13th Annual International Workshop on Innovating the Network for Data Intensive Science — INDIS
sessions.desc: Data networks are the circulatory system for science, discovery, society and industry. But scientific data networking is not a solved problem, and significant challenges remain. These challenges reflect scientists’ persistent needs from data networks: the needs for ever increasing capacity, flexibility, consistency, and collaboration. The theme for the 13th INDIS workshop is Connected Science: Bridging Research and Industry — reflecting not only the role of networking in connecting scientific infrastructure, but also our community’s collaborations across different types of organizations to advance data-intensive science. This year INDIS plans to continue its tradition of having a discussion- and interaction-oriented schedule; based on past feedback, this is always well received. INDIS 2026 delivers an essential complement to the HPC-focused SC26 Technical Program, providing a dedicated platform for HPC researchers to explore data-intensive computing, interconnects, and networking.

sessions.title: 15th International Workshop on Runtime and Operating Systems for Supercomputers (ROSS 2026)
sessions.desc: With increasing levels of parallelism, increased heterogeneity, energy and memory constraints coupled with emerging post-Moore computing architectures like quantum and neuromorphic, a reevaluation of current approaches for extreme-scale operating systems and runtime environments is needed. ROSS is a workshop aimed at identifying looming problems and discussing promising research solutions in the area of runtime and operating systems for extreme-scale supercomputers. Specifically, ROSS focuses on principles and techniques to design, implement, optimize, or operate runtime and operating systems for extreme-scale supercomputers and cloud environments. In addition to typical workshop publications, we encourage novel and possibly immature ideas, provided that they are interesting and on-topic. Well-argued position papers are also welcome.

sessions.title: 21st Workshop on Workflows in Support of Large-Scale Science (WORKS26)
sessions.desc: Scientific workflows have underpinned some of the most significant discoveries of the past several decades. Workflow management systems (WMS) provide abstraction and automation that enable researchers to easily define sophisticated computational processes, and to then execute them efficiently on parallel and distributed computing systems. As workflows have been adopted by multiple scientific communities, they are becoming more complex and require more sophisticated workflow management capabilities. This workshop focuses on the many facets of scientific workflow composition, management, sustainability, and application to domain sciences in an increasingly diverse landscape. The workshop covers a broad range of topics in the scientific workflow lifecycle that include: reproducible research with workflows; workflow execution in distributed and heterogeneous environments; application of AI/ML in workflow management; workflow provenance; serverless workflows; exascale computing with workflows; stream-processing, interactive, adaptive and data-driven workflows; workflow scheduling and resource management; workflow fault-tolerance, debugging, performance analysis/modeling; big data and AI workflows, etc.

sessions.title: 2026 International Workshop on Performance, Portability, and Productivity in HPC
sessions.desc: The Performance, Portability, and Productivity in HPC workshop aims to bring together developers and researchers with an interest in practical solutions, technologies, tools, and methodologies that enable the development of performance-portable applications across a diverse set of current and future high‑performance computers. The topic of Performance, Portability, and Productivity focuses on enabling applications and libraries to run across multiple architectures without significant impact on achieved performance and with the goal of maintaining developer productivity. This workshop provides a forum for discussions of successes and failures in tackling the compelling problems that lie at the intersection of performance, portability, and productivity in high performance computing. This area touches on many aspects of HPC/AI software development and the workshop program is expected to reflect a wide range of experiences and perspectives, including those of compiler, language and runtime experts; applications developers and performance engineers; and domain scientists. For more information see: https://p3hpc.org/.

sessions.title: AgenticAI4HPC’26: The First International Workshop on Agentic AI for HPC
sessions.desc: Recent progress in agentic AI — AI systems capable of autonomous planning, reasoning, adaptation, and tool use — opens transformative opportunities across the HPC research landscape. Beyond system-level optimization, agentic AI can play a pivotal role in code modernization, automated code translation across programming models, performance tuning for diverse hardware platforms, and the long-term sustainability of large scientific software stacks. As HPC systems continue to evolve toward exascale and beyond, developers face increasing challenges in maintaining legacy codes, porting applications to emerging architectures, and achieving performance portability across changing programming models and runtime environments. Agentic approaches offer the potential to autonomously refactor legacy codes, translate between models, recommend architecture-aware optimizations, and iteratively tune applications. AgenticAI4HPC’26: The First International Workshop on Agentic AI for HPC will bring together researchers and practitioners to explore methodologies, systems, and real-world applications that leverage agentic AI to accelerate HPC software development, enhance productivity, and enable sustainable performance at scale.

sessions.title: AI4S: 8th Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Scientific Applications
sessions.desc: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a game-changing technology that has shown tremendous advantages and improvements in algorithms, implementations, and applications. We have seen many successful stories of AI-enhanced scientific applications. Recently, advances in generative AI have revolutionized not just science but the entire society. However, there are a number of problems remaining to be studied to sustain AI in scientific applications in the long term, bridge the gap between AI and scientific applications, and enable wider employment of AI in HPC. The purpose of this workshop is to bring together computer and domain scientists from academia, government, and industry to share recent advances in the use of AI in scientific applications, introduce new scientific problems to the community, and stimulate tools and infrastructures to support AI-enhanced science. The workshop will be organized as plenary talks based on peer-reviewed paper submissions accompanied by keynotes from distinguished researchers and a panel discussion.

sessions.title: EduHPC-26: Workshop on Education for High Performance Computing
sessions.desc: The EduHPC workshop welcomes unpublished manuscripts from academia, industry, and national laboratories on HPC and PDC education at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, as well as professional training and workforce development. We encourage papers at the intersection of HPC/PDC education and other areas, including data science, and internet-of-things and edge (IoT/Edge) computing. Given the increasing relevance of ML/deep learning workloads on HPC systems, we especially encourage pedagogical papers on this topic. Historically, the workshop has accepted contributions from fields such as CS, CSE, DS, and computational courses across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. The workshop aims to foster collaboration among stakeholders within the SC context and provides a platform for discussing pedagogical challenges, solutions, and opportunities for HPC/PDC/DS/AI/ML/IoT education. Activities at the workshop include paper presentations, invited talks and panels, and special sessions for sharing resources and opportunities for collaboration.

sessions.title: HUST-26: 13th International Workshop on HPC User Support Tools
IA^3 2026 — 16th Workshop on Irregular Applications: Architectures and Algorithms
sessions.desc: Data-intensive applications process heterogeneously, employing diverse methods and data structures that exhibit irregular data accesses, control flows, and communication patterns. Modern data analytics applications additionally require supporting dynamic data structures, asynchronous control flows, and mixed parallel programming models. Supercomputing systems are organized around software and hardware optimized for data locality and bulk synchronous computations. Managing irregular behaviors requires a substantial programming effort and lacks integration, leading to poor performance. Holistic solutions to these challenges emerge only by considering the problem from multiple perspectives: from micro- to system architectures, from compilers to languages, from libraries to runtimes, and from algorithm design to data characteristics. Only collaborative efforts among researchers with different expertise, including domain experts and end users, can lead to significant breakthroughs. This workshop brings together scientists from different backgrounds to discuss methods and technologies for efficiently supporting irregular applications in current and future architectures.

sessions.title: PMBS26: The 17th International Workshop on Performance Modeling, Benchmarking, and Simulation of High Performance Computer Systems
sessions.desc: The PMBS26 workshop is concerned with the comparison of high performance computing systems through performance modeling, benchmarking, or through the use of tools such as simulators. We are particularly interested in research that reports the ability to measure and make trade-offs in software/hardware co-design to improve sustained application performance. We are also keen to capture the assessment of future systems. The aim of this workshop is to bring together researchers, from industry and academia, concerned with the qualitative and quantitative evaluation and modeling of high performance computing systems. Authors are invited to submit novel research in all areas of performance modeling, benchmarking, and simulation, and we welcome research that brings together current theory and practice. We recognize that the term "performance" has broadened to include power consumption and reliability, and that performance modeling is practiced through analytical methods and approaches based on software tools and simulators.

sessions.title: RISE 2026: 1st International Workshop on Rising Innovators in Sustainable Exacomputing
sessions.desc:
RISE 2026: Rising Innovators in Sustainable Exacomputing is a half-day, symposium-style workshop dedicated to strengthening the global talent pipeline in high performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI). The workshop spans hardware and system architectures, software environments, algorithms, applications, machine learning, quantum and cloud computing, energy efficiency, and sustainability, while integrating leadership and career development. RISE combines technical excellence with mentorship through a keynote on global collaboration, a cross-sector career panel, mentorship roundtables, and lightning talks highlighting women-led research project spotlights. Interactive elements, including the RISE Research Expertise Map, Global RISE Exhibit, and a community-built Pathways in Computing timeline, foster visibility, networking, and interdisciplinary exchange. By connecting students, researchers, and senior leaders across academia, labs, and industry, RISE establishes an inclusive, recurring platform that advances innovation, collaboration, and sustainable professional growth in exascale computing.
RISE Workshop Link

sessions.title: The 2nd International Workshop for Software Frameworks and Workload Management on Quantum-HPC Ecosystems
sessions.desc: The integration of quantum computing (QC) with high performance computing (HPC) is emerging as a transformative paradigm for addressing complex scientific and engineering challenges. Given current quantum hardware limitations, such as noise, limited qubit counts, and constrained circuit depth, hybrid quantum–HPC (Q-HPC) ecosystems provide a practical path forward by combining complementary strengths. This workshop focuses on software frameworks, AI-enabled orchestration, and workload management strategies essential for scalable Q-HPC integration. Topics include architecture co-design, heterogeneous resource management, networking, fault tolerance, error mitigation, programming models, middleware, benchmarking, and large-scale distributed Q-HPC systems. Emphasis will be placed on open, interoperable ecosystems such as openQSE and on ML/AI techniques for adaptive workflow orchestration, topology-aware scheduling, performance prediction, and autonomous runtime control. Through invited talks, technical presentations, panels, and special sessions, the workshop will foster collaboration across academia, industry, national laboratories, and funding agencies to define research priorities and accelerate AI-driven Q-HPC ecosystems.

sessions.title: The 9th Annual Parallel Applications Workshop, Alternatives to MPI+X (PAW-ATM)
sessions.desc: Supercomputers get faster and more complex every year. MPI, long the dominant model for distributed computation, has adapted by combining with models for intra-node parallelism (e.g., OpenMP, CUDA). These MPI+X hybrids offer performance but demand significant programmer effort to write, debug, and tune applications. Alternatives to MPI+X are worth exploring as programmer productivity becomes a major component of the time to science. Alternatives include parallel programming languages (e.g., Chapel, Regent, Fortran), general purpose libraries (e.g., Charm++, COMPSs, HPX, Legion, UPC++), and domain-specific libraries (e.g., Arkouda, Dask, Spark). With many options to choose from, it is hard for programmers to know which alternative models are appropriate for their application and for programming model developers to understand the opportunities for improvement. PAW-ATM brings together both application experts and programming model developers to disseminate knowledge about available applications and models, as well as advance their design.

sessions.title: XLOOP 2026: The 8th Annual Workshop on Extreme-Scale Experiment-in-the-Loop Computing
sessions.desc: Advancement in computational power and high-speed networking is enabling a new model of scientific experiment, experiment-in-the-loop computing (EILC). In this model, simulation and/or learning modules are run as data is collected from observational and experimental sources. Presently, the amount and complexity of data generated by simulations and by observational and experimental sources, such as sensor networks and large-scale scientific facilities, continues to increase. Several research challenges exist, many of which are independent of the scientific application domain. New algorithms, including artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms, to merge simulation ensembles and experimental data sets must be developed. Data transfer techniques and workflows must be constructed to control the ensembles and integrate simulated and observed data sets. The Workshop on Extreme-Scale Experiment-in-the-Loop Computing (XLOOP 2026) will be a unique opportunity to promote this interdisciplinary topic area. We invite papers, presentations, and participants from the physical and computer sciences.

5th International Workshop on Cyber Security in High Performance Computing
sessions.desc: The goal of this workshop is to bring together researchers and practitioners in cybersecurity and HPC. Security in high performance computing (HPC) has traditionally been an “operational” challenge (i.e., restrict access and usage to certified users). Thus, despite significant advances in our understanding and mitigations of vulnerabilities, the cybersecurity research community has been somewhat disconnected from the HPC community. Recent increases in the heterogeneity of both the underlying platforms of HPC and the community of HPC-level users and applications point to an important and growing need for connection and synergy between these two communities.

sessions.title: 17th Workshop on Latest Advances in Scalable Algorithms for Large-Scale Heterogeneous Systems (ScalAH'26)
sessions.desc: Novel hybrid scalable scientific algorithms are needed with the advent of a variety of novel accelerators, including GPUs, FPGAs, etc., as well as with the growth in size of quantum computing devices, neuromorphic chips, and various AI-specific processors. This myriad of devices requires a unified approach that allows efficient and scalable hybrid approaches combining classical and novel computing paradigms to be implemented at scale. These extreme-scale heterogeneous systems require these novel scientific algorithms to hide the complexity, hide network and memory latency, have advanced communication, and have no synchronization points where possible. With the advent of AI in the past few years, the need for such scalable mathematical methods and algorithms for such hybrid architectures that are able to handle data and compute-intensive applications at scale becomes even more important.

sessions.title: EESP 2026: 3rd International Workshop on Energy Efficiency with Sustainable Performance: Techniques, Tools, and Best Practices
sessions.desc:
The Energy Efficiency and Sustainable Performance (EESP) workshop fosters the exchange of innovative strategies, tools, and best practices to enhance energy efficiency in modern computing environments. As energy costs rise and CO₂ emissions increase, sustainable operation has become critical for HPC, AI, and data center infrastructures. EESP addresses the challenge of balancing performance, power, and sustainability, focusing on actionable, cost-effective solutions for Tier-0/1 and Tier-2 systems. The workshop promotes cross-layer innovation by integrating hardware, software, runtime systems, and data-driven analytics to achieve end-to-end visibility and adaptive energy management. It advances transparency in energy use and carbon emissions, supports hardware innovations (e.g., new architectures and liquid cooling), and enables dynamic adaptation, predictive analytics, and intelligent workload scheduling for real-time optimization. By fostering collaboration between HPC and AI communities, EESP advances reproducible practices and operational insights that empower computing centers, researchers, and industry to implement scalable solutions for long-term sustainable performance.
EESP Workshop Link

sessions.title: High Performance Python for Science at Scale
sessions.desc: This symposium-style workshop aims to connect researchers, developers, and Python practitioners to share their experiences scaling Python-based applications and workflows on supercomputers. The goal is to provide a platform for topical discussion of best practices, hands-on demonstrations, and community engagement via open-source contributions to new libraries, runtimes, and frameworks. Based on talks and demos that survey and summarize the best practices and recent success stories and developments, the workshop provides attendees a forum for expanding their knowledge of tools and techniques as well as opportunities to engage with representatives from the broader Python community.

sessions.title: ISAV26: In Situ AI, Analysis and Visualization
sessions.desc: HPC platforms and applications have reached such large scale, complexity, and heterogeneity, that a major challenge has become the wide gap between our ability to compute extreme-scale data and our ability to gain insight from it to make timely, data-driven decisions. A well known, yet challenging, approach to visual analysis, learning, and processing is performing the tasks in situ, i.e., while the data is still in memory, potentially in lieu of saving the raw data out. Since 2015, ISAV has fostered a community of in situ developers, practitioners, researchers, and users of in situ methods and infrastructure, connecting industry, government laboratories, and academia across all career levels. Through presentations, discussions, and peer-reviewed proceedings of research findings, lessons learned, and early ideas, ISAV illuminates new requirements and gaps driven by science and engineering applications and fosters the application of in situ methods.

sessions.title: First-Timers Orientation
sessions.desc:
Feeling overwhelmed by SC? Don't worry, you're not alone. This conference is a massive, incredible experience, and we want to help you make the most of it.

Join our First-Timers Orientation for a stress-free session where you'll hear directly from our General Chair and seasoned conference volunteers. They'll walk you through everything you need to know, including:

- Navigating the conference schedule and finding your way around the venue.
- Understanding the different event types and what they mean.
- Understanding the various registration options.
- Learning valuable tips and tricks to maximize your conference experience.

Bring your questions. Let’s get you ready to dive into SC26.

2nd Annual Workshop on Large-Scale Quantum-Classical Computing (LSQCC)
sessions.desc: Quantum computing is advancing rapidly, and its integration with high performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly important for enabling practical hybrid computational workflows. In a growing number of domains, research is progressing toward quantum advantage — with quantum computation already addressing problems that strain exact classical methods and increasingly competing with state-of-the-art approximate approaches. These combined methods offer new opportunities for accelerating progress in scientific areas such as physics, chemistry, materials, and optimization by leveraging quantum computing together with established classical and AI-based techniques. The 2nd Annual Workshop on Large-Scale Quantum-Classical Computing (LSQCC) brings together recent research on quantum algorithms, system integration techniques, and emerging hybrid workflows that incorporate HPC and AI components where beneficial. The workshop highlights technical challenges, recent developments, and near-term opportunities for effectively combining quantum computing with complementary approaches.

sessions.title: 6th International Workshop on RESource DISaggregation in High Performance Computing (RESDIS)
sessions.desc: Disaggregation is an emerging compute paradigm that splits existing monolithic servers into a number of consolidated single-resource pools that communicate over a fast interconnect. This model decouples individual hardware resources and enables the creation of logical compute platforms with flexible and dynamic hardware configurations. The concept of disaggregation is driven by various recent trends in computation. From an application perspective, the increasing importance of data analytics and machine learning workloads brings unprecedented need for memory capacity, which is in stark contrast with the growing imbalance in the peak compute-to-memory capacity ratio of traditional system board-based servers. At the hardware front, the proliferation of heterogeneous, special-purpose computing elements promotes the need for composable platforms, while the increasing maturity of optical interconnects elevates the prospects of distance independence in networking infrastructure. The workshop intends to explore various aspects of resource disaggregation, composability, and their implications for future HPC platforms.

sessions.title: 8th International Workshop on Containers and New Orchestration Paradigms for Isolated Environments in HPC (CANOPIE-HPC)
sessions.desc: The ongoing revolution enabled via containerization, virtualization, and new orchestration models has dramatically changed how applications and services are delivered and managed across the computing industry. This revolution has established a new ecosystem of tools and techniques with new, flexible and agile approaches, and continues to gain traction in the HPC community. In addition to HPC-optimized container runtimes, technologies like Kubernetes create a new set of opportunities and challenges. While adoption is growing, questions regarding best practices, foundational concepts, tools, and standards remain. Our goal is to promote the adoption of these tools and introspect the impact of this new ecosystem on HPC/AI use cases. This workshop serves as a key venue for presenting late-breaking research, sharing experiences and best practices, and fostering collaboration in this field. Our eighth workshop iteration will continue to emphasize real-world experiences and challenges in adopting and optimizing these new approaches for HPC and AI.

sessions.title: 8th Workshop on Programming and Performance Visualization Tools (ProTools)
sessions.desc: Understanding program behavior is critical to overcome the expected architectural and programming complexities, such as limited power budgets, heterogeneity, hierarchical memories, shrinking I/O bandwidths, and performance variability, that arise on modern HPC platforms. To do so, HPC software developers need intuitive support tools for debugging, performance measurement, analysis, and tuning of large-scale HPC applications. Data collected from these tools can be far too large and too complex to be analyzed in a straightforward manner. We therefore need automatic analysis and visualization approaches to help application developers intuitively understand the effects that algorithmic choices have on application correctness or performance. The ProTools workshop brings together HPC application developers, tool developers, vendors, and researchers from the visualization, performance, and program analysis fields for an exchange of new approaches to assist developers in analyzing, understanding, and optimizing programs for extreme-scale platforms.

sessions.title: 10th International Workshop on Software Correctness for HPC Applications (Correctness '26)
sessions.desc: Ensuring correctness in HPC applications is one of the fundamental challenges that the HPC community faces today. While significant advances in verification, testing, and debugging have been made to isolate software defects in the context of non-HPC software, several factors make achieving correctness in HPC applications and systems much more challenging than in general systems software — growing heterogeneity (CPUs, GPUs, and special purpose accelerators), massive scale computations, use of combined parallel programming models (e.g., MPI+X), new scalable numerical algorithms (e.g., to leverage reduced precision in floating-point arithmetic), and aggressive compiler optimizations/transformations are some of the challenges that make correctness harder in HPC. As the complexity of future architectures, algorithms, and applications increases, the ability to fully exploit exascale systems will be limited without correctness. The goal of this workshop is to bring together researchers and developers to present and discuss novel ideas to address the problem of correctness in HPC.

sessions.title: High Performance Computing for Environmental and Earth Sciences (HPC4EES)
sessions.desc: With the availability of large-scale weather, climate, and Earth data from multiple sources, including satellites and sensors, existing modeling techniques need further improvement to handle these data volumes. The high performance computing (HPC) community can help. In the last decade, HPC has played an essential role in scaling existing weather modeling methods, enabling improved forecasting and proactive responses to severe weather conditions. However, this area warrants greater attention from HPC researchers to better understand the impact of climate change on future generations and to mitigate sudden disasters, including earthquakes and extreme weather events. Thus, we propose a dedicated workshop about coupling HPC with environmental and earth science. We chose SC as the venue for this workshop to reach a broad segment of the HPC community. The workshop will cover challenges around large-scale environmental modeling and possible solutions from the HPC community.

sessions.title: HPC Systems Professionals Workshop (HPCSYSPROS26)
sessions.desc: The complexity of high performance computing (HPC) systems necessitates advanced techniques in system administration, configuration, and engineering and with staff who are well-versed on the best practices in this field. HPC systems professionals include system engineers, system administrators, network administrators, storage administrators, and operations staff who face problems unique to HPC systems. The ACM SIGHPC SYSPROS Virtual Chapter, the sponsor for this workshop, has been established to provide opportunities to develop and grow relationships focused specifically on the needs of HPC systems practitioners and to act as a support resource for them to help with the issues encountered in this specialized field. This workshop is designed to share best practices for common HPC system deployment and maintenance, to provide a platform to discuss upcoming technologies, and to present the state-of-the-practice techniques that increase performance and reliability of systems, and in turn increase researcher and analyst productivity.

sessions.title: LLVM-HPC2026: The Twelfth Workshop on the LLVM Compiler Infrastructure in HPC
sessions.desc: LLVM, winner of the 2012 ACM Software System Award, has become an integral part of the software-development ecosystem for optimizing compilers, dynamic-language execution engines, source-code analysis and transformation tools, debuggers and linkers and a whole host of programming-language and toolchain-related components. Now heavily used in both academia and industry, where it allows for rapid development of production-quality tools, LLVM is increasingly used in work targeted at high performance computing. Research in, and implementation of, program analysis, compilation, execution and profiling have clearly benefited from the availability of a high-quality, freely-available infrastructure on which to build. This workshop will focus on recent developments, from both academia and industry, that build on LLVM to advance the state of the art in high performance computing.

sessions.title: PDSW’26: The 11th International Parallel Data Systems Workshop
sessions.desc: Efficient storage, movement, and management of data are crucial to application performance and scientific productivity in both traditional simulation-oriented HPC environments and cloud, AI/ML/big data analysis environments. This issue is further exacerbated by the growing volume of experimental and observational data, the widening gap between the performance of computational hardware and storage hardware, and the emergence of new data-driven algorithms in machine learning. The goal of this workshop is to facilitate in-depth discussions of research and development that address the most critical challenges in large-scale data storage and data processing. PDSW will continue to build on the successful tradition established by its predecessor workshops: the Petascale Data Storage Workshop (PDSW, 2006-2015) and the Data Intensive Scalable Computing Systems (DISCS, 2012-2015) workshop. These workshops were successfully combined in 2016, and the resulting joint workshop has attracted up to 45 full paper submissions and 195 attendees per year from 2016 to 2025.

sessions.title: Research Software Engineers in HPC (RSE-HPC-2026)
sessions.desc: Research software engineers (RSEs) are critical to the impact of HPC, data science, and the larger scientific community. They have existed for decades, though often not under that name. The past several years, however, have seen the development of the RSE concept, common job titles, and career paths; the creation of professional networks to connect RSEs; and the emergence of RSE groups at universities, national laboratories, and in industry. This workshop will bring together RSEs and allies involved in HPC, from all over the world, to grow the RSE community by establishing and strengthening professional networks of current RSEs and RSE leaders. We'll hear about successes and challenges that RSEs and RSE groups have experienced, and discuss ways to increase awareness of RSE opportunities and improve support for RSEs. The workshop will be highly interactive, featuring panels, an invited talk, and short submitted talks.

sessions.title: Sovereign AI Supercomputing Cloud Workshop
sessions.desc: As the HPC landscape shifts toward massive-scale AI infrastructures, the pursuit of a sovereign supercomputing ecosystem has become paramount. However, recent industry consolidations — notably NVIDIA’s acquisition of SchedMD — have shattered the illusion that open-source software (OSS) is a guaranteed failsafe against vendor influence. This workshop explores the paradox of modern HPC sovereignty: How can sites build autonomous, transparent infrastructures when critical "open" components are increasingly controlled by hardware vendors? We will evaluate the transition from passive consumption toward active community governance, highlighting initiatives like OpenCHAMI and the High Performance Software Foundation (HPSF). Through technical talks and interactive panels, this symposium seeks to move beyond an idealized view of OSS toward a pragmatic, risk-aware strategy for the next generation of sovereign on-premises infrastructure, ensuring interoperability and resilience in an era of vertical integration.

sessions.title: Twelfth International Workshop on Heterogeneous High-Performance Reconfigurable Computing (H2RC 2026)
sessions.desc: As in the previous 11 years, this workshop will bring together application experts, software developers, and hardware engineers, both from industry and academia, to share experiences and best practices to leverage the practical application of reconfigurable logic to scientific computing, AI/ML, and “big data” applications. In particular, the workshop will focus on sharing experiences and techniques for accelerating applications and/or improving energy efficiency with FPGAs using high-level design flows, which enable and improve cross-platform functional and performance portability while also improving productivity. Particular emphasis is given to cross-platform comparisons and combinations that foster a better understanding within the industry and research community on what are the best mappings of applications to a diverse range of hardware architectures that are available today (e.g., FPGA, GPU, many-cores and hybrid devices, ASICs), and on how to most effectively achieve cross-platform compatibility.

sessions.title: WHPC: Building Community, Building Careers
sessions.desc:
The WHPC@SC26 workshop will be held in Chicago, Illinois, USA, with the goal of fostering a diverse and inclusive HPC community. The WHPC workshop series has become the leading SC event focused on DEI topics. We aim to cultivate skills for valuing a diverse workforce and creating a welcoming environment for all. Following the workshop held at SC24, we have an increased emphasis on diversity and inclusion of all people from underrepresented groups.

WHPC@SC26 will focus on the following topics:
- Building community through real-time networking
- Improving diversity and inclusion for all in the HPC workforce
- Highlighting and supporting early-career researchers from underrepresented groups
- Building a deeper understanding of what diversity, equity, and inclusion means for different groups
- Learning from, and valuing, different experiences and career paths

sessions.title: Workshop on High Performance Fabrics for AI and HPC
sessions.desc: As computing demands surge for AI and HPC applications, networking becomes essential for performance and scaling. AI and HPC fabrics are used in scale-up and scale-out communications. This workshop will cover innovations in AI/HPC fabric architecture, network transport, load balancing, congestion control, network resilience, and network visibility. The workshop will further focus on Ethernet technologies for AI and HPC including Scale-Up Ethernet Transport (SUE-T), Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN), Ultra Ethernet, advanced congestion control, lossless transport mechanisms, telemetry, and fabric management.

7th Workshop on Heterogeneity and Memory Systems (HMEM)
sessions.desc: Heterogeneity is ubiquitous, not only in terms of processing units but also memories and networks. As heterogeneity increases, memory subsystems play an even more important role to attain performance, from their technology to the system architecture to the software management and programming model. While CPU-only compute nodes are becoming rare instances, heterogeneous memory architectures have recently emerged and revolutionized the traditional memory hierarchy. Today’s and upcoming architectures may well comprise multiple memory technologies next to DRAM, accelerators with dedicated memories, or even specific expansion cards hosting memory alone, such as: 3D-stacked memory, high-bandwidth multi-channel RAM, unified/shared memory on accelerators, Compute Express Link (CXL)-based architectures, Huawei's Unified Bus, persistent memory, or MRDIMMs.

sessions.title: AI on HPC: Performance Engineering, Challenges and Opportunities
sessions.desc: How can AI workloads be engineered for optimal performance in modern HPC environments? As AI models grow in scale and complexity, high performance computing (HPC) systems are becoming essential for training and deploying these workloads. However, traditional HPC architectures, designed for batch processing, present unique challenges for AI/ML applications — such as dynamic workloads, high I/O demands, and parallelization intricacies. This workshop explores the intersection of AI and HPC, focusing on performance optimization, scalability, and portability. Topics include AI workload characterization, hybrid AI/HPC workflows, efficient execution strategies, and infrastructure co-design. By fostering collaboration between researchers, practitioners, and system developers, this workshop aims to advance best practices and innovations in AI-enabled scientific computing, aligning with SC26’s themes of exascale readiness and performance portability.

sessions.title: ExaMPI26: Workshop on Extreme-Scale MPI
sessions.desc: MPI is currently the de facto standard for programming HPC systems and developing parallel applications. Development of the MPI standard continues in earnest, with version 5.0 being released within the past year, and features for version 5.1d under active discussion. The aim of this workshop is to bring together researchers and developers to present and discuss innovative algorithms and concepts within the Message Passing programming model, and to create a forum for open discussions on the future of the Message Passing Interface (MPI) in the post-exascale era. Possible workshop topics include and are not limited to algorithms for collective operations, MPI optimization for artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads, data-centric models, scheduling, fault tolerance, MPI optimization in heterogeneous systems, interoperability of MPI with other programming models (e.g., PGAS), integration of task-parallel models in MPI, the role of MPI in "smart" networks, and the use of MPI in large-scale simulations.

sessions.title: FTXS: Workshop for Faults, Trustworthiness, and eXplainability for AI Systems at Scale
sessions.desc: FTXS convenes researchers and practitioners to address trustworthy AI systems at scale under real-world variability. Modern AI/LLM pipelines (training, inference, RAG, and agentic systems) face “gray failures” such as distribution drift, prompt/tool/RAG variability, infrastructure noise, and limited-precision effects. Small perturbations can amplify into hallucinations, instability, miscalibration, irreproducibility, and silent regressions — wasting GPU-hours and undermining confidence in AI-assisted decisions. FTXS organizes discussion around a practical closed loop: Disturb → Degrade → Detect → Diagnose → Defend → Validate. We emphasize explainability as a diagnostic tool for attribution across components (model, retrieval, tools, infrastructure, precision), and we aim to synthesize shared taxonomies, measurement practices, and seed artifacts (checklists, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols) that improve both research and operational practice.

sessions.title: High-Accuracy Computing on Low-Precision Hardware
sessions.desc: This workshop aims to bring together researchers, application scientists, system developers, and industry partners to explore algorithmic and implementation approaches enabling accurate scientific computing on low-precision hardware. As accelerators increasingly favor reduced-precision arithmetic for performance and energy efficiency, many scientific applications continue to require accuracy, stability, and reproducibility. Addressing this widening gap demands community-driven advances across algorithms and scientific software, spanning domain-informed and cross-cutting approaches while building toward reusable, precision-aware libraries and tooling infrastructure. The workshop will feature invited talks and solicited works highlighting mixed-precision methods, error-aware and adaptive numerical algorithms, floating-point emulation libraries, and practical deployment on large-scale systems. The workshop emphasizes building community-driven software ecosystems for broad adoption across domains, reducing duplication, and accelerating impact. By fostering discussion among application developers, numerical experts, and hardware vendors, the workshop will establish best practices, share lessons, and strengthen academia–industry collaboration to make low-precision hardware a reliable component of scientific workflows.

sessions.title: Regional Tech Hub Inauguration
Sixth International Symposium on Quantitative Co-Design of Supercomputers
sessions.desc: The Sixth International Symposium on Quantitative Co-Design of Supercomputers, or SQCS'26, considers combining two methodologies — collaborative co-design and data-driven analysis — to realize the potential of supercomputing more fully. By narrowing in on these two proven methodologies with the broad-community attention of an SC26 audience, we will address a host of identified challenges impacting high performance computing (HPC). The 2026 workshop focus will focus on upcoming machines and emerging technologies. The state of HPC is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving beyond a sole focus on raw peak FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) to prioritizing time-to-solution, energy efficiency, and AI-simulation convergence. The landscape is defined by the rise of "post-exascale" machines, the integration of generative AI into scientific workflows, and the emergence of hybrid quantum-classical architectures. This symposium will bring together leaders in the field to review current efforts across centers and discuss areas that show potential.

sessions.title: The 12th Computational Approaches for Cancer Workshop (CAFCW26)
sessions.desc: Cancer touches everyone. Since being established in 2015, CAFCW continues to bring together the community interested in impacting cancer with HPC and the community with an interest in learning more about HPC impacting cancer challenges. The workshop continues to grow, inviting the cancer and HPC communities to converge at SC, interact, and share insights and advances. The workshop highlights the diversity of opportunities where HPC serves as an essential element for advances in cancer treatments, driving new approaches to understand cancer and enabling translation of insights and new treatments to reach clinical impact. This year, the workshop will emphasize the role of HPC in translating research to clinical application and reaching patients, uniting research, clinic and patient. For over a decade, this workshop has catalyzed new biomedical research by connecting industry, government research laboratories, and academia at the intersection of computation, biomedical science, cancer, and healthcare.

sessions.desc: The landscape of AI for science has shifted dramatically. Beyond building ever-larger models from scratch, the scientific community is increasingly leveraging powerful pre-trained models — adapting them through fine-tuning, domain specialization, and integration into complex AI systems combining reasoning models, knowledge graphs, agentic workflows, and connections to simulators and instruments. These shifts highlight a full stack of interdependent challenges for developers, scientists, and HPC centers, from strategies and infrastructure for sharing data and computing, to frameworks orchestrating multiple models and agents, to methods and tools for ensuring safety, alignment, and rigorous evaluation of scientific reasoning and skills. Progress in any one area both depends upon and accelerates the others. This workshop will highlight advances across this interconnected landscape, emphasizing openness, international collaboration, and community-driven efforts, featuring peer-reviewed papers and invited talks spanning shared infrastructure, open model development, agentic AI systems for science, evaluation and safety, and driving challenge applications.

Eighth Workshop on Interactive and Urgent High Performance Computing
sessions.desc: Interactivity enables the exploitation of HPC in new and revolutionary ways, delivering many new and exciting opportunities for our community. Interactive HPC involves users being in the loop during job execution monitoring a job, steering the experiment, or visualizing results to make immediate decisions. Likewise, urgent computing combines interactive computational modeling with time-sensitive systems in the real world such as the near-real-time analysis of unfolding disasters to inform real-time decision making. Supporting interactive and urgent workloads on HPC requires expertise in a wide range of areas and the solving of numerous technical and organizational challenges. This workshop brings together stakeholders, researchers, and practitioners from across interactive and urgent computing within the wider HPC community. We will share success stories, case studies, and technologies to continue community building around leveraging urgent and interactive HPC as an important tool for scientific research, responding to disasters, and addressing societal issues.

sessions.title: Fourth International Workshop on HPC Testing and Evaluation of Systems, Tools, and Software (HPCTESTS 2026)
sessions.desc: This workshop brings together HPC researchers, operators, and vendors from around the globe to present and discuss state-of-the-art HPC system testing methodologies, tools, benchmarks, procedures, and best practices. The increasing complexity of HPC architectures and growing need to leverage HPC for integrated workflows demands more extensive testing than ever to evaluate the status of the system after installation or software upgrades and ensure operability before it is transitioned to production. Different methodologies are used by HPC centers and vendors to evaluate systems during their lifetime, not only at the beginning during installation and acceptance, but also during maintenance and alongside regular operations. This workshop provides a venue to present and discuss the latest HPC system testing technologies and methodologies. The event will include an opening talk focused on current HPC system testing topics, followed by a series of paper presentations from peer-reviewed accepted submissions, concluding with a panel discussion.

sessions.title: International Workshop on RISC-V for HPC (RISCVHPC)
sessions.desc: RISC-V is an open standard instruction set architecture (ISA) which enables the open development of CPUs and a shared common software ecosystem. There are already over 15 billion RISC-V cores, which are accelerating rapidly. Nonetheless, for all the successes that RISC-V has faced, it is yet to become popular in HPC. Recent advances, however, such as data center RISC-V-based CPUs and PCIe accelerators, mean that this technology is becoming a more realistic proposition for our workloads. This workshop aims to connect those currently involved in RISC-V with the wider HPC community. We look to bring together RISC-V experts with scientific software developers, vendors, and supercomputing center operators to explore the advantages, challenges, and opportunities that RISC-V can bring to HPC. Furthermore, we aim to further expand the RISC-V HPC SIG, enabling interested attendees to participate in one of the most exciting open-source technological activities of our time.

sessions.title: Scale to See: Scalable AI for Scientific Imaging and Spatiotemporal Data
sessions.desc: Scale to See: Scalable AI for Scientific Imaging and Spatiotemporal Data is a half-day workshop at SC that brings together researchers at the intersection of high performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI), large-scale scientific imaging and spatiotemporal data. Scientific imaging and spatiotemporal data — from climate and earth systems to medical imaging, materials science, and cosmology — are increasingly high-dimensional, multimodal, and time-evolving, demanding AI methods that are not only accurate but also scalable, physics-aware, and deployable on leadership-class HPC systems. This workshop focuses on AI methods and systems explicitly co-designed for extreme scale, including HPC-aware model architectures, scalable training and inference pipelines, physics-integrated learning algorithms, and efficient computing techniques for high-dimensional data. Through peer-reviewed papers, invited talks, and panel discussions, the workshop aims to set a research agenda, foster interdisciplinary collaboration, and build a community around AI that operates natively at HPC scale to transform scientific imaging and spatiotemporal analysis.

sessions.title: Sustainable Supercomputing
sessions.desc: Providing a sustainable path for supercomputing is a pressing topic for our community, industry, and governments. Supercomputing has an insatiable appetite for computational cycles, while we face increasing challenges of delivering performance per Watt advances with silicon technology trends. All within the context of the converging needs of HPC and AI, climate change, the drive towards net-zero, and economic pressures driven by geo-political challenges. Improving the sustainability of supercomputing provides many opportunities when the end-to-end cycle is considered. From the design of computational circuits and systems; to the power and cooling that is used to operate them, along with the suite of software tools used to administrate, maintain, and raise operational efficiency of HPC systems, with the increasing pressures from the AI aspects being added to traditional HPC workload and workflows. All elements of the system considered, from compute nodes and interconnects to IO and storage components of the system.

sessions.title: The 1st International Workshop on Edge-Cloud-HPC Operational Continuum (ECHO)
sessions.desc: High performance computing (HPC) is decentralizing into a sensor-edge-cloud continuum. Modern edge AI pipelines for perception and control now face the same systemic bottlenecks that define supercomputing: data-management overhead, interconnect topology, and accelerator utilization. This workshop on Edge-Cloud-HPC Operational Continuum (ECHO) applies an HPC lens to resource-constrained environments, investigating how foundational principles must evolve for non-deterministic edge and cloud infrastructures. We focus on three pillars: (1) exporting HPC rigor to the edge through hierarchy-aware parallelism, co-designed memory management, and high-performance streaming I/O; (2) reclaiming predictability for cloud-native HPC by mitigating virtualization overheads, multi-tenant resource contention, and stochastic provisioning; and (3) expanding HPC influence into adjacent domains, including Edge/IoT, MLOps, and cyber-physical systems via shared metrics, reference workloads, and reproducible benchmarking that reports variance and tail behavior. We invite papers, experience reports, and demos, and we encourage artifact packaging for comparison.

sessions.title: Thirteenth SC Workshop on Best Practices for HPC Training and Education
sessions.desc: The inherent wide distribution, heterogeneity, and dynamism of the current and emerging high-performance computing and software environments increasingly challenge cyberinfrastructure facilitators, trainers, and educators. The challenge is how to support and train the current multidisciplinary users and prepare the future educators, researchers, developers, and policymakers to keep pace with the rapidly evolving HPC environments to advance discovery and economic competitiveness for many generations. The 13th annual full-day workshop on HPC training and education is an ACM SIGHPC Education Chapter coordinated effort, aimed at fostering more collaborations among the practitioners from traditional and emerging fields to explore educational needs in HPC, to develop and deploy HPC training, and to identify new challenges and opportunities for the latest HPC platforms. The workshop will also be a platform for disseminating results and lessons learned in these areas and will be captured in a special edition of the Journal of Computational Science Education.

sessions.title: Thirteenth Workshop on Accelerator Programming and Directives (WACCPD 2026)
sessions.desc: Accelerators are now a central component of modern HPC systems, delivering an increasing share of computational capability and enabling tightly coupled, highly heterogeneous node architectures. This evolving landscape — spanning GPUs, AI/ML accelerators, FPGAs, dataflow devices, and emerging quantum processors — creates both new opportunities and significant challenges in algorithm design, performance portability, and programming model standardization. WACCPD 2026 brings together researchers and practitioners working on programming models, compilers, runtimes, and applications for accelerator-based systems. The workshop focuses on approaches that enable performance, scalability, and portability across diverse architectures, including directive-based models, standard language parallelism, portable frameworks, and task-based and data-centric systems. It also highlights mixed-precision techniques, AI-assisted programming, and hybrid classical–quantum workflows. Through peer-reviewed papers, invited talks, and a panel, WACCPD fosters exchange of ideas and showcases methods and case studies that advance programmable, sustainable, and high-performance heterogeneous computing.

sessions.title: Workshop on Operational Data Analytics in HPC (HPC-ODA)
sessions.desc: Operational data analytics (ODA) provides unique opportunities to analyze, understand, and optimize HPC operations. Readily available open-source frameworks make the collection of telemetry from different operational domains of HPC increasingly easy. However, analyzing the data, extracting actionable knowledge from it, and leveraging it to optimize HPC operations is challenging. While most HPC sites have sophisticated monitoring capabilities in place, their analysis capabilities often do not go beyond visual inspection by humans via dashboards or static thresholds for alarms. Few early adopter sites have pioneered advanced usage of data, but its wider adoption will depend on success stories and the availability of analysis tools and models. This workshop will bring together HPC users, practitioners in HPC operations, monitoring experts, and data analytics researchers to share experiences, discuss state-of-the-art research, and foster collaboration. It will solicit papers with concrete, reproducible, and empirical data gathered through case studies, research for practice, and surveys.

sessions.title: Regional Tech Hub Friday
The Empty Shelf: Vertical Market Failure in Data Storage for HPC and AI

presentations.title: Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy
presentations.abstract: Resolving individual stars in simulations of the Milky Way (MW), where we live, is essential to understanding its formation and time evolution. Recent multi-wavelength, multi-modal observations have shown the detailed structures of the MW. Correspondingly, high-resolution simulations that resolve individual stars with multiphysics are required. Leveraging exascale systems, we present PHEASANT: star-by-star MW galaxy simulations including physics across multiple spatiotemporal scales with up to 5.4 trillion particles, ~10,000 times more particles than the state-of-the-art. On Aurora, our code processes 144 billion particles per second using 60,236 GPUs, approximately three times the throughput of a state-of-the-art N-body/smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulation, while its gravitational interaction kernel achieved 976 PFLOP/s in FP32. The code is highly portable, achieving 101 billion and 135 billion particles processed per second with 37,908 GPUs on OLCF Frontier and 20,736 GPUs on JSC JUPITER, respectively, while maintaining high kernel performance across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.

presentations.title: Exascale Multiphysics Simulations for Liquid Metal Fusion Blankets
presentations.abstract: We present pioneering multiphysics simulations of lead-lithium and water flows in the ITER WCLL fusion test blanket set using NekRS on exascale platforms, including Frontier and Aurora. Developed at Argonne, NekRS is a high-performance, open-source multiphysics solver that employs rapidly convergent high-order spectral element methods with minimal numerical dissipation and dispersion. Advanced multilevel preconditioners, high-order time-splitting schemes, and adaptive communication strategies are enabled through OCCA-based kernels, ensuring portability and scalability across emerging HPC architectures. This work presents the first complete, high-fidelity, high-resolution multiphysics model of a fusion blanket, including turbulent flow resolution, heat transfer, buoyancy, magnetohydrodynamics, tritium breeding and transport, and water activation. We also present the largest spectral element model in NekRS to date and the largest simulation of fusion systems to date.

presentations.title: Crossing the 12,000-Atom Barrier with Heterogeneous Quantum-Classical Supercomputing: Quantum Chemistry of Protein-Ligand Complexes
presentations.abstract: We develop a workflow decomposing a molecule into fragments via quantum embedding and simulating them with a heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) method. We sample fragment electronic configurations on two 156-qubit quantum processors (ibm_cleveland, ibm_kobe), using up to 94 qubits, running 21,006 circuits for over 239 hours, collecting 3B measurement outcomes: the most resource-intensive HQC computation for quantum chemistry to date. We compute fragment wavefunctions via optimized subspace diagonalization on supercomputers Fugaku, Miyabi-G, and ROQUO, achieving 72.5% parallel efficiency with scalable distributed linear algebra kernels. We simulate two protein-ligand complexes spanning dispersion- and electrostatics-dominated regimes (11,608 and 12,635 atoms), demonstrate 40x increase in system size and up to 210x improvement in accuracy over previous state-of-the-art, with HQC matching coupled-cluster (CCSD) accuracy in fragment energies. We present the first HQC protein-ligand binding prediction using a mixed-basis set and an automated end-to-end workflow enabling practical HQC calculations of large protein systems.

presentations.title: Closing the FeMo-Cofactor "Quantum-Advantage'' Gap with Exascale Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: The FeMo-cofactor (FeMoco) of nitrogenase has for nearly a decade been the canonical "killer app" motivating fault-tolerant quantum computing for chemistry: the CAS(113e, 76o) active space is beyond exact diagonalization and remains challenging for every polynomial-scaling classical method. We report the first exascale classical solution of this active space. The resulting code has been tuned for two exascale supercomputers, LineShine and China's New-generation Intelligent Supercomputer (CNIS), reaching sustained performance on 20,480 LineShine nodes of 1.456 EFLOP/s in double precision (58.9% of the machine peak) and 5.626 EFLOP/s in mixed precision. These computational achievements enable the FeMoco ground-state consensus to be reached on 1,280 LineShine nodes within a measured end-to-end wall time of 105 minutes (1.75 h), approximately one-fifth of the best published 8.6-hour single-run projection for fault-tolerant quantum computing on the same active space.

presentations.title: What Production AI Demands from Data Infrastructure
presentations.abstract: Moving AI from pilot projects into production requires more than GPUs — it requires data infrastructure designed for scale. Modern AI workloads depend on continuous access to massive volumes of unstructured data while balancing performance, cyber resilience, governance, and operational simplicity. This session examines how organizations are building AI data pipelines that support ingestion, training, inference, and long-term knowledge retention from a common architectural foundation. We'll discuss practical approaches to reducing unnecessary data movement, improving GPU utilization by bringing data closer to AI workloads, and eliminating storage silos. Attendees will gain architectural guidance drawn from production AI deployments, including proven design patterns and common pitfalls to avoid as AI environments continue to grow.

presentations.title: Building Sovereign AI: Infrastructure for Trusted AI Environments
presentations.abstract:
As governments, research institutions, and regulated enterprises accelerate AI adoption, they face a new challenge: delivering high-performance AI while maintaining sovereignty over data, models, operations, and critical infrastructure. Building sovereign AI environments requires more than governance frameworks, it demands resilient infrastructure architecture, secure operations, and specialized engineering expertise.

This session explores the technical and operational considerations for deploying production-ready sovereign AI environments, including cluster design, workload isolation, data residency, network segmentation, lifecycle management, and operational governance. Using the deployment of Haein, South Korea's national sovereign AI infrastructure, as a prime sovereign example, attendees will gain practical insights into architectural decisions, deployment strategies, and operational best practices to accelerate production while maintaining security, compliance, and trust. Participants will leave with actionable frameworks for building secure, scalable, and trusted AI infrastructure for sovereign, enterprise, and research environments.

presentations.title: The Operational Journey From HPC Cluster to AI Factory: Power, Cooling, Data and Operational Readiness for the AI/HPC Era
presentations.abstract:
AI infrastructure deployments are forcing HPC operators to confront challenges that extend far beyond GPU procurement. Rising rack densities, power constraints, liquid cooling adoption, storage bottlenecks, data pipelines, and evolving operational processes are reshaping how modern HPC facilities are designed and managed.

This presentation shares practical lessons from organizations transitioning from traditional HPC clusters to AI factories capable of supporting training, fine-tuning, post-training, and inference workloads. Rather than focusing on theory, we examine the operational realities of infrastructure planning, facility readiness, workload placement, data management, and day-to-day operations. Attendees will learn how power, cooling, networking, storage, and operational decisions interact, where common bottlenecks emerge, and what steps can be taken to prepare existing HPC environments for large-scale AI adoption.

presentations.title: Bringing HPC to Life: The Convergence of Computing, Technologies and Communities in Health
presentations.abstract:
There is a transformation underway in medicine. Not that long ago, employing AI and HPC to address key challenges in cancer was uncommon. The uses of medical digital twins to help doctors and patients work together for better outcomes were simply flights of fantasy. Today, these are only a few of the developments that are rapidly becoming mainstream, empowered by interdisciplinary communities working together, driving hard to overcome shared challenges in compute, policy, data and many other areas to improve health, medicine and overall wellness.

How did we get here? Where are we going? What does the future hold? These are questions that commonly arise when discussing the transformation in health and life sciences that recent advances in AI and computing have enabled. The talk will deliver insights on how the past decade has created a solid foundation for healthcare innovation, share examples of how data science and AI are continuing to accelerate the pace of change in healthcare worldwide, and provide perspectives on future opportunities and challenges awaiting around the corner!

presentations.title: Sparse Linear Algebra Accelerates Genotype Representation Graph Computation at Biobank Scale
presentations.abstract: Biobank-scale genomic analyses are increasingly constrained by computational costs, as hundreds of thousands to millions of samples and variants must be analyzed together. The genotype representation graph (GRG) compactly encodes population genetic variation to accelerate computation, but the current approach does not exploit modern accelerator architectures. This work introduces Mikado, a new methodology for expressing GRG-based computation using sparse linear algebra primitives. Under a reverse topological ordering of the graph nodes, the GRG adjacency matrix is strictly block-lower-triangular, and the genotype matrix-vector product becomes a sparse triangular solve that can be further decomposed into a pipelined sequence of blocked sparse matrix-vector multiplies. By decoupling computation from graph representation, our approach exposes fine-grained parallelism and enables hardware-optimized sparse primitives on GPUs. Mikado was evaluated across the Perlmutter supercomputer at NERSC and Google Cloud. Mikado achieves an order-of-magnitude speedup for PCA and BOLT-LMM compared with the original GRG traversal approach, including on All of Us Research Program cohorts, demonstrating that advanced computing infrastructure is now central to progress in biological research. Portability across supercomputer nodes and cloud instances makes these gains broadly accessible, providing a scalable, hardware-portable, researcher-friendly tool for population genetics at biobank scale.

presentations.title: DeepSim: SOL-Based Explainable GPU Performance Projection with Multi-Task Learning
presentations.abstract:
Accurate kernel-level GPU performance projection is essential for early-stage architecture design when target hardware is unavailable and only high-level specifications are known. Existing methods face a trade-off: simulators reveal bottlenecks but are slow and require unavailable hardware details, while analytical and end-to-end learning models are efficient yet rely on idealized assumptions and provide limited explainability.

We present DeepSim, an explainable GPU performance projection framework for single-GPU kernels that learns unit-level speed-of-light (SOL) ratios to calibrate bottleneck pressure using multi-task learning. Given target chip specifications and kernel traffic from existing GPUs, DeepSim constructs idealized limiters, predicts per-unit SOL ratios, and maps them to practical limiters reflecting target-chip behavior. Using this representation, DeepSim infers dominant bottlenecks, classifies workloads, and estimates execution time. Across 290K samples and 284 kernels spanning NVIDIA Ampere, Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs, DeepSim achieves 12.29% mean absolute percentage error on held-out B200 and 14.78% on unseen kernels.

presentations.title: EMO: Energy Efficiency Modeling and Optimization for AI Workloads
presentations.abstract:
The massive energy consumption of GPU-accelerated AI workloads challenges sustainable computing. We observe that execution asynchrony (e.g., CPU-GPU, concurrent streams, and multi-GPU) creates slack, allowing non-critical kernels to run at lower frequencies to save energy with minimal performance impact. However, existing approaches struggle to achieve both workload generality and fine-grained slack discovery, while high-fidelity modeling incurs substantial overhead.

We present EMO, a lightweight framework for exploiting these opportunities. EMO constructs a low-level dependency graph capturing execution asynchrony and performs what-if timing analysis to identify slack windows. It then introduces dependency-aware kernel packing, which preserves critical paths while collapsing redundant details, enabling high-fidelity latency-energy modeling with minimal profiling cost. Finally, EMO combines graph analysis and pack-level models to formulate and solve a constrained combinatorial optimization problem for frequency policies under given latency targets. Evaluations show that EMO reduces energy consumption by 15%–28% with only 2%–5% performance loss and negligible overhead.

presentations.title: LEO: Tracing GPU Stall Chains via Cross-Vendor Backward Slicing
presentations.abstract: More than half of the Top 500 supercomputers employ GPUs as accelerators. On GPU-accelerated platforms, developers face a key diagnostic gap: profilers show where stalls occur but provide limited dependency paths explaining why. Furthermore, the same kernel may have different stalls and underlying causes on different GPUs. This paper presents LEO, a root-cause analyzer for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs that performs backward slicing from stalled instructions, considering dependencies arising from registers as well as vendor-specific synchronization mechanisms. LEO attributes GPU stalls to source instructions to explain performance inefficiencies. Across 21 kernel/region evaluation units on three GPU platforms, expert-designed, LEO-informed optimizations deliver per-platform geometric-mean speedups of 1.73×–1.82×; these are not end-to-end application speedups. Our case studies show that (1) the same kernel may require different optimizations for different GPU architectures, and (2) under our LLM protocol, prompts containing LEO's structured diagnostics yield better outcomes than code-only and raw-stall-count prompts.

presentations.title: Interactive Debugger for Performance-Portable Python HPC Kernels
presentations.abstract: We propose pkdb, the first interactive debugger for performance-portable kernels written in Python. Python is widely used in HPC, with frameworks such as PyKokkos translating Python-embedded domain-specific languages to native code that runs across various CPUs and GPUs. pkdb enables standard interactive debugging like breakpoints, stepping, continuation, and variable inspection while preserving actual on-device execution without source modification. Beyond these fundamentals, pkdb introduces three advanced capabilities that exploit the dynamic nature of Python and PyKokkos: (1) live code evaluation, (2) hot-swap, and (3) concurrent kernel comparison. Our performance evaluations on Intel and AMD CPUs and NVIDIA and AMD GPUs show that pkdb introduces limited overhead and is practical for everyday use, and introduces critical debugging features to the Python HPC ecosystem.

presentations.title: ORCA: Steerable Observability for Bulk-Synchronous Parallel Applications
presentations.abstract:
The bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) paradigm powers critical computational workloads from scientific simulations to large-scale machine learning training. Running on tens of thousands of processors, these systems are uniquely sensitive to performance variations that current observability approaches struggle to diagnose—post-hoc analysis of massive traces introduces latency and rigidity that obstructs timely diagnosis.

To address these challenges, we present ORCA, a system for always-on, steerable BSP observability. ORCA enables operators to materialize relevant views from running applications on demand and intervene in response, via a tree-based overlay providing coordinated collection, in-situ SQL analytics, and timestep-consistent control. ORCA accelerates observability workflows across the spectrum. On a real AMR code at 4,096 ranks, ORCA collects equivalent traces at ~2% overhead (vs. 56%–81%), enables up to 7275× faster analyses, and 99.999% in-situ data reduction. In an LLM-driven evaluation of steerability, a performance anomaly that took months to diagnose manually is localized in 27 minutes.

presentations.title: Constructing a Job-Centric Frontier Telemetry Dataset to Accelerate HPC Operations, Systems, and Energy Research
presentations.abstract: Comprehensive analysis of high-performance computing (HPC) systems requires linking workload execution to system behavior. This kind of analysis is vital for diagnosing performance issues, managing capacity, detecting anomalous workloads, and understanding how applications interact with system hardware. However, node telemetry data and job scheduler records are collected and analyzed in isolation and application identification requires a directed effort. We present a job-centric telemetry dataset that unifies scheduler job records with node-level measurements, enabling direct association between workloads and their corresponding power, thermal, and performance characteristics. This dataset, which spans two years of Frontier operations, aims to support a wide range of research and operational applications, including workload characterization, system analysis, and anomaly detection. This paper describes the dataset curation process, including data collection, normalization, and association of telemetry with individual job metadata. To enable further study, the dataset will be published alongside this paper for use by the HPC community.

presentations.title: Understanding Reliability Bottlenecks in LLM Agents for HPC I/O Telemetry Analysis
presentations.abstract: High performance computing (HPC) facilities collect extensive I/O telemetry, but turning it into operator-relevant insight remains a manual, expert-driven process. Tool-using LLM agents could help automate this workflow, but their reliability on realistic telemetry-analysis tasks remains unclear. We study this using CIODI-Bench, a benchmark of 49 expert-curated tasks built from more than two years of public production telemetry from the Polaris supercomputer. Using CIODI-Bench, we compare tool-using agents for HPC I/O telemetry analysis under controlled conditions. We find that the main reliability bottleneck depends on task structure: on constrained extraction tasks, curated semantic grounding improves performance from 73.0% to 93.5%; on data-analysis tasks, process-aware review improves performance by 13.2% over baseline; but on insight-generation tasks, the added orchestration yields no improvement while increasing output cost by nearly 3x. Our analysis results clarify the reliability limits of current agentic approaches and offer practical guidance for building more trustworthy telemetry-analysis agents.

presentations.title: The Design and Organization of the El Capitan Center of Excellence for Application Readiness
presentations.abstract:
El Capitan is the first U.S. exascale system for national security. Its Center of Excellence (COE) enabled co-design and application readiness. The COE's central goal is to prepare applications to use the AMD Instinct MI300A APU and Cray Slingshot interconnect effectively on the first day of delivery, and continuously improve after delivery. Application engagements are driven by a team of eight engineers from HPE and AMD who support approximately 20 applications from three national laboratories. Quarterly hackathons had attendances reaching upwards of 50 participants.

We describe the technical scope, engagement model, and organizational structure that supported COE activities, emphasizing the key components of a high performance computing COE. We highlight five select case studies that demonstrate technical challenges in addressing functionality and performance across many software and hardware updates, often utilizing experimental software to overcome issues. We summarize lessons learned and AI impacts that may benefit future COEs.

presentations.title: TangleLab: A National Hybrid Computing Platform to Unlock Quantum Information Science and Engineering Research and Education
presentations.abstract: TangleLab is a hybrid quantum-classical computing platform under development by the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center in collaboration with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Rigetti Computing and funded by the National Science Foundation (award number 2537076). The platform will integrate GPU-accelerated HPC resources with a superconducting quantum processor to support emerging hybrid applications while exploring architectural models for future heterogeneous cyberinfrastructure. This presentation focuses on the system's architecture and deployment strategy, including integration of classical and quantum resources, scheduling and access models, software environment design, and operational considerations for supporting both research and education. We will also discuss hybrid deployment approaches that combine local quantum hardware with cloud-accessible quantum systems to support scalable workflows as quantum technologies evolve. TangleLab will provide a practical blueprint for HPC centers seeking to integrate quantum computing into production cyberinfrastructure and prepare researchers for the next generation of heterogeneous computing environments.

presentations.title: Turning Quantum Into an HPC Resource: Automation, Virtualization, and Containerization
presentations.abstract:
As quantum computing transitions from the lab to industrial environments, HPC data centers face a fundamental integration gap between traditional automated software stacks and the low-level manual and physical control required for quantum hardware. Because quantum relies on qubits, rather than traditional integrated circuits, it requires a dedicated software architecture to make it compatible with existing compute paradigms.

This presentation outlines how applying the established compute principles of automation, virtualization, and containerization to quantum computing transforms complex quantum systems into deployable, plug-and-play HPC resources. We examine how packaging automated control and optimization software into a containerized sub-system enables quantum hardware to become a seamless compute accelerator.
