presentations.abstract: Speculative decoding can substantially accelerate LLM inference, but realizing its benefits in practice is challenging due to evolving workloads. We present TIDE (Temporal Incremental Draft Engine), a serving-engine-native framework that integrates online draft adaptation directly into high-performance LLM inference systems. TIDE reuses target model's intermediate hidden states generated during inference as training signals for draft adaptation, thereby avoiding additional target model computation and serving-time overhead. It employs adaptive runtime control to activate speculation and draft model training only when beneficial. TIDE exploits heterogeneous clusters by mapping inference and training to appropriate GPU classes. Across diverse real-world workloads, TIDE achieves up to 1.66× throughput over no-speculation baselines while recovering performance on misaligned workloads where static draft models degrade throughput. TIDE also reduces training time by up to 3.02× and storage requirements by 24× compared to existing draft training approaches, and improves system throughput by up to 1.22× on heterogeneous GPU clusters.

presentations.title: LLMProf: Identifying Performance Bottlenecks in LLM Serving Systems with Top-Down Profiling
presentations.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems have become critical cloud workloads, yet their performance diagnosis remains challenging due to rapid software-hardware evolution, dynamic request patterns, and the limitations of existing profiling tools. These gaps force developers to rely on manual heuristics for performance optimization, leading to slow progress and error-prone code. We present LLMProf, a low-overhead profiling framework tailored for various LLM serving systems. LLMProf employs a top-down, multi-level analysis approach that captures only the most relevant metrics at each profiling level to balance detail with minimal performance impact while remaining agnostic to frameworks and hardware. We present case studies that leverage LLMProf to optimize real-world LLM serving workloads, from which we derive a performance diagnosis taxonomy that provides actionable guidance and enables automated postmortem analysis. Our case studies demonstrate that by applying simple optimizations uncovered by LLMProf, we can achieve up to 2.09× throughput improvement.

presentations.title: What Bloats Your Floats? Right-Sizing Numerical Precision for Scientific Computing
presentations.abstract: While FP64 (binary64) remains the standard representation of real numbers in scientific computing, hardware trends increasingly favor low-precision formats optimized for AI workloads. This shift prioritizes throughput and energy efficiency over full-precision capabilities. We challenge the necessity of high-precision arithmetic in PDE-governed simulations, where spatial and temporal discretization errors introduce a physical noise floor that masks the lower-order bits of the FP64 format, rendering them irrelevant. We propose a criterion based on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) with respect to spatial and temporal refinements to evaluate the impact of safe precision reduction on scientific computations. Finally, we present an automated dataflow-centric workflow for targeted lowering within mixed-precision subgraphs in complex scientific applications. Large-scale evaluations of weather and climate applications show that strategic precision reduction on GPUs achieves up to 1.8× speedup without compromising physical fidelity.

presentations.title: LLM Agents Meet Lossy Compression: Benchmark, Demystify, and Optimize Across HPC Architectures
presentations.abstract: LLM coding agents can resolve many repository-level issues, yet their ability to translate and optimize performance-critical HPC kernels across heterogeneous accelerators remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks conflate two distinct capabilities: generating correct target-platform code (translation) and improving throughput under correctness constraints (optimization). We present SZ-BENCH, a benchmark that separates these abilities for scientific lossy compression across CUDA, HIP, and Cerebras, covering nine kernels and five applications. Evaluating four LLM backbones and two agentic workflows, we find large performance variation on GPUs, systematic failure on PE-centric Cerebras targets, and persistent tension between correctness and throughput. Additional reasoning iterations often degrade results. To address these issues, we propose SZ-GEN, a multi-agent workflow that integrates generation, profiling, and validation. SZ-GEN achieves up to 30.05/190.32 GB/s on SZp/CUDA, significantly outperforming baselines, though requiring more search iterations.

presentations.title: Scalable High-Fidelity Macromolecular Docking for GPU-Accelerated Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: Flexible macromolecular docking offers high-fidelity predictions of biomolecular interactions, but remains prohibitively expensive at scale. Among existing approaches, LightDock leverages glowworm swarm optimization (GSO) for accuracy, yet suffers from limited parallelism, irregular computation, and severe load imbalance, preventing efficient execution on GPU supercomputers. We present SparkleDock, a scalable GSO-based docking framework enabling near-real-time flexible docking. We redesign GSO to expose massive fine-grained parallelism at the glowworm-agent level, and restructure the dominant energy scoring computation into a Tensor Core-compatible formulation, enabling efficient execution of irregular pairwise interactions through structured matrix operations. We further introduce a performance-model-driven scheduling for load balancing and out-of-core scaling across GPUs. SparkleDock achieves 9.7× and 18.9× speedups over LightDock on single A100 and H100 GPUs, and delivers over two orders of magnitude acceleration at scale. On 512 GPUs, it reduces docking time from hours to seconds, enabling large-scale, high-fidelity virtual screening previously impractical with flexible docking.

presentations.title: Bridging Precision and Performance Gaps: Scientific Computing on AI-Oriented Architectures
presentations.abstract: The rapid rise of AI-oriented accelerators has reshaped compute systems around low-precision tensor engines, raising a practical question for the HPC community: Under what conditions can such hardware support scientific workloads that demand numerical robustness, irregular memory access, and scalability? Using the Ascend 910 NPU series as a representative tensor-centric platform, we characterize precision, execution, and memory-hierarchy bottlenecks that hinder the direct deployment of scientific codes. From this characterization, we develop and evaluate workload-specific mappings that combine heterogeneous execution, mixed-precision numerical formulations, hierarchical memory orchestration, and communication–computation overlap. Evaluations spanning kernels, numerical solvers, quantum simulation, and Monte Carlo applications show that AI-native NPUs can achieve numerical robustness, competitive performance, and satisfactory scalability when these constraints are addressed in a coordinated manner. Our results provide a state-of-the-practice case study of how scientific workloads can be adapted to tensor-centric architectures, while distinguishing transferable optimization principles from Ascend-specific implementation details.

presentations.title: Scaling Quantum Circuit Optimization via Guided Exploration and Global Context Learning
presentations.abstract: Every circuit gate in a quantum program can add execution errors on noisy quantum hardware, making gate-count reduction important for reliable quantum computing. Rule-based optimizers use greedy search and miss improvements requiring long rewrite sequences. Learning-based methods are promising but constrained by incomplete circuit representations, unfocused exploration, and poor scalability. To address these limitations, we introduce GUIDERQ, a new reinforcement-learning optimizer with three key advances: combining local and global circuit features for richer representations, learned filtering to focus on the most promising candidate actions, and recursive partition-and-reassembly that scales to large circuits while exploring optimization opportunities across partitioning boundaries. Across representative quantum-circuit benchmarks with up to 27,883 gates and three industry-standard gate sets, GUIDERQ achieves geometric-mean gate-count reductions of 33.0%, 34.2%, and 25.1% on the IBM, Nam, and TDG gate sets — up to 34.1% more than Quarl, the state-of-the-art learning-based optimizer — with up to 3× faster search.

presentations.title: Park-n-Ride: Hardware-Aware Compilation and Execution of Bivariate Bicycle Codes on Neutral-Atom Systems
presentations.abstract: Quantum computers are noisy; without quantum error correction (QEC), deep programs fail as qubits lose information due to decoherence. Among QEC approaches, bivariate bicycle (BB) codes offer low overhead and constant-depth syndrome extraction, while neutral-atom arrays provide scalable, reconfigurable qubit layouts. However, executing BB-code primitives on neutral-atom systems requires a hardware-aware mapping that respects movement, zoning, and interaction constraints. We present Park-n-Ride, a system for compiling and executing the BB code on neutral-atom processors. Park-n-Ride introduces a module layout and movement model aligned with neutral-atom constraints, exposes a compact BB-native logical interface for compilation, and integrates scheduling mechanisms that enable efficient execution on zoned architectures. By co-designing BB-code abstractions with hardware execution, Park-n-Ride provides a practical path from qLDPC primitives to resource-efficient, high-throughput execution on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays.

presentations.title: BAHAMAS: A Control Plane for Optimization and Execution of Variational Quantum Circuits
presentations.abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) suffer from unstable optimization due to temporal noise drift and static qubit mappings that distort gradient signals across iterations. We present BAHAMAS, an online control framework that stabilizes noise exposure by adaptively selecting physical mappings via consensus-based fidelity estimation, without requiring simulators, offline training, or prior executions. Across real quantum devices, BAHAMAS improves optimization reliability and supports inference-time retargeting under drift through robust, per-iteration control.

presentations.title: QPAR: A Plug-In Parallel Framework for Qubit Routing
presentations.abstract: Qubit routing, a key stage of quantum compiler, inserts additional operations (e.g., SWAP gates) to ensure quantum circuit instructions are executable on physical hardware. The effectiveness of routing in terms of minimizing additional operations is critical, as they introduce extra overhead and noise. However, existing routing methods often suffer from high computational overhead, limiting their scalability for large-scale circuit compilation. To overcome this limitation, we present QPAR, a plug-in parallel framework to boost the scalability of routing algorithms. The key insight of QPAR is that, while qubit routing is a sequential process, we can first relax the sequential dependencies to enable parallelism and then rebuild them to ensure correctness. QPAR further establishes optimizations to combat potential loss of routing effectiveness caused by parallelization. Experimental results demonstrate that QPAR can accelerate routing algorithms by up to 126.6x, with negligible, even negative, cost increases on a 128-logical-core server.

presentations.title: TETRIS-Q: Tiling-Based Effective Transient-Fault Reduction on Interleaved Superconducting Qubits
presentations.abstract:
The struggle of the hour in quantum computing research is achieving effective suppression of the error mechanisms induced by the interaction of external radiation with superconducting quantum devices. Despite the rapid advancements in quantum error correction (QEC) of recent years, radiation-induced faults are yet to be fully addressed. These events are known to be the cause of simultaneous correlated defects in qubits that lie onto a single substrate, ultimately annulling QEC code effectiveness.

In this paper, we propose to selectively combine substrate-level phonon barriers and QEC interleaving via a planar-mesh tiling algorithm, TETRIS-Q, reaching efficient and effective suppression of radiation events. Our cross-layer solution comes at no extra cost in terms of QEC code execution or decoding time. We model and simulate radiation-induced transient faults over a plethora of barrier and QEC interleaving configurations.

presentations.title: The Anatomy of a Misprediction: Tracking Terrestrial and Orbital Radiation-Induced Errors in Systolic Arrays
presentations.abstract: The increasing use of systolic arrays to accelerate AI in safety-critical domains, such as autonomous vehicles and space systems, makes their reliability a primary concern. Existing approaches often analyze the impact of faults at a single abstraction level, failing to capture how radiation-induced events at hardware level translate into system-level failures. This gap limits the ability to identify which hardware faults lead to critical application errors and to design effective mitigation strategies. To address this challenge, we propose a cross-layer analysis that traces faults from their origin in silicon to their impact on AI models. By exposing tensor processing units to accelerated terrestrial and orbital radiation environments (neutron and proton beams) and combining hardware-level simulations with software-level fault injection, we identify error patterns and propagation mechanisms that result in mispredictions. This end-to-end perspective enables the identification of the low-level sources of errors that lead to critical failures.

presentations.title: BitIR: Cross-Architecture Fault Injection for Resilience Analysis of Heterogeneous GPU Applications
presentations.abstract: Modern GPU-based HPC systems rely on heterogeneous vendor stacks, yet reliability studies are largely limited to single architectures. Consequently, it remains unclear how faults behave across different GPU backends. We present BitIR, a cross-architecture fault injection framework that enables semantically aligned, software-visible resilience analysis across NVIDIA, Intel, and AMD GPUs. BitIR injects deterministic faults at the LLVM IR level, ensuring equivalent bit perturbations prior to backend lowering and enabling direct cross-vendor comparison. Using a set of representative GPU benchmarks, we conduct large-scale injection campaigns on production systems and classify outcomes into masked results, silent data corruption (SDC), failures, and hangs. We find that identical faults produce markedly different behaviors across vendors: Intel most often masks faults but exhibits more hangs when faults escape masking; NVIDIA exposes more overt detectable failures; and AMD alternates between SDC-dominant and failure-dominant behavior depending on the benchmark and fault site.

presentations.title: GPU Faults Across Cloud Providers: Characterization and Operational Insights at Scale
presentations.abstract: Reliability is a critical challenge in operating large-scale GPU training infrastructure across multiple cloud providers. Despite growing interest in GPU fault characterization, no prior work describes the automated systems that manage faults across providers at scale, nor a methodology for continuous reliability improvement. We operate a large GPU training fleet spanning all major CSPs and NCPs, encompassing various GPU architectures with close to 1 billion GPU hours/year. We focus on three production clusters at the highest maturity level (≥98% node availability) across three providers, analyzing 19,564 fault incidents across 5,065 nodes over 5–7 months. To maintain availability, we built a breakfix system with three pillars: scale-up automation, fault triage with provider-specific remediation actions, and repeat-offender management. We report on reliability KPIs: mean time to repair (MTTR), automated triage success rate (ATSR), node recidivism rate (NRR), and present a Pareto-driven methodology for continuous improvement.

presentations.title: Science Is a Distributed System: Rethinking Scientific Infrastructure for the AI Era
presentations.abstract:
Modern science increasingly operates as a distributed system. Experimental facilities generate enormous and complex datasets; networks move them across institutions; supercomputers and AI systems transform them into scientific results; and those results can inform what happens next at the experiment. Yet much of our infrastructure is still designed and operated as a collection of independent facilities. Researchers think in terms of scientific questions, not infrastructure boundaries, but they must increasingly navigate the interfaces between multiple institutions, security domains, software environments, and operational models.

Drawing on a decade of work connecting scientific facilities with NERSC and developing cross-facility computing infrastructure, this talk will explore what it takes to turn a collection of powerful resources into an integrated scientific ecosystem. It will examine lessons learned from building these systems, why the scientist rather than the facility should be the organizing principle, and what happens when AI begins to mediate between human scientific intent and the increasingly complex computational and experimental infrastructure. The next frontier is not another faster machine, but an integrated scientific ecosystem that behaves as one system — one that allows scientists to move seamlessly from observation to insight.

presentations.title: Making Exascale HPC Radio Telescopes
presentations.abstract:
Real-time processing of radio astronomy data presents a unique challenge for HPC centers. The science data-processing workflow contains memory-bound portions, compute-bound portions, io-bound portions and iterative portions with non-trivial convergence, running in both embarrassingly parallel and tightly coupled modes. The storage footprint is equally challenging, requiring the production and ingestion of large numbers of small files along with 1TB-scale single files, with individual surveys easily ingesting PB-scale amounts of data, that when processed can produce PB-scale amounts of science products. This is all coupled together in a complex job dependency graph which has to meet real-world time constraints from radio telescope observations. Simply put, HPC is a core part of a radio telescope.

Dr. Pascal Elahi will present how the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre has worked with world-class radio telescopes such as the MWA and ASKAP telescopes, precursors to the SKAO Observatory SKA-Low and SKA-Mid radio telescopes, to produce science process pipelines that scale on HPC systems. He will highlight the PaCER Program, which has uplifted the software stack, leading to improved efficiency and drastically reduced the storage requirements. He will also showcase BLINK, a Pawsey-developed code which has enabled discovery of radio sources otherwise hidden behind the sheer data volume and compute challenge inherent in raw radio data. We are truly entering the era of real-time processing of the radio sky by HPC-radio telescopes.

presentations.title: Bits to Bites: Securing the Future of Agricultural Production Using AI
presentations.abstract:
Tackling the grand challenges of 21st-century agriculture requires a fundamental shift in the way we envision the role of data science and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, and in the way we build agricultural AI systems. Farmers and policy makers face variable profitability, major crop loss and poor crop quality owing to a number of challenges including labor shortage, weather and production uncertainties, and water scarcity. While there is certainly a growing interest in AI-based solutions because of a rapid adoption of precision agriculture technologies, traditional approaches to developing digital solutions do not necessarily work well in this landscape. A deeply embedded model toward development, that engages AI and data engineers directly with extension scientists and growers, is likely to be more fruitful.

In this talk, Ananth Kalyanaraman will present ongoing developments of scalable AI solutions and tools for the U.S. specialty crop agricultural systems. In particular, he will cover machine learning models and tools for two classes of agricultural applications: 1) farm intelligence: delivering decision support at the farm scale, toward mitigation of weather-induced risks and providing farmers with forecasting capabilities; and 2) water intelligence: delivering decision support at a regional scale, toward seasonal planning of water allocation and reservoir management in snow-dominant watersheds. Through these experiential reports, he aims to provide the audience an idea about the kind of AI solutions and tools that he likes to call “Agricultural AI” that are needed for agricultural ecosystems, and share the lessons learned about the limitations and associated challenges, along with areas where new breakthroughs and investments are needed, to scale AI development and use for enhanced agricultural productivity.

presentations.title: Building Intelligent Systems for STEAM: From Physics to Arts
presentations.abstract:
As HPC systems reach exascale, a single simulation run can generate petabytes of data, and the parallel file system, the traditional path for reading and writing simulation data, has become the bottleneck that limits what can actually be learned from that data. Now imagine multiple simulation runs. Ongoing work with plasma physicists explores integrating high-performance simulation(s) and machine learning so tightly that data never has to touch disk. An in-transit workflow is presented in which one to many simulations are streamed directly into an ML framework, transformed asynchronously in flight, and used to train a model while the simulation is still running. The system and software challenges of porting and coupling such a workflow are many, but the right orchestration among the moving parts can open doors to scientific questions that could never even be posed before. At exascale, the data ecosystem is the experiment, and scientific discovery is determined by how the system manages flow of information. This proof-of-concept points toward a larger vision, one in which supercomputers, AI reasoning, surrogate modeling, autonomous workflows, software infrastructure and human-in-the-loop are integrated into a single, unified ecosystem.

Not every science needs an exascale-sized effort, yet the lessons learned at scale can be applied far more broadly, democratizing the convergence of HPC and AI for science across domains as varied as physics, sports analytics, and cultural-heritage conservation. This talk will conclude with some stories from the humanities. Applying computing across disciplines depends on consistent communication between computer scientists and domain scientists, which is only possible when the two communities work together, made possible via the research software engineering (RSE) workforce.

presentations.title: LLM-PRISM: Characterizing Silent Data Corruption from Permanent GPU Faults in LLM Training
presentations.abstract: Large-scale LLM training is increasingly susceptible to hardware defects stemming from manufacturing escapes and silicon aging. These defects manifest as silent data corruption (SDC) that perturbs gradients and parameters throughout the training process. We present LLM-PRISM, a methodology to characterize LLM pre-training resilience to hardware faults. LLM-PRISM couples RTL-level GPU fault simulation with a stochastic injection engine embedded in Megatron-LM. Through 7,664 training runs across FP16, BF16, and FP8 regimes, we analyze how fault type, rate, and numeric format govern resilience. We find that while LLMs resist low-frequency faults, impact is highly non-uniform; critical datapaths and specific precision formats can induce catastrophic divergence even at moderate fault rates. This study provides the first hardware-grounded, pre-training characterization of SDC resilience.

presentations.title: COPPER: Improving DRAM Reliability with Low Overheads via Cooperative Parallelized Error-Correcting Codes
presentations.abstract: DRAM scaling increases fault rates, motivating stronger and more efficient error correction. However, the transparency between on-die ECC (OD-ECC) in DRAM and rank-level ECC (RL-ECC) in the memory controller introduces substantial storage, reliability, and performance overheads. We propose COPPER, a cooperative ECC mechanism that improves reliability with low performance and area overheads. COPPER exploits the fixed mapping between DRAM data arrays and interface pins to convey a crafted error-location hint from OD-ECC to the memory controller, enabling parallel rank-level cross-checking and decoding without stalling memory transfers. We further propose POD-RMW, which provably parallelizes OD-ECC operations during read-modify-write. Our evaluations show that COPPER incurs only 0.007% DRAM-chip area and at most 0.001% CPU area. With 19.5% storage overhead, COPPER reduces DUE and SDC rates by up to 15x and 430x, respectively, while improving performance by up to 2.1x over prior cooperative ECC approaches under high fault rates.

presentations.title: Temporal Modeling of Soft Error Propagation Using Dynamic Bayesian Networks
presentations.abstract: With the ever-shrinking size of transistors, modern devices have become increasingly susceptible to soft errors that can lead to silent data corruption (SDC), seriously compromising system reliability. Understanding how these corruptions propagate through a program's execution is essential for accurate resilience analysis, yet existing analytical models rely on static assumptions that miss temporal behavior, while fault-injection studies reveal only final outcomes without exposing the intermediate propagation paths. This paper introduces Hydra, a temporal error-propagation framework that constructs a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) from the program execution trace to model how corrupted values traverse dataflow, control-flow, and memory-dependency transitions. Hydra captures masking, reactivation, multi-step propagation, and long-range dependencies, enabling estimation of program-level SDC probabilities without repeated injections and revealing interpretable propagation pathways. Across a diverse benchmark suite, Hydra's predicted SDC probabilities closely match fault-injection results, achieving a mean absolute error of 2.2 percentage points, while substantially reducing computational cost.

presentations.title: Low-Overhead Silent Error Detection for Large Language Model Inference at Scale
presentations.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed across large-scale computing systems, where soft errors can silently corrupt computations and degrade output quality. Existing protection techniques often rely on broad monitoring or expensive checking mechanisms, incurring non-negligible runtime overhead and limiting scalability across architectures and workloads. In this work, we propose TRACE, a lightweight fault-detection technique for generative LLMs. TRACE identifies a small set of critical layers that are most informative under fault conditions, places lightweight activation-based symptom monitors on these layers during inference, and uses a trained model to determine whether a fault has corrupted the generated output. Across 15 LLMs and three datasets, TRACE achieves 95.3% average fault-detection coverage with only 0.56% runtime overhead, a 6.1× reduction relative to prior LLM fault-tolerance techniques. TRACE further remains effective under multi-bit faults and multi-dataset profiling, demonstrating robust detection across diverse fault conditions and workloads.

presentations.title: Near-Real-Time Performance Visualization of MPI Applications: Integrating Performance Analysis Into HPC Education
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing (HPC) has become an essential capability in both industrial practice and scientific research, making the acquisition of practical HPC skills an increasingly important objective in higher education. Parallel programming with models such as MPI and OpenMP is central to this training, and students should gain experience on real HPC clusters rather than on local machines. However, universities often have access only to limited, partitioned, or decommissioned cluster resources, while learners must also master operational concepts such as SSH, SCP, and batch-based job management with systems such as SLURM. In addition, efficient MPI programs require performance analysis, yet established tools are designed for experts and assume prior knowledge of instrumentation, measurement, and interpretation.

EduMPI Suite addresses this gap by providing an educational environment for executing and analyzing MPI programs on HPC clusters in near-real-time. It automatically delivers visual feedback on MPI communication events during execution, enabling students to observe program behavior and understand the performance characteristics. A distinctive feature is the visualization of internal algorithmic communication patterns of collective operations, which are often hidden in professional tools but are crucial for understanding the performance implications of collective communication.

Usability evaluations over multiple semesters show that EduMPI Suite lowers the barriers to practical HPC performance analysis, is recommended by students, and improves the success rate of identifying and explaining performance problems to 96%, compared with 60% for professional analysis tools. Its near-real-time performance analysis is enabled by low measurement overhead <3.8% and low query latency <0.09 s.

presentations.title: Towards Resource-Efficient Parallel Concept Drift Detection in Data Streams
presentations.abstract:
Modern data science increasingly outpaces the efficient use of parallel hardware, creating a need for computational performance engineering. Because HPC tools are not embedded in exploratory data science environments, data scientists lack support for such investigations. This PhD project therefore bridges HPC and data science, using concept drift detection as a case study.

Concept drift—the change in data distributions after ML model deployment—must be detected to ensure robust streaming ML systems. However, the computational overhead of drift detectors (DDs) remains underexplored, even though directly affecting latency, energy consumption, and deployability. This gap motivates the thesis contributions.

First, a framework is introduced for systematically investigating the computational performance of DDs, including complexity analysis, benchmarking and performance analysis. Second, building on this framework, a survey and benchmark evaluate DDs bi-objectively, measuring both runtime and accuracy. The results reveal that computational performance is treated as secondary in the literature, no single detector dominates across scenarios, and higher accuracy consistently requires longer runtimes. Simultaneously, timely drift detection can reduce pipeline runtime by avoiding unnecessary model updates. Third, performance analysis identifies bottlenecks in state-of-the-art DD implementations, particularly inefficient BLAS and OpenMP usage in streaming scenarios. Consequently, the thesis presents MoPEDDs, a modular parallel ensemble of DDs that exploits unused parallel resources improving detection with negligible runtime overhead.

Finally, because performance engineering remains complex for most data scientists, the thesis introduces JUmPER (Jupyter meets Performance). It embeds performance engineering into Jupyter through coarse- and fine-grained monitoring, making HPC expertise accessible where data science happens.

presentations.title: Towards Scalable and Efficient Deep Learning: Structured Optimization Across Training and Fine-Tuning
presentations.abstract:
Modern deep learning systems must balance optimization quality against computation, memory, communication, and reliability constraints, whose relative importance varies across supercomputing architectures. This dissertation develops controlled relaxation as a structured optimization strategy: preserve information essential to learning while relaxing costly requirements in synchronization, curvature representation, and parameterization.

The thesis develops this principle through three contributions. AD-KFAC relaxes global synchronization in distributed second-order optimization while retaining curvature information in asynchronous, versioned, and recoverable state. BD-KFAC replaces dense curvature representations with block-diagonal structure, exposing a controllable trade-off between statistical fidelity and resource cost. RRLoRA relaxes the requirement for an uninterrupted low-rank optimization trajectory by periodically refactorizing the learned update and restarting the learning-rate schedule, allowing the parameterization to evolve without discarding accumulated information.

Together, these methods address complementary bottlenecks in distributed second-order training, resource-efficient curvature estimation, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning while preserving the optimization structure that makes each approach effective. The results support controlled relaxation as a systems-aware design principle: preserve signal-carrying structure, relax constraints that impose disproportionate system cost, and keep the resulting approximation or asynchronous state observable and recoverable. This principle offers a practical framework for designing efficient and reliable machine-learning systems on large-scale supercomputing platforms.

presentations.title: Embrace the Chaos: Harnessing Variability in Accelerator-Rich Systems
presentations.abstract:
HPC and ML workload scaling have led supercomputers to deploy large, heterogeneous systems with extreme power limits. Current GPU thermal design power limits (TDPs) range from 1,400–2,000W, scaling to extreme power budgets at scale. Thus, power has displaced performance as the dominant constraint. My research addresses this challenge by co-optimizing power and performance at scale through cross-stack approaches spanning hardware, firmware, systems, and applications.

Power management (PM) causes performance variation across accelerators, making it hard for users to get repeatable performance and for administrators to balance resource utilization. I was the first to characterize GPU variability across production clusters, uncovering consistent variability. This work guided MLCommons' benchmarking effort on handling variability. To harness this variability, I developed PAL, a cluster scheduler that leverages application-specific variability during job placement to optimize latencies and resource utilization.

Further investigating PM, we found GPU power often spikes above TDP (temporarily), triggering frequency throttling that hurts performance. I investigated these power excursions, especially frequent in compute-intensive workloads, and developed solutions that reduce excursions and improve latency.

As workloads rapidly evolve, new workloads often show different excursion characteristics as well as power/performance variability. To adapt our solutions to new, unseen workloads, I developed Minos, which groups similar workloads using power and utilization characteristics while reducing profiling overheads.

Overall, my research demonstrates the critical impact of excursions and GPU variability on large-scale systems. As power constraints intensify and hardware limits are pushed, this cross-stack co-design offers essential techniques to improve power-constrained supercomputing in the future.

presentations.title: Machine Learning-Based Multi-Objective Optimization for HPC Workload Scheduling
presentations.abstract: As high-performance computing (HPC) systems reach exascale, schedulers that optimize a single objective, typically throughput, prove inadequate for facilities that must simultaneously manage performance, energy consumption, and resilience under substantial workload uncertainty. This dissertation develops and empirically validates a three-component multi-objective scheduling framework built on graph neural networks (GNNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), testing the hypothesis that graph-structured representations of jobs and system state, combined with adaptive multi-objective learning, outperform traditional and single-objective learned schedulers in production HPC environments. The framework comprises (1) GNN-RL, a graph attention network and PPO-based scheduler encoding job dependencies and resource contention; (2) HARMONIC, a Bayesian uncertainty-aware optimizer that separates aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty and balances performance, energy, and resilience via a multi-objective DDPG agent with Pareto-front guarantees; and (3) EA-GATSched, a GATv2-based scheduler driven by a GEOPM-calibrated physics power model and a state-conditioned Pareto-weighting network. GNN-RL and HARMONIC evaluations are complete: GNN-RL improves utilization by 13.8%–20.2% and throughput by 15.0%–50.0% over EASY-backfilling across 377,234 production jobs on three ALCF systems; HARMONIC reduces energy by 10%–19%, improves throughput by 16%–25%, and cuts performance variability by 18%–32% across simulation and a 64-node testbed. EA-GATSched, the framework's in-progress third component, has achieved 27.3%–56.6% energy reduction and up to 95.8% utilization across 389,604 jobs on the same three systems, with cross-architecture GEOPM validation remaining as future work. These two studies draw on overlapping, not additive, job sets from the same ALCF systems and together establish relational, uncertainty-aware, and physics-grounded learning as jointly necessary for sustainable exascale HPC scheduling.

presentations.title: Finite-Element Methods and Exascale Algorithms for Fully Relativistic Noncollinear Pseudopotential Density Functional Theory: From Mathematical Formulations to Efficient Computational Realization and Magnetic Materials Applications
presentations.abstract:
Fully relativistic noncollinear density functional theory (DFT) is essential for simulating spintronic and topological materials but costs 12–30 times more than unpolarized DFT, largely because each electron state becomes a two-component spinor. This cost is dominated by a sparse Hermitian eigenproblem with ~10^8 unknowns and ~10^5 eigenvectors, re-solved every self-consistent-field iteration in complex arithmetic. This thesis co-designs finite-element discretizations, eigensolvers, and GPU implementations within the open-source DFT-FE code.

The central contribution is residual-based Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration (R-ChFSI), which reformulates the Chebyshev recurrence around the residual so that errors from inexact operations shrink with it. Whereas standard Chebyshev filtering stalls, R-ChFSI converges to residuals of 10^-8 with approximate overlap-matrix inverses and FP32/TF32 arithmetic, making reduced precision and compressed communication safe. On Aurora, combining TF32 filtering with 10–12-bit block-floating-point compression of point-to-point messages accelerates filtering by up to 3.5x and the full ground-state solve by 2.27x over FP64, changing the energy by 1.3x10^-10 Ha/atom.

Band parallelization sustains 94% filtering efficiency when strong-scaling an 11,468-electron system to 384 nodes, and calculations reach 78,988 electrons on 800 Aurora nodes. On CPUs, DFT-FE achieves 8x–10x lower minimum wall time than Quantum ESPRESSO at equal accuracy, and GPU runs need 40x–70x fewer node-hours than CPU runs. The thesis also derives consistent forces and stresses and introduces adaptive-coordinate meshes that reduce energy errors up to 28x at fixed degrees of freedom. These capabilities enable a novel study of how vacancies reshape magnetism in the two-dimensional magnet Fe3GeTe2.

presentations.title: PHANTOM: Phase-Aware Power Management for Energy-Efficient LLM Training
presentations.abstract: GPUs enable large-scale LLM training, but high energy consumption and sharp power transients hurt efficiency and reliability. Existing GPU power-management methods are largely reactive and do not exploit the phase structure of training iterations. We present PHANTOM, a predictive, phase-aware dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) framework for sustainable and reliable multi-GPU LLM training. We show that iteration-level power traces exhibit repeatable, fine-grained phase patterns. PHANTOM uses a lightweight temporal convolutional network (TCN) to predict short-horizon GPU power from synchronized hardware events and phase signals, then applies a Pareto-based multi-objective optimizer to choose frequencies ahead of phase transitions, balancing energy efficiency and power stability under real-time constraints. This design is lightweight enough for online deployment without intrusive changes to the training workflow. On multi-GPU LLM workloads, PHANTOM reduces energy by 15%–16%, normalized power-slew rate (NPSR) by 9%–15%, and energy–delay product (EDP) by 10%–11% compared with the default hardware DVFS policy.

presentations.title: Scalable and Efficient Simulation of LLM Training
presentations.abstract: Simulation offers unique values for both enumeration and extrapolation purposes, and is becoming increasingly important for managing the massive machine learning (ML) clusters and large-scale distributed training jobs. In this paper, we build Echo to tackle three key challenges in large-scale training simulation: (1) tracing the runtime training workloads at each device in an ex-situ fashion so we can use a single device to obtain the actual execution graphs of 1K-GPU training; (2) accurately estimating the collective communication without high overheads of discrete-event-based network simulation; and (3) accounting for the interference-induced computation slowdown from overlapping communication and computation kernels on the same device. Echo supports both dense and MoE workloads with high fidelity and further enables GPU memory-aware ex-situ simulation. Echo delivers on average 8% error in training step (~3x lower than state-of-the-art simulators) for GPT-175B on a 256-GPU H800 cluster with 3D parallelism on Megatron-LM under three minutes.

presentations.title: Cross-Layer Energy Analysis of Multimodal Training on Grace Hopper Superchips
presentations.abstract: Multimodal deep learning jointly processes text, images, and video, but scaling models and sequences shifts training bottlenecks from computation toward memory capacity and data movement. DeepSpeed addresses these limits through CPU offloading, activation checkpointing, and sequence parallelism, yet these techniques add communication and system activity that can alter energy efficiency. We present a cross-layer study of multimodal training on NVIDIA Grace Hopper (GH200) systems, characterizing interactions among the application, runtime, and hardware layers. Using controlled experiments across multiple model scales, we evaluate power, energy, runtime, and throughput under offloading and parallelism strategies. Results show that energy efficiency depends primarily on data movement and compute-communication overlap rather than raw accelerator utilization; consequently, runtime-optimal configurations are not always energy-optimal. We derive practical guidelines for selecting offloading modes, sequence-parallelism degrees, and hardware-aware schedules that balance memory pressure, communication cost, time-to-solution, and energy on tightly coupled heterogeneous systems.

presentations.title: Characterizing the Scalability and Performance of Large-Scale AI Training Under Multi-Tenancy
presentations.abstract: Characterizing AI workload performance on modern HPC systems requires understanding both their scalability in isolation and their behavior under concurrent execution. However, the interplay among parallelization strategies, network congestion, compute capability, and interconnect technologies remains poorly understood. This work investigates the performance and scalability of AI models up to 2,400 GPUs. We quantify the communication overheads and their impact across different interconnects by evaluating scale-up, scale-out, and rack-scale configurations under multiple allocation schemes. Finally, we study how multiple concurrent training jobs interfere with each other by designing a realistic noise model. We design a benchmark suite of AI models to evaluate the performance of five distinct parallelization strategies across different supercomputing clusters, including Alps, Leonardo, LUMI, JUPITER, NVL72 GB300, and DGX A100. Our work provides a systematic characterization of the scalability and execution efficiency of distributed AI training, while offering key insights into performance behavior under realistic multi-tenant scenarios.

presentations.title: Advancing HPC Research and Development Workflows with High-Speed Data Transfer and Data Provenance for AI-Driven Science
presentations.abstract:
The rapid adoption of AI in scientific research is increasing the importance of data-centric computing infrastructures that support large-scale data movement, management, and reproducibility. While HPC systems provide the computational foundation for scientific discovery, challenges related to efficient data utilization frequently limit research productivity.

This talk presents research information infrastructure (RII) that integrates data management, high-speed data transfer, and provenance-aware computing for AI-driven scientific workflows. The infrastructure incorporates ultra-high-speed data transfer system (UDTS), which enables efficient disk-to-disk transfer of large datasets across high-bandwidth networks, and data provenance system for HPC (DPS4H), which automatically captures execution histories, file dependencies, and workflow metadata without requiring modifications to existing applications. Proof-of-concept evaluations demonstrated effective utilization of available network resources and practical applicability to data-intensive research environments. By combining scalable data movement and automated provenance collection, RII provides a foundation for reproducible, collaborative, and data-centric scientific computing in the AI and exascale era.

presentations.title: When Fiber Becomes a Sensor: New Applications for Research and Education Networks
presentations.abstract: Research and education networks are built to move massive volumes of scientific data, but the same optical fiber that carries that data can also become a distributed sensor. This session explores how fiber sensing can transform deployed fiber routes into real-time sources of operational and environmental intelligence. By detecting subtle changes caused by vibration, strain, temperature shifts, construction activity, cable movement or seismic events, fiber sensing can help networks identify risks earlier, improve fault isolation and support more resilient high-capacity infrastructure. The talk will introduce key sensing approaches, including distributed acoustic sensing, polarization-based sensing and reflectometry, and explain how AI-driven analysis can turn raw optical signals into actionable insights. Attendees will learn how research and education networks can use fiber sensing to protect critical backbones, reduce maintenance effort and enable new science applications across terrestrial and subsea network environments.

presentations.title: The Global Network Advancement Group: A Next-Generation Multi-Tbps Campus and Global Network System for Data-Intensive Sciences
presentations.abstract:
The Global Network Advancement Group (GNA‑G), through its Data‑Intensive Sciences (DIS) and SENSE/AutoGOLE Working Groups, is developing a next‑generation, multi‑terabit/sec global system to support the rapidly escalating demands of data‑intensive science. Scientific programs such as the LHC, Rubin Observatory LSST, SKA, Cryo‑EM, genomics, and distributed AI/ML workflows now generate unprecedented data volumes, requiring coordinated global infrastructure capable of predictable, high‑throughput, multi‑domain operation.

Building on the progress of previous SC conferences, especially SC25, and state-of-the-art technology and AI/ML developments since then, partner teams from the U.S., Europe, Latin America, Asia and Africa will field more than a dozen Network Research Exhibitions to demonstrate this architecture at scale, while showcasing multi‑domain orchestration, programmable data planes, AI‑driven optimization, digital twin simulation, and multi‑Tbps global data movement. The system supports progressive deployment spanning R&D → advanced production → full production, ensuring coexistence with general R&E traffic while enabling scientific discoveries.

presentations.title: Wafer-Net: A Flexible Hierarchical Interconnection Architecture Based on Wafer-Scale Integration
presentations.abstract: High-performance interconnection networks are typically built upon high-radix routers. As system scale continues to grow, the conventional switch-centric scaling paradigm faces severe challenges in latency, deployment cost, and scalability. This paper proposes Wafer-Net, a flexible hierarchical interconnection architecture enabled by wafer-scale integration. Wafer-Net abstracts distributed on-wafer compute and switch resources into two composable building blocks—the Compute Chiplet Group (CCG) and the Switch Chiplet Group (SCG)—and thereby recasts conventional interconnection networks as a hierarchical structure that combines local high-bandwidth domains with global low-latency switching. We further propose a formal mapping framework based on hierarchical compression transformations and dynamic programming. Using this framework, we instantiate three representative Wafer-Net topologies, which significantly reduce network diameter and cabling overhead while supporting concise and efficient minimal/non-minimal and adaptive routing algorithms. Simulation results show that these Wafer-Net topologies consistently outperform both their conventional counterparts and the wafer-scale baseline in throughput and latency.

presentations.title: Scalable Generation of Distributed-Memory Mappings for Large Tensor Networks
presentations.abstract:
Large-scale tensor networks are a critical class of computations widely used in domains such as computational chemistry, machine learning, and others. Owing to their memory footprint and complexity, their execution requires distributed-memory clusters and deeply efficient communication.

This work proposes an enhanced non-linear formulation that unifies previously proposed modeling and optimization schemes for DAGs of tensor operators. Our new modeling and formulation finds high-performing mappings for large tensor networks. Our key scientific contribution is a novel representation of the hyper-dimensional grid of processing elements. The new abstraction exponentially expands the search space, yielding higher performance and enhanced scalability. Furthermore, we reformulate the mapping to exploit optimization procedures in Google CP-SAT, leading to over 50x scalability improvement relative to prior work.

We evaluate our approach on various DAGs targeting CPU and multi-GPU clusters. Our approach achieves average speedups of 4.01x and 1.73x over the Cyclops Tensor Framework and NVIDIA cuTensorNet, respectively.

presentations.title: GLOW: Accelerating Geometric Multigrid Layers on Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine
presentations.abstract: This paper describes the mapping of geometric multigrid (GMG) onto the Cerebras Wafer Scale Engine (WSE-3). The WSE wafer integrates almost a million cores along with a low-latency 2D mesh network, providing unprecedented on-chip bandwidth and fine-grained communication. Although the architecture is predominantly used for deep learning, we explore the suitability of WSE for accelerating GMG. GMG solves sparse linear systems efficiently by recursively coarsening the grid, which leads to more rapid convergence with less computation. As compared to prior implementations of stencils on WSE, this demonstration highlights the challenges of mapping a layered algorithm – and the full set of operators – onto a dataflow architecture. We compare the performance of this implementation to that of the HPGMG benchmark on an NVIDIA GH200 GPU. Across different GMG configurations and problem sizes, we observe a speedup of up to 25× as compared to a single GH200 node.

presentations.title: SpaDA: A Spatial Dataflow Architecture Programming Language
presentations.abstract: Spatial dataflow architectures like the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine deliver exceptional performance in AI and scientific computing by distributing scratchpad memory across hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs). Yet programming these architectures remains difficult: with no shared memory, data movement requires explicit configuration, and asynchronous task management introduces substantial complexity. We present SpaDA, a programming language that offers precise control over data placement, dataflow patterns, and asynchronous operations while abstracting low-level architectural details. We design and implement a compiler targeting Cerebras CSL through multi-level lowering and unique optimization passes. SpaDA functions as a high-level programming interface and an intermediate representation for domain-specific languages (DSLs), demonstrated here with the GT4Py stencil DSL. SpaDA enables concise expression of operations with complex parallel patterns — including collective operations, multi-dimensional stencils, dense and sparse linear algebra — in 7.49× fewer lines than CSL, achieving over 260 TFlop/s across 730,000 PEs on a single device.

presentations.title: OCEAN: Open-Source CXL Emulation for Hyperscale Architecture and Networking
presentations.abstract: Compute Express Link (CXL) 3.0 introduces fabric-level memory pooling, yet the absence of production CXL 3.0 hardware and the complexity of multi-host configurations pose significant barriers to the research community. This paper presents OCEAN, a high-fidelity, open-source emulation framework that reproduces the fabric-level feature set that distinguishes CXL 3.0—including multi-host memory sharing, dynamic capacity management, and coherent pooling across hosts—using QEMU virtualization and custom Linux kernel modules. OCEAN makes two central technical contributions: active latency injection and a software cache coherence layer implementing MESI-state management with distributed snoop filters to maintain correctness across up to 16 hosts. We validate OCEAN against a real CXL Type-3 device. In addition, case studies on Tigon database workloads quantify the throughput impact of hardware cache coherence—an 11× improvement at full coverage—while a design-space sweep of 12 memory-placement policies on GROMACS demonstrates up to 7% performance variation from policy choice alone.

presentations.title: TPage: Transparent Page Management for CXL-Based Tiered Memory Systems
presentations.abstract: The emerging Compute Express Link (CXL) technique introduces critical management challenges in tiered memory systems, particularly the trade‑off between data migration overhead and memory space efficiency. A 4KB‑based page unit enables fine‑grained memory management but incurs high migration latency and high page table scan overhead. 2MB‑based transparent huge page (THP) improves the migration efficiency but often wastes significant memory space due to the underutilized page space. To resolve the problem, we propose TPage, a transparent page management framework for CXL‑based tiered memory systems. TPage enables four key innovations: (1) PMU‑assisted memory imbalance monitor, (2) two‑phase page table scan, (3) hybrid page hotness tracking, and (4) huge-page‑aware page placement. TPage dynamically monitors inter‑node memory access pressure imbalance and proactively migrates pages to mitigate it. These mechanisms collectively reduce memory bloat and accelerate page migration, speeding up the performance by 3.6× over Transparent Page Placement (TPP).

presentations.title: Quantifying the Cost of Software-Managed Synchronization on Multi-Host CXL Memory
presentations.abstract:
Current multi-host CXL platforms provide shared, byte-addressable memory, but no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations. As a result, the main challenge is not remote-memory latency itself, but the software overhead required to ensure visibility and synchronization.

We quantify this overhead on a real four-host CXL shared-memory system, covering raw memory performance, software-managed publish/observe visibility, and synchronization built from explicit flushes and polling. On our platform, one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs, and each lock acquisition costs 3–5 µs, roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks. These overheads dominate synchronization-heavy workloads: BFS gains nothing from adding a second host; it requires frequent barriers and cross-host exchange. In contrast, triangle counting, which is read-dominated with little synchronization, does speed up when scaling from 32 to 32+32 threads across two hosts. Overall, suitability depends on remote-write intensity, synchronization frequency, and whether hot metadata stays in local DRAM.

presentations.title: Papers in Conversation
presentations.abstract: About Papers in Conversation: Each session highlights three technical papers addressing a common or emerging HPC topic. Following the paper presentations, a 20-minute moderated panel discussion will explore connections among the papers, contrasting perspectives, broader implications, open challenges, and future research directions. Our goal is to go beyond the individual contributions and encourage a conversation that helps the audience understand the larger research landscape, including where the field might be heading.

presentations.title: Towards High-Performance Sparse Graph Attention on Dense Tensor Core Units
presentations.abstract: Sparse graph attention (SGA) is a critical building block of attention-based graph neural networks (GNNs). Existing approaches either optimize individual primitives (e.g., SDDMM or SpMM) in isolation or rely on block-sparse representations, which fail to map graph-sparse workloads efficiently onto dense TCUs. We propose SpG-Attention, a unified framework that bridges sparse graph attention with dense TCU computation. Specifically, SpG-Attention introduces: (1) memory-efficient SGA (ME-SGA) parallel strategies that classify attention multiplications by their reduction characteristics and choose row/column-wise parallelization accordingly; (2) a TCU-friendly condensed-sparse format and customized fused kernels with MMA-aligned tiled execution, discrete-to-contiguous tiled loading, metadata prefetch pipelining, and register-fragment alignment; and (3) input-aware runtime optimizations based on graph statistics and refined by bounded online profiling to handle structural diversity and long-tail degree distributions. Extensive experiments on real-world graphs demonstrate that SpG-Attention achieves average speedups of 2.45x over Fused3S for inference and 2.15x over FlashSparse for end-to-end training.

presentations.title: Distributed Variational Quantum Linear Solver
presentations.abstract: VQLS is a promising hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving linear systems Ax=b, but its practical deployment is hindered by the massive circuit execution overhead required when encoding arbitrary matrices via linear combination of unitaries (LCU) decomposition. Evaluating the VQLS cost function requires quadratic scaling requirement with the LCU terms, resulting in tens of thousands of circuits per iteration and millions of executions across a full optimization trajectory. To address this, we present a scalable, distributed implementation of VQLS that exploits the embarrassingly parallel structure of the gradient-free-based cost function using NVIDIA CUDA-Q conjunction with multi-node distribution for HPC system. Benchmarking on the Perlmutter supercomputer, we validated the VQLS algorithm with a sample tridiagonal Toeplitz and a canonical Hele-Shaw fluid flow problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate near ideal strong scaling and high efficiency weak scaling performance. We also used Nsight to benchmark the distributed framework to explore ideal concurrency.

presentations.title: ZenKO: Guided and Iterative Quantum-Classical Method for Molecular Electronic Structure Using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
presentations.abstract: The electronic structure of molecules is foundational for scientific advancement; however, determining it remains challenging due to the growth of the molecular Hilbert space with system size. Recent approaches address this by using quantum circuits to sample candidate configurations and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to compute the ground state. We propose ZenKO, a novel gradient-based, iterative SQD method that employs a hybrid quantum-classical approach. ZenKO decomposes configuration selection into discovery, validation, and refinement, enabling targeted subspace expansion and guided exploration. Our evaluation demonstrates that, across H₂O, H₁₀, and N₂ molecules, ZenKO improves ground-state accuracy compared to prior iterative methods, while significantly reducing classical cost.

presentations.title: Quantum Sampling Architecture for Protein Structure Reconstruction on Utility-Scale Hardware
presentations.abstract: Predicting the structure of short peptides in protein binding pockets remains difficult: the regime requires physics-based conformational search, yet no existing method performs that search practically on current hardware. We present QSAD, a quantum-classical framework that reformulates peptide structure prediction as amino-acid-level Hamiltonian sampling and replaces iterative optimization with non-iterative Hamiltonian evolution. Executed entirely on IBM Heron R2 across 101 binding-pocket peptides (5-18 residues), QSAD improves prediction accuracy by 27%-71% over all evaluated AI and quantum baselines, with the lowest variance across tested lengths. QSAD also tolerates noise levels 3x-5x beyond typical hardware error rates, where iterative methods fail, and achieves a mean per-case speedup of 27x in quantum execution time relative to VQE. The sampled ensemble further supports approximate reconstruction of protein energy landscapes. These results establish coarse-grained quantum sampling as a practical path for structure prediction where data-driven methods lack sufficient signal.

presentations.title: Real-Time High-Fidelity Bayesian Inference and Forecasting of Tsunamis: A Digital Twin for Tsunami Early Warning Applied to the Cascadia Subduction Zone
presentations.abstract:
Tsunamis resulting from megathrust earthquakes are rare events that can cause devastating socioeconomic damage and loss of life. State-of-the-art early-warning systems rely on simplified physics models that can be inaccurate for near-field predictions, leading to delayed, missed, or false warnings. Tsunami propagation codes typically use shallow-water equations, which omit coupled ocean-acoustic and surface-gravity wave dynamics, while high-fidelity hydrodynamics codes are too computationally expensive for real-time use. My doctoral research develops a digital twin framework for tsunami early warning that incorporates high-fidelity physics, uses Bayesian data assimilation, and leverages GPU-oriented algorithms to enable accurate, real-time forecasts with rigorously quantified uncertainties for the Cascadia Subduction Zone.

The computational advance is an offline–online decomposition exploiting time-shift invariance in the parameter-to-observable and parameter-to-prediction maps. Their block-triangular Toeplitz structure enables fast Fourier transform-based matrix-vector products, delivering approximately one-hundred-thousand-fold speedups over repeated partial differential equation solves. The Bayesian inverse problem is reformulated in the smaller observation space using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, enabling offline factorization and real-time inference.

For a margin-wide Cascadia rupture with 600 hypothetical pressure sensors, the method infers more than one billion parameters and predicts wave heights at 21 locations in under 0.2 seconds on 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, a ten-billion-fold speedup over state-of-the-art methods—a breakthrough recognized with the 2025 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The framework also enables scalable Bayesian optimal experimental design by recasting sensor placement as dense matrix subset selection to minimize uncertainty in inferred seafloor motion or wave-height forecasts. This digital twin paves the way toward accurate, uncertainty-aware tsunami forecasts worldwide.

presentations.title: Subgraph Counting: Methods, Frameworks, and Applications
presentations.abstract:
Subgraph counting and matching are core primitives in network analysis, underpinning applications from computational biology to fraud detection to performance analysis in HPC. Existing methods assume static, small networks, rely on hardware-specific kernels that do not scale across the accelerator ecosystem, and emphasize counting over the harder problem of locating pattern instances. This dissertation addresses all three.

We develop ParaDyMS, a parallel method for counting all motifs of size k ≤ 5 on fully dynamic networks under batched edge insertions and deletions. Rather than recomputing from scratch, ParaDyMS updates motif counts incrementally using only the delta induced by a batch of changes. Implemented in the Kokkos C++ Performance Portability ecosystem, ParaDyMS targets both OpenMP and CUDA from one source, achieving up to 124× speedup over the state-of-the-art static method and outperforming 112 CPU cores with a single GPU.

To address hardware portability, we present PyGB-LAPIS, a compilation pipeline lowering graph algorithms written in Python-GraphBLAS through MLIR and the LAPIS backend into Kokkos-flavored C++. PyGB-LAPIS generates kernels across five sparse storage formats and multiple hardware backends from one source, matching hand-written Kokkos performance while eliminating per-backend engineering effort.

Finally, we develop an exact subgraph matching method that decomposes query and host graphs into size-4 graphlets and searches a compressed graphlet-overlap representation. This supports arbitrary-size queries and, uniquely, resolves multiple simultaneous queries in one pass through a shared search tree rather than restarting per query, with the union graph traversed on the fly and pruned by graphlet frequency to control its size.

presentations.title: Efficient Representation Learning for Heterogeneous Systems and Continual Task Adaptation
presentations.abstract:
This dissertation addresses two fundamental challenges in distributed machine learning: client heterogeneity and continual adaptation to new tasks. It develops efficient fine-tuning and representation-learning frameworks that let distributed models acquire new knowledge and align it across clients without communication bottlenecks or catastrophic forgetting.

First, we introduce a dual-distilled federated learning framework for clients with heterogeneous systems and data. Trainable global prototypes with adaptive margins align local representations and logits without requiring a shared model architecture, enabling robust knowledge transfer and stable convergence.

Next, we propose a communication-efficient federated framework for large language models (LLMs) based on representation fine-tuning. By intervening on hidden states rather than weights, and combining All-But-Me aggregation with dynamic test-time computing, it reduces communication cost while balancing local personalization and global generalization.

We then present SETA, a mixture of sparse experts for task-agnostic continual learning in LLMs. SETA resolves the plasticity–stability dilemma by structurally decomposing the parameter space into shared and task-specific experts, protecting shared knowledge from semantic drift while preserving task-specific features.

Finally, we introduce FedSEAM, which extends sparse experts to federated continual learning. Clients learn experts on private task streams, and the server merges them through subspace agreement: it combines only the update directions clients share, keeps disagreeing directions as client-private experts, and protects prior-task subspaces from being overwritten.

Together, these contributions chart a path toward scalable, resource-aware machine learning systems that bridge decentralized efficiency and continual real-world deployment, learning new tasks across privacy-constrained environments without forgetting.

presentations.title: Genome Variant Representation in Genome LMs and Multi-Omic AI: Efficiency, Scalability, and Medical Actionability
presentations.abstract:
The recent rapid growth and curation of large multi-omic datasets, driven largely by high-throughput sequencing, have provided unprecedented opportunities in medical and clinical research, especially for precision medicine. This presents an opportunity for improved multi-omic deep learning implementations for oncology tasks. However, it comes with a set of challenges, namely:

1. Granularity in genomic variant representation: representing complex, arbitrary-length genomic variant data without destroying spatial context or non-coding regulatory signals in both standalone and multi-omic models

2. Scalability and efficiency: establishing efficient and domain-informed data loading strategies, hyperparameter optimization guidelines and computationally scalable architectural choices, especially for resource-intensive medical applications

3. Systematized multi-omic integration: How can we rigorously evaluate multi-omics integration strategies and assess which combinations of omics modalities yield the most informative biological representations for oncology tasks?

To address these issues, we have made the following contributions. First, we developed a feasibility study into the representation of genomic variant data, leveraging genome language models (gLMs) to capture nucleotide-level dependencies across variable-length somatic variant-associated sequences for pan-cancer classification and survival analysis. Next, we scaled our framework to combine both coding exomes and non-coding regions by implementing input load balancing and architectural changes, improving performance on chosen oncology tasks. Finally, we introduced a generalized, versatile, and modular framework that incorporates key autoencoder architectures for representation learning, enabling exploration and robust evaluation of multi-modal omics integration.

The cumulative findings bridge hardware-efficient scaling, biological representation learning, and cancer-specific multi-omics to drive medical actionability.

presentations.title: Foundation Models for Discovery and Exploration in Chemical Space
presentations.abstract:
Accurate, rapid prediction of molecular properties remains a bottleneck in materials innovation because experiments and conventional simulations are too costly to explore vast, high-dimensional chemical spaces. Scalable and interpretable molecular foundation models can accelerate discovery across chemical space while using computational resources efficiently. We demonstrate this with MIST, a family of molecular foundation models trained with up to an order of magnitude more data and parameters than prior work. To train MIST we developed Smirk, a tokenizer which preserves nuclear, electronic, and geometric information, enabling representation learning across chemical systems.

The largest MIST model has 1.8B parameters and was trained on 2B molecules. Training such a large model is an expensive endeavor. To make model development tractable on an academic compute budget we developed hyperparameter-penalized neural scaling laws which guided identification of compute-optimal model configurations without exhaustive sweeps at every scale, reducing model-development cost by an order of magnitude.

MIST models have been fine-tuned to predict over 400 structure–property relationships spanning domains from psychophysics to electrochemistry. They demonstrate state-of-the-art benchmark performance and enable real-world applications including stereochemical reasoning for organometallics, olfactory perception mapping, and electrolyte formulation design.

Beyond raw predictive accuracy, using mechanistic-interpretability methods we determine MIST learns chemically meaningful concepts during training. Analysis of token vectors, low-dimensional embedding projections and model logits reveals concept-aligned structures not explicitly labeled during training.

Together, these contributions connect molecular representation learning, compute-optimal scaling, and broad scientific validation, establishing scientific foundation models as robust tools for materials discovery and optimization.

presentations.title: Hardware-Aware Matrix-Free Algorithms for Accelerating Large-Scale Finite-Element Simulations on Distributed CPU and GPU Architectures
presentations.abstract:
Large-scale simulations governed by partial differential equations reduce, after finite-element (FE) discretization, to two kernels: operator action on large blocks of vectors inside eigensolvers, and the solution of Poisson or Helmholtz systems inside linear solvers. Both are limited by data movement rather than floating-point throughput, and the traditional assembled sparse-matrix and cell-matrix strategies scale poorly at high polynomial order, the first bound by memory traffic, the second by an operation count that grows as the sixth power of the order.

This dissertation develops hardware-aware matrix-free algorithms that evaluate operator actions on the fly through sum factorization, batched over the multivector dimension. The contributions are batched FE Helmholtz matrix-multivector products, using even-odd decomposition and SIMD vectorization on CPUs and fused register-blocked kernels on GPUs, a matrix-free Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonian action covering nonlocal projectors, real and complex arithmetic and inline constraint handling on AVX2/AVX-512/SVE CPUs and on GPUs with tensor cores and reduced-precision ghost exchange, a distributed-memory GPU fast-diagonalization solver that inverts the FE Laplacian exactly at O(N^(4/3)) FLOPs, and a device-native fused conjugate-gradient solver with a Chebyshev-Jacobi p-multigrid preconditioner.

Measured inside DFT-FE against existing baselines on Summit, Frontier, Fugaku, Polaris, Pravega and Aurora, the operator actions run 2.6x–5.8x faster than cell-matrix. The fused solve runs 5.86x faster than deal.II on 384 Aurora GPUs, and p-multigrid holds it at 5–7 iterations across polynomial orders. On tensor-product meshes one exact solve is 34x–3,186x faster than p-multigrid. The algorithms assume nothing specific to DFT and carry over to higher-order FE applications.

presentations.title: BatchMine: Accelerating Approximate Graph Pattern Mining via Batch Processing
presentations.abstract:
Approximate graph pattern mining, as a fundamental technique in graph analysis, has been widely applied in machine learning, biomedical research, and social network analysis. However, existing solutions still face significant challenges in efficiency and scalability when dealing with complex pattern graphs or giant data graphs. To address these limitations, we introduce BatchMine, an out-of-core system for approximate graph pattern mining. BatchMine leverages three key techniques: (1) a partition-based estimation method to accelerate convergence; (2) a batch-processing framework with adaptive refinement to enhance external-memory access locality and improve convergence efficiency; and (3) a hybrid data layout that balances sampling efficiency and storage overhead.

To the best of our knowledge, BatchMine is the first graph pattern mining system capable of handling graphs exceeding main memory capacity, enabling mining on graphs with nearly 100 billion edges on a single machine within 1,000 seconds. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of BatchMine.

presentations.title: KSPine: Fast Parallel K-Shortest Path Computation via Block-Cut+ Tree Decomposition and Dynamic Caching
presentations.abstract: Efficiently computing K-shortest path (KSP) on graphs is critical for many real-world applications. Existing solutions suffer from query-dependent pruning, limited parallelism, and redundant computation across repeated queries. To address such challenges, this paper presents KSPine, a fast parallel KSP framework. KSPine is built on block-cut+ tree (BC+ tree), a structural decomposition that identifies a compact, query-independent skeleton of the graph using biconnected components and articulation points. This skeleton allows KSPine to prune each query to a small structural subgraph and solve independent sub-KSP problems within each BiCC block in parallel. To combine local sub-KSP results into global top-K paths, we design a merging-based method with early stopping that reduces unnecessary computation. KSPine also introduces a hierarchical dynamic caching mechanism that reuses sub-KSP results across queries, avoiding redundant computation under continuous workloads. On six real-world graphs across various domains, KSPine achieves an average speedup of 1.5× over state-of-the-art methods.

presentations.title: PUMatch: Bandwidth-Efficient DFS-Based Subgraph Matching Under GPU Memory Oversubscription
presentations.abstract: Subgraph matching on massive graphs is hindered by GPU memory oversubscription, where frequent CPU-GPU data transfers create severe performance bottlenecks. Existing unified memory solutions suffer from bandwidth waste due to coarse-grained page transfers, while BFS-based approaches often fail due to intermediate result explosion. To address these challenges, we present PUMatch, a bandwidth-efficient, DFS-based CPU-GPU collaborative framework. PUMatch introduces four key innovations: (1) dual-scale packaging that reorganizes missing neighborhoods into compact CSR units to maximize bandwidth efficiency; (2) a synchronization-free asynchronous coordination protocol for DFS execution; (3) orthogonal warp scheduling with trie-based resumption that operates independently of the SM’s built-in scheduler; and (4) an adaptive hybrid data access scheme that dynamically optimizes data movement via a lightweight learning controller. Extensive experiments on real-world graphs with billions of edges demonstrate that PUMatch achieves up to 10.49× speedup over state-of-the-art BFS baselines and 3.45× over DFS baselines, while reducing PCIe traffic by 73%.

presentations.title: BMS2: Fast Batched Subgraph Matching on GPUs with Structure-Aware Scheduling
presentations.abstract: Batched matching is widely used in drug discovery, software analysis, and social network analysis.
