Its core operation, subgraph matching, is an NP-complete graph algorithm that has been optimized in the HPC field for decades. As for batching scenario, we find that current subgraph matching systems are unable to leverage the common structure patterns of real-world graphs, thereby missing potential optimization opportunities. In this paper, we propose BMS2, a batched matching system with structure-aware scheduling. BMS2 incorporates these intrinsic properties into previous general filter-join strategy: (1) in the filter phase, BMS2 utilizes the presence information of special structure for early termination; (2) in the join phase, we exploit the similarity of batched queries to reuse matching results of common structure. Experiments demonstrate that BMS2 can achieve an order of magnitude performance improvement on GPUs compared to the state-of-the-art with the ability to process two orders of magnitude larger dataset.

presentations.title: Building Multi-Tenant AI Infrastructure at Scale
presentations.abstract:
Every large AI cluster begins with the same goal: deliver GPU infrastructure that can scale reliably. The challenge is that networking quickly becomes far more complex than simply connecting switches and servers. As clusters grow, operators must coordinate edge networking, Ethernet fabrics, InfiniBand, NVLink, and host/DPU networking while continually provisioning, resizing, and maintaining tenant environments.

Drawing on lessons from 60+ GPU clusters and 500,000 GPUs under management, this session explores how networking for AI has evolved beyond traditional data center operations. It examines why organizations outgrow manual configuration and DIY automation, why hardware-enforced multi-tenancy has become a foundational operational requirement, and how experience gained across many deployments helps reduce operational risk.

Attendees will gain practical architectural and operational guidance for designing networking that can support the scale, security, and lifecycle demands of modern AI infrastructure.

presentations.title: Accelerated Services Framework: Programmable Services Using DPUs
presentations.abstract:
Modern data centers, enterprise networks, and AI infrastructure require network services such as security, encryption, traffic management, and segmentation to scale across hybrid cloud and edge environments. In the post-Mythos era lateral movement turns one compromised workload into a breach, hence DC east-west traffic monitoring becomes increasingly critical. Today, these services often rely on dedicated appliances or server software, increasing cost, complexity, power consumption, and operational overhead.

This paper presents an accelerated services framework (ASF) which combines an open-source software abstraction layer for network services and couples it with an open-source composable DPU hardware form factor. This allows for a flexible software front-end that is coupled with scalable hardware. We envision ASF delivering accelerated services and security in multiple form factors such as SmartSwitches, dense Rack-scale nodes, and AI clusters.

ASF calls for vendor neutrality to simplify operations, reduce infrastructure costs, and free server resources for enterprise and AI factories.

presentations.title: From Hero Run to Fleet Proof: Reproducible AI Training Across 512 GPUs
presentations.abstract:
One fast benchmark run does not prove that a large AI cluster will perform consistently in production. This presentation explains how Nscale moved from a single “hero run” to repeatable fleet-level validation across a 64-rack NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 deployment.

We will show how 14 workload configurations, each using 512 GPUs, were repeated across independent allocations to test whether performance held across different racks, NVLink domains, NCCL paths and InfiniBand fabric. The session covers topology-aware placement, firmware consistency, health validation, workload comparability and the preservation of evidence needed to distinguish a genuine fleet capability from an isolated peak result.

Attendees will learn a practical methodology for designing reproducible large-scale training tests, identifying infrastructure variance and deciding when benchmark evidence is strong enough to support production-readiness claims.

presentations.title: Practical HPCQC Integration with QDMI: A Real-Hardware Case Study with IQM Systems
presentations.abstract:
Quantum computers are entering HPC centers, shifting the main challenge from hardware access to integration. Many software paths still rely on vendor-specific adapter chains between user SDKs, schedulers, and backend APIs, which complicates operations and slows the move from pilots to production. We present a practical integration path built on the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI). Using IQM superconducting systems as a hardware case study, we implement an IQM-backed QDMI layer and connect it to two software layers HPC centers already care about: Slurm-based job execution and Qiskit-facing user workflows. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/iqm-finland/QDMI-on-IQM.

The message is that integrating quantum hardware into HPC need not be a bespoke effort per backend. Once the software–hardware boundary is standardized, large parts of the stack become reusable across providers and deployment styles. We do not claim that this removes all HPCQC challenges, but that this boundary can be standardized today.

presentations.title: End-to-End Modeling and Trace-Driven Replay for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Supercomputing
presentations.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical applications increasingly execute as multi-stage workflows spanning HPC nodes, simulators, workflow runtimes, network services, and remote quantum backends. Evaluating such applications is difficult because their end-to-end critical path crosses heterogeneous components with incompatible observability and control interfaces, making reported results hard to reproduce, compare, and extrapolate. We present QTrace, an end-to-end methodology for performance analysis of hybrid quantum-classical workloads. QTrace combines a unified cross-layer tracing schema with a dependency-aware, trace-driven replay engine that preserves workflow causality while enabling controlled perturbation of backend latency, scheduling policy, and reliability-related effects. This supports both faithful reproduction of observed executions and systematic "what-if" studies for future quantum-accelerated systems. We evaluate QTrace on representative iterative and adaptive workloads across simulator-backed and remote-backend settings. The results show that QTrace reconstructs workflow behavior with high fidelity, reproduces observed executions with low replay error, and exposes bottlenecks that are often hidden by backend-centric metrics alone.

presentations.title: A GPU-Accelerated and Geometry-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Optimized PES Scans with CUDA-Q
presentations.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical workloads, particularly potential-energy-surface (PES) scans in quantum chemistry using batched VQE and QAOA, involve many structurally similar Hamiltonians differing only in coefficients. Existing warm-start and meta-optimization strategies reuse parameters between instances but still fixed quantum-classical resources, ignoring cross-instance structural similarities. We present OptiPESS, a GPU-accelerated runtime system for adaptive resource allocation in hybrid quantum-classical execution. OptiPESS introduces the Locality-Occupancy-Variance (LOV) metric, a lightweight, geometry-aware measure of Hamiltonian similarity, coupled with efficient alignment and Pauli-classification passes. Using LOV, OptiPESS performs distance-aware scheduling of iteration and shot budgets, predicting which instances can be skipped, quick-solved, or fully optimized. Implemented atop CUDA-Q with persistent multi-GPU execution and near-linear scaling, OptiPESS reduces classical and quantum evaluations by up to 78.3% and wall-time by up to 74.8% while maintaining baseline accuracy. This demonstrates how lightweight static analysis and adaptive scheduling can transform quantum-classical co-execution from fixed-budget loops into a predictive, resource-aware runtime.

presentations.title: Papers in Conversation
presentations.abstract: About Papers in Conversation: Each session highlights three technical papers addressing a common or emerging HPC topic. Following the paper presentations, a 20-minute moderated panel discussion will explore connections among the papers, contrasting perspectives, broader implications, open challenges, and future research directions. Our goal is to go beyond the individual contributions and encourage a conversation that helps the audience understand the larger research landscape, including where the field might be heading.

presentations.title: Toward Continental Forest Dynamics Modeling at Individual-Tree Resolution on Exascale Systems
presentations.abstract: Modeling continental-to-global forest dynamics at individual-tree resolution is essential for Earth system prediction but has remained computationally impractical because of cross-scale interactions among billions of trees in heterogeneous atmospheric and soil environments. We present GGap, an agent-based forest model designed for exascale systems. GGap employs a Site–Gap–Tree hierarchy that co-locates each site's ensemble on a single GPU to maximize data locality. It leverages two-level parallelism: site partitions run concurrently across MPI ranks, while GPU threads update agents within each rank. To avoid CPU–GPU synchronization, a multi-priority kernel pipeline executes sequential ecological phases entirely on-device, using grid barriers to enforce their order. On Frontier, the largest weak-scaling configuration simulates 10.25 billion agents on 2,048 GPUs at 96.2% parallel efficiency. A 1,000-year contiguous United States simulation across 1,424 sites and 235 species reproduces regional patterns of species composition, forest structure, productivity, and biomass, demonstrating ecologically meaningful continental-scale forest simulation.

presentations.title: Demonstrating the Neuromorphic Advantage on Stochastic Dynamics in Turbulent Flows
presentations.abstract:
Graphics processing units (GPUs) excel at workloads dependent on linear algebra, covering a wide range of topics like artificial intelligence and quantum mechanics. However, in workloads that are not well captured by linear algebra, such as probabilistic systems, GPUs may not provide optimal performance.

In this work, we demonstrate a neuromorphic advantage in energy efficiency for simulating turbulent flows with stochastic methods. We observe energy savings across the board and runtime speed-up for some methods when comparing a neuromorphic platform to equivalent workloads on GPU and CPU. Specifically, our neuromorphic implementation achieves 1.52x speed-up and 37.46x less energy consumption, compared to a GPU running the same 1.5 million random walks over discretized space. For 100,000 walks in continuous space, GPU outperforms neuromorphic in execution time but consumes 2.37x more energy. As the technological landscape for neuromorphic systems rapidly evolves, their performance relative to current hardware is likely to significantly improve.

presentations.title: MakoXC: Rearchitecting DFT Exchange–Correlation with Matrix-Aligned and Knowledge-Organized Sparsity
presentations.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) is essential to materials science and drug discovery, yet exchange–correlation (XC) evaluation remains a major bottleneck. Linear-scaling methods exploit electronic nearsightedness but introduce irregular sparse workloads that underutilize modern AI accelerators. We present MakoXC, a matrix-aligned XC engine that restructures nearsightedness-induced sparsity into regular accelerator-friendly computation. MakoXC combines matrix-aligned cells to organize interactions into dense clusters, sparsity-guided activation to expose implicit sparsity for practical linear scaling, and a kernel-fused pipeline to consolidate fragmented workloads into a compute-intensive execution path. MakoXC achieves average speedups of 67.8x over standard XC evaluation and 4.7x over state-of-the-art linear-scaling methods. Integrated into a production-grade commercial DFT package, MakoXC scales to ubiquitin (1,231 atoms, def2-SVP) on 64 GPUs, completing end-to-end DFT in under five minutes. MakoXC demonstrates how scientific workloads can achieve genuine low complexity while maximizing parallel efficiency on AI accelerators.

presentations.title: From PME to FMM: A Modern Approach to Long-Range Force Calculation in GROMACS
presentations.abstract:
The fast multipole method (FMM) is a potentially scalable method for long-range electrostatics in molecular dynamics (MD) codes such as GROMACS. Most MD codes have relied for decades on the highly optimized particle mesh Ewald (PME) method, but its reliance on fast Fourier transforms introduces all-to-all communication that ultimately limits strong scaling, whereas FMM uses a hierarchical communication pattern in which farther nodes exchange less information.

In this study, we tightly integrate a highly-scalable and GPU-accelerated FMM into GROMACS, which for the first time shows an actual advantage over PME in time-to-solution. We compared both FMM and PME on the ALPS cluster across one to 128 Grace Hopper compute nodes, each equipped with four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs, over multiple MD test systems. Across these systems, including a 44-million-atom simulation, our FMM implementation shows markedly better scalability than GROMACS' highly optimized PME implementation and achieves up to 2.57× speedup at scale.

presentations.title: HSTUFuse: Training-Compatible Efficient Fusion for Long-Sequence Recommenders
presentations.abstract: Generative recommenders improve the modeling of long-range behavioral dependencies through unified causal sequence modeling, where the hierarchical sequential transduction unit (HSTU) serves as a core sequence encoder. However, the original HSTU implementation incurs fragmented operator execution, cross-feature reductions in LayerNorm, padding overhead from dense materialization, and redundant spatial aggregation. We present HSTUFuse, a training-compatible CUDA optimization that decomposes HSTU into three stages—pointwise projection, spatial aggregation, and pointwise transformation—with fused forward and backward implementations. It further replaces LayerNorm with Dynamic Tanh, internalizes jagged-tensor addressing, and combines valid-position computation with causal lower-triangular pruning. ML-1M training runs show stable convergence while retaining recommendation quality close to the PyTorch HSTU. On ML-20M, it achieves per-batch HSTU execution speedups of 19.53× on RTX 4090 and 22.46× on H800, measured using the sum of forward- and backward-pass times.

presentations.title: FitFloat: Read/Write Random-Access Compressed Floating-Point Arrays for GPUs
presentations.abstract: In many floating-point applications that use GPUs, device memory is a bottleneck limiting the maximum problem size. One solution is to use Unified Virtual Memory, but the limited physical GPU memory likely causes page evictions, incurring potentially large performance penalties. We present FitFloat, a drop-in floating-point array replacement supporting user-specified precision on GPUs with the goal of reducing storage requirements of scientific applications while maximizing performance over unified memory. FitFloat targets applications limited by the GPU's memory capacity, allowing larger problem sizes to be efficiently processed. We evaluate the storage savings and performance improvement of our approach relative to using native arrays on 11 single-precision and three double-precision codes from the HeCBench suite on two different GPUs. In the best case, FitFloat yields a speedup of 739 and provides a geometric-mean speedup of 16.1 for the float codes and 20.1 for the double codes on an RTX 4090.

presentations.title: Chisa: Dynamic Logical Way Partitioning for Efficient Caching in Sparse Accelerators
presentations.abstract:
Sparse tensor computations are memory-bound, making on-chip data reuse critical to sparse accelerator performance. Guided cache replacement derives lookahead information from structural relationships between operand tensors, but its effectiveness hinges on the prefetch observation window in SRAM. Under constrained SRAM, the window is inevitably small and guidance becomes noisy or misleading—precisely when caching matters most.

We propose Chisa, a dynamic logical way partitioning scheme for sparse accelerator caches. Inspired by victim caches, Chisa integrates buffer semantics into cache sets: a single role bit lets each way dynamically serve as a logical cache or buffer way without data migration, so mistakenly evicted blocks can be rescued upon reuse. Chisa further incorporates Jaccard similarity-based initialization and rescue rate-based runtime adaptation. On real-world sparse matrices, Chisa achieves geometric mean speedups of 1.23x and 1.27x over the state of the art on SpMSpM and SpMM, respectively, peaking at 4.46x and 4.64x.

presentations.title: High-Performance Tensor Formulation of the Viterbi Algorithm for Hidden Semi-Markov Models
presentations.abstract: Hidden semi-Markov models (HSMMs) are fundamental probabilistic models widely adopted across diverse domains, from computational biology to finance and signal processing. The Viterbi algorithm decodes the most likely state sequence given an HSMM and can be applied iteratively for ab initio model learning. However, existing Viterbi implementations remain sequential, and GPU-accelerated solutions are entirely absent, making HSMM decoding impractical for large-scale workloads. We present a tensor-based formulation of the Viterbi algorithm for HSMMs, restructuring the inner loops into tensor operations that naturally map onto SIMD units and massively parallel architectures. Building on this formulation, we provide optimized implementations spanning single- and multi-core CPUs, and, for the first time, GPU. Experimental evaluation demonstrates speedups of up to 14× on a single core, over 200× with multi-core, and over 570× on GPU over the state-of-the-art sequential baseline, establishing a new performance baseline for large-scale HSMM decoding.

presentations.title: PIMCQG: Co-Designing Billion-Scale Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for Processing-in-Memory
presentations.abstract: Graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) delivers superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for large-scale AI applications, but remains fundamentally bottlenecked by the ”memory wall” on CPUs and GPUs. Processing-in-memory (PIM) offers massive internal bandwidth by co-locating computation with data, making it a natural fit for irregular, memory-bound workloads. However, directly mapping graph-based ANNS onto PIM exposes severe algorithm–architecture mismatches: restricted per-PU memory, costly inter-PU communication, heavy coordination overhead, and weak compute capability, forcing existing PIM-based ANNS to rely on cluster-based algorithms that plateau at low recall. We propose PIMCQG, an algorithm–hardware co-design framework through three optimizations: (1) a compact index reducing PIM-resident footprint by 14.5×; (2) an asynchronous pipelined scheduler fully utilizing host–PIM bandwidth; (3) a multiplication-free distance kernel with <0.08% recall loss. Evaluations on three billion-scale datasets show up to 20×/17.1× throughput over CPU/GPU baselines, 129× over prior PIM accelerators at high recall, and scale across multi-node and emerging PIM architectures.

presentations.title: FluxZK: Scalable and Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proof Computation via GPU Acceleration
presentations.abstract:
Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocols enable privacy-preserving verification but face critical performance bottlenecks at the proof generation stage, particularly when handling large-scale computations that exceed GPU memory capacity. We present FluxZK, a framework that addresses scalability and efficiency challenges through ZKP-specific GPU-based optimizations. Our framework introduces FluxMSM, an efficient multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) implementation that leverages fine-grained parallelism and overlapped data transfer with computation. Additionally, we develop FluxNTT, a high-performance number theoretic transform (NTT) solution supporting both out-of-core and on-GPU computation paradigms. Extensive evaluations on data center GPUs demonstrate that FluxZK scales well to large input sizes of up to 2³⁰ elements, delivering an estimated performance improvement of up to 2.16x over existing solutions in real-world ZKP applications.

Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/SJTU-Liquid/FluxZK.

presentations.title: MPCAR: Scalable and Secure Multi-Party Computation-Based AllReduce
presentations.abstract: Scalable and secure collective communication is critical in modern HPC and AI workloads, especially AllReduce. State-of-the-art (SOTA) solutions use homomorphic encryption (HE) to ensure data privacy, but incur complex key management and overheads, and weak integration with collective algorithms. We present MPCAR, the first multi-party computation-based AllReduce framework, which decouples AllReduce into two phases, data reduction and distribution, and applies tailored secure methods to each. MPCAR employs secret sharing MPC schemes for the data reduction phase and asymmetric one-time-padding-based protection for the distribution phase, while also allowing user-defined secure communication protocols. We co-design these schemes with multiple AllReduce algorithms and implement several system-level optimizations. Evaluated across five platforms spanning AWS and HPC clusters at scale, including two exascale supercomputers and scaling to 8,192 ranks, MPCAR improves latency/throughput by up to 30.5%/41.2%. MPCAR also outperforms SOTA by up to 21.3% on real-world workloads, including DNN applications and three DeepSeek-distilled models.

presentations.title: eFaaS: A Lightweight, Kernel-Bypass Serverless Framework for HPC Workloads
presentations.abstract:
HPC workflows are growing in scale and complexity, demanding elastic resource provisioning and fine-grained parallel execution. While serverless computing is conceptually well-suited due to its on-demand model, existing frameworks are primarily designed for lightweight, event-driven workloads, leading to fundamental mismatches in highly concurrent HPC scenarios.

In such workloads, large numbers of function instances must be created simultaneously, introducing significant startup and communication overhead. Kernel-dependent mechanisms—such as cgroups, namespaces, and the network stack—become bottlenecks: instance initialization triggers heavy lock contention, while cross-node communication incurs additional costs from data copying, serialization, and context switching.

To address these issues, we propose eFaaS, a serverless architecture tailored for HPC. By leveraging eBPF, eFaaS enables lock-free isolation and zero-copy communication, minimizing kernel overhead. Experimental results show that eFaaS maintains stable performance under extreme concurrency, significantly reduces long-tail latency, and achieves end-to-end speedups of 1.27×–3.74× across representative HPC workflows.

presentations.title: The Maverick Architecture: A Runtime-Adaptive Dataflow Paradigm for Exascale Computing
presentations.abstract:
AI is rebuilding compute — and it is exposing the limits of today's infrastructure.

For years, the industry believed the answer was simple: more GPUs, larger clusters, and specialized hardware for every new workload. But as multimodal AI, agentic systems, and increasingly heterogeneous architectures become the norm, the bottleneck is no longer the accelerator. It's the system itself.

The next generation of HPC and AI won't be won by fixed architectures optimized for today's models. It will be won by infrastructure that adapts as workloads evolve.

This session explores why maximizing FLOPS is no longer enough. Using the successful deployment of the Spectra supercomputer at Sandia National Laboratories as a real-world example, we'll examine how adaptive computing is redefining system efficiency, eliminating infrastructure bottlenecks, and preparing HPC for an era where software changes faster than hardware can be built.

presentations.title: Three Ways a Filesystem Panics When a Data Center Goes Dark — and How MooseFS 5 Avoids Them
presentations.abstract:
Distributed filesystems are mostly engineered around disk and server failures. A site outage is a different kind of event: many servers vanish at once, correlated, sometimes deliberately. Systems that treat it as many simultaneous disk failures tend to develop three concrete pathologies: leader election can deadlock because the survivors are no longer a majority; the repair machinery starts re-replicating everything the lost site held, saturating the inter-site link; and there is often no way to tell the system, "This site is down on purpose."

This talk describes how MooseFS 5 addresses each. Election counts sites, not servers — a site votes if a majority of its servers respond. Repair stays inside a site whenever surviving copies or EC parts allow, crossing the WAN only as last resort. Sites carry an explicit three-state lifecycle, so maintenance is not an emergency. Illustrated by MooseFS in production at IMGW-PIB across Warsaw and Kraków.

presentations.title: SMB and NFS behaviors for AI training
presentations.abstract:
Everyone knows NFS is the ideal remote file protocol for Linux and AI; after all, it’s the one everyone uses. So … what if they’re wrong?

In this Exhibitor Forum presentation, we will contrast SMB and NFS behaviors for AI training, showing real results and case studies of a modern SMB server stacked up against its Linux kernel-mode NFSD alternative, all on Linux, to debunk the myth of NFS being the only correct remote file system for Linux. Using tools like MLPerf, VDBench, IOR, and FIO, we will show the specific ways that SMB can be a superior fabric for AI training, checkpointing, and multi-platform data aggregation. You will leave this presentation with a clear understanding of the protocol impacts on AI workloads, the caveats of specific file systems and security measures, and how you can better optimize your AI training and checkpointing regardless of chosen protocol.

presentations.title: "Meet Your Mentor / Senior Peer" Speed Networking
presentations.abstract: Four invited senior peers deliver 5-min lightning talks sharing their technical journeys, expertise development, career transitions, and leadership experiences. The fast-paced session offers opportunities for follow-up conversations and mentoring connections.

presentations.title: (Featured Speaker) From Recovery to Explanation: Deterministic Replay as Evidence for Fault Diagnosis at Scale
presentations.abstract: For two decades, fault tolerance has meant recovery: checkpointing and restart, rollback recovery, consistent cuts — mechanisms that assume the fault announces itself. Something crashes, hangs, or times out; recovery restores a good state and continues.A growing and expensive class of failures in large-scale AI training does not announce itself. The job runs to completion, the loss curve looks healthy, and the model is nonetheless wrong: a parameter declared trainable never receives a gradient; a resume restores weights but not optimizer state; a precision policy silently degrades. These faults waste thousands of GPU-hours and surface days later, discovered by working backwards from an evaluation metric. For this class, recovery is worse than insufficient — applied blindly, it faithfully carries the defect forward across every restart.Such failures require explanation, not just recovery, and explanation requires evidence rather than inference. Telemetry-based root-cause analysis reasons from surface signals about what probably happened; deterministic record-and-replay makes the execution itself available for interrogation.This talk argues that the fault-tolerance community's next primitive is a queryable evidence base. I ground the argument in two prior systems: iReplayer (PLDI 2018), which showed that deterministic replay of production multithreaded programs is affordable and can be performed in place, and an OOPSLA 2020 system that automated root-cause diagnosis over such recordings using replay, hardware watchpoints, and binary analysis. I then examine what large-scale AI workloads change — a semantic gap between bytes and the logical entities of a model; distribution across ranks, where each rank's evidence is self-consistent yet insufficient; and silence, which removes the trigger these mechanisms assume — and describe early work on a semantic attribution layer addressing the first. Throughout, I am explicit about what such evidence establishes and what it does not: provenance is not proof of value correctness.

presentations.title: 13th Annual International Workshop on Innovating the Network for Data Intensive Science — INDIS
presentations.abstract: Data networks are the circulatory system for science, discovery, society, and industry. But scientific data networking is not a solved problem, and significant challenges remain. These challenges reflect scientists' persistent needs from data networks: the needs for ever increasing capacity, flexibility, consistency, and collaboration. The theme for the 13th INDIS workshop is "Connected Science: Bridging Research and Industry" — reflecting not only the role of networking in connecting scientific infrastructure, but also our community's collaborations across different types of organizations to advance data-intensive science. This year INDIS plans to continue its tradition of having a discussion- and interaction-oriented schedule; based on past feedback, this is always well received. INDIS 2026 delivers an essential complement to the HPC-focused SC26 Technical Program, providing a dedicated platform for HPC researchers to explore data-intensive computing, interconnects, and networking.

presentations.title: 14 GPU Programming Paradigms Put to the Test: Performance Portability and Halstead Difficulty in Scientific Computing
15th International Workshop on Runtime and Operating Systems for Supercomputers (ROSS 2026)
presentations.abstract:
With increasing levels of parallelism, increased heterogeneity, energy and memory constraints coupled with emerging post-Moore computing architectures like quantum and neuromorphic, a reevaluation of current approaches for extreme-scale operating systems and runtime environments is needed.

ROSS is a workshop aimed at identifying looming problems and discussing promising research solutions in the area of runtime and operating systems for extreme-scale supercomputers. Specifically, ROSS focuses on principles and techniques to design, implement, optimize, or operate runtime and operating systems for extreme-scale supercomputers and cloud environments. In addition to typical workshop publications, we encourage novel and possibly immature ideas, provided that they are interesting and on-topic. Well argued position papers are also welcome.

presentations.title: 17th Workshop on Latest Advances in Scalable Algorithms for Large-Scale Heterogeneous Systems (ScalAH'26)
presentations.abstract:
Novel hybrid scalable scientific algorithms are needed with the advent of a variety of novel accelerators, including GPUs, FPGAs, etc., as well as with the growth in size of quantum computing devices, neuromorphic chips, and various AI-specific processors. This myriad of devices requires a unified approach that allows efficient and scalable hybrid approaches combining classical and novel computing paradigms to be implemented at scale.

These extreme-scale heterogeneous systems require these novel scientific algorithms to hide the complexity, hide network and memory latency, have advanced communication, and have no synchronization points where possible. With the advent of AI in the past few years, the need for such scalable mathematical methods and algorithms for such hybrid architectures that are able to handle data and compute-intensive applications at scale becomes even more important.

presentations.title: 2011 Tōhoku–Oki Earthquake and Tsunami: Dynamic Rupture and Acoustic–Gravity Simulations
presentations.abstract: This video visualizes data obtained from large-scale earthquake and tsunami simulations based on a dynamic rupture model of the 2011 Tōhoku–Oki earthquake, a magnitude 9.1 megathrust earthquake in the Japan Trench that caused over 20,000 deaths and $300B in damages. The 3D dynamic rupture simulation (Wong et al., Nature Communications, 2026) computes the seismic wave propagation in the Earth, generating the earthquake-induced seafloor motion that is visualized by the seafloor velocity and seafloor displacement fields in the video. These seafloor motion data are used as an input to a 3D acoustic–gravity simulation that computes the coupled ocean acoustic and tsunami wave propagation, which is visualized by the sea bottom pressure and surface wave height perturbations. The implementation of these earthquake and tsunami models is an integral part of an ongoing effort to develop a digital twin for tsunami early warning in the Japan Trench. This work is an extension of the Cascadia Subduction Zone digital twin that was recognized with the ACM Gordon Bell Prize at SC25 (Henneking et al., SC25 Proceedings, 2025).

presentations.title: 2026 International Workshop on Performance, Portability, and Productivity in HPC (P3HPC)
presentations.abstract:
The Performance, Portability, and Productivity in HPC workshop aims to bring together developers and researchers with an interest in practical solutions, technologies, tools, and methodologies that enable the development of performance-portable applications across a diverse set of current and future high performance computers.

The topic of performance, portability, and productivity focuses on enabling applications and libraries to run across multiple architectures without significant impact on achieved performance and with the goal of maintaining developer productivity. This workshop provides a forum for discussions of successes and failures in tackling the compelling problems that lie at the intersection of performance, portability, and productivity in high performance computing. This area touches on many aspects of HPC/AI software development and the workshop program reflects a wide range of experiences and perspectives, including those of compiler, language and runtime experts; applications developers and performance engineers; and domain scientists.

For more information see: https://p3hpc.org/.

presentations.title: 21st Workshop on Workflows in Support of Large-Scale Science (WORKS26)
presentations.abstract:
Scientific workflows have underpinned some of the most significant discoveries of the past several decades. Workflow management systems (WMS) provide abstraction and automation that enable researchers to easily define sophisticated computational processes, and to then execute them efficiently on parallel and distributed computing systems. As workflows have been adopted by multiple scientific communities, they are becoming more complex and require more sophisticated workflow management capabilities.

This workshop focuses on the many facets of scientific workflow composition, management, sustainability, and application to domain sciences in an increasingly diverse landscape. The workshop covers a broad range of topics in the scientific workflow lifecycle that include: reproducible research with workflows; workflow execution in distributed and heterogeneous environments; application of AI/ML in workflow management; workflow provenance; serverless workflows; exascale computing with workflows; stream-processing, interactive, adaptive and data-driven workflows; workflow scheduling and resource management; workflow fault-tolerance, debugging, performance analysis/modeling; big data and AI workflows, etc.

presentations.title: 2nd Annual Workshop on Large-Scale Quantum-Classical Computing
presentations.abstract:
Quantum computing is advancing rapidly, and its integration with high performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly important for enabling practical hybrid computational workflows. In a growing number of domains, research is progressing toward quantum advantage — with quantum computation already addressing problems that strain exact classical methods and increasingly competing with state-of-the-art approximate approaches. These combined methods offer new opportunities for accelerating progress in scientific areas such as physics, chemistry, materials, and optimization by leveraging quantum computing together with established classical and AI-based techniques.

The 2nd Annual Workshop on Large-Scale Quantum-Classical Computing (LSQCC) brings together recent research on quantum algorithms, system integration techniques, and emerging hybrid workflows that incorporate HPC and AI components where beneficial. The workshop highlights technical challenges, recent developments, and near-term opportunities for effectively combining quantum computing with complementary approaches.

presentations.title: 4th Annual Trillion Parameter Workshop: Building Open AI Infrastructure, Models, and Agentic Systems for Science
presentations.abstract: The landscape of AI for science has shifted dramatically. Beyond building ever-larger models from scratch, the scientific community is increasingly leveraging powerful pre-trained models — adapting them through fine-tuning, domain specialization, and integration into complex AI systems combining reasoning models, knowledge graphs, agentic workflows, and connections to simulators and instruments. These shifts highlight a full stack of interdependent challenges for developers, scientists, and HPC centers, from strategies and infrastructure for sharing data and computing, to frameworks orchestrating multiple models and agents, to methods and tools for ensuring safety, alignment, and rigorous evaluation of scientific reasoning and skills. Progress in any one area both depends upon and accelerates the others. This workshop will highlight advances across this interconnected landscape, emphasizing openness, international collaboration, and community-driven efforts, featuring peer-reviewed papers and invited talks spanning shared infrastructure, open model development, agentic AI systems for science, evaluation and safety, and driving challenge applications.

presentations.title: 5th International Workshop on Cyber Security in High Performance Computing
presentations.abstract: The goal of this workshop is to bring together researchers and practitioners in cybersecurity and HPC. Security in high performance computing (HPC) has traditionally been an “operational” challenge (i.e., restrict access and usage to certified users). Thus, despite significant advances in our understanding and mitigations of vulnerabilities, the cybersecurity research community has been somewhat disconnected from the HPC community. Recent increases in the heterogeneity of both the underlying platforms of HPC and the community of HPC-level users and applications point to an important and growing need for connection and synergy between these two communities.

presentations.title: 6th International Workshop on RESource DISaggregation in High Performance Computing (RESDIS)
presentations.abstract: Disaggregation is an emerging compute paradigm that splits existing monolithic servers into a number of consolidated single-resource pools that communicate over a fast interconnect. This model decouples individual hardware resources and enables the creation of logical compute platforms with flexible and dynamic hardware configurations. The concept of disaggregation is driven by various recent trends in computation. From an application perspective, the increasing importance of data analytics and machine learning workloads brings unprecedented need for memory capacity, which is in stark contrast with the growing imbalance in the peak compute-to-memory capacity ratio of traditional system board-based servers. At the hardware front, the proliferation of heterogeneous, special-purpose computing elements promotes the need for composable platforms, while the increasing maturity of optical interconnects elevates the prospects of distance independence in networking infrastructure. The workshop intends to explore various aspects of resource disaggregation, composability, and their implications for future HPC platforms.

presentations.title: 8th International Workshop on Containers and New Orchestration Paradigms for Isolated Environments in HPC (CANOPIE-HPC)
presentations.abstract: The ongoing revolution enabled via containerization, virtualization, and new orchestration models has dramatically changed how applications and services are delivered and managed across the computing industry. This revolution has established a new ecosystem of tools and techniques with new, flexible and agile approaches, and continues to gain traction in the HPC community. In addition to HPC-optimized container runtimes, technologies like Kubernetes create a new set of opportunities and challenges. While adoption is growing, questions regarding best practices, foundational concepts, tools, and standards remain. Our goal is to promote the adoption of these tools and introspect the impact of this new ecosystem on HPC/AI use cases. This workshop serves as a key venue for presenting late-breaking research, sharing experiences and best practices, and fostering collaboration in this field. Our eighth workshop iteration will continue to emphasize real-world experiences and challenges in adopting and optimizing these new approaches for HPC and AI.

presentations.title: 8th Workshop on Programming and Performance Visualization Tools (ProTools)
presentations.abstract:
Understanding program behavior is critical to overcome the expected architectural and programming complexities, such as limited power budgets, heterogeneity, hierarchical memories, shrinking I/O bandwidths, and performance variability, that arise on modern HPC platforms. To do so, HPC software developers need intuitive support tools for debugging, performance measurement, analysis, and tuning of large-scale HPC applications. Data collected from these tools can be far too large and too complex to be analyzed in a straightforward manner. We therefore need automatic analysis and visualization approaches to help application developers intuitively understand the effects that algorithmic choices have on application correctness or performance.

The ProTools workshop brings together HPC application developers, tool developers, vendors, and researchers from the visualization, performance, and program analysis fields for an exchange of new approaches to assist developers in analyzing, understanding, and optimizing programs for extreme-scale platforms.

presentations.title: A case study on the resource utilisation and queue dynamics of an institutional HPC system
presentations.abstract: HPC systems are often evaluated using aggregate metrics that implicitly assume a uniform user population. Using a year-long trace from an institutional HPC system, spanning 4.2 million jobs and 596 users, we show this assumption fails for demand-concentrated workloads: a small cohort drives most computational demand, energy consumption, and the mismatch between requested and actually-used resources. This concentration produces severe queue unfairness governed by job shape: small, backfill-compatible jobs dispatch instantly regardless of priority, while larger jobs do not, so the users best served by the scheduler are not those with the least demand, but those whose jobs fit available capacity. Counterfactual simulation shows targeted interventions recover most of the achievable benefit: resizing resource requests cuts mean queue wait by 67%, and pacing the heaviest 5% of submitters cuts mean wait by 82%. Both the waste and the queue risk are predictable from submission-time metadata alone, enabling proactive management.

presentations.title: A Cloud Accessible Four-Qubit Electron Spin Quantum Processor in a 300 mm Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Process
presentations.abstract:
We present a cloud accessible electron spin qubit quantum processor manufactured using a 300 mm metal-oxide-semiconductor process. Four single-electron spin qubits form a linear array with controllable nearest-neighbor exchange coupling; the unit cell can be tiled without design modification, providing a direct path to larger processors. The system is installed at the UK's National Quantum Computing Centre, where automated calibration maintains operation with minimal human input and users submit circuits through industry-standard frameworks including Qiskit and Cirq. This deployment is a prototype for future HPC integration.

Single-qubit gates are driven by magnetic resonance; two-qubit CPhase gates use electrically modulated exchange coupling. Single-shot readout via a parallel array of charge sensors achieves fidelities above 99% in under 10 µs and supports mid-circuit measurement.

We demonstrate two applications: a variational quantum eigensolver determining the equilibrium bond length of molecular hydrogen, and stabilizer measurements demonstrating the building block of quantum error correction.

presentations.title: A community developed simulator for the Tenstorrent Tensix architecture
presentations.abstract:
Tenstorrent's RISC-V based accelerators have become popular not only for AI and ML, but also as vehicles for exploring HPC workloads more generally. Whilst Tenstorrent document their Tensix architecture in detail and develop their software stack openly, running code has historically required a physical card, and their recently released simulator targets hardware equivalence rather than introspection. In this paper we present a community developed simulator for the Tensix architecture, supporting both the Wormhole and Blackhole generations and integrating seamlessly with the TT-Metal software stack.

Constructed entirely from publicly available documentation, open source software and measurements on physical hardware, it is written in pure Python for readability and ease of modification. An opt-in, provenance-tracked cost model adds timing fidelity incrementally, and typed event streams, per-component tracing and timeline export enable programmers to identify and diagnose performance bottlenecks that the hardware itself hides.

presentations.title: A Comparative Study of Energy Scaling Behavior for AI Training: Wafer or Die Scale
presentations.abstract:
Datacenter electricity consumption is projected to grow rapidly, driven primarily by AI. Meeting this demand sustainably requires understanding how training energy scales with model size, and whether this holds across increasingly diverse hardware, particularly for wafer-scale dataflow accelerators like the Cerebras WSE series, which integrate compute and memory on a single wafer, unlike die-scale GPUs.
We compare a Cerebras WSE-2 and an NVIDIA GH200 as representative wafer- and die-scale accelerators, using a matched sweep of seven CNN and Vision Transformer architectures with batch sizes from 2 to 512 to cross-validate energy models. We find distinct energy-scaling behavior between the two: the WSE-2's dataflow execution makes scaling more predictable, while its high baseline power and lack of workload-controlled power management increase sensitivity to model size and batch size.

presentations.title: A Deployment-Aware Multi-Objective Hyper-Parameter Optimization Framework for Machine Learning
presentations.abstract: State-of-the-art ML models deliver unprecedented performance across computer vision, natural language processing, and multi-modal tasks. These improvements have been driven by significantly growing computational costs, memory footprint, and consequently, energy consumption. Several model compression techniques and hyperparameter optimization strategies have been proposed to address these increases. Most of these approaches, however, target the training phase and often overlook the deployment context and the model usage. We propose a general-purpose framework for ML model optimization, focused on deployment and inference, to assist practitioners by quantifying trade-offs between model accuracy, power consumption, and other deployment-relevant metrics such as latency and memory usage. The proposed system is validated in three use cases: deploying a computer vision model on a resource-constrained edge device, optimizing LLM serving on data center-grade hardware, and running a large-scale benchmark on the Frontier HPC system. The system successfully identifies optimal configurations, demonstrating its versatility and applicability to practical scenarios.

presentations.title: A Distributed HPC/AI Services Ecosystem for the Genesis Mission Platform
presentations.abstract: Modern HPC and AI applications require capabilities deployed, composed, and accessed on demand. However, reusable services must coordinate heterogeneous resources, lifecycles, and low-latency data exchange. We present a distributed service ecosystem for the American Science Cloud (AmSC) of the Genesis Mission, providing mechanisms for deploying, composing, and accessing HPC/AI capabilities. Our contribution is a service-building ecosystem for HPC/AI workflows that separates service management, workflow execution, and data exchange, enabling capabilities to be composed without application-specific integration. We demonstrate the approach through an asynchronous OpenFOAM optimization workflow, showing how HPC/AI capabilities become reusable services across AmSC resources.

presentations.title: A Distributed Mixed-Precision N-Body Engine: Scaling Behavior and the Precision Limits of a Direct-Summation Kernel
presentations.abstract: We report a distributed direct-summation N-body engine used to study two coupled limits: where the single collective per step begins to limit strong scaling, and where reduced-precision arithmetic begins to corrupt the physics. At fixed N = 32768 on one 96-core node, the kernel scales almost ideally to 16 ranks and reaches 57× speedup at 96. In-core phase timers show that the loss beyond 16 ranks comes from one straggling rank, whose peers wait at the collective, rather than from data transfer, which stays under 1% of a step. A precision ladder from FP64 down to FP8 shows that the accumulator, not the individual force terms, sets the error floor: rounding the running sum costs 92×–125× more force error than rounding the terms alone.

presentations.title: A Distributed Particle-Based Volume Rendering Framework for Fugaku and Beyond
presentations.abstract: Modern flagship HPC systems increasingly rely on GPU-accelerated architectures. While GPUs accelerate simulations, CPU resources may remain available, providing an opportunity for in-situ processing and visualization. This community talk presents an ongoing effort to develop a distributed Particle-Based Volume Rendering (PBVR) framework that exploits this CPU/GPU division. Volumetric fields are converted in situ into compact visualization particles using CPUs on the HPC system, while interactive rendering is performed on a GPU-equipped remote client. We evaluate the approach on Fugaku using OpenFOAM and demonstrate particle generation across up to 2,304 compute nodes (110,592 CPU cores). For a separate 432 x 432 x 432 grid measurement at 576 MPI ranks, PBVR particle files were 98.1% smaller than the uncompressed logical Ux payload over 11 steps. We discuss the implementation, initial performance results, and potential applicability to future heterogeneous HPC systems such as FugakuNEXT.

presentations.title: A Distribution-Function GNN Surrogate for Lattice Boltzmann Flows: Adaptive Coarsening Is Where the Speedup Comes From
presentations.abstract: We evaluate a graph-network surrogate for two-dimensional lattice Boltzmann(LBM) flows on both accuracy and wall-clock time per case. The model predicts the increment of the velocity distribution function and reconstructs velocity and density from the LBM definitions; a 49-step rollout (9800 solver steps) completes without diverging. Adding the distribution function to the inputs cuts the velocity error by 20-46%. Static coarsening by variable-radius Poisson-disk selection from geometry alone cuts the node count 22.6-fold while accuracy on the evaluation grid stays on par with the uniform mesh, and cuts the time per case tenfold to 8.9 times faster than the reference solver. On the uniform mesh it is only on par, so the advantage appears solely under coarsening. Against a coarse-grid solver at the same obstacle Reynolds number the surrogate offers robustness, not speed: it returns a solution on all 48 cases, the solver on 42.

presentations.title: A First Look at Conventional Attacks on Scientific Applications
presentations.abstract: How vulnerable are scientific applications to conventional attacks mounted by intentionally manipulating their input? Prior work largely leaves this question unanswered. We begin to answer it by carefully adapting fuzzing and security-focused bug triage to characterize vulnerabilities in scientific codebases. Our process discovers almost 1000 unique crashes (likely distinct bugs) across Enzo, GROMACS, Laghos, and LAMMPS (about 3 million lines of code). Per application, an average of 7.3% of them represent easily exploitable vulnerabilities according to heuristic security analysis. Additionally, 26% of all bugs (51% for GROMACS) are exploitable heap memory safety issues. Cumulatively, we find over 110 distinct vulnerabilities that may permit arbitrary code execution (ACE). Manual inspection confirms the existence of exploitable bugs. Using a coding agent, we generate 59 reproducible proof-of-concept ACE exploits. Our results suggest untrusted data could have catastrophic effects on artifact integrity, creating real risk as computational scientific results drive increasingly consequential societal decisions.

presentations.title: A Free Online Textbook and Interactive Exercises for Introducing Parallel Computing
presentations.abstract:
We present the parallel and distributed computing
(PDC) content of Dive into Systems, a free, online textbook
that covers a broad range of computer systems topics. Dive
into Systems introduces many topics in the TCPP curriculum
including two chapters devoted to parallel computing. Our
textbook is written assuming only a CS1 background of the
reader, and it is designed to be used as a primary textbook for a
range of courses. As a supplement to our textbook, we developed
online interactive learning resources that provide practice to
students learning its content. These resources include interactive
end-of-chapter exercises and novel Ask me Another components,
including four specific to PDC. Ask me Another components
generate new instances of their question type, allowing a user
to generate a virtually infinite number of practice questions. We
also present results of a multi-institutional study that piloted one
of our PDC Ask me Another components.

presentations.title: A Fused Computation-Communication Collective for Irregular Distributed-Memory Applications
presentations.abstract:
Irregular distributed-memory applications often perform local computation and memory operations around a many-to-many communication exchange. We introduce AllScatterApply (ASAP), a fused collective communication primitive for this pattern. ASAP overlaps local and remote operations at fine granularity, scales to 32,000 CPU cores on NERSC Perlmutter, and delivers up to 74× speedup over point-to-point implementations built on the same one-sided runtime library.

We evaluate ASAP on genomic k-mer counting (KC) and connected components (CC). For KC, ASAP achieves 2×–5× speedup over bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) baselines and matches the performance of a hand-tuned asynchronous algorithm. For CC, ASAP is 1.8× faster than both optimized BSP and asynchronous baselines. By avoiding expensive graph partitioning, ASAP also achieves 8.8× faster end-to-end performance than a dedicated asynchronous graph-processing system.

presentations.title: A GPU-Accelerated Blocked Adaptive Randomized Range Finder Based on an Implicit Householder QR Decomposition
presentations.abstract: Low-rank methods can reduce the memory and computational requirements of deep neural network training in approaches such as GaLore. Randomized range finders offer an attractive alternative to singular value decompositions, particularly when the required rank is determined adaptively from a prescribed approximation tolerance. We introduce a blocked adaptive randomized range finder based on an implicit Householder QR decomposition and an optimized hybrid CPU--GPU implementation. The proposed method avoids explicit reorthogonalization. Numerical experiments show that it preserves orthogonality and approximation accuracy in regimes where block Gram--Schmidt without reorthogonalization becomes unstable. The blocked formulation exposes matrix--matrix operations and enables overlap of CPU panel factorization with GPU updates. On an NVIDIA GH200, the overlapped implementation reduces the runtime for the largest tested matrix from 9.91s on the CPU to 0.407s. The method provides a stable and efficient building block for low-rank approximation on heterogeneous systems with applications in computational science and engineering.

presentations.title: A GPU-Friendly SSOR Preconditioner Based on an Approximate Inverse of Triangular Matrices
presentations.abstract: We develop a GPU-friendly variant of the symmetric successive over-relaxation (SSOR) preconditioner for efficient execution of the preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) method on GPUs. To avoid the forward and backward substitutions required by the original SSOR preconditioner, which constitute a major bottleneck on GPUs, we incorporate an approximate inverse of a triangular matrix appearing in the SSOR preconditioner, with a dropping strategy to reduce the cost of applying it. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed SSOR variant against existing parallel SSOR variants on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. The proposed variant substantially reduces the cost of applying the preconditioner by replacing the forward and backward substitutions with SpMVs, while largely preserving the convergence improvement of SSOR. Consequently, despite the additional cost of constructing the approximate inverse, the total PCG execution time is reduced for most of the test matrices, demonstrating that the proposed approach provides an effective GPU-friendly SSOR variant.

presentations.title: A Heuristic Based Cache Miss Classifier
presentations.abstract: Cache misses can limit HPC applications, yet conventional profilers only identify where misses occur and not their root cause. Capacity pressure and cache-set conflicts often produce similar hotspots but generally require different optimizations. Conventional classification uses a fully associative shadow cache but introduces additional state and lookup work. We present an explainable classifier that combines five complementary signals. The signals are computed over bounded counter periods and combined on a signed capacity-conflict scale. The method uses bounded counters and a compact address-history table while diagnosing root causes. Across 12 program configurations and 48 data-object scopes, the classifier agreed in every tested case with the more frequent capacity or conflict label among the independently generated ground-truth misses in that scope. On the Himeno benchmark, CMSA required 2.32 times the runtime of baseline Cachegrind. These results demonstrate the potential of bounded signals for explainable cache diagnoses without shadow-cache labels during prediction.

presentations.title: A Highly Optimized Double-Word Arithmetic Implementation using Versal DSPs
presentations.abstract:
Scientific applications often require high-precision floating-point operations.
Modern FPGAs provide dedicated hardware for single-precision (FP32) multiply-accumulate operations, but double-precision (FP64) still requires costly implementations using lookup tables (LUTs).
As an alternative to FP64, double-word arithmetic can nearly double the precision of FP32 using only single-precision instructions.
In double-word arithmetic, a number is represented as a pair of FP32 values, which is carefully normalized so that its two components never overlap.

This work presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first implementation of double-word arithmetic on FPGAs. We develop both an HLS-based and a hand-optimized implementation.
Our hand-optimized implementation fully exploits the functionality available in the DSP blocks, requiring zero LUTs or flip-flops for multiplication and almost no LUTs or flip-flops for addition.

We evaluate our double-word implementation by comparing to HLS and vendor provided IP, then demonstrate it to be a viable alternative to FP64 on modern FPGA.

presentations.title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Framework for Solving Computational Fluid Dynamics and Nuclear Physics Equations Using Quantum Singular Value Decomposition and Transformation
presentations.abstract: Quantum computing offers a great promise to significantly reduce the computational cost of solving multidimensional partial differential equations (PDEs). However, existing quantum linear solvers, such as the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd (HHL) algorithm, exhibit limited scalability, prolonged execution times, and low accuracy. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical framework comprising two quantum PDE solvers based on quantum singular value decomposition (QSVD) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). The proposed methodology is validated on PDEs from computational fluid dynamics and nuclear engineering — potential flow past a 2D cylinder and a Joukowsky airfoil, and the neutron transport equation (NTE) — using noise-free and noisy simulators and hardware emulators from IBM-Quantum. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed methods.

presentations.title: A JIT framework for Implicit GEMM and FlashAttention Micro-Kernels in RISC-V
presentations.abstract: The RISC-V Vector extension (RVV) is a credible CPU deep-learning inference target, but its software stack lags the silicon: optimized kernels are scarce, and prior co-design studies of RVV convolution use compile-time intrinsic kernels built on the memory-hungry im2col+GEMM formulation, evaluated almost entirely in simulation. We present a lightweight just-in-time (JIT) framework that generates register-blocked, vector-length-agnostic Implicit GEMM micro-kernels for RVV at runtime, once the true vector length and layer shape are known, and integrates them into Intel oneDNN, eliminating the im2col buffer. We characterize six vector widths (VLEN 128-8192 bits) in cycle-accurate gem5 and validate on a BananaPi-F3 board, then extend the infrastructure to JIT FlashAttention. Implicit GEMM reaches 3.28x over scalar in gem5 and 3.08x on silicon; for FlashAttention, runtime generation is fastest up to VLEN=512, the range of every shipping RVV core. An autotuner separates portable tuning knobs (tile height MR) from ISA-specific ones (LMUL, NR).

presentations.title: A Linear-Scaling, Sparse Matrix Electronic Structure Solver on the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine
presentations.abstract: We present a linear-scaling electronic structure solver for the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE), a data-flow architecture integrating more than 900,000 processors on a single silicon wafer. We combine a novel, WSE-optimized sparse-matrix squaring kernel with a sparse, recursive Fermi-operator expansion to construct the density matrix on this massively parallel architecture. Our approach solves the quantum-mechanical eigenvalue problem for one self-consistent-field iteration with a computational complexity that is linear in the number of atoms. For a bulk water system described at the density-functional tight-binding level of theory, we achieve a 31x speedup for a single density-matrix solve relative to a single-GPU reference calculation running on an NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper superchip.

presentations.title: A Locality-Aware Execution Model for Distributed Graph Algorithms using NWGraph and HPX
presentations.abstract:
Graph processing at scale presents many challenges, including the irregular structure of graphs, the latency-bound nature of graph algorithms, and the overhead associated with distributed execution. While existing frameworks such as Spark GraphX and the Parallel Boost Graph Library (PBGL) have introduced abstractions for distributed graph processing, they continue to struggle with inherent issues like load imbalance and synchronization overhead.
In this work, we present a distributed library prototype and a distributed implementation of three key graph algorithms-Breadth-First Search (BFS), PageRank, and Triangle Counting, using C++ mechanisms from the NWGraph library and leveraging HPX's distributed containers and asynchronous constructs.
We evaluate our HPX-based implementations against GraphX and PBGL, showing that a high-performance runtime such as HPX enables the construction of algorithms that significantly outperform conventional frameworks by exploiting asynchronous execution, latency hiding, and fine-grained parallelism in shared memory.

presentations.title: A Model‑Agnostic Orchestration Engine for Multi‑Stage High-Performance Scientific Workflows
presentations.abstract: Scientific workflows increasingly require the integration of independently developed models and heterogeneous data sources. We present a model-agnostic orchestration engine that represents both data sources and simulation models as producers of named variables. Given a requested target, the engine recursively resolves variable dependencies, derives an executable workflow, manages intermediate products through a shared data layer, and dispatches computation through configurable execution backends. We demonstrate the approach using an asteroid-impact wildfire scenario in which a requested fire-spread product automatically resolves the data required to execute WRF-SFIRE on high-performance computing resources. The prototype demonstrates target-driven workflow generation, dependency resolution, provenance tracking, and intermediate-product reuse, providing a foundation for multi-stage cascading-hazard workflows.

presentations.title: A Multi-Layer Workflow for Diagnosing Performance Portability in RAJA Applications
presentations.abstract: Performance-portable frameworks like RAJA enable a single source to run on diverse HPC architectures, but productivity relies on the compiler removing abstraction overhead. When it does not, runtime data show where performance diverges, but not why. We present a multi-layer workflow that diagnoses abstraction-induced divergence by combining runtime measurements with compiler-visible evidence, including GPU resource usage, optimization remarks, and LLVM IR metrics. We apply this workflow to 55 RAJA Performance Suite kernels using HIP and OpenMP backends, three optimization levels, and three problem sizes (1,980 configurations). For selected kernels, the workflow distinguishes optimization-agnostic from optimization-sensitive behavior and links performance losses to the compiler's excessive loop unrolling, register pressure, reduced occupancy, scratch spills, and control-flow complexity. These diagnostics guide source changes that restore native-level performance for four kernels and an optimization-specific transformation that eliminates compiler-induced register pressure in a fifth, providing guidance for understanding and improving performance portability beyond runtime analysis.

presentations.title: A Multi-Phase GPU Pipeline for Biconnected Components
presentations.abstract: Graph biconnectivity is a fundamental primitive for structural analysis, but classical algorithms rely on depth-first search, which is inherently sequential and does not scale to GPUs. We present a multi-phase, GPU-resident pipeline for computing biconnected components on large-scale undirected graphs. Our pipeline first removes 1-core vertices through iterative peeling, then grows depth-capped breadth-first search trees from multiple random roots in parallel, ensuring each vertex joins exactly one tree. We resolve each tree's non-tree edges into local biconnected components, then merge components across tree boundaries using the remaining cross-tree edges. We evaluate our approach on 17 real-world networks on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Our approach substantially outperforms earlier GPU and CPU baselines, including WK-17, WK-18, and CPU-based FAST-BCC, and achieves an average speedup of 2.49x over FAST-BCC-Filter, the current state-of-the-art GPU approach.

presentations.title: A Multi-Task Benchmark for Time Series Foundation Models on R&E Backbone Telemetry
presentations.abstract: Research and Education (R&E) backbone networks support the transfer of petabyte-scale scientific data under stringent timing constraints. However, their operational monitoring remains predominantly reactive, relying on threshold-based alerts and visualization dashboards that provide. limited predictive capabilities and cannot anticipate congestion or anomalous events hours in advance. Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), large neural networks pre-trained on billions of diverse time series, offer a promising route to predictive monitoring, but their adaptation behavior on live R&E backbone telemetry remains poorly characterized. We present a systematic multi-task benchmark of five TSFMs (TimesFM, Moirai, Chronos, PatchTST, and TTM/Granite) across four adaptation strategies and four auto-labeled operational tasks (48-hour utilization trajectory, threshold exceedance detection, peak-timing estimation, and traffic asymmetry forecasting), using 26 months of SNMP telemetry from the AmLight backbone with no human annotation. Our results show that TSFM performance is task-structured: zero-shot models outperform classical baselines on trajectory and timing tasks, where broad pre-training captures diurnal patterns, but do not surpass classical methods on tasks that reward high autocorrelation exploitation. Standard fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting in some architectures. Linear-probe fine-tuning avoids forgetting but introduces a subtler failure: auto-labels designed for one task do not transfer to others, so performance improves only where the label aligns with the target. This label-task mismatch is the central failure mode we identify and characterize. The unifying solution is a frozen backbone with a small, task-specific MLP head trained on the correct auto-label for each objective. With at most 500 auto-labeled windows, this approach surpasses all fine-tuned models on exceedance detection and matches fine-tuning on peak-timing estimation. These results establish that pre-trained TSFM backbones already encode operationally relevant network representations, and that a frozen backbone with a lightweight task head can be a viable foundation for predictive operations on R&E networks.

presentations.title: A Naive D3Q27 Lattice Boltzmann Implementation on the Cerebras CS-3: Comparison with GPUs
presentations.abstract:
The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) is a stencil-based CFD method widely used across engineering fields, in which the domain is divided into a lattice, each element is computed independently, and data is exchanged with adjacent elements. Thus, it is expected to map well onto the Cerebras CS-3, which features large distributed on-chip memory and high-bandwidth inter-PE communication.

In this work, we naively implement a three-dimensional LBM (D3Q27 Model) on the CS-3 by assigning a 1x1xn lattice to each processing element (PE). To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first attempt made to implement 3-D LBM and measure its performance.

On the largest domain, the CS-3 achieves 83.74 GLUPS — a 17.4× and 8.5× speedup over the NVIDIA A100 and GH200 — while sustaining a parallel efficiency of 1.0 under weak scaling. These results indicate that wafer-scale computing can serve as a promising platform for memory-bound stencil computations.

presentations.title: A Next Generation Multi-Terabit/sec Campus and Global Network System for Data Intensive Sciences: The Global Network Advancement Group Data Intensive Science and AutoGOLE/SENSE Working Groups
presentations.abstract:
The Global Network Advancement Group (GNA‑G), through its Data‑Intensive Sciences (DIS) and SENSE/AutoGOLE Working Groups, is developing a next‑generation, multi‑terabit/sec global system to support the rapidly escalating demands of data‑intensive science. Scientific programs such as the LHC, Rubin Observatory LSST, SKA, Cryo‑EM, genomics, and distributed AI/ML workflows now generate unprecedented data volumes, requiring coordinated global infrastructure capable of predictable, high‑throughput, multi‑domain operation.
This system integrates programmable networks (P4, SRv6, PolKA, BGP‑CT), multi‑domain orchestration (SENSE/AutoGOLE), real‑time telemetry (INT, perfSONAR, ALTO, GradientGraph), ML‑driven intelligence (NetPredict, Hecate, GradientGraph), high‑throughput end systems (400G–800G DTNs, GPU nodes), and regional caches/data lakes into a unified, composable architecture. It is validated through global testbeds such as GP4L, FABRIC, NRP, and GRP, and deployed across multi‑Tbps optical infrastructures including APOnet, AmLight, Rednesp/RNP, ESnet, Internet2, GEANT, and StarLight.
At SC25, NRE‑125 and 16 partner NREs demo nstrated this architecture at scale, showcasing multi‑domain orchestration, programmable data planes, AI‑driven optimization, Digital Twin simulation, and multi‑Tbps global data movement. The system supports a progressive deployment model spanning R&D → advanced production → full production, ensuring coexistence with general R&E traffic while enabling the next decade of scientific discovery.
This has been enabled by strong industry support and collaboration, most notably from Ciena, Supermicro, Arista, Dell and Juniper.
This paper presents an overview of the architecture, mechanisms, development trajectory, operational model, and SC25 demonstration results of the GNA-G next‑generation global system, many of the development threads supporting its progressive implementation, and use cases in several disciplines of data intensive science.

presentations.title: A Performance-Portable GPU-Accelerated Solution for Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh Method using Cabana and FFTX
presentations.abstract: One approach to the development of high-performance computing applications is based on libraries that implement algorithmic motifs in a portable, performant and concise fashion. We develop a GPU-accelerated algorithm for Method of Local Corrections, a particle-particle particle-mesh method for simulating incompressible flow in 3D, using such motif libraries. The algorithm comprises of structured grid calculations, local particle interactions, and free-space convolution. We use two motif libraries: Cabana, a motif library for particles, built on top of Kokkos; and FFTX for fast Fourier Transform, that uses the SPIRAL code generation system. By using motif libraries, we obtain a concise and portable implementation (2K lines of code). We compare the measured performance to that predicted by the roofline model and obtain 52\%-86\% on NVIDIA A100, 42\%-61\% on NVIDIA H100, 22\%-42\% on AMD MI100, and 17\%-38\% on AMD MI300A.

presentations.title: A Physics-Informed AI Architecture for One-Dimensional Turbulence Modeling
presentations.abstract: One-dimensional turbulence (ODT) represents turbulent flow on a one-dimensional domain through continuous molecular diffusion and stochastic triplet-map eddy events. This work examines what a deterministic machine-learning surrogate can learn from such a stochastic system. Fourier neural operators trained on individual ODT realizations converge toward ensemble-mean dynamics because future eddy events cannot be inferred uniquely from the instantaneous flow state. Training directly on ensemble averages confirms accurate interpolation across unseen jet velocities and widths, with more than 300× speedup relative to generating the corresponding ensembles. We therefore propose a hybrid physics-informed architecture that mirrors the ODT solver: a neural operator advances the continuous diffusion dynamics, while stochastic triplet-map events are applied explicitly. Using the same eddy sequence, the hybrid model reconstructs individual realizations with a final relative L2 error of 0.028 and approximately 9× faster rollout than the original solver. This decomposition provides a practical framework for learning stochastic turbulence models.

presentations.title: A Portuguese-Language Ecosystem for HPC Education: Design, Formative Development, and Evidence of Adoption
presentations.abstract: This paper presents a Portuguese-language educational ecosystem designed to support the progressive teaching of high-performance computing (HPC). Developed through an independent, author-led initiative, the ecosystem combines two textbooks with reproducible C programs using MPI, OpenMP, and OpenACC, exercises, instructor slides, Colab-compatible laboratory notebooks, interactive learning tools, and training and outreach activities. Its development followed an incremental process in which materials initially used in courses, bootcamps, and programming competitions were reorganized, tested on real systems, and refined through observations and feedback from authentic educational contexts. A preliminary analytical evaluation examines the ecosystem in terms of conceptual alignment, progressive complexity, reproducibility, adoptability, and authentic use. The results indicate that its components form a coherent and reproducible educational pathway covering distributed-memory, shared-memory, and accelerator programming. Although the available evidence supports claims of adoption and sustained use, controlled studies are still required to determine the ecosystem's effects on student learning.

presentations.title: A Probability-Based Static Analysis to Lower Overhead in Floating-Point Exception Detection in NVIDIA GPUs
presentations.abstract: Floating-point exceptions, including NaN, infinity, and division by zero, present significant challenges to GPU-accelerated programs. These exceptions can silently propagate in the programs, leading to inaccurate results that might go unnoticed. Existing tools like FPChecker and GPU-FPX detect these exceptions dynamically but impose significant run-time overhead, making them impractical for large-scale GPU applications. We propose a static analysis framework that allows selective instrumentation of only high-risk floating-point instructions in GPU programs. We achieve this selective instrumentation in two ways: first, by analyzing SASS files on a per-instruction basis, comparing IEEE 754 bit pattern exception probabilities with thresholds; second, by comparing propagated exception probabilities within basic blocks while traversing the data flow graphs.
