We evaluate our framework by testing 19 programs across four CUDA benchmark suites and demonstrate that our approach can eliminate certain checks with at least 90% exception detection coverage.

presentations.title: A Production Compiler Implementation of Hardware Transactional Memory for OpenMP
presentations.abstract: Hardware Transactional Memory (HTM) has long been proposed as an alternative to lock-based synchronization, yet no production-quality compiler support for HTM exists in OpenMP. Several OpenMP extensions have been proposed to expose HTM to programmers, but setbacks in commercial hardware — most notably the security-related disabling of Intel TSX — led much of the community to abandon the effort. In this paper, we show that HTM support can be implemented with modest engineering effort in Clang/LLVM, a widely used production compiler. We adopt a previously proposed OpenMP transaction construct with a single max_retries clause and semantics mirroring the existing critical construct. We detail non-trivial challenges encountered during its implementation in LLVM 23, including two previously unreported correctness pitfalls: one in the transactional fallback mechanism and another in statement emission along transaction control-flow paths. Evaluation on an Intel Xeon shows that OpenHTM outperforms the standard critical construct by up to 1.97×.

presentations.title: A Reflection on a Decade of Grassroots HPC: From Repurposing Decommissioned Racks to Building a Continent-Wide Movement
A Scalable and Sustainable Online Environment for HPC Education: Integrating projectEUREKA! with Local Kubernetes Infrastructure
presentations.abstract: Academic institutions need scalable approaches for providing students and faculty access to high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence without requiring infrastructure expertise. This paper presents an online environment built on the CAMSA cluster at Texas A&M University–San Antonio using K3s, KubeVirt, Ansible automation, and projectEUREKA! to provide browser-based access to local computational resources. Standardized application environments and automated provisioning reduce repetitive configuration and infrastructure-management burdens for learners, instructors, and support staff. Traditional HPC resources remain available alongside Kubernetes, allowing backend complexity to be introduced progressively when appropriate. The approach is evaluated through deployment reproducibility and access-complexity analysis, comparing the skills, dependencies, and actions required to reach a functional computing environment. The resulting architecture provides a transferable, sustainable model for institutions using HPC to support education and training without making HPC expertise itself the educational objective.

presentations.title: A Side-Channel Methodology for DL Model Recovery Using Power Traces
presentations.abstract: Deep learning architecture represents proprietary intellectual property and serves as a basis for model extraction and adversarial attack techniques. By analyzing only the total GPU power consumption, sampled every 20ms via standard telemetry during inference, without access to weights, inputs, activations, or the computational graph, we can reconstruct the sequence of layer types executed. Our methodology involves segmenting the power trace, matching each segment against a library of per-layer power templates using k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), and refining the classification with a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that encodes typical layer transition patterns with a Viterbi decoder. Evaluations across 21 models and 8-layer classes reveal an average layer-type sequence recovery accuracy of 60.1%, reaching up to 92% for some models.

presentations.title: A Single Pane of Glass for AI Supercomputing: Interoperable Access Portals Worldwide
presentations.abstract: Providing simplified access to distributed HPC, AI, and cloud resources is a global challenge. Driven by major investments and user demand for a single pane of glass, the need for interoperable resource portals is clear—yet implementations that work across institutional and national boundaries remain hard. Following a well-received ISC 2026 BoF, this session broadens the conversation to operators of federated research infrastructures across Europe, the U.S., and Asia-Pacific, sharing experiences, challenges overcome, and lessons learned. Through lightning updates, live polling, and moderated discussion, attendees exchange practical approaches to federated identity, allocation, accounting, and site autonomy versus federated consistency.

presentations.title: A Study In High Performance Portability Through Layered Abstractions
presentations.abstract:
In the past year NVIDA's CUDA programming model has grown to include several language extensions and DSLs, most notably with the addition of CUDA Tile, a tile-based parallel programming abstraction. We implemented CUDA Tile not just as a set of language features but as a series of compiler stages based around MLIR, allowing for much richer and more sophisticated code generation.

The effectiveness of this deeper compiler stack and the interaction between thread-level and tile-level parallelism quite honestly took us by surprise, and has provided remarkable insights into the mechanisms by which retargetable parallel abstractions provide excellent performance with a fraction the amount of code, requiring only auto-tuning with no code modification. NVIDIA's accelerated maths libraries are being converted to use CUDA Tile as a result.

We will share these insights and our analysis in this talk, along with additional conclusions from an investigation into how AI coding agents both benefit from and are impeded by Tile- and Thread-level abstractions when optimizing code.

presentations.title: A Study of 4D Julia Sets: Iterations of Z = Z2 + K in the Quaternions
presentations.abstract:
Created in 2005, this work is an exploration of quaternion Julia sets. Quaternions are a four-dimensional number system.

Real numbers: 1 dimension — ( a )
Complex numbers: 2 dimensions — a + bia + bia + bi
Quaternions: 4 dimensions — a + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dk

A quaternion Julia set is the set of starting points ( (a, b, c, d) ) whose iterates remain bounded (they do not escape to infinity). Complex Julia sets typically appear as curves or fractal lines in the plane. Quaternion Julia sets live in four dimensions; the slices we can see often appear as evolving 3D solids. This animation explores those solids as the parameters that generate the set are changed. Motion through the 4D parameter space is created with Hermite splines connecting successive 4D target values. For much of the work, new targets are set every four seconds, producing a slow largo pace of about 60 beats per minute.

Credits

Animation: Dan Sandin
Algorithms: John Hart, Yumei Dang
Programming: Dan Sandin, Shalini Venkataraman
Visionary Leadership: Tom DeFanti
Mathematical Leadership: Louis Kauffman
Music Composition and Performance: Stephan Vankov

Produced at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, UIC, and Calit2, UCSD

presentations.title: A Tale of Two Teams: Scientists Versus the Multi-Agent System
presentations.abstract: We introduce a multi-agent cosmology system designed to access and analyze the largest cosmological simulations in the world. The system is designed as an interactive, end-to-end analysis suite with the goal of accelerating and streamlining complex analysis of cosmological simulations. Instead of benchmarking, in this work we compare the workflow of a real scientific team, reflecting a typical academic researcher group, to one scientist operating the MACosmo system. Both the scientific team and the agentic team found meaningful new information: the agentic system team isolated a distinct population of cool-core clusters residing in dynamically disturbed halos that a dark-matter-only classification would misclassify, while the scientific team derived new observables that aid robust classification through observational data. This work suggests that carefully designed multi-agent systems, used as collaborators, can accelerate and broaden the analysis of cosmological simulations while reaching conclusions that supplement an expert team.

presentations.title: A Taxonomy of Application Properties for Mixed-Precision Autotuning
presentations.abstract:
Modern HPC platforms increasingly rely on reduced-precision hardware for performance and energy efficiency, but many scientific applications still default to FP64. Although parts of these applications may tolerate lower precision, identifying safe and profitable precision reductions remains difficult. Tool-based mixed-precision autotuners help automate this task, yet their success varies widely across applications. Existing work focuses mainly on autotuning tools rather than application suitability.

We present a completed application-centric study of the properties that make mixed-precision autotuning feasible, costly, fragile, or beneficial. Our novel contribution is a taxonomy that organizes these properties into structural, behavioral, numerical/domain, and performance/architectural categories, maps them to autotuning workflow costs, and expresses them as decision gates for readiness assessment.

In the poster session, we will present the framework using visual summaries and examples to discuss tool assumptions, benchmark design, and practical adoption.

presentations.title: A Threat Model for Sensitive-Data Workloads on Multi-Tenant AI Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: Sensitive-data research increasingly requires the GPU scale of national AI supercomputers, yet the governed multi-tenant handling routine in cloud environments has not been established in supercomputing. Extending a Trusted Research Environment (TRE), or Secure Data Environment (SDE), onto such a system distributes security responsibility across three parties---a capacity owner, an infrastructure provider, and a TRE/SDE operator that governs data on infrastructure it neither owns nor operates. We present a threat model for this setting, expressed as attack trees and grounded in FRIDGE, a satellite-TRE architecture deployed as multi-tenant Kubernetes on two bare-metal national systems. It covers three adversaries---a privileged host operator, a malicious co-tenant, and a rogue researcher---and the supercomputing-specific attack surfaces conventional TRE work omits, mapping each attack path to a mitigation and its owning party. Underpinning the design is portable governance across independently-operated TRE/SDE platforms. This is work in progress.

presentations.title: A Tool Infrastructure for Runtime Correctness Checking of Device-Initiated Multi-GPU Communication
A Tutorial for Kokkos: Performance Portability for C++ Applications and Libraries
presentations.abstract: This SC26 tutorial on Kokkos — an HPC, performance portability, open source, C++ library — targets a beginner audience who wants to write efficient code for CPU and GPU hardware, while maintaining only one code base. The course consists of lectures and hands-on exercises, covering the fundamental aspects of the Kokkos library, including parallel construct functions and memory management classes. The materials come from the official, open source Kokkos tutorial, which is freely accessible online. This is a full-day tutorial.

presentations.title: A Unified Semantic Interface Specification for Parallel Programming Tools
presentations.abstract: The growing number of parallel programming models (PPMs) has led to an ecosystem of tools for performance analysis, optimization, and correctness checking. These tools typically embed PPM-specific semantics into their implementations, creating tight coupling that hinders extensibility, maintainability, and semantic consistency across tools. This paper introduces a Unified Semantic Interface Specification (USIS) that decouples PPM semantics from tool implementations and generalizes a proposed MPI interface format. USIS provides deeper semantic coverage, including GPU semantics and an operational data-flow and synchronization layer that enables reasoning about procedures without prior PPM-specific knowledge. USIS is instantiated for MPI, OpenSHMEM, NCCL, and NVSHMEM, with a workflow combining vendor artifacts and curated files to generate the specifications. The resulting descriptions are integrated into two independently developed tools, the SPMD IR project and MUST, replacing their separate PPM-specific semantic representations with a shared specification. The paper identifies aspects that remain inherently coupled to PPMs or tools.

presentations.title: A Viskores-Enhanced Vision Transformer Framework for MRI-Based Cancer Image Classification on Frontier
presentations.abstract: High performance computing (HPC) enables workflows that integrate scientific visualization and artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific discovery. This work investigates the integration of Viskores, a performance-portable visualization framework, into a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based MRI classification pipeline executed on the Frontier supercomputer. Instead of training directly on raw magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data, our approach generates visualization-derived feature representations using Viskores operations, including median filtering, Sobel gradients, Laplacian filtering, texture extraction, Otsu thresholding, and morphological processing. We evaluate these representations on a four-class brain tumor MRI dataset containing 7,200 images and compare them with a conventional raw-image ViT baseline. The best-performing visualization-enhanced pipeline improves classification accuracy from 91.94% to 95.50%. The poster presents the end-to-end HPC workflow, performance comparison, and an ablation study, demonstrating the potential of integrating scientific visualization and AI within scalable, reproducible workflows for medical imaging applications.

presentations.title: A-OASIS: Building an AI-Coupled Atmosphere-Ocean Foundation Model
presentations.abstract: U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) water-for-energy planning requires predictions of precipitation and hydroclimate variability from weeks to years, yet these horizons depend on coupled atmosphere-ocean-land feedback that are difficult to learn from observations. Established dynamical Earth system models and explicit couplers remain the scientific reference, but producing long simulations and forecast ensembles is computationally intensive. This work in progress asks a bounded question: after careful, domain-guided data harmonization, how much of the coupling workflow can a unified AI foundation model learn directly, and where does that strategy become limited? We present the Atmosphere-Ocean Artificial System for Integrated Simulation (A-OASIS), an Aurora-derived model that jointly encodes atmosphere, ocean, and land states in one latent space rather than training and coupling separate emulators. Initial experiments demonstrate stable full resolution distributed training and decreasing validation loss with increased model capacity. These results establish implementation feasibility, driving the next step of validating forecast capability.

presentations.title: AAFLOW+: Stateful Operator Abstraction with Distributed KV Cache Orchestration for Multi-Agent Workflows
presentations.abstract: Multi-agent LLM workflows are distributed GPU-cluster applications that interleave retrieval, planning, and reasoning. However, text-centric agent communication repeatedly rebuilds shared context through expensive prefill, while the resulting KV cache remains confined to local serving runtimes rather than being reused as transferable state. We present AAFLOW+, a stateful abstraction of agentic workflow operators that elevates KV cache to a first-class distributed memory object, with explicit operators for materialization, transfer, fork, composition, and eviction over zero-copy, communication-aware execution graphs. Its cost-based scheduler selects transfer/recomputation using measured bandwidth and prefill costs. Evaluation uses a trace-driven model parameterized by A100/InfiniBand microbenchmarks with Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B. Modeled results show up to $50.2\times$ TTFT reduction at long context, up to $7.63\times$ lower aggregate multi-agent compute cost at 16-agent scale, and $1.72-6.10\times$ lower peak KV memory. Transfer–recompute analysis shows KV transfer dominates recomputation at 25 Gbps and above, placing state sharing squarely within reach of HPC interconnects.

presentations.title: AC-STRR: Training-Aware Visual Token Reduction for Scalable High-Resolution Medical Vision-Language Models
presentations.abstract:
High-resolution chest radiographs produce long visual-token sequences that increase large vision-language model (LVLM) fine-tuning cost and inference prefill latency.
We present \textbf{A}nchor-\textbf{C}ontext \textbf{S}implified \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}etention and \textbf{R}eduction (AC-STRR), a training-aware framework that filters background tokens, preserves locally distinctive anchors, and merges redundant context before the language decoder.
AC-STRR applies the same reduction path during fine-tuning and inference while retaining the original position indices used by Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding.
On VinDr-CXR with Qwen3-VL-8B and Low-Rank Adaptation, AC-STRR reduces fine-tuning time on one L40S by 24.9\% and achieves a 9.07$\times$ combined speedup on eight L40S GPUs over the single-GPU full-token baseline.
It also reaches up to 63.5\% token reduction on native-resolution MIMIC-CXR.
Tuned AC-STRR keeps report quality close to the full-token baseline while lowering prefill latency.
These results suggest that domain-aware token reduction can improve fine-tuning and inference prefill efficiency for high-resolution medical LVLMs.

presentations.title: Accelerated Genetic Programming Hyper-Heuristics for Simulation-Based Scheduling via Agentic AI
presentations.abstract: Python is widely used in scientific research because it enables rapid development and provides rich ecosystems for data analysis, AI and machine learning. However, customised research code can become prohibitively slow as experiments scale. This challenge is particularly acute in discrete-event project-scheduling simulations, where sequential state updates, nested loops, conditional evaluations, and object-oriented structures limit the benefits of compiled numerical and GPU-accelerated libraries. Addressing these bottlenecks typically requires iterative profiling, refactoring, testing, and validation, yet researchers may lack the time or specialised software-engineering expertise for low-level optimisation. This paper presents a systematic refactoring approach using Claude agentic AI on real-world project-scheduling workloads in a high-performance computing environment. Guided by representative benchmarks and correctness checks, the agent identifies bottlenecks, implements targeted optimisations, and evaluates their effects, while the researcher retains final control. Testing runtime reduced from 1,298 seconds to under 200 seconds without changing outputs, saving four million core-hours (NZ$320,000) annually.

presentations.title: Accelerated Quantum Supercomputing: A Hands-On Tutorial on Quantum-Classical Hybrid Workflows Executed on QPUs and GPUs
presentations.abstract: Accelerated quantum supercomputing (AQSC) requires engineers to consider the hardware, software, and infrastructure challenges that arise when integrating quantum processing units (QPUs) into an HPC environment. This tutorial will provide attendees with hands-on experience to learn about AQSC infrastructure being deployed at supercomputing centers around the world. Participants will gain hands-on experience with the Python API of CUDA-Q. Attendees will have access to GPUs and IQM QPUs hosted at Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ). Live demonstrations and hands-on exercises include how to scale workflows, from a simple pip install to deploying multi-GPU, multi-node, and QPU jobs. This will all be tied under two quantum algorithms: sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD: quantum and HPC) and generative quantum eigensolver (GQE: AI and quantum), emphasizing the need for HPC and AI in quantum computing workflows. Attendees will learn about challenges in scaling quantum hardware and advancements in quantum error mitigation (QEM) and quantum error correction (QEC) which address them. They will learn about and execute commonly used QEM and QEC techniques in superconducting devices and perform GPU-accelerated decoding of quantum measurements. Participants will leave with practical skills in building hybrid applications locally and experience in scaling them on AQSC infrastructure.

presentations.title: Accelerated Quantum Supercomputing: AI, HPC, and the Quantum Applications Worth Betting On
presentations.abstract: Quantum processors are not useful in isolation. Today's small-scale QPUs require only modest classical hardware, but as systems scale toward utility and fault tolerance, dependencies on classical HPC and AI grow rapidly. These dependencies span the full stack: real-time decoders for fault-tolerant error correction, AI-assisted state preparation and circuit synthesis, hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, HPC-scale data processing, and verification. The serious questions for the SC community span all timelines: Which applications can quantum-HPC-AI integrated systems meaningfully accelerate now, which become reachable with fault tolerance, and which remain infeasible despite widespread touting? Integration approaches differ widely — RIKEN's Fugaku-IBM/Quantinuum hybrid platform, DOE lab user programs at NERSC and ORNL, NVIDIA's NVQLink GPU-QPU interconnect, and Google and AWS's standalone fault-tolerant roadmaps with classical co-processing serving error correction. These distinct framings reflect different visions for HPC-AI integration, and our community lacks consensus on which application and architecture pairings are optimal.

presentations.title: Accelerating and Scaling Python for HPC
presentations.abstract: Python is powering breakthrough exascale scientific discoveries - come learn how to program the world's largest supercomputers with it! In this interactive tutorial you’ll learn how to write, debug, profile, and optimize high-performance, multi-node GPU applications in Python. You'll learn and master: CuPy for drop-in GPU acceleration of NumPy workflows, Numba for writing custom kernels that match the performance of C++ and Fortran, mpi4py for scaling across thousands of nodes, DragonHPC for workflow acceleration, CppJIT for on-demand interoperability between Python/C++ and automatic bindings generation, leveraging it for compiler-based automatic differentiation of C++ with Clad. Everything is hands-on: short and interactive lectures by expert instructors will be paired with guided Jupyter notebooks that introduce each concept and have you immediately apply it in bite-sized exercises: a mini-app applying various programming models with JAX, CuPy and CppJIT on cosmic web data, and a CARTopiaX CAR T-cell therapy example). We'll use a web-based environment that requires no installs and setup - just a laptop and a browser. Whether you’re a domain scientist seeking faster turnaround or a software engineer evaluating portable acceleration strategies, you’ll leave with a roadmap, skills, and code for bringing scalable Python practices back to your own HPC facility.

presentations.title: Accelerating Fast Fourier Transforms with the RISC-V Vector Extension
presentations.abstract: The RISC-V Vector extension (RVV) enables greater flexibility for Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) and vector processing compared to established extensions like AVX for x86. For Fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) in particular, variable vector lengths, segmented loads and stores, and permutation instructions allow for novel vectorization strategies previously not feasible with traditional SIMD. In this work, different vectorization schemes for FFTs are derived by systematically matching unique RVV features to complex data flows and arithmetic operations. The resulting FFT algorithms are then evaluated on a wide range of RVV 1.0 hardware, including the SpacemiT K1 and K3, the Sophon SG2044, and the SiFive X280. The results demonstrate that achieving high performance across diverse platforms requires four distinct vectorization paths, as the optimal strategy depends heavily on the hardware. Ultimately, these results highlight the necessity of dynamic, run-time kernel selection to sustain optimal performance in FFT across the heterogeneous RISC-V ecosystem.

presentations.title: Accelerating GPU Datalog with Kernel Fusion
presentations.abstract: Recursive Datalog queries such as transitive closure, connected components, and same generation iterate a rule to a fixpoint and express many graph analytics. GPU Datalog engines run each round as a chain of separate relational operators driven by a host loop, paying for repeated sorting, per-round allocation, and a CPU-GPU round-trip. Instead, we run each round as single CUDA kernel over GPU-resident data structure, so a single atomic operation per derived fact deduplicates, tests novelty, and inserts it together. Because the state stays on the device, the whole loop runs on the GPU via a replayed CUDA graph and a conditional graph node, and results are updated in place as edges arrive. On an NVIDIA A100, this cuts end-to-end time by up to 24x for transitive closure and 136x for connected components over MNMGDatalog, beats GPUlog by up to 29x in compute, and updates connected components up to 40x faster.

presentations.title: Accelerating Graph Neural Networks with Decoupled Access-Execute Architectures
presentations.abstract: Graph neural networks address critical problems in content recommendation, fraud detection, and drug discovery. Unlike dense machine-learning models, graph models are often memory bound rather than compute bound, making HBM-based processors a promising alternative to GPUs. This paper first characterizes how graph input locality shapes the architectural requirements of these workloads. It then evaluates locality-aware architectural optimizations, including decoupled memory access and near-memory processing, that enable HBM-based processors to outperform GPUs by up to 7x.

presentations.title: Accelerating HPC Performance Analysis with AI Agents
presentations.abstract: Successful performance analysis typically involves a combination of established workflows, measurement tools, architectural knowledge, performance models, hardware counter analysis, parametric studies, and visualization. AI agents can integrate and automate many of these activities, significantly reducing the effort required to collect, organize, analyze, and interpret performance data. Agents are particularly effective at automating command-line data collection, managing results from parametric studies, applying performance models to known architectures, interpreting well understood hardware counter data, and performing static analysis of compiler reports and generated assembly code. In this talk, we will present several success stories that demonstrate how AI agents can be used to analyze HPC proxy applications and accelerate the performance engineering process. For example, analysis of the RAJAPerf suite on AMD MI300A GPUs identified optimization opportunities that produced a 34× speedup in one kernel. We will also discuss practical lessons learned, including common challenges and limitations encountered when working with AI agents. We will also discuss emerging opportunities for agent-assisted performance analysis, including the skills, interfaces, and rules that performance measurement and analysis tool developers should consider providing to maximize agent effectiveness. Finally, we will highlight AI agent capabilities being developed for current and future releases of the ROCm ecosystem.

presentations.title: Accelerating Materials Discovery with ADAM: An AI Co-Pilot for Physical Experimentation
presentations.abstract: The rapid discovery of new materials for energy storage, advanced computing, and other technologies requires us to remake scientific experimentation beyond the limits of human cognition and manual interaction. Most existing autonomous experimentation relies on deterministic scripts or narrowly-scoped post-hoc machine learning. Large language models offer a fundamentally different capability, in the form of generalized reasoning from natural language goals, but we must still address safe LLM reasoning with real-time instrument feedback in a closed-loop workflow. Here we present ADAM, a multi-agent large language model framework integrating a retrieval augmented generation pipeline grounded in internal documentation, a validated instrument tool registry, and human-in-the-loop oversight positioned at semantic reversibility boundaries. By inferring these boundaries from natural language rather than hard-coded rules, ADAM achieves high autonomy in routine experiments and applies precise human oversight only when needed. We demonstrate this system in two materials characterization and processings examples.

presentations.title: Accurate and Scalable Graph AI for Early and Explainable Health Risk Assessment
presentations.abstract:
Early and explainable health risk assessment can enable proactive and informed medical intervention. Comprehensive assessment, however, relies on intrinsically multimodal clinical data that are often irregular, sparse, and temporally misaligned, making accurate and scalable assessment challenging. We address these two connected challenges: (1) improving the accuracy of early and explainable health risk assessment through Graph AI and (2) scaling Graph AI training to reduce training time and support larger training data volumes.

To address (1), we develop M-GrEEnHeRA, a multimodal graph-based approach for early and explainable health risk assessment that represents multimodal clinical data as dynamic graph sequences and performs spatio-temporal learning over these graphs using Graph AI. To address (2), we develop a distributed producer-consumer (DPC) workflow that tackles key Graph AI training bottlenecks, including memory inefficiency, batch-construction-induced stalls, and GPU load imbalance.

presentations.title: Achieving Performance Portability for Semi-Lagrangian Simulations via Automated Layout and Loop Tuning
presentations.abstract:
Hardware heterogeneity defines the exascale era, and scientific
application performance is increasingly dominated by memory access patterns
rather than operation count.

We analyze the performance profile of a portable semi-Lagrangian
mini-application extracted from the Gysela-X++ tokamak plasma simulation code.
While single-source portability guarantees correctness across architectures, we
show that per- formance portability remains elusive, even when a code is not
intentionally tied to specific hardware features (e.g., tensor cores, cache
size, etc.).

By embedding judiciously placed layout and loop nest tuning points into this
single-source C++ mini-application, simple automatic tuning of its main operator
sequence recovers lost performance at minimal productivity cost. This automated
approach achieves speedups of up to ×1.47 on GPUs and ×1.53 on CPUs over expert
manual optimization, while requiring a fraction of the development time.

presentations.title: ACM SIGHPC Fellows Lightning Talks
presentations.abstract: In partnership with ACM SIGHPC, this year WHPC invites the SIGHPC Computational and Data Science fellows to give a lightning talk about their work.

presentations.title: ACSC Student Presentations
presentations.abstract: The University of Texas at Austin will host this event.

presentations.title: Adapting Classic List-Scheduling Heuristics for Conditional Task Graphs
presentations.abstract: Many scientific and machine-learning workflows are modeled as conditional task graphs (CTGs), in which some branches are chosen at runtime so only one of several alternative sub-graphs executes. Tasks on different branches are mutually exclusive, so a scheduler can overlap them on the same processor. We show that classic list-scheduling heuristics such as HEFT and CPoP can be adapted to CTGs with two small changes: a schedule representation that lets mutually exclusive tasks share a processor, and a priority function that weights each task by its probability of executing. Both are components of the open-source SAGA parametric list scheduler. Exploiting mutual exclusion is the dominant benefit, bringing expected makespan within a few percent of a clairvoyant scheduler. Probability reweighting does not help on generic conditional graphs, but helps decisively when a rare branch contains a heavy task competing with always-executed work for a fast processor, the structure of surrogate-model workflows.

presentations.title: Adaptive Block Mixed-Precision Cholesky Factorization for Large-Scale Space-Time Gaussian Processes
presentations.abstract: Gaussian process models underpin many environmental applications but are limited by the dense Cholesky factorization of an $N \times N$ covariance matrix that costs $O(N^3)$ operations and $O(N^2)$ memory. Low-precision arithmetic can reduce these costs, yet naive \fp{8}, half-, or single-precision Cholesky may fail on ill-conditioned covariance matrices because rounding destroys positive definiteness. We develop an adaptive block mixed-precision Cholesky factorization that partitions the covariance into blocks and assigns each the lowest precision satisfying a prescribed accuracy budget. A condition-number safety factor guarantees completion by preserving positive definiteness after rounding. Applied to a space-time Gaussian process for forecasting storm wind gusts over the northeastern United States, an extreme-weather forecasting task critical to hazard warning, the method scales to 131,589 observations on a single GPU, performs most arithmetic in \fp{8}, preserves the log-likelihood, and makes maximum-likelihood estimation practical at a scale beyond double precision while producing calibrated forecasts with predictive uncertainty.

presentations.title: Adaptive Control with Offline Reinforcement Learning for HPC Power Management
presentations.abstract: Power-capping policies for high-performance computing must reduce energy use without imposing unacceptable delays across heterogeneous applications. PowerSched, deployed on CPU nodes of the Hunter supercomputer at HLRS, identifies per-job operating points through iterative Golden-Section Search (GSS), which requires multiple measurement intervals and can respond slowly to workload changes. We replace this search with an Implicit Q-Learning controller trained offline on approximately 13 million telemetry transitions from 15,000 historical jobs. Using only telemetry already available to PowerSched, the controller requires no application instrumentation and predicts a bounded per-socket power cap every 15 seconds. We integrate it as a prototype behind PowerSched's predictor interface and conduct preliminary single-node experiments on HPL, HPCG, and eight NAS Parallel Benchmarks. Relative to a 400 W/socket maximum-cap baseline, the controller reduces measured node energy by 7.1% across all ten benchmarks with a 1.0% average performance reduction. The results use three independent runs per benchmark.

presentations.title: Adaptive Error Quantization for Lossy Compression of Scientific Datasets
presentations.abstract: Large-scale scientific instruments and applications generate massive amounts of data, creating storage and I/O bottlenecks for analysis. Error-bounded lossy compression methods mitigate this, but certain unpredictable datasets make it difficult to obtain large compression ratios with prediction-based compressors without introducing a large error. This work introduces adaptive error quantization, a novel extension to the SZ3 compressor framework. Our implementation dynamically refines the prediction error of an unpredictable data point by allocating additional error quantization bins through continuous bisection of the error, improving data fidelity for hard-to-compress datasets while minimizing storage overhead. We present a comparison of our adaptive method against the baseline SZ3 compressor on the HACC particle simulation datasets, highlighting our algorithm's advantage when compressing high-entropy fields.

presentations.title: Adaptive Orchestration of Heterogeneous LLMs with Dynamic Escalation for Multi-Agent Collaboration
presentations.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems offer strong reasoning capabilities but often incur substantial computational and operational costs. This work presents an adaptive two-orchestrator framework for coordinating heterogeneous small and large LLMs. Orchestrator-1 (O-1) determines the initial number of expert agents and model tier using task-level risk signals. The primary adaptive component, Orchestrator-2 (O-2) evaluates multiple round-level signals using a heuristic approach and selectively escalates only when the current model configuration is deemed insufficient. After evaluation across various benchmarks using models deployed with vLLM we found that compared with the Large-only configuration, the Small + Large configuration improved accuracy by 0.51–6.67 percentage points, reduced average cost per task by 15.99%–33.65%, and decreased execution time by 8.1%–18.06%. Only 0.10%–3.60% of tasks required escalation, demonstrating the effectiveness of O-2’s signal-driven decision mechanism. These results validate that dynamic escalation can preserve or improve performance while reducing unnecessary use of Larger models.

presentations.title: Addressing Challenges in Collaborative Computational Cancer Policy Research
presentations.abstract:
Two computational artifacts underpin personalized lung cancer screening: a natural history model (NHM) that reproduces disease progression (CHRONOS-Lung), and a decision-analytic framework that converts individual risk into a screening schedule. ENGAGE provides the latter as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), solved once per risk profile across a O(10^8) combinatorial space. Both are written in Julia and were developed at MD Anderson. Since 2020, successive ALCC allocations have let our team run large-scale calibration and analysis campaigns for multiple cancer modeling groups on leadership computing, which made the ENGAGE campaigns conceivable. We review four themes from moving these models onto HPC.

The first was dependency and portability. The POMDP solves relied on a commercial solver, so we moved to the open, JuMP-compatible HiGHS. Scale then exposed fragility local runs never showed, with 230 of 1,000 solves failing at default tolerances. Sweeping three tolerances across 64 combinations identified relaxed settings we adopted. Separately, the Julia projects pinned no manifests, so library drift triggered recompilation on compute nodes, a limited issue locally but a large one when many concurrent compilations fire at once. Pinning environments and amortizing JIT and library-load costs across node-local task batches removed that overhead.

The second was scale. The POMDP campaign produces an enormous number of small files in Julia-specific binary formats, a pattern parallel filesystems handle poorly and one aggravated by sharing an allocation and file systems with other cancer modeling groups. We ran in batches of two million POMDP solves, chaining an archival tar job that triggered the subsequent batch, staged through the scratch file system, and served the resulting archives through a Globus collection. Input handling had similar issues. The solves re-read the same jld2 files repeatedly, so at our scale 55,680 of them contended for the same files, causing I/O deadlock and sharply longer runtimes until we rewrote them to cache the reads.

The third was pluggability. CHRONOS-Lung, the sex-, histology-, and nodule-attenuation-specific NHM, comprises 12 Julia models sharing a 15-state monthly-cycle structure with Gompertz tumor growth and size-dependent stage transitions. Its original calibration was a bespoke extreme-elitist genetic algorithm in Julia, in which the two fittest of 100 individuals produced every child. Because the EMEWS model exploration framework treats both the NHM and the exploration algorithm as pluggable tasks, we could investigate alternatives efficiently, using EMEWS queues for Python to let the open-source Python DEAP library drive the Julia NHM over MPI. We finally adopted a (mu + lambda) scheme with tournament selection, which produced robust fits across the multiple calibration targets.

The fourth was statistical. Calibration had used 1,000-person cohorts for expediency. Scaling studies let us move to 100,000, spending concurrency on reduced uncertainty and better estimator quality rather than wall-clock alone. The calibrated models reproduced their SEER targets closely and validated against four independent external cohorts.

Throughout, the governing question was how much domain code must change to meet HPC constraints and how much the workflow layer can absorb on its behalf.

presentations.title: Adopting Emerging AI Frameworks in HPC Environments
presentations.abstract: Computational scientists use HPC in two primary ways: to run simulations and to process data, iterating until a new observation emerges. As scientific computation becomes more sophisticated and resource-heavy, researchers increasingly turn to AI/MLtools to accelerate discovery. Yet before these tools can be used, scientists often spend undue time on tasks like environment setup, dependency management, model acquisition, and determining the correct way to run each framework on shared HPC systems. This demands a system that can streamline and standardize these setup tasks, so that scientists can focus on analysis rather than infrastructure. With a reproducible, well-defined workflow for deploying and running AI tools on HPC, we can accomplish this goal. In this work, we demonstrate such a workflow using four widely used AI tools: Stable Diffusion (text-to-image generation), vLLM (high-throughput large language model inference), Ollama (lightweight local LLM serving), and AlphaFold3 (protein-structure prediction).

presentations.title: Advanced Architecture Testbeds: Community Resources for HPC-AI Research
presentations.abstract: Testbeds play a vital role in assessing the readiness of novel architectures for upcoming supercomputers for the exascale and post-exascale era. These testbeds also act as co-design hubs, enabling the collection of application operational requirements, while identifying critical gaps that need to be addressed for an architecture to become viable for HPC. Various research centers are actively deploying testbeds, and our aim is to build a community that facilitates the sharing of information, encouraging collaboration and understanding of the available evaluation resources. This BoF will facilitate the exchange of best practices, including testbed design, benchmarking, system evaluation, and availability.

presentations.title: Advanced MPI Programming
presentations.abstract: The vast majority of production parallel scientific applications today use MPI and run successfully on the largest systems in the world. Parallel system architectures are evolving to include complex, heterogeneous nodes comprising general-purpose CPUs as well as accelerators such as GPUs. At the same time, the MPI standard itself is evolving to address the needs and challenges of future extreme-scale platforms as well as applications. This tutorial will cover several advanced features of MPI that can help users program modern systems effectively. Using code examples based on scenarios found in real applications, we will cover several topics including efficient ways of doing 2D and 3D stencil computation, derived datatypes, one-sided communication, hybrid programming (MPI + threads, shared memory, GPUs), topologies and topology mapping, neighborhood and nonblocking collectives, some of the new performance-oriented features in MPI-4, and the new application binary interface (ABI) in MPI-5. Attendees will leave the tutorial with an understanding of how to use these advanced features of MPI and guidelines on how they might perform on different platforms and architectures.

Agentic AI Augmentation for Recursive Mixed-Precision Linear Solvers
presentations.abstract: High performance computing increasingly relies on low-precision hardware for throughput, yet scientific applications demand numerical accuracy. Recursive mixed-precision algorithms address this, but extending them to new solvers requires expert-level knowledge. This work investigates agentic AI augmentation to transfer knowledge from a recursive mixed-precision Cholesky solver to new algorithms, evaluating in-context learning (ICL) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), using implementations, documentation, and mathematical formulations as structured knowledge. We find that full-context ICL enables frontier LLMs to generate a high-performance recursive mixed-precision LU factorization achieving up to a 4.9x speedup over cuSOLVER FP32 on H200 GPUs while preserving accuracy, whereas PEFT memorizes the framework but fails to generalize, showing that expert-designed HPC implementations can serve as reusable knowledge for AI systems. At the poster, I will present our knowledge-transfer framework via figures comparing runtime and speedup across ICL prompting levels and models, fine-tuning accuracy results, and our recursive mixed-precision framework and future directions.

presentations.title: Agentic Computing and Services for the Computing Continuum
presentations.abstract: AI applications increasingly span a computing continuum from edge sensors through cloud to HPC centers, yet most are still assembled and operated manually. This BoF convenes the SC community around agentic, service-oriented cyberinfrastructure: software agents, exposed as composable services, that sense continuum state, decide where to train and deploy models, act through a shared control plane, and learn from outcomes. Drawing on experience from the NSF ICICLE AI Institute and invited external perspectives, participants will debate autonomy levels, trust, provenance, evaluation, and emerging protocols such as MCP, and identify steps toward community benchmarks and interoperable agentic cyberinfrastructure.

presentations.title: Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach
presentations.abstract: Quantum frameworks each define their own Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect, so porting a circuit to a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) runtime needs a hand-written pass per dialect. Our translator selects among three paths: a deterministic compiler path for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), a large language model (LLM) agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes the source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators, comparing output distributions by total variation distance (TVD). For smaller open-weight models we replace retrieval-augmented generation with inline context engineering and add a guardrail-assembler that rebuilds valid QIR from incomplete output. Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 5-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD. On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.

presentations.title: Agentic Orchestration of HPC Applications in Cloud
presentations.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are serving as a catalyst of change for research practices, influencing the daily lives of staff scientists, software engineers, and system administrators. Adopting LLM-based agents promises new degrees of autonomy, where categories of human work and decision making are replaced by goal-oriented systems. This transition necessitates novel architectural paradigms and solid understanding of the strengths and limitations of LLMs. In this work, we design agents to conduct the entire life-cycle of an HPC application experimental run in cloud -- creation and build of a container, deployment in Kubernetes, optimization, and orchestration of a scaling study. We execute the study for five well-known HPC applications to build multi-platform container images and optimize figures of merit across 21 instance types in Kubernetes. We present a successful agentic scaling study, designs that improve work time to completion, and suggested best practices for agentic design and collaboration.

presentations.title: Agentic WAN‑Native LLM Orchestration: From User‑Driven Inference to Geographically Distributed Model Instances Across Internet2, PNRP, and SCinet via NRP and SENSE
presentations.abstract: SENSE-NRI(TomL), CalTech-NRI(HarveyN), StarLight-NRI(JoeM)

presentations.title: Agentic-ready data management workflow for material science
presentations.abstract:
Material science increasingly integrates experimental,
computational, and literature-derived evidence resulting in data
that are potentially incomplete or inconsistent; and that are
fragmented across instruments, notebooks, file systems, simulations,
and publications. This data fragmentation hinders the
promise of using large language model (LLM)-driven agentic
workflows to reason across natural-language, tabular, textual,
and image-based data with limited human intervention. To
close this gap, we present a methodology spanning domain
characterization and schematization, data inventory, integrated
data management via a lakehouse architecture, and automated
dataset enhancement for agentic interpretation. Our solution
enables an automated data workflow pipeline that can leverage
specific agentic data skills, semantically find correspondence
in the domain schema (generated), generated relevant queries
(with validation mechanism) for entries into data-lakehouse and
aggregate relevant data for a specific task/analysis We demonstrate
its value by comparing the potential of an agentic-ready dataset
vs. a “vanilla” baseline.

presentations.title: AgenticAI4HPC’26: The First International Workshop on Agentic AI for HPC
presentations.abstract: Recent progress in agentic AI—AI systems capable of autonomous planning, reasoning, adaptation, and tool use—opens transformative opportunities across the HPC research landscape. Beyond system-level optimization, agentic AI can play a pivotal role in code modernization, automated code translation across programming models, performance tuning for diverse hardware platforms, and the long-term sustainability of large scientific software stacks. As HPC systems continue to evolve toward exascale and beyond, developers face increasing challenges in maintaining legacy codes, porting applications to emerging architectures, and achieving performance portability across changing programming models and runtime environments. Agentic approaches offer the potential to autonomously refactor legacy codes, translate between models, recommend architecture-aware optimizations, and iteratively tune applications. AgenticAI4HPC’26: The First International Workshop on Agentic AI for HPC will bring together researchers and practitioners to explore methodologies, systems, and real-world applications that leverage agentic AI to accelerate HPC software development, enhance productivity, and enable sustainable performance at scale.

presentations.title: Agents at Your Service: Reuse-First Workflow Composition with Laminar 3.0
presentations.abstract: Large language models show promise as software development assistants, but their tendency to hallucinate makes them unreliable for directly generating workflow implementations in specialized coordination languages. This paper presents Laminar 3.0, an evolution of the Laminar serverless framework that integrates a bounded, prompt-chained pipeline of role-specialized LLM agents to support workflow discovery and composition. It introduces an LLM-driven metadata generation mechanism to enrich the workflow registry, a hybrid retrieval mechanism combining semantic search, lexical search, and LLM-based re-ranking, and a retrieval-first, constraint-guided generation pipeline that proposes workflow skeletons only when no suitable artifacts exist. Laminar 3.0 prioritizes reuse and synthesizes only the coordination layer, leaving host semantics under developer control. Experiments show semantic retrieval remains robust even for compressed queries, achieving 79% top-1 and 81% top-3 retrieval, while the generation pipeline produces skeletons with a CodeBLEU score of 0.946, substantially outperforming direct generation with vanilla prompting.

presentations.title: Agents of Intelligence: Lowering the Barrier to AI for Domain Scientists
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how science is done, yet most domain scientists face a steep barrier to adopting it. The landscape of models, platforms, and data pipelines is fragmented, and navigating it rewards tacit expertise accumulated over years of practice. We present Agents of Intelligence (AoI): a modular, composable, human-in-the-loop framework of AI agents that sense workflow context, automate routine decisions, recommend models and compute resources, and learn from usage. AoI is grounded in interviews with 11 Schmidt AI postdoctoral researchers spanning eight scientific domains, and it integrates with the National Data Platform to support the full research lifecycle from data acquisition through model deployment, making AI-assisted science accessible across domains.

presentations.title: AI Agents for Data Infrastructure: From Telemetry to Optimization
presentations.abstract: The talk will explore how AI agents could reshape the way we understand, manage, and optimize data infrastructure. Drawing on examples from telemetry preprocessing, diagnosis, and I/O optimization, I will discuss the opportunities and challenges and invite the community to help build shared benchmarks and open experimental environments.

presentations.title: AI Agents for Nuclear Science: Evaluation of Vaults, Skills, and Multi-Agent Verification
presentations.abstract: Scientific AI agents increasingly assist researchers in software development, workflow orchestration, data analysis, and simulation-driven discovery. However, scientific environments impose requirements beyond those of general-purpose assistants, including domain-specific knowledge integration, reproducibility, correctness verification, and continuous adaptation to evolving software ecosystems. In this paper, we present a design of scientific agents evaluated across four nuclear-fuel specialists spanning open-ended research to deterministic workflow execution. We evaluate the impact of structured knowledge vaults and reusable skills on agent performance, execution cost, and reliability and find that across five foundation models, the answer quality improves by roughly 1.2x-1.5x more than they raise execution cost. We describe a correctness-verification agent that traces cited references to validate outputs, reducing relative grading error against manual evaluation and discuss a path toward collaborative multi-agent systems combining agents that follow our design. The study provides practical guidance for building scalable, trustworthy scientific AI agents.

presentations.title: AI and ML for HPC Workload Analysis: From Isolation to Reproducibility — Building Common Benchmarks
presentations.abstract: HPC facilities each build operational data analytics in isolation, with no shared benchmarks to compare methods or reproduce results across sites. This seventh-edition BoF convenes the community around a common goal: shared standards, open benchmarks, and cross-facility collaboration for HPC workload analysis. Using the HPC ODA Commons, introduced to the community at ISC 2026, as a working exemplar, we examine how standardized schemas and benchmark recipes enable reproducible comparison across systems. We present an emerging multi-facility study, invite sites to contribute data, schemas, or models, and work together to prioritize analyses and plan a community report.

presentations.title: AI for Quantum at the Quantum Science Center: Towards Building a Connective Layer Across the Quantum Computing Stack
presentations.abstract: We present the AI for Quantum efforts of the Agentic Software team at the Quantum Science Center (QSC), Oak Ridge National Laboratory, advancing a unifying thesis: that artificial intelligence can serve as the connective and accelerating substrate of the quantum computing stack. Our portfolio spans three axes. For **knowledge infrastructure**, Quantum RAG grounds frontier models in curated quantum corpora, and the Quantum Computing LLMWiki provides a machine-readable knowledge resource. For **evaluation**, the Quantum Computing Benchmark Leaderboard rigorously benchmarks frontier models on quantum code generation, coupled with a hard benchmark and shared-task problems developed for IEEE Quantum Week (QCE). For **domain reasoning and systems**, ChatQEC, FTQEC, and hardware-aware error correction lower the barrier to reasoning about codes and decoders under realistic device constraints, while a multi-agent framework decomposes quantum-HPC workflows across specialized agents. We further extend EPIC toward quantum-HPC co-execution, integrating these capabilities into a unified orchestration substrate.

presentations.title: AI for Science with Python on AMD Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: Running Python workloads at scale is becoming increasingly important in the scientific landscape of today, especially given the rise of AI as a partner in scientific development and discovery. We will show various ways of deploying AI workloads (including AI agents) at scale running on AMD GPUs: our focus will be on AI for science on heterogeneous types of systems with variety of deployments (i.e. wheels and containers) and job schedulers (Slurm and Kubernetes). We will provide a walkthrough of AMD Inference Microservices (AIM) and how this inference engine can be used by scientists to deploy their Python AI workloads.

presentations.title: AI for Science: Building the future engines of scientific discovery
presentations.abstract: The U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is a national initiative to accelerate scientific discovery through artificial intelligence, with the ambitious goal of doubling research productivity and impact within a decade. This collaborative effort brings together DOE's 17 national laboratories, universities, and industry partners to build an integrated AI-powered discovery engine that addresses critical challenges in energy systems, materials manufacturing, biotechnology, fundamental science, and strategic technologies. The mission has selected 278 projects spanning 13 science themes and secured over $800 million in partner commitments, including a landmark $1 billion U.S.-Japan partnership. At its core, the initiative aims to create a coordinated scientific discovery system that integrates supercomputing resources, curated scientific data, AI models and agents, and experimental facilities into reusable workflows that close the loop from hypothesis generation to experimental validation. The ultimate vision is to develop AI systems that can propose falsifiable theories, design and execute their own experiments, provide calibrated uncertainty, and serve as public infrastructure accessible to researchers worldwide. However, the presentation emphasizes that success requires addressing AI for science not merely as a model problem, but as a comprehensive scientific-system problem encompassing data, theory, experiments, compute, incentives, governance, and human judgment working in concert.

presentations.title: AI on HPC: Performance Engineering, Challenges and Opportunities
presentations.abstract: How can AI workloads be engineered for optimal performance in modern HPC environments? As AI models grow in scale and complexity, high performance computing (HPC) systems are becoming essential for training and deploying these workloads. However, traditional HPC architectures, designed for batch processing, present unique challenges for AI/ML applications — such as dynamic workloads, high I/O demands, and parallelization intricacies. This workshop explores the intersection of AI and HPC, focusing on performance optimization, scalability, and portability. Topics include AI workload characterization, hybrid AI/HPC workflows, efficient execution strategies, and infrastructure co-design. By fostering collaboration between researchers, practitioners, and system developers, this workshop aims to advance best practices and innovations in AI-enabled scientific computing, aligning with SC26’s themes of exascale readiness and performance portability.

presentations.title: AI Supercomputers: Evolution or Revolution?
presentations.abstract: AI has had a profound impact on the supercomputing ecosystem, with dramatic advances in technology, size, and scale of supercomputers being deployed. While there is no doubt that AI software is very different from scientific computing applications, underneath the software, how different are the supercomputers powering the AI revolution? Have AI workloads fundamentally changed the technology used to build supercomputers that are the foundation of scientific computing, or have AI workloads just accelerated in time the path that scientific computing was already on? In this panel, our experts will examine this question, looking at the hardware and software that power the world’s largest supercomputers for both HPC and AI, and discuss the implications this has on organizations who rely on these systems and how this affects the next generation of professionals starting out in a supercomputing field that is changing faster than it has in its 60+ year history.

presentations.title: AI-Assisted Engineering in HPC
presentations.abstract: Software engineering is changing rapidly as AI-assisted programming becomes accepted. Tools and approaches have matured rapidly from “vibe-coding” to using complex and highly productive agentic harnesses. In this session, we will discuss the implications for the scientific programming community, with a particular focus on HPC software. This includes systemware, middleware, and tools used to operate, manage, and maintain HPC systems, as well as parallel simulation and modelling software used in HPC settings. Topics include trustworthiness and validation for AI-generated software, career futures and professional implications for systems engineers and research software engineers, security implications, and emerging current "best performance practices."

presentations.title: AI4S and Sovereign Supercomputing in Japan
presentations.abstract:
In December 2025, the Japanese government adopted its first AI Basic Plan under the AI Promotion Act, positioning AI research and development, including the computing infrastructure behind it, as a national priority. In line with this, MEXT is promoting AI for Science (AI4S) and strengthening Japan’s computing infrastructure for it through two major initiatives. First, the RIKEN Center for Computational Science (R-CCS) introduced RIKYU in 2026, a supercomputer for AI4S development with 1,600 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. RIKYU complements Fugaku in developing and applying scientific foundation models, and its resources are also available to MEXT’s AI4S research programs, including ARiSE and SPReAD1000.
Second, MEXT’s FY2025 supplementary budget supports four university centers that provide National Infrastructure Systems (NIS) in HPCI, the framework for sharing computing resources across Japanese universities and research institutes, to expand shared GPU resources and make their use more efficient for AI4S. The four centers at Hokkaido Univ., Univ. of Tsukuba, UTokyo, and Kyushu Univ. have agreed to share operational know-how and standardize practices, and UTokyo will serve as an HPCI hub that links jobs across resource-providing centers.
This talk presents both efforts and discusses how national infrastructure for AI4S can be operated and shared across institutions.

presentations.title: Algebraic Breadth-First Search on the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine
presentations.abstract: Graph traversal is memory bound on conventional hardware: irregular access defeats the cache hierarchy. The Cerebras WSE-3 gives each of its 900,000 cores its own 48 KB of SRAM, turning irregular access into local access, but leaves them coordinating over a 2D mesh and a slow host-device link. We present an algebraic BFS that runs entirely on device, avoiding the link that host-callable SpMV kernels would cross every iteration. Sweeping Graph500-specification R-MAT graphs from scale 10 to 20 across PE grids up to 750x750, we find adding cores helps only up to a point, past which larger collectives outweigh the smaller share of work per PE. At that turning point up to 89% of device time goes into collectives, while exporting results costs two orders of magnitude more than the search itself. Within the kernel, distributed on-chip memory removes the memory wall and leaves collective communication as the next target.

presentations.title: Algorithms & Applications
presentations.abstract:
This session highlights how quantum algorithms are being applied to real scientific problems in combination with large-scale classical computing. Speakers will present recent progress on end-to-end applications in areas such as chemistry, biomedicine, and materials science, with a focus on the role HPC plays in making these workflows practical, from pre- and post-processing to error mitigation and verification at scale. Rather than treating quantum hardware in isolation, the talks emphasize how algorithm design is shaped by the surrounding classical infrastructure, and what this means for the path toward utility-scale quantum-classical computing.

The session brings together perspectives from clinical research, a national HPC center, and quantum hardware vendors, offering a view of how applications are being developed across different platforms and institutions.

presentations.title: AMAI: Algebraic Modelling of Distributed AI Computations for Symbolic Performance Analysis
presentations.abstract: Developing large-scale AI systems requires extensive on-machine tuning: engineers evaluate hundreds of parallel configurations by trial and error, at considerable cost in accelerator rental and compute time. Existing performance models are either tied to specific frameworks or too coarse for modern distributed workloads. We present AMAI, a performance analysis framework featuring (i) a declarative domain-specific language for describing distributed deep-learning computations, and (ii) compositional cost semantics that map programs into symbolic models of time and per-device memory. Models are parameterized by hardware constants and structural variables that define the parallelism configuration. As a result, descriptions can be analyzed at any scale and reused across machines. Predictions stay within 3 percent of measured step time and peak memory across batch-size and data-parallel scaling when analyzing the training of Qwen3.5 0.8B on a multi-node NPU cluster.

presentations.title: Americas HPC Collaboration: Building Workforce Pathways for HPC, AI, and Quantum
presentations.abstract: Building on a decade of Americas HPC Collaboration (AHPC) BoFs, this SC26 session will formalize the Education and Workforce Development Chapter and outline a practical roadmap for its first year. The BoF will focus on areas where collaboration can make a concrete impact: system-facing training for people who deploy and support HPC/AI infrastructure, using the Oak Ridge Computing Academy (ORCA) as one example; a panel on emerging AI and quantum training needs with academia and industry participants; and student cluster competition experiences that demonstrate the value of hands-on learning. Participants will identify shared assets, pilot activities, and institutional commitments.

presentations.title: An Agentic Evaluation Framework for AI-Generated Scientific Code in PETSc
presentations.abstract:
While LLMs have accelerated scientific code gen-
eration, comprehensively evaluating generated code remains
challenging. Many benchmarks emphasize functional correctness
or task completion, which is insufficient for code built on pro-
duction HPC libraries, where solver selection, API conventions,
memory management, parallel awareness, and performance also
matter. We introduce PETSCAGENT-BENCH, a multidimensional
benchmark and agent-based framework for assessing whether
AI-generated scientific code uses a production HPC library as
an expert would. A tool-augmented evaluator compiles, executes,
and measures code and combines deterministic checks with
LLM-based assessments in a 14-evaluator pipeline spanning five
categories: correctness, performance, code quality, algorithmic
appropriateness, and library-specific conventions. A2A and MCP
enable black-box evaluation of compatible coding agents. Across
realistic PETSc problems, frontier models generate readable,
well-structured code but struggle with correctness on challeng-
ing problems and with library-specific conventions even when
code compiles and runs—limitations that conventional pass/fail
evaluation does not capture.

presentations.title: An Agentic Workflow for Legacy HPC Modernization: Converting the Two-Electron-Integral Core of GAMESS
presentations.abstract:
Modernizing legacy Fortran is a problem of volume: the transformations are individually routine, but the codebases are enormous, and the work goes undone. We propose an agentic workflow operating at production scale. Three prompt-specialized agent roles operate under a version-controlled specification the agents themselves authored, while humans hold a small number of gates. Safety is anchored to an exact verification oracle inherited from the domain.

We apply the workflow to the two-electron-integral routines of GAMESS (General Atomic and Molecular Electronic Structure System), converting twelve source files (56,448 lines, 225 subroutines) from fixed-form Fortran 77 to free-form Fortran 2008. The agents ran as Claude Code roles in isolated worktrees. Because GAMESS's user community treats its printed test energies as canonical, we adopt bit-for-bit reproduction as the merge criterion. All twelve files pass the 51 standard tests with zero chemistry-relevant differences and the Jenkins continuous-integration test suite.

presentations.title: An AI-Anchored Pathway into HPC Practice: Design and Initial Evaluation of a Three-Day Summer School in Vietnam
presentations.abstract: High Performance Computing (HPC) education increasingly serves students entering through artificial intelligence and data-intensive applications, despite uneven preparation in parallel programming and shared computing environments. This paper presents the design and initial evaluation of a three-day, practice-oriented HPC summer school for 36 selected students, of whom 34 attended at least one session, using a real Slurm cluster. The curriculum connected AI workloads with cluster access, resource management, OpenMP and MPI, GPU execution, reproducible environments, and an AI/HPC workflow challenge. We analyzed participation and assessment records, 25 post-school survey responses, and operational observations. Slurm and data-intensive AI workflows received the highest perceived-practicality ratings (4.12/5 and 4.08/5), while parallel programming presented the greatest knowledge load (3.36/5). The findings highlight the importance of teaching-assistant support, explicit instructional scaffolding, and reliable infrastructure, providing practical design lessons for institutions developing short, hands-on HPC training programs.

presentations.title: An ELF-Aware DMA Engine for Distributed-Memory Accelerators
presentations.abstract: Distributed-memory, many-core accelerators are often bottlenecked by the task of transferring data to and from the local memories. Existing solutions place much of the orchestration burden onto the host processor. Instead, we propose an ELF-aware DMA engine that parses an ELF file from host memory and uses off-the-shelf DMA and interconnect IP to transfer data with minimal host intervention. We also extend the ELF format to encode both high-fan-out load and many-to-one gather operations in one file. On our FPGA proxy modeled after a kilocore accelerator, our design is 4.8× faster than host memcpy and 39% faster than scatter-gather DMA on load, with host preprocessing reduced to two register writes. Extrapolation to the kilocore scale suggests the engine costs roughly 1.6% of PE capacity. For many-core distributed-memory accelerators, we conclude that this approach is a viable middle ground between the host manually transferring bytes and a custom NoC/DMA stack.

presentations.title: An Exascale Universe in Warm and Cool
presentations.abstract:
This image opens onto a world that feels at once immense and intimate: a turbulent landscape constructed from data generated by one of the largest cosmology simulations run on exascale supercomputers. Vast orange forms move across the frame like heated clouds, molten currents, or a weather system caught mid-motion. Cooler blue structures gather around and beneath them, forming translucent streams and pockets that suggest an opposing climate. Their overlap turns temperature into a visual conversation — warm and cool masses pressing together, passing through one another, and creating a layered terrain with no familiar ground or horizon.

The orange and blue bodies are isosurfaces extracted from temperature data: boundaries that give form to conditions that cannot ordinarily be seen. Their fine wireframe skins deliberately retain the visual language of early computer graphics. Rather than conceal the construction of the image behind smooth, seamless surfaces, the mesh makes the digital scaffold visible. It recalls the moment when computer-generated worlds announced themselves through grids, polygons, and luminous lines — an artificial landscape honest about the machinery that makes it possible.

Across this shifting terrain, small magenta, violet, and pale spheres drift like beads, sparks, or distant lights. Each represents an element from the simulation and can stand for an extraordinary amount of matter — many solar masses compressed into a point of visual scale. Individually, they appear delicate; collectively, they trace a crowded and intricate environment.

By combining translucent temperature forms, deliberately exposed polygonal meshes, and floating matter, the work lets computational data become a place to linger. It invites the viewer to move between recognition and uncertainty: to see clouds, currents, constellations, and cellular structures, while remembering that the landscape is entirely constructed from a numerical model. The result is an artificial world with its own texture, atmosphere, and visual history — an image where calculation becomes environment.

presentations.title: An In Situ Computational-learning Framework for the Simulation of the Cardiac Electrical System of a Patient-specific Human Heart
presentations.abstract:
Cardiac arrhythmias are associated with abnormal
propagation of electrical activity through the heart. High-
resolution simulations can capture these dynamics but generate
large data volumes that are expensive to store and transfer. Fixed
output intervals may save redundant states while undersampling
periods of rapid electrical propagation. We propose an adaptive
in situ workflow that learns when simulation states should be
retained. An offline teacher identifies informative voltage states,
and a lightweight causal neural network is embedded directly in
the parallel simulation to make runtime output decisions. The
selected nonuniform data are then used to train a continuous-time
neural operator. Compared with uniform temporal sampling, the
adaptive strategy stores fewer states while improving prediction
accuracy on unseen simulations. The results demonstrate an in
situ connection between high-performance cardiac simulation and
neural operator learning.

presentations.title: An Integrated In-Situ Visualization Framework for Interactive Analysis and Surrogate Modeling
presentations.abstract: Image-based in-situ visualization has become a mature approach that not only helps mitigate notorious I/O bottlenecks, but also facilitates exploratory visual analysis by enabling interactive exploration in the spatiotemporal domain. This approach generates a large collection of visual representations from different viewpoints, and in this work, we extend this approach to surrogate modeling, using the generated visualization images as a common representation that bridges human-centered interactive visual analysis and machine learning. During in-situ visualization, metadata required by existing information-entropy-based smart visualization techniques are also generated. Unlike previous smart in-situ visualization approaches, which try to output only the set of most information-rich rendering images, the proposed framework also outputs the complete set of rendered images for offline surrogate modeling. Our initial results demonstrate the feasibility of training surrogate models directly from the image-based representation generated for visual analysis, enabling learned approximation without requiring the original simulation data.

presentations.title: An LLVM Pass for Automatic Skeletonization of MPI Applications
presentations.abstract:
We present an LLVM pass that automatically skeletonizes MPI
applications: it statically identifies computations that do not affect
the arguments of MPI calls and removes them, producing a much faster
program that preserves the original's communication semantics. The
pass operates on the LLVM IR, propagating a communication
variable status backward from MPI call sites through the program's
data and control dependencies, and handles the non-trivial engineering
challenges (recursion, loops, dynamic libraries, memory allocation)
that arise when applying this analysis to real, non-trivial HPC codes
such as Lulesh and miniFE. We validate that the generated skeletons
reproduce the communication pattern of the original application, and
illustrate one concrete use of this technique: accelerating MPI
runtime tuning by running the parameter search on the skeleton rather
than on the full application.

presentations.title: An MLIR Dialect for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
presentations.abstract: To achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC), a compilation pipeline must address quantum error-correcting codes, syndrome extraction, magic-state distillation, and physical-gate decomposition. We introduce ftqc, an open-source dialect for MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation) that treats these concerns as first-class constructs in the intermediate representation (IR). Logical qubits are type-safe static single-assignment (SSA) values parameterized by their error-correcting code and distance, letting the compiler enforce code and distance compatibility at the type level.
