The dialect provides operations covering the logical life-cycle: encoded initialization, transversal Clifford gates, T gates and Toffoli gates by magic-state injection, syndrome extraction, and distillation. A resource estimator derives physical-qubit counts and logical error rates directly from ECC metadata in the IR, and three validated backends emit OpenQASM 3, QIR (Quantum Intermediate Representation), and Stim. Across four benchmarking quantum circuits, end-to-end compilation completes in under 15 ms, and a full logical-error-rate sweep through Stim runs in under 4 s.

presentations.title: An Omnistat-Guided Workflow for Energy-Efficiency Analysis
presentations.abstract: Large-scale accelerator applications can exhibit variation in device activity and completion times as workloads evolve. Allocation-wide averages may obscure whether reduced activity reflects improved energy efficiency or devices waiting for slower ranks. We present an Omnistat-guided workflow that aligns timestamped node- and accelerator-level telemetry with application timers and algorithmic steps. Omnistat operates in user mode and requires no modification or recompilation. We demonstrate the workflow using a 64-node CRK-HACC cosmological hydrodynamics simulation spanning 512 GCDs and 625 steps. Its evolving particle distribution illustrates how computational heterogeneity manifests in application timings and system telemetry. Dynamic load balancing is disabled to provide a controlled configuration. The analysis shows how cross-rank timing variability propagates to accelerator utilization, frequency, power, and energy. Relating step energy to cross-device power dispersion identifies intervals for load-distribution analysis and phases that may benefit from power management, making Omnistat a practical first-pass diagnostic layer for subsequent profiling and optimization.

presentations.title: Analog Computing for Science: From Emerging Technologies to a Shared Research Agenda
presentations.abstract: Analog computing is re-emerging as a broad approach to scientific computation, offering opportunities beyond energy efficiency, including low-latency physical dynamics, reduced data movement, computation integrated with sensing, and new methods for simulation, optimization, and artificial intelligence. Yet progress remains fragmented across physical substrates, applications, architectures, mathematics, and software. This highly interactive BoF will bring the SC community together to identify challenges, promising workloads, shared infrastructure, and opportunities for collaboration. Building on the DOE ASCR report Basic Research Needs for Analog Computing for Science, participants will prioritize research directions and help shape a community agenda for analog and hybrid analog-digital computing.

presentations.title: Analytical Resource Management for Fine-Grained MoE Computation-Communication Overlap
presentations.abstract:
Fine-grained computation-communication overlap lets distributed Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference start communication on partial results. Compute and communication cooperative thread arrays (CTAs), however, contend for finite streaming-multiprocessor (SM) residency and progress in discrete waves, and a fixed partition cannot adapt to workload or kernel changes.
We present a wave-quantized analytical model and launch-time resource manager that selects the communication-CTA count from routed-tile counts, kernel occupancy, residency constraints, and split-level readiness dependencies before launch, without profiling or recompilation.
We integrate it into the COMET A100 implementation and evaluate three MoE models on four A100 GPUs under three parallelism configurations at the GEMM2+GatherRS operator, complete post-router MoE layer, and complete-model prefill levels.
Speedups over COMET reach 4.218×, 2.584×, and 1.439× at these levels, respectively.
At every feasible TP=2/EP=2 sequence length of at least 4096, our implementation outperforms Megatron core-TE and FastMoE TP+NCCL.

presentations.title: Analyzing the Impact of Architectural Design Decisions on Performance Across Generations of NVIDIA GPUs
presentations.abstract: The high performance computing (HPC) industry is moving past an era in which each new generation of devices provided uniform performance improvements across all workloads. In this work, we profile a diverse suite of applications across multiple generations of NVIDIA HPC GPUs to evaluate how architectural design decisions translate into real-world application performance, in terms of speedup and energy efficiency. The suite of applications was hand-picked to represent the modern HPC landscape; it covers scientific computing, AI inference, AI training, and targeted microbenchmarks. GPU-level performance counters, execution time, power, and energy measurements were collected and analyzed to identify which architectural improvements provide the greatest benefit, which are less impactful, and what workload characteristics determine their effectiveness. Relative to the increase in transistor count, the data exhibits significant performance gains among Tensor Core bound applications, expected gains in memory-bound applications and below-expected gains in vector throughput-bound applications.​

presentations.title: Analyzing User Logs as a First Diagnostic Step in Open OnDemand
presentations.abstract: Open OnDemand (OOD) session failures generate developer-centric logs that may confuse researchers and burden HPC support staff with routine tickets. While large language models (LLMs) provide readable failure explanations, unconstrained models can hallucinate non-existent root causes. We present \textit{LogLight}, an asynchronous diagnostic panel running inside the OOD session card under the invoking user's Linux privileges without elevated service state. LogLight enforces a four-source trust hierarchy that prioritizes deterministic extraction from logs and scheduler accounting, incorporates an advisory site playbook, and restricts the LLM strictly to narrative synthesis. In a blind evaluation across 30 production sessions, binding deterministic findings into prompts significantly improved diagnostic accuracy and attribution over log-only inputs. Grounding enabled a lightweight Mistral-7B model to match the diagnostic performance of a GPT-OSS-20B model, offering an efficient, user-scoped architecture for failure analysis.

presentations.title: Anchor: Delivering Consistent Performance on Noisy Cloud-Based Quantum Computers
presentations.abstract: Quantum computers are becoming an important part of high-performance computing (HPC), with hybrid quantum-classical algorithms combining quantum processors with classical HPC resources. However, unlike classical accelerators, near-term quantum computers do not provide consistent performance. The quality of a program's output can vary from day to day on the same machine and from machine to machine on the same day, making results difficult to reproduce and limiting the use of quantum computers in scientific workflows. We present Anchor, a technique that combines machine-learning-based fidelity prediction with linear programming to distribute program executions across multiple circuit mappings. Compared with state-of-the-art noise-adaptive compilation, Anchor reduces output performance variability by 73% on average.

presentations.title: Annotation-Driven Migration of CUDA Programs to Tenstorrent Blackhole
presentations.abstract: Tenstorrent Blackhole combines distributed local memories, explicit inter-core communication, and Tensix cores decoupling data movement from computation. CUDA offers a substantial HPC software base but leaves physical data placement and scheduling largely implicit. Migrating CUDA HPC kernels to Blackhole requires spatial mapping across cores and per-core coordination of compute and data-movement kernels. We present an MLIR-based compiler deriving data placement, inter-core communication, and tile computation from a statically shaped affine CUDA subset. Declarative annotations express choices not fixed by the source, including compute/DM operation placement and streaming granularity. We evaluate it on Gaussian elimination, five-point stencil, and symmetric rank-k update. Relative to our compiler's default realizations, the best measured configurations achieve a 4.2× speedup for BF16 Gaussian and 2.1–2.2× for FP32 Gaussian and Jacobi. A choice's performance impact can reverse with surrounding policies, precision, and loop schedule, motivating comparison of alternative per-core realizations rather than independent policy selection.

presentations.title: Antarctica: Looking Through the Ice Into the Past
presentations.abstract:
This work is an interdisciplinary collaboration between artists, designers, scientific researchers, and visualization experts. The team aimed to address two primary objectives. To start, we incorporated the human language of art to set the foundation for science communication to open the conversation between communities and the scientific endeavors of the scientist, a part of the NSF Center for Oldest Ice Exploration (COLDEX). The second aim was to assist the team, Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues, in understanding the ice sheet layers they are currently studying.

Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues use airborne ice-penetrating radar, gravity, and magnetic surveys to image the internal structure of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet and the geology hidden beneath more than three kilometers of ice. Their work spans three key regions of East Antarctica — the South Pole region, Dome A, the Allan Hills, and Dome C. These measurements reveal how ice has flowed, deformed, melted, and interacted with the underlying landscapes over millions of years. One of their primary goals is to locate regions where the oldest continuous ice has remained preserved and to understand how the ice sheet layers have changed over time to predict future movements.

Incorporated in the video are artistic representations of the data reflecting the ice sheet layers of Antarctica. These scientifically directed visualizations of the data were transformed into 3D prints that proved to be valuable in communicating with colleagues to determine the next drilling site in Antarctica to test hypotheses. Additionally, the 3D printing allowed the scientists to see and hold a physical representation of their findings.

presentations.title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
presentations.abstract: LLM agents can make expert scientific workflows accessible through natural language, but a plausible response does not establish that the requested computation ran. This matters at synchrotron facilities, where calibration and integration are multi-step operations over terabyte-scale datasets. We present APEXA, a deployed framework coordinating 61 tools for synchrotron data reduction. A deterministic execution-integrity guard prevents it from returning results for tool calls that did not execute, and the same tool layer enforces motor safety: across 50 adversarial scenarios and four models, it produced 0/200 violations against a simulated EPICS controller, versus 15/200 for a prompt-only baseline. We also introduce APEXA-Bench, 58 facility tasks organized by scientific correctness and physical consequence. On real APS beamline data, one prompt recovered detector geometry and integrated a full attenuation and exposure sweep. Trustworthy scientific agents need deterministic validation of execution, not model-side assurances. We release the framework, benchmark, and traces.

presentations.title: Applications, Libraries, and Tools in Modern Fortran (alt.fortran)
presentations.abstract: Fortran plays a crucial role in numerous applications. This BoF provides a forum for Fortran developers to engage with the language's modern programming features. With features introduced in recent language revisions, Fortran 2023 supports modern programming practices and high performance computing (HPC). This BoF gathers developers from diverse domains to share experiences and explore Fortran's evolving capabilities. After some brief presentations, the session will focus on an interactive discussion where audience members will be encouraged to share their own experiences and ask questions of our experts.

presentations.title: APQF: Agentic Profiling-Guided Structured Pruning and Mixed-Precision Quantization with Adaptive Fine-Tuning
presentations.abstract: Deep neural networks are powerful but too large to run cheaply on edge devices. Pruning and quantization help, but deciding how and where to compress a model is still manual, or relies on algorithms that are hard to apply across architectures. We introduce APQF, an agentic profiling-guided framework that combines structured pruning, mixed-precision quantization-aware training, and accuracy recovery in one automated pipeline. A profiling agent measures cost distribution and pruning sensitivity, which then drive per-group pruning ratios, per-layer bit-widths, and the recovery strategy. Our experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 show that APQF compresses convolutional and transformer models further than a joint pruning and quantization baseline at comparable or higher accuracy, and stays stable across different planners, including free open-weight ones.

presentations.title: ARC-FL: Fault-Tolerant Federated Learning via Error-bounded Lossy Compression and Unequal Error Protection
presentations.abstract: Federated Learning(FL) trains models across clients without sharing local data, but its iterative training process requires frequent transmission of model updates and introduces high communication overhead. Error-bounded lossy compression can effectively reduce this overhead. However, existing studies mainly focus on data reduction and accuracy but have limited attention to communication reliability. Compressed bitstreams are sensitive to transmission errors, and a few corruptions can cause an entire model layer to fail reconstruction. We propose ARC-FL, a framework that combines hierarchical compression with unequal error protection. ARC-FL assigns model layers to three protection levels by parameter update magnitude and uses a layer-wise fallback for partial decoding failures. At a BER of 3E-3, equal error protection(EEP) with strong protection fails to maintain model convergence in several configurations. Meanwhile, ARC-FL preserves meaningful accuracy across all tested architectures and datasets and achieves up to 7.5x the accuracy of EEP in the most affected configuration.

presentations.title: ArchAgent: Agentic AI for Heterogeneous System Design Across Chip, Scale-Up, and Scale-Out Domains
presentations.abstract: The design space for modern AI/HPC systems has expanded rapidly across compute architectures (GPUs, dataflow processors, and RISC-V accelerators), memory technologies (HBM, GDDR, and SRAM), and interconnects (NVLink, UALink, Infinity Fabric, InfiniBand, Slingshot, and Ultra Ethernet). No single architecture is optimal for LLM training, LLM serving, and AI-coupled HPC, while the resulting combinatorial design space is too large for manual exploration. We present \textbf{ArchAgent}, a hierarchical multi-agent framework in which an LLM-based planner decomposes system design into chip, scale-up, and scale-out subproblems handled by specialist agents. A deterministic analytical evaluator closes the loop, ensuring all performance estimates come from analytical models rather than the LLM. On a mixed AI+HPC workload under a 1 MW power budget, ArchAgent discovers heterogeneous designs delivering a 1.93× weighted geometric mean speedup over a homogeneous GPU baseline, outperforming 100-evaluation hill climbing (1.65×) after only 18 evaluations.

presentations.title: Architecting Multi-Petabyte Data Migration in a Live HPC Environment: From Strategy to Execution
presentations.abstract: Large-scale storage migrations are among the most challenging operational activities in high-performance computing (HPC) environments due to the need to preserve workflow continuity while moving petabyte-scale datasets across storage platforms. This paper presents the planning and execution of a live migration of 900 research projects totaling 3.28 PB of data across 3.30 billion files from Lustre-based storage to a VAST Data filesystem. We implemented a technology-agnostic namespace using automount abstractions and dual datapaths to decouple workflow migration from data movement. Supported by a custom toolchain for metadata-preservation, our pipeline integrated project prioritization, pre-copy transfers, incremental synchronization, and automated validation. Despite being a fully-managed migration, this framework minimized administrative overhead, preserved filesystem integrity, and achieved zero user-reported tickets for workflow disruption.

presentations.title: AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System for Intelligent HPC User Support
presentations.abstract:
AI question-answering assistants increasingly serve user support at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities, but they offer no systematic way to judge answer quality in production or attribute a bad answer to the component at fault, and they stay static after deployment apart from knowledge-base updates.

We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline that scores each production interaction, identifies whether a failure lies in missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and routes it to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core pairs answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test separating information absent from the corpus from information present but never retrieved. Controlled harness training, supervised by expert references and null-edit controls, improves the pipeline itself.

Across 2,174 support turns AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%, and harness training raised agreement with expert labels from 108/150 to 123/150 turns, a governed self-evolution driven by production evidence.

presentations.title: Asynchrony Promotes Scalable Recovery of Iterative Linear Solvers from Silent Errors
presentations.abstract: Distributed memory linear solvers are the workhorse of many scientific HPC applications and are also close counterparts to AI algorithms. The increasing scale and heterogeneity of HPC systems renders them susceptible to silent data corruption (SDC). Physics based checksums (PBCs) can detect SDC errors locally on each computing node. Detection can be followed by rollback to a checkpoint: however, this localized checkpointing does not scale optimally as fault rates increase. Increased asynchrony in Krylov solvers promotes scalability of fault recovery from SDC errors. We focus on the s-step communication-avoiding conjugate gradient (CACG), and describe the algorithmic changes needed to implement PBCs to protect all portions of the CACG algorithm. Our results show that local recovery incurs much lower overhead and remains scalable at much higher node counts and fault rates compared to global recovery and that as fault rates increase, the benefit of asynchrony increases.

presentations.title: Auditing drug-response transfer at scale: an HPC-parallel, IMPROVE-conformant control pipeline
presentations.abstract:
Deciding which cell-line-to-clinic drug-response transfer gains are real, rather than artifacts of a
favorable seed or an uneven cohort, is not one large computation but thousands of small independent ones: each claim must be scored one drug at a time, under leak-free cross-validation, against a matched negative control, and repeated over seeds. We present the HPC harness that makes this audit routine on a single multi-GPU node. The pipeline is IMPROVE-conformant - one data model and one central metrics module across cell lines, xenografts, organoids, and patients - and its unit of work is a (dataset, method, drug-shard, seed) tuple. Drugs are partitioned disjointly by p mod num_shards so workers never race; a flexible pinned-slot scheduler auto-detects the device count and keeps exactly one job per GPU, refilling each device the instant its job exits; and several small experiments are packed onto disjoint GPU subsets to saturate the node. The statistical nulls are the primary parallel workload-per-drug label permutations and a 5,000-resample paired bootstrap fan-out with the same sharding, and a memory-efficient attention kernel fits a genomic foundation-model probe into 16GB. The same scripts scale down to one GPU, so every result is bit-reproducible. Run at this scale with a null on every claim, the science is sobering: a feature-free base-rate predictor reproduces a published transfer model's discrimination (r=0.94 across four cohorts), the training loss beats the encoder
(0.81 vs 0.42 rank correlation).

presentations.title: Automated Design Space Exploration of ARM CMN-Based HPC Architectures: A Case Study for the European Rhea Family Processors
presentations.abstract: The Network-on-Chip (NoC) is a major determinant of memory-system performance in modern high-performance computing (HPC) processors. Configurable coherent interconnects such as Arm Coherent Mesh Networks (CMNs) represent large design spaces involving request and home nodes, memory interfaces, queue resources, and node placement. This paper presents an automated multi-objective design-space exploration methodology combining automated Design Space Exploration (DSE) framework, Arm Performance Models, and industrial architecture-generation tools. The methodology is evaluated on a representative CMN-S3 subsystem defined in the context of future processors of the European Rhea family, exploring the organization of the coherent interconnect and memory subsystem while keeping the compute architecture fixed. Results highlight the importance of balancing request and home/cache resources to sustain DDR bandwidth while controlling implementation cost. The automated exploration identifies the same Pareto optimal configurations as exhaustive evaluation using only $26$ of $343$ valid configurations, reducing total exploration time from approximately $140$~h to $2$~h.

presentations.title: Automated Isolation of Vulnerable Workloads
presentations.abstract: Kubernetes and OpenShift support scientific services, data platforms, and artificial-intelligence workflows at high performance computing facilities. Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (RHACS/StackRox) identifies vulnerable images, policy violations, and risky deployments, but operators still must interpret risk and coordinate containment. That handoff is slow; immediate deny-all isolation can interrupt shared services before owners remediate. We present an automated, risk-based system that converts RHACS findings into controlled Kubernetes NetworkPolicy actions. A shared backend classifies risk, assigns configurable remediation windows, stores workload state, and applies or removes managed policies. Dashboard, CLI, operator, REST API, and Splunk integrations support manual and automated response. Namespace scoping, policy simulation, rollback, opt-out metadata, and structured audit events preserve operational control. Prototype validation demonstrates end-to-end detection, tracking, containment, and recovery for representative vulnerable workloads. Together, these mechanisms make response timing visible, repeatable, and recoverable instead of relying on ad hoc operator judgment.

presentations.title: Automated Task Placement for Hybrid HPC-Serverless Workflows
presentations.abstract: Serverless computing offers HPC workflows elastic capacity, but only some tasks fit its runtime and memory limits, and finding them has required manual placement. We separate two questions that manual placement conflates: deployment-independent candidacy, which combines platform limits with task-level heuristics and is settled before execution, and deployment-dependent placement, which turns on how much workflow parallelism the local allocation absorbs. Our framework combines static DAG analysis with one bounded profiling run per task type to assign each a candidacy class, then splits candidates across local and serverless backends without per-task input. In a single-run campaign on Epigenomics, Seismology, and Cycles, hybrid execution reaches the lowest observed makespan of three strategies, but the margin tracks how capacity-constrained each workflow is: 65.0% on Seismology against 4.9% and 9.0%. Withholding the task types the analysis rejects lowers observed makespan a further 9.8–39.9%, and dispatch costs a median of 221 µs.

presentations.title: Autonomous Science Network: A Grassroots Community for Trustworthy Science
presentations.abstract: Autonomous experiment operation is demonstrating the ability to dramatically improve the pace of scientific discovery. This BoF convenes a community to continue building on the early two-year roadmap, discussing how different teams are using agentic workflows to improve the potential for new discovery and to address the related need to verify the new results.

presentations.title: Awards and Closing Remarks by ISAV OC
Awards Ceremony and Conclusion
Back to the Future for HPC and Cancer: The Transformative Next Decade in Cancer Research and Cancer Care
presentations.abstract: A decade ago, in 2016, the U.S. National Cancer Institute and the U.S. Department of Energy announced their truly unique collaboration to take advantage of each agency's strengths, bringing together the power of emerging exascale systems and the collective data, knowledge, and wisdom of the cancer community. With the advances of the last decade in HPC, AI, and availability of cancer clinical and research data, the opportunities ahead are tremendous to improve cancer care. Enabled by HPC, the next decade will be truly transformative as clinical opportunities and potential are realized, research connections are made, and the paths for translation of data science insights to treat patients are widened. The panel will reflect on the experiences and advances of the past decade, share insights on current challenges, and look ahead to the future as HPC unites communities to take on cancer.

presentations.title: BASE: A Reusable Streaming Preprocessing Accelerator for Heterogeneous FPGA Systems
presentations.abstract:
Modern heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) systems increasingly rely on FPGA-based accelerators to improve throughput and energy efficiency for data-intensive applications. However, many streaming workloads remain constrained by byte-level preprocessing and data movement, which can dominate end-to-end execution time.
This paper presents BASE (Byte-level Analytics and Statistical Engine), a reusable streaming preprocessing accelerator that integrates statistical feature extraction directly into the FPGA communication path. BASE performs single-pass histogram generation, entropy estimation, variance computation, and byte-transition analysis while data is transferred through the AXI DMA interface, overlapping preprocessing with communication and reducing host-side computation.
Using deployment-time FPGA bitstream screening as a representative workload, experiments on the ZCU104 show that BASE reduces preprocessing latency by 5.04× and improves end-to-end execution time by 4.23×. On the U55C, BASE achieves 1.32× preprocessing and 1.78× end-to-end speedups. These results demonstrate BASE’s potential as a reusable building block for streaming analytics in reconfigurable HPC systems.

presentations.title: Batched GPU Execution for High-Throughput Combinatorial Search
presentations.abstract: Simplifiable strong uniquely solvable puzzles (SUSPs) connect combinatorial search to upper bounds on the matrix-multiplication exponent. The process of evaluating each candidate requires expensive parallel workloads, which have been handled efficiently using GPUs. However, the existing search sent one candidate at a time to a GPU, so allocation, data transfer, and synchronization cost all the benefits of fast evaluation on a GPU. We redesigned the search by batching same-size candidates into one kernel launch. Besides that, we also optimized the workflow by decoupling GPU work from multi-threaded search expansion on the CPU. In our experiments, the single-GPU pipeline raised end-to-end throughput by 3.09–5.75 times, while the double-GPU pipeline could achieve over 11 times. With a new, better search program, we found a new (79, 10)-SUSP, improving on the best width-10 result reported by Anderson and Le.

presentations.title: Benchmarking Agentic AI Workflows with Charliecloud
presentations.abstract:
Agentic AI workflows are an emerging paradigm in the AI space that enable autonomous agents
to drive the traditional prompt token response through multi-step reasoning, tool calling, and
planning phases. Recent advances to orchestrate production level frameworks such as these
are trending towards using LLM inference engines such as vLLM and model abstraction layers like LiteLLM. Charliecloud enhances this work by leveraging portability across diverse HPC
systems. In this talk, we address why such frameworks are leveraging these tools with
Charliecloud and how we can assess end-to-end performance of these workflows through
benchmarking.

presentations.title: Benchmarking AI Vector Databases for Genesis Mission
presentations.abstract:
In support of the Genesis Mission, the U.S. government's national AI initiative, Circe is an HPC-hosted AI service environment that supports model access, custom knowledge databases, and external tool integration. A central feature of Circe is effective retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which requires streamlined vector databases. This work aims to identify and recommend the best-performing vector database backend for Circe's RAG services, promoting efficient and accurate query retrieval at scale.

We benchmarked five databases—Qdrant, Redis, Weaviate, ChromaDB, and Elasticsearch—using Qdrant's vector-db-benchmark framework, comparing their scalability, query speed, latency, and retrieval accuracy across three configurations. Redis achieved the strongest baseline performance, with Weaviate following closely behind. With tuning, Weaviate reached the highest throughput (3,002.3 requests per second), while Qdrant demonstrated the largest proportional improvement (620.0 to 1,504.3 requests per second). We conclude that Weaviate is the strongest candidate for maximum query speed, while Qdrant offers the greatest flexibility for tuning.

presentations.title: Benchmarking Physical GCD Placement Effects on Performance, Energy, and Co-Execution
presentations.abstract: GPU-accelerated supercomputers expose large populations of nominally identical resources that are often treated as interchangeable, even though physical device variability can affect performance and energy efficiency. This is particularly relevant for multi-die accelerators and workload co-execution, where outcomes depend on both workload compatibility and physical placement. We characterize these effects on Frontier using six synthetic workload classes. A solo campaign covers 600 node allocations and 4,800 AMD Instinct MI250X Graphics Compute Die (GCD) observations, while co-execution evaluates all workload pairs across 72 representative physical placements using matched solo baselines. Across the sampled population, best-to-worst GCD differences reach 18.7% in performance, 32.3% in average GPU-package power, and 36.9% in energy. Complementary co-executions approach ideal overlap and reduce energy by approximately 40%. Workload compatibility determines whether sharing is beneficial, while physical GCD placement determines its magnitude and stability, motivating GCD-aware scheduling to improve science per watt.

presentations.title: Beyond FLOPS and Kernels: Benchmarking Agentic Science and the Future Role of Python
presentations.abstract:
Python has become the dominant language for scientific computing, AI, and high-performance computing workflows. As supercomputing enters an era increasingly shaped by foundation models, autonomous agents, and AI-guided scientific discovery, the community faces a fundamental question: what should we benchmark next?

This panel brings together leaders from HPC, AI, and scientific software to discuss how benchmarks can continue to influence system architecture in the age of agentic workflows. Should future benchmarks measure isolated kernels and application performance, or end-to-end scientific outcomes? How do we evaluate systems that combine simulation, machine learning, retrieval, reasoning, and autonomous decision-making? And what role should Python play as the orchestration layer for increasingly heterogeneous and distributed computing environments? Panelists will explore whether Python can serve as the foundation for next-generation benchmarks and how benchmark design can guide the architecture of future AI-enabled supercomputers.

presentations.title: Beyond Job Submission: Developing System Literacy through Productive Struggle
presentations.abstract: High-performance computing training reliably teaches users how to submit jobs. It rarely equips them to reason about why their work behaves as it does on a shared system. At a PEARC26 Birds-of-a-Feather session on system literacy, practitioners nearly all agreed that users should hold a working mental model of system behavior, and nearly all reported that users do not. We argue that this gap persists because system literacy is formed incidentally rather than taught: users assemble their own models from documentation, experience, and chance interactions, producing models that vary widely in accuracy and surface as uneven productivity on shared infrastructure. We locate the mechanism by which such models are revised in productive struggle, the calibrated difficulty skilled facilitators already sustain when they diagnose the misconception behind an error rather than only correcting it. Whether that practice can be scaled is the question we pose.

presentations.title: Beyond the Add-On: Absorbing Quantum Into the HPC Ecosystem
presentations.abstract:
Quantum computing has often been integrated with HPC systems as an add-on: scheduled through custom adapters, monitored through bespoke hooks, bolted onto facilities as parallel infrastructure. This reflects how most sites operate today, but it stops short of deep integration and does not provide the right foundation for the decade ahead.

The alternative view holds that quantum and HPC should be designed as one holistic system from the start, with quantum resources running through the same schedulers, workflow engines, and observability systems already in place. SC26 arrives at an inflection point: nine DOE national laboratories are actively deploying quantum systems, IBM has published its Quantum-Centric Supercomputing reference architecture, and DOE has launched the $293 million Genesis Mission targeting quantum-AI-HPC convergence. The systems are going in. This panel asks how to design that integration correctly from day one rather than assembling it as a series of bolt-ons.

presentations.title: Beyond the GPU: The Future of AI Acceleration in the Zettascale Era
presentations.abstract: The rapid evolution of AI is driving unprecedented innovation in computing architectures, from GPUs and AI accelerators to novel memory, networking, and system designs. This BoF brings together leaders from industry, academia, and national laboratories to discuss emerging directions in AI acceleration for future zettascale systems. Rather than focusing on specific products, participants will explore common challenges in architecture, programmability, scalability, energy efficiency, software ecosystems, and deployment at scale. The session will emphasize audience interaction, community discussion, and roadmap development, providing attendees an opportunity to help shape the future of AI acceleration and AI-enabled supercomputing.

presentations.title: Beyond the helpdesk: a lightweight, reproducible model for just-in-time HPC learning and support
presentations.abstract:
Formal HPC courses and individual helpdesk interactions address different user needs, but leave a gap for users who need timely guidance on practical problems without requiring a full course or a one-to-one support case. JSC HPC Support Corner, a monthly one-hour online session designed to make HPC expertise more accessible. It has the following structure: a 10-15 minute expert presentation, topic-specific Q&A, open discussion, and live troubleshooting. Participants can submit questions in advance in a shared document, and Zoom breakout rooms can be used for dedicated discussions. The sessions also serve as an orientation and awareness-raising channel, helping users discover services and workflows that are not necessarily covered in formal courses or encountered through individual support requests.

This work describes the educational rationale, distributed organisation, lessons learned, evaluation, and a reproducible workflow that other HPC centres can adapt as a complement to formal training and ticket-based support.

presentations.title: Beyond the Terminal: Career Coaching
presentations.abstract: The afternoon career coaching sessions give students the opportunity to participate in focused career conversations with HPC and AI professionals. These 10-15 minute, one-on-one sessions are designed to give students personalized guidance on career questions, résumés, graduate school decisions, job searches, technical growth, and professional next steps. Students will select their preferred coach in advance and are encouraged to come prepared with specific questions and goals so they can make the most of each conversation.

presentations.title: BFS-FAR: Fragment-Local Asynchronous Relaxation with Host Reconciliation for Breadth-First Search on UPMEM
presentations.abstract: Breadth-first search (BFS) is difficult to accelerate because of irregular memory accesses, limited computation per edge, and frequent synchronization. Processing-in-Memory (PIM) offers high memory-level parallelism, but level-synchronous BFS is ill-suited to UPMEM because DRAM Processing Units (DPUs) cannot communicate directly and must coordinate through the host. To address this, we present BFS-FAR, an execution model that replaces strict level-by-level synchronization with fragment-local progress and update-aware reconciliation. BFS-FAR partitions graphs into per-DPU CSR fragments, performs in-place local relaxation, and reconciles replicated levels through a parallel host-side minimum reduction. Experiments on R-MAT and synthetic graphs using up to 2,540 DPUs show 18.0-86.5 algorithm-only speedups over PrIM-BFS, although CPU_64T remains faster because host-mediated coordination still limits complete BFS performance. These results highlight execution model and communication granularity as key design considerations for irregular PIM workloads.

presentations.title: BFS-FAR: Fragmented Asynchronous Breadth-First Search on UPMEM Processing-in-Memory
presentations.abstract:
Breadth-first search (BFS) is difficult to accelerate because of irregular memory access, low work per edge, and frequent synchronization. On UPMEM Processing-in-Memory systems, DPUs cannot communicate directly, so existing PIM-BFS designs rely heavily on host-mediated frontier exchange.

We present BFS-FAR, a completed fragmented BFS design that combines locally asynchronous relaxation within each DPU with host-side minimum-level reconciliation. Its key contribution is allowing improved levels to be reused within the same DPU launch, reducing repeated global frontier exchange and host coordination. Experiments using up to 2,540 DPUs cover R-MAT graphs with approximately 262K–4.2M vertices and 4.2M–67.1M directed edges, and controlled-size synthetic graphs ranging from 200K vertices and 10M edges to 13.6M vertices and 730M edges. BFS-FAR achieves 18.0×–86.5× algorithm-only speedup over UPMEM baseline, PrIM-BFS.

The poster will present the BFS-FAR workflow, performance results, timing breakdowns, DPU scaling, and the effects of locality and workload balance.

presentations.title: Bigger Networks, More Trajectories: Scaling Exact Stochastic Simulation on GPUs Through Sparse Storage and a Warp-ary Propensity Tree
presentations.abstract:
Exact stochastic simulation of biochemical networks requires large trajectory ensembles for increasingly large reaction models, creating two main bottlenecks: dense model storage can exceed device memory, while serial reaction selection costs O(M) per step.

We built an exact GPU Gillespie solver in Lattice Microbes software that stores stoichiometry and the reaction dependency graph in a compressed sparse row format and selects reactions using a warp-cooperative 32-ary propensity tree in O(log₃₂M). Our major contribution combines sparse storage with warp-cooperative logarithmic selection for exact GPU SSA. The solver is implemented and validated against StochKit2; release in Lattice Microbes v3.0 is planned.

On an NVIDIA B200 across five models with 18–58,276 reactions, memory use decreases by ~800×, enabling up to 100K trajectories where other tools run out of memory. This poster presents the algorithm, sparse data layout, scaling, and comparative performance, including up to ~20× higher throughput where competing tools still fit.

presentations.title: Biological Interfaces
presentations.abstract:
Water at biological interfaces contributes substantially to the mechanical behavior of membranes, yet how it responds to mechanical stress is not well characterized. This artwork was developed from molecular simulations, which examined how lateral tension influences interfacial water in lipid model membranes representative of mammalian and bacterial composition under physiological conditions.

In the resting state, interfacial water organizes into hydrogen-bonded networks, with small ring-like arrangements linking adjacent lipid. In the video, these ring-like arrangements are highlighted by the glowing planes between golden spheres. When lateral stress is applied, these arrangements persist in one mammalian membrane type, while in the other, stress-induced flattening of the membrane surface causes interfacial water to become partially decoupled from the lipid interface. This differential behavior points to a close relationship between a membrane's mechanical properties and the structural organization of its associated water network, offering insight into the mechanisms by which interfacial water contributes to membrane resilience under mechanical load. Whilst the video is mostly for aesthetical purposes, the findings of the molecular simulations suggest that interfacial water is not merely a passive boundary layer but an active participant in membrane stability that responds dynamically to stress, with implications extending across biophysics, drug design, and the study of biological adaptation.

presentations.title: Bit-Identical Substitution of LLM-Translated C++ into Production Fortran, and What It Certifies
presentations.abstract: LLM Fortran-to-C++ translation is usually evaluated by compilation success, similarity metrics, or tests on isolated functions. However, none of these establishes substitutability: whether a translated function can replace the original in production without changing results. Reported here are two migration campaigns held to that standard by VIT (Verified Incremental Translator). VIT generates the interoperability code, and the LLM writes only the algorithmic function body. Each body passes two bit-identical gates, replay against captured production state and whole-simulation baselines. ROSCO, a wind-turbine controller, was fully translated to C++; 2.56 million nontrivial outputs match exactly across 27 scenarios. In OpenFAST’s AeroDyn, ten times ROSCO’s size, 33 of 507 procedures are translated under the same gates and tool. Of fourteen injected defects, three pass both gates. Thus, bit-identity certifies agreement on exercised inputs, not equivalence of two implementations, and as translation becomes inexpensive, the verification oracle becomes the limiting factor in migration.

presentations.title: Blended Infrastructure for Advanced Computational Workflows: From Accelerated Discovery to Agentic Automation
presentations.abstract: As HPC accelerates into an era of hybrid infrastructure and pervasive AI, computational research increasingly calls for optimizing blended on-prem and cloud infrastructure for advanced workflows that will accelerate future discoveries. This session begins with the drivers: cutting-edge science workflows challenging traditional infrastructure, and agentic AI workflows that autonomously drive the entire scientific loop from hypothesis generation to results analysis. We then review the current capabilities and gaps for managing and using blended HPC infrastructure as the backbone of these advanced workflows. Attendees will engage in discussion and interactive polling, collaboratively identifying gaps and opportunities for the community to address.

presentations.title: BlueField Assisted Resiliency Framework
presentations.abstract:
Efficient checkpoint/restart mechanisms are critical for high-performance computing systems, where long-running applications must quickly recover from failures to maintain productivity and resource efficiency. However, all current checkpoint/restart mechanisms rely on the host CPU, introducing cache contention and operating-system jitter. To address this issue, we present a BlueField-Assisted Resiliency Framework, AURORA: Accelerated User-space Remote Offload for Resilient Applications.
Unlike traditional methods that consume significant CPU resources, SmartNIC-assisted checkpoint/restart offloads IO-bound processes to the SmartNIC, allowing truly parallel operation between the host and its recovery mechanism. Through experimental microbenchmarks, we show that AURORA dramatically reduces host overhead, unlocking up to 10% faster runtimes for CPU-bound HPC workloads when compared to traditional host-based mechanisms.

presentations.title: Boiling the Ocean ... Literally
presentations.abstract:
The video shows monthly averaged sea surface temperature anomalies in the North Atlantic since 1980. The colors represent warming and cooling up to 2026 compared to the monthly averages from 1980 to 1995. The visualization highlights the rapid speed at which our oceans have been warming in a period of just over 45 years.

The video was made as realistic as possible with satellite imagery, realistic atmosphere thickness and density, a topography map and the use of ray-traced renders to present the data as realistically and prominently as possible.

presentations.title: Brain Dump: HPC Experts Volunteer To Be Replaced by AI
presentations.abstract: To cement their legacies, a group of HPC luminaries have generously volunteered to be replaced by AI. They have kindly agreed to provide expert responses to prevalent chatbot queries regarding HPC, thus generating natural-intelligence content for AI training. We must acknowledge, however, that our experts may have ulterior motives regarding some topics, and we must take steps to avoid data poisoning. We need audience participation from people like you to detect and label fallacious content!

presentations.title: Breaking the Chain: Geometry-Native State Preparation with ASPIRE
presentations.abstract: Loading data into quantum computers is a key bottleneck threatening end-to-end quantum advantage. Compilers for structured states, like matrix product states (MPS), help manage this bottleneck in quantum chemistry, finance, and many-body simulation. Approximate MPS preparation typically uses layered staircases of nearest-neighbor gates. We present Adaptive State Preparation by Iterative Removal of Entanglement (ASPIRE). ASPIRE approximately compiles state-preparation circuits by selecting gates using the state's entanglement geometry and target processor's connectivity. It scores candidate qubit pairs on entanglement removability and identifies layers of parallel long-range gates removing the most entanglement. We test ASPIRE on Hamiltonian ground states and multivariate amplitude-encoded functions, including qubit connectivity, hardware noise, NISQ, and early-fault-tolerant settings. For states with long-range entanglement, ASPIRE typically achieves higher fidelities and shallower circuits than existing methods, even including classical optimization. ASPIRE is a competitive, resource-frugal protocol, especially promising for applications tolerant to imperfect fidelity, like quantum phase estimation guide states.

presentations.title: Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines : From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine
presentations.abstract: In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView's ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum J\"ulich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.

presentations.title: Bridging Reasoning and Verification: A Generative AI Approach to Chemistry
presentations.abstract: While modern language models can perform high-level chemical reasoning, they often struggle to propose solutions to chemical design tasks that adhere to known principles of chemical validity or synthesizability. Here, we introduce CHARGE, a Chemistry-tool Augmented Reasoning-based Generative framework that combines large-scale reasoning models with automated tool calling to tackle molecular discovery and design challenges. We integrate cheminformatics utilities and neural-network property predictors into the reasoning loop, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation, verification, and refinement without user intervention. Across 10 molecule design tasks, CHARGE consistently designs molecules with improved properties compared to the unaugmented LLM baseline. For the task of predicting chemical synthesis outcomes, we show that the tool-assisted reasoning of CHARGE increases synthesis prediction accuracy from 12% to 40%. Together, these results point towards an agentic AI chemistry workflow, whereby LLMs provide flexible scientific reasoning and orchestration, while robust cheminformatics tools verify and guide the molecular design.

presentations.title: Bridging the Semantic Gap in Long-Term Agent Memory Retrieval
presentations.abstract: LLM-based agents perform well across many tasks but still struggle with long-term interactions requiring coherence, continuity, and personalization. LLM-based agents often use RAG-style memory systems to retrieve past experiences, but direct query–memory similarity can fail when user queries and fine-grained memories are semantically misaligned. We address this semantic gap with an iterative, anchor-guided retrieval strategy inspired by spreading activation in associative memory. Starting from a small set of seed memories, the method expands through global semantic associations and local temporal neighbors, while a path-aware cross-encoder selects complementary evidence across multiple hops. Retrieved memories are accumulated and reused as anchors for further exploration.

presentations.title: Bringing OpenACC to LLVM’s Offload Stack: Dialect Contracts, Lowering Boundaries, and a First-Class ACC Runtime
presentations.abstract: OpenACC support in LLVM spans Flang and Clang frontends, an MLIR acc dialect with in-dialect transforms, and an offload runtime. Frontends already lower directives into acc IR. This paper presents the dialect design and IR contracts that keep transforms frontend-agnostic via type and operation interfaces rather than source-language IR. The mid-level form lets the compiler discover OpenACC's implicit aspects, notably data attributes and parallelism. We describe the compiler-runtime boundary: what MLIR decides versus what the runtime ABI must understand, including non-contiguous values whose layout is deferred to the runtime. We then present libacctarget, an OpenACC runtime in LLVM Offload that shares infrastructure with libomptarget via libompaccsupport while owning ACC-specific mapping, reference counting, async queues, and map kinds. We evaluate a Fortran-first path: a derived-type field-section case study, SPECaccel measurements of implicit data and late privatization, and the OpenACC VV suite as a probe of contracts that execute end to end

presentations.title: Bringing Quantum Computing to the HPC Datacenter
presentations.abstract: As quantum computing matures, challenges with the adoption of this technology shift from theoretical feasibility to practical deployment within established supercomputing infrastructures. This BoF examines the holistic framework required to operationalize quantum systems, from the physical datacenter floor requirements to the high-level application layer. We dive into the complex interplay between infrastructure installation, platform requirements, security protocols, and the necessary evolution of the software stack to support quantum algorithms and hybrid QC-HPC workflows. As such, this BoF outlines a strategic blueprint for building resilient, high-performance quantum-classical hybrid computing environments suitable for next-generation scientific discovery.

presentations.title: Buffer
Building a Kubernetes-first, sovereign HPC system: OpenCUBE
presentations.abstract: Based on the need to define a vendor-neutral deployment-ready platform for European hardware we set out develop a software stack for system and user management, promoting performance, energy efficiency, and programming efficacy in a heterogeneous computing system. We will report on how the OpenCUBE testbed system is now using OpenCHAMI, Talos, and the Slingshot network, together with classic storage as well as OpenFAM, to implement an ‘everything is a container’ k8s-based environment on SiPearl’s Rhea processor and Semidynamic’s RISC-V accelerator bitstream (EPAC2).

presentations.title: Building a Local Chapter as Civic Infrastructure: Chicago Women in HPC and the Quantum × HPC Pathways Initiative
Building a Trusted Agentic AI system for HPC Systems Management
presentations.abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) systems are large, complex environments comprising thousands of compute nodes, high-speed networks, storage systems, and dedicated management infrastructure. Despite the availability of advanced monitoring and management tools, users and administrators often face challenges due to the volume of operational data, the complexity of system interactions, and the expertise required to effectively interpret and act on available information. Recent advances in agentic AI (artificial intelligence) offer new opportunities for more autonomous, context-aware, and collaborative system management. In this work, we present an HPC Systems Management Copilot that integrates a collection of intelligent agents capable of interacting with job schedulers, monitoring frameworks, system databases, and other HPC management services. The copilot provides real-time assistance to users and administrators through a unified natural-language interface. We also present an experimental evaluation assessing the capabilities, effectiveness, and safety of the proposed system across representative HPC management scenarios.

presentations.title: Building an HPC User Documentation Process Via Layers of Writing Infrastructure
presentations.abstract: We are technical communication scholars working as guest faculty researchers at Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF) at Argonne National Laboratory in Lemont, IL. We research documentation processes for high performance computing (HPC). We are building an applied theory of writing infrastructure to model these processes. Building and maintaining user documentation that is responsive to changing user needs and technologies for complex computing systems, such as the exascale machine Aurora, is challenging. It is a whole-facility endeavor that depends on layers of writing infrastructure that are built incrementally over time. This poster builds on our model of the documentation process for the supercomputer Aurora. It traces the timeline of building the layers of writing infrastructure, such as cross-cutting committees, networked communication tools and diverse document types, to illustrate how the process was implemented. Takeaways include the importance of a collaborative culture for documentation and a metric-driven culture of continuous improvement.

presentations.title: Building and Managing Exascale HPC/AI Supercomputing Infrastructure
presentations.abstract:
Designing and operating exascale infrastructure for HPC and AI workloads is no longer a distant challenge — it is accelerating faster than ever, bringing unprecedented complexity in performance, cost, scalability, and security. National labs, hyperscalers, neo-clouds, commercial enterprises, and academic centers all face these problems, often arriving at very different solutions shaped by their workloads, regulatory contexts, supply chains, and economics.

This 90-minute panel brings together operators from across the sector to compare approaches, debate trade-offs, and surface the practical lessons most worth carrying across organizational boundaries. Topics under discussion include cost-effective scaling, exascale data movement, security and multi-tenancy, energy and power management, and operational resilience.

The panel delivers insights that benefit the broader HPC and AI ecosystem — turning isolated operational lessons into a shared, comparative view, aligned with the theme of SC26: HPC Unites.

presentations.title: Building Gigawatt-Scale Infrastructure for AI
presentations.abstract: The explosive scale of generative AI models demands highly specialized infrastructure. This panel explores the critical challenges of building and scaling dedicated AI clusters tailored specifically to the modern model lifecycle: massive-scale pre-training, nuanced post-training, and high-throughput, capacity-demanding inference. As models scale to trillions of parameters, infrastructure must deliver unprecedented compute density, ultra-low latency interconnects, data processing, reliability requirements, parallelisms, and continuous I/O throughput. Our panelists will dissect the unique hardware and software bottlenecks inherent to each phase. We will debate the most effective strategies for mitigating hardware failures at scale, optimizing distributed storage pipelines, and tackling power constraints. This interactive 90-minute session will equip attendees with actionable insights into architecting the resilient, high-performance systems required to power the next generation of generative AI breakthroughs.

presentations.title: Building Research Computing Capacity Through Collaborative Visualization
presentations.abstract: Access to high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) does not ensure their effective use in research. Investigators also need workflows that fit their data, expertise, and research questions. This extended abstract describes a collaborative approach to research computing at the University of Chicago Research Computing Center. The approach combines scientific visualization, GPU-accelerated analysis, and hands-on support across research disciplines. Three examples illustrate its application: biomedical image segmentation using 3D Slicer and MONAI, a cultural heritage reconstruction deployed to a display wall and a VR headset, and Gaussian splat workflows for interactive digital twins. A browser-based viewer also supports remote exploration and the exchange of annotations. Beyond individual projects, five workshops have engaged more than 75 participants. These activities show how reusable workflows, consultation, and training can connect computing resources to research practice.

presentations.title: Building Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories with the INTERSECT Federated Ecosystem
presentations.abstract: Failure resilience in federated ecosystems for instrument science presents a critical challenge. Failures disrupt experiments and make them potentially useless, wasting valuable resources and creating setbacks. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Self-driven Experiments for Science / Interconnected Science Ecosystem (INTERSECT) offers a federated ecosystem for instrument science, enabling autonomous experiments, self-driving laboratories, smart manufacturing, and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven design, discovery, and evaluation. This paper documents the recent advances in creating a resilient INTERSECT ecosystem. The proposed solution includes a resilient architecture with resilience design patterns, a resilient system of systems (SoS) architecture, and a resilient microservices architecture; and a resilient software development kit with reliable service communication and asynchronous and synchronous failure detection and notification. The resilience capabilities are demonstrated for an autonomous additive manufacturing process with a real-time feedback loop.

presentations.title: Building Scalable Agentic Systems for Science: Concepts, Architectures, and Hands-On with Academy
presentations.abstract: Agentic systems, in which autonomous agents collaborate to solve complex problems, are emerging as a transformative methodology in AI. However, adapting agentic architectures to scientific cyberinfrastructure—spanning HPC systems, experimental facilities, and federated data repositories—introduces new technical challenges. In this half-day tutorial, we introduce participants to the design, deployment, and management of scalable agentic systems for scientific discovery. We will present Academy, a Python-based middleware platform built to support agentic workflows across heterogeneous research environments. Participants will learn core agentic system concepts, including asynchronous execution models, stateful agent orchestration, and dynamic resource management. A guided hands-on session will help attendees build and launch their own agentic workflows. It will include case studies in materials discovery, biology, and chemistry. This tutorial is designed for researchers, developers, and cyberinfrastructure professionals interested in advancing AI-driven science with next-generation autonomous systems.

presentations.title: Building Skills and Community Through HPC in South Africa
Building the Scientific Data Fabric Community for AI-Driven Discovery
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific discovery, but today's cyberinfrastructure was designed for workflows in which data are collected, stored, analyzed, and archived as largely independent activities. Modern science increasingly requires continuous interaction among instruments, data repositories, workflows, AI services, edge devices, HPC systems, and scientists across institutional boundaries. This BoF brings together researchers, facility operators, cyberinfrastructure developers, and domain scientists to discuss the next generation of scientific data infrastructure. Through examples from astronomy, geosciences, materials science, medicine, and high-energy physics, participants will identify common infrastructure challenges and define a community roadmap for interoperable, federated scientific data ecosystems.

presentations.title: Cache-Driven Super-Linear Scaling in a Python Fluid Solver
presentations.abstract: Turbulent convection transports heat in stars, planets, and the Earth’s atmosphere, and simulating it demands extreme-scale computing. We present DHARA, a modular fluid solver written in Python (NumPy, CuPy, mpi4py) with compiled stencil kernels for CPUs and GPUs. On the CPU-based Shaheen III (KAUST), DHARA scales to 786,432 cores for compressible convection, and its strong scaling is super-linear: adding cores speeds up each step by more than the ratio of the core counts. Profiling explains why. As the domain is split across more cores, each subdomain’s stencil working set drops into the fast L1/L2 caches, so cache misses collapse, leading to a better than doubling of the per-core throughput. The same code carries over to the Frontier (OLCF) and Polaris (ALCF) GPU systems with near-ideal strong scaling.

presentations.title: CADI: Semi-Automatic Insertion of Host-Device Data Transfer Directives Based on Code Analysis
presentations.abstract: In heterogeneous computing using directive-based parallel programming models such as OpenACC, programmers typically need to explicitly specify host-device data transfer directives, increasing programming effort. Existing automatic approaches may introduce runtime overhead that can degrade performance. To reduce programming effort while preserving opportunities for performance optimization, we propose a semi-automatic approach that combines static code analysis with runtime memory tracking while allowing programmers to specify transfer directions. Based on this approach, we present CADI (Code Analysis-based Data-transfer directive Insertion), a foundation for semi-automatically inserting data transfer directives. CADI automatically determines the base address and transfer size required for each directive, while the programmer specifies the transfer direction to retain control over performance-related data movement. CADI achieved execution performance comparable to manually optimized implementations on the Himeno benchmark, indicating minimal runtime overhead. The poster presents the design of CADI, its code analysis and runtime mechanisms, and experimental results.

presentations.title: CAFCW26 Virtual Posters
presentations.abstract: Highlights of the CAFCW26 Virtual Poster Presentations.

presentations.title: Can LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code?
presentations.abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly integrated into software development, yet HPC remains demanding for them. Their performance has been measured for low-level, kernel-based parallel programming paradigms, but task-based and workflow orchestration paradigms, despite growing importance, have seen less rigorous evaluation. We extend the ParEval benchmark, originally demonstrated on C++ kernel-level models, to task-based paradigms and demonstrate it on PyCOMPSs, asking whether LLMs generate correct and efficient task-based parallel code. We further propose a multi-tier prompting scheme, from programming-model knowledge to infrastructure-aware coding, and evaluate the first two levels. Across 21 models, correctness and efficiency decouple: the most correct model is among the least efficient, and only one frontier model is strong in both. Open-weight models close the gap to the previous commercial generation with framework-specific guidance. The main barrier is framework knowledge, not the parallel algorithm, and correct code still achieves limited efficiency at the studied problem size.

presentations.title: Can Regional Collaborations Save HPC?
presentations.abstract: AI-driven workloads are outpacing what any single institution can afford, power and cooling constraints are tightening, and the workforce required to support next-generation HPC is in short supply. Regional collaboration is increasingly proposed as the answer — but does it actually work? This panel directly confronts that question. Drawing on operational experience from national HPC centers, regional networks, and campus research computing programs, panelists will debate the economics of cost-sharing, the governance challenges of federated infrastructure, and the realities of shared staffing and data management. Informed by the March 2026 NSF-CASC Workshop on NAIRR regional hubs and PEARC community discussions, the panel is structured as a moderated debate designed to surface genuine divergence/agreement and drive toward actionable insight for institutions making long-term infrastructure decisions right now.

presentations.title: CAPIO: Safe Kernel-Bypass of Commodity Devices using Capabilities
presentations.abstract:
Securing low-latency I/O in commodity systems forces a fundamental trade-off: rely on the kernel’s high overhead mediated interface, or bypass it entirely, exposing sensitive hardware resources to userspace and creating new vulnerabilities. This dilemma stems from a hardware granularity mismatch: standard MMUs operate at page boundaries, making it impossible to selectively expose safe device registers without also exposing the sensitive control registers colocated on the same page. Existing solutions, enforce an isolation model that cannot protect sub-page device resources.

We present CAPIO, the first architecture to leverage hardware capabilities to enforce fine-grained access control on MMIO. Unlike prior page-based protections, CAPIO utilizes unforgeable capabilities to create precise, sub-page “slices” of device memory. This enables the kernel to delegate latency-critical hardware access to userspace applications while strictly preventing interaction with co-located privileged registers. We demonstrate that CAPIO achieves the latency improvements of kernel bypass while enforcing byte-level access control of resources.

presentations.title: Career Pathways
presentations.abstract: Navigating your career is a challenge that all early-career professionals must face. Career pathways will vary depending on those in academia, government research lab, or industry. In this panel, we will hear from professionals in each of these sectors to hear about their unique experiences and challenges as they embarked upon their career roadmap.

presentations.title: Characterizing and Auto-Tuning 175B-Parameter LLM Training on Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 Accelerators
presentations.abstract: Training large language models on production HPC systems requires parallelism configurations tailored to accelerator memory, interconnect topology, and software maturity. We present an empirical study of GPT-style training on Intel Data Center Max 1550 GPUs in SuperMUC-NG Phase 2, using the upstream Megatron-DeepSpeed stack without custom kernels, evaluating 3.6B-, 20B-, and 175B-parameter models to quantify how tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, micro-batch size, and gradient accumulation affect throughput and feasibility. Results show a pronounced penalty when tensor-parallel collectives cross the eight-tile node boundary, while more micro-batches amortize pipeline bubbles until throughput saturates. Bayesian optimization of the 175B space yields a configuration reaching 58.91 TFLOP/s per tile; scaling to 128 nodes (1024 tiles) retains 91% weak-scaling and 82% strong-scaling efficiency. We derive an empirical cost decomposition from pipeline depth, micro-batch size, and gradient accumulation that bounds what further auto-tuning alone can deliver on this system.

presentations.title: Characterizing Cooperative I/O Caching for Data Loading at Scale on Aurora
presentations.abstract:
Deep-learning jobs on exascale systems begin by reading identical files: Python packages, then training data from a shared filesystem, forcing thousands of processes to issue near-identical requests at once and slowing startup for the whole machine. Cooperative caching can relieve this by serving redundant reads locally, but it adds overhead, so it is not always worthwhile. We ask when it pays off.

We characterize Copper, a cooperative read-caching filesystem, against direct Lustre reads on Aurora, measuring PyTorch startup and ResNet-50 dataset loading, cold and warm, from 2 to 2,048 nodes. We find a crossover: as scale grows, Copper's bounded coordination cost overtakes direct reads whose cost climbs with contention. At 2,048 nodes, startup through Copper is ~3× faster cold, ~11× faster warm. Import-torch results are complete; a synthetic file-size guideline is in progress.

The poster presents the crossover and its mechanism, inviting discussion of when cooperative caching should be applied.

presentations.title: Characterizing Failure Types Across HPC and AI Clusters
presentations.abstract:
High-performance computing studies conclude that user error causes most job failures, while large-scale AI training reports attribute most interruptions to hardware. The two are rarely compared, because they publish failure evidence in incompatible forms: attributed causes, scheduler outcome labels, or bare event rates.

We survey 162 public datasets and reports, assign each an evidence verdict, and normalize the usable evidence into an eleven-class taxonomy tagging each failure type as a cause, a symptom, or an outcome label. The resulting denominator-disciplined maps cover 38 systems across 44 matrix columns, and include a GPU error-class characterization spanning five hardware generations.

Read on common footing the literatures agree: failure rates are similar but exposure is not, counting failures and weighting by compute give opposite priority orders, interconnect leads attributable GPU hardware failures, and the largest logged error class is application-induced. The survey table, taxonomy, and source quotations are released as a public artifact.

presentations.title: Characterizing GPU Performance in AI Inference with Power Metrics
presentations.abstract: Large language model inference is increasingly limited not only by raw compute capability, but also by memory bandwidth, runtime behavior, and GPU power efficiency. We study how LLM inference performance and energy use vary across hardware platforms and inference frameworks. Experiments are conducted on NVIDIA's Jetson Thor, and A100 and H200 GPUs using two inference frameworks: vLLM and Hugging Face Transformers. Three open-weight LLMs are evaluated. For each hardware, framework, and model combination, inference metrics are collected. Pareto and histogram analyses are used to study the trade-off between throughput and energy efficiency. To connect inference behavior to hardware limits, BabelStream benchmark's triad kernel is used to measure host-memory and GPU-memory bandwidth. In addition, roofline analysis separates prefill and decode phases to show when performance is compute-bound or memory-bound. These measurements help explain why the Jetson Thor can be energy-efficient, while A100 and H200 provide higher throughput but consume more power.

presentations.title: Characterizing LLM Inference Performance on a WebAssembly Runtime
presentations.abstract: WebAssembly (WASM) has drawn attention as a portable binary format and a promising substrate for AI workloads. Delegating computation to a native backend through wasi-nn promises portability with native speed, yet to our knowledge this approach has not been evaluated quantitatively for LLM inference. We compare LlamaEdge, a WASM-based LLM runtime, with native llama-cli on a multi-socket node, aligning backend, build settings, and prompts so that only the execution environment differs. Across 1B–8B models, thread counts, context lengths, and GPU offload ratios, performance is equivalent under full GPU offload, while CPU-only execution shows a gap of up to 1.38×. We attribute this gap primarily to the in-page offset of the work buffer, set by the host-side allocation path, rather than WASM overhead. Confining cores and memory to one node reduces the gap to 1.07–1.13×, and allocating the work buffer from the main heap narrows it further to 1.02–1.04×.

presentations.title: Characterizing Low-bit Deployment of 3D Medical Image Analysis on Portable AI Supercomputer
presentations.abstract: The sensitivity of patient data limits the direct deployment of web-based generative AI and other cloud-hosted models in clinical environments, motivating secure, on-premise inference. However, local deployment is constrained by computational resources, memory capacity, and hardware portability, particularly for demanding tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation. In this work, we investigate low-bit post-training quantization (PTQ) for efficient offline deployment on the NVIDIA DGX Spark, a compact system with a Grace-Blackwell accelerator and 128 GB of unified memory. Using a unified TensorRT quantization workflow, we deploy nine representative 3D segmentation models spanning CNN- and transformer-based architectures, from 5.7M to 1.46B parameters, and evaluate them on the BTCV abdominal CT benchmark. Eight of nine models can be quantized to 8-bit weights and activations (W8A8) without meaningful accuracy degradation. Compared with full-precision inference, W8A8 achieves 3.9x-7.2x higher inference speed while substantially reducing memory consumption, enabling efficient, portable, privacy-preserving 3D medical image inference.

presentations.title: Characterizing Network Behavior of Distributed LLM Inference on a Four Node Edge Cluster
presentations.abstract: Desk-side AI accelerator clusters enable local LLM execution, yet their networked system behavior remains uncharacterized. We evaluate a four-node NVIDIA GB10 (Grace Blackwell Architecture) cluster connected via a commodity Ethernet switch across twenty distributed inference configurations spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. Four key findings emerge. First, decode is memory-bandwidth bound: single-node and pipeline-parallel setups achieve 0.69–0.86 of the memory-bandwidth roofline, while tensor parallelism divides per-node weight reads to accelerate decoding by up to 2.5x over RDMA, inverting standard datacenter trade-offs. Second, link bandwidth is not a bottleneck; per-node traffic consumes under 4% of the 200 Gb/s link without congestion. Third, communication latency remains critical, as RDMA over Converged Ethernet lowers end-to-end token latency by 2.0x to 7.1x compared to TCP. Finally, enabling expert parallelism alters inter-node traffic by less than 0.5%, reflecting vLLM’s default all-reduce backend rather than an intrinsic property of expert parallelism.

presentations.title: Characterizing Scaling Performance of LLM Inference on GPU-Based Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly important for scientific computing and agentic coding workflows. With growing model sizes, a single node on current-generation HPC systems no longer suffices for LLM inference. Inference must span slower scale-out interconnects and combine different parallelization strategies. This combinatorial space of strategies is large, and each configuration places different demands on the hardware. Which configuration performs best at a given scale, workload, and model architecture remains unclear. To address this, we empirically sweep hundreds of parallel deployment configurations across models and workloads on two leadership-class systems.
