We analyze scaling trends and find optimal configurations for different workloads and performance metrics, aiming to provide actionable insights for HPC practitioners.

presentations.title: Characterizing Simulation-AI Coupled Workflows on Frontier: Benchmarks and Digital-Twin Replay
presentations.abstract: Simulation–AI workflows now consume a large share of HPC cycles, shifting usage away from traditional modeling and simulation and leaving users and facility policymakers without a clear picture of how these coupled workloads consume system resources. We present a framework that characterizes the HPC resource usage of distributed simulation–AI workflows across six machine learning architectures used for AI training and inference. The framework couples a simulation–AI benchmarking suite with a digital twin of the system, built by extending, customizing, and integrating existing components. We port the benchmarks to the OLCF Frontier supercomputer and run six 64-node experiments, one per architecture, capturing computation, I/O, and energy telemetry without instrumenting any component's source. A translator bridge makes the collected telemetry replayable by the digital twin. We further demonstrate what-if scenario evaluation—energy projections at larger scales and outcomes under alternative scheduling policies—illustrating the framework's broader utility.

presentations.title: Charliecloud: Image Build Optimization for AI Workloads
presentations.abstract:
Charliecloud is a lightweight, unprivileged container runtime for HPC. Its Git-based image build cache has structural advantages over standard layer-based caches and performs competitively, as we have previously shown. Because Git cannot track all file types or the metadata to rebuild images, Charliecloud supplements it with a complete image traversal per build instruction. Since this traversal time increases with image size, we sought to reduce it.
Our approach recursively watches for changes to the image with inotifywait, a commandline tool that reports file “events” via the Linux inotify interface. Because inotifywait can sometimes miss events, we add a verification step that walks new directories. Surprisingly, monitoring speeds up some instructions but slows down others. The major gains from monitor-informed updates shrink as more files change and eventually become slowdowns, because they must be added to Git individually. This motivates a hybrid strategy that captures monitoring’s benefit while minimizing its cost.

presentations.title: Cheap Plans, Costly Trades: Host-Device Tradeoffs for SpGEMM on AiM
presentations.abstract: Sparse matrix–matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) is bandwidth-bound, the kind of kernel a memory-side accelerator ought to absorb, but the processing-in-memory hardware that ships is built for AI inference. We map 𝐶 = 𝐴 · 𝐴 onto SK hynix’s Accelerator-in-Memory (AiM), whose fixed-function units multiply dense bfloat16 vectors but cannot compute an address, so the host must place every product in advance. The mapping trades host planning for device time; we measure the trade over four designs, from almost no planning to a simulator-in-the-loop search. A single packing pass cuts device time 7×–122×, every further plan buys at most 8.5× more, and on a single product each plan costs more host time than it saves.

presentations.title: Cheaper by the Batch: Shared Traversal for Genotype Graph Editing
presentations.abstract:
Adding nodes in a graph while reusing existing structure is a recurring computational problem.
In population genetics, this problem arises in genotype representation graph (GRG), a DAG that losslessly encodes genetic variation across thousands of samples by sharing subgraph structure.
In GRG, mutation’s carrier is encoded as leaf nodes reachable from the node it is assigned to.
Current approaches update mutations individually.

This paper introduces a batched mutation-remapping algorithm that replaces independent traversals with a shared reverse-topological pass, identifying reuse candidates for a batch at once.
The pass propagates compact bit-parallel per-mutation state and uses an adaptive sparse/dense carrier set representation spanning rare-to-common variant densities.
Batching adds memory-scalablility to split-based parallelism, which replicates graph and traversal state per worker.
Our remapping approach is evaluated on standalone scenarios and end-to-end allele polarization workload.
It is up to 10.5$\times$ faster than independent remapping while preserving exact carrier-set semantics.

presentations.title: Chemically Accurate End-to-End Classical Simulation of Qubitization-Based Quantum Phase Estimation on 1,024 GPUs
presentations.abstract: Qubitization-based quantum phase estimation (QPE) is a core algorithm for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC), and molecular ground-state energies are among its most promising applications. Resource estimates predict the qubits and gates required, while end-to-end simulation directly tests whether the resulting circuits achieve the target accuracy; yet a naive chemical-accuracy H4 circuit needs 99 qubits and 1.78 billion gates. We combine established qubit- and gate-reduction techniques with distributed state-vector simulation using our prior communication optimizations for hierarchical GPU interconnects, on ABCI-Q's 1,024 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The H4 circuit shrinks to 28 qubits and 0.32 billion gates, runs in 1.5 hours, and yields a one-million-shot measurement distribution whose peak lies 0.53 milli-Hartree from the exact full configuration interaction (FCI) energy, within chemical accuracy. These runs check, at small scale, that estimated resources deliver the target accuracy. The poster also presents each reduction stage's effect, strong scaling, and remaining bottlenecks.

presentations.title: CI for E4S: Build and Test Automation for a Containerized HPC-AI Software Stack
presentations.abstract: Modern HPC-AI software depends on complex webs of applications, libraries, and accelerator toolchains across many hardware platforms. E4S addresses dependency conflict resolution by distributing Spack-provisioned, containerized HPC-AI stacks across x86\_64, AArch64, and ppc64le, with CPU, CUDA, ROCm, and oneAPI variants. However, building, testing, and keeping stacks updated presents major challenges for small teams. We describe the GitLab CI pipeline and E4S Testsuite built to automate this: staged binary caching, Spack-driven environment builds, Docker/Singularity image generation, and per-package smoke tests. As of E4S 26.06, this approach drives about 200 CI jobs per pipeline, builds up to 127 CPU packages per architecture, and exercises 236 tests, with full x86\_64 CPU builds completing in 5 to 8 hours, and in minutes when cached. Automation has reduced maintainer workload, improved reproducibility, and lowered barriers to external contributions, demonstrating that CI automation is instrumental to sustaining community-maintained HPC-AI ecosystems at scale.

presentations.title: CLASP: Index Compression for Finite Element SpMV
presentations.abstract: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) in finite element methods is memory-bound, with index storage consuming a significant fraction of bandwidth. We exploit mesh connectivity to partition the assembled matrix into element-wise blocks each covering at most B = 256 nodes, enabling 8-bit column indices and 16-bit row pointers, a 4x index compression over standard CSR. We show that the encoding is provably compressive with node duplication overhead bounded by $1 + O(B^{-1/d})$ for d-dimensional meshes. We present three GPU kernels: partitioned CSR, partitioned CSR with shared-memory buffering, and a prefix-sum-based COO variant. We test our kernels on four NVIDIA GPU generations and show that the proposed encoding results in a faster SpMV operation achieving 1.4x-1.7x speedup over cuSPARSE CSR. We further show that COO-variant is more suitable for high-bandwidth-equipped GPU systems. A direct CPU implementation of partitioning CSR kernel with vectorization achieves up to 2x speedup over Intel-MKL for SpMV operation.

ClusterBench: A Framework for Cluster-Wide Continuous Benchmarking and Regression Testing
presentations.abstract: Data centers need tooling that validates an entire installation rather than individual nodes, at acceptance and at regular intervals thereafter. This requires dispatching identical benchmarks to every node in a single submission, and therefore cluster-aware scheduling. This paper presents ClusterBench, a framework for cluster-wide continuous benchmarking. It ships with a benchmark collection targeting each component: CPU, GPU, memory, interconnect, and I/O. Because measurements are repeated throughout the cluster's lifetime, ClusterBench collects data across space and time. Comparison against earlier runs detects performance regressions introduced by software changes, such as kernel updates or new library versions. The measurements also form a dataset for research on hardware variability. On the NHR@FAU clusters Helma, Alex, and Fritz, variation within a single component stays within 1%. Variation across specimens reaches 5%, despite nodes identical by specification. Correlating performance with power draw, frequency, and temperature shows that this relationship differs between air- and liquid-cooled nodes.

presentations.title: Co-Design for new processor and system architectures at JSC
Co-designing MoE Architectures and System Stacks for Scalable Training on Leadership Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown exceptional promise as scientific foundation models. However, substantial pre-training costs pose a major bottleneck in training high-quality models. The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has emerged as an effective solution to this problem. Preceding MoE studies have been conducted on NVIDIA platforms, while many scientific foundation models are trained on supercomputers with diverse accelerators. By examining pretraining strategies on a dataset sourced from scientific texts and porting state-of-the-art MoE training techniques to the ROCM-stack on Frontier, we identify crucial factors to achieve high training throughput. For the first time, we show that it is possible to scale training of massive MoE models on clusters with thousands of GPUs. Leveraging these insights, we train a suite of MoE models for science, called SMOREs. Evaluations of these models against standard benchmarks such as SciQ and ARC-Challenge show that they outperform their dense counterparts in the early phases of training.

presentations.title: Co-Designing the NIC and Transport: Simpler Hardware, Scalable Communication
Coconut: An HPC-Native Inference Framework for Neural Surrogates in MPI Simulations
presentations.abstract: Neural surrogates can accelerate hybrid PDE solvers, but whether a surrogate delivers a speedup can only be determined in situ, because deployment configuration strongly affects its performance, and current HPC infrastructures support this exploration poorly. We present Coconut, an HPC-native inference framework that fits the MPI programming model and exposes deployment options at two levels: batch size, numerical precision, device placement, and inference backend at the model level, and process topology at the architecture level. A microbenchmark quantifies the cost of the embedded Python interpreter required by the PyTorch Inductor backend, showing when this model-safe execution path becomes efficient. In an industrial thermal multiphase-flow simulator, a thermodynamic surrogate moves from a 2.4× kernel-level slowdown to a 34.12× speedup over the original kernel and 2.51× over a multithreaded batched baseline, carrying through to application-level throughput gains. Deployment choices decide whether a surrogate pays off; Coconut enables their in situ evaluation.

presentations.title: Code Generation with MLIR for the OPS Structured-Mesh DSL
presentations.abstract:
Structured-mesh applications underpin high-performance scientific simulations, yet performance portability across CPUs and GPUs demands substantial compiler and runtime support. We present an MLIR-based compiler
framework for OPS, a structured-mesh DSL, that captures OPS abstractions at runtime and JIT-lowers them to OpenMP and CUDA backends. A key contribution is adapting the predominantly value-semantic xDSL stencil compilation stack to OPS’s buffer-semantic model, where pre-allocated datasets have memory identity and update semantics. This demonstrates that shared MLIR stencil infrastructure can accommodate lower-level, production-oriented DSLs without redesigning their programming model. The framework introduces an OPS
dialect and staged lowerings for parallel loops, data accesses, stencils, and execution policies. Evaluation of representative structured-mesh applications, including the OpenSBLI research code on multicore CPUs and an NVIDIA H100 GPU, shows performance competitive with OPS’s mature source-to-source backends, substantial memory-bandwidth utilization, closely matched GPU kernel times, and amortized JIT overheads, providing a practical path for modernizing DSL compilers.

presentations.title: CoDISAR: A Composable Disaggregated Infrastructure for SAR Backprojection
presentations.abstract: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is a remote sensing technology, used on moving platforms such as aircraft. Challenges arise when generating high-resolution images due to the computational complexity of image formation algorithms. Traditional approaches generate the images offline or deploy high-throughput hardware onboard the aircraft. Onboard compute is restricted by drone constraints including size, weight, and power. We propose CoDISAR, a solution where accelerators are distributed in the field, accessible via composable disaggregated infrastructure. This enables drone swarms to support high-resolution SAR imaging in near-real time, where drones can request GPUs from pools of resources. We examine the effects on time-to-image for the backprojection algorithm using distanced accelerators. Network latencies attributed to distances of up to 1000 km are inserted to evaluate the performance of CoDISAR against typical compute resources available on drones. Modeling indicates that our solution can generate high-resolution images up to 5x faster over classical methods.

presentations.title: CoEncode: Reclaiming Idle Encoder GPUs in Multi-Tenant Multimodal LLM Serving
presentations.abstract: Disaggregated multimodal LLM serving improves stage isolation but can leave dedicated encoder GPUs substantially underutilized. We present CoEncode, a workload-aware encoder pooling approach that uses model-specific capacity profiles to provision fractional GPU resources and colocate encoder workloads while accounting for end-to-end pipeline conditions. Our evaluation shows that CoEncode maintains comparable end-to-end TTFT SLO attainment while improving SLO goodput perGPU by 19.3% and reducing encoding energy consumption by 45.9%. These results demonstrate the potential of encoder pooling to improve resource and energy efficiency without sacrificing end-to-end serving quality.

presentations.title: Collaborative Partitioning of Hybrid Quantum–Classical Workloads: Cost-Model-Driven Planning for Tensor-Network/QPU Execution
presentations.abstract: Quantum processors sit beside CPUs and GPUs in HPC centers, yet nothing decides, before execution, which part of a workload belongs where, and on a noisy device that decision needs two currencies at once, wall-clock time and error. We supply the missing layer for matrix-product-state simulation. A computation is partitioned at one bond: the weakly entangled side is contracted exactly, the strongly entangled fragment becomes a single ancilla-free staircase circuit driven by a seam register of fewer qubits, whose sampling cost is bounded by chi^2 /epsilon^2 and adapts to the Schmidt spectrum. A planner prices every candidate: classical time and quantum time from transpiled gate durations, against a four-term error envelope, always retaining a classical fallback, and emits a per-run receipt comparing prediction with measurement. On 64-site Ising chains the envelope covers the realized error on every executed plan, and the planner correctly declines the QPU.

presentations.title: Collecting Infrastructure-Level Measures for Energy Analysis in Modern Computing Infrastructures
presentations.abstract:
Modern HPC facilities are complex environments in which all components are tightly coupled; consequently, precisely modeling and accounting for energy consumption requires approaches that go beyond instrumenting individual compute nodes.
Aiming for a cluster-wide vision, we designed a scalable data collection pipeline that aggregates fine-grained measurements from multiple subsystems—spanning component loads, software and hardware counters, sensors and energy—ensuring consistent sampling frequencies and synchronized data acquisition across the infrastructure.
We present a dataset of comprehensive metrics collected at 1 Hz over one month from a production research data center supporting heterogeneous workloads, including HPC, Kubernetes services, and distributed storage.
To illustrate what this approach makes possible in practice, we analyze two case studies—distributed I/O and large-language-model inference—showing how cluster-wide measurement reveals system-level dynamics missed by localized instrumentation.
The proposed dataset and collection methodology provide a foundation for future work on predictive modeling, energy-aware resource management, and more efficient computing infrastructures.

presentations.title: Colourful Wind Assistance
presentations.abstract:
The video shows the flow past two wing sails arranged in tandem, representative of wind-assisted propulsion devices. The simulation was performed with x3d2, a high-order finite-difference incompressible-flow solver developed within the Xcompact3d framework (https://www.incompact3d.com). The simulation uses the immersed-boundary method to represent the foil geometry, together with non-periodic streamwise inflow/outflow boundary conditions and periodic transverse boundaries.

The calculation uses a uniform Cartesian mesh of approximately 381 million grid points. Based on the wing-sail chord and imposed inflow velocity, the Reynolds number is approximately 28,000. The case is an illustrative demonstration of the numerical methodology rather than a full-scale wing-sail prediction. Simulations were run in double precision on an NVIDIA Grace Hopper GH200 GPU using x3d2’s CUDA backend.

presentations.title: Communication Libraries in HPC and AI
presentations.abstract: The world's largest supercomputers for scientific discovery are also premier systems for artificial intelligence model training and inference. While traditional HPC compute has predominately leveraged the MPI standard, AI workloads have increasingly focused on collective communication libraries, such as NVIDIA's NCCL and AMD's RCCL, which are optimized for high throughput and GPU-native usage. This Birds of a Feather (BoF) session at the SC Conference (SC) aims to delve into the intricacies of collective communication libraries, focusing on the comparison between the widely adopted Message Passing Interface (MPI) and NCCL/RCCL, as well as other key messaging libraries, such as SHMEM.

presentations.title: Communication Strategies for Wafer-Scale Iterative Solvers
presentations.abstract: Collective communication strongly affects the performance of iterative scientific applications. Conjugate gradient repeatedly computes global dot products that require reductions across many processing elements. This work evaluates chain and hierarchical XY two-phase reductions on a Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine. We developed a reproducible workflow for compiling wavelet programs, executing them on hardware, collecting distributed timer values, and producing graph-ready data. Measurements across 262,144 processing elements show a payload-dependent crossover. XY two-phase communication performs best for small payloads, but chain communication becomes faster as the payload grows. These results motivate adaptive collective selection based on message size.

presentations.title: Community Discussion and Q&A
Completion-Driven, Staging-Free AlltoAllv with Local-NIC Balancing
presentations.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training workloads use imbalanced AlltoAllv collectives at bandwidth-bound message sizes. On Frontier, one-sided AlltoAll can beat RCCL and Cray-MPICH, but only with the right schedule and only as per-peer fetches shrink. Other approaches balance load across a node's NICs by explicitly copying data between GPUs, which costs GPU staging buffers and overlaps that copy with network traffic only coarsely. We introduce CURLEW, a completion-driven, GPU-staging-free RDMA AlltoAllv with dynamic local-NIC balancing. CURLEW achieves near-flat bandwidth across GPU counts and message sizes on balanced patterns, is 1.9x faster than previous work at max-to-mean skew above 8, and reduces end-to-end training time of a 201B-parameter model by 22% at a capacity factor of 1.25.

presentations.title: Complexity and Scale in AI-Assisted Workflow Management: A Federated Learning Case Study
presentations.abstract: Federated learning over medical images is a demanding workflow application. Each round fans out across parallel client jobs and converges on an aggregation step that feeds the next round. At scale this yields 101 sub-workflows and 2,679 jobs on GPUs at four sites, which takes an expert months to build, mostly on workflow mechanics rather than science. We ask how far AI assistance can automate such workflows. An LLM agent, grounded in a released plugin of Pegasus-specific skills, first produces a reviewable specification of checkable constraints and acceptance criteria, then generates the executable workflow. A validation loop repairs runtime failures, checks code against those constraints, and regenerates the implementation from the specification alone. We evaluate three LLM agents, report end-to-end runs on the FABRIC testbed, and show how conformance checking against the specification caught three silent errors that failure-driven debugging missed, including one that trained 1,700 jobs on random tensors.

presentations.title: Compliance, ColdFront, and Chaos: Tooling to Align HPCC User Life Cycles and Research Impacts with Changing Regulatory Landscapes
presentations.abstract:
As federal research funding in the United States becomes subject to additional compliance regulations, better understanding the research being done at high-performance computing centers (HPCCs) takes on new importance in HPCC system management. However, aggressive compliance regulations can often be at odds with the flexibility required to serve large user bases performing cutting-edge research, resulting in ad hoc measures, inconsistent applications, and disorganized communication.

This paper presents a case study of implementing new tooling and user life cycle management workflows to standardize user and project relationships at a large R1 university's HPCC. These relationships are structured to provide insight into compliance needs, while integrating with the popular HPCC management system ColdFront for research output tracking. The development and deployment process is provided in detail, including specification development, technical discussion of tooling, collaboration across the university, and user-facing considerations during a 30-month roll out process affecting over 11,000 user accounts.

presentations.title: Compositional Energy Modeling of Layer-Resolved GPU Training
presentations.abstract: We present a compositional energy model for layer-resolved GPU training on AMD MI300X and NVIDIA H100 datacenter GPUs. Instead of fitting whole-run energy, the model assigns energy coefficients to hardware work classes, including matrix-engine convolutions, GEMM kernels, bandwidth-bound layers, gradient all-reduce, and static device power. Coefficients are calibrated in situ from steady-state replays of production ResNet-50 training kernels, then composed over full runs whose classes interleave, overlap, and contend for shared resources. On MI300X, coefficients calibrated on a native HIP implementation transfer to unmodified PyTorch without refitting, predicting energy to -7.3% at one GPU and +8.5% at sixteen GPUs. On H100, a frequency-dependent active-state term scoped by matrix-pipe utilization gives 9.0% mean absolute error over 42 operating points and 6.4% where the architecture took part in no modeling decision. Residuals identify missing vector work, state power, and operating-point effects. Power-cap sweeps show that per-operation energy falls by 20-41% from 750 W to 450 W on MI300X, so coefficients must be remeasured or corrected when the operating point changes.

presentations.title: Compression for AI and Scientific Data
presentations.abstract: Large-scale numerical simulations, experimental instruments, observational platforms, and modern AI workloads generate and consume unprecedented volumes of data, creating critical challenges for storage, I/O, communication, and analysis. Data compression—particularly error-bounded lossy compression—is a key enabling technology to address these challenges. This half-day tutorial reviews the motivations, fundamental principles, and algorithmic foundations of lossy compression for scientific and AI data workflows. It introduces core compression stages (decorrelation, approximation, and encoding) and examines their realizations in state-of-the-art compressors. It emphasizes trustworthiness through error control, uncertainty quantification, and application-specific quality metrics. New this year, we consistently incorporate compression for AI and data-driven workflows, including training data, model states (e.g., embeddings and activations), and communication buffers in distributed and federated learning. The 70-minute hands-on session covers generic compressors and demonstrates a novel generation of lossy compression framework for building practical, customized compression pipelines using real-world datasets, including ones from participants if available. Leading researchers in AI and compression researchers and developers present the tutorial targeted at beginners and practitioners seeking to understand and apply lossy compression in modern HPC and AI environments. It builds upon and significantly extends the highly rated SC17–SC25 tutorial series with new content on AI integration, trustworthiness, and next-generation workflows.

presentations.title: Computers as Information Channels: A Common Yardstick for the Post-Moore Hardware Zoo
presentations.abstract: We propose a novel measurement unit for computing performance that's grounded in information theory. Modern computing systems are increasingly diverse, supporting low-precision formats, hardware specialization, and emerging paradigms such as analog, quantum, and neuromorphic hardware. Traditional metrics like floating-point operation (flop) counts no longer accurately capture this complexity. Instead, we frame computation as the transformation of information through a channel and define performance in terms of the mutual information between a system’s inputs and outputs. This approach measures not just the quantity of data processed, but the amount of meaningful information encoded, manipulated, and retained through computation. Our proposal aims to provide a principled, implementation-agnostic foundation for evaluating performance.

presentations.title: Conclusion
Confidential Supercomputing: Essential Evolution or Elegant Illusion?
presentations.abstract: Sensitive workloads across health sciences, financial modeling, and AI/ML on proprietary data increasingly demand confidentiality guarantees traditionally out of scope for supercomputing infrastructure. Confidential computing—hardware-enforced trusted execution environments established in cloud and edge contexts—is proposed as a path to securing computation at HPC scale. But is this achievable, or does it conflict with the principles that make supercomputers fast? This BoF gathers the HPC community to debate whether confidential supercomputing is a necessary, achievable evolution or an aspirational posture satisfying compliance optics without meaningful security. Join us to map where it genuinely delivers—and where gaps remain.

presentations.title: Congestion-Aware Collective Communication for Composable Disaggregated GPUs
presentations.abstract: Traditional server-centric data center design relies on a fixed ratio of compute and memory, limiting adaptability to evolving workloads, particularly in AI. Composable Disaggregated Infrastructure (CDI) addresses this by enabling on-demand composition of disaggregated devices. We focus on the intersection of GPU disaggregation and MPI collective communications, introducing an emulation methodology that uses available hardware to emulate PCIe-based disaggregated GPUs. While high-end servers run collectives over high-bandwidth intra-node interconnects, PCIe-based disaggregated systems introduce congestion, making it challenging to identify the best-performing algorithm for each collective. We propose a congestion-aware scoring model that estimates congestion at step granularity and, grounded in a Hockney-based bandwidth model, predicts the absolute communication latency of each algorithm on different PCIe topologies. Experimental results show the model predicts absolute latency within an average accuracy of 94.73%, 93.25%, and 93.94% for Allgather, ReduceScatter, and Alltoall, respectively, providing an effective, profiling-free tool for algorithm selection in GPU-disaggregated systems.

presentations.title: Connecting Skills, Training and Community: Lessons from Building the HPC Workforce
presentations.abstract: Developing the High-Performance Computing (HPC) workforce requires more than technical infrastructure and expertise. People entering the HPC community arrive with different levels of experience, skills and career goals. This manuscript reflects on my experience as a Community Manager across SHAREing and CAKE, two initiatives within the UK Digital Research Infrastructure programme. Through SHAREing, I have contributed to approaches that help learners identify knowledge gaps, explore relationships between HPC concepts, navigate existing training resources and build personalised learning pathways. Through CAKE, I have worked to make the wider HPC landscape more visible, accessible and connected through community events, outreach and knowledge exchange. These experiences highlight the complementary roles of skills development and community building in creating an HPC ecosystem where individuals can access opportunities, develop their expertise, connect with others and thrive.

presentations.title: Connecting the Quantum and HPC Communities: A Tutorial on High-Performance Software for Quantum Computing
presentations.abstract: Quantum computing has the potential to revolutionize many fields in the 21st century. Over the past decade, numerous quantum computers have been made publicly available. However, the effectiveness of the hardware is heavily reliant on the software ecosystem—a lesson drawn from classical computing's evolution. Unlike classical systems, which benefit from mature electronic design automation (EDA) and high performance computing (HPC) tools for handling complexity and optimizing performance, quantum software is still in its infancy. One of the goals of this tutorial is to educate the HPC community on quantum computing and to bring these two communities closer together. To this end, the tutorial covers two key topics at the intersection of classical and quantum software: quantum program compilation and the integration of quantum devices into HPC environments. Furthermore, the tutorial showcases how expertise in classical HPC can address key challenges in the quantum software stack. All of the above is accompanied by hands-on demonstrations based on the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT)—an open-source collection of high-performance software tools for quantum computing developed by the Chair for Design Automation at the Technical University of Munich, and the Munich Quantum Software Company.

presentations.title: Consumption-Aware Memory Prediction for Scientific Workflows
presentations.abstract:
Distributed scientific workflow tasks exhibit signif-
icant variation in memory consumption, making accurate peak
memory estimation critical for resource management and avoid-
ing out-of-memory (OOM) failures. Existing workload schedulers
rely on static features like file sizes or tool names, which fail to
capture non-linear memory scaling. We present Consumption-
Aware Memory Prediction (CAMP), a closed-loop framework that
utilizes fine-grained, consumption-level provenance—the exact
number of bytes a task reads—measured dynamically via eBPF
kernel probes. To minimize tracing overhead across parallel task
executions at scale, we develop an active-learning-based, multi-
gate selective auditing policy that samples only the most informa-
tive workflow tasks for model retraining. We evaluate CAMP on
thousands of production-scale bioinformatics workflow records
executed under Slurm. Compared to size-based scheduling base-
lines, incorporating dynamic data-consumption features reduces
prediction median absolute percentage error by up to 40.31%.

presentations.title: Continental-Scale, High-Order, High Spatial-Resolution Ice Flow Modeling Based on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs)
presentations.abstract: Solving time-independent stress-balance equations to predict ice velocity is the most computationally demanding part of ice-sheet simulations, both for memory and execution time. In this study, we develop numerical algorithms that use the parallel processing power of graphics processing units (GPUs) and implement them in the Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (ISSM) three-dimensional (3-D) Blatter-Pattyn higher-order (HO) module. Our setups are based on the ISSM Antarctic model from the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison for CMIP6 (ISMIP6), with about 10^7 degrees of freedom (DoFs), and a higher-resolution version with about 10^8 DoFs. We compare the GPU-accelerated 3-D HO ISSM stress balance module to the standard CPU-based version. We evaluate predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness. The poster will present the science question being investigated in this study, the methodology, results, and implications of the findings, and will outline future research objectives.

presentations.title: Continuum Computing: Agentic AI for Intelligent Orchestration
presentations.abstract: Continuum computing (digital continuum) is a distributed ecosystem spanning edge devices, scientific instruments, cloud platforms, data centers, supercomputers, and quantum systems. As these infrastructures become increasingly complex, agentic AI offers new opportunities for intelligent orchestration of computation, data, workflows, and heterogeneous resources. This BoF will explore how collaborative AI agents can enable autonomous scientific computing while ensuring trust, resilience, and human oversight. Topics include multi-agent coordination, AI-driven resource management, autonomous workflows, foundation models for scientific computing, and new programming models. The session will identify key research challenges and foster cross-disciplinary collaboration to advance the next generation of intelligent continuum computing.

presentations.title: Conversations on Neurodiversity
presentations.abstract: This fireside chat explores neurodiversity within the HPC community. Join speakers from Microsoft and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory as they discuss workplace interactions, mentorship, and vital resources for neurodiverse individuals.

presentations.title: Copy2: Data Sync Tool For High Performance Storages
presentations.abstract: The rapid growth of scientific and AI workloads challenges HPC centers to efficiently move large datasets across high-performance storage systems. Data movement at this scale is constrained by I/O bandwidth, metadata processing, filesystem semantics, and resource consumption, while existing open-source and commercial solutions may lack required performance, resource guarantees, or cost effectiveness. Motivated by a large-scale storage migration at our HPC facility, we developed copy2, a resource-aware transfer tool for parallel and distributed storage systems including Lustre and VAST Data. copy2 combines fine-grained parallel metadata traversal, inode-based hard-link preservation, highly concurrent asynchronous I/O, and bounded memory management. Component-level and end-to-end evaluations across diverse file sizes and counts show 2-4x higher transfer bandwidth and 3-5x lower energy consumption than rclone and fpsync, while adhering to user-defined memory bounds. Production deployments involving hundreds of millions of files further demonstrate its effectiveness for predictable, high-throughput scientific data movement at scale.

presentations.title: Core-Level Performance Engineering
presentations.abstract: While many developers put a lot of effort into optimizing large-scale parallelism, they often neglect the importance of an efficient serial code. Even worse, slow serial code tends to scale very well, hiding the fact that resources are wasted because no definite hardware performance limit (“bottleneck”) is exhausted. This tutorial conveys the required knowledge to develop a thorough understanding of the interactions between software and hardware on the level of a single CPU core and the lowest memory hierarchy level (the L1 cache). We introduce general out-of-order core architectures and their typical performance bottlenecks using modern x86-64 (Intel Sapphire Rapids) and ARM (NVIDIA Vera) processors as examples. We then go into detail about x86 and AArch64 assembly code, specifically including vectorization (SIMD), pipeline utilization, critical paths, and loop-carried dependencies. We also demonstrate performance analysis and performance engineering using the Open-Source Architecture Code Analyzer (OSACA) in combination with a dedicated instance of the well-known Compiler Explorer. Various hands-on exercises will allow attendees to make their own experiments and measurements and identify in-core performance bottlenecks. Furthermore, we show real-life use cases from computational science (sparse solvers, molecular dynamics) to emphasize how profitable in-core performance engineering can be.

presentations.title: Correctness Evidence for I/O Optimizations in VPIC-Kokkos: Preliminary Results
presentations.abstract: Scientific input/output (I/O) optimizations require clear correctness evidence that application developers can review. We study deterministic export tests and scientist-vetted end-to-end analyses within the Kokkos implementation of the Vector Particle-in-Cell (VPIC) application. These validations rely on different oracles and target different properties. This work in progress explores what kinds of correctness evidence should be provided alongside an application I/O optimization.

presentations.title: Correctness Testing of HPC Scientific Software in the Age of AI-Generated Code
presentations.abstract: Effective software testing plays a critical role in guaranteeing the performance, correctness, and reproducibility of software. Testing high-performance computing (HPC) software poses unique challenges due to massive parallelism, concurrency and heterogeneity, the scale of target platforms, lack of oracles, and application-specific verification and verification. These challenges are now amplified by AI coding tools generating and translating HPC code faster than humans can review it. In this BoF, a panel of experts and the audience will discuss methodologies and challenges in HPC software testing, including verification of AI-generated code to deepen our understanding of this crucial aspect of HPC software development.

presentations.title: Correlation-Aware Uncertainty Visualization of Multivariate Data with Many-Core Acceleration
presentations.abstract: This research addresses a fundamental limitation in state-of-the-art uncertainty visualization of multivariate data: omission of statistical correlation between underlying data fields. Existing approaches either ignore correlation, yielding overconfident or underconfident uncertainty estimates and potentially misleading visualizations, or rely on computationally expensive Monte Carlo integration that limits practical applicability. We enable efficient, scalable, and reliable correlation-aware uncertainty visualization by modeling bivariate uncertainty using correlated Gaussian distributions and multivariate uncertainty using kernel density estimation (KDE), both capturing data correlation. We develop analytical frameworks for Gaussian and KDE models to propagate uncertainty into extracted level sets, providing the first rigorous study of correlation effects on multivariate level-set uncertainty while eliminating costly numerical integration. Compared to Monte Carlo methods, our approaches achieve speedups of up to 500x on equivalent serial and parallel hardware using the Viskores library. Results on synthetic and real-world datasets underscore the criticality of correlation-aware uncertainty quantification for trustworthy data analysis.

presentations.title: CQTwin: A Digital-Twin Toolkit for Operational Analytics of HPC Schedulers
presentations.abstract: HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet the data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab for what-if exploration. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies, revealing how the same workload would have unfolded under different decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, supporting real-time decision-making. The dashboard covers the complete workflow---workload characterization, experiment configuration, and multidimensional comparison---letting users see which policies suit a workload and at what trade-offs. We validate CQTwin on Argonne Leadership Computing Facility production traces spanning 2016--2023.

presentations.title: Cross-Fabric Policy Reasoning for Hybrid InfiniBand/Ethernet HPC Systems
Cross-Stack Resilience for Extreme Scale AI: Coordinated Recovery for Training and Inference
presentations.abstract:
Resilience has become significantly more complex for AI workloads. AI models distribute parameters, communication state, and inference caches across thousands of devices. Collective communication has moved onto the critical path of application execution, with large-scale training synchronizing at every step and parallel inference invoking collectives very often. In these environments, a single device or rank failure can affect training progress, model quality, and inference latency. Also, large-scale training and latency-sensitive inference now run on mixed CPU, GPU, and accelerator systems with multiple fabrics and tiers of storage. Large-scale scale-up, scale-out and heterogeneous systems all exacerbate the problem by spreading state across tightly coupled nodes and distributed domains.

Checkpoint/restart remains essential, but it is no longer sufficient as a stand-alone strategy for AI workloads. This paper treats resilience as an optimization problem and proposes a cross-stack resilience architecture that coordinates recovery across applications, framework, communication, storage, orchestration and system telemetry.

presentations.title: CUDA-Enabled Actors: Rekindling GPU Execution in the C++ Actor Framework
presentations.abstract: The C++ Actor Framework (CAF) once provided OpenCL-based GPU acceleration within the actor model, but this capability is no longer supported. This paper presents CUDA-Enabled Actors, a CUDA-based extension that re-establishes a practical path to GPU execution in CAF while preserving an actor-oriented programming interface. CUDA support is implemented through a thread-safe command runner that serves as the execution interface for launching CUDA kernels through an actor-oriented API and gives users finer control over host--device memory transfers. The resulting design hides much of the complexity of GPU programming while retaining the modularity and abstraction of the actor model. Experiments demonstrate that CUDA-Enabled Actors provides actor-oriented GPU execution with modest overhead relative to native CUDA, supports execution across multiple GPUs, enables recovery from worker failures, and improves resource use for irregular workloads, establishing it as a practical foundation for GPU-enabled applications in CAF.

presentations.title: CURATE: Leveraging LLM Agents to Compose, Catalog, and Deploy Reproducible Workflows
presentations.abstract: Agentic code generation has the potential to accelerate the development of computational workflows while also reducing barriers to entry. However, a key gap remains: existing coding agents focus on code generation and do not address the entire workflow lifecycle, including deployment and sharing. As a result, users develop and stitch modules independently while managing deployment on their own. To address this gap, we propose CURATE (Composition, User-in-the-loop, Reuse, and Automated Task Execution), a novel human-in-the-loop multi-agent system that uses LLM agents to manage and develop composable workflows across their entire lifecycle. A key feature of the system is a catalog that allows for the storage and reuse of modules across workflows. Module catalogs provide a foundation that can be expanded to support FAIR principles by facilitating the sharing and reuse of curated modules and subgraphs. We demonstrate the feasibility of our system with an initial prototype and 6 experiments.

presentations.title: Custodian: Enabling Automatic Performance Engineering Agents on the NERSC HPC System
presentations.abstract: The advancement of Large Language Models and the rapid evolution of AI assistants and agents create an opportunity for the development of highly specialized HPC agents to enable automatic performance analysis. In this paper, we present Custodian, an HPC performance analysis agent that analyzes previously collected job telemetry and application-output data to characterize application behavior, identify potential performance bottlenecks, and transform performance metrics into natural language descriptions and figures that suggest optimizations or highlight computing inefficiencies. We validate Custodian’s telemetry-derived application states and roofline analyses against NVIDIA Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute across four representative applications executed on NERSC Perlmutter. Finally, we discuss the tradeoffs, cost, productivity and systems applicability of HPC agents on the NERSC HPC system.

presentations.title: Customized End-to-End Services for Science Workflows via SENSE
presentations.abstract: nri114

presentations.title: CXDVirt: Low Latency Kernel Module Based CXL-SSD Emulation
presentations.abstract: CXL-SSDs promise memory-semantic access to NAND-scale capacity through a small in-device DRAM cache, but scarce hardware makes emulation central to CXL-SSD research. Cylon, a state-of-the-art emulator, runs workloads in a VM, intercepting DRAM misses to inject NAND latency. We show this VM machinery adds over 3μs per miss, exceeding high-performance NAND read latency, while repeated VM exits inflate tail miss latencies several-fold. We present CXDVirt, a kernel-module-based CXL-SSD emulator that removes the VM entirely: the device is exposed through host devdax, hits run natively via the MMU, and a custom page-fault path models NAND latency on misses. CXDVirt preserves CXL-SSDs’ bimodal latency profile while reducing per-miss latency 1.4–1.6× (4.1× at P99.9); with eight threads its miss latency only doubles, against 8–9× for Cylon behind QEMU’s global lock. CXDVirt stays within 5% of remote DRAM without NAND traffic, where Cylon is 3.1–3.6× slower, and enables configurable eviction and prefetch policy studies.

presentations.title: DAOS Update: Version 2.8 and MLPerf Storage
presentations.abstract: The Distributed Asynchronous Object Storage (DAOS) is an open source software-defined high performance storage system that has redefined performance and scalability for a wide spectrum of AI and HPC workloads. This PDSW26 WiP session presents the new features in DAOS 2.8, as well as DAOS results for the MLPerf Storage v3.0 benchmarks.

presentations.title: DART: ML-Accelerated Surrogate for Real-Time CFD Digital Twins
presentations.abstract:
Experimental aerodynamics facilities stream
surface-pressure measurements continuously, but the CFD
models used to interpret those measurements require minutes
to hours per evaluation. This multi-order-of-magnitude gap
prevents deploying the model inside the experiment’s control
loop. We present DART, a workflow engine that represents
a CFD digital-twin pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of
typed computational steps and makes surrogate substitution a
first-class operation: a machine-learned model replaces a node’s
implementation while preserving its declared input/output
contract, so adjacent stages remain unchanged. DART then
monitors the substituted loop by comparing prediction residuals
to incoming measurements and raises an alarm when the
surrogate leaves its fitted regime. On a steady aerodynamic
pipeline, a substituted surrogate answers in 4.1 ms what the
solver answers in 220s while reproducing 99.5% of held-out
lift variation. On an unsteady cylinder benchmark, an alarm
calibrated only on trusted-regime data detects out-of-envelope
deployment within six shedding cycles.

presentations.title: Data Centers and Water: Socioenvironmental Risks in Times of Digital Expansion
Data Layout and Differentiation for Efficient Training of Physics-Informed Deep Operator Networks
presentations.abstract: Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks reduce dependence on simulation-generated training data, but their training requires higher-order spatial derivatives at many function-coordinate pairs, causing severe computational and memory costs. We reorganize PI-DeepONet training around its tensor-product structure. Our compact data layout eliminates duplicated Branch inputs and Trunk coordinates, enables GEMM-based contraction, and shares Trunk derivatives among input functions. We further compare forward-mode automatic differentiation, zero coordinate shift, and explicit derivative propagation. In a completed two-dimensional Navier–Stokes benchmark, the optimized implementation achieved a 4.87-fold speedup and a 144-fold reduction in peak GPU memory for a representative case while preserving numerical equivalence. The implementation has also enabled a three-dimensional indoor ventilation demonstration. The poster will present the data layouts and differentiation strategies using schematic diagrams, summarize the complete performance sweep, and show the three-dimensional predicted flow fields as an animation.

presentations.title: Data Readiness for AI in HPC: Building a Community Around Dimensions, Metrics, and Tools
presentations.abstract: AI now drives discovery across HPC science, yet models are only as trustworthy as the data they use. Many teams still lack a shared way to judge whether their data is ready for AI. This BoF brings together the HPC and scientific communities to define data readiness for AI using seven practical dimensions: quality, understandability, fair and unbiased representation, structure and organization, feature importance, governance covering ethics, security and privacy, and AI-specific needs such as labels and distributions. Through short talks and open discussion, we will compare practices, identify gaps, and begin building shared metrics, tools, and benchmarks.

presentations.title: Data-Driven GPU Performance Model for Molecular Dynamics in Computational Drug Discovery
presentations.abstract:
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations increasingly rely on GPU acceleration to meet the computational demands of large biomolecular systems. However, predicting application performance across diverse molecular systems and heterogeneous GPU architectures remains challenging due to complex heterogeneous MD kernels with varying compute and memory demands. Conventional analytical models, including Roofline analysis, provide only coarse estimates and cannot capture the heterogeneous execution characteristics of modern MD workloads.

This work presents a hierarchical, reasonably explainable surrogate model that integrates molecular descriptors, simulation parameters, GPU architectural features to learn architecture-aware representations of MD execution on GPUs. Proposed teacher-student model's knowledge distillation removes the dependence on expensive runtime profiling while maintaining strong accuracy across previously unseen GPU architectures, providing a practical foundation for architecture-aware performance modeling in computational drug discovery.

presentations.title: Data-Driven Static MIG Planning for an H200 Research Cluster
presentations.abstract:
Research computing clusters support GPU workloads ranging from small interactive jobs to large full-device training runs. Exposing each GPU as a monolithic resource wastes capacity because many jobs require only a fraction of a GPU. Modern GPUs, such as the NVIDIA H200, support Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitioning, but real-time reconfiguration is impractical for heterogeneous, continuously arriving HPC workloads.

We frame MIG planning as an operational data analytics problem, using long-term production telemetry to make a one-time provisioning decision. We construct a slot-level demand matrix and formulate layout selection as an exact mixed-integer linear program (MILP), evaluating planners by weighted fulfillment. Our optimal layout improves in-sample fulfillment from 66.8% to 98.1%, reaches 97.6% on held-out data, and 99.7% on raw demand. A simple greedy planner achieves the same optimum due to a near-zero LP integrality gap (<0.001%). The layout is robust to demand inflation, and deploys directly with Slurm GRES.

presentations.title: DataCrumbs: Efficient Cross-Layer Data Capture for Explainable I/O Performance in HPC Storage Stacks
presentations.abstract: Modern scientific workloads move large data volumes through deep, complex I/O stacks in high-performance computing (HPC) systems. State-of-the-art tools such as Darshan capture API-level statistics describing what happened, not why, so performance variation is often dismissed as jitter without direct evidence. Emerging approaches such as eBPF enable fine-grained, low-overhead collection, but naively applied they produce overwhelming data volumes. We present DataCrumbs, an I/O monitoring tool that uses function probing to collect selective, fine-grained performance data across the full I/O stack, from user-space runtimes to kernel-space file-system paths, enabling explainable I/O analysis. DataCrumbs instruments 8,723 functions at only 0.1% profiling and under 3% tracing overhead, while a time-windowed, parallel event-association algorithm scales cross-layer root-cause analysis. Across four workloads, DataCrumbs exposes cross-layer insights invisible to user-space-only tools, including a tuned read-ahead insight that cuts Montage's POSIX I/O time by 1.35x. DataCrumbs thus enables selective, fine-grained, explainable I/O analysis for real HPC workloads.

presentations.title: Death by a Thousand Spreadsheets: Consolidating Infrastructure Data with NetBox
presentations.abstract:
If you work in HPC infrastructure, you know the drill: rack elevations in one spreadsheet, IPs in another, cable maps in Visio if they exist at all, and the rest living in someone's head. It works fine until that person is out sick or leaves.
This talk covers NetBox Enterprise as a replacement for that patchwork: DCIM for racks, devices, and cabling, IPAM for address space and VLANs, plus the extra tooling at the Enterprise tier. Most of the time is spent live in the tool: building out inventory, mapping topology, and showing what it looks like to consolidate scattered infrastructure data into one place instead of five.
The goal isn't to sell anyone on NetBox, but to give a realistic look at what the migration involves, what it fixes, and what it doesn't so you can decide if it's worth doing at your own site.

presentations.title: DECARD: A Runtime for Distributed and Heterogeneous Architectures Based on Dataflow
presentations.abstract:
Distributed heterogeneous architectures improve performance by mapping application components to specialized resources, but exposing architectural details increases programming and runtime complexity. Program Execution Models (PXMs) abstract application dependencies from scheduling and data-movement mechanisms. The Codelet Model is a dataflow-inspired PXM based on explicit dependencies among codelets grouped into Threaded Procedures.

This paper presents DECARD (Distributed Execution Codelet Accelerated Runtime for Dataflow), an extension of the Codelet Model for distributed heterogeneous systems. DECARD defines hierarchical components for node-level scheduling, communication, codelet scheduling, and execution, implemented using C++, OpenMP, and MPI. Evaluation shows a stable runtime cost of 1.14--1.23~$\mu$s per codelet, 10.55$\times$ shared-node speedup from 4 to 48 cores with 87.95% efficiency, and 96.67% distributed scaling efficiency across five 48-core nodes. Communication and 2D stencil experiments further characterize token transfers and application-level execution, establishing DECARD as a platform for studying distributed dataflow execution.

presentations.title: Decay-Driven Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Preference-Aware Power Control in HPC
presentations.abstract: Energy efficiency is a fundamental constraint in HPC systems, where electricity costs rival hardware costs and power budgets limit deployable performance. RL suits runtime power control, but online training is impractical in production, and offline RL needs a separate agent per operating point since preference weights are fixed beforehand. We present DDMORL, a Decay-Driven Multi-Objective RL framework for single-node energy management that exposes one application- and hardware-agnostic control: a user-specified scalar acceptable performance decay δ ∈ [0,1]. A lightweight, application-specific progress-to-power-cap model generates preference-aligned signals from this target, removing the need for learned interpolators or per-point agents, while letting the offline-trained policy control power live via Intel's RAPL. We evaluate DDMORL on compute- and memory-bound HPC benchmarks, showing decay levels map reliably to power caps delivering substantial energy savings within the requested degradation limit; the approach is application- and hardware-agnostic and generalizes to other nodes for production deployment.

presentations.title: Decentralized Scheduling of Scientific Workflows
presentations.abstract:
Modern scientific workflows are evolving with the emergence of the Compute Continuum, which integrates geographically distributed, heterogeneous, and dynamic computing resources across HPC systems, cloud platforms, edge devices, and scientific facilities. In this context, traditional centralized Workflow Management Systems (WMSs) face scalability and fault-tolerance limitations, motivating the exploration of decentralized scheduling mechanisms.

In this paper, we present a general approach for implementing decentralized scheduling in WMSs, enabling distributed task submission, collaborative task allocation, and remote task execution. Using this approach, we implement a fully decentralized consensus-based scheduler in which agents collectively agree on task assignments without relying on a central coordinator or shared global state. The scheduler is integrated into the COMPSs WMS and evaluated on the MareNostrum 5 supercomputer using a distributed GridSearch application.

The results demonstrate improvements in workflow execution time and load balancing across agents. Our general approach provides a foundation for implementing decentralized scheduling mechanisms.

presentations.title: Deciding whether a generative quantum eigensolver can work before running it
presentations.abstract: Generative quantum eigensolvers map naturally onto hybrid quantum-classical HPC systems. Configuring one means choosing an operator pool, a reference state, a circuit depth, and a simulator. With the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model as our testbed, we find that a symmetry calculation constrains all four choices. The pool and reference state fix how much of the state space a circuit can explore. That dimension names the cheapest exact simulator and the shortest circuit expressing a generic target. Exploiting the symmetry, a permutation-symmetric simulator reaches 1000 spins on one GH200 superchip. A companion test, one energy evaluation per pool token, asks whether any token improves on the reference state. Neither the calculation nor the test needs a run or the ground state, and together they explain three campaigns. A third and costlier scan fixes the working depth. Of its two pre-registered predictions, one held and one failed.

presentations.title: Deep codesign of advanced technology systems
Deep Learning at Scale: Engineering High-Resolution Scientific AI Models
presentations.abstract: Deep learning is increasingly used in scientific applications involving high-dimensional, high-resolution data. As models, datasets, and data resolutions scale, so does the need for efficient, distributed training on high performance computing (HPC) systems. This tutorial addresses practical challenges in training scientific AI models on high-resolution data, including data throughput, memory pressure, and communication overhead in distributed HPC workflows. Participants will learn to profile and build efficient data pipelines, optimize single-GPU performance, and scale training across GPUs and nodes using data, tensor, and spatial (domain) parallelism. Through hands-on examples drawn from scientific use cases, we will show how different model families, such as transformers, convolutional neural networks, and neural operators, benefit from these parallelization strategies. We will emphasize the performance trade-offs among computation, memory, and communication that determine scalability for high-resolution scientific workloads. Attendees will gain experience running optimized workloads on GPU-based supercomputers and learn strategies they can apply to train scientific AI models that exceed single-device memory limits while scaling efficiently.

presentations.title: Democratizing AI Accelerators for HPC Applications: Challenges, Success, and Support
presentations.abstract: A recent surge in novel AI accelerator hardware has sparked intense interest in running HPC applications and driven algorithmic research on these architectures. However, the maturity levels of associated tooling and software stacks vary significantly, with gaps in documentation and support. This BoF aims to explore trends in AI accelerators for HPC, ideal programming models, software stack support, code portability, training resources, and common challenges. We hope to foster a community of users interested or experienced in using AI accelerators for HPC applications.

presentations.title: Dependency-Preserving GPU Work Decomposition for Earthquake Rupture Simulation Using the Fast Domain Partitioning Method
presentations.abstract: The Fast Domain Partitioning Method (FDPM) reduces the time and memory complexity of boundary-integral-equation simulations of earthquake rupture. Its matrix-generation phase exposes independent element pairs, but each pair's three slip-direction series produce hundreds of coefficients reused by closed-form evaluations throughout a time window. A one-thread-per-pair mapping exceeds register capacity, whereas distributing only the evaluation across threads routes coefficients through device memory. GPU-kernel and thread boundaries therefore cannot be chosen independently. We propose dependency-preserving work decomposition that jointly selects both boundaries from producer–consumer dependencies and GPU resource and execution constraints. For FDPM, one fused kernel handles each series and one warp lane owns each term-specific coefficient–evaluation chain, keeping coefficients on chip and exchanging only low-volume scalars. On an NVIDIA H100, matrix generation runs about 12× faster than a direct OpenACC port on the same GPU. With additional time-evolution optimizations, the whole simulation runs 45× faster than the production A64FX baseline.

presentations.title: Deriving Vendor-Agnostic GPU Metrics from AMD MI300A and NVIDIA H100 Hardware Counters
presentations.abstract:
Large-scale scientific applications increasingly run on GPUs from multiple vendors, and comparing performance across architectures is essential to porting and tuning codes. Such comparisons rely on hardware counters, but AMD and NVIDIA expose counter sets designed independently, with different names, granularities, and semantics, and no correspondence between them exists. We construct and validate a mapping between AMD MI300A and NVIDIA H100 hardware counters for FP64 compute and memory-hierarchy metrics, scoring each candidate pair across 12 kernels from the RAJA Performance Suite. Counters that appear comparable can measure different quantities: AMD reports FP64 instructions per wavefront without indicating how many of its 64 threads were active, which makes it report up to 3.19× more FP64 FLOPs than NVIDIA for the same kernel. We show how to correct this, and report every mapping we tested, including those that agree poorly and the metrics for which no
mapping exists.

presentations.title: Descriptive Execution of HPC Applications and Workflows
presentations.abstract: The means to execute and orchestrate software in high performance computing (HPC) has changed from human-written code to descriptive prose. We assess the extent to which an agentic framework can optimize and run an HPC scaling study with a low-latency network in Amazon Web Services, translate job specifications between workload managers, and design and run workflows. In job translation experiments, agents convert 982 of 1,000 specifications between Slurm and Flux, all validated by production Flux, matching human-written performance in all but one case. In the scaling experiments, agents deploy and optimize applications, demonstrating scaling through the largest size of nodes. In the bioscience workflow, the agent reproduces an expert-written variant-calling pipeline almost exactly -agreeing with the reference call set in 18 of 19 evaluable runs - through many distinct yet functionally equivalent implementations. This information is invaluable for enabling multi-cluster application deployment, with scheduling and transformation handled by agents.

presentations.title: Design the Plant and the Control Together
presentations.abstract:
Exascale cooling plants are often sized and operated by convention, making it unclear how much energy can be recovered through control and how much performance is fixed by plant design. We developed and validated a digital twin of the Frontier supercomputer cooling plant using one year of operational telemetry, then optimized control settings, coolant flow, subloop topology, and life cycle cost and carbon. The novel contribution is an end-to-end co-design framework showing that implementable control recovers 27.8% of annual cooling energy, while optimized flow allocation reduces topology sensitivity by 93%, leaving embodied carbon as the main remaining design criterion.

The study has completed model validation, annual optimization, topology enumeration, and life cycle analysis. During the poster session, we will use a system diagram, validation plots, energy savings comparisons, topology results, and a life cycle decision map to show why control should be optimized before hardware redesign.

presentations.title: Designing Open, Heterogeneous System Monitoring Around OpenCHAMI
presentations.abstract: While modern management platforms like OpenCHAMI streamline cluster orchestration, they do not inherently provide the comprehensive monitoring and data collection required to observe every facet of a next-generation data center. Operating heterogeneous, large-scale systems requires a unified, open-source observability framework capable of aggregating distributed logs, metrics, and traces across thousands of bleeding-edge compute nodes. This BoF session brings together HPC systems engineers, data center architects, and site reliability engineers to discuss the architecture, integration challenges, and best practices for building robust telemetry pipelines around OpenCHAMI, ensuring operational visibility, rapid fault isolation, and open-source compliance in next-generation supercomputing environments.

presentations.title: Developing a Numerical Algorithm with CIVL Model Checking in the Loop
presentations.abstract: Verifying a numerical algorithm in a large scientific simulation is challenging: the framework is too big to model-check, and the unit tests exercise only sampled inputs. We report a case study developing a new cloud-in-cell (CIC) deposition algorithm for Flash-X, a multiphysics simulation framework, keeping the CIVL model checker in the loop. Rather than verify the algorithm within Flash-X, we extract only the interfaces the algorithm needs into a small, self-contained C model, and check the algorithm there. Treating particle positions as symbolic values, CIVL proves two physical properties---mass conservation and the deposition location---over the continuum of admissible positions, and verifies memory safety and freedom from MPI deadlocks and data races across rank distributions within bounds. Writing the verifying properties first and rechecking them at each stage turned CIVL into a design guardrail. It also surfaced a defect that our random-seed tests missed. We report its benefits, cost, and tradeoffs.

presentations.title: DGEMM with Ozaki Scheme I/II on FP4 Tensor Cores: A Base-13 E2M1 Limb Representation
presentations.abstract: This paper proposes a method and its implementation for emulating FP64 matrix multiplication (DGEMM) by constructing, on FP4 (E2M1) Tensor Cores, Ozaki schemes I and II. The key property is that every FP4 value becomes an integer when doubled, and that shifting this integer set by multiples of 13 covers all integers. Converting an arbitrary integer into base-13 FP4 limbs keeps intermediate sums error-free in FP32 accumulators. By the same principle, the integer GEMM of INT8 Tensor Cores can be emulated bit-exactly on FP4. When FP4 Tensor Cores have twice the throughput of FP8, Ozaki scheme II theoretically achieves slightly higher performance than its FP8 counterpart. This paper further proposes kernel optimizations raising the attained fraction of peak performance. We verify this on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, achieving performance competitive with an existing FP8-based implementation of Ozaki scheme II, and exceeding it at a large problem size (16384^3).

presentations.title: Diagnosing and delivering repairs for Fortran GPU offload compiler defects
presentations.abstract: Many production simulation codes reach GPUs through directive-based Fortran offload, where compiler support is immature. Compiler suites are built largely from single-construct tests, leaving the clause combinations applications write thinly covered. We use a production flow solver as a compiler-validation instrument: golden files and grindtime detect a defect, metamorphic probes confirm it, and a C-to-Fortran differential and bisection localize it. Three months yielded 45 defects across the AMD, Cray, and Intel toolchains and 18 patches. About a dozen sit below any directive, in Fortran lowering, the back end, or the linker; several reproduce only under OpenACC. Fifteen give wrong answers with no diagnostic, so 42\% of what we found passes a compile-and-run suite. Delivery, not repair, delays users: Cray CCE 21.0.2 ships two defects whose upstream repairs predate its declared base by three and four months, and five merged fixes await a vendor build absent for 109 days.

presentations.title: Diamond Agent: Agentic Control of Federated HPC Resources as a Service
presentations.abstract: Efficiently aggregating and orchestrating computing power across heterogeneous clusters for HPC workflows faces four practical challenges: preserving workflow context across independently administered clusters, moving large datasets between sites, reasoning about site-specific environments and scheduler policies, and exploiting live queue and resource states for efficient task scheduling. To this end, we design Diamond Agent, an agentic system that enables intelligent execution of HPC workflows across heterogeneous clusters. Diamond Agent provides an agent-facing workspace and skills that unify cross-site resource discovery, resource specification, data movement, task execution, and result retrieval. Diamond Agent translates high-level agent actions into valid site-specific executions, moves data through Globus Transfer, and uses live system capability and queue information to select feasible placements. Its event-driven continuation mechanism decouples agent actions from long-running batch jobs: persistent services monitor remote execution and resume the agent only when a result or decision-relevant event is available.

presentations.title: Diamond Agent: Agentic Control of Federated HPC Resources as a Service
presentations.abstract: We present Diamond Agent, an agentic system that enables intelligent execution of HPC workflows across heterogeneous clusters with typed skills as the interface. Diamond Agent provides an agent-facing workspace and skills that unify cross-site resource discovery, resource specification, data movement, task execution, and result retrieval. A centralized Diamond Agent instance can operate multiple supercomputers without being deployed separately on each login node. Diamond Agent translates high-level agent actions into valid site-specific executions, moves data through Globus Transfer, and uses live system capability and queue information to select feasible placements. Its event-driven continuation mechanism decouples agent actions from long-running batch jobs: persistent services monitor remote execution and resume the agent only when a result or decision-relevant event is available.

presentations.title: Digital Twins in HPC: From Shared Definitions to Shared Standards
presentations.abstract: The HPC community now has a working definition of the digital twin, anchored in the 2024 NASEM report. What it lacks are standards to operationalize that definition across the full lifecycle. This BoF brings together practitioners from novice to expert, spanning scientific computing, biomedicine, infrastructure, and data centers, to surface the most urgent gaps: data homogenization across heterogeneous sources, verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ) at every lifecycle stage, and the emerging role of agentic AI as both enabler and new source of complexity. We will map the landscape, identify active efforts, and determine what coordinated community action looks like.

presentations.title: Digitizing the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary: Accelerating Document Analysis with VLMs and HPC Infrastructure
presentations.abstract: The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary (CAD), completed in 21-plus volumes over 90 years (1921–2011), is a foundational Akkadian lexical reference locked in print and print-derived images. Manual text generation from dictionary scanned images requires domain expertise and is time-consuming. We present a generalizable pipeline that converts dense mixed-script dictionary pages into accurate UTF-8-encoded structured data. The HPC-enabled pipeline combines image preprocessing and layout segmentation with Vision Language Model (VLM)–based Optical Character Recognition (OCR), prompt engineering, and post-processing. In few-shot experiments on the gold standard dataset, Claude Opus 4.6 achieved a 1.45% CER and 5.75% WER on the training set (for optimal prompt design and selection) and 1.49% CER and 4.73% WER on the validation set. Using the pipeline, running on CPU compute nodes, we extracted raw text in less than a week, with domain expert text verification underway to finalize the scholarly dataset for human-environment history research.

presentations.title: Disk-to-Disk File Transfer Experiment on an End-to-End 400 Gbps Line Between Japan and the USA by MMCFTP
presentations.abstract: nri102s1,NRE109

presentations.title: Dispatch Granularity in Quantum-HPC ADMM Optimization: Implications for Near-Real-Time Computing
presentations.abstract:
Iterative-consensus decomposition enables combinatorial optimization problems exceeding a single quantum processing unit (QPU) by solving coupled block subproblems and
reconciling them at a consensus barrier. We evaluate whether sub-solver quality or execution mode governs performance. Across 880 byte-identical sub-QUBOs of widths 6–13, non-variational digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization (DCQO) and variational QAOA match exact enumeration at widths ≤ 7 under equal per-circuit shot budgets, whereas classical simulated annealing produces materially larger gaps. When routed onto the measured coupling map of the 54-qubit IQM Emerald, DCQO and QAOA circuit depths differ by at most 9% at supported widths. Their principal distinction is dispatch granularity: DCQO requires one circuit per block and permits round-level batching, whereas QAOA requires 25 sequential circuit evaluations per block in our execution model. Thus, for near-real-time hybrid optimization, execution-mode selection matters more than sub-solver choice.

presentations.title: Distinguished Address: Rethinking Security for AI: Enforcing Boundaries for AI Agents
presentations.abstract: As organizations adopt AI agents that execute code, access data, and coordinate across shared HPC infrastructure, every allowed action becomes a security decision. This talk explores how NVIDIA OpenShell brings isolation, deterministic policy enforcement, and controlled network access, unlocking actual enforceable agent runtime boundaries. Safe adoption requires extending zero trust to agent behavior, making continuous monitoring and governance foundational to how organizations grant, oversee, and govern agent autonomy.

presentations.title: Distinguished Paper Recognition and Closing
Distinguished Speaker Talk: "Developing a task-based compressible Navier-Stokes solver - lessons learned and future developments"
presentations.abstract:
Leveraging task-based programming to efficiently execute scientific computing necessitates substantial adaptation of algorithms and software architectures in comparison to standard and established MPI implementations.
