In this context, the Hypersonic Task-based Research (HTR) solver is one of the examples of software for scientific computing that has adopted a task-based architecture. HTR is a compressible Navier-Stokes solver, and it is specifically designed for the study of reacting multiphysics flows at high Mach numbers. It employs finite-difference algorithms for discretizing the transport equations on curvilinear structured grids. The entire solver operates within the environment provided by the Legion runtime and is routinely utilized on hundreds of GPUs for scientific discoveries related to hypersonic turbulence, electrified combustion, and rocket burner ignition.
Over the years, the HTR solver has undergone significant updates and refactorings to enhance its capabilities and achieve improved performance while maintaining portability and maintainability. This talk aims to delve into some of the design decisions and trade-offs made during this development process. The primary objective is to shed light on the strengths and potential areas for improvement of this type of runtime from the perspective of an end user.

presentations.title: Distinguished Talk: Scaling Autonomy: Federated Agentic Middleware and Serverless Systems for Scientific Computing
presentations.abstract: Scientific discovery increasingly relies on integrating large-scale experiments, simulations, and AI models across diverse computing environments. However, existing workflows and middleware often struggle with the complexity of scaling across federated resources and lack the autonomy needed to overcome human bottlenecks. In this talk, I will present a vision for autonomous, agent-driven science enabled by federated serverless systems. I will show how agentic middleware can orchestrate stateful, collaborative agents across heterogeneous resources, relying on serverless computing to provide elastic, on-demand execution at extreme scale. Drawing on our prior work with Parsl, funcX, Globus, and Academy, I will present examples that demonstrate how federated agentic systems can deliver high-throughput, resilient, and scalable scientific computing, enabling more autonomous and efficient discovery.

presentations.title: Distributed Shared Timestamped Memory
presentations.abstract:
Parallel discrete-event simulation (PDES) and agent-based modeling and simulation (ABMS) are two important modeling and simulation paradigms used in domains such as network simulation, epidemiology, and transportation. Both must coordinate distributed state as simulation time advances, yet common approaches in each paradigm sacrifice either performance through blocking synchronization or scalability and simplicity through rollback mechanisms to do so. Moreover research in each field has largely progressed in isolation.

We present a partitioned distributed versioned array that can serve as a common global distributed memory layer in both PDES and ABMS for more flexible synchronization schemes. By allowing each rank to maintain multiple versions of a shared datastructure available at the same time, our approach enables unbalanced workloads to drift out of lockstep without rollbacks or neighborhood barriers. We demonstrated increased performance using this scheme on common benchmarks from both PDES and ABMS paradigms, against state of the art runtimes.

presentations.title: Distributed Sparse P-bit Ising Machines for CPU Clusters
presentations.abstract:
Ising computing is a novel paradigm for combi-
natorial optimizations. Ising machines built from probabilistic
bits (p-bits) update each vertex from a weighted sum over
its graph neighbors forming an inherently irregular workload.
Distributing the sampler across Message Passing Interface (MPI)
processes or ranks lets each rank update its own p-bits while
restricting communication to halo p-bits. We characterize this
trade-off on 12 MAX-CUT instances using the GPI-2 one-
sided communication at 2-8 processes, sweeping synchronization
frequency and comparing two primary samplers for the first
time: Stochastic Simulated Annealing (SSA) and Probabilistic bit
Simulated Annealing (PSA). Poorly partitioned graphs can see
a speedup upto 53x from relaxed synchronization. The quality
cost, however, is set by density rather than halo/owned ratio.
Sparse graphs lose under 1% even at high halo ratios, while
dense instances lose 8.6%. PSA yields better solutions in 83% of
configurations whereas SSA runs up to 3.4× faster.

presentations.title: Distributed SpMV with HClib-Actor: A Case Study in Alternatives to MPI-Based PETSc
presentations.abstract: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) exhibits irregular computation and communication patterns that challenge distributed-memory execution. This paper presents a case study of distributed SpMV using HClib-Actor, an actor-based programming and runtime system implementing the Fine-grained Asynchronous Bulk-Synchronous Parallel (FA-BSP) model. We explore four HClib-Actor-based implementations as alternatives to MPI, varying matrix partitioning and sparse storage format, which together determine the communication direction and local traversal order. We evaluate their weak and strong scalability on synthetic and real-world graph matrices using up to 1,536 CPU cores, with PETSc as a highly optimized MPI baseline, on the Georgia Tech PACE Phoenix cluster. Our results show that HClib-Actor achieves good scalability on relatively well-balanced workloads and outperforms PETSc in several configurations, although performance remains sensitive to workload distribution. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of HClib-Actor for distributed SpMV and motivates further exploration of partitioning, scheduling, storage, and communication strategies.

presentations.title: Distributed Volumetric Generation of Neuronal Morphology at Scale
presentations.abstract: Large-scale electron microscopy connectomes enable the study of neuronal morphology, but annotating and proofreading these datasets remains effort-intensive. Generative models offer a complementary approach, learning from manual reconstructions to synthesize neuronal structures. Dense volumetric occupancy grids are directly compatible with connectomics workflows, but cost grows cubically with linear resolution which is unfavorable for sparse objects like neurons. We present a distributed generative pipeline with this representation and characterize its cost–fidelity tradeoff. We extract 46,582 axonal and dendritic fragments under a fixed 20 µm field of view and train a compartment-conditioned 3D convolutional variational autoencoder at different resolutions. Generated fragments are evaluated using geometric and topological descriptors calibrated against natural variation in the data. Across up to 256 NVIDIA A100 GPUs on Polaris, our pipeline retain 74–85% strong-scaling efficiency for training and generation is sharded to produce one million fragments in 3.1 s at 64³ and 5.25 min at 256³.

presentations.title: DMSim: Configurable Data Management Simulation Framework for Scientific Computing Grid
presentations.abstract: Modern computing-grid simulators often emphasize system configuration and job allocation while simplifying data-management behavior, despite its stateful impact on performance. In data-centric infrastructures such as the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG), replica placement and transfer policies influence network contention, staging delay, storage utilization, and resiliency, yet production-scale evaluation is difficult. We present DMSim, a configurable data-management simulation framework for scientific computing grids. DMSim extends CGSim with a lightweight global file-system manager and SimGrid-based communication modeling to track replicas, simulate contention-aware transfers, and support configurable policies. It models reactive transfers triggered by job inputs, proactive background replication and rebalancing, and explicit drop-in transfers for irregular behaviors. We validate DMSim using historical PanDA and Rucio records, reconstructing initial file locations and comparing simulated transfer-queue times with production observations. Simulated staging times fall above bandwidth-based lower bounds and below observed job queuing times, supporting reproducible policy evaluation at scale in controlled experimental settings.

presentations.title: Do AI Workloads Fail Differently? A Cross-Cluster Characterization of Failure Types in AI and HPC Systems
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing studies conclude that user error causes most job failures, while large-scale AI training reports attribute most interruptions to hardware. The two literatures are rarely read together, because they publish failure evidence in incompatible forms: attributed causes, scheduler outcome labels, or bare event rates.

We surveyed 162 public datasets and operational reports, assigned every one an evidence verdict, and normalized the usable evidence into an 11-class taxonomy that tags each failure type as a cause, a symptom, or an outcome label. The resulting denominator-disciplined maps cover 38 systems across 44 matrix columns and include a GPU error-class characterization spanning five hardware generations. The work is complete: every value passed three verification passes, and the artifact is public.

presentations.title: DOE Genesis Mission
Does New Hardware Improve Carbon Impact of HPC systems?
presentations.abstract: The carbon footprint of computing systems is growing rapidly, driven by exponential AI growth. Many studies have suggested approaches such as fast hardware upgrades, using renewable power, and extending system lifetime to improve overall carbon efficiency and reduce carbon footprint. We analyzed carbon efficiency of the top 500 high performance computing (HPC) systems. It shows that a combination of key factors affects carbon efficiency. We propose tempered hardware upgrade, where hardware upgrades are performed while considering carbon optimization, accounting for both new and old hardware's embodied carbon. We evaluate several approaches and find that optimizing for just one factor: performance, operational carbon, or embodied carbon fails to improve carbon efficiency, sometimes worsening it or yielding negligible gains. For example, a fast hardware upgrade worsens embodied carbon efficiency by 0.9x but slightly improves operational carbon efficiency by 1.1x, however increasing embodied and operational carbon emissions by 125.5% and 47.2%, respectively. In contrast, tempered hardware upgrade improves embodied carbon efficiency by 1.7x and operational carbon efficiency by 19x, while increasing embodied carbon emissions by only 12.7% and reducing operational carbon emissions by 86.2%. We conclude that a balanced approach is required to improve carbon efficiency and reduce carbon footprint of systems.

presentations.title: Domain Bounds as a Silent-Fault Detector for AI-Ready Scientific Data
presentations.abstract: We address an incipient type of data-based faults, driven by increasing data reuse in AI-enhanced computational science workflows. A dataset is created under specific conditions; its categories, measures, and labels depend on that context, but that context is usually unavailable downstream and abandoned when datasets are used to train models. We propose encoding this context, called domain bounds, with the data to which it applies. A domain bound flags apparently valid data proposed for reuse in an incompatible context, even when every value falls within its expected range. We present cases from computational science and biomedicine where missing domain bounds allow silent reuse errors, and show why description and provenance approaches miss them. Our detector uses standard data container technologies and catches faults from a taxonomy of published cases, at a cost independent of dataset size. It caught 17 of 18 injected domain-bound reuses that lineage and descriptive records accepted.

presentations.title: Domain-Aware Power Rebalancing under Node-Level Power Caps on Aurora
presentations.abstract:
Node-level power capping is a scalable mechanism for enforcing electrical, thermal, and scheduling constraints on exascale systems. On a heterogeneous node, however, a single
cap hides a second decision: how platform firmware distributes the constrained budget among GPUs, CPU cores, memory, and the CPU uncore. This paper characterizes the hidden allocation
on the Aurora supercomputer. More importantly, under constrained node caps, firmware can keep the CPU uncore near its minimum even when application progress depends on data movement, increasing runtime enough to raise total board energy. We introduce U-PullUp, a lightweight GEOPM agent that uses recent GPU copy-engine activity as a data-movement signal and requests a higher uncore frequency while leaving the node cap active. Across the nine SPEChpc workloads, U-PullUp reduces board energy by up to 34.2% relative to default power control at the same cap, while the best configuration for each workload reduces energy by 19.6% on average.

presentations.title: DPGraph: Code Optimization with Dynamic Program Graphs Using Heterogeneous GNNs
presentations.abstract: Heterogeneous high-performance computing systems require selecting suitable devices (e.g., CPU or GPU) and optimization parameters such as vectorization and interleave factors. Existing LLVM-IR-based program representations mostly rely on static information and may miss runtime behavior important for performance optimization. We propose DPGraph, an execution-flow-aware program graph representation that augments fine-grained LLVM-IR-based program representations with dynamic data dependencies to better capture runtime program behavior and identify effective optimization configurations. We evaluate DPGraph on vectorization and interleave factor prediction, CPU/GPU parallelism detection, and optimal loop-order prediction tasks. Across these tasks, DPGraph achieves around 13.6%, 7.06%, and 7.05% higher performance gains than state-of-the-art approaches, respectively. DPGraph is also data- and compute-efficient: it achieves 13.6% better speedup than MIREncoder while using over 40X fewer training samples and reduces training time by about 86% for CPU/GPU configuration prediction compared to state-of-the-art method ConTraPh.

presentations.title: DPUCrumbs: Dissecting DPU Pathways
presentations.abstract:
Data processing units (DPUs) such as NVIDIA's BlueField-3 increasingly used to offload MPI collectives, compression and data movement in HPC.
Yet cost of offload is spread across every layer between the application and the card.
Existing tools observe one layer at a time, each on its own clock, so host, driver and card cannot be joined into one timeline.
A slow offload is therefore observable but not explainable.
We present DPUCrumbs, an eBPF-based tracer that extends DataCrumbs across PCIe onto the card.
It captures application calls, DOCA and ibverbs entry points, MLX5 driver and kernel's DMA and IOMMU paths.
NIC hardware timestamps then place both endpoints on one time axis.
On a DOCA RDMA ping-pong, DPUCrumbs measures PCIe crossings at 13.2 and 8.6 µs, shows the DPU responding in 0.82 µs and and and reveals that reply waits 6.1 µs at the NIC before host consumes it, at 3.6% overhead.

presentations.title: Drava: An Event-Driven Runtime for Scientific Pipelines with Agentic Configuration Optimization
presentations.abstract:
Next-generation X-ray science (XRS) detectors are driving continuous, multi-stage streaming pipelines with facility-scale data rates approaching petabytes per second. These workflows require real-time reconstruction, AI inference, and feedback-driven control under strict performance and energy constraints, yet current software stacks often require manual tuning of batching, transport, and resource decisions.

We propose Drava, an event-driven runtime for scientific streaming pipelines. Developers express application stages as reusable components, while Drava manages scheduling, batching, data movement, and execution across heterogeneous resources. Integrated with ptychography and tomography applications, Drava sustains high-rate streaming at about 31 kHz. Compared with PvaPy, it handles unpaced input without dropping frames and achieves up to 2.36× higher throughput. Batching improves throughput by up to 2.44×, while agentic Bayesian optimization identifies a configuration 2.24× faster than the best manual configuration. Drava also exposes throughput-energy trade-offs for performance- and energy-aware scientific workflows.

presentations.title: Drava: An Event-Driven Runtime for Scientific Pipelines with Agentic Configuration Optimization
presentations.abstract: Across scientific domains, detectors increasingly produce data faster than it can be transmitted, forcing analysis to run near the instrument. The analysis uses multi-stage pipelines that may include reconstruction and inference under latency and throughput constraints. Current solutions leave key performance choices such as batch size, inter-stage data transport, and resource placement to manual tuning that is brittle and time consuming. We introduce Drava, an event-driven runtime for edge scientific streaming pipelines. Developers express stages as reusable callbacks, while Drava manages scheduling, batching, data movement, and transport-aware execution across heterogeneous resources. On ptychography and tomography pipelines, Drava sustains 31 kHz on the runtime path and runs up to 2.36× faster than a PvaPy baseline that drops frames beyond 2 kHz. Drava remains ~2.6× faster than hand-tuned loss-free PvaPy, while its observability enables agentic optimization that finds a configuration 2.24× faster than the best manual one and exposes energy–throughput trade-offs.

presentations.title: Dynamic and Static Workflow Orchestration for Large-Scale Uncertainty Quantification Campaigns
presentations.abstract:
Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is an essential component of computational science workflows. As the size of UQ campaigns continues to grow, efficiently orchestrating large ensembles of parallel simulations on High Performance Computing (HPC) systems becomes increasingly challenging. While workflow management frameworks simplify campaign execution, the choice of an orchestration strategy can significantly influence resource utilization, execution efficiency, and overall time to solution.

This paper evaluates two paradigms for large-scale campaigns on a parallel hemodynamics application use-case. The first approach employs dynamic task scheduling using EasyVVUQ and Dask Distributed, where simulations are executed through a pool of dynamically managed workers. The second approach relies on scheduler-native job arrays, where simulation instances are submitted as independent batch jobs.

The methodology combines strong scaling experiments with UQ campaigns executed under both orchestration strategies. The results provide practical guidance for selecting workflow execution strategies and highlight the trade-offs between dynamic and static workflow orchestration models.

presentations.title: Dynamic Planning for Scalable Data Movement in Accelerated Query Engines
presentations.abstract:
At scale, structured-data processing is often a data-movement problem. Joins and aggregations must choose whether to shuffle, broadcast, or reduce intermediate results,
and the right choice can depend on data properties that are hard to predict prior to execution. In this paper, we introduce dynamic planning, a query-optimization method that lets operators choose data-movement strategies at runtime. We have implemented this approach in GPU Polars, where RapidsMPF actors observe table chunks and exchange metadata before selecting a strategy. Controlled microbenchmarks and a PDS-H Q9 case study confirm that dynamic planning makes sensible runtime decisions while preserving both stability and performance.

presentations.title: E-dLLM: Energy-Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference via Phase-Aware DVFS
presentations.abstract: Existing diffusion LLM (dLLM) serving systems focus on optimizing latency and throughput, while their energy efficiency remains less studied. We show that dLLM decoding moves between compute-bound cache-refresh and memory-bound cache-reuse phases, and that decoding configurations create a broad accuracy–energy trade-off. We present E-dLLM, which combines configuration selection with phase-aware dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). On LLaDA-8B, reactive DVFS reduces energy by 17% with less than 1% latency overhead, while preserving model outputs.

presentations.title: E4S: An HPC-AI Software Ecosystem for Science
presentations.abstract:
E4S, an HPSF project, provides a broad HPC-AI software ecosystem for science [https://e4s.io]. E4S is a curated, Spack based software distribution of 100+ HPC, EDA, and AI/ML packages. It features AI tools such as PyTorch, OpenClaw, NVIDIA NemoClaw, NVIDIA NeMo, NVIDIA BioNeMo, vllm, Ollama, Huggingface CLI, JAX, OpenAI, Google's Gemini API based chatbot, and other supporting tools including langchain, pandas, and SciKit-Learn. E4S supports containerized, bare-metal installation, and deployment on commercial cloud platforms with support for AWS, Azure, OCI, IBM, and Google Cloud. It includes Codium, an IDE, Jupyter notebook, and visualization tools such as VisIt and ParaView all launched from a web browser without installing any additional software. These tools provide an
open platform for education and research in HPC-AI.

presentations.title: Early Lessons From Characterizing Unified CPU-GPU Memory on DGX Spark
presentations.abstract: NVIDIA DGX Spark integrates an Arm CPU and Blackwell GPU behind one coherent LPDDR5X memory pool. A roofline view captures throughput, but the shared-memory programming model can blur where CPU–GPU memory-policy costs are charged. We isolate three attribution factors: ownership state, lifecycle boundary, and timing window. Handoff tests show cold first touch reaches 35x steady reuse, with managed-family paths still 1.6x–1.7x above steady at 256 MiB. Lifecycle tests show explicit and mapped host paths spend 264 ms and 246 ms in 256 MiB setup+teardown, versus 0.22–0.24 ms for managed-family paths. In a 400 MiB-per-array vector addition, end-to-end and steady-state timing change policy ranking. Unified physical memory simplifies data visibility, but it does not remove ownership, lifecycle, or timing-window cost attribution.

presentations.title: EcoShift: Performance-Aware Power Management for Power-Constrained Heterogeneous Systems
presentations.abstract: Power constrained HPC systems increasingly execute heterogeneous CPU–GPU applications under strict cluster wide power limits. Existing power management policies typically rely on fair sharing or utilization based heuristics, overlooking application specific sensitivity to CPU and GPU power caps and therefore allocating reclaimed power inefficiently. We present EcoShift, a performance aware framework for cluster wide power management. EcoShift combines online performance prediction with a dynamic programming allocator that distributes reclaimed power among CPU–GPU applications to maximize average performance improvement. We evaluate EcoShift through emulation on two heterogeneous platforms equipped with Intel CPUs and NVIDIA A100 or H100 GPUs across diverse CPU–GPU workloads. EcoShift consistently outperforms state of the art policies, delivering up to 6% higher average performance while strictly maintaining the cluster wide power constraint.

presentations.title: Ecosystems for Scientific Computing in the Age of AI
presentations.abstract: AI is rapidly reshaping scientific software through code generation, simulation acceleration, intelligent workflows, and emerging agentic systems. Yet the software ecosystems, collaboration models, trust frameworks, and workforce practices that underpin high performance computing (HPC) were built for a different era. Drawing on findings from a recent workshop series (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03413), this BoF invites the international community to challenge assumptions, identify emerging priorities, and help define the next generation of scientific computing ecosystems. Discussion will focus on human-AI collaboration, trust, sustainability, user experience, and workforce evolution — turning shared insights into actionable directions for the community.

presentations.title: EduHPC-26: Workshop on Education for High Performance Computing
presentations.abstract: The EduHPC workshop is devoted to the development and assessment of educational innovations and resources in high performance computing (HPC) and parallel and distributed computing (PDC), with a particular focus on undergraduate and graduate education. We encourage contributions at the intersection of HPC/PDC education and other areas, including artificial intelligence, data science, and internet-of-things and edge (IoT/Edge) computing. Given the increasing relevance of ML/deep learning workloads on HPC systems, we especially encourage pedagogical papers on this topic. Historically, the workshop has accepted contributions from fields such as CS, CSE, DS, and computational courses across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. The workshop aims to foster collaboration among stakeholders within the SC context and provides a platform for discussing pedagogical challenges, solutions, and opportunities for HPC/PDC/DS/AI/ML/IoT education. Activities at EduHPC'26 include a featured speaker, presentations of our peer-reviewed papers, and a special session focusing on innovative HPC/PDC assignments.

presentations.title: EESP Closing Remarks
EESP Welcome Remarks
EESSI as a Vendor-Neutral, Community-Driven Stack for Heterogeneous HPC and Cloud
presentations.abstract:
Managing workloads across rapidly diversifying hardware—spanning x86, Arm, and emerging RISC-V CPUs alongside competing NVIDIA and AMD GPU architectures—demands a software infrastructure that is genuinely independent, vendor-neutral, and resilient against ecosystem lock-in.
This talk introduces the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI), a community-governed software stack designed to provide an autonomous, transparent foundation for heterogeneous scientific computing. Supported through the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking via the MultiXscale Centre-of-Excellence, EESSI delivers an on-demand, streaming distribution architecture (powered by CernVM-FS) that decouples scientific applications from specific host operating systems and single-vendor software ecosystems. By dynamically serving microarchitecture-optimized binaries across diverse CPU targets and GPU acceleration platforms without compromising performance, EESSI eliminates single-site redundancy and prevents vendor-driven stack fragmentation.

Ultimately, we demonstrate how establishing a shared, institutionally neutral software ecosystem ensures long-term scientific reproducibility, and returns software governance to the open scientific community.

presentations.title: Effective Communication
presentations.abstract: Every early-career professional will have to effectively communicate results, challenges, and ideas during their career. Effective communication can be very challenging, but is a necessary skill that, when perfected, will bolster any early-career professional. In this session, we will first focus on how to craft an effective written abstract that conveys the main message to the reader with a short paragraph. Then, we will dive into how to structure an oral presentation for maximum effect with an audience.

presentations.title: Efficient and Portable Support for Overdecomposition on Distributed GPU Platforms
presentations.abstract: Overdecomposition enables asynchronous many-task runtimes such as Charm++ to overlap communication with computation and to balance load dynamically. Its benefits are well established on CPUs, but GPUs favor large kernels and bulk transfers, so fine-grained execution risks prohibitive launch, synchronization, and communication overheads. We investigate whether overdecomposition can be sustained efficiently on GPUs and portably across vendors. We find that the dominant costs arise not on the device but from host-side serialization, in vendor-specific ways, and can be mitigated transparently by the runtime: by parallelizing kernel submission and completion detection across processes and threads sharing each GPU, and by routing every message through device-to-device paths. In a single-source Charm++/Kokkos environment running unchanged on NVIDIA and AMD systems, these techniques reduce the minimum effective task granularity on Task Bench from 26-37μs to 4μs, and overdecomposed Jacobi2D, MiniMD, and LULESH match MPI performance on up to 64 A40 and 32 MI250X GPUs.

presentations.title: Efficient Bayesian Spatially Clustered Factor Analysis with Adaptive Parallel Gibbs Sampling
presentations.abstract: Multivariate spatial data exhibit both spatial heterogeneity and spatial contiguity. Classical exploratory factor analysis (EFA), which assumes a globally homogeneous structure, is ill suited to capture these features. This paper proposes Bayesian spatially clustered factor analysis (BSCFA), which embeds a Bayesian approach within the spatially clustered factor analysis (SCFA) framework. BSCFA retains the spatially adaptive grouping mechanism of SCFA and shifts it from point estimation to posterior inference conditional on the estimated partition, providing conditional uncertainty quantification for group specific factor models given the final partition. In addition, conjugate priors introduce Bayesian regularization, which stabilizes group specific parameter estimation and is particularly beneficial when individual spatial groups contain limited samples. To overcome the computational burden of running full MCMC chains at each outer iteration, we develop a suite of optimization strategies including state projection, warm-start Gibbs sampling, adaptive short chain lengths, and group wise parallel execution, which collectively yield an approximately 23.6-fold speedup. Simulation studies demonstrate that BSCFA outperforms both EFA and SCFA in terms of loading covariance estimation accuracy and model selection criterion. Applied to built environment data from 1,535 stations in the Tokyo metropolitan area, BSCFA identifies spatially contiguous clusters with clear functional differentiation. The factor structures reveal regional variations in urban functionality, achieving a BIC reduction of 25.9% compared to SCFA and 31.2% compared to EFA.

presentations.title: Efficient cosmological friends-of-friends computation with fine-grained optimizations
presentations.abstract: One computationally intensive part of cosmological simulations is identifying clusters. One method to do this is via the friends-of-friends (FoF) algorithm, which is functionally equivalent to finding incremental connected components. Optimizing FoF for large, imbalanced datasets is challenging due to load and communication imbalance. In this paper, we present a parallel approach that integrates a tree traversal library with a union-find library. While this combination provided a foundational framework, we discovered that it fell short of meeting the rigorous performance demands of complex cosmological data. To overcome this, we designed and implemented a series of fine-grained optimizations tailored to the unique memory and processing patterns of the algorithm. We demonstrate that our approach achieves significant performance gains for highly imbalanced outputs without compromising cluster accuracy or quality. Finally, we analyze these results and identify remaining opportunities for further improvement in scalable cluster finding.

presentations.title: Efficient Distributed GPU Programming for Exascale
presentations.abstract: Over the past decade, GPUs became ubiquitous in HPC installations around the world, delivering the majority of performance of some of the largest supercomputers, steadily increasing the available compute capacity. Four exascale systems (Frontier, Aurora, El Capitan, JUPITER) use GPUs as the core computing devices. To take advantage of these GPU-accelerated systems with tens of thousands of devices, application developers need to have the proper skills and tools to understand, manage, and optimize distributed GPU applications. In this tutorial, participants will learn techniques to efficiently program large-scale multi-GPU systems. While programming multiple GPUs with MPI is explained, also advanced tuning techniques and complementing programming models like NCCL and NVSHMEM are presented. Tools for analysis are shown and used to motivate and implement performance optimizations. The tutorial teaches fundamental concepts that apply to GPU-accelerated systems of any vendor in general, taking the NVIDIA platform as an example. It is a combination of lectures and hands-on exercises, using the JUPITER system for interactive learning and discovery.

presentations.title: Eighth Workshop on Interactive and Urgent High Performance Computing (WIUHPC)
presentations.abstract:
Interactivity enables the exploitation of HPC in new and revolutionary ways, delivering many new and exciting opportunities for our community. Interactive HPC involves users being in the loop during job execution monitoring a job, steering the experiment, or visualizing results to make immediate decisions. Likewise, urgent computing combines interactive computational modeling with time-sensitive systems in the real world such as the near-real-time analysis of unfolding disasters to inform real-time decision making. Supporting interactive and urgent workloads on HPC requires expertise in a wide range of areas and the solving of numerous technical and organizational challenges.

This workshop brings together stakeholders, researchers, and practitioners from across interactive and urgent computing within the wider HPC community. We will share success stories, case studies, and technologies to continue community building around leveraging urgent and interactive HPC as an important tool for scientific research, responding to disasters, and addressing societal issues.

presentations.title: Emblase: Using Tiled as an AI-Ready Data Access Service for Live Scientific Workflows
presentations.abstract: Scientific user facilities such as the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II) need reliable paths from beamline acquisition to machine-learning analysis and scientist-facing interaction. We present a Tiled-centered architecture that publishes scientific data and inference results through one interface while keeping compute, model-registry, and language-model services replaceable. As an institutional partner in the American Science Cloud (AmSC), we developed Emblase to demonstrate an application that uses AmSC-provided compute, model-hosting, and LLM inference services in a live NSLS-II Soft Matter Interfaces (SMI) scattering workflow. Data acquisition creates Bluesky runs that Tiled exposes to an event-driven inference service. The service resolves a versioned physics-informed machine-learning model, processes incoming frames, and writes embeddings and associated products to Tiled for dashboard inspection. Authenticated Tiled tools support grounded natural-language interaction. The architecture keeps live experimental state behind one scientific interface while allowing deployment-specific choices for compute and AI services.

presentations.title: Emerging Personas and Tools for Hybrid Quantum-HPC Systems
presentations.abstract: Quantum computing is entering an era where quantum processing units (QPUs) with tens to hundreds of qubits are increasingly integrated with high-performance computing (HPC) systems to support hybrid quantum-classical workloads. This paradigm, often referred to as Quantum-Centric SuperComputing (QCSC), introduces new operational, software, and infrastructure challenges. In this paper, we identify and characterize six distinct personas involved in QCSC environments. Particular attention is given to emerging roles that arise at the interface between quantum and HPC systems. We analyze the responsibilities and tools associated with each persona and examine their differing requirements for operational data. Consistent data representations and analytics frameworks will be required to support diverse users across the quantum-HPC ecosystem. By defining personas and their data needs, we provide a foundation for future discussions in this critical area.

presentations.title: Emerging Storage Technology
presentations.abstract:
The AI and HPC community is scrambling to accommodate the explosive demand for memory and storage capacity and new technologies. Does one solution fit all in storage components and architectures? What new differentiators matter across varied usages like out-of-core HPC computation on huge data sets, context memory cache capacity for LLM inference, 10x-higher IOPs for vector databases and GNNs, scaled checkpointing, and multitenant security?

To spark creativity and frame emerging opportunities, this panel gathers leading experts from academia in usage models, and vendor technologists for storage microcontrollers, object/file systems, and network storage acceleration that engage in storage innovation. The audience will gain new knowledge of emerging tech and new perspectives on topics that they may have recently heard of. Just as for each of the last several years of this Panel/BoF, speakers and audience contributors will archive reference material to accelerate moving the broader community forward.
Panel Session Link

presentations.title: Empowering K-12 Education through HPC-enabled AI and Computational Thinking: A Living Lab Case Study
presentations.abstract:
As High Performance Computing (HPC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) become ubiquitous, there
is a critical need to bridge the gap between advanced computational research centers and K-12
educational environments. This lightning talk and demo present a case study of a piloted
collaboration between Penn State University, Cornell University, and the Milton Hershey School
(MHS). By establishing a “Living Lab” ecosystem, this initiative provided hands-on AI and
computational training for K-12 teachers while simultaneously developing the conversation for
applied AI solutions for complex school administration challenges. We demonstrate how
open-ended “lessons learned” conversations can demystify advanced technologies for non-
traditional disciplines and outline future directions for K-12 and HPC center partnerships. This
work has led to a state-wide “Listening Tour” funded by the Pennsylvania Department of
Education for additional conversations with K12 school districts across the state, that
may continue to build and further develop this andragogical workforce training approach.

presentations.title: Enabling Performance Isolation for Co-scheduled Workflows
presentations.abstract: Heterogeneous systems such as NVIDIA GH200 and GB200 pair powerful GPUs with substantial CPU capacity, but GPU jobs targeting these systems frequently leave much of the CPU capacity idle, lowering CPU utilization and overall system throughput. Co-scheduling CPU workloads alongside GPU jobs improves resource utilization, but can introduce interference and undermine performance predictability. We present a proof of concept for co-scheduling CPU and GPU jobs on GH200 nodes with hardware-enforced resource isolation using Arm Memory System Resource Partitioning and Monitoring (MPAM) for CPU, L3-cache, and memory bandwidth and InfiniBand QoS for host network traffic. We augment existing resource isolation mechanisms in Slurm to allocate jobs to dedicated CPU and GPU "shards" with allocations for compute cores, L3-cache, memory bandwidth, and network bandwidth. This proof-of-concept implementation provides a practical framework for evaluating co-scheduled workloads with hardware-enforced resource isolation and establishes an operational model for multi-tenant co-scheduling on heterogeneous HPC/AI nodes.

presentations.title: Enabling Radio Astronomy to Use French Supercomputers
presentations.abstract:
Next-generation radio telescopes, such as the SKA, will generate exascale data volumes requiring national supercomputing resources. However, the radio astronomy community faces systemic barriers in accessing French HPC centers due to the Zone à Régime Restrictif (ZRR), a cybersecurity regime enforcing individual accountability that conflicts with the community's shared-account model.
To reconcile these requirements, we leverage a "Scientific Application as a Service" framework using Ephemeral Buffers and Application Microservices, extending it with a proposed named service account model. We validate this approach by deploying the DDF Pipeline—a calibration imaging pipeline for the LOFAR telescope (an SKA pathfinder)—on the Jean Zay supercomputer. Our results show data transfer throughputs up to 137.9 MB/s download and 28.73 MB/s upload , and a reduction in execution time from 68.8 to 8.7 hours on 24 nodes (~7.9x speedup). Finally, validated cross-center executions between Jean Zay and Adastra demonstrate the feasibility of future cross-facility workflow integration.

presentations.title: Enabling Topology-Awareness for Performance Improvement: A Case Study with Trinetra-A HPC Network
presentations.abstract:
As HPC systems scale, the physical connectivity of
the underlying network plays an increasingly significant role in
application performance. The effectiveness of a parallel
application is strongly influenced by how well process placement
reflects the network topology.

This paper presents a methodology designed to enable
topology-aware process placement on Trinetra-A, a high-speed
switchless 3D torus network developed by C-DAC, highlighting
the key considerations and challenges involved in the process. Our
approach involves application communication analysis and a
process mapping framework that leverages existing process
mapping tools to implement topology-aware process placement.

We evaluate the methodology using MPI benchmarks and a
real application, achieving peak latency improvements of 89% for
MPI_Alltoall, 68% for MPI_Alltoallv and 8% for MPI_Allgather,
along with a 68% improvement in heFFTe application
performance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of
optimized placement on Trinetra-A and provide a reference that
can be readily adopted by HPC network developers.

presentations.title: End-to-end GPU-native communication in GROMACS simulations with PME task specialization
presentations.abstract:
Strong scaling of molecular dynamics simulations is increasingly limited by communication latency as per-step execution time becomes shorter. In task-specialized GROMACS runs, particle-particle (PP) tasks exchange coordinates and forces with particle-mesh Ewald (PME) tasks every time step through CPU-mediated MPI communication, exposing host synchronization on the critical path of a step that is otherwise entirely GPU-resident. We present an NVSHMEM-based GPU-native redesign of these pipelined producer-consumer communication phases. Our design combines stream-triggered and kernel-initiated communication, fuses PME force communication with receiver signaling, and is tuned for NVLink and RDMA interconnects to reduce
control-path overhead and increase overlap, improving end-to-end performance by up to 15%. This work extends GPU-native communication beyond halo exchange toward end-to-end
GPU-resident GROMACS execution, while highlighting the challenges that symmetric allocation without team-based support poses for task-specialized applications.

presentations.title: Energy and Carbon Footprint of the x3d2 CFD Solver on AI-First and HPC-Class GPUs
presentations.abstract:
Estimates of the energy and carbon cost of computation are almost never checked against direct measurement. We instrument x3d2, a compact, high-order finite-difference CFD solver, across three GPU architectures and a 24-core server CPU.

While an AI-first accelerator uses 1.27x–1.40x lower energy than either HPC-class GPU, hardware selection is second-order: shifting a job's start time across 12 months alters emissions by 28x. Four standard carbon-accounting tools, all correctly configured, agree within 1.3x on that accelerator while overestimating energy measured at the wall socket by 1.9x–2.9x. On an A100 node, the same tools land within 0.64x–1.11x of whole-node energy.

The measurement campaign is complete: 124 instrumented runs on two platforms, plus a 36-run arm on a third, with full per-run telemetry and a complete analysis pipeline.

During the poster session, we will guide attendees through the power telemetry, visual tool-accuracy breakdowns, and the practical realities of carbon-aware scheduling.

presentations.title: Energy and Cost-Aware Control at Scale: Multi-Dimensional Frequency Steering on AMD MI300A
presentations.abstract:
Energy and Power have become a first-order concern for large HPC and AI installations.
The optimization targets are no longer limited to production peak throughput, but include
stable output under electrical limits, carbon constraints, and infrastructure cost pressure.
This paper presents an extension to an operational control approach (PowerSched) that mitigates some of these concerns. The work reports on a PowerSched extension towards multi-dimensional frequency steering of GPU architectures that targets CPU boost frequencies, GPU clocks and memory/interposer-related controls, The control plane supports policy shaping through a configurable objective term, so operation can be shifted at runtime along an energy--performance--cost trade-off axis. Challenges and solutions for multi-dimensional steering algorithms are discussed, including mutual constraints, discrete-valued tunables, and noisy telemetry. First results for AMD mi300a architecture are presented. The results indicate performance gains up to 10% relative to the uncapped system and energy-efficiency gains up to 30%.

presentations.title: Energy-Aware Performance Characterization of Kokkos Kernels Across Precision Levels
presentations.abstract:
Kokkos is a performance-portable programming model used in GPU-accelerated HPC applications comprising kernels with diverse computational and memory behaviors. We characterize kernels from two applications to evaluate how FP32, FP64, and mixed FP32/FP64 affect arithmetic intensity, performance throughput, and GPU energy consumption. We introduce an Energy-Aware Roofline Model that incorporates energy into performance analysis and a Thermal-Aware Inter-Kernel Energy Model that visualizes energy consumption alongside duration, GPU temperature, and execution order.
We study both applications with: (1) fine-grained, application-level instrumentation through the Kokkos Performance Tools PAPI Connector and (2) coarse-grained PAPI instrumentation applied to a dedicated-kernel benchmark using vendor-specific power management components.
Our analysis shows that precision effects vary by application, kernel, and workload. Mixed FP32/FP64 kernels generally achieve arithmetic intensity comparable to FP32, with modestly lower throughput and, in most cases, a modest increase in energy consumption. FP64 kernels generally exhibit the highest energy consumption among the evaluated precisions.

presentations.title: Energy-Efficient Coupled Simulations with Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling
presentations.abstract: Dynamic inter-solver load imbalance in coupled multiphysics simulations leaves faster solvers idle at synchronization points, wasting energy. We investigate whether dynamic voltage and frequency scaling can exploit this slack without increasing time-to-solution. Our runtime framework combines preCICE for coupling and timing with MERIC for energy monitoring and online CPU-frequency control. A controller based on the Jitter algorithm maps each solver’s active fraction to a target frequency, while an energy model estimates savings from activity, power, and frequency-induced slowdown. We evaluate the method on a partitioned, iteratively coupled 2D air-water heat transfer problem using DUNE on the Barbora and Karolina clusters. On Barbora, total energy-to-solution fell by 13% with negligible runtime overhead, while the faster air solver used 28% less energy. On Karolina, solver runtime is dominated by communication overhead, causing DVFS to unnecessarily slow the simulation and significantly increase energy-to-solution.

presentations.title: Energy-Efficient Streaming FPGA Accelerator for DeepSeek Sparse Attention Decode
presentations.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces long-context inference cost by scoring all cached tokens and attending only to the top-$k$. At batch one, however, GPUs execute this operation inefficiently because its dependent scan, exact selection, and irregular gather provide insufficient parallelism. For exact per-query DSA, we show that the bottleneck is primarily architectural: after eliminating host-side kernel-launch overhead, the kernel reaches at most 1.19% of GPU INT8 peak across 4K--128K contexts. We present a streaming FPGA accelerator that fuses index generation and sparse attention while retaining intermediates on chip. It reduces per-head scores immediately, finds the exact top-$k$ threshold by counting rather than ranking, and fetches each selected key/value vector once for all heads. On AMD Alveo U55C, post-route power is \SI{11.324}{\watt}; against an RTX 6000 Ada running the quantized kernel, it achieves $8.0$--$10.2\times$ lower energy and $3.9$--$6.4\times$ lower energy--delay product.

presentations.title: Enhancing Data Center Efficiency and Throughput by Co-Scheduling
presentations.abstract:
Many HPC data centers have supercomputers with separate CPU-only and GPU compute nodes to support different workloads.
One approach to increase system throughput is to run CPU-only jobs on unused CPU resources on the GPU nodes.
Analysis of the workload running on NERSC's supercomputer showed that approximately 60% of Perlmutter's GPU node-hours employed fewer than 12 CPU cores and less than 128GB host memory.
The remaining 52 CPU cores and 128GB host memory could be used by co-scheduled CPU-only jobs.
However, it is critical that the co-scheduled CPU-only jobs and GPU jobs have controlled/bounded interference.
This preliminary study assesses the feasibility of co-scheduling in production.
Testing of the NERSC-10 benchmark applications on NVIDIA Grace-Hopper nodes using Memory System Resource Partitioning and Monitoring (MPAM) and network/InfiniBand quality of service for performance isolation measured a 70% throughput increase from co-scheduling compared with no co-scheduling, while maintaining an acceptable level of performance
isolation.

presentations.title: Ensemble PBVR: Interactive In Situ Visualization of Ensemble Statistics on Rendering Particles
presentations.abstract: Ensemble statistics are classically computed after every member has been written to storage. Forming them during the run instead requires gathering field data on the compute nodes, at the cost of global communication and memory copies. We present ensemble PBVR, which forms them from visualization particles instead: one set of particles circulates through the members by a ring exchange, and the mean, variance and coefficient of variation accumulate at the particle positions during batch execution. Gradients used as volume-rendering normals follow analytically from a chain-rule expansion that closes with four accumulated quantities per particle, and the target field is defined at run time by a user-supplied algebraic expression. We apply it to a 72-member CityLBM urban plume dispersion ensemble on a GPU supercomputer. Against a post hoc ParaView workflow it reaches the first image 4 to 30 times faster and transfers 60 times less data.

presentations.title: Entropy on the Edge of Collapse
presentations.abstract: This is a dynamical rendering of a detailed three-dimensional simulation of the explosion of the very-rapidly rotating core of a massive star that is exploding as a supernova. Rapid rotation leads to a powerful jet-like explosion along the two poles, accompanied by the generation and tangling of strong magnetic fields. This movie depicts the earliest phases of the supernova explosion that is simultaneously giving birth to a rapidly rotating radio pulsar.

presentations.title: EnvAgent: Multi-Agent Approach to Building Science Environments in the Clouds
presentations.abstract:
Environment configuration remains a fundamental yet overlooked challenge in software engineering, requiring precise management of operating systems, dependencies, and hardware constraints. Existing LLM-based software engineering workflows often rely on predefined Dockerfiles or manual scripts, or exclude repositories with difficult environments, limiting generalization.

We present ENVAGENT, a multi-LLM-agent workflow that automatically synthesizes, builds, and verifies hardware-aware Dockerfiles from repositories. We further introduce ENVAGENT+, a resource-provisioning agent that infers computational requirements and allocates compatible resources, and ENVBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating environment reconstruction fidelity.

We evaluate ENVAGENT on 54 repositories from Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench across seven programming languages. Results show that ENVAGENT improves runnable counts by 16.2% and FCS scores by 33.91% over baselines, enabling reliable evaluation of repositories that existing approaches fail to configure.

presentations.title: Error-Explicit Low-Precision Factorizations for Iterative Refinement
presentations.abstract:
Recent NVIDIA GPUs prioritize low-precision throughput while native FP64 stagnates, falling from $37$ to $1.25$\,TFLOP/s between B200 and B300.
Mixed-precision iterative refinement factorizes in FP32 but retains the FP64 matrix $A$ for residual evaluation, requiring $12n^2$ bytes of persistent storage.
We present two refinement algorithms that remove this dependence.
Split-$A$ iterative refinement (SA-IR) represents $A$ as two FP32 words, while error-explicit iterative refinement (R-IR) stores the FP32 factorization residual $R=PA-LU$ and discards $A$, reducing storage to $8n^2$ bytes.
R-IR inherits refinement's convergence condition, and in our tests its accuracy is limited by residual evaluation rather than FP32 storage of $R$.
Across five GPUs the advantage tracks the FP32:FP64 ratio.
On B300 at $n=32{,}768$, SA-IR is $25\times$ faster than emulated FP64 and $1.4\times$ faster than vendor refinement, and R-IR is $24\times$ faster at $8192$ right-hand sides.
Streamed construction of $R$ peaks at $8.24$--$8.57n^2$ bytes, reaching $n=184{,}320$ where $12n^2$ will not fit.

presentations.title: Ethics in HPC: With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility
presentations.abstract: The implications of HPC technology on society and the environment prompt us, as a community, to discuss and understand our direct and indirect impacts. This BoF is highly interactive and aims to facilitate discussion within the community, relating ethical behavior and societal norms to the design of HPC solutions and autonomous/intelligent systems. The BoF will feature breakout groups and then converge to a plenum discussion. By furthering this dialogue, we can ensure that the HPC community advances its commitment to technology for the benefit of humanity as a whole. We do not expect to reach conclusions, but raise ideas.

presentations.title: Evaluating AI Agents for Scientific Workflow Maintenance
presentations.abstract: AI coding agents could help maintain scientific workflows, but a repair that executes successfully may still duplicate calculations, compromise provenance, or change the scientific meaning of a result. We propose evaluating such repairs through the scientific and operational properties they must preserve. A pilot implementation explores this idea through twelve compact software maintenance tasks, with examples spanning safe recovery, portable analysis records, and scientific post-processing. Separate exploratory experiments provide preliminary motivation: some repairs passed all functional-component checks while failing scientific or robustness checks, and agents sometimes claimed completion despite failing independent assessment. These observations support distinguishing basic functionality from evidence of reliable workflow maintenance. They do not establish comprehensive task coverage or readiness for production use. We invite discussion of which properties should underpin such evaluations, whether component-level performance predicts reliability in integrated workflows, and how human oversight and computational cost should shape decisions about agent autonomy.

presentations.title: Evaluating All-Reduce Operations in DDP Training with FABRIC: Framework for Architecture, Backend, and Reduction Interchange Comparison
presentations.abstract: Distributed deep learning increasingly relies on large GPU systems, where distributed data parallel (DDP) training replicates models across devices and synchronizes gradients each step. As model sizes and GPU counts grow, gradient synchronization becomes a major overhead. Although many optimized all-reduce algorithms exist, they are often embedded in different communication libraries or stack layers, making controlled comparison in full training workflows difficult. We present FABRIC (Framework for Architecture, Backend, and Reduction Interchange Comparison), an open-source, portable, and extensible framework for evaluating PyTorch DDP across communication backends and collective strategies. Using DDP communication hooks, FABRIC integrates alternative all-reduce algorithms without modifying PyTorch internals or training code, enabling reproducible comparisons across models, datasets, and backends including MPI, NCCL, and RCCL, and letting researchers add and benchmark custom communication methods. Experiments on Frontier and Polaris reveal meaningful performance differences among synchronization strategies. The poster presents FABRIC's architecture, extensibility, and productivity, and current results.

presentations.title: Evaluating Function-Level Accuracy and Performance of SIMD Math Libraries with FP32 Inputs
presentations.abstract:
SIMD math libraries are important building blocks for high perfor-
mance computer arithmetic. We evaluate unary IEEE 754 binary32
(FP32) AVX2 functions implementations from AOCL-LibM, GNU
libmvec, SLEEF, and Intel SVML. We exhaustively test every fi-
nite FP32 encoding against a 256-bit MPFR oracle. Most of the
functions achieve smaller error than the library-level bounds, but
several AOCL and SLEEF functions exceed stated accuracy bounds.
For performance evaluation, we identify and test data-dependent
performance paths from cheap SIMD execution to expensive fall-
backs. Cheap SIMD paths outperform matched scalar calls, but
expensive corrections can make vector functions slower than scalar
routines. This work fills a gap by providing the community with a
per-function, per-input reference for the accuracy and performance
of FP32 AVX2 math libraries.

presentations.title: Evaluating Fused Weight-Decompression General Matrix Multiplication for Quantized LLM Inference in SYCL
presentations.abstract: General matrix multiplication (GEMM) constitutes major computation load in Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Although weight quantization is the de facto standard of modern LLM inference, the GEMMs are often sub-optimized for non-CUDA backends, such as SYCL. A fused weight-decompression GEMM could potentially raise throughput via removing intermediate VRAM traffic. This paper evaluates the efficacy of the fused kernel for INT8 weight-quantized LLM inference in SYCL: We conduct standalone microbenchmarks to isolate the GEMM throughput and accuracy, followed by an inference-engine integration of the fused path that demonstrates its end-to-end gain. At the kernel level, the fused path is 1.20–1.36× faster than the baseline in GEMM. In LLM inference, the fused path raises prefill throughput by 20–57%. It closes the prefill gap against a CUDA backend from over 40% to within 7–26% where the model fits both devices, and surpasses CUDA where the Intel GPU's larger memory avoids layer-offloading.

presentations.title: Evaluating In-Network Collectives for AI/ML workloads with ATLAHS
presentations.abstract: In-network collectives (INC) can accelerate many collective network operations by moving computations away from the CPU, either into the NIC or into switches. The benefits are reductions in both traffic and latency, at the cost of higher system complexity. Designers of AI/ML training and inference systems have to balance network costs and the performance impact of network features on current and potentially future workloads. The ATLAHS toolchain allows us to study the impact of latency, bandwidth, and topology changes on workload performance, while supporting simulations of unprecedented scale. In this work, we add INC support to ATLAHS and report the impact on collective performance for groups of up to 1024 ranks, and on Llama-2-7B training performance at up to 64 GPUs.

presentations.title: Evaluating OpenMP API Version 6.1 Target Kernel Language
presentations.abstract: The OpenMP API has steadily evolved into a comprehensive, highly portable alternative to vendor-specific APIs for GPU acceleration. The upcoming OpenMP 6.1 specification introduces two key features for code acceleration: access to dynamic shared memory and multidimensional, kernel-like programming. In this paper, we provide an overview of these newly standardized features for C++ and Fortran codebases. We implement a functional prototype based on the official LLVM infrastructure, extending both the Clang and Flang compilers to support these additions. We evaluate our implementation across several C++ and Fortran benchmarks, confirming that these new OpenMP capabilities effectively help close the performance and expressiveness gap with vendor-specific APIs. During the evaluation, we also observe a few remaining opportunities where OpenMP could become even more competitive for specific computational patterns.

presentations.title: Evaluation of LLVM Flang for Production HPC Applications and Modern Fortran Features
presentations.abstract: In 2025, LLVM released its first Flang Fortran compiler version considered ready for widespread evaluation. We know of no published assessment of Flang compiling a workload-derived portfolio of high-performance computing (HPC) applications. We address this gap using workload data from the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), which supports more than 10,000 scientists on approximately 1,000 projects. We selected ten Fortran packages heavily used at NERSC with available source code and compiled them using recent versions of Flang on NERSC’s Perlmutter system. Seven compiled without code modifications, though some required build-system changes. Three compiled after minor source edits, mostly to address Fortran standard violations. We evaluated seven additional packages selected for their use or enablement of standard Fortran parallel features: multi-image execution and do concurrent. Six such codes compiled with most or all unit tests passing.

presentations.title: Every State, Every Loop, All at Once: Reaching the Outer Loop of an Autonomous Laboratory
presentations.abstract:
An autonomous laboratory's inner loops are already closed, but the loop
spanning synthesis, measurement, and simulation closes through a person, where
a result changes the next decision. An agent placed there is blind, because the
state it needs lives in someone's head, in tools that disagree, and in files
that cannot be queried. We present \texttt{reach}, an intelligent state layer
holding knowledge, execution, and operational state as one navigable graph,
kept consistent across its many writers. With that state addressable, an agent plans
a campaign and decides each next step while the scientist supervises along a
trust gradient. We contribute (i)~the state layer architecture; (ii)~the seam
contract, implementable by any long-running external system; and (iii)~an
integration study at the Autonomous Chemistry Lab, where the deployed layer
drove an agent-planned vial-transfer chain and carried a measured diffraction
pattern through a vendor application into agentic Rietveld refinement.

presentations.title: Evolution in Scientific Deep Learning: A Data-centric Study
presentations.abstract: Deep learning over the past six years has shifted away from highly specific models in favor of a generic yet tunable paradigm, but the I/O and data movement implications of this shift remain uncharacterized. We address this gap by profiling modern deep learning applications at LLNL using DFTracer, combining function-level and application-level profiling to trace compute, communication, and I/O in a previously unexplored manner across the stack. We find that similarities to classical deep learning bottlenecks still exist; however, novel inefficiencies from customizable in-situ preprocessing - arising from a need for heterogeneous data access and tunable graph representations - are increased and unaccounted for in optimizations. We suggest optimizations such as utilizing more effective data structures and offloading graph representation/transformations to the GPU, and aim to continue the study by profiling additional scientific codes with broader stack tracing.

presentations.title: Evolution of Python Compiler for GPUs
presentations.abstract: The Python programming language is famous for being highly productive and newcomer friendly but suffers runtime performance. Over the last decade, one attempt to close this performance gap is to build compilers for domain specific languages (DSL) and compile to native code. The LLVM/MLIR ecosystem has played a pivotal role in creating easy pathways for developers to build DSLs and become the dominant methodology for doing so. As GPUs have grown in complexity, Python DSLs have also become more popular leading to a new programming model, Tile Programming. These two trends have led to an explosion of Python DSLs. Join us as we talk about the Past, Present, and Future of Python compilers for GPUs.

presentations.title: Examining QRMI as a Unified Interface for Quantum-HPC Integration
presentations.abstract: The efficient and scalable integration of quantum resources into HPC environments requires standardized mechanisms for resource management, scheduling, and workflow orchestration across diverse and heterogeneous infrastructures. The Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) addresses this challenge through a thin, vendor-agnostic middleware layer that provides standardized APIs for scheduling, executing, and monitoring quantum workloads while exposing quantum resources as first-class schedulable resources alongside CPUs and GPUs. Previous work demonstrated QRMI integration with the Slurm workload manager. This paper extends the validation of QRMI to a broad range of workload managers, encompassing traditional batch schedulers, a cloud-native orchestration platform, and a graph-based scheduler. We examine the integration patterns, implementation requirements, and scheduler-specific considerations associated with each environment and compare QRMI with alternative approaches to quantum resource integration. We demonstrate that QRMI provides an abstraction layer that minimizes scheduler-specific modifications while enabling consistent access to heterogeneous quantum resources across both on-premises and cloud environments.

presentations.title: Exascale Biomedical Digital Twins: From Biophysical Simulation to Clinical Impact
presentations.abstract:
Biomedical digital twins represent a frontier for exascale computing and AI, offering transformative potential for proactive healthcare, precision medicine, and medical-device innovation. However, translating complex human physiology into real-world clinical workflows introduces critical HPC challenges in model fidelity, speed, data integration, regulatory validation, and deployment cost.

This panel brings together leaders across academia, medical devices, and modeling software: Dr. Amanda Randles (Duke University; computational digital twins and HPC biophysical simulations), Darrell Swenson (Medtronic; HPC integration in medical device development), and Dr. Mark Palmer (Synopsys; clinical translation, simulation, and enterprise digital twin adoption). Using cardiac digital twins as a primary high-impact case study, the panel will explore the broader roadmap for biomedical HPC. The session is structured around interactive debate and direct audience engagement to address a central question: What must the supercomputing community solve next to make high-fidelity biological digital twins routine, scalable, and impactful across clinical and industrial settings?

presentations.title: Execution-Path- and Restriction-Aware Autotuning for MPI Collective Operations
presentations.abstract: Machine-learning autotuning selects MPI collective algorithms by benchmarking candidates and predicting the fastest for each execution configuration. Existing methods often assume that all candidates are valid throughout the configuration space and that measurements reflect their actual execution paths. These assumptions fail when restrictions cause silent fallback or compositional algorithms invoke nested collectives whose performance depends on the policy being trained. We present an execution-path- and restriction-aware framework for MPICH \texttt{MPI_Bcast}. It partitions the configuration space by algorithm restrictions, trains corresponding submodels, and combines them into a unified runtime policy. A multistage procedure first trains an intermediate policy using independent algorithms, then benchmarks compositional algorithms under that policy to build the final model. On Polaris, the intermediate policy improves \texttt{smp} performance by up to $2.275\times$; the final policy achieves speedups of up to $30.71\times$ over default MPICH and $2.76\times$ over ACCLAiM.

presentations.title: Expanded Slurm container runtime support
presentations.abstract: Slurm 26.11 will add a new runtime plugin capability intended to replace the existing OCI container support as well as become the key integration point for all container runtime engines going forward. This capability will enable the community to build lua bindings to properly adapt Slurm to each container runtime, and will enable greater workflow composability with a diversity of emerging workloads. Runtime plugins will continue to enable command line interface flexibility while extending support to the Slurm REST interfaces. Further this capability will enable container runtimes to properly layer namespace usage with Slurm's administrative namespace plugins.

presentations.title: Experience Meets Innovation: Intergenerational Collaboration in HPC
presentations.abstract:
Success in high performance computing (HPC) and research depends on bringing together diverse perspectives, experiences, and approaches to problem-solving. This panel explores the value of intergenerational collaboration in the workplace and how teams can thrive by leveraging the unique strengths of each generation.

Featuring professionals from a broad range of career stages, panelists will share their experiences working across generations, discuss common challenges and opportunities, and highlight strategies for building inclusive, high-performing teams. Attendees will gain insights into fostering mutual learning, bridging communication styles, and creating environments where institutional knowledge and fresh ideas come together to drive innovation.

Whether you are early in your career or a seasoned professional, this discussion will provide practical takeaways for strengthening collaboration and advancing success in the research and high performance computing community.

presentations.title: Experiences with and Best Practices around Cooling Distribution Units (CDUs)
presentations.abstract: Cooling distribution units (CDUs) are becoming necessary to meet the cooling demands of modern compute and network systems. We present the experiences NSF NCAR has had with the CDUs on our HPE Cray EX test and production systems. Along with various topics including finding leaks, expansion tank issues, replacing pumps, and properly torqueing components, we will give a list of best practices we have developed for dealing with these specialize HPC system components. Included in our presentation is an artifact for querying the Redfish endpoints of the CDU system and populating a timeseries database for plotting CDU values over time.

presentations.title: Exploiting Memory Contiguity in Stencil Applications for Extreme Scalability on Heterogeneous Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: Exascale computing requires the development and execution of applications with massive scalability capabilities. Iterative Stencil Loop (ISL) applications are an important class of scientific applications with high scalability potential. EPSILOD is a tool designed to simplify the development and execution of ISL applications in heterogeneous distributed environments. This work proposes and evaluates new techniques in EPSILOD to optimize data communication in distributed ISL applications running on multi-GPU, multi-node systems. Specifically, it explores multidimensional partitioning policies and techniques to optimize MPI communications, including both host-staging and GPU-aware MPI, by automatically creating data contiguity in memory based on the chosen partitioning policy. Experimental results are presented using up to 1,024 NVIDIA GPUs across 256 nodes and up to 8,192 AMD GPUs across 1,024 nodes, showing significant improvements in strong and weak scalability across various scenarios and ISL applications.

presentations.title: Exploiting the Interplay of Compute- and Memory-Bound kernels in MPI Applications
presentations.abstract:
Parallel applications are typically designed for synchronous, lock-step execution, treating communication stalls as performance hazards. Yet, in a communication-light application with infrequent synchronization that alternates between compute-bound and memory-bound phases, an MPI communication stall can unintentionally relieve memory-bandwidth contention.
We demonstrate this using a Parallel Optical Flow Solver combining a compute-bound Ray Tracing kernel with a memory-bound Optical Flow kernel and negligible inter-process communication. Natural desynchronization and overlap between the two phases yield substantial speedup, with peak performance when the number of processes concurrently executing the memory-bound phase per ccNUMA domain remains near the memory-bandwidth saturation point. We further show that MPI asynchronous progress can significantly degrade performance by increasing concurrent memory-bandwidth contention. To study the underlying mechanisms, we develop a tunable dual-kernel microbenchmark, showing that substantial application or system noise is required to achieve full desynchronization. Finally, we validate these findings with a bandwidth-aware, model-based simulator.

presentations.title: Exploring DAOS as a Burst Buffer for Nx100 Gbps Scientific Streaming
presentations.abstract: Scientific experiments are shifting from batched-file acquisition to online streaming readout, where O(1) MB detector frames flow directly to HPC facilities for real-time processing. Each HPC node runs a multi-stage workflow, and the slowest stage determines the overall throughput. On a pair of 100 Gbps nodes, throughput drops from 35 Gbps to 6 Gbps once downstream processing is enabled. Based on a 2024 experiment, we estimate that streaming live data would require about 300 Perlmutter nodes. This work explores Distributed Asynchronous Object Storage (DAOS) as a burst buffer that decouples the counting-house upstream from HPC downstream processing, such that fewer nodes can absorb the same traffic. Writing raw 8.6 KB packets to DAOS through an asynchronous queue achieved 32 Gbps end-to-end, limited by a single DAOS connection. Ongoing Aurora experiments suggest near-linear client-side scaling. We outline open challenges: small-object read penalties, tail latency under continuous production, and the throughput–latency trade-off.

presentations.title: Exploring Sparse Matrix Multiplication Operations on Cerebras CS-3 Platforms
presentations.abstract:
In recent years, novel AI accelerators have emerged as promising alternatives to GPUs for AI model training and inference. The Cerebras CS-3 has demonstrated strong performance on machine learning and some scientific applications. While the benefits of Cerebras systems for dense workloads are well demonstrated, their potential for sparse workloads, particularly for large matrices with substantial memory requirements, is not yet understood.

In this work, we study two sparse linear algebra kernels, sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) and sampled dense-dense matrix multiplication (SDDMM), on the CS-3. We propose low-level CS-3 designs and optimize them for I/O performance, memory footprint, and scalability. Our evaluation shows that the CS-3 kernels can outperform the CPU by up to 100x for SpMM and 20x for SDDMM on 90% sparse matrices, with SpMM performance improving as matrix dimensionality increases. However, beyond 99% sparsity, our kernels suffer performance degradation and approach or underperform state-of-the-art CPU libraries.

presentations.title: Exploring the Exascale Universe
presentations.abstract: Recent exascale cosmology simulations are producing multi-petabyte datasets with unprecedented volume, resolution, and physical fidelity in support of next-generation observational surveys. These datasets allow us to visualize the evolution of cosmic structure across enormous spatial and temporal scales and to generate synthetic observations for direct comparison with survey data. They also provide powerful inputs for AI, including emulators and digital twins, as well as agent-based approaches that can streamline complex, multi-step scientific queries and analyses across datasets whose scale and complexity make traditional exploration increasingly difficult.

presentations.title: Exploring the Genesis Platform Capabilities to Accelerate Scientific Discovery in OPAL
presentations.abstract: Autonomous, cross-facility science requires capabilities that no individual project should have to build for itself: managed execution for long-lived services, versioned distribution of models to remote compute systems, governed access to large language models, a shared substrate for experimental data, and end-to-end provenance. The U.S. Department of Energy Genesis Mission platform, delivered through the American Science Cloud, provides these as reusable services. This paper reports how the Genesis platform enables cross-facility experiments and accelerates scientific discovery. We explore the plant phenotyping workflow of the Orchestrated Platform for Autonomous Laboratories as the exemplar: it couples Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Advanced Plant Phenotyping Laboratory with the Frontier supercomputer. In a 40-day nickel-treatment campaign, the resulting workflow replaced roughly twelve hours of manual analysis with interactive queries returning in seconds to minutes.

presentations.title: Exploring the Performance Portability of Modern Programming Languages
