presentations.abstract: This poster evaluates the performance portability of Julia, Mojo, Python, and Rust across NVIDIA and AMD accelerators using four scientific benchmarks: seven-point stencil, BabelStream, Hartree–Fock, and miniBUDE. Native CUDA and HIP implementations were ported idiomatically to KernelAbstractions.jl (Julia), Mojo, Triton (Python), and CubeCL (Rust), respectively, and assessed in single and double precision. Results highlight the tradeoffs each language makes with its programming model and compiler design. Although these languages are relatively immature, they demonstrate promising potential for productive, performance-portable high performance computing (HPC) development.

presentations.title: Exploring Tree-Based Approaches for Collective Communications on Cerebras WSE-3
presentations.abstract:
Collective operations are a key performance factor on the Cerebras WSE-3, a wafer-scale processor with 900,000 cores on a 2D mesh. At this scale, communication distance strongly affects latency, making locality a first-order concern in the design of collective algorithms.

We develop tree-style schedules that minimize communication distances for 1D Reduce, the building block of 2D collectives and AllReduce. We port Bine trees, the locality-optimized binomial trees we recently introduced, to the WSE-3; implement balanced binary-tree reductions; and introduce unbalanced binary trees as well as two-phase variants with tree-based outer phases. Each schedule is paired with an analytical cost model and implementation-level optimizations such as fused receive-send transports. On the official cycle-accurate simulator, our schedules outperform fixed-pattern state-of-the-art algorithms by up to 1.63x.

presentations.title: Extending ecoHMEM to Arm: Automatic Data Placement Using Statistical Profiling Extension
presentations.abstract: The growing diversification of high-performance processor architectures and adoption of heterogeneous memory systems introduce new challenges for performance portability and efficient memory management. As Arm-based platforms gain relevance in HPC and technologies such as HBM and CXL memory expansion become widespread, mechanisms that automatically exploit memory heterogeneity are increasingly important. Precise sampled hardware events have proven valuable for characterizing memory behavior across processor families, but their use on Arm has only recently become feasible with the Statistical Profiling Extension (SPE). In this work, we extend the ecoHMEM automatic data-placement framework to Arm-based systems by leveraging SPE to obtain precise memory-access information. We design and implement the required profiling infrastructure and analyze its key tradeoffs. Experimental evaluation on an Arm system with emulated memory heterogeneity demonstrates the feasibility of integrating SPE into automatic data placement, achieving performance improvements of up to 22% over mainstream NUMA strategies.

presentations.title: Extending I/O Observability to Explainability for Targeted Optimization
presentations.abstract: HPC I/O profilers such as Darshan report POSIX-level metrics but do not trace the kernel stack: VFS, page cache, block layer, NVMe driver, and storage media. We present PEARL, an eBPF-based cross-layer tracing plugin for DataCrumbs, that builds one causal timeline per request from syscall to disk completion. We evaluate PEARL on Chameleon Cloud with IOR workloads. Page-cache faults account for 82% to 93% of kernel I/O time, a signal Darshan cannot capture. PEARL traces the same requests at 9.0 to 15.7 microseconds where Darshan reports 0.45 to 5.88 milliseconds. Overhead is negligible and within system noise. PEARL moves profiling from reporting what happened to explaining why, enabling targeted evidence-based optimization.

presentations.title: Extending MPI One-Sided Communication with Lightweight Notification-Based Synchronization
presentations.abstract:
As high-performance computing systems scale toward many-core architectures, hybrid programming models combining message passing and task-based execution require efficient communication and synchronization. However, integrating communication and synchronization into these models remains challenging.

We present two contributions to address these challenges. First, we introduce Task-Aware LPF (TALPF), a task-integrated implementation of the Lightweight Parallel Foundations library supporting asynchronous communication and relaxed synchronization while preserving the analyzable Bulk Synchronous Parallel model and enabling overlap of computation and communication. Second, we extend a notification-based MPI communication model to support multiple occurrences of the same notification identifier, enabling fine-grained synchronization without additional overhead. This mechanism is exported through Task-Aware MPI (TAMPI) and underpins Two-Sided RDMA (2SR), which emulates two-sided MPI semantics using one-sided operations with notifications.

We evaluate these contributions on the MareNostrum5 supercomputer and demonstrate competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art task-aware and MPI one-sided implementations while improving programmability, safety, and portability.

presentations.title: Extending the Life of HPC Systems in Resource Constrained Environments
Extending the Life of HPC Systems in Resource-Constrained Environments: A Path from a Student Cluster Competition to Sustainable Computing in Africa
presentations.abstract:
In resource-constrained environments, High Performance Computing (HPC) often runs on repurposed hardware, making energy, rather than acquisition, the main expense. Building on PEARC '26 work, this extended abstract assesses repurposed systems by their Productivity-to-Energy (PTE) ratio rather than raw performance. CPU frequency, set through Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS), and the number of active cores were tuned jointly on a repurposed dual-socket node. Compared with a 16-core, 3.5 GHz baseline, the best configurations lowered energy consumption by 49.60% for HPCG and 30.62% for OpenFOAM.

The abstract also traces the path of the author from no prior HPC knowledge, through a national Student Cluster Competition, to international recognition in just over a year. It further considers how extending the life of hardware reduces both the operational and embodied emissions of HPC in Africa.

presentations.title: Extending the Performance Portability of Julia to Long-Vector Architectures
presentations.abstract:
The architecture of computing infrastructures is becoming increasingly diverse, making performance portability critical.
In the Julia language, JACC (Julia for Accelerators) provides performance portability across CPUs and GPUs.
However, JACC was not designed with long-vector architectures in mind, which effectively hide memory latency and deliver high sustained performance in memory-bound applications.
In this paper, we extend the performance portability of Julia to long-vector architectures by developing an execution backend for the NEC Vector Engine within JACC.
We compare JACC applications against native implementations on three GPU models and two VE models, with little or no architecture-specific code depending on the benchmark.
Our results show that the relative performance exceeds 90% on all architectures in most cases, and demonstrate that our backend extends the performance portability of JACC from CPUs and GPUs to long-vector architectures.

presentations.title: FAB-Cache: A Programmable Multi-Site Caching Service for Remote Dataset Retrieval Using FABRIC
presentations.abstract:
Scientific datasets, which often range from gigabytes to hundreds of terabytes, are frequently accessed within research institutions and shared among collaborators distributed globally. Thus, efficiently distributing these large-scale datasets to researchers has become a growing challenge.
We present FAB-Cache, a programmable, multi-site caching service deployed on NSF FABRIC testbed to accelerate access to remote scientific data. FAB-Cache chains NGINX proxies across geographically distributed FABRIC nodes and caches requested data on demand. It uses perfSONAR throughput measurements to select proxy paths. This design combines distributed storage and network measurements to support a stateful service within the network. We evaluate FAB-Cache using real-world scientific datasets retrieved across multiple FABRIC sites. Cache hits substantially outperform direct downloads over the public Internet, while cache misses achieve comparable or higher throughput in several scenarios. These results demonstrate the potential of FABRIC infrastructure to support flexible data distribution services for scientific workflows.

presentations.title: Fabrica: Agentic CUDA-to-CSL Translation and Optimization for Wafer-Scale Systems
presentations.abstract: Porting GPU kernels across architectures requires more than syntax translation. CUDA embeds work decomposition through threads, blocks, and memory accesses; the Cerebras Software Language (CSL) demands explicit data movement across a processing-element mesh with distributed SRAM, fabric communication, event-driven tasks, and host/device coordination. We present Fabrica-Bench, 54 paired CUDA-to-CSL tasks, and Fabrica, an agentic framework combining target knowledge, execution, failure-directed repair, and correctness-gated optimization. With Claude Opus 4.8, Fabrica raises success from 6/28 (single attempt) to 26/28; 22 match or beat CSL references (16 speedups). In a Sonnet 4.6 ablation with repair loop and budget fixed, retrieved Cerebras knowledge raises success from 1/15 to 7/15, while structured design records improve neither 40-run comparison. Across 46 tasks, Fabrica passes 35, with a 3.42x geometric-mean speedup among passing held-out programs and up to 83x on ReLU. Target-specific knowledge and staged feedback, not prompt structure alone, drive cross-architecture kernel generation.

presentations.title: Fair, Random IO Operations are Hard
presentations.abstract: The IO500 Committee continuously works to improve and expand what the IO500 benchmarks cover to keep them both current and relevant. The latest change we have been working on is a random 4 KiB read phase. Our first attempt yielded some unexpected results prompting a deep dive and re-implementation from scratch. Where we are now requires community feedback to ensure the best path forward.

presentations.title: Fantastic Hardware Counters and How to Use Them for Noise-Resilient Performance Modeling
presentations.abstract: Performance models are a key instrument in HPC, exposing scalability bugs early and predicting scaling behavior. Most empirical models, however, rely on time measurements, which can be distorted by noise. Hardware counters offer a robust alternative, but not every counter is noise-resilient and reflects scaling behavior. We close the loop between noise-resilience analysis and performance modeling. Building on NORC, we introduce a selection stage combining a knee-based cutoff on noise-resilient counter rankings with a modeling-quality assessment that compares counter models from a benchmark suite against ground truth via lead-exponent deviation, then clusters redundant counters. The selected counters feed two strategies added to Extra-P that derive a model's term structure from the counters and fit only the coefficients from runtime. Evaluated using PolyBench, Kripke, and RELeARN, our approach reduces model error by up to 75% while keeping measurement effort at a standard Extra-P level.

presentations.title: Fast and Accurate ML Surrogates from Simulation: An HPC Liquid-Cooling Models Case Study
presentations.abstract: ExaDigiT is an open-source state-of-the-art digital twin framework for liquid-cooled HPC facilities. This framework models cooling systems using Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU)-based thermo-fluid simulators, which are computationally expensive and impractical for large-scale and real-time applications. This paper develops deep learning surrogates from a baseline LSTM through Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) variants to a Deep Multi-scale \& Multi-physics Network (DeepM\&Mnet) architecture. The paper builds on comprehensive data analysis that revealed structural properties of the cooling system: primary-secondary loop dynamic decoupling, spatial independence among Cooling Distribution Units (CDUs), and variable-dependent thermal time constants. Because most of these outputs are strongly persistent, we score against a persistence baseline in addition to $R^2$. Evaluated across 2,827 outputs (11 $\times$ 257 CDUs), the model beats persistence on 1,541 of the 1,799 outputs that carry learnable structure (85.7\%); the remaining 1,028 are shown to be persistence-locked, in particular, one group at a measured sensor noise floor. The mean $R^2$ is 0.926 (median 0.999), and at the 60\,s evaluation window, one forward for all 257 CDUs costs 4.1\,ms against 79.3\,s of FMU wall clock, a 19{,}514$\times$ speedup, turning a 10{,}000-member uncertainty ensemble run from 220 hours into 41 seconds. Architectures agree on aggregate $R^2$ to within 0.0002.

presentations.title: Faster Biobank-Scale Genomics Through Sparse Linear Algebra on Genotype Representation Graph
presentations.abstract: Biobank initiatives include half a million phased genomes, outpacing the tools available to analyze them. Conventional genotype formats treat variants independently and fail to exploit the shared ancestry structure underlying population genetic variation. Prior work introduced the genotype representation graph, a compact graph encoding that captures shared ancestry directly but relies on traversal algorithms that map poorly onto modern accelerators. Here, we show that this computation can be expressed exactly as sparse linear algebra: under a topological ordering, the graph’s adjacency matrix becomes strictly block triangular, so the core genotype matrix–vector product reduces to a block sparse triangular solve. Further, we decompose this solve into a pipelined sequence of blocked sparse matrix-vector multiplications, exposing fine-grained parallelism and enabling mature, hardware-optimized primitives in place of hand-tuned kernels. The result is substantial, portable speedups across accelerator hardware, from cloud deployments to supercomputers.

presentations.title: Faster Post-Outage Testing at Full Machine Scale
presentations.abstract: System testing after outages is a standard workflow across HPC centers. When returning from an unplanned outage, the main focus is identifying any degraded hardware and quickly returning the system to production. We have developed a post-outage testing tool called pray4us that checks the full machine with component-wise tests, provides a simple to interpret pass/fail answer, provides specific actions to take if failures are encountered, and runs end-to-end at full scale with all tests in a short wall-clock time. We cover the pray4us tool and discuss using it to investigate a Slingshot-11 bandwidth problem uncovered by the tool. Through the tool we have discovered the bandwidth problem is correlated with message size suggesting a stall event rather than a degraded network component. This may be related to enabling Prioirty Flow Control on our Slingshot-11 network, so next steps for our tool includes recording NIC level counters looking for pause frames.

presentations.title: Faster Scientific Multi-dimensional data analytics with NVIDIA cuPhoton
presentations.abstract: Observatories and telescopes, lasers and X-ray light sources, and other high-throughput instruments generate image data faster than CPU-bound pipelines can process it to support timely decisions. The computational bottleneck is rarely one slow kernel, but rather an end-to-end workflow that spans from the sensor/simulation to a decision: load, read, HPC processing and analysis, AI-signal detection. Modern facilities routinely accumulate petabytes of multidimensional data across a single survey or experiment campaign. With CPU-first implementations, it can take hours to months—sometimes a year or more—to obtain scientifically useful results from data the instrument produced in seconds. These delays make it harder for scientists and engineers to extract insights to make informed decision and advance their research. What is missing is a GPU-native path that covers every stage from the sensor to the decision, not a faster version of any one step. I will talk about how NVIDIA cuPhoton provide open-source NVIDIA CUDA-X toolkit of GPU-accelerated building blocks for that path, spanning use cases from spectral and optical astronomy to time-domain laser/X-ray analysis. By keeping image data on the GPU from sensor read through classification—on either single to hundreds of GPUs—cuPhoton collapses the wait to as low as microseconds, resulting in a tight loop that researchers can run interactively, shortening time to insight and letting facilities keep pace with the data their instruments are producing.

presentations.title: Fatal Attraction
presentations.abstract:
Supermassive black holes are among the largest objects in the Universe. Their masses range from at least one hundred thousand to many billions of times that of our Sun. In a tidal disruption event, a star is captured by the black hole’s gravitational field.

This artwork illustrates the different phases of destruction of a star by the tidal field of a supermassive black hole.

The right panel combines multiple instants of times highlighting the enormous stretch incurred by the star as it is pulled back toward the black hole.

The left panel shows the star after its first orbit around the black hole. The star is then subsequently destroyed when colliding with its own accretion stream.

presentations.title: FBench: A Flexible Benchmark for CFG-Based What-If Exploration of HPC I/O Patterns
presentations.abstract: The I/O performance of large-scale HPC applications depends on a complex interplay of access patterns, middleware optimizations, and file system configurations. To explore these effects without rerunning full applications, we introduce FBench, a flexible, code-transparent benchmark for what-if analysis. FBench leverages context-free grammars (CFGs) derived from Recorder traces to either generate a simplified global configuration file or replay I/O patterns on-the-fly without preprocessing. It supports POSIX and MPI-IO and injects optimization hints via JSON. FBench reproduces IOR's scaling within 6.9%, captures the irregular file-per-process pattern of HACC-IO, and reveals a 30% collective/independent gap on Lustre that striping cannot close.

presentations.title: Featured Speaker
presentations.abstract: A fireside chat with the US Department of Energy ASCR Facilities Directory Ben Brown.

presentations.title: Featured Speech: From Vision to Impact: Lessons in National-Scale Collaboration and Research Impact from the Exascale Era
presentations.abstract: The delivery of the nation’s first generation of exascale supercomputers was one of the largest and most consequential collaborative efforts in the history of high-performance computing, spanning national laboratories, universities, and industry partners across the country. Lori Diachin helped lead this effort as Deputy Director and then Director of the U.S. Department of Energy's Exascale Computing Project (ECP) from 2018 through 2024. In this keynote, she will reflect on the technical, organizational, and human leadership lessons drawn from that journey: what it takes to align a multi-institutional team around a shared mission, how to sustain momentum through a decade-long research and engineering effort, and why mentorship and inclusive leadership are essential to building the next generation of computing talent. Drawing on her career across national laboratories and DOE programs, she will offer practical guidance for early- and mid-career researchers navigating their own paths in HPC and AI, and a candid look at what national-scale collaboration in science really requires.

presentations.title: Featured Speech: Holistic Power Efficiency: Squeezing Computing out of Every Watt
Featured Talk: BURGS: Breaking the Perception Barrier in Undergraduate HPC Systems Research
presentations.abstract: Systems research can look intimidating from the outside: technically demanding, hard to enter, and disconnected from the things students care about. In this talk, I’ll share how the Broadening Undergraduate Research Group for Systems (BURGS) breaks that perception barrier by creating a welcoming community where undergraduates can engage directly in hands-on HPC systems research -- and what we learned from more than 200 graduates along the way.

presentations.title: Featured Talk: Hotness tracking in CXL hardware
presentations.abstract: Growing application memory demands are motivating heterogeneous memory systems that combine local DRAM with CXL-attached capacity. Their performance depends on identifying which data should occupy the faster tier and adapting placement as access patterns change. M5 and ARC are two complementary approaches to hardware–software co-design for CXL memory management. M5 uses device-side page and subpage tracking to guide migration, while ARC adapts the counting organization to workload behavior using shared hardware storage. Through measurements on real CXL prototypes, we examine how the location, granularity, and organization of hotness tracking influence migration decisions and application performance, highlighting trade-offs and opportunities for coordinating memory monitoring and placement.

presentations.title: Featured Talk: The Amazing World of Programming for Accelerators: From GPUs to SmartNICs and QPUs (Among Many Others)
presentations.abstract: Hardware heterogeneity is not anecdotal anymore, but rather the norm. Furthermore, it is not any longer limited to the now-customary CPU+GPU system architectures. These days we haveSmartNICs, processing-in-memory (and its variants), quantum accelerators, FPGAs, vector processors, and a plethora of domain-specific accelerators, to name only a few, admittedly indifferent degrees of maturity and adoption. Application developers always struggle to figure out the right programming model(s), language(s), strategies (…) to make their codes future-proof.While AI-programming has quickly become the norm, we still want to understand AI-generated code (at least for the time being). In this talk, I will go over the current landscape of hardwareheterogeneity and its programming, my expectations for the upcoming future, and some solutions that my group has been working on for a variety of accelerator technologies.

presentations.title: FFUSE: I/O Fault Injection and Resilience Scoring for HPC and AI Workloads
presentations.abstract: As HPC and AI/ML workloads increasingly share storage, filesystem faults (errors, partial I/O, latency spikes, silent corruption) can cause crashes or undetected data loss. To our knowledge, no systematic comparison of HPC and AI responses to identical filesystem faults, or unified cross-domain metrics, exists. We present FFUSE, a FUSE-based framework injecting seven filesystem fault categories transparently at the application I/O layer, and FIORE, a metric for failures without error reporting. Across 27 runs per workload, LAMMPS (HDF5 checkpoints) had lower crash (29.6% vs. 51.9%) and failure (44.4% vs. 66.7%) rates than ResNet-50 (pickle-based checkpoints). FIORE was 0.333 (LAMMPS) and 0.222 (ResNet-50), indicating ResNet-50 reported a larger share of its failures. Checkpoint format was associated with differences in I/O-layer fault behavior; a small paired pilot holding the application fixed suggests format can alter recovery outcomes but cannot isolate its effect. These results may inform checkpoint reliability in converged HPC–AI systems.

presentations.title: FHE-STREAM: Characterizing Memory Access Behavior in Fully Homomorphic Encryption Workloads
presentations.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data, but adoption is limited by high memory overheads. The Residue Number System makes FHE arithmetic practical on CPUs while expanding each polynomial into a fragmented, pointer-based collection of limb arrays. Standard HPC memory benchmarks use flat, contiguous arrays and cannot capture how these structures behave under irregular access. We present FHE-STREAM, a microbenchmark suite that reproduces the memory layout of production RNS-based FHE libraries and measures the gap between the bytes an algorithm intends to move and the bytes the memory system actually transfers. Validation against hardware DRAM counters shows this gap is driven by cache-line utilization rather than access irregularity alone: cache-line-granular or coarser access shows little amplification, while sub-cache-line random access substantially increases traffic. This ordering predicts real cost, with OpenFHE relinearization spending more than half its runtime waiting on memory, providing measured targets for accelerator and library designers.

presentations.title: Fidelity-Aware Scheduling of Quantum Circuits on Multi-QPU Systems
presentations.abstract:
High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) platforms expose multiple Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) that may differ in size, topology, native gates, and noise characteristics. For current noisy devices, errors compound along the compiled circuits quickly, and minimizing them, that is, maximizing the circuits' execution fidelity, is essential for reliable results.
Fidelity depends on the compilation to a specific target device: the same high-level circuit may produce different executables and, therefore, different expected fidelities across QPUs.
We present a low-overhead fidelity-aware scheduling framework for multi-QPU systems based on a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that estimates, before compilation, the expected fidelity of each circuit on each available QPU. Then, a tunable scheduler uses these estimates to control the trade-off between execution fidelity and parallelism. Results show that this framework allows for approximating an exhaustive fidelity-based assignment, saving computational resources compared to a brute-force approach that compiles each circuit on every device.

presentations.title: Field-Preserving Gaussian Splatting for Interactive Visualization of Large-Scale Cosmological Simulations
presentations.abstract: Large-scale cosmological simulations generate hundreds of millions of particles, making interactive visualization computationally expensive. Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) provide an efficient compressed representation of particle datasets, but existing GMM-based renderers incur additional computational overhead from depth-plane sampling and alpha compositing, while Gaussian splatting methods are designed for photorealistic rendering rather than scientific visualization. We present a field-preserving Gaussian splatting framework that combines GMM compression with orthographic projection and GPU tile-based rasterization to reconstruct additive particle density and continuous scalar attributes directly from compressed Gaussian representations. Built on the gsplat framework, the proposed renderer executes entirely on the GPU for interactive visualization. Experiments on the Illustris-3 (94,196,375 particles) and HACC cosmological simulations (331,644,184 particles) achieve density PSNRs of 43.27 dB and 46.07 dB, respectively, while sustaining up to 92 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

presentations.title: Fine-Grained Application-Aware Congestion Mitigation with Telemetry-Tuned Weighted SRv6 Policies
presentations.abstract:
Modern wide-area and research networks support
many different types of applications, each with its own perfor-
mance requirements. Because of this diversity, no single routing
strategy such as shortest path, least-utilized path, or Equal-
Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) can consistently deliver the best results
for every application. Existing telemetry mechanisms such as
IOAM and gNMI are fundamentally class-agnostic and operate
at 10–500ms timescales, while current SRv6-TE systems rely on
controller-driven path switching based on out-of-band statistics.
In this paper, we present a class-aware, in-header congestion
feedback mechanism for SRv6 that (i) encodes traffic engineering
(TE) class identity in the SRH Tag field, (ii) appends per-hop,
per-class congestion evidence in a Telemetry Tuned Weight -SRv6
(TTW-SRv6) record carried in-band with the SRv6 tunnel, and
(iii) uses load balancing algorithms per class within a distributed
architecture. A new architecture is presented where a trusted edge classifier
analyzes flow behavior.

presentations.title: Fine-Tuning Foundation Models for Micro-CT Image Segmentation Using HPC Platforms
presentations.abstract: Foundation models have demonstrated exceptional performance in computer vision, but adapting them to scientific imaging requires domain-specific datasets, scalable training methodologies, and high-performance computing (HPC) resources. This work presents methodologies for fine-tuning and deploying foundation models for synchrotron X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) image segmentation. We describe the adaptation of SAM3 for instance segmentation and DINOv3-Seg for semantic segmentation. We present strategies for data preprocessing, model configuration, loss design, and hyperparameter optimization for fine-tuning these models. We further describe scalable fine-tuning on local GPU servers through a web-based training interface and on the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) through Slurm-based job submission. Finally, we present distributed inference strategies on NERSC and the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF), enabling near real-time segmentation of large synchrotron datasets across hundreds of GPUs. Together, these methods provide guidance for adapting, training, and deploying foundation models for large-scale scientific image segmentation at synchrotron facilities.

presentations.title: First-Timers Orientation
presentations.abstract:
Feeling overwhelmed by SC? Don't worry, you're not alone. This conference is a massive, incredible experience, and we want to help you make the most of it.

Join our First-Timers Orientation for a stress-free session where you'll hear directly from our General Chair and seasoned conference volunteers. They'll walk you through everything you need to know, including:

- Navigating the conference schedule and finding your way around the venue.
- Understanding the different event types and what they mean.
- Understanding the various registration options.
- Learning valuable tips and tricks to maximize your conference experience.

Bring your questions. Let's get you ready to dive into SC26.

presentations.title: Flow Through a Pebble-Bed Reactor in NekRS
presentations.abstract: The pb146 case in NekRS is a benchmark computational fluid dynamics problem that simulates flow through a packed bed of 146 spherical particles, representing a simplified pebble-bed reactor geometry. It features a densely packed arrangement of spheres inside a cylindrical domain, producing complex flow behavior with tight gaps, recirculation zones, and turbulent interactions that are challenging to resolve numerically. Using NekRS’s high-order spectral element method, the case captures detailed boundary-layer physics and serves as a realistic yet standardized workload, making it widely used for testing solver accuracy, scalability, and performance on GPU-based high performance computing systems.

presentations.title: Flux: Workload Management for HPC and AI/ML Simulation in Cloud
presentations.abstract: Modern scientific workloads require automation and elasticity beyond the reach of traditional HPC schedulers. Developed over a decade at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Flux is the next-generation workload manager powering El Capitan, the world's #1 exascale system. Flux is unique for its graph-based, hierarchical resource management, enabling seamless portability and performance for complex workflows. Recently, the project joined the High Performance Software Foundation (HPSF) and was integrated with the Kubernetes Kubeflow Trainer for AI/ML. Participants will explore Flux foundations before diving into advanced capabilities for on-premises, cloud, and Kubernetes environments. We will cover the orchestration of heterogeneous workloads that require interplay between simulation, analysis, and services. Through lectures and hands-on, energetic tutorials that include interactive questions and terrible jokes, attendees will have fun and learn the ins and outs of scheduling in the exascale era. Tutorial content will range from getting started with job submission to running Flux with the Kubeflow Trainer in Kubernetes, and orchestrating a workflow under the scope of agentic science. Importantly, Flux Framework has never had the opportunity to give a pure Flux tutorial at the SC conference, and an influx of interest and questions make this year a unique opportunity to address this gap.

presentations.title: Fourth International Workshop on HPC Testing and Evaluation of Systems, Tools, and Software (HPCTESTS 2026)
presentations.abstract: This workshop brings together HPC researchers, operators, and vendors from around the globe to present and discuss state-of-the-art HPC system testing methodologies, tools, benchmarks, procedures, and best practices. The increasing complexity of HPC architectures and growing need to leverage HPC for integrated workflows demands more extensive testing than ever to evaluate the status of the system after installation or software upgrades and ensure operability before it is transitioned to production. Different methodologies are used by HPC centers and vendors to evaluate systems during their lifetime, not only at the beginning during installation and acceptance, but also during maintenance and alongside regular operations. This workshop provides a venue to present and discuss the latest HPC system testing technologies and methodologies. The event will include an opening talk focused on current HPC system testing topics, followed by a series of paper presentations from peer-reviewed accepted submissions, concluding with a panel discussion.

presentations.title: FP64 Performance and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation on HPC Systems
presentations.abstract:
A growing industry narrative holds that native double precision can be deprioritized in HPC accelerators, on the hypothesis that low-precision tensor cores can emulate FP64 on demand, and that most workloads are bandwidth-bound. This paper evaluates those claims and the importance of FP64 in scientific computing. We show roofline profiling data of representative HPC workloads across common computational motifs, to evaluate the arithmetic-intensity and accuracy. We also consider FP64 emulation via the Ozaki method to ascertain some of the possibilities and limitations.

These results indicate that emulation should not be evaluated as a replacement for FP64, but as an optimization for the subset of workloads whose dominant computation is sufficiently large, dense, and GEMM-like: this is less than 10\% of the HPC ecosystem. Even in this favorable regime, GEMM speedup is not sufficient: numerical behavior, workspace requirements, matrix shape, and integration overhead determine whether the benefit survives at application scale.

presentations.title: FPGA-Accelerated Simulation of a RISC-V Vector Architecture
presentations.abstract: A profusion of RISC-V-based system-on-chip (SoC) accelerator architectures has emerged in the past few years, fueled by AI and high performance computing. In many of these architectures, the RISC-V CPU serves as a control processor to route data and instructions to specialized IP blocks. Design, implementation, optimization, and validation of such architectures requires modeling and simulation of the integrated SoC at the register transfer level (RTL) in software simulators and FPGA. In this work, we evaluate the performance of a RISC-V scalar core augmented with the ARA2, a multi-lane floating-point vector unit, on workloads that are challenging for software RTL simulation. To accelerate evaluation, we map the RTL design to a low-cost FPGA development board. Here, we implement a heterogeneous system in which an ARM CPU manages benchmark setup, execution, and result collection for the RISC-V system, enabling fast, autonomous performance evaluation of the ARA2 vector processor.

presentations.title: From a Last-Week Add-On to First-Day Practice: Three Years of Integrating MPI Performance Analysis into HPC Education with EduMPI Suite
presentations.abstract: Performance analysis is essential for scalable MPI programs, yet tool and workflow complexity often relegates it to the end of Parallel Programming courses. EduMPI Suite lowers this entry barrier by automating cluster execution, measurement, and near-real-time analysis while visualizing MPI communication from the first program. This paper presents a three-year experience report on its integration into HPC education. We trace the transition of performance analysis from a last-week add-on to a recurring element of MPI development, using unpublished historical survey evidence and individual 2025 questionnaire data. Earlier cohorts perceived performance analysis as unnecessary, difficult, or unintuitive. In the final study, all students recommended introducing EduMPI Suite early in the course. Of 33 students, 29-33 rated it higher than conventional tools for understanding program behavior, interpreting communication, identifying bottlenecks, obtaining visual feedback, and navigating the tool. These findings support embedding performance analysis throughout MPI education before transitioning learners to professional environments.

presentations.title: From Access to Impact: Designing HPC–Quantum–AI Workflows for Scientific Productivity
presentations.abstract:
Quantum computing is increasingly being integrated into HPC environments, yet its impact on scientific discovery, especially in combination with AI workflows, remains limited by a more fundamental challenge: usability. Today’s hybrid quantum–HPC–AI workflows are fragmented, manually assembled, and difficult to reproduce, requiring users to navigate multiple abstraction layers, toolchains, and system constraints. At the same time, the user base is expanding beyond quantum experts to domain scientists who require intuitive, reliable, and scalable workflows.

This panel examines how to move from access to impact by focusing on the design of user-centered quantum–HPC–AI workflows. Drawing on perspectives from scientific computing, data workflows, system design, and applied research, panelists will explore workflow bottlenecks, abstraction strategies, orchestration challenges, and the role of AI. The discussion will focus on what is required to make hybrid systems usable in practice and how to translate emerging capabilities into measurable scientific productivity.

presentations.title: From Answering to Acting: An AI Agent for Research Computing User Support
presentations.abstract: RCD/HPC centers increasingly run support chatbots, but these answer from static documentation and cannot handle information that changes or act when a user needs something done. We describe our experience building an agent for a national cyberinfrastructure program that both answers questions from live infrastructure data and takes actions on the researcher’s behalf, such as registering them for events, posting announcements, and filing tickets, under their own federated identity, with user data kept inside institutional infrastructure and a confirmation step before consequential writes. Because help is only useful if it stays good, we evaluate answers with a judge validated against human reviewers, which separates the agent from plain retrieval (0.97 vs. 0.47), and we run that evaluation two ways: a release gate that catches our own regressions, and a drift detector that catches when the underlying information has gone stale.

presentations.title: From Candidate to Confirmed: A Verification-First Agenda for Open Autonomous Science
presentations.abstract: Automation, robotics, and LLMs are reshaping scientific discovery, generating hypotheses, designs, and analyses faster than humans can review them. Over the past year, multi-agent systems have produced laboratory-validated hypotheses, and interface standards like MCP and A2A have begun connecting agents to scientific tools and to one another. Progress on generation has outrun the infrastructure needed to trust it. Agents nearing expert performance on closed-ended questions complete only a small fraction of open-ended research tasks, no system has self-validated a novel discovery end to end, and a widely cited autonomous-discovery result was corrected after its novelty claims were contested. Verification, not generation, is now the binding constraint on autonomous science, and the open-model community is well positioned to address it. We propose a verification-first agenda of open, reproducible evaluation, end-to-end provenance for agentic workflows, and interoperable, accountable agent interfaces, artifacts that belong in shared open infrastructure alongside the models themselves.

presentations.title: From Diagnosis to Prediction: the AI frontier in Screening and Precision Prevention.
From Discovery to Patient Impact: Bridging the Translational Gap
presentations.abstract: Bringing biomedical discoveries from the research environment to the bedside requires more than technology. It requires collaboration across disciplines, institutions, and perspectives. This panel brings together participants from the Regional Technical Hub representing academia, national laboratories, industry, and clinical practice to share their experiences using AI, high performance computing, and other advanced technologies to accelerate biomedical research and translation. Panelists will explore the opportunities and challenges of cross-disciplinary collaboration, translating innovation into practice, integrating new tools into clinical workflows, and responsibly working with sensitive biomedical and clinical data. Together, we will consider how we can bridge the translational gap and harness emerging technologies to improve outcomes for patients.

presentations.title: From dispersed training materials to a centralized learning solution: The conceptualization of the SDSC Learning Hub
presentations.abstract:
HPC centers accumulate decades of training materials — slides,
documents, videos, code, and repositories — but as these collections
grow, so does the challenge of helping users find what’s relevant to
them under FAIR principles. We present the SDSC HPC Learning
Hub, a user-centered prototype connecting learners with training
resources drawn from a corpus spanning 2018 to the present (500+
cataloged materials). A novel feature is the use of learning paths
that can be customized to user activities. In this paper, we report on
the current public prototype, evaluation methodology, and lessons
learned for organizations transforming fragmented educational
collections into coherent learning environments.

presentations.title: From GPU-Accelerated Systems to Modern NVIDIA and AMD Superchips: Analyzing Energy and Power of a Heterogeneous SYCL Application
presentations.abstract:
Recently, the landscape of heterogeneous HPC systems has changed drastically once more, from classic GPU acceleration to tightly coupled systems such as the NVIDIA Grace Hopper superchip and the AMD MI300A APU.
Since energy consumption is a critical factor for the sustainable operation of HPC facilities, we analyze a heterogeneous SYCL application capable of CPU-GPU co-execution to investigate how power draw, energy consumption, and performance evolve in this ongoing transition.
Comparing heterogeneous and GPU-only scenarios, we find that the trade-off between maximum performance and minimum energy consumption observed in a conventional system persists even in modern superchips.
Furthermore, we observed significant energy savings in GPU-only settings on NVIDIA's GH200 platform compared to a classic GPU-accelerated system, driven by an over 140W lower CPU idle power draw. In a GPU-only scenario, AMD's MI300A APU achieves almost 19 percent lower runtimes than the NVIDIA GH200, while consuming only 1.03 times the energy.

presentations.title: From Idle to Urgent: A Resource-Harvested HPC Workflow for High-Fidelity Seismic Estimation
presentations.abstract: We propose an Urgent Interactive HPC workflow that dynamically integrates high-fidelity 3D nonlinear analysis with surrogate neural networks (NNs) to enable rapid decision-making during large-scale earthquakes. This approach achieves both "Resource Harvesting", which utilizes idle computing capacity during non-emergency periods, and immediate response during crises. By developing two specialized HPC kernels, the proposed method reduces energy-to-solution by 76% and improves throughput by 3.7-fold during normal operations to efficiently construct training datasets, while during emergencies, it couples NN-based inverse analysis with physics-based simulations and dynamic refinement to reduce conventional computational costs by over 97.9%, enabling the generation of highly reliable spatial time-history ground motion distributions within 30 minutes post-earthquake.

presentations.title: From Microbenchmarks to LLM Inference: An End-to-End Analysis on the Energy Efficiency of the Grace Hopper Superchip
presentations.abstract: The NVIDIA Grace Hopper (GH200) Superchip introduces a tightly integrated CPU-GPU architecture with shared power management, enabling new opportunities for energy-efficient high performance computing and AI inference. However, the impact of its power controls across different workloads remains largely unexplored. We present an end-to-end analysis of the GH200, spanning power sensor validation, HPL and HPL-MxP benchmarking, and LLM inference using Llama-3.1-8B. Our study quantifies the interaction between module and GPU power limits, evaluates energy-performance trade-offs, and analyzes operational and total cost of ownership. We demonstrate highly accurate onboard power measurements, identify workload-dependent optimal power settings, and show that mixed precision and inference workloads respond differently to power capping. During the poster session, we will present our experimental methodology, discuss the observed trade-offs, and highlight practical guidelines for energy-efficient deployment of GH200-based HPC and AI systems.

presentations.title: From Millions to Billions: Scaling Explicit Red Blood Cell Modeling on Exascale Systems
presentations.abstract: Explicitly resolving deformable red blood cells (RBCs) at physiological scale remains a fundamental challenge in computational hemodynamics due to high levels of memory, communication, and initialization demands. We present the first explicit billion-scale RBC simulation using HARVEY, a massively-parallel fluid–structure interaction solver characterizing high-fidelity deformable cell simulations. By combining scalable cell packing, distributed data management, and heterogeneous CPU–GPU execution, we initialize and simulate 4.95 billion RBCs within a 1 mL blood volume using 9,400 Frontier nodes (601,600 CPU cores and 75,200 AMD GPUs). The simulation occupies 3.76 PB of CPU memory and 1.44 PB of GPU memory while maintaining approximately 75% weak-scaling efficiency near full-system scale. These results extend explicit RBC modeling from millions to billions of cells and establish the computational foundation for physiologically-scaled cell-resolved blood flow simulations.

presentations.title: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and AI for Science
presentations.abstract: Many valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized because they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or subject to data-sovereignty restrictions. Federated AI therefore provides essential infrastructure for training models across institutions while keeping data local. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community on moving federated AI from pilots to dependable multi-site production. The analysis uses a five-domain readiness framework and two frontier-scale deployments: federated large language model training across three U.S. National Nuclear Security Administration laboratories using heterogeneous NVIDIA and AMD accelerators, and cross-facility fine-tuning spanning Aurora, Polaris, Frontier, and Perlmutter across Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD systems. We highlight systems challenges in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; summarize best practices for privacy, security, and decentralized trust; and identify open problems in asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts that motivate an international open-science working group.

presentations.title: From YAML to Insight: Interactive Visualization of hws Hardware Samples
presentations.abstract:
The hws library provides a simple, easy-to-use way to capture hardware metrics for CPUs and GPUs from various manufacturers, including NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel. Having a holistic view of how an application interacts with the underlying hardware is crucial for application developers optimizing not only for peak performance but also for other targets such as energy efficiency. Up until now, hws has exported the hardware samples as YAML files, leaving the data analysis and visualization of the results to the user.

Therefore, in this e-poster, we present a companion visualization tool for hws that generates interactive, standalone HTML reports, enabling users to quickly gain insights from hws data with minimal setup effort. Our interactive research e-poster will include a live version of the visualizer embedded as an iframe, allowing visitors to freely explore the tool with example scenarios and quiz questions on their own using the touchscreen.

presentations.title: FTXS 2026 : Closing remarks
presentations.abstract: Closing remarks for the FTXS 2026 workshop.

presentations.title: FTXS: Workshop for Faults, Trustworthiness, and eXplainability for AI Systems at Scale
presentations.abstract:
FTXS convenes researchers and practitioners to address trustworthy AI systems at scale under real-world variability. Modern AI/LLM pipelines (training, inference, RAG, and agentic systems) face “gray failures” such as distribution drift, prompt/tool/RAG variability, infrastructure noise, and limited-precision effects. Small perturbations can amplify into hallucinations, instability, miscalibration, irreproducibility, and silent regressions — wasting GPU-hours and undermining confidence in AI-assisted decisions.

FTXS organizes discussion around a practical closed loop: Disturb → Degrade → Detect → Diagnose → Defend → Validate. We emphasize explainability as a diagnostic tool for attribution across components (model, retrieval, tools, infrastructure, precision), and we aim to synthesize shared taxonomies, measurement practices, and seed artifacts (checklists, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols) that improve both research and operational practice.

presentations.title: Fulfillment: Artistic Encounters with the Hidden Labor and Environmental Footprint of High Performance Computing
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing (HPC) has become one of the defining infrastructures of contemporary society. Beyond enabling scientific discovery, HPC increasingly powers artificial intelligence, climate modeling, logistics, digital commerce, autonomous systems, and large-scale simulation. Despite its transformative role, HPC largely remains invisible to the public, obscuring the vast networks of human labor, material extraction, energy consumption, and environmental impact required to sustain computational infrastructures.

This project argues that artistic practice can make HPC visible, not only by visualizing scientific data, but by revealing the social, ecological, and political systems in which computational infrastructures are embedded. Rather than treating HPC solely as a technological achievement, the work positions it as part of a cultural-material landscape whose hidden operations shape everyday life.

Fulfillment is an interdisciplinary virtual reality artwork developed at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory (EVL), University of Illinois Chicago, in collaboration with anthropologists, designers, and computer scientists from several research institutions spanning the U.S., Europe, and Asia with support from the National Science Foundation. This proposal is for a public exhibition of the Fulfillment project as part of the Art Gallery Program at the SC26 conference. While the original work investigates global logistics and supply chain capitalism, this exhibition reframes those systems through the computational infrastructures that increasingly govern them. Warehouses, AI-driven optimization, cloud computing, data centers, predictive algorithms, and real-time simulation are presented as interconnected expressions of contemporary HPC ecosystems.

presentations.title: Fully GPU-Accelerated Distributed Full Configuration Interaction Beyond Trillion-Determinant Scale
presentations.abstract: Full configuration interaction (FCI) provides exact reference energies for benchmarking approximate quantum chemistry methods including emerging quantum algorithms, but its applicability is severely limited by exponential computational and memory requirements. To enable practical large-scale FCI calculations, we present a fully GPU-accelerated distributed implementation that combines chunk-based determinant partitioning, a hybrid GPU–CPU memory scheme, and GPU-native communication using NVIDIA NCCL. The proposed implementation computes the fully converged ground-state energy of NH2OH/6-31G with 1.7 trillion determinants in 13.4 hours and demonstrates execution of C2H4/6-31G with 2.4 trillion determinants, representing the largest determinant space reported to date for an uncompressed FCI implementation. It scales efficiently on up to 1,024 GPUs, and achieves up to a 58× speedup over our previous CPU-based implementation. These results establish the practicality of trillion-determinant FCI calculations on modern GPU clusters and provide large-scale exact benchmark data for validating approximate quantum chemistry methods.

presentations.title: Future directions from NSF's Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure
presentations.abstract: In this talk Katie Antypas, Senior Science Advisor for Cyberinfrastructure at the US National Science foundation with provide an update and future directions for computing, data infrastructure, coordination services for HPC systems, software and workforce development infrastructure from the Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure. She will also provide an update on the NAIRR: a Super Intelligence Infrastructure for Science and the newly awarded NAIRR Operations Center.

presentations.title: GarageWork: A Shared Testbench Abstraction for Software Simulation and FPGA Testing
presentations.abstract: GarageWork is a lightweight FPGA testing framework that enables the same cocotb testbench to be used for both software RTL simulation and FPGA-accelerated hardware simulation. A shared abstraction hides backend-specific interfaces, while synthesizable Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) dispatchers provide design-under-test (DUT)-specific control and test operations on the FPGA. GarageWork is intended for rapid bare-metal testing of standalone designs and on-chip processing logic for scientific sensors, rather than full SoC-level prototyping. The framework has been validated on AMD Alveo V80 FPGAs with several internal designs and provides initial support for AI-assisted generation of DUT-specific test components.

presentations.title: GDSight: Per-Operation Cross-Layer Attribution for GPUDirect Storage
presentations.abstract: GPUDirect Storage (GDS) copies NVMe data into GPU memory, bypassing the CPU data path and the identity linking an operation to the device work it causes. To our knowledge, no external GDS tool attributes a device command to its causing application operation: cuFile stops at the call, counters report only aggregates, and time-based matching fails once submission is asynchronous, even at one operation in flight. We present GDSight, which attributes each NVMe command to the operation that caused it, whether it entered cuFile or fell back to POSIX. Using eBPF, it matches commands by timing and by physical address, and only address survives asynchrony. On unmodified KvikIO, NIXL and HDF5 we pin pathologies to their cause: a silent bypass cuFile’s counters miss, 4× device amplification, and 22× tail inflation. We show that each diagnosis resolves to a measured intervention, worth up to 17× where throughput is the limit, or none.

presentations.title: GenASPEN: Agentic AI for Automatic Performance Modeling of HPC Codes
presentations.abstract: The growing heterogeneity of HPC programming models and hardware architectures has made automated performance modeling more essential and more difficult. Compiler-based frameworks such as COMPASS and MAPredict need programming model-specific integration; frontier LLMs are flexible but predict runtime poorly; custom LLMs buy accuracy at prohibitive cost. We present GenASPEN, an agentic AI framework that assigns each task to the component best equipped for it: a Code Translation Agent (a context-aware chain-of-thought pipeline over GPT-OSS 120B, or a Code Llama 7B assistant fine-tuned with ChatHPC) converts CUDA/HIP kernels into ASPEN application models, and a Performance Modeling Agent combines them with machine and analytical models to predict FLOPs, loads, stores, and execution time on modern GPUs. Across 22 benchmarks on NVIDIA H100 and AMD MI300A, GenASPEN reaches 98.5% operation-count and 94.40%/93.09% execution-time accuracy, beating four frontier LLMs on 16 of 22 kernels with zero manual annotation.

presentations.title: Geometry-Routed Attention for Multi-Magnification Histopathology Fusion in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
presentations.abstract:
Multi-view histopathology provides multiple histopathological images (HI) at different magnifications and tissue regions for each patient. Existing methodology includes complex fusion based learning architecture. However, existing state-of-the-art deep fusion models fails to capture the acquisition geometry of the multi-view HI. On the recently released Multi-Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC) benchmark, a self-attention fusion module was reported to under-perform plain feature concatenation, suggesting that unstructured attention cannot recover the scale-and-region relationships from a small cohort of 925 training patients.

In this work, we proposed dot-product based Geometry-Routed Attention fusion model (GRA), that incorporates a low-parameter routing that considers the acquisition geometry along with tumor core/edge regions prior directly into the attention logits. We study two realizations, ALiBi-style bias (GRA-P) and a learned per-relation routing (GRA-R). We validate our proposed methodology on Multi-OSCC dataset comprising of six classes with HI captured under three magnification factors. GRA-R attains a mean test AUC of 77.97%, with the highest class specific AUC for recurrence of 91.27%. Our results surpass existing benchmark Concat by 2.97% on mean multi-class performance. In particular, GRA-R surpass existing state of the art by 4.89% for lymph node metastasis and 5.04% for tumor differentiation. Additionally, the data-scaling ablation demonstrates that the GRA-R largest performance yield in low-data regimes, highlighting the utility of the proposed model under limited training data. Component-wise ablations further demonstrate that both acquisition-geometry and region-aware routing terms contribute independently to the overall performance.

presentations.title: GIFT: Geometry-Informed Low-Precision Gradient Communication for LLM Pretraining
presentations.abstract: Gradient communication is a major scaling bottleneck in large language model (LLM) pretraining. While FP8 can substantially reduce communication cost, direct quantization in Euclidean coordinates can distort highly anisotropic gradients. We present GIFT, a geometry-informed gradient communication method that transforms gradients into more isotropic coordinates before low-precision quantization. To make this practical, GIFT uses a one-sided, low-rank geometry approximation and applies it selectively to layers most sensitive to quantization error, while leaving the optimizer, training recipe, communication collective, and FP8 format unchanged. Across Llama-style models with approximately 600M and 2B parameters, GIFT achieves downstream performance comparable to Muon training with FP32 gradients. On 64 NVIDIA GH200 Superchips, GIFT reduces end-to-end training step time by 10.87% for Llama-600M and 17.05% for Llama-2B relative to FP32 gradient communication.

presentations.title: Global Network Advancement Group Data Intensive Science WG
Global Research Platform
GNNs Beyond HBM: Compressed, Bit-Exact Feature Streaming for Out-of-Core Training
presentations.abstract: Graph neural networks increasingly train on node-feature matrices that exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory: ogbn-papers100M's is ~57 GB, beyond a commodity 8-40 GB card. Out-of-core systems (GIDS, Ginex, MariusGNN, GraphBolt, HMGraph) already stream features from host memory past HBM, but always uncompressed. GnnPress compresses the streamed feature store: it exposes an ordinary float array to the GNN while storing features compressed and materializing only a small, double-buffered resident window. On an NVIDIA A100-40GB, GnnPress trains ogbn-papers100M (52.9 GiB), which out-of-memories an in-core layout. A lossless zstd codec is bit-identical to the in-core run every epoch (max|dloss|=|dacc|=0), including under mini-batch SGD; a GPU-native lossy codec, cuSZp, reaches 3.13x while perturbing training loss by at most 1e-6 over 30 epochs. Mini-batch SGD reaches 61% accuracy at a measured 1.7 GiB peak GPU (31x below in-core). Compressing the feature stream, not merely avoiding OOM, distinguishes GnnPress from prior uncompressed out-of-core GNN training.

presentations.title: Governed Agents: An Evidence-Based Architecture for the Computing Continuum
presentations.abstract: Agents can automate model selection, data curation, placement, retraining, and recovery across edge, cloud, and HPC resources, but this autonomy can turn uncertain model outputs into costly, privacy-sensitive, or irreversible actions. We define a governed agent as one whose proposed actions pass machine-checkable gates for context validity, decision uncertainty, policy compliance, execution feasibility, and auditability. Drawing on results from the NSF ICICLE AI Institute and related work, we present an architecture that integrates semantic typicality, runtime anomaly detection, neuro-symbolic verification, uncertainty-aware evaluation, lossless model compression, and modular agentic data curation. These mechanisms form a governance plane that mediates a sense-decide-act-learn loop across the computing continuum. Because current evidence remains component-level, we specify a falsifiable integration protocol, evaluation metrics, and failure tests to determine whether governed autonomy improves utility without obscuring risk or shifting excessive burden to human operators.

presentations.title: GPU Code Generation for OpenACC Kernels construct in a Modern MLIR-Based Compiler
presentations.abstract: The OpenACC kernels construct asks the compiler to discover and exploit parallelism inside a region that may mix parallel and sequential loops, intervening sequential code, reductions, and control flow that can guard those loops. Mapping such regions to GPUs is harder than compiling the more prescriptive parallel construct: the compiler must decide where synchronization and launch boundaries fall, not only how to schedule a single nest. We describe an MLIR-based Fortran OpenACC pipeline with three strategies for kernels: (1) splitting kernels into sequenced host-side device launches; (2) a single cooperative grid with grid-scoped barriers; and (3) CUDA Dynamic Parallelism (CDP), launching child grids from a device driver kernel. The strategies share most of the parallelism-lowering stack and diverge on how nests are ordered, synchronized, and bridged. We detail their CUDA mechanisms and mappings, and evaluate them on proxy applications and a synthetic suite that isolates the axes driving strategy choice.

presentations.title: GPU Device Compilation in ClangIR: Lowering CUDA and HIP Kernels Through the CIR Pipeline
presentations.abstract: ClangIR (CIR) is a high-level, MLIR-based intermediate representation that preserves source-level semantics between the C/C++ AST and LLVM IR, but its support for heterogeneous programming models has been largely unexplored. We present a path for compiling CUDA and HIP code through CIR, and show that it requires almost no new IR surface: kernels and device functions reuse cir.func, CIR’s intrinsic-call mechanism, and a small set of carry-across attributes lets whole-module runtime registration be deferred until a later pass can synthesize it. A single principle organizes the design—each decision is made at the earliest pipeline stage that has the information it needs—so the language-parameterized pipeline serves NVPTX and AMDGPU. Across PolyBench/GPU, our implementation compiles all benchmarks for NVPTX and AMDGPU architectures and runs them at parity with original Clang on an NVIDIA H100 and an AMD MI300X, at a compile-time cost of roughly 3%.

presentations.title: GPU-Accelerated de Bruijn Graph Traversal for Genome and Metagenome Assembly
presentations.abstract:
De novo genome and metagenome assembly often relies on De Bruijn graph traversals to reconstruct microbial genomes. Effective GPU implementation of this phase of the assembly is complicated by the presence of highly variable and unpredictable walk lengths, leading to severe warp divergence and memory requirements that are not known a priori.

We present a GPU-accelerated de Bruijn graph traversal adapted from MetaHipMer2 that uses a three-pass walk design to address these challenges. First, bounded walks enable more uniform work distribution and reduce warp divergence while bounding memory requirements in the first traversal phase. Second, symbolic walks determine the memory required to store generated sequences without requiring dynamic memory allocation. Finally, connection walks link subsequences generated in the first stage. Compared to the parallel CPU implementation in MetaHipMer2, our GPU implementation achieves a 45.84× speedup on a 440-million-k-mer dataset, substantially reducing single-node assembly time without affecting assembly quality.

presentations.title: GPU-Aware h5py: A Pure-Python Extension for HDF5--GPU Data Movement
presentations.abstract:
GPU-accelerated scientific computing in Python needs to move data from
on-disk HDF5 files into GPU memory. We present a pure-Python extension
to h5py adding GPU-aware reading, writing, and reduction without
modifying its C extension or the HDF5 library. It carries h5py's
index-based, NumPy-style slicing unchanged from disk through host memory
to GPU-resident CuPy or PyTorch arrays, addressing a selection
identically regardless of the result's location. Internally, every
read, write, and reduction path pins host memory once, reuses it across
calls, and overlaps host-to-device transfer with the next piece's
storage read, optionally fusing a caller-supplied transform or reduction
into the same stream at no extra cost until the computation outweighs
the transfer. Measurements on real hardware show index-addressed reads
costing only for what is selected, host memory staying flat as dataset
size grows over an order of magnitude, and fused compute staying hidden
behind I/O until per-piece compute cost overtakes it.

presentations.title: GPU-Initiated Data Movement for Accelerator-Centric HPC
presentations.abstract: Accelerator applications must move data between GPUs while computation continues, yet conventional host mediation delays transfer submission until control returns from an OpenMP target region. GiOMP moves the initiation point into GPU execution, so movement begins at data readiness and overlaps independent work. Using OpenMP target offloading, GiOMP provides device callable PUT, GET, and completion operations over HPE Slingshot. Its proxy path sends dynamic requests through a CPU worker, while its GPU trigger path releases prepared network operations without later CPU submission. On Tioga, a fused pipeline on two nodes achieves up to a 1.23× speedup over GPU aware MPI, with 5.6 to 6.8 microseconds attributed to eliminating a target relaunch. Jacobi weak scaling reaches 1.87× on Tioga and 1.82× on Delta AI. Remote GPU memory is the first concrete target of a broader GPU driven data movement layer, with future investigation of storage facing staging and in transit consumers.

presentations.title: GPUH5: A GPU-first I/O Library for Scientific Data
presentations.abstract: \I/O is a bottleneck in GPU-accelerated science, yet scientific data-format libraries run only on the host. A kernel cannot write where its data lives: it must exit and copy its array before HDF5 can run, so the write point becomes a kernel boundary. Systems that let a GPU initiate I/O give up the data model, emitting flat, untyped byte ranges. We present GPUH5, a GPU-first I/O library for persistent kernels. It keeps HDF5's hierarchical paths and chunked arrays, replacing the container format with a key-value store, so the host precomputes every chunk's key and an in-kernel write reduces to enqueuing a pointer, light enough that the producer holds 98.8% achieved occupancy. On a single-GPU Gray-Scott simulation writing 380 snapshots to NVMe, GPUH5 hides 96% of the I/O its synchronous twin exposes, finishing 1.9× faster than default HDF5.

presentations.title: Gradient-Free Optimization of Quantum Circuits Parameters for Hybrid Machine Learning
presentations.abstract: Quantum Machine Learning generally aims to build more accurate models by using quantum mechanical principles to better capture complex correlation across data features. Existing methods scale poorly with the number of both data samples and features, making them very challenging to train on real quantum devices beyond trivial datasets. We introduce a new hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for supervised classification, which uses gradient-free optimization to learn the quantum circuit parameters and builds the final classical model from the quantum circuits measurements. We experiment over a variety of datasets and show that this algorithm performs better than standard Quantum ML algorithms in most cases, while being more scalable to larger datasets and fully trainable on current quantum devices.

presentations.title: Graph500 Announcement
Green Shift: Resize the GPU, Not the Process
presentations.abstract:
GPUs are multiplexed across workloads using NVIDIA MPS, MIG, and CUDA Green-Contexts. Multiplexing maximizes utilization while isolation keeps tail latency predictable. But MPS and MIG are inefficient: resizing a partition requires restarting the bound processes and reloading model weights and state, incurring seconds of idle downtime that grows with model size. This poorly fits modern inference, where many models share a GPU and their compute demands shift constantly.

Green-Contexts instead change a process’s Streaming-Multiprocessors (SMs) budget on the fly, with no restart or reload, lowering reconfiguration time and GPU idle gaps. However, they target intra-application resource management, lack notion of multi-tenancy, and are not natively supported in PyTorch/vLLM. We introduce Green Shift, which repurposes Green Contexts for multi-tenant inference. On an NVIDIA H100, Green Shift cuts a large model’s reconfiguration downtime from roughly 30s to ~3s (>10× reduction), and uses ~1.5 to 2× less energy during the resize than MPS.

presentations.title: Guarded, State-Aware Orchestration for Schema-Constrained Scientific Model Execution
presentations.abstract: Trained scientific prediction models are often released as code, notebooks, or command-line tools requiring programming and exact schema knowledge, limiting access for domain researchers. Natural-language front ends can reduce this barrier, but standard LLM function calling provides a tool interface rather than workflow semantics for accumulating, validating, executing, and revising scientific inputs. We present guarded, state-aware orchestration for schema-constrained scientific model execution: the workflow collects inputs over multiple turns, constrains tool arguments with a typed schema, blocks incomplete execution, narrates results, and defines correction, what-if steering, and reset semantics. We instantiate the workflow for protein-corona prediction with a backend of 178 per-protein classifiers achieving 87.13% AUC-ROC. Evaluation using a cloud-hosted LLM produced 98.5% feature-extraction accuracy over 300 cases; a separate reliability evaluation of six interaction scenarios over 50 nanoparticle configurations passed all 300 scenario evaluations. These results demonstrate a testable extension of LLM function calling to scientific workflow orchestration.

presentations.title: Guest Panel Talk: From Facility Endpoints to Portable Experiments
Hall Pass: Per-Action Authorization for Shared Agents
presentations.abstract:
Autonomous agents deployed across federated research infrastructure are most valuable when shared across teams, yet few frameworks provide a way to control who may invoke which of an agent's actions. An owner must choose between keeping a private copy of an expensive agent or exposing one that any caller can use, inspect, or terminate. We examine three models for authorizing calls to a shared agent and prototype the third in the Academy middleware, backing per-action permissions with Globus Groups and enforcing them on the message path. We demonstrate with a shared SAM3 agent on Purdue Anvil.

At the poster we will walk through the three models and where each enforces access, then present overhead measurements and a larger shared-agent deployment on Anvil with results collected after initial submission.

presentations.title: Hands-On Outreach: Bridging AI, Supercomputing, and the Public
presentations.abstract: As AI rapidly reshapes public interest in computing, the HPC community has a unique opportunity to demystify these technologies and introduce foundational computational concepts. This interactive Birds of a Feather (BoF) session brings together HPC educators, trainers, and outreach practitioners to explore, facilitate, and evaluate hands-on AI outreach activities. Participants will test proven activities, discuss engagement best practices, and collaborate to design new resources using both human-led and AI-assisted frameworks. Attendees will walk away with a toolkit of reusable activities, insights into AI-driven content generation, and a collaborative network to strengthen HPC outreach community-wide.

presentations.title: HARD: Leveraging FleCSI for Heterogeneous Multi-Material Hydrodynamics
presentations.abstract:
Simulating multi-material hydrodynamic systems with disparate equations of state requires maintaining sharp material interfaces without numerical diffusion, a challenge for traditional methods that compromise accuracy or computational efficiency.

In this poster we extend HARD, a multi-material hydrodynamics code built on FleCSI that employs the Ghost Fluid Method enhanced with a multi-material Riemann solver for physically consistent interface treatment. Our novel contributions include sparse data structures reducing memory footprint by 25% and FleCSI backend optimizations enabling exceptional GPU scalability. We achieve 98.3% weak scaling efficiency on 32 CPU nodes and 81.3% on 16 GPU nodes, with single GPU nodes delivering 12.2× speedup over 128-core CPU nodes.

The implementation is complete and validated against analytical solutions and experimental data through shock tube, Rayleigh-Taylor instability, and 3D shock-bubble benchmarks.

Our poster will demonstrate performance metrics, showcase high-resolution 3D simulations, and provide live comparisons between CPU and GPU execution on representative multiphysics problems.

presentations.title: Hardware Aware Evaluation for Statistical Estimators: A Selection Rule and Reproducible Benchmark
presentations.abstract: Statistical estimators are almost always compared on accuracy only. We compare them on accuracy and compute cost together, on the hardware they would run on, and measure how often the recommendation changes. A rule selects a deployment configuration: an estimator with its implementation, device and fidelity setting. Three rules, error only, a balanced score of normalised error and run time, and a compute budget, are evaluated on six runtimes (four NVIDIA GPUs, an AMD MI300A node and a CPU only runtime), a covariance family, a regression family and two downstream tasks on real data. Weighing run time against error changes the recommended covariance estimator on 37 to 44% of decision groups on every accelerator; in the regression family the configuration changes on 72 to 85% of cells, the estimator does not. An adequate compute budget keeps out of sample performance; a tight budget and the balanced score do not.

presentations.title: Hardware-Aware Compilation of LLM-Generated, QEC-Encoded Quantum Circuits via Constraint-Aware Graph Retrieval
presentations.abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end workflow combining a locally hosted LLM for circuit generation, a deterministic stabilizer-code module for QEC encoding, and Constraint-Aware Hardware Graph Retrieval for identifying suitable connected hardware regions. We evaluate six compilation strategies across 720 method–configuration combinations, covering six IBM calibration snapshots, five three-qubit circuit families, and four optimization objectives. Compared with unoptimized raw mapping, the multi-candidate hardware_aware strategy reduces mean circuit depth from 956 to 468 and two-qubit gate count from 657 to 268. Compared with full-device Sabre, improvements are smaller, reducing depth from 488 to 468 and two-qubit gates from 281 to 268. Greedy CAHGR alone underperforms conventional baselines, demonstrating that calibration-aware region selection must be combined with effective placement and routing. Conclusions are limited to compilation efficiency because execution quality uses a no-fault proxy rather than logical fidelity or hardware execution.

presentations.title: Helios: A Disaggregated MySQL Database That Scales Without Replication
presentations.abstract: Modern in-memory transaction engines can outpace a single SQL query processor, but scaling through replicas or shards adds propagation or coordination. Helios is a disaggregated MySQL database that scales query processing without read-serving replicas.
