Multiple read/write-capable MySQL nodes share one in-memory LineairDB engine, which validates consumed point and range reads and orders commits to provide external consistency. To avoid row-at-a-time RPCs, Helios compiles MySQL's chosen execution plan into a dependent read plan. Embedded DuckDB executes consistent analytical queries over the same PAX layout using epoch cuts and before-images. Our prototype achieves 40.5k transactions/s with four MySQL nodes at 1,024 TPC-C sessions, 3.24x the one-node throughput. On TPC-H SF=10, Helios is 2.20x faster than TiDB with TiFlash and 62.4x faster than MySQL with InnoDB. We present the architecture, consistency mechanisms, and performance results through diagrams and benchmark figures.

presentations.title: Heterogeneous Energy Characterization of GPU-Powered Datalog Engines
presentations.abstract: Datalog’s declarative rules support recursive analytics in databases, program analysis, and machine learning, yet the energy behavior of GPU-powered Datalog engines remains largely unexplored. We present the first heterogeneous CPU–GPU energy characterization of these systems, evaluating five engines across hash-based, index-nested-loop, sorted/hash-indexed, and DataFrame-based designs on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We measure total CPU–GPU energy, hardware-counter-based instructions per joule, and energy–delay product using Powerlog, a lightweight harness that samples GPU power through NVML and CPU-package power through RAPL while running unmodified engines. Results show that the fastest configuration is not always the most energy-efficient. Engine choice changes total energy by up to 3×, while CPUs account for 32–55% of total energy. Scaling from one to four GPUs reduces runtime by up to 2.9× but increases energy by 24–42%. Our reproducible methodology and artifacts support energy-aware Datalog system design and fair cross-engine comparison.

presentations.title: High Performance Computing for Environmental and Earth Sciences (HPC4EES)
presentations.abstract: With the availability of large-scale weather, climate, and Earth data from multiple sources, including satellites and sensors, existing modeling techniques need further improvement to handle these data volumes. The high-performance computing (HPC) community can help. In the last decade, HPC has played an essential role in scaling existing weather modeling methods, enabling improved forecasting and proactive responses to severe weather conditions. However, this area warrants greater attention from HPC researchers to better understand the impact of climate change on future generations and to mitigate sudden disasters, including earthquakes and extreme weather events. Thus, we propose a dedicated workshop about coupling HPC with environmental and earth science. We chose SC as the venue for this workshop to reach a broad segment of the HPC community. The workshop will cover challenges around large-scale environmental modeling and possible solutions from the HPC community.

presentations.title: High Performance Python for Science at Scale
presentations.abstract: This symposium-style workshop aims to connect researchers, developers, and Python practitioners to share their experiences scaling Python-based applications and workflows on supercomputers. The goal is to provide a platform for topical discussion of best practices, hands-on demonstrations, and community engagement via open-source contributions to new libraries, runtimes, and frameworks. Based on talks and demos that survey and summarize the best practices and recent success stories and developments, the workshop provides attendees a forum for expanding their knowledge of tools and techniques as well as opportunities to engage with representatives from the broader Python community.

presentations.title: High Speed Network Processing for Scientific Computing in the Open Cloud Testbed
presentations.abstract:
This paper presents an FPGA-based SmartNIC
architecture designed to address critical network challenges
in data-intensive scientific computing. As scientific workflows
increasingly demand high-bandwidth data movement and realtime
monitoring across wide-area networks, the Open Cloud
Testbed (OCT) provides an ideal platform for investigating
in-network processing solutions at line rate.

Our approach focuses on implementing network visibility, optimization,
and orchestration capabilities through FPGA acceleration.
The proposed system leverages P4-programmable dataplane
functions to support packet parsing, marking, telemetry
extraction, traffic steering, and machine learning inference—all
without requiring host CPU intervention or modifications to application
servers.

Our framework integrates SciTags, which associates network traffic with
scientific context through packet marking. Our
high-performance network bridge counts packets by their
SciTag values, as identified in the IPv6 Flow Label.
Experiments on AMD U280 FPGAs in OCT
demonstrates the feasibility of this approach, showing imperceptible
processing latency and line-rate packet handling, while
accurately monitoring scientific data flows.

presentations.title: High Value, Petabyte-scale Data at JHU
High-Accuracy Computing on Low-Precision Hardware
presentations.abstract:
This workshop aims to bring together researchers, application scientists, system developers, and industry partners to explore algorithmic and implementation approaches enabling accurate scientific computing on low-precision hardware. As accelerators increasingly favor reduced-precision arithmetic for performance and energy efficiency, many scientific applications continue to require accuracy, stability, and reproducibility. Addressing this widening gap demands community-driven advances across algorithms and scientific software, spanning domain-informed and cross-cutting approaches while building toward reusable, precision-aware libraries and tooling infrastructure.

The workshop will feature invited talks and solicited works highlighting mixed-precision methods, error-aware and adaptive numerical algorithms, floating-point emulation libraries, and practical deployment on large-scale systems. The workshop emphasizes building community-driven software ecosystems for broad adoption across domains, reducing duplication, and accelerating impact. By fostering discussion among application developers, numerical experts, and hardware vendors, the workshop will establish best practices, share lessons, and strengthen academia–industry collaboration to make low-precision hardware a reliable component of scientific workflows.

presentations.title: High-Performance and Smart-Networking Technologies for HPC and AI
presentations.abstract: High-performance networking technologies are generating a lot of excitement towards building next-generation high-end computing (HEC) systems for HPC and AI with hundreds of thousands of servers with the latest CPU and GPU technologies, and a variety of application workloads. This tutorial provides an overview of these emerging technologies, their architectural features, current market standing, and suitability for designing HEC systems while delivering scale-up and scale-out principles. We present a holistic view of the major scale-out interconnects that power today’s supercomputers, such as IB, HSE, RoCE, Omni-Path, AWS-EFA, Slingshot, Tofu-D, and Ultra-Ethernet Consortium, followed by scale-up interconnects like NVLink/NVSwitch, AMD Infinity Fabric, CXL, and ESUN. We also highlight how the features of these networking technologies are integrated into libraries such as UCX, Libfabrics, and how these libraries are utilized in upper-level libraries such as MPI. The more advanced topics include discussions on DPU/IPUs and AI hardware such as Cerebras, Microsoft's Maia accelerator, and Meta's MTIA inference engine. Throughout the tutorial, we introduce four hands-on exercises to help attendees learn from the ground up (network-level concepts to MPI library integration) and how the network forms the foundation for designing HEC systems with scalable performance for HPC and AI workloads.

presentations.title: High-Performance Star-M SVD for Big Data Compression
presentations.abstract: In the era of big data, effectively compressing large datasets while performing complex mathematical operations is crucial. Tensor-based decomposition methods have shown superior compression capabilities with minimal loss of accuracy compared to traditional matrix methods. Under the star-M tensor framework, tensors can be decomposed in a matrix-mimetic way, including using the star-M SVD. This tensor SVD has optimality guarantees and has shown exceptional performance on specific types of data, but software implementations have been mostly limited to productivity-oriented languages. In this work, we present our development of a shared-memory parallel, high-performance solution designed to efficiently implement the underlying algorithms. This software will enable optimal compression of extensive scientific datasets, paving the way for enhanced data analysis and insights.

presentations.title: Hitting the Memory Wall: Why Cache Miss Tolerance Defines CPU Performance Now
presentations.abstract: The memory wall is the defining bottleneck in today's AI, automotive, data center, and HPC SoCs. CPUs operate at GHz frequencies with single-digit nanosecond cycle times, yet DRAM latency remains stubbornly at 60–100 ns, and MMIO accesses across complex Networks-on-Chip can take even longer. No single architectural feature can solve this alone — it demands a multi-dimensional defense. This article shares our experience using Google's FlatBuffers library as a memory subsystem stress test on the Andes 46-series RISC-V core. Our evaluation found outstanding transaction capability delivers up to 39% architectural benefit when memory accesses are independent, but only 6% under pointer-chasing patterns. The 46-series attacks this problem from every angle: outstanding transactions to exploit memory-level parallelism, hardware prefetching to anticipate access patterns, and software prefetch to give programmers direct control.

presentations.title: HOLOS: A Gradient-Descent-Based Design-Space Exploration Framework for Hierarchical AI Accelerator Systems
presentations.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has increased demand for hierarchical accelerator systems spanning processing elements, tiles, accelerators, and clusters. Exploring these systems is challenging because hardware parameters and software mappings interact across multiple levels. We present a gradient based design space exploration framework that unifies hardware and software co design using compact tiling factors for data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism together with per accelerator PE array and tile dimensions. The minimum required hardware is inferred directly from each mapping, reducing a conventional O(hardwarexmappings) search to O(mappings). A differentiable per operation model estimates latency, area, and energy. Compared with Calculon, our model achieves 0.99 Pearson correlation and approximately 4 percent mean absolute percentage error across 13B to 540B parameter LLMs. Under realistic memory and interconnect constraints for GPU system, the search reaches within approximately 1 percent of optimal energy delay product while evaluating 27 to 64 times fewer designs.

presentations.title: How far can network congestion awareness improve scientific workflow scheduling?
presentations.abstract:
Scientific workflows execute on shared HPC infrastructures, where network congestion remains a persistent phenomenon. Congestion arises
from communication contention among tasks within the same workflow or across concurrent workflows, often increasing makespan. We show that the impact of congestion can be mitigated by delaying task execution; however, only when two conditions are satisfied: (i) a shared communication bottleneck exists, and (ii) there is available slack outside the workflow critical path. We propose the Valley-Filling Admission (VFA) mechanism, which holds off-critical-path transfers out of the congestion crest and releases them into the idle-bandwidth valley. Using realistic network telemetry, VFA reduces workflow makespan by up to 9.2% for SoyKB and 11.2% for the 771 GB Chip-Seq workflows. We evaluated VFA with simulations across three network topologies, driving eight workflows and a real execution trace against a congestion-free baseline, and systematically sweeping the slack margin, contention factor, workflow concurrency, and telemetry staleness.

presentations.title: How Much Can We Compress Field Images for Smart Agriculture?
presentations.abstract: Camera-based smart-agriculture systems capture visual evidence of weeds, diseases, and pests, but multi-megapixel images are costly to transmit over low-power field networks. Many systems therefore perform on-device analysis and transmit only compact summaries, preventing remote visual verification. Image compression can reduce this burden, but must preserve information needed for downstream analysis. We present a preliminary task-level study using four annotated sugar-beet field images compressed with JPEG and JPEG~2000 over a 2--16$\times$ range, rerunning the same species-level weed detector on each reconstruction. Results show that lossy compression can substantially reduce image size while retaining useful detection performance, with JPEG~2000 consistently outperforming JPEG at the task level. We also find that similar PSNR values do not necessarily imply similar detection utility. However, payloads remain costly even at compression ratios that preserve detection quality, motivating agriculture-specific compression methods that more aggressively reduce data while protecting task-relevant visual information.

presentations.title: How Must HPC Education Change for a World Where AI Generates Our Code?
presentations.abstract: In the near future (if not already) HPC software will be generated by AI. The question is not “if” we must adapt, but “how” we will adapt. Everything about our software will be impacted. In this BoF, we will focus on training: How does what we teach have to change to accommodate the necessary shift in skills in the AI era? We need ideas from across the community and people who will dedicate the time to debate these ideas, digest them, and produce a position paper to drive the change we need in HPC. It all starts with this BoF.

presentations.title: How the NERSC User Community Connects
presentations.abstract: High performance computing centers, such as NERSC, serve thousands of projects and users across many science domains and funding offices, yet staff have few systematic ways to see how these communities form, persist, and connect for planning and outreach. As an exploratory step toward surfacing actionable insights from allocation data, 2020–2026 Perlmutter allocation records are turned into yearly project and user networks, and community detection, weighted betweenness bridge detection, and liaison ranking. Null-model and matched-popularity tests confirm the structure is real and actionable: communities stay above the 95% null modularity band every year; about 10% of projects carry 66%–74% of cross-office connectivity; and the top 200 liaison candidates reach 69% of active users. To our knowledge, this is the first network analysis of an HPC facility’s community.

presentations.title: How the Paradigm of Scientific Computing Evolves Through the Genesis Mission
HPC and AI Water Usage: Findings From 11 Leading Supercomputing Centers
presentations.abstract: High-density artificial intelligence (AI) and high performance computing (HPC) workloads are increasing thermal loads and making water use an important facility consideration. This study establishes an operational baseline from 11 large HPC facilities using a 35-question survey covering cooling systems, water consumption, WUE, blowdown, water quality, and conservation barriers. Facilities with hybrid/adiabatic cooling report a lower WUE, indicating higher water efficiency among surveyed sites, while evaporative facilities generally reported higher WUE. Cooling-tower blowdown accounted for approximately 15%–33% of facility water use at surveyed evaporative sites. Higher cycles of concentration (CoC) can reduce water use, but water chemistry can limit operation. The study also identified a definite water-energy trade-off, particularly during peak summer conditions. Finally, closed-loop liquid cooling does not necessarily eliminate on-site water use; water consumption depends on the outdoor heat-rejection method.

presentations.title: HPC Carpentry: A New Carpentries Lesson Program
presentations.abstract:
The HPC Carpentry project, an effort to provide hands-on workshop-based instruction for novice users of HPC systems, has long been well-aligned with the broader educational mission of the Carpentries project, using open-source materials to bridge the gap between resources and the skills needed to use them effectively.

Having been adopted as a new lesson program within the Carpentries, it is time to reconnect with the larger HPC community, seeking feedback on strategic planning, and identifying new audiences where the solutions developed during the Carpentries incubation and adoption process can add value and strengthen the world of HPC education.

presentations.title: HPC Developments for Fusion Energy Applications
presentations.abstract: The growing interest in fusion energy to power massive data centers has created an urgent need to accelerate plasma science codes. Both experimental capabilities and computational workflows are complex and often render current technologies inefficient, which results in a severe lack of data. Implementation of plasma codes becomes complicated due to variations in software and hardware architectures. A potential solution is to develop an abstraction layer to connect infrastructure to application codes. This BoF focuses on identifying the needs for development and standardization of an abstraction layer, and the relevant functionalities/data structures that would be most useful to abstract.

presentations.title: HPC Education Across Institutional Boundaries: Leveraging NCShare's Statewide Cyberinfrastructure
presentations.abstract:
Most introductory HPC training assumes a local cluster, local staff, and a local allocation process-resources many institutions lack. NCShare, an NSF-funded coalition of North Carolina institutions, operates shared statewide cyberinfrastructure, including NVIDIA H200 GPUs, open to all member campuses.
We describe the design and operation of the NCShare HPC Workshops, a free series taking participants from no prior HPC experience to a completed scientific job. Co-taught by NCShare staff and instructors across member institutions, the curriculum covers access, storage and data movement, containers, CPU-parallel and GPU-accelerated applications, and scientific visualization.
Two design decisions follow from the shared infrastructure. With no environment-module system, containers are the primary route to scientific software making a participant's first environment portable and reproducible. Because allocation latency is the main barrier to participation, workshops run on a dedicated scheduler partition.
We report workshop assessment, post-workshop usage, and release all materials for reuse.

presentations.title: HPC Education and Training: Emerging Opportunities and Challenges
HPC Graph Toolkits and the GraphBLAS Forum
presentations.abstract: Graph analytics is foundational to scientific discovery, national security, artificial intelligence (AI), and industrial innovation, yet sparse, irregular, and evolving graph workloads continue to challenge HPC systems. This BoF convenes developers and users of high-performance graph toolkits to exchange updates, compare combinatorial and algebraic approaches, and define priorities for converged workflows spanning simulation, data analytics, AI, instruments, edge platforms, clouds, and supercomputers. Discussion will address GraphBLAS, interoperability, dynamic graphs, heterogeneous execution, provenance, trustworthy reasoning, and sustainable open infrastructure, producing concrete community directions for research, software, standards, benchmarks, infrastructure investment, and cross-sector collaboration. The outcome will guide collaborative work beyond SC26.

presentations.title: HPC Infrastructure Management at Scale
presentations.abstract: HPC infrastructure management at scale depends on more than golden images: operators must build, version, and deploy the right operating-system image to the right node role safely, repeatably, and without interrupting running jobs. The HPC OS project replaces a Satellite-driven provisioning model, where behavior depended on Web UI host parameters and Ansible overrides, with a central patching source for on-premises clusters. Layered RHEL, Rocky Linux, and Ubuntu CPU/GPU images are built with Packer and Ansible, stored as versioned artifacts, tracked with release metadata, and deployed through MAAS, orchestration, and post-deploy Ansible. In scale testing across 300 CPU/GPU nodes, the most stable operating point was 100 concurrent deployments, driven by AWS SSM and Shell-specific tradeoffs rather than MAAS; Satellite stabilized at about 60 nodes. We present lessons for replacing build-centered automation with a reproducible image build and deployment platform for large HPC environments.

presentations.title: HPC means Heterogeneity, Performance and Complexity
presentations.abstract:
The variety of applications using or seeking to use high-performance computing (HPC) resources is growing, as is their demand for computing power and data management. Meanwhile, the physical limits of Moore's law are prompting the development of new computing solutions, including a growing range of custom-designed processing units and accelerators, as well as emerging techniques such as quantum and neuromorphic computing. Data centres and HPC hosting sites face the challenge of designing systems that can meet the needs of diverse applications, integrate different processing technologies and minimize energy consumption and operational costs. This is resulting in increasingly heterogeneous system designs comprising multiple partitions or modules with different node architectures. However, such diversity also increases the complexity on the side of system operation, parallel programming, performance analysis, and application optimization.
This talk reviews current trends in the HPC landscape, highlighting key challenges and opportunities for the HPC/AI community.

presentations.title: HPC Next: Reflections and Progress on the RISC-V Ecosystem
presentations.abstract:
RISC-V is an open standard instruction set architecture (ISA) enabling the open development of CPUs and a shared software ecosystem. There are already over 30 billion RISC-V cores, which are accelerating rapidly. Nonetheless, for all the successes that RISC-V has enjoyed, it is yet to become popular in HPC. Recent advances, however, such as data center RISC-V-based CPUs and PCIe accelerators, mean that this technology is becoming a more realistic proposition for our workloads.

This BoF aims to connect the RISC-V and HPC communities. We will explore how the technology is progressing and identify lessons learnt from previous years' predictions.

presentations.title: HPC Procurement, Energy Efficiency, and Sustainability
presentations.abstract: Energy efficiency has evolved from an operational objective into a contractual engineering requirement for next-generation HPC systems. This BoF explores how procurement contracts shape future supercomputer design by comparing approaches from Australia, Japan, and Europe. Maciej Cytowski (Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre) examines Australia’s shift from voluntary guidelines to grid-firming, water-saving, and renewable-backing mandates. Masaaki Kondo presents Fugaku to FugakuNEXT, emphasizing procurement strategies for higher simulation performance within a power envelope. Maria Grazia Giuffreda discusses energy-to-solution requirements and software optimization clauses. An interactive forum debates how procurement clauses drive architectural choices, software portability, sustainability, and innovation in late-2020s deployments.

presentations.title: HPC Security in the AI Era: Standards, Compliance, and Governance
HPC Systems Professionals Workshop (HPCSYSPROS26)
presentations.abstract:
The complexity of high performance computing (HPC) systems necessitates advanced techniques in system administration, configuration, and engineering and with staff who are well-versed on the best practices in this field. HPC systems professionals include system engineers, system administrators, network administrators, storage administrators, and operations staff who face problems unique to HPC systems. The ACM SIGHPC SYSPROS Virtual Chapter, the sponsor for this workshop, has been established to provide opportunities to develop and grow relationships focused specifically on the needs of HPC systems practitioners and to act as a support resource for them to help with the issues encountered in this specialized field.

This workshop is designed to share best practices for common HPC system deployment and maintenance, to provide a platform to discuss upcoming technologies, and to present the state-of-the-practice techniques that increase performance and reliability of systems, and in turn increase researcher and analyst productivity.

presentations.title: HPC User Support in the AI and Exascale Era
presentations.abstract:
As HPC enters an era of extreme heterogeneity and AI integration, user support is a critical strategic enabler. However, rising system complexity and finite staffing strain traditional models. To thrive in the AI and exascale era, a collaborative community approach is essential.

This BoF session invites practitioners, providers, and users to collaboratively reshape HPC support. Featuring insights from facility leaders on managing rapid AI adoption, an interactive live survey, and open group discussions, participants will share experiences regarding scaling, AI automation, and knowledge transfer. Outcomes will form a post-conference report dedicated to fostering a sustainable, community-driven support ecosystem.

presentations.title: HPC–Quantum Integration: Software, Systems, and Hybrid Workflows
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing are coming together to enable hybrid workflows that combine classical and quantum resources within a single computing environment. As quantum technologies evolve at different paces, integrating them into HPC systems introduces challenges for software, hardware, and scientific applications.

This panel brings together perspectives from HPC centers, quantum hardware development, and academic research to examine how HPC–quantum integration is approached in practice. Panelists will discuss software and systems layers enabling hybrid execution, including programming models, workflow orchestration, and middleware connecting HPC environments to quantum resources.

Drawing on early integration efforts, the discussion will highlight how communities are engaging with hybrid workflows — from deploying and evaluating quantum resources within HPC facilities to developing hardware and exploring algorithms and use cases. Panelists will share insights into challenges such as latency, resource management, as well as differing expectations around performance, usability, and readiness across quantum paradigms.

presentations.title: HPC-CARLA: Closed-Loop Evaluation of Autonomous Driving Agents as a Resilient, Schedulable HPC Workload
presentations.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation of autonomous-driving policies spans many conditions, but CARLA servers on shared GPU clusters often fail after producing valid episodes. We present HPC-CARLA, which runs these campaigns through a multi-node queue and reuses one simulator service per GPU. It restarts failed services and harvests episode checkpoints independently of job state. Its declarative pipeline framework brings six policies under one audited execution model. Across five agents on A100, HPC-CARLA retained 13,059 valid route evaluations; 94.3% came from jobs that ultimately failed. Three L40S campaigns tested another GPU and driver stack, although score agreement depended on the agent. As A100 coverage expanded, the relationship between an offline difficulty score and driving performance reversed, so the revised dispatcher gives per-agent coverage requirements precedence over that scalar. Together, the campaigns show why workflow state must include simulator health, episode progress, and condition coverage.

presentations.title: hpcGPT: A Flexible Framework for Agentic User Support in HPC
presentations.abstract: High-performance computing centers spend significant staff time addressing recurring user questions about account management, software environments, job scheduling, and system architectures. Analyses of historical support tickets show that a small number of topics account for a disproportionate share of user requests, yet much of this knowledge remains buried in closed tickets and dispersed documentation. We present hpcGPT, an agentic command-line support assistant that combines OpenCode, a provider-independent terminal interface, with Model Context Protocol tools. The system delivers contextualized responses by integrating site documentation, historical ticket knowledge, and live cluster information, while preserving the ability to escalate unresolved issues through existing ticketing workflows. We describe the system architecture, MCP tool ecosystem, and ticket knowledge pipeline, including data ingestion, PII scrubbing, and retrieval mechanisms. Finally, we report on a pilot deployment in a production HPC environment and discuss its potential to improve user support, accelerate access to expertise, and reduce staff workload.

presentations.title: HPCMosaic: Adaptive Dashboard for an Evolving HPC User Base
presentations.abstract:
High-performance computing (HPC) resources are increasingly accessed by researchers outside of computational disciplines, yet HPC interfaces have not kept pace with this shift. Dashboards remain organized around system components rather than modern user goals, exposing complexity that generates extraneous cognitive load and drives incomplete, unresolvable support tickets to overburdened help staff.

This paper presents HPCMosaic, an HPC dashboard framework built on three design principles: adaptability, where the interface adapts to each user's workflow rather than imposing a fixed layout; progressive disclosure, surfacing common workflows clearly while keeping advanced options accessible; and closing the support loop, embedding guided request forms within relevant widgets to automatically capture technical context and route submissions to support staff. A composable widget architecture underpins all three principles, allowing contributors to extend the dashboard without modifying core framework code.

HPCMosaic is deployed in production at a large research university's HPC center and is available as open-source software.

presentations.title: HPCTESTS Panel 2026
presentations.abstract: The HPCTESTS panel hosts all five presenters for a final discussion on the workshop's topics and presented work.

presentations.title: HPL and HPL-MxP at Exascale on Aurora: Performance Engineering and Characterization
presentations.abstract: Running HPL and HPL-MxP at exascale requires more than optimized numerical kernels; it requires coordinated performance engineering across communication, resource mapping, runtime configuration, CPU--GPU interaction, and mixed-precision execution. This paper reports experience from large-scale benchmarking campaigns on Aurora, the Intel-based exascale supercomputer at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Aurora progressed from 0.585 EF/s on 5,439 nodes to 1.01 EF/s on 9,234 nodes in FP64 HPL, while HPL-MxP reached 11.64 EF/s on 9,500 nodes. We describe the system-level choices behind these results, including locality-aware rank, GPU, memory, and NIC placement; explicit CPU--GPU pipelining; host-buffer MPI and transport configuration; phase-specific NIC assignment; AMX-accelerated mixed precision; and a hybrid point-to-point/collective path introduced after synchronization stalls at scale. This experience-based study concludes with practitioner guidance separating Aurora-specific findings from broader principles for tightly coupled heterogeneous systems.

presentations.title: HPPSS Featured Speaker
HUST Morning Break
HUST Survey
HUST Welcome
HV-Coll: Co-Designing Collective Communication with Vectorized Homomorphic Compression
presentations.abstract: Inter-node collective communication constrains large-scale scientific simulations and distributed AI. Error-bounded lossy compression can reduce data volume, but prior CPU frameworks underuse memory bandwidth with scalar packing, lose compression ratio (CR) at SIMD-friendly block sizes, and repeat decompress–operate–compress (DOC) work during reductions. We present HV-Coll, which co-designs a block-aligned representation, SIMD encoding, outlier-aware fixed-length encoding, compressed-domain addition, and MPI collective schedules. Evaluated on 3,584 CPU cores, HV-Coll's homomorphic compression is up to 8.1x faster than hZCCL's scalar DOC workflow, and its outlier-aware encoding improves CR by up to 27.2%. HV-Coll collectives reach up to 47.2x, 23.4x, 43.8x, and 67.6x speedups over native MPI for Bcast, Scatter, Allreduce, and Alltoall, respectively.

presentations.title: IA^3 2026 — 16th Workshop on Irregular Applications: Architectures and Algorithms
presentations.abstract: Data-intensive applications process heterogeneously, employing diverse methods and data structures that exhibit irregular data accesses, control flows, and communication patterns. Modern data analytics applications additionally require supporting dynamic data structures, asynchronous control flows, and mixed parallel programming models. Supercomputing systems are organized around software and hardware optimized for data locality and bulk synchronous computations. Managing irregular behaviors requires a substantial programming effort and lacks integration, leading to poor performance. Holistic solutions to these challenges emerge only by considering the problem from multiple perspectives: from micro- to system architectures, from compilers to languages, from libraries to runtimes, and from algorithm design to data characteristics. Only collaborative efforts among researchers with different expertise, including domain experts and end users, can lead to significant breakthroughs. This workshop brings together scientists from different backgrounds to discuss methods and technologies for efficiently supporting irregular applications in current and future architectures.

presentations.title: IA^3 Debate
Icebreaker and networking
presentations.abstract: An interactive session to help participants find shared research interests and make lasting connections.

presentations.title: IDIA: A review of over a decade of data-intensive computing and a look at the future
Impact of GPU Multistreaming on Task-Based DAG Execution in Dagger.jl
presentations.abstract:
Task-graph runtimes like Dagger.jl can now run independent tasks across multiple concurrent GPU streams, raising two questions: how should tasks be assigned to streams, and do more streams improve performance regardless of placement?

We benchmark four policies (round-robin, random, SDQ, and locality-aware) across four DAG topologies (linear, diamond, chainlink, tangled) and four stream counts (1, 2, 8, 32) on an NVIDIA H200 and an AMD MI300A. Every policy speeds up with more streams, but placement matters. At 32 streams, round-robin is fastest, averaging 4.5x speedup on H200 and 2.5x on MI300A, with SDQ close behind on H200 (4.0x). Locality-aware assignment issues 1.6x to 8x fewer synchronization events but reaches only 2.5x and 1.5x, so policy choice alone changes wall-clock time by up to 2.2x.

At the poster, we will walk attendees through the DAG-topology taxonomy and policy comparisons, and discuss which policy suits each workload and hardware backend.

presentations.title: Impact of Overheads in Disaggregated Systems on Job Turnaround Times
presentations.abstract: Disaggregated systems dynamically attach accelerators to and detach them from compute nodes over a network. They can thus allocate the exact number of accelerators requested by each job, reducing idle accelerators. However, resource disaggregation incurs two overheads. The communication latency between compute nodes and accelerators increases the execution times of jobs, and the reconfiguration to attach and detach accelerators takes time. These overheads may make job turnaround times longer, but their effects remain unclear. We investigate their effects using a scheduling simulator, which we developed for disaggregated systems. The results show that an approximately 20% increase in execution times, reconfiguration times of 90 seconds or longer, and a shortage of accelerators make turnaround times longer than those in traditional systems. We also show that introducing fixed compute nodes, to which accelerators remain attached and require no reconfiguration, reduces turnaround times. We finally summarize considerations for administrators adopting disaggregated systems.

presentations.title: In-Network Computing with SmartNICs for HPC Applications
presentations.abstract: The past few years have witnessed an increased level of support for and deployment of programmable network adapters, known as "SmartNICs." These enhanced network devices offer standard packet processing capabilities as well as advanced "in-network" computing features built around programmable lightweight processing cores, FPGAs, and even CPU- and GPU-based platforms capable of running separate operating systems. SmartNICs have gained rapid adoption for data center tasks, including infrastructure management, packet filtering, and I/O acceleration. Increasingly these devices are also being explored for high-performance computing (HPC) and AI application acceleration. This tutorial provides an in-depth exploration of the state of the art in SmartNICs and the emerging software ecosystems that support them. Attendees will participate in hands-on exercises designed to demonstrate how SmartNICs can be leveraged to accelerate HPC and AI applications. Topics include packet processing frameworks such as P4, I/O acceleration techniques, MPI offloading, and algorithmic adaptations for utilizing SmartNIC processors. Participants will have the opportunity to run these exercises on cutting-edge platforms, including NVIDIA BlueField-3 Data Processing Units (DPUs), using cloud-based environments such as USC’s NETLAB and the FABRIC testbed. The tutorial will also highlight additional strategies for optimizing applications to effectively use SmartNICs as communication accelerators in HPC systems.

presentations.title: Inference Services and Agents on HPC: Scaling Scientific AI for Academic Community
presentations.abstract: Initiated at SC25 to explore AI inference services in the academic HPC community, this BoF returns to address the fast-evolving landscape of inference services, agentic AI, tool services, and AI4Science. This practitioner forum brings centers and researchers together to share practical insights and experiences spanning infrastructure, software, and use cases. This session aims to cultivate collaborative solutions for AI developments. The goal remains to foster a sustained, cross-institutional "community of practice" bridging academic and governmental HPC centers and the user community to foster collaborations in this area.

presentations.title: Informing Probabilistic Tsunami Forecasting with Massive Earthquake Ensembles: FFT-Based Multi-GPU Source-to-Waveform Generation and Posterior-Start Flow Matching
presentations.abstract:
Cascadia tsunamis can reach nearby coastlines within minutes, demanding rapid probabilistic forecasts from early seafloor-pressure observations. Gaussian Bayesian inference is fast but cannot capture non-Gaussian earthquake variability, while generating large simulation ensembles is expensive.

We developed a distributed FFT-based source-to-waveform pipeline that reuses precomputed physical responses, generating full-scale Cascadia waveforms in 24 ms per rupture on 64 GB200 GPUs after setup. Our contribution couples this scalable generator with posterior-start flow matching, which transports the pressure-conditioned Gaussian posterior into an earthquake-informed, non-Gaussian distribution. Trained on one million stochastic ruptures, the model reduces RMSE by 79% and CRPS by 86% relative to the Gaussian baseline across 4,096 held-out events.

presentations.title: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night
presentations.abstract: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night (IOAN) is a multi-player VR experience that brings the rhythms of the cosmos to life in an endless remix instrument. Created from 758,457,209 magnitude readings for 817‚373 astronomical objects captured by the AST3 robotic telescopes in Antarctica, the experience transports players inside of a field of objects at the heart of the Large Magellanic Cloud. Within a multiplayer VR arena, and floating inside a luminous field between the Earth and the Large Magellanic Cloud, multiple players explore and collaboratively create new visual and sound remixes to perform the AST3 dataset as a soundscape for external visitors to the VR arena. The collaborative experience is inspired by communal percussion and multiplayer instruments. Real-time database queries, selections, and filtering operations enable multiple players in VR to collaboratively interact with the objects in the field to create data remixes from astronomical data. Visitors to the arena see and hear the virtual world in correct spatial relation to their real-world positions through spatialized 4K portals and spatialized ambisonic audio that align the physical space of the arena installation with the inner space of the multiplayer virtual environment.

presentations.title: Instrumentor: Customizable and Generic Instrumentation for LLVM
presentations.abstract: Instrumentation-based tools are essential for developing high-performance, efficient, and correct codebases in HPC and AI domains. However, code instrumentation mechanisms remain highly fragmented across compiler infrastructures, and LLVM is no exception. Building these tools usually requires developing custom LLVM passes, a tedious and repetitive task that demands deep knowledge of compiler internals. In this paper, we introduce the LLVM Instrumentor, a generic and customizable LLVM pass that instruments IR driven by user-provided configurations. The Instrumentor, configurable through a JSON file or programmatically, simplifies the development of new instrumentation-based tools by providing a wide coverage of instrumentation features. To demonstrate its versatility and ease of use, we present several instrumentation tools built with just a few lines of JSON configuration and runtime code.

presentations.title: Interactive Knowledge Graph Supporting Self-Directed and Personalized High Performance Computing Education
presentations.abstract: Across universities, compute centers, and industry partners, significant resources are put into developing educational materials for researchers and developers in high performance computing (HPC). It is important to acknowledge that the range of research backgrounds in HPC is beneficial for the community in many ways but poses challenges for education. In particular, many HPC users and developers would benefit from foundational knowledge that may seem obvious to computer scientists. We propose an interactive knowledge graph of fundamental concepts of HPC, allowing learners to choose their own starting point and navigate forwards or backwards through related topics. This content is delivered through accessible, short lecture videos featuring animations that are delivered by HPC specialists. These videos are supplemented with formative assessments, and all of the concepts are structured into an interactive knowledge graph which specifies dependencies between concepts so that the learner can find their own pathways through the learning journey.

presentations.title: Interactive Visualization of Data Center Monitoring Data on a 3D Cluster Model
presentations.abstract: Modern data centers generate large volumes of heterogeneous monitoring data. While conventional two-dimensional visualization tools are effective for many analytical tasks, they provide limited spatial context at system and facility scales, particularly for cooling and network infrastructures. This paper presents a framework for spatially contextualized visualization of monitoring data using a realistic 3D cluster model. The approach maps multi-layer monitoring data onto a 3D representation, enabling both system-level overviews and detailed node-level inspection. Metrics are encoded using color-based textures and chart-based visualizations. Blender serves as the visualization platform, providing extensibility, high-quality rendering, and support for interactive and immersive exploration. The framework is demonstrated using a realistic model of the Karolina cluster. A generalized pipeline for parametric model creation is also introduced. It transforms tabular input data into a structured JSON representation and subsequently into Universal Scene Description (USD) format, enabling reusable and extensible 3D model generation.

presentations.title: International Demonstration of 400 Gbps 8K Uncompressed Video Processing Using SRv6-Based In-Network Computing
presentations.abstract: nri102s1

presentations.title: International Workshop on RISC-V for HPC (RISCVHPC)
presentations.abstract:
RISC-V is an open standard instruction set architecture (ISA) which enables the open development of CPUs and a shared common software ecosystem. There are already over 15 billion RISC-V cores, which are accelerating rapidly. Nonetheless, for all the successes that RISC-V has faced, it is yet to become popular in HPC. Recent advances, however, such as data center RISC-V-based CPUs and PCIe accelerators, mean that this technology is becoming a more realistic proposition for our workloads.

This workshop aims to connect those currently involved in RISC-V with the wider HPC community. We look to bring together RISC-V experts with scientific software developers, vendors, and supercomputing center operators to explore the advantages, challenges, and opportunities that RISC-V can bring to HPC. Furthermore, we aim to further expand the RISC-V HPC SIG, enabling interested attendees to participate in one of the most exciting open-source technological activities of our time.

presentations.title: Interoperable Performance Prediction through Standardized Metadata Capture and Analysis
presentations.abstract: Accurately estimating execution times is essential in HPC, where users must request resources and wall-clock limits before execution. However, execution information relevant to prediction is typically scattered across profilers, schedulers, and workflow engines using incompatible representations. We argue that execution data should instead be treated as a standardized, reusable artifact of workflow execution rather than a disposable input to a single predictor. We present an architecture that captures distributed resource usage, packages it as Workflow Run RO-Crates, and persists it in a queryable hybrid storage architecture (ProvStor), enabling any execution environment producing compatible metadata to contribute to and reuse a shared knowledge base. We showcase an enactment of this architecture using the COMPSs workflow management system, introducing a SLURM-aware profiler, and show its value through a hybrid prediction methodology that combines the analytical Universal Scalability Law with Machine Learning models.

presentations.title: InterQnet: Heterogeneous Quantum Network Demonstrations at ARQNET
presentations.abstract: no NRI

presentations.title: Introduction to MLIR
presentations.abstract:
MLIR is rapidly becoming the infrastructure of choice for building domain-specific languages (DSLs) and compilers for high performance computing — examples include OpenAI’s Triton, NVIDIA’s cuTile, and AMD’s AIR/AIE. Dialects are a core concept in MLIR, enabling data types and operations to be defined at different levels of abstraction, along with passes to systematically transform the programs through a hierarchy of dialects for optimized execution on target platforms. In-tree dialects like Linalg define operations that can represent common computation paradigms like tensor contractions and convolutions.
This tutorial will introduce MLIR and provide an understanding of the steps to build a DSL compiler to target CPUs and GPUs. Starting with an overview of core MLIR concepts, like dialects, operations, types and interfaces, the tutorial will give participants hands-on experience in building an optimizing compiler using MLIR. At the end of this tutorial participants should have a good understanding of the power of transformations in MLIR and how to use them.

presentations.title: Investigating ET-SoC-1 Vector and Parallel Performance with sGEMM
presentations.abstract:
The Ainekko (formerly Esperanto) ET-SoC-1 is a massively parallel RISC-V accelerator. Its compute array comprises 1024 dual-threaded in-order ET-Minion cores (2048
harts) operating at 600 MHz, each core providing an eight-lane 256-bit packed-single (PS) SIMD datapath shared by its two harts, with access to LPDDR4X memory at a nominal 133 GiB/s. This paper presents a performance investigation using single-precision general matrix multiplication (sGEMM) as the benchmark kernel. Two device kernels are implemented and
evaluated on the ET-SoC-1, these are a register-blocked packed-single (PS) SIMD baseline with two-step software pipelining, and a TensorFMA32 kernel that drives the same FMA datapath
through the per-core tensor micro-operation sequencer, with double-buffered A scratchpad loading. Because both kernels are bounded by the same arithmetic peak, the comparison isolates
the effect of operand delivery from that of arithmetic width. Performance is compared against four CPUs references and two GPUs.

presentations.title: Invited Talk
Invited Talk #1 - The Future of Q-HPC Software Tools and Frameworks
Invited Talk #2 - Hybrid Q-HPC Workflow/Workload in Scientific Computing
Invited Talk - Full stack sustainability: Looking at opportunities from Data Centres through to Applications, Adrian Jackson, EPCC
presentations.abstract: In this talk Adrian Jackson will outline some of the research activities underway at EPCC to improve the sustainability of computational research in the UK and global. As EPCC operates it's own data centre, has hardware and software researchers, and works closely with application developers and users, we are well position to impact efficiency and therefore sustainability across the whole computing stack. We will cover data centre optimisations, computing hardware innovations, storage and application efficiency improvements, and emerging workload performance in the AI inference space as well aim to explore where best to apply innovation to enable sustainable HPC.

presentations.title: Invited Talk 1
Invited Talk 2
Invited Talk with Eric Nielsen, Senior Research Scientist with the Computational AeroSciences Branch at NASA Langley Research Center
Invited Talk with Pradeep Dubey, Intel Senior Fellow
Invited talk: "Distributed HPC in Julia without MPI"
presentations.abstract:
MPI has long been the default substrate for distributed scientific computing, but it is not the only path to scalable performance—and in Julia, it is often not the most productive one. This talk surveys the landscape of MPI-free distributed computing in Julia, centered on the standard-library Distributed package and its surprisingly performant primitives for remote execution, data movement, and cluster management. I will review which widely-used Julia packages already run on top of Distributed, and how their capabilities compare to their MPI-based counterparts.
The core of the talk focuses on Dagger.jl, a task-based parallel runtime that provides unified support for both Distributed and MPI: every algorithm expressed in Dagger runs unchanged across either backend, as well as across multi-CPU and multi-GPU configurations. I will highlight Dagger's Datadeps API, which lets users express data dependencies declaratively and have the scheduler automatically handle communication, synchronization, and placement—whether the underlying transport is Distributed or MPI. Through concrete examples, I will show how this abstraction delivers portability without sacrificing performance, and close with an overview of the current state of distributed computing across the broader Julia package ecosystem.

presentations.title: Invited talk: "From MPI+X to Domain-Specific Abstractions: Building Sustainable Weather and Climate Software"
presentations.abstract:
Weather and climate models are large and complex collections of mathematical modelling software. They can take more than a decade to develop and can be in use for a quarter of century or more. They also typically undergo constant revisions and improvements from teams of developers. The proliferation of programming models in the MPI+X paradigm is therefore particularly problematic as cost of developing and maintaining multiple X implementations for different architectures in such a code base becomes prohibitive. The rapid evolution of the programming models has exacerbated the problem. Fortran has been the de facto standard programming language for weather and climate applications and can considered a low-level domain specific language for numerical computation. The ability to write code that in some sense looks likes the maths is part of its appeal and enables developers to be productive. The invasive level of parallel code additions required for performance degrades the sustainability of the code base.
One approach to solving these problems has been to raise the level of abstraction from a general-purpose language to a domain specific language (DSL). Here domain specific information is encoded in and exploited by the programming model for optimisation purposes. Key to this approach is a strong separation of concerns between the science/maths code and the parallel and optimisation code. This approach enables developers to write code which looks like maths whilst allowing the portability and performance by having different routes to optimised codes for different architectures. This comes with the cost of designing and maintaining the DSL.
The Met Office is part of the Momentum partnership and is developing the Momentum modelling software system. The atmosphere model, LFRic, is developed and co-designed in a its own DSL, embedded in Fortran. Part of the DSL is the python domain specific compiler, PSyclone. The advantages and limitations of the this approach are discussed, including the consequences of design choices such as embedding the DSL in Fortran. Some performance results from LFRic are presented as evidence to support the arguments. Finally, how emerging agentic programming techniques may complement DSL-based approaches and what this implies for future weather and climate software development is considered.

presentations.title: Invited Talk: Billions of Edges per Hour: Generating and Partitioning Dynamic Contact Networks on Heterogeneous Exascale Systems
presentations.abstract: Agent-based simulations of population health model each individual's movement and contacts over time. At national scale this produces a dynamic, highly irregular graph: hourly contact networks whose size swings from millions of edges at night to tens of billions during the day, with heavy skew toward dense urban locations. Storing these networks explicitly is impractical and partitioning them by agent or location count leaves severe load imbalance. This talk presents ENABLE, a hybrid CPU-GPU framework developed to address these problems. GPUs generate each hour's contact network directly from activity schedules, and a GPU implementation of Uniform Cost Partitioning balances contact edges across ranks, while CPUs run the disease dynamics in an asynchronous pipeline. For a 350-million-agent population, generating edges on the GPU instead of storing them reduces memory per simulated hour from about 250 GB to 1.3 GB. On the Frontier supercomputer, ENABLE reaches 82% strong-scaling efficiency at 1,120 ranks and holds weak-scaling efficiency above 75% on up to 1,200 GPUs. Roofline analysis shows both partitioning kernels are memory-bandwidth bound, each using about 78% of peak HBM bandwidth on the MI250X. The talk closes with open problems in streaming mobility data, keeping results deterministic across rank counts and scaling dynamic-graph simulations toward virtual population health twins.

presentations.title: Invited Talk: From Code Generation to Performance Reasoning: Agentic AI for the Autonomous HPC Stack
Invited talk: From Streaming Data to Timely Decisions: Infrastructure for Urgent Science
presentations.abstract: Urgent science describes time-critical, data-driven scientific workflows that can leverage distributed data sources in a timely way to facilitate important decision-making. Despite the exponential growth of available digital data sources and the ubiquity of non-trivial computational power to process this data, realizing urgent science workflows remains challenging. This talk will explore application use cases, the requirements and challenges of urgent computing, and how the National Data Platform (NDP) can support AI-enabled urgent science workflows.

presentations.title: Invited Talk: Genesis Mission and the Next Generation of Verified Scientific Workflows
Invited talk: High RISC, High Reward: The Journey from Ratified Specs to RVA23 Superclusters
Invited Talk: How to Beat CPU/GPUs on both Performance and Programmability: The UpDown Graph Supercomputer
presentations.abstract: Making graph algorithms fast and scalable on traditional architectures and GPUs often involves breaking them into large, coarse-grained computational blocks that access similar regions of memory. We show that graph algorithms, which have tremendous vertex- and edge-level parallelism, can be scaled as fine-grained programs on suitable architectures. Specifically, we investigate graph algorithms on the UpDown architecture and show how this many-threaded, cache-less architecture enables simple, fine-grained parallel graph algorithms to be both fast and scalable. Single-node UpDown performance is 28x (geomean) over an H200 GPU, and that same program scales to 1000’s of nodes. We evaluate the system three ways: simulation, analytical projection models, and selected validation studies at scale (simulation of 16,384 UpDown nodes, using 256 supercomputer nodes). These results show the UpDown system can achieve 680K giga-traversed edges per second (GTEPS) for PageRank and 989K GTEPS BFS, exceeding prior results significantly. The realism of UpDown models has been validated by commercial activity at Chicago UpDown Computing (www.chupdown.com).Beyond performance, the insights for programming are significant. Our measurements suggest that not only is programming difficult – for distributed memory and GPU-SIMT – it is unproductive. That is, the resulting programs are not performant. for example, we have measured up to 5x higher total memory traffic for GPU implementations compared with UpDown. And the trend is for increasing UpDown advantage as algorithms grow in complexity suggest that kernel and linear algebra library based approaches face significant challenges.

presentations.title: Invited Talk: Torsten Hoefler: AI Infrastructure at Hyperscale - The Role of (Ultra) Ethernet
presentations.abstract: The rapid rise of generative AI is driving an unprecedented expansion of hyperscale infrastructure. Modern AI services generate trillions of tokens per day, requiring ever larger clusters and making efficiency a first-order challenge. While specialized accelerators such as Maia 200 are essential for delivering performant and cost-effective inference, their capabilities can only be fully realized through a scalable and efficient network fabric. This talk explores the co-design of next-generation AI infrastructure, from accelerator architecture and large-scale inference systems to the communication challenges posed by massive distributed workloads. I will argue that networking has become the defining system bottleneck and discuss the role of Ethernet in addressing it. Finally, I will present the vision behind Ultra Ethernet and its evolution into a high-performance, open networking platform capable of supporting the communication demands of future AI and HPC systems at hyperscale.

presentations.title: Invited Talk: Victor Fung (Georgia Tech & Lila Sciences)
presentations.abstract: Victor Fung will discuss autonomous science and the emerging integration of AI reasoning, scientific tools, and automated experimentation to accelerate scientific discovery.

presentations.title: IO500: The High-Performance Storage Community
presentations.abstract: The IO500 is the de facto benchmark standard for HPC storage. Official IO500 lists have been released at ISC and SC events since SC17 and now have over 300 entries. The purpose is to foster the high-performance storage community and ensure forward progress towards the common goals of creating, sharing, and benefiting from a large corpus of shared storage data. IO500 also serves as the largest repository of detailed HPC storage information for researchers and system designers to analyze and evaluate over time. A key BoF highlight is the presentation of the latest IO500 Production and Research lists.

presentations.title: IRISX: Performance Portable Scientific Computing via Code Generation and Runtime Co-Design
presentations.abstract:
Contemporary HPC, cloud, and embedded systems combine heterogeneous processors, and using them effectively requires careful trade-offs among kernel implementation, multi-device orchestration, and data transfers. Domain scientists need a framework that dynamically discovers performance-portable solutions from the characteristics of the application and the
underlying multi-accelerator platform. We propose IRISX, which integrates the SPIRAL code generation system with the IRIS runtime to deploy architecture-optimized kernels together with a portable abstraction for multi-device heterogeneity. IRISX transforms computation at the kernel, task, and graph levels—through kernel, task, and DAG fusion—to fit each target ar-
chitecture, and a hybrid analytical and ML model selects near-optimal configurations in 96% of unseen cases. On a partial differential equation library evaluated across Frontier, Aurora,
and multiple ExCL systems, IRISX delivers up to 25.9× speedup over unoptimized execution, up to 10× over the Proto library, and up to 74× over a StarPU implementation.

presentations.title: JACC.Async: Performance-Portable Asynchronous Multi-GPU Programming with Just-in-Time Compilation
presentations.abstract:
We present JACC.Async, a new feature of Julia for ACCelerators (JACC), the performance-portable metaprogramming framework built on the just-in-time (JIT) and LLVM compiled
Julia language. JACC.Async enables scientific applications to exploit asynchronous executions across multiple GPUs through a high-level, portable, and easy-to-use interface. Despite the fact that asynchronous multi-GPU execution is essential for achieving high performance on modern systems, existing solutions often rely on low-level, vendor-specific programming models and complex synchronization mechanisms. JACC.Async addresses this reliance by providing the first JIT-based solution for asynchronous multi-GPU computing, offering a unified abstraction that overlaps computation, communication, and data movement across diverse accelerator architectures. JACC.Async supports the two major GPU vendors (NVIDIA and AMD). Scientific workloads based on the conjugate gradient algorithm were used to evaluate JACC.Async on modern multi-GPU platforms featuring NVIDIA A100 GPUs and AMD MI250X GPUs. The results demonstrate that JACC.Async achieves scalable performance with minimal modifications to existing applications.

presentations.title: JASMIN in July (Per Day): Brownian Bouquet
presentations.abstract:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Brownian Bouquet, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one day in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Stochastic Sea (which instead plots one spindle for one hour), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case a bouquet of flowers. The flower-like nature is encouraged by coercing the spindle centers into a sunflower-inspired pattern.

Brownian Bouquet invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

presentations.title: JASMIN in July (Per Hour): Stochastic Sea
presentations.abstract:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Stochastic Sea, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one hour in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Brownian Bouquet (which instead plots one spindle for one day), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case suggestive of a filamentary superstructure such as galactic super-clusters or a network of synapses. The spindle centers are randomly distributed across the composition, reinforcing this impression of a complex, interconnected structure.

Stochastic Sea invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

presentations.title: JForce: Fortran on AI Hardware via OpenMP Offloading and XLA JIT Compilation
presentations.abstract:
Modern accelerator increasingly rely on tensor-oriented execution units and compiler stacks originally developed for AI workloads, yet Fortran HPC applications cannot readily exploit them through existing toolchains.
The OpenMP \verb|workdistribute| construct defines a restricted class of Fortran array computations whose semantics closely resemble tensor computation graphs.
However, executing such regions on domain-specific accelerators still requires bridging the semantic gap between Fortran/OpenMP and tensor compiler infrastructures.
We present JForce, a Just-In-Time compilation and execution framework that intercepts the high-level MLIR representation of an OpenMP region, translates it into StableHLO, and compiles it using XLA.
JForce delegates tensor computation to XLA while retaining the standard OpenMP runtime for host--device data mapping and integration with the remaining OpenMP code.
We evaluate JForce on CPUs, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and Google TPUs, demonstrating portable execution across heterogeneous backends and competitive performance for sufficiently large or repeatedly executed workloads.

presentations.title: Julia for High Performance Computing
presentations.abstract:
This full-day, six-hour hands-on tutorial introduces participants to using the Julia programming language effectively in high performance computing (HPC) environments, from first principles to end-to-end deployment on a leadership-class system. The first portion introduces fundamental aspects of the language and emphasizes Julia’s unique features for scientific computing: mathematical syntax, multiple dispatch, type inference, LLVM-IR code inspection, modern package management, and performance pitfalls. Participants will work through notebook-based exercises that highlight key language features and progressively introduce parallel programming models for CPU and GPU. Attendees will learn node-level performance-portable approaches with KernelAbstractions.jl and JACC.jl and an introduction to Dagger.jl and kernel auto-tuning using the KernelTuner.jl framework.
The last portion focuses on building, running, and analyzing a realistic HPC application — an open-source Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion PDE solver (GrayScott.jl) — then scaling the application across nodes with MPI.jl. We also cover parallel I/O (ADIOS2.jl), scaling measurements, and GPU profiling using vendor tools. For this portion, we invite participants to apply for access to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF) Odo training system (32 nodes of the Frontier supercomputer) until November 5. Please find instructions to register for an Odo account (subject to approval) and materials in our tutorial repository: https://github.com/JuliaParallel/julia-hpc-tutorial-sc26.

presentations.title: Julia for HPC
presentations.abstract: The “Julia for HPC” BoF provides a place for the HPC community with interests in the Julia programming language as an LLVM front-end to close the gaps between high-productivity languages and the performance of compiled languages. We invite participants from industry, government, and academia to discuss their experiences, identify and learn about opportunities and gaps. Topics include Julia adoption for quantum computing, auto-tuning, mixed precision, and agentic AI. The fifth consecutive BoF continues the “Julia for HPC” engagement with the SC community, and complements the tutorial on Julia for HPC at SC26. Presentations will be posted here: https://github.com/JuliaParallel/julia-hpc-bof-sc26.

presentations.title: JUNIQ Benchmark Suite: A Decade of Application Benchmarks on Quantum Computers
presentations.abstract:
As quantum computing hardware rapidly evolves, traditional metrics like gate fidelity and Quantum Volume are insufficient for predicting real-world utility. Researchers and industry users need objective, application-centric benchmarks to gauge when quantum processors will be ready for practical tasks. However, the lack of standardized infrastructure often leads to non-reproducible performance claims and makes it difficult to track progress across different hardware generations and technologies.

We present the JUNIQ Benchmark Suite (JBS), a large collection of benchmark problems and a vendor-agnostic, open-source initiative designed to track quantum technology readiness over decades. Unlike suites focused on synthetic benchmarks, JBS (https://go.fzj.de/juniq-benchmark-suite-page) emphasizes application-domains including computational biology, logistics, and hardware-diagnostics.

JBS hosts an extensive repository of empirical performance data collected over more than a decade (2016–2026) across over 30 analog and digital quantum processing units, tracking quantum technology readiness over successive hardware generations.

presentations.title: JUPITER: From Consistent Imaging to Continuous Benchmarking
presentations.abstract: This invited talk presents the full JUPITER installation journey — from an empty data center to consistently maintaining 6000 nodes. We describe how we envisioned the JUPITER Management Stack during procurement and system design, the benchmarks selected to assess system performance, and the lessons learned during installation. We cover how reference databases are rendered into configuration and compute node images, and how continuous benchmarking during operations detects system degradation over time. We close with lessons from what went wrong and how we plan to evolve this process for future systems in the era of AI-enhanced operation at exascale.

presentations.title: K2S-Gate: A Secure Kubernetes-to-Slurm Gateway with Unified Service Catalogs for Web-Based AI and HPC Applications
presentations.abstract: The rapid growth of AI and high performance computing (HPC) applications demands seamless integration of cloud-native and HPC environments, yet heterogeneous software stacks keep these systems isolated, limiting unified deployment of and access to web-based applications. This work presents K2S-Gate, a secure Kubernetes-to-Slurm gateway that bridges cloud-native and HPC infrastructures through a unified web platform. K2S-Gate introduces a job-to-service transformation paradigm that converts Slurm batch jobs into dynamically accessible web services, enabling one-click execution on HPC compute nodes without SSH tunneling or port forwarding. It also provides a template-based Unified Service Catalog for deployment across heterogeneous environments. For secure, scalable access, K2S-Gate integrates a Secure Access Layer combining single sign-on (SSO), an OAuth2-based identity provider (IdP), and an Istio ingress gateway. Validated on the KISTI-5 supercomputer and integrated into the MyKSC portal, K2S-Gate demonstrates its practicality in real-world HPC environments.

presentations.title: Kamo: Bringing Many-Core Scalability to MySQL
presentations.abstract:
MySQL’s SQL ecosystem is widely used, but its default InnoDB storage engine does not scale well under high concurrency. Kamo is a prototype DBMS built on MySQL that substantially extends the initial LineairDB storage-engine integration. Our contributions include named tables, relational insert/update/delete semantics, secondary and composite indexes, ordered scans, and broader MySQL handler coverage sufficient to execute all five BenchBase TPC-C transaction classes. The current prototype has been implemented and evaluated on single-node and semi-synchronously replicated configurations, reaching up to 18.7× the request throughput of MySQL/InnoDB under the evaluated settings.

In the poster session, we will present Kamo’s system architecture, the key relational and MySQL-integration extensions, and end-to-end TPC-C and YCSB-A results. We will also discuss the observed scaling behavior, current bottlenecks, and limitations of the prototype.

presentations.title: Keeping up the Pace: Growing AMD Flang's OpenMP Offloading Ecosystem
presentations.abstract: Contemporary supercomputers are massively parallel, heterogeneous systems with accelerators---mostly graphics processing units (GPUs)---that provide additional compute and memory performance. Fortran continues to have a large developer base with new code written every day. The OpenMP Application Programming Interface (API) thus constitutes one of the key programming languages to support developers in their need to write portable, high-performance code for such heterogeneous systems. In this paper, we will highlight the evolution of the AMD Fortran Compiler (AMD Flang) in the past twelve months. As AMD Flang is based on LLVM Flang, much of the evolution is also relevant for the LLVM project via pull requests that have been contributed or will be contributed in the future.

presentations.title: Key Features Coming to OpenMP API Version 6.1
presentations.abstract: The OpenMP Architecture Review Board releases new versions of OpenMP every 2-3 years. This year, we will release OpenMP API version 6.1 just before SC26. Feature champions from the OpenMP Language committee will highlight key features in the OpenMP API version 6.1 through short lightning talks with rounds of discussion to give participants ample opportunity to interact with OpenMP experts, ask questions, and provide feedback. We will also include talks from vendors supporting compilers to discuss timelines for support of OpenMP API features.

presentations.title: Large Scale Sorting on UPMEM Processing-in-Memory Architectures
presentations.abstract: Sorting is fundamental in many data-intensive applications, and its memory-bound nature limits parallel efficiency on parallel processors. Processing-in-Memory (PIM) architectures co-locate DIMM Processing Units (DPUs) with memory and are designed to mitigate the memory bottleneck, but their distributed memory model, lack of peer-to-peer communication between DPUs, and lightweight cores yield several challenges. We present PIM-Sort, a comparison-based sorting algorithm designed for large-scale execution on the UPMEM PIM platform, the first commercially produced PIM system. We design PIM-Sort to address the architectural challenges above, and evaluate it on a UPMEM system with 2546 operational DPUs across uniform and skewed inputs up to 155 GiB. PIM-Sort outperforms a parallel CPU baseline on a separate, higher-bandwidth platform by up to 1.24x on 79 GiB of uniformly distributed data (the largest input that fits in a single DPU wave), while the multi-core CPU remains faster on heavily duplicated inputs where cache reuse yields a performance advantage. We find that PIM-Sort is more energy efficient (up to 35%) than the parallel CPU algorithm even when the latter strongly benefits from cache reuse.

presentations.title: Large-Scale Distributed State-Vector Simulation of IQPE for Early-FTQC
presentations.abstract:
