Iterative quantum phase estimation (IQPE) is promising for Early-FTQC because it recycles one ancilla, but classically validating molecular workloads requires distributed state-vector simulation, where qubit reordering and GPU-to-GPU data movement limit scalability.

We present a communication-aware IQPE implementation in chemqulacs-gpu. Building on published Lazy Qubit Reordering for topology-aware mapping reuse, our IQPE-specific contributions are rank-global Z folding that avoids unnecessary reordering, rank-MSB probability evaluation without amplitude gathering, and their integration for systems-scale execution. All components are implemented and evaluated on ABCI-Q. A 32-qubit chlorine workload retains 90.2% parallel efficiency from 2 to 1,024 H100 GPUs, and the widest completed run uses a 41-qubit, 32-TiB complex-FP64 state vector across 1,024 GPUs.

At the poster, circuit and data-movement diagrams will explain the techniques, while scaling plots and a large-run table will support discussion of communication costs, memory limits, and practical IQPE simulation.

presentations.title: LASSI-EE: LLM-based Automated Refactoring of Parallel Scientific Codes for Energy Efficiency
presentations.abstract: Energy efficiency is a critical objective for high-performance computing, yet optimizing scientific applications for energy has traditionally required deep expertise and substantial manual effort. This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can generate energy-efficient parallel codes when guided by empirical execution feedback, and whether their optimizations adapt to the target application and architecture. We propose LASSI-EE, an automated refactoring framework integrating runtime power profiling, energy-aware prompting, self-correcting feedback loops, and an LLM-as-a-Judge for screening generated code. To quantify expected savings under LLM non-determinism, we introduce energy-reduction@k, a metric that accounts for all generation attempts, including failures. Across twenty-two scientific benchmarks and applications on NVIDIA A100 and AMD MI100 GPUs, compiled at full optimization, LASSI-EE achieves expected energy savings of 29% for a single attempt and 48% when selecting the best of three. Average reductions reach 34%-36% among passing energy-reducing refactorings, largely preserving or improving runtime without precision-reducing transformations.

presentations.title: LASSI-Verify: Adaptive Empirical Verification of LLM-Generated Parallel Scientific Code Transformations
presentations.abstract:
Large language models transform parallel scientific code faster than
humans can review. Existing pipelines accept transformations that
compile, run, and satisfy an LLM judge, none of which evidences behavior
preservation, while whole-program formal proof remains impractical for
kernels lacking formal specifications. We present LASSI-Verify, a
work-in-progress adaptive empirical verification framework treating the
source's observable behavior as its specification and grounding
acceptance in three tiers: invariant assertions, observational
equivalence, and metamorphic relations. A seeded witness chain, added
after observing LLMs delete timed work to fabricate speedups, supplies
iteration-integrity evidence toward operational equivalence, and every
failure doubles as a repair signal. Because a verifier must itself be
verified, we grade benchmark checks before trusting them as oracles. In
preliminary results, the framework rejected all 13 oracle-detected
defects across 350 self-corrected variants of 16 HeCBench CUDA kernels,
while an LLM judge, reasoning over code text and output rather than
executed state, accepted three.

presentations.title: Lead Invited Talk (Satoshi Matsuoka, Director of Riken Center for Computational Science)
Learning When to Unroll-and-Unmerge on GPUs: Experiences with Reinforcement Learning in LLVM
presentations.abstract:
Branching hurts performance on GPU architectures, so unmerging control flow inside a loop looks like a poor optimization. Prior work showed otherwise: unmerging recovers information that a control-flow merge destroys, and pairing it with unrolling helps further.
The static heuristic developed in prior work performs poorly on many applications.
On an NVIDIA A100 across HeCBench, it loses to doing nothing: -4.9% mean improvement where +10% was available, and 23.9% of loops made slower. Its rule cannot express a quarter of the best decisions.

We port the transform to a newer LLVM and build a reinforcement learning pipeline that decides per loop whether to unmerge and which unroll factor to use, using measured kernel time as feedback. Two agents fit their training loops but neither transfers, because profitability follows the application rather than the loop. Adapting on two loops of the target cuts regressions to 9.5% and reaches +4.0% at best.

presentations.title: Learning Within the Laws of the Hardware: Rethinking Multi-GPU Performance Modeling and Workload Characterization
presentations.abstract: Performance modeling enables runtime estimation, scalability analysis, and bottleneck identification without committing large-scale compute resources. However, existing methods rely on either analytical or empirical models: the former are interpretable and generalize by construction but are limited in accuracy by architectural assumptions, while the latter are accurate only where training data exists and offer no insight into performance-limiting factors. Addressing these concerns, we propose hardware-informed neural networks (HINN), applying the physics-informed neural network (PINN) methodology to multi-GPU performance modeling, where the governing "physics" consists of hardware-derived architectural laws. HINN retains established analytical models as differentiable priors and learns residual corrections subject to hardware-derived constraints enforced via automatic differentiation across the domain. Evaluated on five HPC applications on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, HINN achieves 7.6% and 9.9% median relative estimation error for kernel and communication predictions, while enabling extrapolation to unseen configurations and automated bottleneck classification.

presentations.title: Leveraging and Evaluating LLMs for Scientific Computing
presentations.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are progressing at an impressive pace. They can solve complex problems while presenting the opportunity to leverage their capabilities for scientific computing. Despite their progress, even the most sophisticated models can struggle with simple reasoning tasks and make mistakes, necessitating careful verification of their outputs. This tutorial focuses on these two important aspects: (1) leveraging LLMs to assist scientific computing code translation and automatic parallelization, and (2) presenting best practices for evaluating and comparing LLMs within the scientific computing context. Designed specifically for students, researchers, and engineers at beginner and intermediate levels, the tutorial features four hours of presentation and two hours of hands-on experience. Attendees learn the fundamentals of LLM design, development, and use cases for scientific computing. The tutorial deep-dives into three key topics for scientific computing: automatic parallelization, sequential code translation (Fortran to C++), and parallel code translation (OpenMP to Cuda) with the CodeScribe, LASSI, and PARACODEX tools. Attendees also learn various complementary methods to test and evaluate LLM responses rigorously. At the end of the tutorial, attendees are equipped with solid foundations, knowledge, and practical experience to leverage and evaluate LLMs for scientific computing and to transform theoretical insights into actionable solutions.

presentations.title: Leveraging high performance computing for simulation of snowpack liquid water content using SnowModel
Leveraging Sparsity for LLM Inference in a Commercial Processing-in-Memory Prototype
presentations.abstract: LM decoding is bounded by the memory wall: weights and KV cache move every token, and the low-arithmetic-intensity matrix–vector products of decode leave throughput set by bandwidth rather than compute. Bank-level PIM attacks this by keeping weights resident and computing in place, but its lockstep execution cannot skip zeros. We present the first end-to-end sparsity-aware inference framework for bank-level PIM. A column-union cost model shows that lockstep cost is set by the union of columns (or KV tokens) a bank-group must visit, not the nonzero count. Activation-aware weight pruning aligns surviving columns across rows and matrices, while a group-aligned adaptation of query-aware KV selection collapses the attention scan. Against a measured NVIDIA H200 at batch-1, this work cuts per-token latency by 4–7× and, beyond moderate context, undercuts the GPU’s most energy-efficient batched configuration (crossing near 10K, around 6× lower at 128K), while preserving accuracy and extending on-board context.

presentations.title: Ligand Dynamics Control Structure, Elasticity, and High-Pressure Behavior of Nanoparticle Superlattices
presentations.abstract: The spherical clusters in this image are a molecular dynamics simulation of lead sulfide nanocrystals, each seven nanometers wide, coated with radiating oleic acid ligands that allow such particles to self-assemble into an ordered crystal called a nanoparticle superlattice. The underlying research found that below a critical ligand coverage density, nanoparticles collapse and fuse together, while above it, the ligand layer cushions the structure enough to withstand applied pressures up to nearly 56 gigapascals while largely retaining its ordered arrangement. The image renders this simulated nanoscale structure alongside additional micrographs of nanoparticle superlattice material from the same body of research.

presentations.title: Lightning talks
presentations.abstract:
Talk 1: Phuong Cao - Diagnose cluster failures and recover from such failures/attacks for edge AI LLMs

Talk 2: Dante D. Sánchez-Gallegos - On the management of data on the computing continuum to support urgent applications

Talk 3: Albert Reuther - Interactive and Urgent HPC and Cybersecurity Challenges
Talk 4: Tanu Malik - Interactive Yet Reproducible: Portable, Auditable Notebook
Workflows on HPC

presentations.title: LightshowAI-Agent: An MCP-Based Agentic Framework for Real-Time and Reproducible X-Ray Absorption Spectral Analysis at Scientific User Facilities
presentations.abstract: Identifying an unknown phase from X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) data requires a multi-step pipeline spanning candidate retrieval, surrogate inference, spectral alignment, expert-informed ranking, and provenance tracking across independent databases, models, and services that scientists coordinate manually. We present LightshowAI-Agent, a framework that automates and orchestrates this pipeline. Scientific capabilities are exposed as typed tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), providing access to the Materials Project database, XAS prediction surrogates, and American Science Cloud (AmSC) model services. Versioned skill files carry domain-specific analysis procedures that experts can inspect and revise independently of prompts. Reproducibility is supported by logging agent and model activity through MLflow and analysis metadata through Tiled. We demonstrate a workflow identifying a TiO2 polymorph from Ti K-edge spectra streamed from the NSLS-II Quick X-ray Absorption and Scattering (QAS) beamline.

presentations.title: Limitations of Generative Inverse Design for Scientific Simulations
presentations.abstract: Generative inverse design for scientific simulations addresses a many-to-one problem: generating distinct inputs whose forward simulations approximate a target output. Our prior work generated image-based initial conditions directly, but simulations often construct initial conditions at runtime from configuration variables. We shift the task upstream by generating variables whose effects propagate through intermediate representations before producing the final output. We use a deterministic heat-diffusion proxy with Cosine Phase and Perlin Noise geometry functions that create diverse material-layout patterns. Conditional normalizing flows generate input variables conditioned only on observed final states, and the resulting simulated outputs are evaluated against the corresponding targets. Variable-inclusion ablations isolate geometry and thermal variables, while posterior-factorization ablations compare full-joint, chained-joint, and disjoint decompositions. Results show error arises primarily when modeling geometry variables, whereas posterior factorization provides little improvement over baselines. These findings suggest the final outputs may not retain enough information about upstream variables and intermediate representations.

presentations.title: Linalg vs MDH: Why Reduction Semantics Matter
presentations.abstract:
Data-parallel computations are performance-critical building blocks in domains like scientific computing and machine learning. In the MLIR ecosystem, the Linalg dialect—in particular linalg.generic—is a central abstraction for such computations, yet it does not treat reduction operators as first-class, compiler-visible constructs.

To address this gap, we propose the mdh dialect: it makes reduction (combine) operators explicit—including user-defined operators beyond standard pointwise cases—thereby enabling reduction-aware code generation and richer expressivity for reduction-based computations. Our experiments on GPU and CPU—across linear algebra, deep learning, data mining, and quantum chemistry workloads—isolate the effect of explicit reduction operators, estimating the relative performance opportunity if linalg.generic exposed such operators.

presentations.title: LinkPass: Transparent RDMA Link Failover and Recovery for Collective Communication
presentations.abstract: Optical links in high-bandwidth AI clusters are prone to failures from temperature, vibration, dust, and other factors, causing temporary or permanent disconnections or intermittent packet loss. In tightly synchronized distributed training, a single flapping link between a network interface card (NIC) and top-of-rack switch can stall every participating rank. We present LinkPass, a shim beneath the network-plugin interface shared by NVIDIA NCCL and AMD RCCL that transparently masks such failures. LinkPass uses an RDMA probe mesh to detect stalling links, fails traffic over across healthy NUMA-proximate NICs to avoid backup bottlenecks, and reverts traffic when the original NIC recovers. Operating entirely over standard InfiniBand Verbs, LinkPass is transparent to collective libraries and training code and agnostic to GPU and NIC vendors. Evaluations show that LinkPass prevents link flaps from crashing jobs, significantly increasing mean time between failures and reducing required checkpointing frequency.

presentations.title: Liquid Cooling Interfaces: Optimizing Temperature, Telemetry, Water, and Heat Reuse
presentations.abstract: As direct liquid cooling scales, the interface between IT systems and facility mechanical infrastructure becomes more critical. This BoF explores four challenges. First, high-temperature cooling (heat-reuse, IT thermal margins) and dew point (prevent condensation). Second, warm-water fluid quality (filtration and added chemicals to prevent corrosion, biological growth, and scaling). Third, temperature and fluid dynamics with rapid workload power swings (volumetric expansion, pump cavitation, facility response characteristics). Fourth, integrating telemetry into IT systems and building automation (predict thermal excursions, reduce trapped capacity). This session is intended for facility engineers, system integrators, operations, administrators, architects, and researchers in energy-efficiency and sustainability.

presentations.title: LLBPE: Linked-List Based GPU-Parallel BPE Tokenizer
presentations.abstract: Every LLM inference begins with tokenization, which converts raw input bytes into the discrete token sequence the model consumes. For text, this step is often implemented using Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), an algorithm originally introduced for data compression. BPE has traditionally run on the CPU with extensive optimization, but recent work has moved it to the GPU for higher throughput. We show that these GPU implementations are bottlenecked not by computation but by data movement. We develop LLBPE that represents the token sequence as an array-based linked list so that each merge reduces to a constant-time pointer update. Furthermore, LLBPE fuses rank lookup, minimum selection, and merging into a single kernel to eliminate redundant hash map queries. LLBPE achieves up to 5.2× higher throughput than the best existing GPU implementation and 24.6× over optimized CPU implementations, at the cost of minor discrepancies in tokenized output.

presentations.title: LLM–Driven Root Cause Analysis of BGP and BFD Flap Events
presentations.abstract:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) flaps are key indicators of network instability. Frequent up/down transitions can increase latency, cause packet loss, and lead to Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations by repeatedly disrupting traffic forwarding and routing convergence. Root causes of the flaps can range from physical link failures to protocol misconfigurations and policy violations, making diagnosis costly and time-consuming, as operators must correlate evidence across devices, interfaces, protocols, logs, and performance metrics. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising alternative, as they can integrate and reason across heterogeneous operational evidence to accelerate root cause identification and reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR). However, their effectiveness depends on explicit diagnostic reasoning, structured explanations, and validation of inferred causes against operational evidence. API-based LLMs also raise privacy concerns, while locally deployed open source alternatives require careful evaluation of their diagnostic accuracy and operational
performance. In this paper, we present an LLM-based prototype for automated root cause analysis of BGP and BFD flap events. The prototype uses locally deployed open-source LLMs to correlate protocol logs with topology, service state, and forwarding information, identifying likely root causes and affected network entities. We evaluate the approach through controlled failure
experiments in a Mininet-based testbed and through operational analysis of events from a production BGP/BFD testbed. The results show that prompt design substantially affects root-cause accuracy, with structured, domain-specific prompts enabling several medium-sized models to achieve perfect accuracy. Entity-extraction performance varies more widely across prompts and models, while model selection also affects inference latency. These findings suggest that locally deployed LLMs can support accurate, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving analysis of BGP and BFD flap events.

presentations.title: LLM-Driven Root Cause Analysis of BGP and BFD Flap Events
LLMs as Packagers of HPC Software
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing (HPC) software ecosystems are heterogeneous, with applications depending on hundreds of external packages across diverse build systems and configuration options. Package managers such as Spack automate dependency resolution, but rely on manually authored recipes encoding intricate build knowledge that becomes increasingly labor-intensive to maintain. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for software engineering tasks, but synthesizing HPC package recipes remains challenging: the output must capture dependency, configuration, and platform constraints that are often fragmented across repositories and prior packaging practice.

We present a systematic study of what context and feedback LLMs need to synthesize valid Spack recipes, isolating the effects of repository metadata extraction, reference retrieval, and iterative repair. Structured build information improves installation success from approximately 43% in minimal-context settings to 100% in the best configuration, showing that metadata distillation, reference packages, and diagnostic feedback are essential for HPC package synthesis.

presentations.title: LLVM-HPC2026: The Twelfth Workshop on the LLVM Compiler Infrastructure in HPC
presentations.abstract: LLVM, winner of the 2012 ACM Software System Award, has become an integral part of the software-development ecosystem for optimizing compilers, dynamic-language execution engines, source-code analysis and transformation tools, debuggers and linkers and a whole host of programming-language and toolchain-related components. Now heavily used in both academia and industry, where it allows for rapid development of production-quality tools, LLVM is increasingly used in work targeted at high performance computing. Research in, and implementation of, program analysis, compilation, execution and profiling have clearly benefited from the availability of a high-quality, freely-available infrastructure on which to build. This workshop will focus on recent developments, from both academia and industry, that build on LLVM to advance the state of the art in high performance computing.

presentations.title: Load Balancing and Communication Bottlenecks in SpMV on the Cerebras WSE-3
presentations.abstract:
SpMV is a fundamental kernel in scientific computing, but irregular memory access limits its scalability on conventional parallel systems. The Cerebras CS-3 distributes all data across on-chip SRAM on a two-dimensional PE mesh, so accessing non-local data becomes inter-PE communication rather than a memory-hierarchy traversal. Whether this low-latency advantage is sustained at scale remains unclear.

We present the first execution-time breakdown of SpMV on the CS-3. Our novel contribution is identifying, under load balancing, which component dominates among computation, inter-PE communication, reduction, and synchronization wait. Load balancing achieved a 3.40x speedup for Poisson3Da, while inter-PE communication reached 71.2% of execution time for F1. We evaluate five matrices from the SuiteSparse collection.

At the poster session, we will walk visitors through our execution-time breakdown charts, explain the bottleneck transition using a simple broadcast-round model, and discuss implications for communication-aware SpMV on wafer-scale processors.

presentations.title: Load-Balanced Communication Overlap for Lattice H-Matrix–Vector Multiplication on GPU Clusters
presentations.abstract:
Lattice hierarchical H-matrices provide a structured low-rank representation for parallel boundary element method solvers, but the concentration of dense and poorly compressible submatrices near the matrix diagonal causes load imbalance under conventional process-grid mappings.
We develop a lattice-H-matrix-specific design for load-balanced communication overlap on GPU clusters.
The design combines a one-dimensional column-cyclic task assignment with a coarse-grained diagonal/off-diagonal decomposition.
The assignment distributes the expensive diagonal-block workload across processes, while the decomposition allows the collective reduction of off-diagonal contributions to proceed concurrently with diagonal-block GPU kernels.
An MPI+OpenACC implementation was evaluated on NVIDIA GH200 nodes using the HBI earthquake simulation application.
The proposed design distributes the dominant diagonal-region workload more evenly and achieves up to a 3.08x speedup over the conventional two-dimensional process-grid implementation.

presentations.title: Lowering the Barrier to HPC/AI: Open OnDemand at Recod.ai
Lowering the Barrier: Leveraging JupyterHub for K–12 AI and Data Science Outreach
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and data literacy are becoming increasingly important for a competent STEM workforce, yet infrastructure barriers present a significant bottleneck for access, especially in the K-12 space. High-performance hardware such as GPUs requires significant funding to procure and host, which puts them out of reach for most school systems. Meanwhile, institutions of higher education possess the requisite hardware and often have underutilized compute capacity, but these resources are typically homed within a secure research ecosystem that creates friction for students unfamiliar with cluster computing concepts. To bridge this gap, we present our implementation of JupyterHub for a series of high school AI summer camps, highlighting the key design choices that contributed to the nearly 100% engagement of participating students.

Machine Learning for a Gamma-Ray Telescope Using Stream-HLS
presentations.abstract:
Machine learning is becoming an important contributor to data acquisition for science, performing many tasks more efficiently than previously utilized techniques. Scientific instrumentation frequently is required to separate the actual signals of interest from background signals, and machine learning has often been applied to this task. However, manually designing and tuning the HLS implementation of onboard neural network inference is labor-intensive, and the resulting designs often have significant room for improvement.

Automated dataflow HLS tools could be used to implement inference on an instrument's onboard FPGA. We focus on a recent tool - Stream-HLS. Here, we assess the suitability of the Stream-HLS framework to implement a background rejection task for a gamma-ray telescope. The Stream-HLS design proves to be able to fit the flight part (XC7K325T), whereas the hand-tuned baseline does not. Moreover, the Stream-HLS design achieves ~1.9X higher throughput, while leaving 43% of the available DSPs idle.

presentations.title: Machine Learning-Based Performance Prediction for RISC-V Vector (RVV) Processors
presentations.abstract: The RISC-V Vector extension (RVV) offers rich architectural flexibility for data-parallel HPC workloads, but its vast microarchitectural design space is expensive to explore by cycle-accurate simulation, so machine-learned surrogates have become the standard substitute. Two questions that decide whether such a surrogate is useful are rarely examined: where its features come from, and how its generalization is measured. We study both on a gem5 model of the Ara vector unit, sweeping vector and memory-system parameters across TSVC2 kernels and training regression models on static, dynamic, and interaction features. We find that hardware configuration alone predicts CPI poorly, at 52.6% error under leave-one-kernel-out validation, while program features recovered from the compiled binary reduce this to 25.4%. More consequentially, the validation protocol dominates the reported accuracy: on identical data, features, and models, a random split reports 0.28% error against 23.2% when whole kernels are held out.

presentations.title: Magellan: A Carbon-Aware Task Scheduler for Geo-Distributed Systems
presentations.abstract:
Magellan is a decentralized carbon-aware task scheduler that reduces the carbon footprint of long-running, stateful workloads through checkpoint-restart migration across geo-distributed infrastructure. Prior carbon-aware systems have largely relied on simulation and targeted stateless or batch jobs while overlooking the real overheads of wide-area migration.

Magellan addresses these gaps through three primary contributions: a decision engine that jointly balances computational progress, carbon emissions, migration overhead, and monetary cost under an explicit budget cap; a decentralized bidding and destination-arbitration protocol with a checkpoint-restart runtime using CRIU for unmodified processes and native checkpoints for ML and HPC workloads; and validation on CloudLab and Google Cloud under real WAN conditions and measured destination capacity constraints. Across 72 annual scenarios and three workload classes, Magellan reduces lifecycle carbon by up to 92.8% (13×) with 11.6% lower makespan at approximately neutral cost. The poster presents the architecture, migration workflow, decision model, testbeds, and key carbon-cost-performance tradeoffs.

presentations.title: MailRail: Mitigating Incast Congestion with User-space, Node-based Flow Control
presentations.abstract: Irregular workloads, such as those stemming from Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, frequently induce severe incast congestion in large-scale parallel environments. Existing fabric-level congestion control mechanisms rely on reactive, link-level rate limiting that degrades overall throughput. While receiver-driven, credit-based flow control offers a proactive alternative, scaling process counts reduces memory slots per rank below usable thresholds, rendering traditional rank-based accounting untenable. To address this challenge, we introduce MailRail, an out-of-order, asynchronous messaging framework, along with a novel user-space, node-based credit flow control system. By shifting credit accounting from individual processes to shared per-node pools, our proactive, fabric-agnostic approach maintains sufficient credit availability even as process density grows, enabling processes to dynamically utilize freed credits without waiting for receiver-side redistribution. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that node-based flow control achieves an 1132× speedup over unconstrained execution at an adversarial incast ratio of 4096:1 while adding minimal overhead on uniform workloads.

presentations.title: Malleable OpenFOAM: Communication-Efficient Dynamic Reconfiguration for CFD
presentations.abstract:
We introduce the first malleable implementation of OpenFOAM, the most widely used open-source CFD solver, allowing it to dynamically change its node allocation mid-run instead of staying fixed for the job's duration. The system uses communication efficiency (CE), measured live by TALP/DLB, to trigger resizing via the DMR framework, which handles checkpoint-restart at a new node count. The key technical contribution is identifying which runtime objects must be redistributed at reconfiguration using OpenFOAM's AUTO_WRITE flag to isolate true solver state, while discarding stale cached objects that otherwise cause deadlocks at scale.

Tested on a 92M-cell automotive CFD benchmark on the MareNostrum 5 supercomputer, the controller successfully converges from both under- and over-provisioned starting points to the target CE band. This malleable implementation of OpenFOAM automatically selects resources so users only pay for the efficient run and do not waste resources or wait longer for results.

presentations.title: Mallet: An Open-Source Formal Verification Flow for Agile Domain-Specific Accelerator Development
presentations.abstract: Custom domain-specific accelerators are gaining attention for the significant performance gains they deliver on specialized workloads: scientific instruments utilize custom accelerators to sustain extreme data rates, and molecular dynamics accelerators can achieve orders-of-magnitude speedups over general-purpose supercomputing systems. However, their increasing complexity and specialization make verification challenging, allowing design flaws to escape detection and leading to incorrect results. Formal verification can fill this gap, but accelerator designs shift quickly, formal properties are hard to write, and LLM-generated designs often mirror bugs in the very properties meant to catch them. We present Mallet, an open-source formal verification flow for the Chisel stack. Mallet renders properties from human-specified AXI memory-map annotations, so design-spec drift is caught at compile time, and issues them to multiple model-checking engines, producing an adjudication matrix that ranks proof strength and flags vacuous passes. We demonstrate Mallet across five AXI4-Lite DUTs and a fault-injection suite.

presentations.title: Managing HPC Software Complexity with Spack
presentations.abstract: Modern scientific software stacks rely on thousands of packages, from low-level libraries in C, C++, and Fortran to higher-level tools in Python and R. Scientists must deploy these stacks across diverse environments, from personal laptops to supercomputers, while tailoring workflows to specific tasks. Development workflows often require frequent rebuilds, debugging, and small-scale testing for rapid iteration. In contrast, preparing applications for large-scale HPC production involves performance-critical libraries (e.g., MPI, BLAS, LAPACK) and machine-specific optimizations to maximize efficiency. Managing these varied requirements is challenging. Configuring software, resolving dependencies, and ensuring compatibility can hinder both development and deployment. Spack is an open-source package manager that simplifies building, installing, and customizing HPC software stacks. It offers a flexible dependency model, Python-based syntax for package recipes, and a repository of over 9,000 packages maintained by more than 1,600 contributors. Spack is widely adopted by researchers, developers, cloud platforms, and HPC centers worldwide. This tutorial introduces Spack’s core capabilities, including installing and authoring packages, configuring environments, and deploying optimized software on HPC systems. Attendees will gain foundational skills for automating routine tasks and acquire advanced knowledge to address complex use cases with Spack.

presentations.title: Mark Your Calendars: CDER Community Announcements
presentations.abstract: This time slot is for anyone in the CDER community to make a short announcement about projects of interest to the PDC/HPC educational community.

presentations.title: Mastering OpenMP Tasking: From Start to Free-Agent Tasks
presentations.abstract: OpenMP® is the leading, portable, and widely supported directive-based programming model. Already in 2008, the OpenMP API introduced tasking to support the creation of composable parallel software blocks and the parallelization of irregular algorithms. Developers usually find the OpenMP language easy to learn. However, mastering the tasking concept requires a change in the way developers reason about the structure of their code and how they expose its parallelism. Our "Mastering Tasking" tutorial has been designed for the SC audience to learn about the tasking concept in detail and to understand code patterns as solutions to many common problems. Throughout all topics, we showcase the additions brought with OpenMP versions 5.0 through 6.1 and explain how to adopt codes. For this tutorial, we assume attendees understand basic parallelization concepts and know the fundamentals of the OpenMP API. First, we introduce the OpenMP tasking language features in detail and then focus on performance aspects, such as introducing cut-off mechanisms, exploiting task dependencies, and preserving locality. The new free-agent tasks introduced with OpenMP version 6.0 are covered in detail. Extensive case studies accompany all topics. As a full-day tutorial, we will include hands-on sessions.

presentations.title: MATCH: Multimodal Alignment Through Contrastive Learning of Heterogeneous Sensor Streams at Static Nodes
presentations.abstract:
Multimodal environmental sensing networks routinely capture temporally co-occurring conditions across incompatible representations: an RGB frame, a thermal frame, an audio clip, and environmental readings share no common feature space. We present MATCH, a contrastive learning framework that combines frozen, domain-matched pretrained backbones with lightweight trainable projection heads to align real-world node data across all four modalities in a shared 512-dimensional embedding space without task-specific labels. A multi-view InfoNCE loss aligns all six modality pairs. Evaluated on a 195-observation held-out test set from a single deployed node, retrieval improves over random across all six pairs, with RGB↔Thermal strongest — notably, 73.3% of its incorrect top-5 retrievals fall within ±2 hours of the correct time of day, versus a 20.4% chance baseline, indicating the learned space captures coarse diurnal structure.

At the poster we'll present our architecture, cross-modal retrieval examples, quantitative alignment results, and discuss next steps toward node-specific adaptation.

presentations.title: Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
presentations.abstract:
We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes.
The B300 is not a uniform successor to the B200: it trails by up to 5.6$\times$ on convolutional inference, 8$\times$ on 3D vision transformer training, 24--27\% on 70B LLM throughput, and 16$\times$ on double-precision Quantum ESPRESSO.
We resolve the convolutional deficit using per-GPU board power rather than throughput alone: on the affected workloads the B300 draws only 36--53\% of its 1100\,W envelope, whereas on ViT-Large, which it wins, both parts saturate at 95--97\% of TDP.
Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost.
Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1$\times$ in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build.
We give per-workload procurement guidance.

presentations.title: Measured WAN Traffic Reduction from Federated Edge AI in a Distributed Cosmic-Ray Sensor Network
presentations.abstract:
Scientific instruments are increasingly built from large numbers of small, heterogeneous edge devices that operators cannot inspect or trust. Citizen-science cosmic-ray networks, in which commodity smartphones act as particle detectors, are an extreme example. Centralizing raw observations from such networks is the default architecture, but its wide-area traffic grows with every observation, and it requires participants to surrender raw data. We present an end-to-end federated alternative and attempt to measure its network behavior on smart-phone
data. Our system trains a compact artifact-rejection classifier for smartphone cosmic-ray detections entirely in the browser. Hits never leave the phone; clients exchange small weight payloads with a FedAvg coordinator on the National Research Platform. At matched accuracy, federation cuts WAN traffic 3.2–11.4 x, governed by per-client data volume, not client count, locating the crossover. We also address aggregator hardening and validation against a low-cost calibrated muon telescope.

presentations.title: Measurement Error for CPU Performance Counters
presentations.abstract: Understanding supercomputers’ performance and behavior is critical for their optimization and acquisition. Performance counters, which count the number of various types of CPU events, are the primary means of profiling CPUs. However, they may be inaccurate due to measurement errors. We can identify measurement error if we can calculate the true event count, but the true count is obscured by hardware and software unknowns. We handle hardware unknowns by measuring events that do not depend on the hardware implementation, and we handle software unknowns by carefully configuring standardized benchmarks. While we find measuring errors up to 0.45% of the true count, the measuring errors we find are typically much less than 0.01%.

presentations.title: Measurement-Driven Contention-Aware, Herd-Safe Stripe Placement for Lustre
presentations.abstract:
Parallel file systems such as Lustre are shared by many concurrent jobs, so the write bandwidth observed by a single job fluctuates over time as other jobs place load on the same object storage targets (OSTs). Users can change how files are placed across OSTs, yet it remains unclear when doing so is beneficial. Based on measurements from three production Lustre systems, this paper finds that the contrast between busy and idle OSTs is a property of the moment rather than of the system, so the decision to tune has to be measured per job: always tuning costs 13% in the worst case, never tuning 43%.

Building on this observation, the paper presents CASTOR, a client-side tuner that operates without special privileges. It measures per-OST latency using a small write-probe, determines whether tuning is worthwhile, selects a layout with a simple model, and randomly distributes jobs across cool OSTs to prevent them from converging on the same targets. Across three file systems and six workloads, CASTOR demonstrates that an unprivileged write probe can detect contention and that randomly selecting among cool OSTs prevents concurrent tuners from colliding. Where a contrast exists, placement raises bandwidth by up to 1.85x and cuts its variance by up to 4.7x. The central lesson is that whether to tune is itself a measurement problem, and one that has to be solved before any layout is chosen.

presentations.title: Measuring Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) Dependability via Wide Area Network Fault Injection
presentations.abstract: Hybrid high-performance computing and quantum computing (HPC-QC) systems rely on quantum networks for secure communication, yet their dependability under real-world conditions has not been systematically studied. This work presents a fault injection study of BB84 QKD using QFabric, a quantum-network emulation platform built on the FABRIC testbed. Unlike simulators, QFabric routes classical sifting traffic over a real WAN link, enabling cross-layer fault injection. We find that polarization fidelity, rather than packet loss, determines QBER, with no significant interaction between the two; detector efficiency similarly affects key rate independently of packet loss. However, individual runs at marginal fidelity still exceed the security failure threshold from ordinary variance alone, despite a mean QBER that appears safely below it, while no such failures occur at higher fidelity. This shows that aggregate QBER statistics can mask real per-session security risk, and that cross-layer fault interaction in BB84 depends on the specific physical mechanism involved.

presentations.title: Measuring the Impact of the Better Scientific Software Fellowship Program
presentations.abstract:
The Better Scientific Software Fellowship (BSSwF) Program was launched in 2018 in the U.S. to recognize, develop, and support leaders advancing practices, processes, and tools for better scientific software. Over eight years, the program has supported 43 Fellows and 43 Honorable Mentions across institutions and career stages to advance developer productivity and software sustainability and strengthen the scientific software community. A 2025 impact assessment
examined program reach, contributions to developer productivity and software sustainability, and effects on careers, mentorship, and community engagement. Based on a landscape analysis, review of Fellow projects, and interviews with Fellows, findings indicate that the program expanded professional networks and visibility and created opportunities for collaboration, mentoring, and career advancement. Program elements include community-facing projects, professional engagement, mentoring, and dissemination of Fellows’ work. BSSwF provides a model and insights for training, professional engagement, networking, and workforce-development programs supporting individual careers and the broader scientific
software ecosystem.

presentations.title: Mechanism-Aware Analysis of Cross-Platform GPU Fault-Injection Outcomes
presentations.abstract:
HPC test practitioners frequently compare fault injection results across GPU platforms, software stack versions, and computing facilities. Standard outcome categories such as masked faults, silent data corruptions (SDCs), and detected unrecoverable errors (DUEs) provide useful campaign summaries, but matching labels or distributions do not necessarily indicate comparable behavior. We present a mechanism aware method for interpreting cross platform GPU fault injection results and apply it to six reproducible cases on production NVIDIA, Intel, and AMD GPU systems. The cases show that bit position can determine whether a test completes with SDC or causes device failure, that aligned injections can become different effective faults after backend lowering, and that faults reaching control or address logic may remain masked. We recommend
retaining lightweight runtime evidence for all tests and performing targeted propagation analysis on key cases before declaring cross-platform results equivalent.

presentations.title: Medical Digital Twins: Can HPC Unite the Future for Health Globally?
presentations.abstract: Medical digital twins are an exciting area of investment and rapid innovation and hold tremendous potential to realize the promise of precision medicine and improved health. The successful adoption of medical digital twin approaches requires a community effort, spanning a full range of stakeholders with the individual or patient at the center. With an esteemed group of experts in medical digital twins, the panel will help attendees understand the world of medical digital twins, what it means and what it holds in store. The panel will also discuss several areas where HPC plays or could play a role in helping to unify and connect medical digital twin stakeholders in such areas as varying disciplines, anatomical systems, interoperability, data access and privacy, proprietary and open, AI and mechanistic models, clinics and research, education, and many more areas essential to the development and adoption of medical digital twins.

presentations.title: Megabytes in Murmuration: From 8-MB X-Ray Projections to Interpretable TB-Scale Structure Through Automated HPC
presentations.abstract: Synchrotron tomography beamlines routinely produce large sequences of two-dimensional X-ray projection images as their primary experimental output. Individually, these images often provide limited scientific value: the features of interest in biological samples typically emerge only after transformation into three-dimensional reconstructed volumes. This transformation is computationally demanding, requiring sustained high-throughput data transfers, and multiple processing steps — even more so for samples larger than the field of view. We describe the automated data acquisition and processing system implemented at the EMBL P14 beamline at PETRA III, Hamburg, Germany, and the underlying computing architecture that enables the beamline users to inspect interpretable three-dimensional representations of their samples shortly after X-ray exposure.

presentations.title: Meganeura: Vulkan and Metal as a Performance-Portability Layer for GPU Training and Inference
presentations.abstract: Meganeura explores Vulkan and Metal as a common foundation for GPU inference and training. Implemented in Rust, it combines computational graph compilation with bounded, automatic kernel tuning, aiming to keep the engine small and general while adapting to different hardware. We examine this approach across NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple GPUs, using PyTorch as a reference. Our evaluation considers not only steady-state performance, but also preparation time, numerical validation, memory use, and practical deployment barriers. We discuss how graphics APIs can support machine learning alongside rendering, where their execution model helps or limits performance, and what observability is needed to understand those trade-offs. The work asks how much performance portability a compact engine can achieve without maintaining separate implementations for each vendor.

presentations.title: Mentorship in Practice: Building Relationships for Early-Career Growth
presentations.abstract: Early-career professionals are often told to “find a mentor,” with little guidance on where to start or how to navigate the relationship once they have one. This panel brings together professionals with experience as both mentors and mentees to discuss how these relationships begin, what makes them useful, what to talk about, and how they can evolve over time. Panelists will also discuss the distinction between mentors and sponsors and share their thoughts on building a broader network of people who can offer guidance, perspective, and advocacy at different career stages. The moderated discussion will be followed by an open Q&A, where attendees are invited to bring their own questions and experiences into the conversation.

presentations.title: MiniLlama-Infra: Micro-Architecture Ablation of LLM Inference on Commodity GPU Accelerators
presentations.abstract: Quantizing LLM weights to INT8 can reduce storage yet still slow inference when GPU access patterns are poorly matched to the hardware. We present MiniLlama-Infra, a transparent from-scratch CUDA inference engine for Llama-3.2-1B and a six-stage micro-architecture study. Archived Nsight Compute measurements on an RTX 4060 Laptop show that naive INT8 GEMV reduces memory throughput from 58.1 to 19.2 GB/s and increases latency from 289.1 to 298.5 µs. A warp-cooperative mapping improves coalescing and available parallelism together, reducing kernel latency to 52.3 µs, a 5.7× speedup. Matched Stage 5/6 experiments further show that W8A8 improves decoding throughput by 15.8% on RTX 4060 Laptop and 12.8% on A100 SXM4, with estimated GPU energy-efficiency gains of 17.0% and 8.4%. Additional A100 kernel experiments, selected historical cross-generation and 3B results, and a compiled-engine perplexity pilot extend the evaluation while explicitly bounding the scope of the claims.

presentations.title: Mixed Feelings About Mixed Precisions
presentations.abstract: What if we have been oversolving in computational science and engineering for decades? Are low-precision arithmetic formats only for AI workloads? How can HPC applications exploit mixed-precision hardware features? This BoF invites the HPC community at large interested in applying mixed precisions into their workflows and discussing the impact on time-to-solution, memory footprint, storage, data motion, and energy consumption. Experts from scientific applications/software libraries/hardware architectures will briefly provide the context on this trendy topic, share their own perspectives, and mostly engage with the audience via a set of questions, while gathering feedback to define a roadmap moving forward.

presentations.title: Mixed Precision at Scale: From Peak FLOPs to Trusted Science
Mixed-Precision Cholesky Factorization for Semidefinite Programming Using Ozaki Scheme II
presentations.abstract: This paper explores the accuracy and performance of a mixed-precision Cholesky factorization based on the INT8 Ozaki scheme II. Within the tiled Cholesky algorithm, we apply an optimized Ozaki scheme II to the symmetric rank-k update (SYRK), while keeping the diagonal factorization (POTRF) and the triangular solve (TRSM) in double precision. We further introduce a look-ahead technique and a dynamic tile size scheduler. On a server whose GPU has limited FP64 throughput, our implementation attains a 3.04x speedup over the OpenBLAS dpotrf routine while retaining double-precision accuracy. We also examine how the number of slices affects the backward error and the relative forward error, and find that 15 slices are required to preserve double-precision accuracy within the range covered by our experiment. Finally, we integrate the proposed factorization into a double-precision semidefinite programming solver and obtain a 1.47x speedup on an SDP benchmark instance (1et.2048).

presentations.title: MLPerf: A Benchmark for Machine Learning
presentations.abstract: As AI workloads scale exponentially, evaluating machine learning infrastructure requires rigorous, standardized benchmarking. This Birds of a Feather session brings together HPC researchers, hardware architects, and software engineers to discuss the future of the MLPerf benchmark suite. The discussion will address critical scaling challenges, heterogeneous accelerator evaluation, and performance metrics for disaggregated infrastructure. Participants will collaborate on driving reproducibility and expanding benchmarks to encompass emerging, complex AI workloads. Join us to share deployment insights and directly shape the benchmarking roadmaps guiding the next generation of supercomputing systems.

presentations.title: mmgal.jl: Fast, Differentiable Modeling for Millimeter-Sky Inference
presentations.abstract:
Generating realistic millimeter/sub-millimeter (mm/sub-mm) sky simulations is essential for de-blending sources and understanding cosmic dust-obscured star formation, but remains computationally expensive. While the previous tools could simulate only a small fraction (<0.25%) of the mm-sky, the next-generation telescopes are now mapping nearly 25% of the sky at high sensitivity, probing the faintest and farthest populations of galaxies. Interpreting this data and de-blending sources effectively requires accelerating forward modeling and inverse problem-solving techniques.

In this paper, we present SkyMatch.jl, a fast and differentiable framework for computing mock mm-sky maps and catalogs. Leveraging the Reactant.jl compiler, SkyMatch.jl automatically optimizes the simulation's tensor computations to run efficiently on multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Overall, SkyMatch.jl achieves speedups of up to 90× on CPUs and 3300× on GPUs, enabling us to realistically simulate data from state-of-the-art mm-wave telescopes and interpret the resulting source populations.

presentations.title: Moderated Panel Discussion
Modern High-Performance I/O: Leveraging Files and Objects
presentations.abstract: As more diverse applications move to high performance computing (HPC), the I/O workload has also become more varied. The community has spent three decades improving large-scale parallel file systems, but object stores provide new approaches and novel interfaces. At the same time, traditional parallel I/O approaches and abstractions have evolved under the covers to make use of both novel object stores and classic parallel file systems. In this full-day tutorial we will explore several object storage technologies and discuss both old and new approaches to getting maximum performance from them. With a mix of lectures and hands-on exercises, attendees will learn about object storage design and usage. We will also tackle how the classic I/O software stack has evolved to make use of object stores, as well as provide attendees with the knowledge to know when file systems and object stores are the most appropriate storage approach for their applications. By the end of the day, attendees will know a bit more about what these new storage systems are doing while at the same time learning how to use libraries and tools to hide the details.

presentations.title: Modernizing Hercules for GPU-Accelerated Earthquake Ground Motion Simulation on NVIDIA GPUs
presentations.abstract: Physics-based earthquake ground motion simulations, in order to achieve a desirable maximum frequency for practical applications, require billions of finite elements and tens of thousands of explicit timesteps, making the element-local force operators, inter-rank exchange, and output path all important to end-to-end performance. We present a modern GPU-resident implementation of Hercules, an octree-based finite-element earthquake simulator. The implementation maps effective stiffness, BKT viscoelastic attenuation, and explicit displacement update to CUDA; retains the primary field histories on the accelerator; exchanges boundary data through CUDA-aware MPI; and limits host transfers to data required by non-accelerated paths and output. On early-access NVIDIA GB200 resources, a fixed 67.1-million-element problem attains a 25.02X speedup on 64 GPUs, while a weak-scaling sweep maintains 95.6% efficiency from one to 64 GPUs and grows to 4.29 billion elements. At equal scaling-unit count, one GPU is 5.4–7.8 times faster per timestep than one 144-core NVIDIA Grace--Grace node. A 2-Hz simulation of the 2013 Mw 6.4 Ruisui earthquake contains 1.584 billion elements and 40,000 timesteps. It completes the solver in 1007.05s on 32 GPUs and 558.06s on 64 GPUs, speedups of 5.86X and 10.58X over 32 CPU nodes. Unfiltered station histories agree with the CPU implementation to a relative L2 error of 1.215e-5 and a minimum component correlation above 0.9999. These results demonstrate that GPU residency and accelerator-aware communication make Hercules practical for high-resolution production ground motion simulations without changing its established numerical model.

presentations.title: Mojo-Driven Performance Portability for LBM
presentations.abstract:
Lattice-Boltzmann methods (LBM) have emerged as a prominent approach for simulating fluid dynamics, owing to their inherent parallelism and suitability for high-performance computing on both multicore CPUs and GPUs.
In this study, we investigate Mojo, a low-level framework designed to bridge Pythonic programming with high-performance computing, and compare its performance portability against established parallel programming frameworks such as CUDA, HIP, and SYCL using lid-driven cavity simulations.
Our results show that template metaprogramming in Mojo enables high-performance portability without requiring manual loop unrolling.
Compared with FluidX3D, Mojo achieves application efficiencies above 80% across GPUs, although its performance is lower on CPUs, resulting in a 0.59 performance portability score for D3Q19-fp32 across all evaluated architectures, programming models and optimisations.
These results highlight Mojo's potential as a productive and efficient programming model for heterogeneous computing, but also suggest room for improvement on CPU platforms.

presentations.title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
presentations.abstract: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4\% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.

Morphogenesis
presentations.abstract:
Long before computers, Alan Turing asked how a smooth egg becomes a spotted, striped, branching creature. His answer, reaction-diffusion, is the chemistry of pattern itself. Here that chemistry runs as living paint: two competing substances diffuse and react across a field, blooming into coral, fingerprints, dividing cells, and restless worms, cycling endlessly through nature's vocabulary of form.

But look closely, and the field is split into three vertical territories, each a separate GPU. The luminous seams between them are the secret of large-scale simulation: the halo exchange, where neighboring processors trade their edge values every timestep so the pattern can flow seamlessly across boundaries. Gold packets pulse along the seams and communication is made visible.

This is how we simulate weather, galaxies, and combustion: cut reality into pieces, solve each in parallel, and stitch the edges back together. The pattern is the phenomenon; the seams are the high performance computing. Turing's morphogenesis is computed the way modern science actually computes it.

presentations.title: Mosaic: Ephemeral, Capability-Aware Scheduling Across Heterogeneous Rack-Scale Systems
presentations.abstract:
Heterogeneous HPC racks combine CPU, GPU, and FPGA resources with workloads that need different hardware and software stacks. Hardware-compatible placement alone fails when persistent workers diverge in operating-system images, libraries, drivers, or runtime versions. Separate provisioning, container, and accelerator recovery paths further fragment admission and failure handling.
We present Mosaic, a Slurm-complementary lifecycle controller combining version-aware admission, capability-based dispatch, and explicit reset boundaries. Workers register capabilities and observed versions; Mosaic admits compatible workers and dispatches tasks through set inclusion and profile compatibility. It supports fast per-job userspace replacement, broader diskless PXE-to-RAM worker replacement, quarantine, and requeue.
On a heterogeneous rack-scale testbed, Mosaic reaches all-workers-ready for 32 concurrent workers under one controller in about 17s. Per-job images reproduce the expected package environment in 100% of runs, versus 45.83±14.55% with periodic Ansible and 24.17±10.17% with periodic reimaging. After failure, Mosaic restores a verified configuration in about 1.5s.

presentations.title: Move Metadata, Not Data: A Register-in-Place Lakehouse for Large Autonomous-Driving Datasets
presentations.abstract: Even when autonomous-driving data is available on shared storage, analysis pipelines often copy and reorganize it. To register sensor files without copying them, we built an Apache Iceberg lakehouse that records their locations and metadata. We registered about 647,000 lidar and radar Parquet files from a resident ∼13TB sample of NVIDIA’s 133 TB PhysicalAI Autonomous Vehicles dataset. Registering these Parquet files over NFS took approximately 2 h 8 min, based on log timestamps. In a separate four-scale experiment, registration time grew approximately linearly with file count. Timed after warm-up in that experiment, eleven queries over metadata or materialized tables had median latencies of 21–352 ms as total registered rows grew 36×; these timings do not characterize general sensor or media scans. Deployment also exposed an ownership hazard when DROP TABLE PURGE unintentionally deleted ∼11TB of source data. We describe safeguards and are developing a copy-based baseline.

presentations.title: MPI Windows as an Abstraction for CUDA Interprocess Communication
presentations.abstract: CUDA interprocess communication (IPC) allows direct pointer access to GPU allocations of peer processes. Applications are required to handle export, collective exchange, per-peer import, pointer caching, failure handling, and cleanup. We show that these operations can be managed through an MPI window instead, using existing MPI shared-window query mechanisms. We implement this approach in WinIPC, a library that intercepts MPI window operations through the MPI profiling interface. We evaluate the approach using distributed matrix transpose, five-point stencil, and CUDA-enabled LULESH. We demonstrate peer-pointer access across 32 GPUs on eight physical nodes of a GB200 NVL system. For distributed transpose with accumulation at matrix order 1024, the single-kernel direct implementation achieves 2.44x the throughput of GPU-aware MPI. At matrix order 6912 on 32 GB200 GPUs, this variant reaches 20x the GPU-aware MPI rate. Moreover, we identify an allocation-time restriction of fabric-enabled IPC that limits its use with container-managed GPU buffers.

presentations.title: MPI-CCOB: Benchmarking MPI Overlap on CPU and GPU Systems
presentations.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the MPI Communication–Computation Overlap Benchmark, or MPI-CCOB, a configurable benchmark for evaluating overlap in MPI applications on CPU and GPU systems. Motivated by domain-decomposition applications, the benchmark organizes processing units into one-, two-, or three-dimensional Cartesian topologies, producing different numbers of concurrent neighbor-exchange requests. It supports both compute-bound and memory-bound workloads to examine how computational characteristics affect overlap. Since not all MPI implementations support asynchronous progress, MPI-CCOB also provides an optional user-level progress thread per processing unit. By controlling workload characteristics and communication-progress mechanisms, our benchmark reveals the conditions required for effective overlap. Experiments with MPICH and Open MPI show that active progress enables nearly complete overlap during compute-bound workloads. However, overlap decreases substantially under memory-bound workloads on both CPU and GPU systems, even when communication is continuously given the option to progress.

presentations.title: MPICH: A High-Performance Open-Source MPI Implementation
presentations.abstract: MPICH is one of the most widely used open-source implementations of the MPI standard and the foundation for many vendor MPI libraries powering today's HPC systems. This BoF brings together MPICH developers, industry partners, and HPC users to share the latest project developments, discuss support for emerging architectures and MPI features, and explore future directions for the MPI ecosystem. This year's session will also discuss opportunities for community engagement and contributions to MPICH. Attendees are encouraged to participate in an interactive format, ask questions, share experiences, and help shape the future of one of HPC's core software infrastructures.

presentations.title: Multilingual GPU Communication Libraries with LLVM Bitcode and CUDA LTOIR
presentations.abstract:
GPU applications combine kernels produced by multiple compiler frontends with
production device libraries implemented in CUDA C++. Reimplementing libraries
per frontend is costly, especially communication libraries whose code depends
on host-created transport state. We show linkable device IR can serve as an
interoperability boundary for stateful GPU libraries without sacrificing
baseline performance. We package \nvshmem{} and \nccl{} implementations as
LLVM bitcode and CUDA LTOIR and consume them from CUDA C++, CUTLASS Python, and
numba-cuda-mlir. Across RMA benchmarks, packaged IR preserves latency and
bandwidth relative to conventional CUDA C++ linkage, reaching 98~GB/s. Across
both libraries, CUTLASS Python stays within 3.7\% of CUDA C++ latency and
delivers at least 90.7\% of its bandwidth, reaching \nccl{} bandwidth parity.
Fused GEMM+AllGather experiments show packaged communication IR composes with
tensor-core computation, while LTOIR remains within 0.57\% of baseline across
every tested \nccl{} shape. Results establish linkable device IR as a
performant multi-frontend library boundary.

presentations.title: My Coauthors Don’t Sleep: Agentic AI and Trust in Computational Science
presentations.abstract: This panel will discuss the role of agentic AI and ML in the predictive science setting, with a focus on impacts to computational science and HPC. In particular, questions related to trustworthy agentic AI for science will form the core theme, as enabled by explainability and interpretability methods, as well as robust treatment of uncertainty in models and data. What are the particular challenges and opportunities for agentic workflows for modSim at exascale? How can uncertainty quantification be a scaffold for scientific AI/ML, and what are the pitfalls? This discussion will lay the foundation for future work in HPC co-design at the interface of theory, software, and hardware optimization as we prepare for new paradigms of predictive modeling and simulation in the era of agentic AI.

presentations.title: N-VEG: 3D Gaussian Encoding for Neural Volume Compression
presentations.abstract: Research in Implicit Neural Representations has led to new lines of compression methods for large 3D volumetric data, offering aggressive compression ratios and direct data lookup without decompression. While these methods perform well at compression, they struggle to learn high-frequency information; though this is addressable by a variety of encoding methods, they add significant memory overhead, hampering compression goals. Other methods inspired by novel view synthesis attempt to model volumes explicitly with primitives, e.g. 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. In this work, we present a hybrid approach to volume compression that learns in-tandem a 3D Gaussian reconstruction and Neural representation of the input scene. We treat the 3D gaussians as an encoder for a small neural network, with latent feature vectors attached to each primitive. When sampling the volume, spatial locations are weighted by overlapping gaussians; feature vectors are then interpolated, harmonically activated, summed, and decoded by an MLP. Here, the 3D Gaussian encoder is a lagrangian alternative to global encoding structures, like hash grids, allowing the INR to be detail-aware when learning its encoding. This strategy achieves greater reconstruction quality than primitive-only reconstruction methods, while retaining fast training times and aggressive compression ratios, making it a viable in-situ volume compression technique.

presentations.title: NAAIR
National Data Platform, National Research Platform and Open Science Data Federation: How They Collectively Enable Data-Intensive Science
presentations.abstract: Our work examines VFL through the lens of policy-aware execution across distributed infrastructure. We present communication-efficient VFL methods and evaluate their trade-offs among execution time, computational cost, model utility, and privacy considerations. This work fits well the SCinet Research Exposition because it demonstrates how advanced networking and geographically distributed research infrastructure influence the practical deployment of privacy-preserving AI workflows. Rather than simulating a distributed deployment, we execute VFL workflows on FABRIC, including the CIENA node, in an environment representative of the infrastructure that SC attendees develop and operate. Our findings support the adoption of policy-aware collaborative machine learning by identifying effective execution strategies for distributed scientific settings.

presentations.title: National Data Platform, National Research Platform and Open Science Data Federation: How they collectively enable data-intensive science
presentations.abstract:
Data sharing is a critical challenge in modern scientific research, where progress depends on efficiently managing and processing massive volumes of data. To tackle these storage and performance demands, the Open Science Data Federation (OSDF) was created to establish a global research data distribution network. Originally built on the Open Science Grid’s StashCache, OSDF now runs on the Pelican Platform to strengthen its infrastructure.
The Pelican Platform adds several major upgrades to the OSDF, including precise GeoIP routing, origin and cache web interfaces, centralized registration, director services, host advertising systems, and detailed status telemetry. Together, these tools provide a precise, highly controllable, and stable global data-sharing framework. Benchmarking tests confirm that Pelican offers a robust, distributed infrastructure, allowing key initiatives—including the National Data Platform (NDP), National Research Platform (NRP), and Open Science Pool (OSPool)—to effectively simplify data orchestration for complex scientific workflows.

presentations.title: National Lab Strategies
presentations.abstract: This session brings together representatives from national laboratories and supercomputing centers that are building or operating quantum computing capabilities alongside their HPC systems. Each speaker will give a short talk on their organization's strategy, covering plans, lessons learned, and priorities for integrating quantum computing into HPC environments. The talks will be followed by a panel discussion on common challenges and how institutions across regions can work together to move quantum-HPC integration forward.

presentations.title: Nautobot
Navigating Complexity: Achieving Performance Portability in the Evolving Landscape of Accelerated HPC Systems
presentations.abstract: With the increasing demand for AI in HPC, there has been a rapid rise in accelerated architectures, portable programming models, and frameworks. The already-daunting task of programming for interconnected accelerated systems has become even more complex. This BoF, organized by IXPUG, will focus on portable programming across a wide range of heterogeneous architectures—including Intel, NVIDIA, AMD, and ARM supporting diverse simulation, data analytics, and AI workloads. The session will explore key challenges, state-of-the-art solutions, and emerging best practices for programming across these systems, identifying common principles and methodologies that support development and long-term maintenance across sites, architectures, and scientific applications.

presentations.title: Navigating Mixed-Precision: Tools and Techniques for Floating-Point Error Profiling
presentations.abstract: Floating-point arithmetic is the bedrock of scientific computing, yet it frequently introduces subtle errors and non-deterministic behavior in numerical software. As the HPC community shifts toward mixed-precision execution to unlock performance and energy-efficiency gains, developers require robust methodologies to rigorously analyze floating-point error accumulation. This tutorial provides a comprehensive introduction to two state-of-the-art tools designed to guide precision-tuning decisions in both CPU and GPU-accelerated applications. The first tool is FPChecker, which leverages the Clang/LLVM compiler infrastructure to perform static and dynamic analysis of C/C++ applications. The second is NixNaN, a high-performance profiler built on the NVIDIA NVBit dynamic instrumentation framework, engineered to detect floating-point exceptional values arising during CUDA kernel execution without requiring source modification or recompilation. Throughout this session, participants will learn (1) to assess the floating-point dynamic range of applications, (2) to visualize the propagation of rounding errors, and (3) to isolate performance-critical numerical issues, such as overflows, and NaNs. The tutorial emphasizes a hands-on approach: attendees will engage with accessible examples (e.g., simple linear solvers) configured to run locally on their laptops. In the advanced session, we transition to real-world impact, where participants will apply these tools to larger numerical libraries (e.g., Hypre).

presentations.title: Navigating the Spectrum of Science Workloads with ESnet JLab FPGA Accelerated Transport (EJFAT)
presentations.abstract:
Cross-facility workflows are no longer optional but a requirement for the success of current and future science campaigns. From remote labs to multi-institutional science campaigns, advances in instrumentation and technological innovation are enabling experimental and observational scientific user facilities to generate data faster than processing and storage can handle.

Our work explores EJFAT as a potential solution to these challenges. While EJFAT has been shown to be performant and scalable, this paper explores considerations for integrating EJFAT into real-world scientific experiments. We explore two applications: one highly integrated, the other highly generalizable. The first is a highly tuned and optimized workflow for pushing data as fast as possible to meet the goals of scientific experiments, while the second is a general ecosystem lowering the barrier for scientists to leverage HPC resources with minimal effort representing two common classes of applications typical found in scientific user facilities.

presentations.title: ND-Locate: Localizing Non-Determinism in MPI Applications
presentations.abstract: Large-scale MPI applications can yield different scientific results from identical inputs due to non-deterministic execution, yet current tools offer little help in pinpointing its source. We present ND-LOCATE, a framework that localizes execution-level non-determinism to application functions, achieving Pearson correlations up to 0.97 on benchmark applications and identifying the code regions responsible for output variability in the production cosmological simulator Enzo.

presentations.title: Network-Aware Caching in Distributed CMS XRootD Systems via Data-Driven Forecasting
presentations.abstract: High-Energy Physics experiments such as the Compact Muon Solenoid distribute petabyte-scale datasets across geographically dispersed sites, imposing sustained load on wide-area research networks. Although in-network caching mitigates repeated transfers, deployed policies remain reactive rather than anticipatory. In this work, we propose a two-stage predictive caching framework trained on 8.4 million XRootD session records from 25 cache nodes across four domains. In Stage-1, a gated recurrent unit model forecasts near-future dataset accesses. In Stage-2, directories and files within predicted datasets are identified through non-parametric resolution. Simulation results show that an architecturally decoupled side-cache preserves baseline performance. Over 23 days at a single cache node, it displaces 115 GB of wide-area traffic, reducing wide-area volume by 1.6% and improving the hit rate by 1.4–1.6 percentage points. This study demonstrates that predictive caching depends not only on prediction accuracy, but also on selecting prediction granularity and integrating predictions with cache operation.
