Nexus: Malleable Physical Infrastructure for Dynamic Workload Convergence
presentations.abstract: Contemporary research environments demand the integration of heterogeneous computing paradigms. This poster introduces Nexus, an incubator research project and empirical testbed designed to deploy complex, dynamic bare-metal infrastructure. Nexus bridges bare-metal immutability with cloud-native orchestration to enable the automated convergence of disjoint computational paradigms onto unified, reproducible hardware.

presentations.title: nFlows: Enabling Efficient Data Movement in Data-Intensive Scientific Workflows on Non-Uniform Memory Access Architectures
presentations.abstract: Data movement across the memory subsystems of modern supercomputers is a major performance bottleneck for data-intensive scientific workflows. Preserving locality and minimizing data movement are key strategies to address this, yet support in workflow scheduling remains limited. nFlows is a runtime system for studying data movement in scientific workflows and prototyping memory-topology-aware scheduling algorithms. This version targets the main memory subsystem, focusing on Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) architectures, which dominate modern compute-node design. We use nFlows to execute workflows under a traditional FIFO scheduler and a NUMA-aware FIFO scheduler from prior work, collecting traces for both. Our analysis shows some workflows are negatively affected when execution spreads across NUMA nodes, and NUMA-aware scheduling mitigates this: executions reading at least 60% of their data locally rise from 27.64% to 68.33%, executions with a makespan improvement rise from 3.07% to 11.71%, and best-case makespan reduction increases from 10.22% to 44.28%.

presentations.title: No Bits Left Behind: A Precision-Preserving On-Wafer Reduction for FP64 GEMM
presentations.abstract:
Wafer-scale AI engines pack hundreds of thousands
of cores onto a single die, but their arithmetic is low-precision,
with no native double precision (FP64)—the workhorse of sci-
entific computing. We emulate FP64 matrix multiply (GEMM)
entirely on the wafer, to the accuracy of a true FP64 computation,
using the Ozaki scheme to split each operand into bfloat16
slices. On a grid with no shared memory, the Ozaki slices
must be reduced on the wafer itself in extended precision;
otherwise the reduction would discard the low-order bits the split
preserves. Accuracy is FP64-class at every size we measured, up
to 3360 × 3360, and we scale FP64 GEMM to span∼50% of
the wafer. The method extends to complex FP64 through a host-
side Karatsuba wrapper and drives a Newton–Schulz solver to
FP64-class residuals.

presentations.title: No-Restart Elasticity in an Adaptive Runtime System for Cloud-Native HPC
presentations.abstract: Exploiting discounted spot instances for HPC requires changing an application's resource allocation at runtime, shrinking ahead of an interruption and expanding onto replacement capacity. Existing mechanisms implement rescaling as a full teardown and cold restart, where restart accounts for up to 95\% of the overhead, growing with node count and, on GPUs, with CUDA context initialization. We present a no-restart rescaling mechanism for Charm++ in which surviving processes never exit: it negotiates membership with a lightweight external coordinator, reconciles UCX endpoints with the new cluster view, and returns to the top of runtime initialization while preserving live application state. A rescaling operation costs 8--15\,ms on CPUs and 7--11\,ms on GPUs at 4--32 instances, two orders of magnitude below restart-based implementations. GPU device state persists in place, eliminating the checkpointing daemons previously required. End to end, eight simultaneous interruptions cost 0.2\% of runtime on CPUs and 0.6\% on GPUs.

presentations.title: Novel Profiling Pipeline for Replay-Based Performance Analysis
presentations.abstract: Replay-based profilers collect hardware metrics by executing the same code multiple times with different metric groups. While this overcomes hardware-counter limits, it breaks down for multi-GPU applications: interdependent kernels in NCCL and NVSHMEM require ranks to progress together but independent replay passes are susceptible to divergence. We present a coordinated pipeline for replay-based profiling of multi-GPU applications. To preserve correctness, we introduce a profiler-side synchronization mechanism and a heuristic kernel-grouping algorithm that replays dependent kernels in lockstep across ranks. We introduce a bundling-based metric distribution algorithm that partitions metric sets across profiler instances. The pipeline merges per-process reports into a unified profile and supports report clustering for scalable exploration. We implement the profiling pipeline in NVIDIA NCU and evaluate our metric distribution implementation. Replay coordination eliminates deadlocks in interdependent workloads, while metric distribution reduces the maximum replay count by up to 3.50× versus single-GPU profiling with profiling data quality preserved.

presentations.title: Numerical Linear Algebra in the Age of Coding Agents
presentations.abstract: Since SC25, a revolution has taken hold: coding agents have moved from curiosity into nearly every institution's pipeline, and "vibe coding" is now how much software, numerical included, gets written. That matters for numerical linear algebra (NLA), whose libraries underpin modern science and whose trustworthiness was built over 50 years of human expert engineering. Now, when a plausible NLA kernel is nearly free to generate, what holds that trust together? This BoF gathers established leaders and younger NLA scientists from academia and industry to open a discussion, so our community shapes this shift rather than being swept along.

presentations.title: NVIDIA Vera: A Microarchitecture-Level Comparison with Grace, Turin, and Granite Rapids
presentations.abstract:
The majority of new HPC systems are centered around NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel CPUs. Vera is NVIDIA’s latest data-center CPU, including its first custom data-center core design, Olympus. This paper investigates Vera in comparison to AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids, using NVIDIA Grace as a baseline. We navigate up the performance ladder, from microbenchmarks that isolate performance metrics, through NAS kernels and miniapps, to single-socket performance of a range of scientific codes.

We find that Vera achieves the best performance of the architectures evaluated in most codes tested, and that this gain is primarily attributed to its high memory bandwidth, effective Spatial Multithreading implementation, and low-latency memory subsystem aided by the architecture’s predictive structures. While Vera represents a major leap over its predecessor, we show that its comparatively modest floating-point performance trails Intel and AMD in a small number of compute-bound workloads reflecting NVIDIA’s GPU focus for such workloads.

presentations.title: Obleth: Fair Multi-Tenant LLM Serving for Self-Hosted Campus Infrastructure
presentations.abstract: LLMs are becoming more popular, and costs are continuing to rise. Many universities are looking to host LLMs on local infrastructure to meet compliance, cost, and data-sovereignty requirements. Most AI gateways assume a cloud-provider backend, one that handles seemingly unlimited connections and natively supports capabilities that many self-hosted models lack. This is why I created Obleth, a source-available AI gateway designed for locally hosted infrastructure. Obleth's standout features include: a weighted fairshare admission scheduler dividing inference capacity proportionally across tenants; a Slurm cluster provisioner for opportunistic compute on preemptible partitions with automatic preemption recovery; an auto router that selects the best available model from a registered fleet based on capability, capacity, and cost; runtime-configurable capability extensions (boons) for things like on-premise content policy enforcement and MCP tool integration; and per-request pipeline tracing requiring no external telemetry. We evaluate fairness guarantees and gateway overhead with an included reproducible benchmark harness.

presentations.title: OBSERVE: An Observable, Sustainable, and Fault-Tolerant Runtime for Hyperparameter Optimization on Production HPC Systems
presentations.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) has become a fundamental component of deep learning (DL) workflows, yet executing long-running optimization campaigns on High Performance Computing (HPC) systems remains a challenge, due to sustainability, computational costs, interruptions, heterogeneous hardware, and limited runtime visibility. Existing HPO frameworks primarily optimize the search effectiveness, while operational aspects required by HPC environments are neglected. This work introduces OBSERVE, an HPC-native framework for Bayesian Optimization (BO) offering energy-aware multi-objective optimization, fault tolerant checkpointing, and runtime observability. The framework is validated on the ClimateBench and MLPerf-DeepCAM benchmarks across heterogeneous HPC platforms with different schedulers and GPU architectures, and execution is tested by parallelizing the DL training in multi-GPU environments and the HPO process itself. Results confirm that the framework preserves the optimization effectiveness of BO while enabling resilient execution and exposing energy-performance trade-offs. More broadly, this work lays the foundation for energy-aware HPO as a runtime service in HPC infrastructures.

presentations.title: Offset-Aware Coalescing for Fine-Grained Scattered Reads in HPC Reproducibility Analytics
presentations.abstract: Data-intensive workloads in scientific computing, e.g., in-situ and ad-hoc data processing for numerical reproducibility analysis, exhibit I/O patterns dominated by small, non-contiguous reads from large files. Although many HPC frameworks overlap I/O with computation, existing interfaces, e.g., POSIX and io_uring, are primarily optimized for sequential or large-block access. Workloads issuing many random reads therefore incur high system-call overhead, inefficient batching, and underutilized bandwidth. We present SCISSOR, an I/O runtime for workloads dominated by fine-grained random access. SCISSOR applies gap-aware offset coalescing to merge nearby requests into contiguous segments, reducing kernel interactions and increasing effective I/O size. A regression-based performance model selects batching and coalescing parameters that balance I/O and computation throughput. Finally, SCISSOR leverages io_uring to issue large asynchronous batches with minimal context-switch overhead. On HPC reproducibility analytics over large-scale cosmology simulations (HACC), SCISSOR achieves 3.6× and 42× higher end-to-end throughput on average over io_uring and POSIX memory-mapped baselines, respectively.

presentations.title: Oil on Canvas: Galactic Center on Palette
presentations.abstract:
My painting (Oil on Canvas) translates a radio-astronomy observation of our galaxy's heart into a dusky, nebular atmosphere, its aubergine and violet field that surrounds the Milky Way's core.

The source of my interpretation of the galactic center stemmed from discussions with Prof. Florina Ciorba from the University of Basel (UniBas), Switzerland, who is the co-founder member and PI of the UniBas node of the SKACH project — The SKA (Square Kilometre Array) of Switzerland Consortium (SKACH, https://skach.org/about-skach/). The underlying data comes from the 1.28 GHz MeerKAT galactic center mosaic created by Heywood et al. (2022), released by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO). The image that inspired me and my painting is a re-rendered version by J.C. Muñoz-Mateos and branded by SKACH (the Swiss SKA Consortium) and SKAO (the Square Kilometre Array Observatory).

https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/milky-way-center-meerkat-and-webb/

presentations.title: On Big Data, Big Simulations, and Big plans for AI in Climate Sciences
presentations.abstract: Climate science is being transformed by the convergence of AI, simulations, and high-performance computing. This talk explores how data compression and representation learning can extract knowledge from massive climate datasets, how Gordon Bell Award-winning simulations are pushing the frontiers of weather and climate modeling, and how DaCe enables automatic optimization and differentiation of legacy Fortran codes for modern heterogeneous systems. Building on these advances, I will outline a roadmap toward an AI climate scientist: a system that unifies observations, simulations, scientific reasoning, and machine learning to accelerate discovery, formulate hypotheses, and ultimately become a collaborative scientific partner in understanding and predicting Earth's changing climate.

presentations.title: On Multimodal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture models for Tokamak Plasma Dynamics
presentations.abstract: Experimental tokamak diagnostics are multimodal, heterogeneous, and sparsely sampled across discharges, making reusable pretrained representations valuable for plasma modeling. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn predictive latent representations without reconstructing every modality. We adopt TokaMark, a 14-task benchmark built from 11,573 MAST discharges, and introduce Tokamak JEPA (T-JEPA), a multimodal adaptation of V-JEPA~2.1 coupling a spatial poloidal magnetic-flux representation with six diagnostic encoders through bidirectional cross-attention. Across frozen, partial, and full adaptation, T-JEPA shows selective transfer, with frozen representations competitive for flux-map and plasma-current prediction. Our task-specific end-to-end models reduce NRMSE by 11.8--22.5\% relative to matched TokaMind FT-Base warm-starts on Groups 1--2, while normalization, actuator conditioning, and effective batch size affect accuracy and stability. Controlled studies show limited warm-start benefits and greater reliability when explicit coefficient targets are retained. Overall, task-specific optimization remains strongest for peak accuracy, while T-JEPA provides a basis for reusable multimodal representations across tokamak diagnostics.

presentations.title: On preprocessing heterogeneous HPC telemetry for use in foundation models and digital twins
presentations.abstract: HPC facilities publish telemetry supporting foundation-model training and digital-twin replay but lack common fields, units, and privacy conventions. We extend REDI and AIDRIN to HPC telemetry via a new domain processor and agentic telemetry skill, and apply SetGo, forming an end-to-end pipeline that transforms heterogeneous telemetry into AI-ready and digital-twin-ready datasets. For digital twins, we demonstrate cross-facility replay fidelity: naively replaying Marconi100 telemetry through a Frontier twin violates its physical power envelope on 10.23% of samples; renormalization reduces this to 0.0042%. The pipeline supports representative replay and targeted emulation. For foundation models, we find static scheduler metadata alone gives no signal for predicting job-level details; however, ExaFM predicts job runtime with R2 = 0.960 when conditioned on a pre-anonymization identity embedding; without it, transferring that head to Marconi100, unseen during pretraining, reaches R2 = 0.716. We close with actionable recommendations for publishing AI- and digital-twin-ready telemetry toward future pretraining corpora.

presentations.title: One API, Five Memories: Measuring Unified Memory Across NVIDIA and AMD Architectures
presentations.abstract:
Managed memory promises one pointer that both the CPU and the GPU can dereference, with the system deciding where the pages live.
We measured what that promise means on five systems: NVIDIA H100 NVL, GH200, GB10, and AMD MI300A and MI300X, running one benchmark identically on all of them: a page-granular pointer chase bracketed by device- and host-resident anchor buffers, cross-checked by an operating-system residency probe, and probing placement, lifecycle costs, memory pressure, memAdvise hints, and concurrency.
The five systems follow four different placement rules.
The same managed access costs 244ns on an empty H100 and 40152ns when GPU memory is full; the GH200 degrades eightfold under the same pressure, the GB10 not at all.
Hints rescue the H100 by 40x, harm the GH200 by up to 44x and are inert on single-pool systems.
A routine operating-system update rewrote the MI300X's placement rule on unchanged hardware and ROCm.

presentations.title: One Bus Accident Away from Death: The Fragility of HPC I/O Tools
presentations.abstract:
HPC I/O tools are essential for understanding application performance, yet a small number of individuals often drive their development and maintenance.
This work investigates the maintainability of open-source HPC I/O tools using CHAOSS-inspired metrics, analyzing repository activity, contributor distributions, code ownership, and maintenance continuity.
We examine how development responsibilities are distributed across projects and identify potential dependencies on key maintainers.
The results highlight the human sustainability risks behind HPC I/O software and motivate greater consideration of maintenance resilience within the HPC community.

presentations.title: One Page, Two DMAs: Writing 400 GbE TCP Streams to NVMe Without Touching the Data
presentations.abstract: Data transfer nodes write wide-area TCP streams to storage. On a 400GbE testbed, the buffered-write path delivers only 138Gbps on a server whose SSDs sustain 453Gbps: cores saturate copying, dirty-page throttling stalls the application, and stalls leak into TCP as window collapse and spurious retransmissions. We present zcp_ingest, which establishes an end-to-end alignment invariant that lets a NIC RX page serve unmodified as a storage write buffer, using only mainline mechanisms. Header-data split plus one TCP_MAXSEG option makes virtually all payload bytes arrive page-aligned; TCP_ZEROCOPY_RECEIVE maps NIC-written pages into userspace; io_uring writes them to NVMe via O_DIRECT — virtually all payload bytes reach storage without CPU copying. With deterministic sender-side placement (SRAP), 16 flows sustain 373.4Gbps — 2.7x the buffered baseline and 97.4% of the path ceiling — with bit-exact terabyte-scale transfers and 4.4x lower CPU cost. Controlled violations establish one-flow-per-queue placement as a prerequisite for fair, drop-free, reproducible operation.

presentations.title: One Year After MPI 5.0: Impact and What's Next?
presentations.abstract: The Message Passing Interface (MPI) API is the most dominant programming approach for HPC environments. Its specification is driven by the MPI Forum, an open forum consisting of MPI developers, vendors, and users. This year, the MPI Forum published the latest version of the standard, MPI 5.0. We will take a look at the new features and will discuss what they mean for the users of MPI. We will also discuss ongoing work toward the next version of the MPI standard, with lightning talks from the working groups, and get feedback from the community.

presentations.title: One-Sided: A Portrait of the New OpenSHMEM Standard
presentations.abstract:
In MPI, every memory transfer requires negotiation. The sender announces. The receiver posts a matching receive. Both wait. This is the contract at the heart of parallel communication — and this visualization begins there, in the weight of it: 256 processing elements, bilateral arcs crossing in every direction, a single REQUEST suspended at its target with no response coming.

Then the model changes.

OpenSHMEM eliminates the contract. Any process can write directly into any other's memory. No handshake. No prior agreement. The target is simply — a destination.

This 90-second visualization is a portrait of that principle, built entirely from real benchmark data captured on an HPE internal research cluster: four nodes, 256 processing elements, HPE Slingshot fabric.

The visual language is built around directionality. 256 PEs are arranged in four organic galaxy clusters — Realms α, β, γ, δ, 64 PEs each — with arcs cycling through one source cluster at a time so the viewer can track individual operations to their specific destinations, not interpret a global blur. Periodic spotlights isolate single PE-to-PE operations. The contrast with the MPI opening is deliberate and exact.

The data behind the animation is 500,000 real GUPS operations — Giga Updates Per Second, a standard benchmark for irregular remote atomic writes — captured live on the HPE Slingshot fabric. Each arc is a real operation. The pattern it makes is not designed; it is measured.

The closing act shows the full system in motion, with the GUPS source code, an operation counter climbing to 500,000, and the key argument: this workload cannot be handled without a global synchronization barrier in MPI — a cost that scales with every PE added. In OpenSHMEM, it just runs.

presentations.title: Online Load Balancing of High-Order Mixed-Element Simulations on Heterogeneous Architectures
presentations.abstract: Scale-resolving simulations performed on clusters can be expensive, spanning hours to months. Efficient use of shared HPC resources increasingly involves allocations combining devices with different throughputs, requiring effective load partitioning across heterogeneous architectures. This work develops an online, distributed, diffusion-based repartitioning strategy driven by observed MPI wait-time statistics at runtime. The method infers cost imbalance to derive a target load distribution, then incrementally relocates interface-adjacent elements across ranks while preserving the existing partition structure. Integrated into the open-source compressible Navier–Stokes solver PyFR, the method is evaluated for flow around a circular cylinder at Re = 3900. Online load balancing achieves 101%, 116%, and 119% of homogeneous sum-of-parts performance targets across three heterogeneous configurations. Completed RK45 simulations achieve 2.4x, 2.8x, and 7.7x time-to-solution speedups.

presentations.title: Open MPI State of the Union 2026
presentations.abstract:
Open MPI continues to advance portable, high-performance communication for increasingly heterogeneous, accelerator-rich systems and workloads. Over the past year, the community has advanced MPI-5.0 conformance, expanded accelerator support, improved collective performance, and worked with partners across the HPC ecosystem. We'll discuss what Open MPI has accomplished over the past year and present a roadmap for the next year.

One of Open MPI's strengths lies in its diversity: we represent many different viewpoints across the HPC community. To that end, many developers from the community will be present to discuss and answer your questions both during and after the BoF.

presentations.title: Open OnDemand User Group Meeting
presentations.abstract: This BoF is meant to be an open discussion to guide the future roadmap for Open OnDemand (openondemand.org), by getting feedback from the community on the prioritization of the various tasks planned for the next few years. OOD is extremely relevant to ongoing discussions within the HPC community about user interfaces and science gateways. The session leaders, all part of the OOD development team, will jointly develop the content for the presentation in advance to ensure a wide range of viewpoints and topics are presented. We will also consult with our user advisory group in advance for their suggestions.

presentations.title: Open Polarity
presentations.abstract: This image depicts the 3D structure of the Sun's open coronal magnetic field from a snapshot of the “Live Prediction” HPC simulation developed by Predictive Science Inc. as part of their research for the August 12, 2026, total solar eclipse. See eclipse.predsci.com for more details on the simulation, which was created using the Magnetohydrodynamic Algorithm outside a Sphere Fortran code (github.com/predsci/mas) at a resolution of over 50 million cells. It ran faster than real time using 24 128-core EPYC Turin 9745 CPUs (3,072 total cores) on NASA's Athena supercomputer.

presentations.title: Open Source and Sovereign Infrastructure for HPC and AI
presentations.abstract:
Open source has long been at the heart of HPC infrastructure management. Traditional HPC platforms have been well served by software stacks designed to meet this specific purpose.

A new era brings new demands for HPC and AI. Open source infrastructure management faces new challenges on many fronts.

This session features leading practitioners of a new generation of software-defined open HPC-AI infrastructure. The session will present a diverse range of open source solutions for current use cases, including advantages and disadvantages. Common problems will be identified and solutions shared. Attendees will be invited to share their experiences.

presentations.title: Open-Source Hardware Tools: Advancing Architecture Research and Chip Prototyping
presentations.abstract: As demand for specialized architectures grows in the post-Moore era, this BoF will foster a sustained community around chip prototyping using open-source hardware tools. Building on themes explored in previous editions of this BoF at SC24 and SC25, the session will focus on practical tool experiences, current gaps, domain-specific accelerators, AI-assisted design workflows, and chip prototyping as an emerging HPC workload. Invited speakers from architecture, open-source EDA, accelerator design, and HPC will seed discussion. Expected outcomes include actionable insights, stronger collaboration, and follow-up community initiatives to advance open-source chip prototyping.

presentations.title: OpenACC Forum — The Future of Programming Accelerators with Directives
presentations.abstract: Through its mission to reduce time to science by nurturing parallel computing skills, the Open Accelerated Computing Consortium (OpenACC) invites you to explore the future of directive-based programming. In the age of agentic coding assistants, this BoF examines the evolving roles of OpenACC, OpenMP, standard language parallelism, and abstraction libraries like Julia for Accelerators or Kokkos for GPU-resident runtimes. Panels including compiler developers and community leaders will summarize the current state of programming for accelerators, followed by open discussion comparing practices and imagining new futures. Developers, researchers, compiler vendors, and the broader HPC community are welcome to shape the conversation.

presentations.title: OpenCCL: A Proposed Open Standard and Reference Implementation Unifying *CCLs for Performance, Portability, and Productivity
presentations.abstract: NVIDIA's NCCL is the de-facto GPU communication API for distributed AI, but it is a toolkit rather than a specification: its semantics are thin, it is tied to one vendor's stack, and other *CCLs re-implement or fork it. OpenCCL proposes an open standard and reference implementation: a normative specification with an ABI-stable header over pluggable transports and collective engines, so one library spans vendors and fabrics without application changes. OpenCCL runs unmodified NCCL codes and addresses all 33 entry points of NCCL 2.23.4. On Slingshot-11 it builds on RAPIDS Cascade APIs: kernel-initiated transfers behind a stream-triggered interface that fits NCCL semantics. Preliminary results on LLNL's Tuolumne, an El Capitan-class system, outperform RCCL and Cray MPICH for Allreduce from 256 bytes to 16 KiB, and Cascade outperforms Cray MPICH and our earlier stream-triggered MPI for small messages. MSCCL's AllToNext is implemented. The poster invites participation in standardization, implementation, and AI adoption.

presentations.title: OpenCHAMI Community Birds of a Feather
presentations.abstract: HPC centers are modernizing how they provision and operate clusters as systems become more heterogeneous, security-sensitive, and composable. OpenCHAMI, an HPSF emerging project, is an operator-led open-source control plane that brings cloud-like APIs and modular services to HPC system management. This BoF will help newcomers understand what OpenCHAMI enables today, give current users a forum to compare deployments and priorities, and invite operators, vendors, and developers to shape the roadmap. We will discuss adoption paths, including but not limited to xCAT transitions, and collect community feedback on tooling, integration, documentation, and operational requirements.

presentations.title: OpenCHAMI for Deployment of Inference Services
presentations.abstract:
AI workloads at HPC sites increasingly expect Kubernetes, while traditional workloads still run under batch schedulers such as Slurm. Both layers are now shaped by vendors, so sites have good reason to keep control of the layer beneath them: how nodes are discovered, booted, configured and reassigned. If that layer is open and site-controlled, a site can change what runs on top without rebuilding its infrastructure.
This talk describes our use of OpenCHAMI, a community-governed, open-source system management platform, as that layer. Building on earlier work presented at SC25, where nodes are moved between Slurm and Kubernetes using kexec-based fast booting, we combined OpenCHAMI's discovery, boot and metadata services with a small set of custom OpenShift artifacts. This lets us add bare-metal nodes to an OpenShift cluster as workers on demand. The immediate goal is to shorten the time from idle hardware to a serving model, often called "time to first token." We also want the provisioning path to be independent of any single workload manager or Kubernetes distribution.
We will share the architecture, where the integration was simple and where it depended on distribution-specific pieces, and what that tells us about portability. We will close with ongoing work: extending the approach to other Kubernetes management stacks, and the experimental OpenCHAMI Operator, which runs the OpenCHAMI control plane itself as a Kubernetes-native resource.

presentations.title: OpenCosmo Visualization: In-Browser Exploration of Cosmological Particle Data
presentations.abstract: Querying a cosmological simulation and seeing it are usually separated by a dedicated tool, a preprocessing step, and a broken workflow. The OpenCosmo Visualization Application (OVA) closes that gap inside the OpenCosmo Portal: a completed query opens directly into an interactive 3D view of the queried particles, in the same browser tab, with no export, installation, or preprocessing. Built on WebGL2 and Babylon.js, OVA adds per-type controls, dynamic filtering by scalar range, a 3D clipping plane, screen-space selection statistics, and one-click immersive WebXR on top of point rendering. Even on integrated laptop graphics, OVA ingests and renders 5M points of a HACC halo end-to-end in about 6.7 seconds, sustains 114.8 FPS, and records zero blocking main-thread tasks.

presentations.title: OpenEvolve-Driven Selection and Tuning of Ozaki-Scheme GPU Matrix Multiplication
presentations.abstract: Ozaki-Scheme is an established numerical method for emulating high-precision GEMM on low-precision GPU hardware. Using it means navigating a costly accuracy/performance tradeoff across algorithm variants and their tuning parameters. This work automates that process with a multi-stage pipeline combining rule-based variant selection with an LLM-driven evolutionary tuner (OpenEvolve). New features include a monotonicity-constrained XGBoost classifier predicting whether an accuracy target is reachable before spending GPU time and a throughput-priority mode trading bounded accuracy for up to 106.6% higher GFLOPS. A per-island-search fix stabilizes OpenEvolve convergence, widening the best-valid range from about 45-50K to 61-108K GFLOPS. In the Quantum ESPRESSO AUSURF112 workload, native cuBLAS remains 1.21x faster than the tuned complex-GEMM configuration, and the pipeline reaches 20.6x native cuBLAS on GB10 versus 1.42x on GH200. At the poster session, we will talk through the pipeline, presenting five result panels: throughput mode, feasibility classifier, OE-search convergence, AUSURF benchmark, and GH200/GB10 hardware comparison.

presentations.title: Opening Invited Talk: Tightly Coupled and Customizable Heterogeneity
presentations.abstract:
The slowing of Moore’s Law and the rapid growth of AI are pushing systems toward greater specialization across compute, memory, networking, and storage. At the same time, AI for Science is bringing simulation, analytics, training, inference, and agentic execution into increasingly connected workflows that need to share and move data efficiently. No single architecture is well suited to every part of these workflows.

This talk looks at tightly coupled and customizable heterogeneity as a way to build systems around these changing needs. A key focus will be macroheterogeneity, where different computing architectures work together as part of a larger system and each part of a workflow can run where it fits best. We will also look at customizable scale-up hypernodes, bringing compute, memory, accelerators, and high-bandwidth fabrics together in configurations shaped by workload needs. The goal is not simply to add more forms of heterogeneity, but to make them easier to couple, customize, and use as part of an end-to-end AI-HPC system.

presentations.title: Opening Panel Discussion - Uniting Research, Clinic and Patient
presentations.abstract: This panel will explore the different ways in which HPC works to unite cancer research, clinical care, and the patient experience, both directly and indirectly.

presentations.title: Opening Remarks by ISAV OC
Opening Remarks from Workshop Chair
OpenQSE: Building an Open Quantum-HPC Software Ecosystem
presentations.abstract: Quantum computing resources are increasingly integrated into HPC and cloud environments, but software stacks remain isolated, vendor-specific, and often proprietary. OpenQSE is a community effort developing an open, modular ecosystem of vendor-neutral specifications to close the interoperability gaps that fragment hybrid quantum-classical workflows. This BoF will briefly share the initiative's roadmap and working-group progress, then open the floor for structured discussion with HPC facility staff, application teams, vendors, and researchers to identify priorities and shape the direction together. The intended outcome is a prioritized set of integration artifacts the community identifies as most urgent for near-term development.

presentations.title: OpenSHMEM: Toward a Unified GPU-Aware Auxiliary Specification and 2.0
presentations.abstract: OpenSHMEM is a community-driven partitioned global address space (PGAS) API for low-overhead, one-sided asynchronous communication across diverse HPC architectures. This BoF will present progress since the 1.6 specification and discuss ongoing work toward OpenSHMEM 1.7, the proposed GPU auxiliary specification for accelerator support, and the longer-term OpenSHMEM 2.0 roadmap. As heterogeneous systems become the norm, the session will bring together users, implementers, middleware and tool developers, hardware vendors, and HPC facilities to share experiences, discuss evolving requirements, and help shape a simple, portable, and vendor-neutral future for OpenSHMEM.

presentations.title: Operational Data Analytics: Agentic AI for HPC Facilities
presentations.abstract: Operational data analytics (ODA) has become essential for understanding and optimizing HPC systems. However, converting the vast amounts of operational data they generate into actionable insights still requires significant manual effort and domain expertise. Agentic AI has the potential to extend traditional analytics by reading telemetry, correlating signals, diagnosing problems, and drafting fixes for an operator to approve. This BoF will explore the state of the art in agentic AI’s applicability to ODA, promising use cases, limitations, and governance challenges. Participants will share experiences and discuss how agentic AI can enhance future HPC operations and efficiency.

presentations.title: Operationalizing Workflow Support on Slurm: A Site Toolkit for Choosing Nextflow Deployment Strategie
presentations.abstract: Workflow-manager deployment choices determine which Slurm objects exist, how much controller load a workflow creates, and where accounting, policy, and failure isolation apply. We present an operator-run toolkit that freezes site and workload state, executes clean-start trials, attributes RPC demand to the benchmark identity, validates scientific completion, audits the campaign, and produces offline analyses. We apply it in three replicates to native Slurm, job arrays, HyperQueue, and Flux using a real 4,823-task Nextflow alignment workload on ASU’s Phoenix production cluster, with a private Dev cluster providing co-tenancy-free context. On Phoenix, arrays reduced both walltime and attributable RPC demand in every paired comparison while retaining per-element Slurm control. Flux reduced RPC demand further but ran longer than arrays; HyperQueue’s fastest median was not stable across replicates or clusters. We provide a constraint-first decision procedure, deployment configurations, and operational guidance for selecting a defensible site default.

presentations.title: Ops Knowledge That Stops Evaporating: Building an Evergreen Documentation, Search, and Monitoring System on an Agent CLI
presentations.abstract: Operational knowledge in HPC has a half-life measured in shifts. Queries get re-derived, negative results re-litigated, and incident reports cannot be reproduced months later. We describe a small, vendor-neutral system deployed at a large GPU-cluster site, and how to build your own in four weeks. Six pieces, five most sites already have: a terminal-native agent CLI, Model Context Protocol servers exposing telemetry read-only, versioned markdown procedures, a git repository, a local search index, and a few hundred lines of generator code. The load-bearing idea is not the model; it is a write-back rule under which any agent reading the knowledge verifies and extends it in the same task. The same repository distributes it: stable procedures become versioned skills, shipped to the team as a plugin through pull requests. A second-order effect surprised us: when a monitoring page costs a minute, dashboards become disposable. We close with anti-patterns and limits.

presentations.title: OPSERVE: Opportunistic LLM Inference over Fragmented GPU Capacity in HPC Systems
presentations.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference is an important GPU workload, while batch-scheduled HPC systems often leave nodes transiently idle because available resources cannot satisfy queued jobs. Our analysis of a year-long HPC trace finds that this unused capacity accounts for 9.81% of total node-hours and changes on timescales of seconds. Exploiting such transient capacity therefore requires serving decisions to adapt to resource availability and request demand. We present OpServe, a malleable LLM serving system that combines persistent and transient inference workers, adapts worker roles between prefill and decode, and reuses completed prefill state through shared KV storage. We evaluate three request traces with Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B. When both OpServe and a fixed prefill/decode baseline sustain the request arrival rate, OpServe reduces p95 end-to-end latency by 1.5–2.1×. Under overload, adaptive allocation reduces queue growth and yields up to 14.3× lower observed p95 end-to-end latency.

presentations.title: OptimasX: An Agentic End-to-End GPU Performance Optimization Workflow in the Code Editor
presentations.abstract: Optimizing a GPU kernel costs 30 manual steps before code changes: pick a profiler, reach a remote system, submit a job, read the report. Domain scientists hold the most GPU hours and the least profiling expertise, so no one tunes the code with the most to gain. OPTIMAS removes two steps by guiding a language model with runtime evidence, but assumes the user can produce it. We transformed OPTIMAS into OPTIMASX, a multi-agentic system that produces the evidence and removes all 32 steps. From a VS Code extension, OPTIMASX profiles code, reads evidence, proposes changes, checks correctness, and measures runtime. The extension holds workflow state, so a queued job or backend restart cannot end the session. On an A100, OPTIMASX reached 4.80× on XSBench and 1.19× on Sobol with bit-identical output, and extends to Cholla and eight HeCBench apps. The speedups are OPTIMAS’s, and the end-to-end automation is ours.

presentations.title: Optimizing Bloom Filters on Modern GPUs
presentations.abstract: Bloom filters are a fundamental data structure for approximate membership queries in applications ranging from analytics and databases to genomics. Deployed as prefilters, they eliminate irrelevant data before expensive downstream processing. As data-processing pipelines move onto GPUs, filtering must remain GPU-resident and keep pace with other stages. Although Bloom filters have been extensively optimized for CPUs, few implementations target GPUs, where fixed SIMD layouts map poorly to SIMT hardware and leave performance potential on the table. We present an architecture-aware GPU Bloom filter with tunable vectorization for performance portability across workloads, memory regimes, and GPU architectures. On NVIDIA B200, it sustains over $92\%$ of the measured random-access bound. At comparable false-positive rates, it outperforms the state-of-the-art GPU baseline by $15.4\times$ for lookup and $11.35\times$ for construction. These gains bring accurate Bloom filters to GPU-scale throughput previously reserved for high-error variants. The implementation is openly available in NVIDIA's cuCollections library.

presentations.title: Optimizing HPC Performance for CDC-Based Storage and Reconstruction of High-Resolution Imagery
presentations.abstract: High-resolution imagery is increasingly used for community asset management, environmental monitoring, and disaster response. These missions preserve details needed for inspection, but they can generate hundreds of gigabytes of data, creating long-term storage and transfer burdens. To reduce this burden, this study evaluates conditional diffusion compression (CDC) for storing and reconstructing high-resolution imagery on GPU supercomputers. We do not propose a new compression model. Instead, we study how CDC should be configured to make better use of HPC resources. Using 100 RGB images from Galveston, Texas, on NCSA DeltaAI GH200, we compare checkpoint and tiling settings by measuring compression ratio, runtime, throughput, peak GPU memory, image quality, artifacts, object detection, and segmentation stability. The balanced b00064 checkpoint with 256 × 256 tiling reduces peak GPU memory to 1.57 GB, reaches 45.4 images per hour, and keeps a 79.98× compression ratio.

presentations.title: Optimizing Podman Storage Performance on Shared Filesystems
presentations.abstract:
By default, Podman assumes that container image storage resides on local disks, reflecting its heritage as a developer-friendly tool designed for single workstations or servers. Currently it stores individual container layers as extracted tarballs using OverlayFS to merge them into a container file system. While efficient locally, extracting each layer to disk triggers metadata-heavy operations that perform poorly on shared filesystems like NFS and Lustre.

This presentation explores alternatives being proposed within the Podman ecosystem to address these limitations. Specifically, we will examine the imagefs storage plugin, which implements two backends optimized for shared filesystems: EROFS and SquashFS. SquashFS is well-known in the HPC community and we will also the potential of EROFS. We will present the storage plugin implementation, analyze its performance implications, and discuss how direct enhancements to the Podman ecosystem can alleviate container image storage challenges in HPC environments.

presentations.title: Optimizing Semiconductor Device Simulations through Low-Precision Arithmetic
presentations.abstract:
Architectural changes in GPUs, especially the boost in low-precision computational units, pose significant challenges to traditional, FP64-based high-performance computing (HPC) applications, while also presenting opportunities.
Adopting reduced-precision data formats is a promising avenue to exploit the increased throughput capabilities. However, straightforward data conversions may lead to degraded accuracy or even erroneous results. For a given application, only an in-depth analysis of its numerical stability can reveal the potential of low-precision arithmetic. In this work, we consider the open-source quatrex package, a quantum transport solver capable of breaking the sustained FP64 Eflop/s barrier, to illustrate trade-offs between accuracy losses and computational speed-ups when moving from high- to low-precision formats.
We use three representative benchmark structures to explore the application's numerical properties.
Applying the gained insights to a larger, more realistic system, we achieve up to 51% higher throughput while maintaining accurate results, on 40% fewer HPC resources than the FP64 reference.

presentations.title: Optimizing system memory bandwidth with micron CXL memory expansion modules on intel Xeon 6 processors
presentations.abstract: High-Performance Computing (HPC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads typically demand substantial memory bandwidth and, to a degree, memory capacity. CXL memory expansion modules, also known as CXL "type-3" devices, enable enhancements in both memory capacity and bandwidth for server systems by utilizing the CXL protocol which runs over the PCIe interfaces of the processor. This paper discusses experimental findings on achieving increased memory bandwidth for HPC and AI workloads using Micron's CXL modules. Memory expansion via CXL boosts read-only bandwidth by 24% and mixed read/write bandwidth by up to 39%. Across HPC and AI workloads, the geometric mean of performance speedups is 24%.

presentations.title: ORBIT: An AI-Powered Assistant for NOC Operations in a Data-Intensive Science Network
presentations.abstract: High-performance networks are critical infrastructure for data-intensive science, and their effective management relies on efficient incident response in Network Operations Centers (NOCs). This paper introduces the Operations Response \& Business Intelligence Toolkit (ORBIT), an AI-powered assistant that enhances incident response by consolidating information from disparate, siloed systems. ORBIT delivers synthesized results directly into the operator's primary work interface, applying agentic AI principles through a centralized reasoning service and a common model-access gateway. The system ensures transparency by logging all AI-generated outputs for operator review and rigorously controls access to sensitive data. In this paper, we describe the ORBIT architecture, present a selection of initial results from operational testing within ESnet’s NOC, and share lessons learned during its development and deployment; the complete findings are available in a companion technical report. Our findings highlight the importance of prompt engineering and a human-in-the-loop design for building trust and facilitating adoption.

presentations.title: ORBIT: An AI-Powered Assistant for NOC Operations in a Data-Intensive Science Network
presentations.abstract: ESnet shares its pragmatic journey developing AI tools that deliver measurable improvements to Network Operations Center efficiency. Rather than chasing trends, ESnet focused on AI-assisted ticket resolution. This presentation details two concrete applications — Intelligent Resolution Guidance that proactively surfaces relevant documentation, and Adaptive Incident Summarization that generates audience-tailored ticket summaries. Through systematic stakeholder engagement and incremental development, ESnet demonstrates how responsible AI implementation can genuinely augment operational capabilities. Attendees will gain practical insights on balancing AI capabilities with limitations, ensuring tools address real workflow pain points while integrating seamlessly into existing processes, and learn from both successes and challenges encountered.

presentations.title: Orchestrating QCSC Workflows in Containerized HPC Environments
presentations.abstract:
Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) is emerging as a model for scientific discovery in which quantum processors work alongside HPC resources as part of larger computational workflows. Realizing this model requires more than access to a quantum processor: applications must coordinate heterogeneous resources, manage different execution environments and support workflows that span HPC schedulers, workflow managers and quantum execution layers.

In this talk, we present our work integrating openQSE and QCSC-Prefect to develop and orchestrate QCSC workflows. openQSE provides a software stack for integrating quantum resources into HPC environments, while QCSC-Prefect uses Prefect to orchestrate quantum and classical workflow stages. We use these components within a containerized development environment that supports workflow development, debugging and integration testing before moving to larger HPC systems and quantum resources.

We demonstrate this approach using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD), a hybrid quantum-classical chemistry workflow that combines quantum sampling with classical processing and HPC-based diagonalization. Through this example, we illustrate how containerized environments can simplify workflow integration and validation while preserving flexibility in the underlying execution resources. We conclude with practical lessons and challenges from developing and validating the SQD workflow across the heterogeneous quantum and HPC execution stack.

presentations.title: Orchestrating the Future: Heterogeneous Disaggregation at Scale for Agentic AI Workloads
presentations.abstract:
As agentic AI and dynamic dataflow models increasingly dominate modern compute landscapes, monolithic architectures struggle to maintain optimal cost-performance ratios. This panel explores the heterogeneous disaggregation of AI workloads, addressing the critical systems-level challenges of orchestrating complex models across diverse, next-generation accelerators.

Panelists will discuss the evolution of software infrastructure, alongside advanced scheduling strategies required to manage dynamic execution and cost-aware SLAs. By decoupling memory, compute, and networking, we can achieve highly efficient, scalable execution in fragmented environments. Join experts as they debate the future of hardware-software co-design, evaluate marginal cost-efficiency trade-offs across contemporary AI hardware, and outline the system software innovations necessary to fully realize the potential of disaggregated infrastructure at scale.

presentations.title: Orion: Observability framework for hybrid workflow-centric I/O monitoring in HPC systems
presentations.abstract: Scientific workflows depend on efficient data exchange, making practical, low-overhead I/O performance visibility essential for HPC optimization. Existing I/O monitoring tools force extreme choices, such as tracing all I/O events or using only coarse profiling, which either inflates data volume or hides attribution context. We design ORION, a workflow-centric I/O monitoring framework that enables users to dynamically choose temporal and spatial monitoring granularity for different regions. ORION provides multi-faceted I/O profiling across time, processes, and files at low overhead; captures critical I/O events in high-interest regions while preserving aggregated views elsewhere; and reconciles traces with profiles at 0.35M–1.15M events/s for scalable analysis. On large-scale workloads, including Montage and Llama fine-tuning, ORION Selective Aggregation identifies critical bottlenecks with 6.8×–36× fewer trace events at 100% ordered top-k severe-bottleneck accuracy, and is portable across two heterogeneous LLNL systems. These results demonstrate that adaptive-granularity monitoring makes high-fidelity I/O analysis practical at HPC scale.

presentations.title: Orrery: Modeling and Simulation of GPU-direct MPI Communication with SimGrid
presentations.abstract: Simulation of HPC applications is an essential tool for analyzing system design trade-offs and enabling effective hardware–software co-design. As modern supercomputers increasingly rely on GPU acceleration, MPI implementations have evolved to support GPU-aware communication, enabling direct GPU data transfers. Modeling these mechanisms is therefore critical for simulating HPC applications on current systems. In this paper, we introduce Orrery, an interposition layer built on SimGrid’s SMPI to model GPU-aware MPI communication using existing collective implementations and flow-based simulation. Orrery intercepts GPU memory allocations, kernel launches, data transfers, and MPI operations, and models their execution in SimGrid according to target system specifications, enabling simulation without requiring physical GPUs. We validate Orrery using CUDA-aware MPI microbenchmarks and a Jacobi solver on up to 32 nodes of the MUSICA supercomputer and demonstrate that it reproduces key GPU-aware MPI mechanisms

presentations.title: Out-of-View Depth and Motion Prediction in Robotic Endoscopy
presentations.abstract: The endoscope can observe only a narrow cone of the surgical field. Tissue leaving this cone deforms, which can lead to injuries if unnoticed. The hidden region has no visible pixels, so depth and motion must be predicted rather than measured. Reusing the last observed depth is a strong baseline over short intervals, but its error grows as tissue deforms, reaching 9.05 mm at the longest interval. We adopted a pretrained V-JEPA2-AC encoder with low-rank adaptation, where two decoders predict depth and optical flow for the hidden region from a reference RGB-D frame and a later view showing 16% of the frame. Under leave-one-organ-out cross-validation on four ex vivo DRENDS organs, with CRCD in every training fold, the adapted model reduces hidden-region depth RMSE from 6.852 to 6.197 mm, and endpoint error against RAFT pseudo-flow from 3.285 to 3.004 px relative to assuming zero motion.

presentations.title: Overlay Containers in Apptainer
presentations.abstract:
Apptainer recently added the concept of overlay containers. Unlike OCI which natively uses many layers, Apptainer has always been based on a container image of one layer, which has advantages especially for HPC environments. It has also always supported overlay images, but they were solely for runtime and were of limited use. Apptainer now has an overlay option at build time that creates a container image that has only the defined additions/changes along with information to identify the base image, not the base image itself. The intended use case is for a software project to produce a shared base image containing the bulk of the software of the project, and for individual project members to each add their much smaller modifications in their own overlay container image. This aids especially in distribution, since the larger images change less often and can be pre-distributed using a more appropriate method.
~

presentations.title: PaFEx: Cross-platform Floating-point Exception Detection using LLVM and PAPI
presentations.abstract: Detecting floating-point exceptions defined by IEEE 754 across GPU vendors remains a conundrum, owing to varying hardware support for exception reporting. Existing tools address this problem through vendor-specific detection, requiring developers to use different tools to examine exception behavior on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. As HPC applications are deployed across different GPU architectures, this fragmentation limits the portability of diagnosing exceptions in GPU kernels. We present PaFEx, a cross-vendor tool that inserts runtime exception checks into GPU programs at the LLVM intermediate representation(IR) level. PaFEx runs on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, through shared exception checking logic, with vendor specific handling of device intrinsics and runtime integration. Across several HPC benchmarks, PaFEx incurs a geometric-mean slowdown of $1.30\times$ on NVIDIA and $1.70\times$ on AMD, measured over end-to-end execution. We also compare PaFEx with baseline tools, GPU-FPX and FloatGuard, examining similarities and differences in exception detection coverage and reporting.

presentations.title: Panel Discussion
Panel Discussion and Q&A: Challenges in AI-enabled Q-HPC Integration
Panel Discussion: Navigating the Future of Scientific Workflows
Panel: "Is Explicit Communication Obsolete? Compilers, Runtimes and On What Matters Next"
presentations.abstract:
As domain-specific accelerators gain importance and workloads increasingly exhibit structured, predictable communication patterns—particularly in machine learning, scientific computing, and tensor operations—the role of explicit communication primitives deserves renewed scrutiny. This panel examines whether the compiler and runtime stack should bear greater responsibility for inferring and optimizing communication, potentially relegating explicit APIs to legacy status.

The rise of Tile IRs and polyhedral compilation frameworks suggests a future where communication becomes an emergent property of program structure rather than a programmer directive. When tiling strategies, data dependencies, and memory hierarchies can be analyzed statically or just-in-time, do we still need developers to manually orchestrate point-to-point sends, broadcasts, and reductions? Or does the irregularity and dynamism of real applications—adaptive meshes, sparse data, load imbalance—ensure that explicit control remains essential?

This discussion will explore the tension between programmer productivity and performance portability, examining where today's compilation technology succeeds in hiding communication complexity and where it fails.

Panelists will debate whether the next decade belongs to smarter runtimes that auto-parallelize and auto-communicate, or whether the most demanding applications will always require the fine-grained control that only explicit communication provides.

presentations.title: Panel: Career Pathways Across Academia, Labs, & Industry: A Global View
presentations.abstract: How do careers in HPC and AI really unfold, and how do you move between academia, national labs and industry? Panelists share candid perspectives on career-defining decisions, and building expertise. The panel includes open Q&A, so participants can bring their own career questions.

presentations.title: Panel: Security of Interactive and Urgent sessions in the era of hacking AIs
presentations.abstract: The panel session will be a curated discussion about the featured talk, paper presentations, and lightning talks. Topics for the discussion are likely to include challenges with scheduling and running urgent streaming HPC jobs, tools for interactive HPC, use of agentic agents for interactive and urgent HPC, and security challenges with running interactive and streaming HPC systems.

presentations.title: Parallel and Accelerated Dependent Partitioning
presentations.abstract: Dependent partitioning is a flexible framework for compactly describing and efficiently computing partitions of distributed data structures that contain indirections and interconnected references. These data structures are commonly found in scientific applications, which operate over meshes, graphs, and sparse tensors. However, existing implementations of dependent partitioning process the individual elements of their input data sequentially on CPUs. This limitation makes dependent partitioning an expensive component of application initialization, and hinders its use in dynamic or on-line contexts. In this work, we present parallel algorithms for computing dependent partitions, and show that these algorithms perform well on accelerators like GPUs. Across a series of microbenchmarks and existing applications that use dependent partitioning, we show that our work achieves speedups of 9.4–9,807× for computing dependent partitions. We then show that our algorithms enable dynamic and on-line partitioning during steady-state execution.

presentations.title: Parallel Computing 101
presentations.abstract: This tutorial provides a comprehensive overview of parallel computing, emphasizing those aspects most relevant to the user. It is suitable for new users, students, managers, and anyone seeking an overview of parallel computing. It discusses software and hardware/software interaction, with an emphasis on standards, portability, and systems that are widely available. The tutorial surveys basic parallel computing concepts, using examples from multiple engineering, scientific, machine learning, and data analysis problems. These examples illustrate using MPI on distributed memory systems; OpenMP on shared memory systems; MPI+OpenMP on hybrid systems; and CUDA or compiler directives on GPUs and accelerators. It discusses numerous parallelization and load balancing approaches; performance improvement tools; and an overview of recent developments such as machine learning on accelerators and data analysis via parallel versions of Python. The tutorial helps attendees make intelligent decisions by covering the primary options that are available, explaining how the different components work together and what they are most suitable for. Extensive pointers to web-based resources are provided to facilitate follow-up studies.

presentations.title: Parallel Restore-Optimized Snapshot Compression for Cost-Efficient Inference Serving
presentations.abstract: Inference services incur cold-start costs from KV-cache profiling and CUDA-graph construction. Container checkpoints avoid repeated initialization, but large memory images consume storage and serial reconstruction delays restoration. We present PROCS, a parallel, restore-optimized compression method for CRIU snapshots. PROCS stores pages in VMA-bounded, page-addressable blocks, supports partial and incremental reads, and reconstructs bounded batches using reusable workers. It coordinates parallel restoration of private mappings, memory-backed files, and anonymous shared memory under restore-wide CPU and buffer limits. We implement PROCS in CRIUgpu and evaluate five SGLang inference models. With 256 KiB blocks and serial restoration, PROCS reduces snapshot size by 12.5–45.5% and restore-to-first-token latency by 7.2–44.7% relative to uncompressed CRIUgpu. At fixed parallelism, 1 MiB blocks reduce size by 6.2%, checkpoint time by 12.4%, and restore-to-first-token latency by 22.5% relative to 4 KiB encoding. For Qwen3.5 27B FP8, increasing decompression parallelism to 16 threads reduces CRIU’s restore latency by 25.8%.

presentations.title: Parallel Shortest Hyperpath Update in Large Dynamic Hypergraphs
presentations.abstract: Finding shortest paths is a well-studied graph problem, with parallel approaches for both static and dynamic settings. However, most existing methods target dyadic networks, where each edge represents an interaction between only two vertices. Many real-world systems involve group interactions, which are modeled more naturally by hypergraphs, where a hyperedge may connect any number of vertices. Moreover, these interactions are often time-dependent, leading to frequent topological changes in the underlying hypergraphs. Yet no scalable approach exists to efficiently update shortest paths, or hyperpaths, in large dynamic hypergraphs. To address this gap, we propose a parallel shortest hyperpath update method that uses a dynamic data structure to maintain the hypergraph, identifies the subgraphs affected by temporal changes, and efficiently updates previously computed shortest hyperpaths. Experiments show that our GPU-based implementation outperforms the recomputation-based baseline by an average speedup of 28.6x and up to 178.3x on large real-world hypergraphs.

presentations.title: Parameterized Verification of Deterministic MPI Programs
presentations.abstract: We consider the problem of verifying a message passing program in which the number of processes is a parameter NP and each process knows its unique ID. Processes communicate using send and receive commands which specify a single destination or source. To verify the program, the user provides functions specifying the number of messages sent from process i to process j, the level of each communication event in the happens-before hierarchy, and a fact that holds for the k-th message sent from i to j. These are used to transform the program to a parameterized sequential program which can be verified using any techniques appropriate for such programs. We realize this approach in an extension to Frama-C/Wp to verify C/MPI programs.

presentations.title: ParslBox: Computational Materials Workflow Executor for AI Agents on High Performance Computing Systems
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can autonomously construct large computational materials workflows, but executing these adaptive, fine-grained workloads efficiently across diverse high performance computing (HPC) systems remains challenging. We present ParslBox (PBX), a lightweight workflow execution toolkit for computational materials applications on HPC systems. PBX provides a local job database, fine-grained CPU/GPU resource management, portable execution across heterogeneous HPC systems, and command-line, Python, and Model Context Protocol interfaces for both users and AI agents. Scalability was demonstrated on up to 2,000 nodes and 24,000 concurrent workers while maintaining low orchestration overhead. Strong-scaling studies using LAMMPS with MACE models and VASP demonstrated transparent execution of production scientific applications. Agentic benchmarks showed reliable workflow construction across multiple closed-weight and open-weight language models. End-to-end agent-driven generation of machine-learned force fields for molten LiCl-NaCl and LiCl-KCl systems further demonstrated autonomous orchestration of complex multi-stage HPC workflows.

presentations.title: ParslBox: Computational Materials Workflow Executor for AI-Agents on High-Performance Computing Systems
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can autonomously construct large computational materials workflows, but executing these adaptive, fine-grained workloads efficiently across diverse high-performance computing (HPC) systems remains challenging. We present ParslBox, a lightweight workflow execution toolkit for computational materials applications on HPC systems. ParslBox provides a local job database, fine-grained CPU/GPU resource management, portable execution across heterogeneous HPC systems, and command-line, Python, and Model Context Protocol interfaces. Scalability was demonstrated on up to 2,000 nodes and 24,000 concurrent workers while maintaining low orchestration overhead. Strong-scaling studies using LAMMPS with MACE, and VASP demonstrated transparent execution of scientific applications. Agentic benchmarks showed reliable, repeatable job registration at scale across multiple closed-weight and open-weight language models. End-to-end agent-driven generation of machine-learned interatomic potentials for molten LiCl-NaCl and LiCl-KCl systems further demonstrated autonomous orchestration of complex multi-stage HPC workflows. Overall, ParslBox provides a portable, low-overhead execution layer for computational campaigns on leadership-class systems.

presentations.title: Past the FLOPS Era: Memory-Bandwidth Disaggregation as a Design-Space Coordinate for LLM Accelerators
presentations.abstract: LLM accelerator design inherited FLOPS-era HPC assumptions that today’s production serving no longer satisfies, foremost one high-bandwidth pool sized for weights. Key/value cache bandwidth demand overtakes weights at deployment batch sizes. We characterize accelerators by two bandwidth scalars (βw ,βs) and workloads by state-to-weight ratio ρ(n) and weight reuse r. Per decode latency splits across the two pools, and a local-minimum theorem proves the shared-pool corner strictly dominated past b·ρ(n) = 1, with the penalty at most 2×. The two-tier gain at equal cost rises from 1.6% at the balance point to 34% at 512K context, while one compromise design recovers 3.9%. Only 0.11% of the feasible designs in a 1,270,129-point space come within 10% of optimal. The contribution is a coordinate system in which memory-centric codesign can be reasoned about in hardware terms, not only at the serving layer: how the optimum migrates with context, and the trade-offs induced.

presentations.title: PATH: Path-Aware Adaptive Traffic at the Host for High-Performance Data Transfers

presentations.title: PathLlama: Domain-Adapted Language Models for Cancer Surveillance at Scale
presentations.abstract:
Population-based cancer surveillance depends on converting narrative pathology reports into structured tumor characteristics. Automated coding must handle ambiguous reports and rare tumor categories while allowing difficult cases to remain under expert review [1]. We investigate whether domain-specific continual pre-training improves cancer registry coding by a general-purpose language model with tunable abstention.

We adapted Meta Llama 3 8B [2] on 16.1 million clinical and cancer-registry records containing approximately 7.0 billion words from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program, MIMIC-III [3], and MIMIC-CXR [4]. The supervised dataset comprised 4,054,951 pathology reports from six SEER registries, with case-level splits. Five classification heads predict site, subsite, laterality, histology, and behavior, each with an additional abstention output. Development and evaluation ran within the secure CITADEL environment on Frontier. Supervised fine-tuning used Fully Sharded Data Parallelism [5], bfloat16 precision, partial layer freezing, and 64 nodes with 256 AMD MI250X modules.

A Deep Abstaining Classifier-inspired objective [6] learns when to defer each task. During training, a validation controller adjusts each task’s abstention penalty toward a chosen accuracy target among accepted predictions. The DAC is a tunable parameter and we tested it at both the 95% and 97.5% target configurations. At inference, the highest-scoring output determines the label or abstention, without confidence thresholding.

We compared domain-adapted PathLlama-adap with PathLlama-base, the same backbone fine-tuned directly using identical supervised protocols, on 395,299 held-out reports from five registries. The 95% target configuration used random sampling; the 97.5% configuration used sequential sampling, intended to stabilize controller updates through deterministic record coverage. Target and sampler effects were not tested separately. Comparisons were made within each configuration; targets were not guarantees of test accuracy.

PathLlama-adap produced more correct automatic labels per test report in all ten task/configuration comparisons and deferred fewer reports in nine, while accuracy among accepted predictions differed by at most 0.4 percentage points. For histology at the 95% target, abstention fell from 55.8% with PathLlama-base to 53.4% with PathLlama-adap, and macro F1 over the same 566 test classes increased from 0.4541 to 0.4782. At the 97.5% target, abstention fell from 75.5% to 73.7%, and this F1 increased from 0.3145 to 0.3366. For rare histology classes (11–50 test reports each), the mean fraction correctly auto-coded per class was 22.4% with PathLlama-adap versus 3.8% with the Hierarchical Self-Attention Network (HiSAN) at the 95% target. This secondary benchmark does not isolate continual pre-training.

Domain adaptation was associated with more correct automated cancer labels while maintaining similar accuracy among accepted predictions. Tunable abstention provides a mechanism for balancing automated coding with expert review. Findings remain descriptive and internal: each arm had one run, all test registries contributed training data, corpus overlap was unquantified, and additional pre-training exposure was not controlled. External, replicated evaluation is needed before operational use.

presentations.title: PauLIB: HPC Strategies for Pauli-Arithmetic-Based Quantum Computing Workloads and Simulations
presentations.abstract:
As quantum devices become accelerators within classical HPC deployments, the efficiency of the classical partition becomes critical. Workloads such as Hamiltonian manipulation, observable backpropagation, and Pauli-based compilation reduce to bulk arithmetic on Pauli strings and sums.

We present HPC strategies for this arithmetic, demonstrated in PauLIB, a header-only C++20 library: a bit-packed binary symplectic representation reducing Pauli multiplication to a bitwise XOR and population count; a sorted, struct-of-arrays layout replacing hash maps and exposing contiguous word arrays to SIMD units and GPU warps; and deterministic OpenMP parallelism with race-free output partitioning.

These strategies deliver orders-of-magnitude higher throughput and smaller memory footprint than Qiskit and PauliEngine, plus a speedup from a CUDA outer-product kernel on an H100. Two case studies, g-sim and truncated Pauli propagation, inherit these gains and scale unchanged from a laptop Arm CPU to a 72-core HPC Arm server. PauLIB is open source with C++ and Python interfaces.

presentations.title: PAW-ATM Intro
PDO Drug Screening Studies for Evaluating and Training AI Drug Response Prediction Models
presentations.abstract:
Background: Anti-cancer drug response prediction (DRP) is important for precision oncology and therapeutic development. Most DRP models are trained on drug screening data of immortalized cancer cell lines, which differ substantially from patient tumors in genomic and molecular characteristics and treatment response. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) better recapitulate patient tumors, but PDO drug screening data remain scarce.

Methods: We conducted four drug screening studies using PDOs from colorectal cancer, head and neck cancer, and sarcoma, generating matched treatment responses and omics data with multiple screening technologies. The four datasets contain: (1) 27 colorectal and 20 head and neck cancer PDO lines, 37 compounds, and 1,316 experiments (pairs of PDOs and compounds); (2) 4 colorectal PDO lines, 100 compounds, and 400 experiments; (3) 5 colorectal PDO lines, 40 compounds, and 200 experiments; and (4) 9 colorectal and 1 sarcoma PDO lines, 100 compounds, and 1,000 experiments. Screening technologies included multiplane high-content imaging using Rhodamine-Phalloidin, Caspase-3/7, To-Pro-3, and Hoechst staining, and ATP-based CellTiter-Glo assays. Overlapping PDO–compound experimental pairs across three of the studies enabled cross-platform correlation analyses to evaluate the reproducibility of PDO drug screening experiments. Using PDO response data, gene expressions, and drug molecular features, we evaluated six DRP algorithms (DeepTTC, UNO, GraphDRP, HiDRA, IGTD, and LightGBM) under two scenarios: (1) training models on cell-line drug screening data including 465,329 experiments and testing on the four PDO datasets; and (2) training models on cell-line data plus part of the PDO data and testing on the held-out PDO data. Both random-split and cancer-blind cross-validations were used; cancer-blind splits shared no cancer models across training, validation, and test sets.

Results: For shared experiments across studies, response measurements showed moderate agreement, with Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.371–0.645. In scenario 1, mean R² across the six algorithms for the four PDO datasets was 0.07, 0.25, -0.26, and 0.24 with random-split cross-validation, and 0.11, 0.25, -0.25, and 0.27 with cancer-blind cross-validation, indicating limited transferability of models trained only on cell-line data to PDOs. In scenario 2, mean R² improved to 0.73, 0.72, 0.55, and 0.71 with random splits, demonstrating a substantial benefit from incorporating PDO data in training. Under cancer-blind validation, scenario 2 achieved R² values of 0.57, 0.48, -1.40, and 0.58, improving prediction performance on three datasets compared with scenario 1.

Conclusion: We provide four AI-ready PDO drug screening datasets containing treatment responses, PDO multi-omics, and drug molecular features for the development and benchmarking of DRP models. Response measurements from different studies and technologies showed moderate consistency, supporting cross-study comparison while revealing platform variability. Across six algorithms and two validation schemes, models trained with both cell-line and PDO data generally outperformed models trained on cell-line data alone, showing the importance of including PDO data in training when predicting PDO responses. Lower and more variable performance under cancer-blind validation highlights the challenge of generalizing across cancer models. Future work will investigate transfer learning approaches that pre-train on large cell-line data and fine-tune on limited PDO data to improve generalization to new PDOs.

presentations.title: PDSW’26: The 11th International Parallel Data Systems Workshop
presentations.abstract: Efficient storage, movement, and management of data are crucial to application performance and scientific productivity in both traditional simulation-oriented HPC environments and cloud, AI/ML/big data analysis environments. This issue is further exacerbated by the growing volume of experimental and observational data, the widening gap between the performance of computational hardware and storage hardware, and the emergence of new data-driven algorithms in machine learning. The goal of this workshop is to facilitate in-depth discussions of research and development that address the most critical challenges in large-scale data storage and data processing. PDSW will continue to build on the successful tradition established by its predecessor workshops: the Petascale Data Storage Workshop (PDSW, 2006-2015) and the Data Intensive Scalable Computing Systems (DISCS, 2012-2015) workshop. These workshops were successfully combined in 2016, and the resulting joint workshop has attracted up to 45 full paper submissions and 195 attendees per year from 2016 to 2025.

presentations.title: Peachy Parallel Assignments (EduHPC 2026)
presentations.abstract:
Peachy Parallel Assignments are tested and ready-to-adopt assignments to teach parallel and distributed computing concepts. They are selected competitively for being "cool and inspirational" so that students spend time working on them. After selection, they are presented at the Edu* series of workshops.

This article describes three assignments presented at the EduHPC 2026 workshop. The first is an unplugged assignment that introduces MapReduce concepts by having students count word occurrences in a popular children's book. In the second assignment, students parallelize a power grid simulation using multiple parallel programming abstractions (OpenMP for shared memory systems, MPI for distributed memory systems, and CUDA/HIP/OpenCL for GPUs).
