For the third assignment, they perform distributed fine tuning of a Large Language Model (LLM), a popular but extremely resource-intensive application.

presentations.title: Pelicanvil: A Web Platform for Discovering, Browsing, and Accessing Federated Datasets on HPC
presentations.abstract: Pelican is a data-federation platform, and the Open Science Data Federation (OSDF) is a national federation built on it, letting researchers pull external datasets into HPC workflows without maintaining a local copy. Whether this is viable in practice remains unclear. A feasibility study benchmarking Pelican/OSDF against local and object storage on a production HPC cluster found performance workable but surfaced two barriers: no federation-wide catalog surfaces dataset metadata, search, and streamability up front, and whether a dataset streams per file or downloads depends on how it's packaged at the origin. In response, we built Pelicanvil, an infrastructure-agnostic web platform running inside a production cluster's Open OnDemand portal that gives researchers a single interface for discovering, browsing, and accessing federated datasets, through generated code snippets or direct download. This work offers HPC support teams a measured answer on Pelican's production readiness and a concrete response to the barriers found.

presentations.title: PerfDecode: Accelerating LLM Decoding on Systolic Arrays via Performance Modeling
presentations.abstract:
The autoregressive nature of large language model
(LLM) decoding results in matrix multiplications with small
token dimensions, which underutilize systolic arrays and exhibit
low arithmetic intensity. Efficient execution of these workloads
requires jointly improving processing-element utilization and
coordinating data movement with computation under limited
on-chip memory. We present PerfDecode, a performance-model-
guided approach to accelerating LLM decoding on systolic
arrays. PerfDecode reorganizes matrix multiplication execution
to exploit idle processing elements and pipeline data movement
with computation. At its core, an analytical performance model
captures DMA transfer and launch overhead, systolic-array com-
putation, reduction and write-back costs, and on-chip memory
constraints to automatically determine blocking configurations
for different matrix shapes. On AWS Trainium2, PerfDecode
consistently outperforms tiled matmul across diverse decode
operators in Llama-3-8B and Llama-3-70B, achieving geometric-
mean speedups of 2.73× and 2.85×, respectively.

presentations.title: Performance Analysis of Inline Compression on Sparse Matrix Vector Multiplication ​
presentations.abstract: Sparse matrix vector multiplication (SPMV) plays a critical role in scientific computing. From computational fluid dynamics, to artificial intelligence, to economics problems, the use cases are vast. Additionally, the data required for high performance computing (HPC) jobs is quickly outgrowing available memory storage. In-line compression aims to mitigate this memory bottleneck by keeping data compressed in storage and only decompressing as needed. We analyze the effects of performing this in-line compression with SPMV and apply various optimizations to examine their effects on execution time and the overall memory footprint.

presentations.title: Performance Analysis of Phaseless Auxiliary Field Quantum Monte Carlo
presentations.abstract: Predicting molecular behavior requires knowing a molecule's ground-state energy, a calculation whose exact cost grows exponentially with system size. Phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (ph-AFQMC) approximates this energy via guided random walks, where accuracy and cost depend heavily on the quality of the trial wavefunction used to steer the walk. We compare two quantum methods for preparing this trial wavefunction, the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and the Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE), benchmarked on NERSC Perlmutter using linear hydrogen chains. At H8 (16 qubits), GQE reduces end-to-end pipeline wall-time by roughly 5x relative to ADAPT-UCCSD, while matching VQE-family accuracy near equilibrium bond length. These results motivate extending the study to H10 chains and multi-node scaling to determine whether GQE's cost advantage persists at larger, more strongly correlated systems.

presentations.title: Performance Characterization of GPU Sharing Strategies for LLM Inference
presentations.abstract: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs), demand has grown for LLM inference services that run continuously within High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments. Because inference requests vary over time, GPU resources dedicated to a single model may remain idle during periods of low demand. Sharing these resources among multiple inference workloads can improve GPU utilization. This paper compares two approaches for concurrently serving multiple models on a single NVIDIA H100 PCIe GPU: software-level GPU sharing using vLLM and hardware-level GPU partitioning using vLLM in combination with Multi-Instance GPU (MIG). We evaluate both approaches while varying the number of concurrently running models and the offered load. The results show that MIG-based GPU partitioning provides stable performance and slightly outperforms software-based GPU sharing when all GPU instances are fully utilized. In contrast, software-based GPU sharing exploits otherwise idle GPU resources, achieving higher throughput and lower latency when fewer models run concurrently.

presentations.title: Performance comparison and analysis of macroscopic cross section lookup kernel on Cerebras CS-3 and NVIDIA GPUs
presentations.abstract: The Cerebras CS-3 integrates approximately 900,000 processing elements in a two-dimensional mesh and provides high memory bandwidth and an exceptionally high B/F ratio, making it attractive for memory-bound scientific workloads. We evaluate a computational kernel that abstracts the macroscopic cross section lookup in XSBench, a Monte Carlo particle transport mini-app, characterized by low arithmetic intensity and irregular random memory accesses. We measure maximum performance, strong scaling, and weak scaling on CS-3, analyze the factors contributing to its improvement over CS-2, and compare it with optimized implementations on NVIDIA GH200 and A100 GPUs. Without additional optimization, the CS-3 implementation achieves 9.44E+09 lookups/s and an 11% higher geometric-mean performance than CS-2. Under identical experimental conditions, it delivers 6.34× and 11.90× higher throughput than GH200 and A100, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of CS-3 for irregular, memory-intensive lookup workloads. Our analysis also highlights how wafer-scale architecture benefits this challenging class of kernels.

presentations.title: Performance Evaluation of a Heterogeneous CPU-GPU Framework for Real-Time ECG Analytics
presentations.abstract: Real-time cardiac digital twins require analytics pipelines that are both computationally efficient and diagnostically accurate. This paper presents a heterogeneous high performance computing framework integrating OpenMP parallelized CPU preprocessing with a CUDA-accelerated convolutional neural network for ECG beat classification using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. The preprocessing pipeline achieved a 4.85× speedup and 79% runtime reduction using eight CPU threads. The GPU classifier achieved 78.17% accuracy, a macro-ROC–AUC of 0.773, and throughput of 175,712 beats/s, representing an 11.2× improvement over CPU batch inference. A Digital Twin Readiness Assessment Framework evaluated predictive performance, computational efficiency, scalability, and deployment feasibility. Results indicate that preprocessing and inference satisfy real-time requirements, while classification of minority arrhythmia classes remains the primary limitation. Future work will focus on optimizing the classification model to improve minority-class performance and overall digital twin readiness.

presentations.title: Performance Improvement of Multi-Dimensional Parallel Loops in Kokkos
presentations.abstract: This paper presents performance improvements for tightly nested multi-dimensional parallelism in the Kokkos library. We show how this can be implemented for GPU and CPU backends, which leads to improved performance and code maintainability. A widely used library like Kokkos needs to be updated in a manner that is friendly to the users and the developers. Using various benchmarks, we show how our work enables Kokkos users to write performance-portable code in a productive manner.

presentations.title: Performance Portability of Multi-GPU Hydrodynamics: SCALSALE with MPI+OpenMP Target Offload
presentations.abstract:
Directive-based offload enables portable GPU execution from one source, yet evaluations usually use microbenchmarks or compact kernels. We extend SCALSALE, a Modern Fortran full multi-material Lagrangian--Eulerian hydrodynamics proxy application, to multi-node GPU execution using MPI+OpenMP without vendor-specific paths. This required restructuring branch-heavy Eulerian advection and replacing host-staged halo exchange with GPU-aware MPI over device-resident buffers.
Tests on NVIDIA A100 and Intel Max 1550 GPUs and an Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ CPU yield weak-scaling efficiencies of 84%-91% within a GPU node, 88%-91% acrosss three GPU nodes, and higher 95%-96% across CPU nodes because longer computation amortizes communication.
Using Pennycook's metric with hierarchical-Roofline efficiencies, performance-portability scores are 34.9% (Eulerian) and 37.9% (Lagrangian) over all platforms, and 44.1% and 42.2% over the GPUs, respectively. Streaming kernels attain 63%-83% of their ceilings across architectures, whereas the dominant advection sweep ranges from 84% to 13%, identifying the optimization target.

presentations.title: Performance Tuning of HPC and ML/AI Applications with the Roofline Model on GPUs, APUs, and CPUs
presentations.abstract: The Roofline performance model offers an insightful and intuitive method for extracting the key execution characteristics of HPC and ML/AI applications and comparing them against the performance ­bounds of modern CPUs and GPUs. Its abilities to abstract the complexity of memory hierarchies and identify the most profitable optimization techniques have made Roofline­-based analysis increasingly popular in the HPC and ML/AI communities. Although different flavors of the Roofline model have been developed, there remains a need for a systematic methodology when applying them to analyze applications running on multicore and accelerated systems. The tutorial aims to bridge this gap on both CPUs and GPUs by both exposing the fundamental aspects behind different Roofline modeling principles as well as providing several practical use­ case scenarios that highlight their efficacy for performance and energy optimization as well as understanding performance portability. This tutorial presents a unique combination of instruction in Roofline by its creator, hands-on instruction in using Roofline within NVIDIA’s, AMD’s, and Intel’s production performance tools, and discussions of real-world Roofline use cases at NERSC, ALCF, and OLCF. The tutorial presenters have a long history of collaborating on the Roofline model and have presented several Roofline-­based tutorials.

presentations.title: Performance-Portable Exact Gaussian Process Regression in Python via SYCL and oneMath
presentations.abstract:
Modern multi-vendor GPU environments force a choice between portable code and native performance.
GPRat is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the HPX asynchronous many-task runtime, tiled algorithms, and CPU/CUDA BLAS backends.
We contribute a UXL Foundation oneMath backend with a hybrid HPX/SYCL design, extending GPRat to AMD and Intel GPUs.
The new SYCL backend comes within \qty{3}{\percent} of native CUDA on an NVIDIA A30 at the largest problem size and outperforms the GPflow and GPyTorch libraries by up to $1.75\times$ and $2.17\times$ on the A30 and up to $1.79\times$ and $4.62\times$ on an AMD Instinct MI210.
On an Intel Arc B580, a consumer-class card with FP64 throughput below our CPU's, the unmodified SYCL backend trails GPRat's CPU backend.
Overall, oneMath's dispatch to vendor-native BLAS lets a single SYCL codebase match CUDA on NVIDIA and outperform established Python GP frameworks on AMD, without vendor-specific code.

presentations.title: Performance-Portable GPU Acceleration of MOM6 with Standard Fortran and OpenMP
presentations.abstract:
We describe a performance-portable GPU implementation strategy for the MOM6 ocean model, where portability is realized through a single codebase built on language standards while maintaining competitive performance on target CPU and GPU platforms. The implementation uses standard Fortran ``do concurrent`` as the kernel-level expression of parallelism, with OpenMP support for device-data residency and GPU-aware MPI communication.

Performance results show GPU acceleration of the dynamic core up to 3x relative to a single-socket CPU baseline while preserving bitwise-identical CPU and GPU results. Fixed-domain tests show scaling across multiple H100 GPUs. Module-level timings show that solver taxonomy guides the porting strategy but does not by itself predict realized speedup.

presentations.title: Performance-Portable GPU Acceleration of the Hybrid PIC Code dHybridR
presentations.abstract: Hybrid particle-in-cell simulations are widely used to study kinetic processes in collisionless astrophysical and space plasmas, yet the high cost of large-scale three-dimensional runs has largely confined production studies to two dimensions or restricted domains. To address this challenge, we present a performance-portable GPU implementation of the hybrid particle-in-cell code dHybridR. It combines OpenMP target offloading with specialized SYCL kernels for the most expensive operations in a unified CPU-GPU codebase for Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs. On the exascale supercomputers Aurora and Frontier, dHybridR achieves weak scaling efficiencies of 86%–97% at 49,152 accelerators on each machine, and at 256 particles per cell, its full-node GPU throughput is up to 32x that of the vectorized CPU implementation at approximately 90% less energy per particle-update. To our knowledge, no other hybrid particle-in-cell code has reported GPU performance at this scale. These advances lower the barrier to large-scale three-dimensional hybrid-kinetic simulations.

presentations.title: perfSONAR in the Cook County Community
presentations.abstract: NRI106, NRI107

presentations.title: Perlmutter-Agent: Design and Early Deployment of a Local, Tool-Grounded LLM Assistant for HPC Incident Investigation
presentations.abstract: HPC incident investigation requires system administrators to correlate metrics, logs, and ticket history across heterogeneous data sources. We present Perlmutter-Agent, a locally deployed, tool-grounded large language model (LLM) assistant for incident investigation on NERSC’s Perlmutter supercomputer. An orchestrator converts Slack messages into structured requests and dispatches them to specialized metrics, logs, and ticket sub-agents. Guided by site-specific agent skills, the sub-agents query operational data through MCP servers and return evidence that the orchestrator summarizes into likely causes. All agents use an open-weight Qwen3.8-27B model served locally by vLLM, keeping operational data from external model providers. In a restricted beta, 339 of 380 user requests (89.2\%) completed successfully; diagnostic accuracy and operator usefulness remain to be evaluated.

presentations.title: PERNIX: High-Throughput SIMD Floating-Point Compression
presentations.abstract: Scientific applications increasingly spend time and energy moving floating-point data between CPUs, memory, and accelerators. PERNIX is an open-source C++ library for block-wise floating-point compression and decompression on CPUs, motivated by the transfer and storage of electron repulsion integrals in CP2K. It combines established quantization with novel SIMD bit-packing and unpacking kernels for AVX2, AVX2+BMI2, and AVX-512-VBMI. Table-driven permutations, shifts, and sign extension enable efficient processing of non-byte-aligned widths. ARM NEON and SVE2 backends are under development. We evaluate in-core throughput, cache and DRAM behavior, and end-to-end host-to-device and device-to-host PCIe pipelines. The poster presents the 512-bit format, SIMD design, measured-versus-modeled throughput, and end-to-end transfer results.

presentations.title: Photonics for AI and HPC: Breaking the Bandwidth and Power Barrier
presentations.abstract: As AI and HPC systems scale to unprecedented levels, traditional electrical interconnects are becoming a limiting factor. Silicon photonics offers a promising path to address bandwidth, energy efficiency and interconnect scalability constraints, but questions remain around deployment readiness, integration complexity and ecosystem maturity. Led by industry analyst Dan Olds, this session brings together experts from Penguin Solutions, Marvell and Micron to explore photonic interconnects from multiple perspectives. Panelists will discuss the technology’s value today, the technical and operational challenges ahead, where photonics can make the greatest impact, and what the broader ecosystem must do to accelerate real-world adoption.

presentations.title: PILOT: Parallel Implementation via LLM-Oriented Translation
presentations.abstract:
This paper presents PILOT, a Python-based workflow that automates the translation of serial C/C++ source code into parallel implementations targeting selected backends using Large Language Models (LLMs). The workflow implements an iterative compilation-error correction cycle that maintains multi-turn conversational context with the LLM, enabling automatic recovery from synthesis errors in successive rounds. Functional correctness is verified automatically by comparing the outputs of the original serial
program and the translated parallel version. PILOT further quantifies the achieved parallelization quality by measuring the execution speedup relative to the serial code. The system is evaluated across five state-of-the-art LLMs spanning diverse architectures. Tests were conducted on fifteen computational benchmarks and four parallel models. Results show that compilation success rates range from 88% to 100% depending on the backend, with MPI and Go achieving perfect compilation across all models. Kernel-level speedups reach up to 48.75× for Go and 31.84× for OpenMP on favorable benchmarks.

presentations.title: PInsight: Enabling In-Situ Performance Analysis for Parallel Applications
presentations.abstract:
Performance analysis of parallel HPC applications is today a
post-mortem workflow: measurement data is collected during a
run, then moved and analyzed after the application terminates,
and each tuning hypothesis costs another full execution. In this
paper, we present PInsight (Performance Insight), a frame-
work that leverages this iterative structure to enable in-situ
performance analysis of applications spanning MPI, OpenMP,
CUDA, and HIP in a single time-aligned trace. PInsight combines
asynchronous tracing via LTTng with rate-controlled per-region
sampling measurement, under a four-mode domain architecture
with fine-grained filtering, tracing windows, node-level GPU
activity policies, and runtime reconfiguration without application
restart. Its analysis toolkit, both scripts and GUI, can consume
the traces both post-hoc and in situ: window-end actions rotate
the trace and launch analyses during execution with sub-second
pause, turning a long-running application into a sequence of
measure–analyze windows

presentations.title: Placing the Control Plane: Cloud-Native Federated Learning across Batch-Scheduled HPC
presentations.abstract: The United Kingdom's AI Research Resource (AIRR) opens national supercomputers to a community familiar with always-reachable cloud services. With batch-scheduled HPC, a user requests a time-bounded allocation that is then reclaimed. Federated Learning (FL) exposes this tension, pairing a long-lived control plane with short-lived training. We characterize the resulting placement asymmetry: the coordination server sees only model updates and control metadata, so it can sit on neutral infrastructure, whereas the client control process is bound to the participating site's data and must remain within its trust boundary. The outbound-only connection this implies is also how edge clients connect, though the batch-scheduler mismatch is specific to HPC. We demonstrate a cross-silo federation spanning three independently administered systems (Isambard-AI, Isambard 3, and Zenith) using unmodified production FL frameworks (FLARE-wrapped Flower), measure the cost the client placement incurs, and propose Kubernetes-as-a-service as the in-boundary home for the persistent process.

presentations.title: Platform-Agnostic Kernel Fusion Pipeline for Linear Algebra Kernels in MLIR
presentations.abstract:
We present a platform-agnostic transformation pipeline that blends kernel fusion
and algebraic optimization. Our approach begins with tensor-form linear algebra
operations in a Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) module and
automatically discovers compatible producer-consumer regions. The operations in
each region are represented and composed in Einstein notation. We use exact
operand-subset dynamic programming to select a binary contraction order,
lexicographically minimizing scalar multiplication work followed by logical
intermediate volume. The selected contractions are reconstructed in MLIR, and an
automatic partitioner selects connected fusion groups according to removable
logical storage, parallel-domain compatibility, and reduction topology. After
bufferization, the selected groups are outlined, their concrete memory
dependences are checked, compatible parallel loops are fused, and eligible
intermediates are forwarded as scalars. We implement the complete transformation
in Linear Algebra Performance through Intermediate Subprograms (LAPIS), an
MLIR-to-Kokkos compiler framework, so one optimized module can target backends
supported by Kokkos execution spaces.

presentations.title: Plenary Talk: Jerry Chow
Plenary Talk: Tanner Crowder
Plexus-v2: Extreme-Scale GNN Training with Communication-Free Sampling and 4D Hybrid Parallelism
presentations.abstract: GNNs are widely used for learning on graph datasets derived from various real-world scenarios. Learning from extremely large graphs requires distributed training, and mini-batch training is a popular approach for parallelizing GNN training. Existing distributed mini-batch approaches have significant performance bottlenecks due to expensive sampling methods and limited scaling when using data parallelism. We present Plexus-v2, a four-dimensional hybrid parallel framework for scalable mini-batch GNN training that combines communication-free distributed sampling, three-dimensional parallel matrix multiplication, and data parallelism. Plexus-v2 introduces a uniform vertex sampling algorithm, enabling each process to construct its local shard of subgraph without any inter-process communication. Combining 3D PMM with data parallelism enables Plexus-v2 to scale to much larger GPU counts than vanilla data parallelism with significantly lower communication overheads. We evaluate Plexus-v2 on five graph datasets and scale to 2,048 GPUs/GCDs. On Perlmutter, Plexus-v2 achieves 3.5x end-to-end training speedup over the best-performing SOTA frameworks on ogbn-products.

presentations.title: PMBS Discussion
PMBS Welcome
PMBS26: The 17th International Workshop on Performance Modeling, Benchmarking, and Simulation of High Performance Computer Systems
presentations.abstract:
The PMBS26 workshop is concerned with the comparison of high performance computing systems through performance modeling, benchmarking, or through the use of tools such as simulators. We are particularly interested in research that reports the ability to measure and make trade-offs in software/hardware co-design to improve sustained application performance. We are also keen to capture the assessment of future systems.

The aim of this workshop is to bring together researchers, from industry and academia, concerned with the qualitative and quantitative evaluation and modeling of high performance computing systems. Authors are invited to submit novel research in all areas of performance modeling, benchmarking, and simulation, and we welcome research that brings together current theory and practice. We recognize that the term "performance" has broadened to include power consumption and reliability, and that performance modeling is practiced through analytical methods and approaches based on software tools and simulators.

presentations.title: Portable, High-Performance and Differentiable Ocean Simulations with Unstructured Grids in Julia
presentations.abstract:
Ocean models are increasingly required to be two things at once: performance-portable
across heterogeneous accelerators, and differentiable, so that adjoint sensitivities are available for state estimation, parameter calibration, and gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we introduce a software package for simulating the ocean system with these attributes, implemented in Julia. Anonymized.jl is a shallow-water ocean dynamical core discretized with the TRiSK scheme on unstructured Voronoi meshes, following the MPAS-Ocean software written in Fortran. Anonymized.jl is designed to run on CPUs and GPUs with architecture-independent kernel implementations and supports differentiable programming. Here, we describe the implementation of two configurations within Anonymized.jl and benchmark their performance on different accelerator devices.

presentations.title: Porting and Benchmarking Chapel on Emerging RISC-V Hardware: An HPC Viability Study
presentations.abstract:
The Chapel programming language recently added support for the RISC-V architecture.
Here we discuss what changes were needed for Chapel to work on RISC-V as well as lessons learned from the porting process.
We use some of Chapel's extensive benchmark suite to gain further insight into the suitability of the RISC-V architecture for future HPC use.
We compare performance on SiFive P550 and Unmatched boards and a Sophon SG2042 with a variety of other recent HPC CPU platforms.
Various portability and performance anomalies arose on different architectures and are discussed.
While the RISC-V machines represent smaller preliminary offerings and not HPC-class hardware, these results still provide hope that RISC-V hardware can become viable for HPC in the near future.

presentations.title: Porting Codes to the NextSilicon Maverick-2 Dataflow Architecture: Early Experience, Best Practice and Performance
presentations.abstract: Porting parallel code to accelerators such as GPUs, FPGAs, or AI Accelerators often requires major changes. In contrast, the new NextSilicon Maverick-2 dataflow architecture and framework transparently accelerate OpenMP code without explicit offloading statements, offering a practical energy-efficient high-performance computing (HPC) platform. We present preliminary best practice, porting experience, and early performance results for the Maverick-2 architecture, its programming models, and the OpenMP-based code-to-device development workflow. The in-house proxy apps used in the benchmark cover several application domains typical for the tier-2 HPC system at NHR@ZIB: computational fluid dynamics, large-eddy simulations, molecular dynamics, and electronic structure theory.

presentations.title: Portrait of Data Center
presentations.abstract:
A supercomputer has vital signs: a temperature, a metabolism, and a heartbeat. This piece paints them. Streaming GPU telemetry (utilization, power draw, temperature, and interconnect traffic) drives a generative flow field: thousands of particles drift and glow, each colored by heat, brightened by power, their speed set by how hard the machine is thinking. Nothing is invented; every gesture is a reading of the machine's own body.

The work is deliberately multi-dimensional. One dimension is data, which is the honest mapping of live signals to light. Another is choreography, drawn from Martha Graham's foundational language of modern dance: contraction and release. Graham built movement from the body's core, a gathering inward that coils tension, then an expansive release outward. Here the machine's heartbeat performs exactly that: on each slow breath the particles are drawn toward the core, gathering; then, on the release, they are expelled outward in a bloom of light and sparks, timed to the pulse. As load climbs from idle to peak, the breath deepens and the release becomes a throw. A supercomputer that is moving through its own register, from rest to full, dramatic exertion.

The third dimension is metaphor: the data center as a living, feeling body, its telemetry the score to which it dances. By borrowing Graham's grammar of gather-and-expel, the piece asks the audience to read a machine not as cold infrastructure but as a performer; one whose choreography is authored not by a human hand but by the physics of computation itself. High performance computing, rendered as contemporary dance.

presentations.title: PortWarp: A Cycle-Accurate GPU-Accelerated HPC Network Simulator Using Port-per-Thread Model
presentations.abstract: The cycle-accurate modeling methodology, used by popular tools such as BookSim2, Gem5, and SST, has become a de facto standard for modeling HPC networks and systems. However, single-threaded cycle loops limit the system size and time scales that can be explored. In this work, we developed PortWarp, a new cycle-accurate approach that efficiently models exascale-class HPC network designs by leveraging GPU accelerators. Because the thread-per-port mapping is hardware-agnostic, the identical validated build achieves 445x speedup on an NVIDIA H100 and 513x speedup on a B100 GPU, with the additional gain coming entirely from newer hardware. Per-port-occupancy instrumentation confirms that in the saturation regime where those speedups are realized, nearly every port-thread performs useful work each cycle. Overall, we are encouraged by PortWarp's performance gains and believe this modeling approach could be applied to other HPC computer systems modeling domains.

presentations.title: Powering Africa’s AI Future: Affordable Renewable Energy Pathways for Sustainable HPC and Datacenters
Pre-Training AuroraGPT on Intel XPUs
presentations.abstract: AuroraGPT pre-trains open foundation models for science on Aurora, an HPE Cray EX system of ~127,000 Intel Max-series XPUs and one of the largest non-NVIDIA GPU systems in production. Training at this scale on a SYCL/oneCCL stack, rather than CUDA/NCCL, surfaces portability and reliability problems the usual toolchain does not address. We present an open, portable stack: ezpz, a launcher that runs the same unmodified PyTorch script across Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, and an experiments/ezpz fork of TorchTitan. The completed AuroraGPT-2B run reached 7.77T tokens; on the migrated stack, an in-flight 20B run matches that fully-trained 2B's peak evaluation scores at comparable compute while consuming ~17x fewer tokens. We detail the failures behind these numbers: a silent loss-reporting bug caught only by bit-exact regression, an 80B instability that NaN'd three optimizers, and a launcher-native auto-retry protocol that eliminated a silent-failure mode responsible for nine lost runs in two weeks.

presentations.title: Predict Before Replay: Joint FEC and Flight Control for Reliable Scale-Up Links
presentations.abstract: Scale-up accelerator fabrics send latency-sensitive flits over serial links at hundreds of gigabits per second. Their reliability pipeline first relies on FEC, then detects residual failures and replays unacknowledged data. At these line rates, delayed feedback lets later flits enter the replay window before a residual failure is reported, so standard replay can amplify one corrupted flit into a suffix retransmission. This paper presents PREFACE, a pre-FEC controller for temporally correlated burst errors. A two-state Bayesian filter converts corrected-symbol observations into a next-flit burst posterior and jointly selects FEC strength with an outstanding-flit cap. We implement PREFACE in ns-3 with publicly verifiable UALink 200G 1.0 replay semantics. PREFACE improves goodput by 10.52%, lowers P99 latency by 50.75%, cuts replay by 47.52%, and improves modeled ring AllReduce by 13.1–27.0%.

presentations.title: Predicting and Explaining Alzheimer Disease Using UK Biobank: An Auditable, Cost-Sensitive HPC Pipeline for Feature Discovery
presentations.abstract:
Age is the strongest known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, and when it is left in the feature set it dominates both prediction and explanation. This work presents an auditable pipeline over UK Biobank tabular data, built for SLURM job arrays on the Discoverer supercomputer. It removes direct age and event-timing fields, reduces 4,366 candidate features to 95 with every removal logged, and fits a sparse lasso logistic regression on a cohort of 10,550 participants.

Test AUC falls from 0.84 with age kept to 0.75 in the controlled model. The features that remain most important by SHAP are vascular, body-size, lipid and blood markers, led by systolic blood pressure, weight and small-LDL cholesterol. At an assumed 1% prevalence, only about 1 in 74 positive predictions would be a true case, so the pipeline is positioned for hypothesis generation, not screening.

presentations.title: Predicting the Energy-Optimal GPU Clock for Production VASP Jobs Before They Run
presentations.abstract: VASP is a dominant HPC workload, and while many users are migrating their workflows to GPUs, not every job uses the hardware efficiently. Lowering the GPU clock for these jobs can reduce their energy consumption with limited impact on performance. However, the right clock differs from job to job. We present a model for per-job energy optimization, one that chooses each job’s clock from its input files alone, before the job runs. Every job’s slowdown follows the same machine-wide curve as the clock drops, scaled by a per-job sensitivity, and this shared curve carries 99.72% of the variance across jobs. Hence choosing the clock needs only the sensitivity, predicted from the submitted files. Under a 5% slowdown budget the selection saves 14.25% of GPU-board energy on 310 production GH200 jobs at 5.45% mean slowdown, and the median job lands on budget at 4.92%. The error concentrates in the most clock-sensitive jobs, whose sensitivity is underpredicted, but it falls as the corpus grows, so the remedy is more training data. Finally, the model transfers. We show sensitivity carries across machines, so a single calibration job maps the model onto an A100, and a handful of jobs settles the delivered clocks.

presentations.title: Predictive Modeling of Effective Peak Throughput for Regional In-Network Caching
presentations.abstract:
Large-scale scientific experiments, particularly in high-energy physics, generate massive datasets repeatedly accessed worldwide. Regional in-network caching reduces redundant long-distance transfers through efficient local data sharing. To optimally allocate bandwidth, we must understand and predict peak cache throughput behavior.

We analyzed three years of cache hit and miss throughputs from the Southern California Petabyte-Scale Cache and built a machine learning model to forecast daily peak throughput. We examined three peak metrics: maximum, 99th percentile, and 95th percentile. Each distinctly guides resource allocation, as maximum captures all traffic but wastes capacity, while percentiles cover most traffic at lower bandwidth.

Results show one-day-ahead forecasts closely following demand, but accuracy degrades at longer horizons. Future work includes enhanced long-horizon models and more granular hourly models.

In the poster session, I’ll explain caching, describe peak throughput trends, and discuss results, limitations, and future work from forecasting.

presentations.title: Prefetching in Disaggregated Memory Systems
presentations.abstract:
The growing prevalence of memory-intensive applications has exposed several limitations of traditional server architectures. Disaggregated memory systems address some of these limitations by enabling memory and compute resources to scale independently. However, disaggregation introduces new challenges, particularly the high latency of remote memory accesses. In this work, we present an approach for mitigating remote-access latency in multi-rack disaggregated memory systems. We also discuss broader open challenges and research
opportunities in memory-system design.

presentations.title: Preparing for HPC & AI Careers
presentations.abstract: In the first part of the workshop, students will explore the range of roles available across HPC and AI, including research, systems and infrastructure, GPU and performance engineering, research software engineering, applied machine learning, and developer relations. The workshop will also cover how to evaluate graduate school options, build strong resumes and portfolios, search for roles effectively, and prepare for interviews and offers.

presentations.title: Principles and Practice of High-Performance AI Training and Inference
presentations.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have led to significant growth in model scale, computational demands, and system complexity, creating both new challenges and opportunities. Modern AI frameworks and systems such as PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang, and distributed middleware including torch.distributed, Megatron-LM, and DeepSpeed enable scalable training, fine-tuning, inference, and deployment across the full AI model lifecycle. This tutorial provides an overview of recent trends in AI and highlights the convergence of AI and high performance computing (HPC), emphasizing the role of advanced hardware architectures, memory systems, and high-speed interconnects in enabling scalable AI workloads. We present an end-to-end view of the AI lifecycle, including training, fine-tuning, hyperparameter optimization, and inference, with a focus on parallelization strategies for large-scale models such as GPT, LLaMA, DeepSeek, and ViT. We discuss key system challenges related to compute, memory, and communication, and examine how modern communication runtimes and software stacks can efficiently leverage heterogeneous CPU/GPU architectures. We also highlight co-design efforts utilizing NCCL and MPI communication backends to support large-scale distributed AI workloads on modern HPC systems. Throughout the tutorial, we include hands-on exercises to provide attendees with practical experience in distributed AI on modern GPU clusters.

presentations.title: PRISM: Lightweight Surrogation for Lossy Compression Quality Prediction
presentations.abstract:
Error-bounded lossy compression is indispensable for managing the data deluge in exascale
scientific workflows, yet selecting compressor configurations requires evaluating quality
metrics (CR, PSNR, SSIM) that are expensive to compute directly. Deep surrogate models
address this bottleneck but must be retrained from scratch whenever new data fields,
compressors, or metrics are introduced, creating a combinatorial scaling problem. We present
PRISM, a lightweight framework that trains a single foundation backbone and adapts to new tasks via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), removing the need
for full retraining. Evaluated on the Hurricane Isabel application across eight fields, four
compressors, and three metrics, PRISM achieves MAPE below 10% in 81 of 96 tasks using
rank-4 adaptation with under 1% trainable parameters (107x reduction), and is more
accurate than from-scratch training when samples are scarce. By amortizing one reusable
backbone across the task space, PRISM offers scalable compression quality prediction for
large-scale HPC workflows.

presentations.title: PRISM: Task-aware Slimming for Edge-Cloud LLMs
presentations.abstract: While LLM compression techniques for cloud and HPC environments often assume diverse, unpredictable workloads, edge deployments typically serve fixed, single-task objectives. We identify two important distinctions in edge-based serving: first, unlike cloud inference which is bound by attention and KV-cache transfers, edge inference is primarily bottlenecked by MLP layers; second, layer and weight importance exhibit strong, task-specific sensitivity signatures. Building on these insights, we present PRISM, a task-aware compression framework for edge-cloud LLM serving. In cloud, PRISM profiles per-task sensitivity using causal ablation and AWQ-style quantization error, generating an execution layer mask and a precision weight mask to form a task-specialized inference DAG. On the edge, a novel sliding-chunk scheduler minimizes the resident memory footprint by streaming weights and overlapping I/O with computation. Evaluated on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5 across four tasks, PRISM reduces peak memory by up to 2.9x and end-to-end latency by up to 26% compared to dense baselines.

presentations.title: Privacy Foundations for Multi-Institutional Scientific Artificial Intelligence
presentations.abstract: Scientific AI, from foundation models to federated analysis pipelines, is becoming shared infrastructure across national laboratories, universities, hospitals, and industry. Its privacy risks often concern an institution’s participation, strategy, or capability rather than single records. Differential privacy, federated learning, secure computation, trusted execution, and provenance each protect parts of the stack, but their guarantees rarely compose across mixed-trust institutions, access tiers, and autonomous agents. This perspective recasts privacy as an assurance problem defined by six elements: protected asset, observer, channel, permitted disclosure, guarantee, and evidence. A lifecycle claim register for a composite cross-institutional scenario reveals two gaps specific to leadership-class facilities: scheduler metadata exposes institutional participation, and instrument-attached control loops leak research strategy through timing and accelerator contention. Six priorities emerge: institution-level guarantees, agent-communication privacy, cross-tier information flow, privacy-compatible reproducibility, leadership-scale accounting, and instrument side channels. We offer a common form for stating, comparing, and auditing otherwise fragmented privacy claims.

presentations.title: Probe Less, Learn More: Characterizing and Correcting eBPF Instrumentation Overhead
presentations.abstract: We demonstrate that although eBPF and bpftrace are widely used for low-overhead tracing, their overheads are large when considering microsecond-scale events. We decompose these overheads into two parts that were not considered separately by prior work: a fixed floor paid for every probe that fires, and per-operation work layered on top. We measure these overheads on a controlled single-syscall harness, then characterize how overheads scale as probes accumulate: overhead is driven by the number of distinct events that fire (~42 ns each), not by the number of probe definitions (~3 ns per additional probe on an already-traced event). For example, a bare probe costs ~50 ns while a single map update or timestamp adds 100–300 ns. From these measurements we derive an observability budget that predicts, before any probe is attached, how much a proposed trace will distort its target and therefore how faithfully the event can be observed.

presentations.title: Procurements Under Pressure: Adaptive Strategies for HPC Centers in an Uncertain World
presentations.abstract: HPC computing centers face mounting procurement risks driven by geopolitical tensions, semiconductor supply constraints, and AI-driven demand for GPUs. Leading-edge fabrication is concentrated among a small number of fabs worldwide, leaving centers exposed when disruptions strike. What was once a predictable multi-year planning cycle has become a landscape of uncertainty. This BoF brings together center directors, vendors, and system integrators from across the international HPC community to develop shared adaptive strategies — from flexible RFPs to extended machine lifetimes. Community participation is central: the goal is not to deliver answers, but to build them together.

presentations.title: Profiling and Optimization Opportunities for SmartNIC-Assisted MoE Inference
presentations.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models improve capacity through sparse expert activation but introduce bursty all-to-all communication and rank-level imbalance during inference. We profile decode-stage Mixtral-8x7B inference on a 4-GPU vLLM data- and expert-parallel setup and observe up to 3.63 ms expert-compute rank skew. We propose a SmartNIC-assisted dispatch design with destination batching, expert-aware admission, blocked-chunk reordering, and credit-based dispatch. A deterministic C++ simulator shows that the full policy reduces average expert-flow-chunk latency by 17.1% and packet count by 74.9% on the profiled workload, with 8.6–18.9% latency reduction across nine routing and arrival workloads. We further implement a trace-driven FPGA/HLS prototype on an AMD/Xilinx U280. A 1,024-chunk board-level replay executes without runtime errors and exactly matches simulator chunk records, demonstrating implementability of the proposed scheduling kernel.

presentations.title: Programming Novel AI Accelerators for Scientific Computing
presentations.abstract: Scientific applications are increasingly adopting artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to advance science. There are specialized hardware accelerators designed and built to run AI applications efficiently. With a wide diversity in the hardware architectures and software stacks of these systems, it is challenging to understand the differences between these accelerators, their capabilities, programming approaches, and how they perform, particularly for scientific applications. In this tutorial, we will cover an overview of the AI accelerators deployed at ALCF, focusing on SambaNova, Cerebras, and Tenstorrent systems along with architectural features and details of their software stacks. Through hands-on exercises, attendees will gain practical experience in refactoring code and running models on these systems, focusing on use cases of pre-training and fine-tuning open-source large language models (LLMs) and deploying AI inference solutions relevant to scientific contexts. The tutorial will provide the attendees with an understanding of the key capabilities of emerging AI accelerators and their performance implications for scientific applications.

presentations.title: Programming Your GPU with OpenMP: A “Hands-On” Introduction
presentations.abstract: If you are an HPC programmer, you know the OpenMP® API. Alongside MPI, the OpenMP API is the open, cross-vendor foundation of HPC. As hardware complexity has grown, the OpenMP programming model has grown as well, adding GPU support in OpenMP 4.0 (2013). With over a decade of evolution since then, OpenMP GPU technology is a mature option for programming any GPU you are likely to find on the market. While there are many ways to program a GPU, the best way is through the OpenMP API. Why? Because the GPU does not exist in isolation. There are always one or more CPUs on a node. Programmers need portable code that fully exploits all available processors. In other words, programmers need a programming model, such as OpenMP, that fully embraces heterogeneity. In this tutorial, we explore GPU programming with the OpenMP programming model. We assume attendees are familiar with multithreading, so we will focus on the directives that define how to map loops onto GPUs and optimize data movement between the CPU and GPU. Students will use their own laptops (with Windows, Linux, or macOS) to connect to remote servers with GPUs and all the software needed for the tutorial.

presentations.title: Proper Rewards: Post-Training Time Series Foundation Models with Scoring-Rule GRPO
presentations.abstract: Temporal data are central to science, yet post-training methods that drive major advances in language modeling remain underexplored for time series foundation models (TSFMs). Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve model capabilities but tends to narrow the model's output distribution, causing overconfident probabilistic forecasts. We resolve this tension by combining group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with rewards based on proper scoring rules. Scoring-rule GRPO elicits calibrated predictive distributions: trajectory-level rewards improve general-purpose forecasting, whereas functional-level rewards specialize the predictive distribution for a task-specific quantity. Across diverse dynamical systems data, post-training with the energy-score reward reduces RMSE by 54% and in-distribution functional forecast error by 57% relative to the pre-trained model. These results show that proper scoring rules are promising rewards for temporal reasoning. Because the prediction quality of this post-training strategy transfers across tasks, it moves TSFMs closer to being truly foundational for scientific applications.

presentations.title: Proposal of a Transparent Dynamic Core Allocation Method for MPI/OpenMP Hybrid Parallelization
presentations.abstract:
Load balancing is essential for maximizing performance and energy efficiency in MPI/OpenMP hybrid applications on supercomputers. While dynamic core binding (DCB) mitigates process-level imbalances by dynamically binding CPU cores, conventional methods require manual source code modifications. We propose a fully transparent DCB method eliminating user-level code alterations. By leveraging OpenMP Tools (OMPT) and Profiling MPI (PMPI) via a dynamically linked shared library, our method automatically intercepts computation phases and calculates load parameters from actual computation time by subtracting MPI wait time from the execution time of OpenMP parallel regions.

Evaluations on the Miyabi-C supercomputer using a Lattice H-matrix application demonstrate up to a 1.54x speedup and 32.0% energy reduction on a single node. Furthermore, 16-node tests demonstrate performance and energy benefits at scale.

Our poster will feature architectural diagrams of the OMPT/PMPI integration and performance graphs comparing static mapping, conventional DCB, and our transparent approach.

presentations.title: PROV-AGENT-LOOP: Provenance Data Management for Agentic Loop Engineering
presentations.abstract: AI agents governed by Large Language Models modify code, inspect logs, revise plans, invoke tools, spend tokens, and decide whether objectives have been satisfied, affecting computational outcomes in ways that require accountable provenance. This paper introduces PROV-AGENT-LOOP, a W3C PROV-compatible model that represents objective-plan-act-evaluate cycles as queryable provenance. The model builds on PROV-AGENT, aligns with MAS, BDI, ReAct, Reflexion, and MAPE-K concepts, and captures loop structure, communication, evaluation, authorization, delegation, and invocation evidence. We implement PROV-AGENT-LOOP in Flowcept, integrating agentic, workflow, machine-learning, scheduler, and telemetry records in one Provenance Database. We validate the model on Frontier, where an AI agent adapts a Dask-based training campaign. The database answers eight cross-domain queries with 100% structural evidence completeness under OPL+DPL, more than double the workflow-only baseline, while Codex token usage and database footprint are reported as observed values rather than controlled overhead.

presentations.title: PULSE: Parallel Uncertainty-guided Landscape Sampling Engine for In-Situ Molecular Dynamics
presentations.abstract: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations generate massive streams of high-dimensional data. However, biologically significant events are rare, transient, and not known ahead of time. Modern MD workflows execute many trajectories concurrently, but most adaptive sampling methods analyze trajectories in offline batches, delaying feedback and wasting computational resources on redundant exploration. We present PULSE, a scalable in-situ framework that closes the feedback loop between simulation and analysis through a synchronized producer-consumer runtime. PULSE performs online conformational state identification, detects previously unexplained regions of the conformational landscape, and adaptively redirects computational effort toward these regions during execution. We evaluate PULSE on two protein systems, Villin Headpiece and beta-lactoglobulin. Compared to conventional adaptive sampling, PULSE drives 70.77% and 37.17% of newly sampled conformations, respectively, into regions that the baseline never explored. We demonstrate end-to-end execution on eight GPUs and show that PULSE maintains nearly constant coordination overhead across concurrency levels up to 32 trajectories.

presentations.title: Pumped Two-Phase Cooling for the Next-Gen Chips with Heat Flux Over 4 W/mm2
presentations.abstract: Pumped two-phase cooling is a promising solution for the increasing heat flux of next-generation GPUs. This study presents a pumped two-phase cooling distribution unit (CDU) and loop architecture and compares the thermal performance of a two-phase cold plate with the same design operating with PG25 coolant. Test results show that the two-phase cold plate can dissipate over 3500 W, while both refrigerant and PG25 cooling can meet the projected thermal requirements of future GPUs with average heat flux above 1 W/mm² and hotspot heat flux above 3 W/mm². Although cooling performance is ultimately limited by fluid thermophysical properties and flow conditions, the thermal challenges of upcoming GPU generations remain manageable. Future work will investigate alternative cold plate materials and thermal conductivity optimization to further enhance cooling performance.

presentations.title: Python as the Connective Tissue of the Genesis Mission: From Exascale Workflows to Federated Scientific Agents
presentations.abstract: The DOE Genesis Mission aims to couple AI, exascale computing, experimental facilities, and autonomous laboratories into an integrated discovery platform, and much of what holds that platform together is written in Python. Large-scale simulation campaigns, AI training and inference pipelines, workflow orchestration, provenance capture, and multi-agent systems all converge on a shared Python layer that lets scientists compose resources across institutional and facility boundaries. Drawing on experience designing agentic systems for scientific resource discovery and workflow composition, performance studies of workflow execution on leadership-class machines, and a decade of community building around scientific workflows, this talk examines where Python succeeds as the orchestration fabric for AI-coupled science and where it strains, from startup and coordination overheads at scale to environment portability across facilities, concurrency, and the cost of provenance and governance in autonomous loops.

presentations.title: Python-Based Distributed Training on AMD GPU Supercomputers: Lessons from Data, Pipeline, and Tensor Parallelism on LUMI
presentations.abstract: The growing computational demands of foundation AI models have made distributed training essential on modern supercomputers. This work presents an empirical study of data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism for Vision Transformer training on the LUMI supercomputer, an AMD GPU-based leadership-class HPC system. Using Python-based frameworks including PyTorch, FairScale, TensorFlow DTensor, and Colossal-AI within containerized ROCm environments, we evaluate framework compatibility, portability, implementation complexity, and reproducibility. Our findings show that software ecosystem readiness significantly impacts scalable AI training. PyTorch DDP and TensorFlow DTensor demonstrate reliable execution, while several CUDA-dependent approaches face deployment challenges on AMD architectures.

presentations.title: Q/A and Closing Remarks
QC-HPC Ecosystem
presentations.abstract:
This session explores how the quantum-HPC ecosystem is taking shape from the vendor and technology-provider side. Speakers will share how their platforms, runtimes, and system software are being designed to integrate quantum processors into existing HPC environments, from job scheduling and resource management to GPU-accelerated classical computing and hybrid programming models. The talks emphasize practical integration paths: what is already working in production, what interfaces and standards are emerging, and where the remaining gaps lie.
The session brings together perspectives from GPU and accelerator providers, HPC software developers, and quantum hardware vendors, offering a view of how the building blocks of a quantum-classical computing stack are coming together across the industry.

presentations.title: Qdislib: Implementation and Evaluation of Circuit Cutting and Sampling Techniques for Quantum Circuits
presentations.abstract: Circuit cutting enables quantum circuits to exceed the qubit limits of current quantum hardware and simulators by partitioning circuits into independently executable fragments. However, different cutting strategies introduce distinct trade-offs in computational overhead, sampling complexity, and reconstruction accuracy. We present a systematic evaluation of the four circuit-cutting techniques implemented in Qdislib, an open-source framework for scalable hybrid quantum–classical execution across CPUs, GPUs, simulators, and QPUs. Our study compares theoretical complexity, reconstruction accuracy, execution time, and distributed scalability, highlighting an optimized wire-cutting implementation that reduces fragment scaling from 8^k to 3^k+4^k and a Hadamard-based gate-cutting method that eliminates mid-circuit measurements while preserving accuracy. The poster will present the Qdislib workflow, implementation details, and experimental results, providing practical guidelines for selecting circuit-cutting strategies on HPC systems and quantum hardware.

presentations.title: QoS Coverage Maps for Placement and Readiness in Urgent Digital Twins
presentations.abstract: Urgent continuum workflows may miss deadlines because of poor task placement, delayed artifact readiness, insufficient compute capacity, or excessive full-fidelity execution time. We isolate placement and readiness while holding capacity and fidelity fixed. We introduce QoS coverage maps, which vary offered load and readiness delay, and classify whether the primary diagnostic target (tau) of 50% on-time completion is met by the best-performing of three non-learning baselines, learned placement, advance artifact staging, or neither. The threshold separates operating regions. For wildfire, learned placement improves on-time completion by up to 85.5 percentage points, while increasing readiness delay from 0 to 10 s at 1.0 fps reduces completion from 87.7% to 0.4%. For earthquake-tsunami, learned placement adds no coverage relative to the primary baseline because 96.4% of critical-path computation is fixed to HPC. At tau = 50%, 10 of 30 tested conditions remain uncovered in each workflow, motivating capacity scaling or bounded approximation.

presentations.title: QR-Omega: Communication Avoiding 2.5D Householder QR
presentations.abstract: Orthogonalization is a key step in Krylov methods, tensor-network algorithms, least-squares solvers, and emerging machine-learning methods. Householder QR is numerically robust for orthogonalization, but on GPUs its performance is often limited by data movement and synchronization. We present QR-Ω, a hierarchical 2.5D Householder QR formulation that extends hierarchical QR with four execution operations: Split, Replicate, Combine, and Pipeline. These operations control how data is partitioned, replicated, reduced, and overlapped across the GPU memory hierarchy while preserving the Householder elimination order. On an NVIDIA H200, we compare QR-Ω with tuned cuSOLVER, MAGMA, and SLATE implementations in FP64, FP32, TF32, and 3×TF32. Across matrix sizes up to n = 131,072, QR-Ω approaches matrix-multiplication throughput while maintaining small numerical errors in FP64, FP32. Our implementation surpasses the state-of-the-art libraries cited above in performance by up to two times without loss of accuracy, while maintaining advantage in all tested sizes and precisions.

presentations.title: QSPredictor: Runtime Prediction for Tensor-Network based Quantum Circuit Simulation on GPUs
presentations.abstract: Tensor networks enable the simulation of large quantum circuits with limited entanglement, potentially reaching hundreds of qubits. For circuits with higher entanglement, predicting runtime before execution is important for assessing simulation feasibility, wait times, and resource utilization in quantum-centric computing systems. Metrics that allow runtime estimation, such as treewidth, are NP-hard to calculate and change with each specific circuit, complicating usability in HPC schedulers. Circuits belonging to different families or algorithms present a similar structure that allows grouping through cheap characterization, providing information relevant to total runtime. We present QSPredictor, a Transformer-based predictor of tensor network planning, contraction, and total runtime using structural circuit properties and OpenQASM text, and compare it against a family-aware baseline. To improve data efficiency, QSPredictor selects representative training circuits followed by conditioned k-means++ selection. Under the complete proposed pipeline, QSPredictor achieves a total-runtime MAPE of 7.09% and a log-space R² of 0.9906.

presentations.title: Quantifying Workload Exposure in HPC Power Telemetry at Operational Sampling Rates
presentations.abstract: HPC centers publish power telemetry to support monitoring, scheduling, and optimization. While this telemetry is published for operational use, it can also reveal information about the workloads on a system. Prior work shows workloads leave signatures in high-frequency telemetry. How much of that signature survives at the coarse rates used in production is unknown. We study workloads using CPU power telemetry from Intel RAPL at approximately 1 kHz, downsampled to intervals as coarse as 60 s, measuring recoverability for resource classes and for individual workloads on unseen problem sizes. Recoverability declines as sampling coarsens, from 0.87 to 0.71 for resource class and 0.74 to 0.54 for workload identity. In short jobs, temporal information distinguishing individual workloads disappears under coarse sampling, while the steady power composition remains. At coarse rates, distinct workloads remain identifiable while similar ones become indistinguishable. Thus, coarsening the sampling rate is a practical but incomplete privacy control.

presentations.title: Quantum Computing: State of the Industry and Illinois’ Ecosystem
Quantum Jumps: From NISQ to FTQC to Hybrid HPC
presentations.abstract: Quantum computing is experiencing accelerating transitions, from noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices to fault-tolerant quantum computers, and from quantum computers being objects of research to their becoming scientific computation tools. Quantum programming habits and assumptions must be revisited, and for the HPC community, this is more than an incremental hardware upgrade; it affects entire stacks. This session will explore how compilation workflows, execution models, and algorithmic strategies are expected to change to incorporate error correction and integrate with production HPC workflows. Thought leaders from the quantum industry, HPC, and academic research will exchange perspectives and engage the audience in discussion.

presentations.title: Quantum Safe Networking — QKD — Any Attempt To Observe the Quantum Channel Leaves Evidence
presentations.abstract: No NRI

presentations.title: Quantum-HPC Workflows Across Multiple Quantum Computing Platforms: Two Case Studies
presentations.abstract:
We describe the Quantum-HPC hybrid system comprising the supercomputer Fugaku, the QPUs Quantinuum Reimei and ibm\_kobe, and the Tierkreis hybrid workflow software.
We present two demonstrations of the system at work.
In the first we compute the excited states of a biomolecular system using Fugaku and Reimei to
handle classical and quantum parts of the workflow respectively.
In the second, Fugaku coordinates Reimei and ibm\_kobe working together in a combined VQE + QPE workflow to compute the ground state energy of a simple system.

presentations.title: Query-Driven Visualization Over Compressed Scientific Data via Data–Index Co-Compression
presentations.abstract:
Large-scale scientific simulations routinely produce petabyte-scale datasets, making error-bounded lossy compression indispensable for alleviating storage and I/O bottlenecks. However, most visualization pipelines still reconstruct the entire compressed dataset before analysis, even when a visualization query accesses only a small subset of the volume, resulting in substantial computational overhead and limited interactive responsiveness.

We apply data–index co-compression to enable efficient query-driven visualization, jointly compressing block-level index with scientific data to support selective decompression while minimizing index overhead. During visualization, only the compressed blocks satisfying the query predicate are decompressed, avoiding unnecessary data access and reducing end-to-end visualization cost.

Experimental evaluation on three representative scientific applications demonstrates substantial end-to-end acceleration, achieving up to 50.1× speedup over conventional full-decompression workflows while preserving comparable visualization quality.

presentations.title: QuLore: An Adaptive Security Framework To Extend Quantum-Safe Communications
Radiation: When Steels Fall Apart
presentations.abstract:
This visualization uses a high performance computing-based workflow to reveal the atomic-scale structure of neutron-irradiated steel. Highlighted in the image are nanoscale defects and chemical features that formed or evolved as a result of irradiation.

The specimen examined in this study was prepared from an HT-9 alloy irradiated to 0.68 displacements per atom (dpa) at 478 degrees Celsius in Idaho National Laboratory’s Advanced Test Reactor. The visualization combines two correlative datasets collected from the same specimen: a two-dimensional image acquired using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and a three-dimensional dataset acquired using atom probe tomography (APT).

The combined datasets reveal several complex microstructural features associated with radiation damage. These include spherical clusters enriched in nickel and silicon, dislocation lines decorated with solute clusters, and a grain boundary exhibiting radiation-induced solute segregation. The dataset also captures a pre-existing vanadium nitride precipitate. Characterizing these features is important because they can influence the physical and mechanical properties of the alloy.

Using high performance computing and advanced deep-learning methods, this image-based workflow improves feature identification and enables more accurate spatial correlation of the complementary TEM and APT datasets. The multimodal computational model under development uses structural information obtained from TEM to support further analysis of the APT dataset and improve the identification and characterization of solute clusters.

This visualization is composed entirely of experimental data obtained from TEM and APT measurements. Rendering the datasets in this form allows researchers to more effectively interpret correlative measurements, identify and analyze complex radiation-induced features, validate computational methods, and communicate scientific findings.

presentations.title: Rapid Dataflow Buffer Sizing for DNNs via Parallel RTL Control-Flow Simulation for FINN
presentations.abstract:
In dataflow architectures, first-in-first-out (FIFO) buffers decouple pipeline stages
working at different rates. Appropriately sizing FIFOs prevents deadlocks and sustains throughput, yet remains a difficult problem for automated deep neural network (DNN)-to-accelerator compilers. As DNNs increase in size and complexity, existing techniques suffer from excessive runtime, inaccurate results, or unacceptable manual modeling effort.

We present a FIFO sizing approach based on iterative simulation of mixed RTL/HLS black-box
designs. Two innovations manage the cost of cycle-accurate simulation: a resource-aware search algorithm that operates at memory-primitive granularity rather than
raw depth, minimizing simulation rounds; and a scalable, MPI-capable, massively layer-parallel simulation of only the control path, greatly accelerating individual runs.

Integrated into the FINN DNN-to-accelerator compiler and evaluated on a range of DNNs
against three existing techniques, the approach delivers near-optimal FIFO depths with guaranteed performance at an average of 2.88x the speed of the best competing approach offering the
same guarantees.

presentations.title: Rapid Earthquake-to-Tsunami Waveform Generation via Large-Scale Multi-GPU FFT Convolution Applied to the Cascadia Subduction Zone
presentations.abstract:
Data-driven methods for earthquake and tsunami early warning rely on large
ensembles of rupture scenarios and their resulting waveforms, but generating
such datasets with repeated high-fidelity seismic and tsunami simulations is
prohibitively expensive. We exploit the linear time-invariant structure of both dynamics to precompute elastic Green's functions and acoustic–gravity adjoint responses, reducing the source-to-waveform map to two consecutive %block lower-triangular Toeplitz matvecs.
convolution operators.
We evaluate these convolutions with a distributed, FFT-accelerated GPU pipeline that partitions the large seafloor grid across GPUs and directly generates the final observation waveforms.
We demonstrate the scalability of this pipeline for the Cascadia Subduction Zone with 963 subfaults, 2,416,530 seafloor grid points, 64 observation locations, and 256 timesteps, requiring 9.45~TiB of aggregate GPU memory. On 64 GB200 GPUs within one NVL72 domain, the pipeline generates waveforms in 24 ms per rupture once the response operators are resident, enabling large rupture ensembles to be evaluated within minutes.

presentations.title: RDMA control over lossy Ethernet: A new approach using synchronized clocks
presentations.abstract: Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) underpins storage and increasingly AI systems, reducing transfer latency and host CPU overhead. Traditional deployments rely on lossless fabrics, using priority flow control, credit-based flow control, congestion notification, and substantial switch memory for skid buffers. Can RDMA operate over lossy Ethernet at a single priority without in-network enhancements? Rather than implementing sophisticated loss recovery on RDMA-capable NICs, we explore end-to-end congestion control driven by one-way delay measurements. Pervasive software clock synchronization enables senders and receivers to estimate path congestion by subtracting send timestamps from receive timestamps and use these estimates to pace transmissions. Evaluations demonstrate sub-microsecond delay measurement accuracy, enabling fine-grained RDMA control. RDMA achieves near-zero packet loss and queueing delay over lossy Ethernet while coexisting harmoniously with legacy TCP traffic. These results establish delay-based, end-to-end congestion detection and mitigation as a compelling alternative to conventional in-network mechanisms for supporting RDMA on shared Ethernet fabrics.

presentations.title: Real-time Optimization of Simulation and Data Processing Pipelines for Experiments on Exascale Computing Platforms
presentations.abstract: Current and next-generation large-scale experiments, especially in high-energy physics and cosmology, involve increasing volumes of data that require exascale computing power to analyze and model. Exascale machines present challenges for workflow scaling and efficient resource usage. We propose a multi-stage task scheduling approach for optimizing resource usage and task scheduling for these workflows. We demonstrate task scheduling for an example Monte Carlo Simulation pipeline from the Short Baseline Near Detector (SBND), and present theoretical and numerical tools for modeling task scheduling in these workflows that can be used to identify optimal scheduling strategies and choose resources for a given problem size.

presentations.title: Real-Time Scientific Data Streaming to HPC Nodes: Challenges and Innovations VI
presentations.abstract:
Emerging scientific needs are driving a new class of workflows that require near real-time processing, urgent computing, and time-sensitive decision-making. The traditional "compute-store-analyze" paradigm, which relies on dumping massive datasets to file systems for post-processing, has become an unsustainable bottleneck. It introduces unacceptable latency, and often renders high-frequency data analysis practically impossible.

This BoF discusses this challenge by exploring the architectural shift from file-based workflows to high-performance streaming. In this new paradigm, storage is treated not as a buffer for post-processing, but as a sink for final scientific results, while analysis, visualization, and reduction occur in-transit or in-situ.

presentations.title: Recall Is Not Honesty: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Architectures for Trustworthy HPC Operational Analytics
presentations.abstract: Agentic systems answer operational queries over HPC telemetry for domain scientists who cannot verify the responses. Trustworthiness requires recovering the facts telemetry supports and refusing the questions it does not, since no facility instruments everything it runs. Existing architectures are built for capability on the assumption that reliability follows, and inference remains untested. We compare five configurations, one tool-using agent and four multi-agent designs varying only in inter-agent communication and shared-state structure, on EPIQ, a new benchmark of 55 multi-intent queries over Fugaku job telemetry with 119 verifiable facts and 25 unanswerable sub-questions. The single agent recovers the most facts (84.9%) but refuses least. Pairing peer messaging with typed dialogue-act fields refuses most (92.0%) while matching single-agent recall within noise, at 2.5 times the tokens. Refusal follows whether agents exchange results at all; typing those exchanges recovers recall. Agent count explains neither. Recall and refusal must be designed for separately.

presentations.title: Reconverse: A new scheduling library for multithreaded task-based runtime systems
presentations.abstract: Task-based runtime systems, including Charm++, provide benefits not available with MPI, such as dynamic load balancing and automatic computation-communication overlap. Charm++ is currently built on top of an old scheduling layer called Converse. However, Converse lacks many features that are essential for distributed multithreaded performance, and other programming models cannot directly use the Converse scheduler. To solve these problems, we present Reconverse, a new scheduling layer for task-based runtime systems. Reconverse is a separately-compiled library that can be linked to Charm++ or other runtime systems. Compared to Converse, Reconverse contains experimental features for optimizing fine-grained applications such as lottery queue scheduling. Reconverse also supports new machine layers such as LCI, a new communication layer for multithreaded runtime systems. We show that Reconverse improves performance compared to Converse on multiple benchmarks and also demonstrated speedups of up to 2x on large-scale applications, showing the benefits of Reconverse for multithreaded distributed workloads.

presentations.title: Reducing Confusion and Broadcasting Understanding: An Empirical Study of the Semantics of NCCL
presentations.abstract: We present a foundation for formalising the semantics of NCCL, the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library. NCCL is a key component in distributed machine learning and HPC stacks that utilise NVIDIA GPUs. By combining analysis of the official documentation with empirical testing of the library, we present several key insights that characterise the concurrent programming model of NCCL. This includes the introduction of the concept of command matching, and novel explanations of the conditions under which undefined behaviour may be observed.

presentations.title: Refuse To Guess: A Declared Precondition in a UXarray MCP Server Caught What No Model Checked
presentations.abstract: We wrapped UXarray, a Python library for unstructured earth meshes, in a Model Context Protocol server so that language models call the library rather than reimplement it. Beyond schema validation, the server declares scientific preconditions that must hold before it computes. We tested what that buys across 480 runs: six mesh-analysis tasks, four interfaces, four models, five trials. One task was rigged to have no honest answer, asking for a remap onto a target grid with zero overlap with the source data. All 60 server-backed runs reported the server’s structured refusal. Writing their own code against the same library, models produced a confident number in 10 of 20 runs and, in all 20, never noted that the target lay outside the data. Across the other five tasks, interface changes were mostly within noise. This is one server and one library, but it isolates a mechanism model capability did not supply.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Ameen Salahudeen
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Andrea Jett
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Avinash Maurya
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Becky Gillespie
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Bob Grossman
presentations.abstract: Robert L. Grossman, PhD, is the Frederick H. Rawson Distinguished Service Professor in Medicine and Computer Science and the Jim and Karen Frank Director of the Center for Translational Data Science at the University of Chicago. He joined the faculty in 2010 and served as the chief research informatics officer (CRIO) of the Biological Sciences Division from 2011-2024. He is also the Chief of the Section of Biomedical Data Science in the Department of Medicine. He is the principal investigator for the National Cancer Institute Genomic Data Commons (GDC), a platform for the cancer research community that manages, analyzes, integrates, and shares large-scale genomic datasets in support of precision medicine. The GDC is used by more than 150,000 researchers each month. He has also built data commons to support research in other areas, including cardiovascular diseases, infectious diseases and medical imaging. His research interests include data science, AI, and machine learning.
