He is the founder and a partner at Analytic Strategy Partners, which helps companies develop AI strategies, and a Director of the Open Commons Consortium (OCC), which is a not-for-profit that manages and operates data commons and data meshes to advance scientific and biomedical research. He served as a member of the NOAA Scientific Advisory Board (SAB) from 2017-2024 and as a member of the Frederick National Laboratory Advisory Committee (FNLAC) from 2014-2021. He earned his PhD in applied mathematics at Princeton University and an AB in mathematics from Harvard University.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: John Towns
presentations.abstract: John Towns is the Deputy Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications. He leads the NSF-funded ACCESS Coordination Office, as part of the overall ACCESS Program supporting researchers and educators nation-wide in the use of advanced computing systems, and plays key roles in the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot as co-Chair of the Allocations Working Group and Chair of the Coordination Team. He also serves as executive sponsor of NCSA’s Quantum Program Office, a partnership with the Illinois Quantum Information Science and Technology Center (IQUIST), to advance quantum research. With over 35 years of experience, Towns has held leadership roles in numerous national and international initiatives supporting advanced research computing. He holds M.S. degrees in Physics and Astronomy from the University of Illinois and a B.S. in Physics from the University of Missouri-Rolla.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Jordan Fauser
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Maria Jaromin
presentations.abstract: Maria Jaromin brings a multidisciplinary background spanning computational engineering, technology transfer, research development, and compliance. She currently leads the Healthcare Innovation Program Office at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois Urbana‑Champaign. In this role, she fosters and advances cross‑disciplinary research collaborations across the university and with external partners, with a focus on integrating advanced technologies into health and biomedical research. Prior to her current position, Maria served as a Technology Manager in the Office of Technology Management at the University of Illinois System, where she managed an intellectual property portfolio in engineering and physical sciences. Her work included evaluating the patentability and commercialization potential of university innovations, negotiating legal agreements, and educating researchers on technology transfer processes and policies. Maria began her career at the Illinois Applied Research Institute as a Research Engineer, specializing in modeling and simulation to enhance the efficiency, safety, and performance of engineering systems and processes. She holds a bachelor’s and master’s degree in Power Engineering from the Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland; a Licentiate of Engineering in Energy Technology from the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, Sweden; and an MBA from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Matt Zajac
Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Michelle Hoffmann
presentations.abstract:
Michelle Hoffmann, Ph.D. has been serving since August of 2021 as the Executive Director of the Chicago Biomedical Consortium (CBC), a consortium of biomedical researchers across Northwestern, the University of Illinois at Chicago, the University of Chicago, and six other Chicagoland institutions, that is generously supported by the Searle Funds at The Chicago Community Trust (CCT), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and The Walder Foundation. The CBC's mission is to find and fund research that will most likely become commercial biomedical applications driving Illinois's economic development.

In her time as Executive Director, Dr. Hoffmann has reorganized the CBC, developed a process to scout and build biopharma applications of Illinois's academic researchers, organized the greater entrepreneurial community and market it to coastal investors and biotech, and trained local PhD talent in the business of early science commercialization. Before this role, from 2019-2021, Dr. Hoffmann was the Senior Vice President of Deep Tech at P33, a privately funded nonprofit charged with elevating Chicagoland's innovation economy and driving inclusive economic growth.

Before P33, Hoffmann spent 15 years helping life sciences companies grow, most recently as a senior vice president at Boston-based Back Bay Life Science Advisors, an integrated strategy and investment firm for global life science companies, venture-backed startups and their investors. During her nine years at Back Bay, Hoffmann led projects for large, publicly traded companies and small, private, venture-backed health care and life sciences companies.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Nicholas Chia
presentations.abstract: Nicholas Chia is a Computational Biologist at Argonne National Laboratory whose work spans artificial intelligence, cancer biology, complex systems, and translational medicine. He received a B.S. in Physics from Georgetown University and a Ph.D. in Physics from The Ohio State University, followed by postdoctoral training in biocomplexity, collective effects, and evolution at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Prior to joining Argonne, Chia spent more than a decade at Mayo Clinic, where he served as Waterman Endowed Co-Chair of the Microbiome Program, Director of the Beyond DNA Multi-omics Strategic Theme within the Center for Individualized Medicine, Associate Director of the Microbiome Program, and Associate Professor of Medicine. During that time, he helped build Mayo’s microbiome and multiomics programs and contributed to the introduction of technologies that ultimately supported 19 laboratory-developed tests reaching clinical go-live. His research has focused on colorectal cancer, cancer evolution, microbial ecology, genome-scale metabolic modeling, and the integration of multi-omic data into clinical and biological discovery. He is recognized for early work applying inverse reinforcement learning to cancer evolution, framing tumor progression as an adaptive process and developing computational approaches to infer the evolutionary pressures that shape disease trajectories. At Argonne, his work has expanded into AI for Science, scientific reasoning, biological foundation models, and large-scale computational biology. He is a contributor to BioAlchemy, a large-scale biological reasoning corpus derived from the scientific literature, and leads and collaborates on programs spanning scientific reasoning, causal inference, disease modeling, population health, biological foundation models, and AI-enabled discovery. His work leverages leadership-class computing resources to develop and evaluate AI systems for scientific research. Across national laboratories, academic medicine, and interdisciplinary research programs, Chia has worked on problems that require the integration of large-scale data, mechanistic modeling, and decision-making under uncertainty, with applications ranging from cancer and microbiome science to scientific reasoning and AI-driven discovery.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Prem Kumar
presentations.abstract: Prem Kumar is the John A. Dever Professor of Information Technology at the McCormick School of Engineering and Applied Science at Northwestern University. His primary research focus is on photonic devices and their applications utilizing the principles of nonlinear and quantum optics (>$30M cumulative research funding). Recent projects have included: generation, distribution, and ultrafast processing of photonic entanglement for applications in quantum information networks; novel quantum light states for precision measurements, imaging, and sensing; and novel optical amplifiers and devices for networked classical optical communications. Although Dr. Kumar’s primary appointment is in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, an affiliation with the Applied Physics program allows him to recruit multidisciplinary students into his research group, a privilege that has proven extremely beneficial for his research interests that lie at the interface of basic quantum science and applied information technology. Because of this interdisciplinary exposure, Ph.D. graduates from his research group (37 completed, 5 in progress) have gone on to build careers in academia, industry, and US national labs. His group has cumulatively published >500 research papers (Google Scholar h-index: 69), including 1 edited book, 2 book chapters, 6 patents, >200 peer-reviewed journal papers, 45 articles in hard-bound volumes, and >300 conference papers with >100 invited. From Feb’13 to Jan’17, Dr. Kumar was on leave from Northwestern to be at DARPA, where he served as a Program Manager in the Defense Sciences Office. At DARPA, Dr. Kumar created and managed a ~$20M/year portfolio of programs in basic and applied sciences, targeting a diverse range of topics that included neuroscience and engineering, ultrafast laser science and technology, precision navigation and timing, stand-off chem-bio defense, quantum effects in biological environments, and quantum information science and technology. He was also program manager for the Defense Science Study Group, which allowed him to interact with young academic faculty from universities across the US in various national defense settings. For his strong portfolio of programs in basic science and technology and his mentoring of DARPA Risers—young, noteworthy performers on DARPA programs—Dr. Kumar was selected Program Manager of the Year in 2015 and awarded the Secretary of Defense Medal for Outstanding Public Service in 2016. Prior to joining DARPA, Dr. Kumar served on the National Academies Committee that issued the 2012 landmark study: “Optics and Photonics: Essential Technologies for Our Nation,” which spawned the National Photonics Initiative (NPI). From 2018 to 2024, Dr. Kumar served on the NPI Steering Committee, lending his expertise to issues pertaining to the National Quantum Initiative. Dr. Kumar is a Fellow of Optica (formerly OSA), APS, IEEE, IoP (U.K.), AAAS, and SPIE. He has been a Distinguished Lecturer for the IEEE Photonics Society, Hermann A. Haus Lecturer at MIT, recipient of the Quantum Communication Award from Tamagawa University in Tokyo, Japan, and the Walder Research Excellence Award from the Provost’s office at Northwestern University. From 2020 to 2025, he served as the Editor-in-Chief of Optica, the flagship journal of The Optica Publishing Group (formerly OSA) for high-impact research. Currently, he co-chairs the National Academies Committee on Atomic Molecular and Optical Sciences, and was recently appointed to the External Advisory Board for NTT Basic Research Laboratories in Atsugi, Japan. Internal to Northwestern, he serves on the Executive Committee for the Institute at Northwestern for Quantum Information Research and Engineering (INQUIRE). Beginning Fall’26, he will also serve as the Interim Chair of the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Ravi Madduri
presentations.abstract: Ravi is a senior computer scientist working in the intersection of HPC/AI and biomedicine. His research interests are in building sustainable, scalable services for science, reproducible research, large-scale data management, analysis using HPC and AI. He leads the PALISADE-X project that is developing Privacy-preserving Federated Learning framework to build robust, trust-worthy AI models. He co-leads the MVP-CHAMPION project, which is a collaboration between VA and DOE and develops methods to perform large-scale genetic data analysis using DOE’s high performance computing capabilities, including methods for generating PRS scores in Prostate Cancer, genome-wide PheWAS on Summit supercomputer. Additionally, Ravi served as MPI for an NHGRI R01 on creating a cloud service for large-scale genomics analysis and was one of three key contributors to the National Institutes of Health $100M Cancer Biomedical Informatics Grid (caBIG), which linked 60 NIH-funded cancer centers and clinical sites engaged in cancer research. For his efforts in project management, tool development, and collaboration, Ravi received several Outstanding Achievement Awards from NIH. For his work on “Cancer Moonshot” project, he received the Department of Energy Secretary award in 2017.

presentations.title: Regional Tech Hub Meet and Greet: Volodymyr Kindratenko
presentations.abstract: Volodymyr Kindratenko serves as the Assistant Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he also holds the position of Director for the Center for Artificial Intelligence Innovation (CAII). He is an Adjunct Associate Professor in the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and a Research Associate Professor in the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. Prior to his current role, Dr. Kindratenko led NCSA's Innovative Systems Laboratory, a center-wide research initiative focused on evaluating emerging computing technologies for high-performance computing applications. Dr. Kindratenko earned his D.Sc. degree from the University of Antwerp, Belgium, in 1997. His research interests encompass high-performance computing, special-purpose computing architectures, cloud computing, and machine learning systems and applications. His work has received funding from NSF, NASA, ONR, DOE, and industry. Dr. Kindratenko has published over 140 papers in refereed scientific journals and conference proceedings and holds five US patents.

presentations.title: Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Memory Scaling in HPC Workloads on Cloud
presentations.abstract: Memory over-provisioning results in resource underutilization when HPC workloads run on Kubernetes. The default Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) cannot anticipate phase-driven memory spikes for first-run HPC jobs. In this work, we present a reinforcement learning recommender called VERA that formulates vertical memory scaling as a Markov Decision Process and trains an agent on 3,353 real Prometheus traces. Evaluated on a live Google Kubernetes Engine cluster using LAMMPS, graph analytics, in-memory analytics, and MLPerf 3D-UNet, the RL agent reclaims 31.6% of the available memory headroom and incurs at most one OOM event while VPA reclaims -7.9% over the same runs, raising memory provisioning, and its recommendation would have been insufficient to avoid OOM in 30 runs. The results demonstrate that an observation-driven RL recommender could outperform retrospective heuristics for dynamic memory scaling.

presentations.title: Reliable Numeric Fault Detection During Edge TPU Inference
presentations.abstract: Detecting floating-point exceptions during Edge TPU inference is structurally hard: the accelerator has no floating-point unit, and attaching it fuses the mapped partition into one opaque operation whose values never leave the chip, so tensor inspection is impossible there. We instead read the host CPU's floating-point status register before and after each inference, which every floating-point operation in the pipeline sets because all of them execute on the host. Across five stock models, register polling detected 100% of exception-raising faults, tensor scanning 98.8%, and output inspection 24.6%. Polling adds under 1% to latency; the optional tensor scan costs 7% to 58%. Detection holds on the accelerator, where 90% to 99% of tensors become unobservable. The tool also counts int8 saturation, targeting the 72% of output-corrupting faults that raise no exception.

presentations.title: Repository-Scale Performance Characterization of the IO500 Benchmark
presentations.abstract: The IO500 benchmark provides a common basis for evaluating high-performance computing (HPC) storage systems, while its growing submission repository also offers an opportunity to study performance behavior across systems and time. This work presents a repository-scale characterization of 294 post-reset IO500 submissions from 116 sites spanning 2019–2025. We combine descriptive and temporal analysis with phase-level correlation, scale-sensitivity analysis, and benchmark-log examination to investigate how performance characteristics represented by individual benchmark phases relate to composite rankings. The results show strong relationships among phases measuring similar I/O behavior, but weaker and scale-sensitive relationships between bandwidth and metadata performance. Temporal and log-level analyses further reveal information that is not apparent from aggregate scores alone. These findings demonstrate the value of analyzing IO500 results beyond leaderboard rankings and identify important considerations concerning system scale, benchmark execution, and repository provenance when using community benchmark data for comparative and longitudinal HPC performance analysis.

presentations.title: Reproducibility of Computational Research: Building a Community of Practice for the AI Era
presentations.abstract: Reproducibility remains a fundamental challenge for computational science and AI-enabled research. Building on successful BoFs at SC22, SC24, and PEARC22-PEARC25, we established the Reproducibility of Computational Research Community of Practice, which now includes an active mailing list, public website, webinar series, and emerging working groups. This interactive BoF will engage the SC26 community in shaping the next phase of this effort by sharing community progress, launching working groups, and exploring how AI can improve the capture of reproducible computational artifacts while addressing new challenges. The session welcomes researchers, research computing professionals, software developers, librarians, and cyberinfrastructure practitioners.

presentations.title: Reproducible Benchmarking for High Performance Computing Applications
presentations.abstract: Benchmarking is integral to overall practices of HPC, AI and ML. A hierarchy of benchmarks allows comparison of machines to each other, vendors to respond to new procurements, and compute facilities to evaluate offers when selecting new platforms. Within a developer community, benchmarks allow an application’s performance to be evaluated and improved over time. Despite the importance of benchmarking, the process of performing a benchmark is challenging and requires many manual steps, such as researching the appropriate workloads, determining how to compile the software, acquiring execution steps, and extracting the correct metric for comparison. Collectively, these steps pose a high barrier for new users to perform a benchmark and an even higher barrier to executing these benchmarks across a wide set of compute facilities. This hands-on half-day tutorial provides a detailed introduction to a suite of open-source tools and their capabilities (Benchpark and Ramble) to enable reproducible benchmarking of HPC systems. The tutorial is structured to address reproducibility aspects including encoding of the run and build instructions for a given application and hardware system. Attendees of this tutorial will leave with foundational skills in conducting reproducible benchmarking using these tools for defining build and run instructions.

presentations.title: Research Infrastructure as enabler of New Scientific Research
presentations.abstract: While much scientific research is possible using traditional mechanisms (such as paper and pencil), research infrastructures play an important role in enabling new scientific research that's not possible otherwise. This talk will cover this aspect, with a bend towards data-intensive science through networking and distributed systems research infrastructures.

presentations.title: Research Software Engineers in HPC (RSE-HPC-2026)
presentations.abstract:
Research software engineers (RSEs) are critical to the impact of HPC, data science, and the larger scientific community. They have existed for decades, though often not under that name. The past several years, however, have seen the development of the RSE concept, common job titles, and career paths; the creation of professional networks to connect RSEs; and the emergence of RSE groups at universities, national laboratories, and in industry.

This workshop will bring together RSEs and allies involved in HPC, from all over the world, to grow the RSE community by establishing and strengthening professional networks of current RSEs and RSE leaders. We'll hear about successes and challenges that RSEs and RSE groups have experienced, and discuss ways to increase awareness of RSE opportunities and improve support for RSEs.

The workshop will be highly interactive, featuring panels, an invited talk, and short submitted talks.

presentations.title: Resolving Placement–Residency Conflicts in Multi-GPU Task-Graph Runtimes
presentations.abstract:
In multi-GPU task-graph runtimes, task placement affects both execution time and data locality. Earliest-finish-time (EFT) placement accounts for communication required by the current task but not how placement changes data residency for later tasks, potentially increasing subsequent communication. We observe that some placement-residency conflicts expose model-level slack, allowing lower-copy alternatives without extending the modeled completion of committed work.

We propose a communication-aware task placement scheduler that evaluates lower-copy alternatives and admits them only when they preserve modeled completion relative to the EFT choice. We implement the scheduler in CUDASTF and evaluate it on five task-graph workloads on an eight-GPU NVIDIA L4 platform. On the two workloads where placement changes, the scheduler reduces modeled input-copy volume by 39-81% and improves performance by 1.18-1.31x over the EFT baseline, while retaining EFT placement when no admissible alternative exists.

presentations.title: Resource Adaptivity in the GPTune Autotuning Framework
presentations.abstract:
Autotuning frameworks often consist of various phases, such as sampling, modeling, and search, each with different resource requirements. Hence, traditional, static resource management for such frameworks often leads to wasted resources since not all allocated resources are used throughout all phases of the tuning process.

To address this inefficiency, we demonstrate the use of dynamic resource management for autotuning frameworks, building on the well-known GPTune framework. The original GPTune implementation uses MPI Spawn to launch processes for each phase within a static allocation. We adapt the implementation to use MPI Sessions and Dynamic Processes with PSets (DPP), expressing resource needs of each phase using DPP's generic, graph-based abstraction. This allows resource managers to adapt allocation to current resource needs.

Our evaluation shows that dynamic resource management can reduce the resource usage of GPTune by 46% compared to the static GPTune version.

presentations.title: Resource Contention in Point-to-Point Overlapping GPU Communication with NVSHMEM
presentations.abstract: Overlapping communication with computation is necessary at scale, and the communication library sets how cheaply that overlap can be had. We study point-to-point halo exchange overlapped with compute on a GH200 Grace Hopper platform with InfiniBand, comparing host-initiated GPU-aware MPI against device-initiated NVSHMEM and NCCL. Using a synthetic benchmark, we determine for which shared resource each backend competes. We then apply the communication models to a memory-bound workload, the SU(3) staplesum implemented with the hila framework. We find that in the memory-bound regime the constraint is HBM utilization rather than SM occupancy with an added L2 cost consistent with evicting the compute kernel's reused working set. Device-initiated NVSHMEM is fastest wherever communication is exposed, reaching 99% overlap efficiency in weak scaling at 128 GPUs and extending usable strong scaling 4X from 16 to 64 GPUs over non-overlapped execution. Every optimization reduces either L2 pressure or latency overhead in point-to-point communication.

presentations.title: Rethinking QDMI: Expanding the Quantum Device Abstraction to the Software Stack
presentations.abstract:
The increasing number of quantum devices being installed on-site in High Performance Computing (HPC) and data centres is creating a need for standardised interfaces to enable tighter integration. Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI) is an emerging interface that address this challenge by providing low-level abstractions to enable seamless integration into HPC environment. It is designed to support multiple quantum modalities behind a unified interface, and it evolves in line with requirements. However, QDMI is versatile enough to be adapted as an interface for quantum software stacks.

In this work, we introduce the concept of stack-as-a-device and implement a proof of concept QDMI device for Munich Software Stack that is deployment at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre. We detail our implementation and know-how regarding the life cycle management of the software stacks and quantum jobs.

presentations.title: Revisiting Distributed Particle-Based Volume Rendering on Fugaku and Beyond
presentations.abstract: Large-scale simulations produce substantial data, making data output and interactive visualization costly. We implement and evaluate a distributed particle-based volume rendering (PBVR) workflow on Fugaku that separates CPU-based particle generation from interactive rendering on a GPU-equipped local PC. Building on JAEA's PBVR framework, we integrate in-situ particle generation into OpenFOAM using VTK and KVS. Experiments demonstrate scalability to 110,592 CPU cores (2,304 MPI processes with 48 OpenMP threads each). Separate evaluations on a smaller model show output data reductions of approximately 55%–90%. Although particle generation adds computation, reduced output can offset this overhead by lowering I/O costs. This architecture also offers a model for utilizing available CPUs during GPU-dominated simulations. At the poster session, we will present the system architecture, integration workflow, scalability results, and opacity-dependent data reduction.

presentations.title: Rigorous Evaluation of LLM Components in HPC Research
presentations.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as components inside HPC research workflows. They are used from code generation and translation, to agentic tool use for debugging, profiling, and experiment orchestration. While these systems can accelerate development, they also introduce new challenges for rigorous evaluation: outputs are stochastic, behavior is sensitive to prompts and configuration, commercial models change silently over time, and the true contribution of the LLM is often confounded with many other experimental factors. As a result, a growing number of papers report results using LLMs in their study without sufficient transparency, suitable baselines, or statistically sound measurements. This tutorial will teach participants a practical framework for rigorous evaluation and reporting of LLM components in HPC research. We cover what must be reported for reproducibility, how to design experiments around stochastic components, and when and how to incorporate human validation. We then focus on HPC-specific evaluation and the unique challenges that arise in using LLMs in HPC research. Throughout, we highlight common pitfalls and provide guidance and templates that participants can directly apply to their own projects and papers.

presentations.title: Risk-Oriented Contracts for Non-Functional Requirements in Computing-Continuum Workflows
presentations.abstract: Continuum workflows move artifacts across edge-cloud heterogeneous resources, exposing them to disclosure, corruption, unauthorized modification, unavailability, and excessive-volume risks. Enforcing the corresponding non-functional requirements (NFRs) introduces energy and execution-time overheads. Here, we present a risk-oriented contract-realization layer (CRL) that represents risk mitigations as mandatory and optional contract clauses, translating them into pipelines of NFR mechanisms. The CRL profiles candidate realizations using empirical execution-time profiles and utilization-based power models. It admits only candidates that satisfy all mandatory clauses and whose estimated energy and makespan remain within the active admission thresholds while maximizing optional-clause coverage. The selected realization provides workflow management systems with artifact-level NFR pipelines, which are materialized as tasks. We evaluate the CRL across four workflow directed acyclic graphs, multiple deployment plans, contract profiles, and heterogeneous continuum resources. For a balanced contract profile, the CRL achieves 84% admitted optional-clause coverage, compared with 67% for a global-uniform policy.

presentations.title: RLSA: Adaptive LLM Gating for Multi-Agent HPC Scheduling Agents
presentations.abstract: In decentralized scheduling of scientific workflows, multiple LLM-based agents reason over heterogeneous resources to bid for jobs. However, LLM reasoning incurs substantial latency and compute cost, limiting scalability in high-throughput environments. We therefore ask whether an LLM is necessary for every decision, and study adaptive LLM gating, where an RL-trained policy learns to choose between an LLM and a fast surrogate from downstream scheduling reward. We propose RLSA (Reinforcement Learning-enhanced Scheduling Agents), trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) under a reward balancing makespan, resource balance, and inference cost. In a controlled auction, RLSA halves LLM calls per job (4.00 to 2.06) while preserving makespan relative to always-LLM bidding (7686 vs. 7285 seconds). We further validate it with a real LLM bidder and a 17-VM FABRIC deployment where LLM calls grow sub-linearly with the number of bidders, positioning RL-based adaptive gating as a cost-control layer for LLM-based scheduling agents.

presentations.title: ROSS'26 Invited Opening Talk: Challenges in Integrating Quantum and HPC
presentations.abstract: As quantum computing transitions from experimental to practical, integrating it into the High-Performance Computing (HPC) ecosystem alongside CPUs and GPUs is essential. However, managing this heterogeneous, often geographically distributed infrastructure introduces significant systems challenges in resource scheduling, workflow orchestration, security, and interoperability. This talk examines these hurdles from a runtime and systems software perspective. Drawing on experiences building quantum-centric platforms, we will explore how operating systems and resource managers must evolve to make quantum resources first-class citizens in future HPC environments.

presentations.title: RSE-HPC Short Break
Runtime Power Feasibility for Small Modular Nuclear Reactor-Powered Datacenters
presentations.abstract: Datacenters are exploring on-site small modular reactors (SMRs) for low-carbon power, but reactor power carries multi-hour state that conventional power scheduling does not capture. A power maneuver that is feasible when requested can become infeasible hours later as iodine–xenon dynamics evolve. We expose reactor feasibility through a runtime layer that checks the projected reactor state before the workload scheduler commits to a maneuver. Using eight Google Borg workload traces and PJM grid data, we evaluate reactor- and workload-aware policies at one-minute resolution. At low reactor margin, workload-aware scheduling without reactor state leaves 172 MWh unserved and averages 7.4 reactor shutdowns, while adding projected reactor feasibility reduces unserved work to 169 kWh with no shutdowns. Fixed recovery delays do not reproduce this behavior, and sensitivity experiments examine lookahead, enforcement margin, and reactor-model mismatch.

presentations.title: Sample Count Is Not Enough: Candidate-Generation Strategy Shapes the Energy and Performance of LLM Test-Time Scaling
presentations.abstract:
Test-time scaling can improve large language model reasoning by generating and combining multiple candidate responses. The inference budget is described by the number of generated candidates, N, but N tells us how many candidates are generated, not how they are executed. The same budget can come from one batched call or several sequential calls. Using Phi3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on 500 GSM8K prompts, increasing N from 1 to 8 improves accuracy by 8.4 and 18.4 points, but accuracy alone does not show its system cost. Fixing N = 8, we compare
four generation schedules, 1×8, 2×4, 4×2, and 8×1, measuring latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy. On A100 GPUs, eight serial calls use 4.64–4.86× as much energy
and have 5.77–6.12× the P95 latency of one batched call, confirmed across A100 nodes and SciQ/V100 experiments. Candidate count alone cannot describe system cost; evaluations should also report generation schedule and GPU-level metrics.

presentations.title: Saving Energy Costs and Time on Supercomputers: Scheduler-Integrated Recurring Node Shutdown Exploiting Malleable Jobs
presentations.abstract: Supercomputers consume electricity around the clock, yet photovoltaic generation can make power cheaper and cleaner by day than at night. Thus, shutting down idle nodes overnight could reduce energy cost but risks longer job waiting times. This paper studies scheduler-integrated shutdown policies that proactively power down a share of the nodes during recurring off periods, such as nights. To compensate, we exploit malleable jobs, which the scheduler shrinks before shutdowns to release nodes and expands afterward. In 270 simulations on job sets from three production supercomputers, we evaluate shutdown shares up to 30% under rigid and malleable scheduling with varying fractions of malleable jobs. Shutting down 30% of the nodes benefits both operators and users once 25% of the jobs are malleable. Compared with rigid scheduling without shutdown, operators save up to 12.5% of the daily electricity cost and users up to 56.2% of their job turnaround time.

presentations.title: SC26 Awards Ceremony and SC27 Launch
Scalable AMG Preconditioning for DG Neutron Diffusion Solvers on Manycore CPUs
presentations.abstract: Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretizations of diffusion-type operators, including neutron transport, produce sparse systems that bottleneck simulation throughput. Standard incomplete LU (ILU) preconditioners exhibit O(h−1 ) iteration growth and prohibitive fill-in. This work presents a Smoothed Aggregation Algebraic Multigrid (SA-AMG) preconditioner for 3D DG systems, implemented via Trilinos/MueLu and Kokkos, demonstrating O(1) mesh-independent convergence on the Takeda Benchmark Model 1 up to 7.1e6 unknowns, yielding a 158× speedup over ILU. A strong scaling and roofline analysis across three manycore topologies — Intel Sapphire Rapids, AMD Genoa, and NVIDIA Grace — shows all solver phases memory-bound. On both dual-socket nodes, scalability regresses or halts at the socket boundary due to inter-NUMA traffic in the fine-grid solve, while the single-socket Grace platform sustains its efficiency and achieves the lowest time-to-solution despite fewer cores. These results identify memory topology, rather than core count, as the dominant scalability factor for heterogeneous reactor transport calculations.

presentations.title: Scalable and Multi-NIC Parallel Trees Collective Algorithms for MPI Scatter, Gather, and Broadcast
presentations.abstract: Broadcast, Scatter, and Gather are MPI collectives critical to HPC and DL application scalability. As GPU clusters rely on multiple NICs per node for inter-node bandwidth, traditional single-tree algorithms fail to exploit this bandwidth for large messages. We propose a GPU-based, multi-NIC-aware design for large-message MPI Scatter, Gather, and Broadcast that partitions each collective across multiple independent binomial trees, each mapped to a distinct NIC, enabling communication to proceed concurrently across all rails. We implement and evaluate our design in Open MPI on two GPU platforms, full-mesh NVLink and NVSwitch, at 16, 32, and 64 GPUs. Compared to Open MPI, our design achieves latency reductions of 52.5%, 82.8%, and 74.6% for Scatter, Gather, and Broadcast on full-mesh, and 57.0%, 79.8%, and 74.3% on NVSwitch. A step-complexity analysis shows our design reduces critical-path communication rounds from ⌈log2 p⌉ to ⌈log2(p/g)⌉, where g is rails per node, yielding better scalability at scale.

presentations.title: Scalable Hierarchical Multi-NIC GPU-Aware MPI Alltoall via Hamiltonian Decomposition
presentations.abstract: Alltoall is a communication-intensive collective, realizing a full-mesh exchange among all processes, which relies on RDMA's Reliable Connection (RC) transport for inter-node communication, requiring a dedicated Queue Pair (QP) per peer and exhausting on-NIC memory as peer count grows. We propose a GPU-aware MPI Alltoall that avoids vendor-specific transports, decomposing the full-mesh exchange graph into edge-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles so each process has a small, fixed number of direct peers, combined with a pipelined, multi-NIC exchange overlapping intra- and inter-node communication. Experimentally, at 36 and 72 GPUs, we reduce measured QPs per NIC by up to 98% and 93% versus Open MPI and NCCL, matching an analytical model projecting 66%-98% reductions up to 1152 GPUs. Our design achieves up to 34% and 36% lower Alltoall latency than Open MPI and MVAPICH-Plus, matches NCCL's latency using MPI, and delivers up to 1.2x and 1.66x higher heFFTe throughput than Open MPI and MVAPICH-Plus.

presentations.title: Scalable In-Domain Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Dense Representation Transfer in High-Resolution Plant Imaging
presentations.abstract:
High-resolution plant imaging enables detailed characterization of plant
morphology, but dense scientific imaging analysis remains limited by costly pixel-level
annotations, large image dimensions, and variable imaging conditions. This
work proposes a scalable in-domain self-supervised foundation model for
high-resolution poplar imagery. A masked autoencoder with a ViT backbone is
pretrained on more than 10 million multi-species plant image tiles using distributed
training. The learned representations are benchmarked for fine-grained dense
prediction and coarse global retrieval under limited supervision and realistic
downstream conditions. Across limited annotations, cross-view variation, and
resolution degradation, the in-domain FM achieves a Mean Dice of 0.8686 and a
Pooled Dice of 0.8959, outperforming an ImageNet-pretrained MAE by 0.0694 and
0.0613, respectively. Increasing pretraining scale further
improves dense feature transfer, suggesting that scalable in-domain pretraining
can reduce domain gaps in high-pixel-dimension scientific imaging.

presentations.title: Scalable OpenCHAMI Node Infrastructure Collection (SONIC)
presentations.abstract: Reliable hardware telemetry is foundational to HPC cluster operations, enabling proactive thermal management, power optimization, and failure prediction. HPC monitoring systems often struggle with data loss, service interruptions, and scalability limitations. This work presents a BMC telemetry system deployed on Los Alamos National Laboratory's SI research cluster that achieves high availability through event-driven architecture combining intelligent polling, triple-redundant data paths, and fault-isolated services. Intelligent polling reduces network overhead by 81% while maintaining sub-second latency. A centralized consumer with batched writes achieves 82% reduction in database CPU utilization. Load testing collected over 77,000 samples across multiple load levels, demonstrating counterintuitive inverse scaling where consumer performance improves as cluster load increases. The poster will present the hybrid architecture pipeline, performance metrics under realistic workloads, and Grafana visualization dashboards demonstrating operational deployment on a nine-node production testbed.

presentations.title: Scalable Performance Diagnostics on Leadership Computing Platforms
presentations.abstract: Exascale supercomputers Frontier and Aurora provide infrastructure for executing applications across thousands of compute nodes, with massive MPI tasks, intensive CPU multi-threading, and heavy computation offloaded to GPUs. These heterogeneous workloads pose significant challenges for performance measurement and analysis tools. We refined the hpcanalysis framework as a multi-layered infrastructure consisting of a C++ ingestion engine for high-throughput, selective access to performance measurement slices, a query interface for extracting slices via specialized queries, and a Python API for high-level analytical tasks. This provides a scalable, efficient, interactive interface that ingests measurements for an execution across 100K MPI ranks on Aurora in under 10 seconds. We also designed HpcDataFrame, a GPU-accelerated substitute for the Pandas library, offloading heavy computations to NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, achieving speedups of up to 314x over Pandas processing. Collectively, our contributions provide a scalable substrate for performance diagnostics at the absolute limit of modern supercomputing.

presentations.title: Scale to See: From Extreme-Scale Computing and Scalable AI to New Scientific Discovery
presentations.abstract: Modern scientific problems increasingly demand more than faster computation—they require fundamentally new computational capabilities. This talk explores how the convergence of AI, mathematical modeling, and extreme-scale computing can transform scientific computing from solving known problems faster to enabling questions that were previously computationally inaccessible.Through examples in computational imaging, inverse problems, and Earth-system science, I will discuss how scaling AI to unprecedented model sizes, spatial and temporal resolutions, and ensemble sizes can reveal structure, quantify uncertainty, and enable scientific inference that is difficult or impossible at conventional scales. I will highlight how advances in AI algorithms, architectures, and HPC systems work together to create these new capabilities, and discuss opportunities and challenges for the next generation of scientific discovery.

presentations.title: Scale to See: Scalable AI for Scientific Imaging and Spatiotemporal Data
presentations.abstract: Scale to See: Scalable AI for Scientific Imaging and Spatiotemporal Data is a half-day workshop at SC that brings together researchers at the intersection of high performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI), large-scale scientific imaging and spatiotemporal data. Scientific imaging and spatiotemporal data—from climate and earth systems to medical imaging, materials science, and cosmology—are increasingly high-dimensional, multimodal, and time-evolving, demanding AI methods that are not only accurate but also scalable, physics-aware, and deployable on leadership-class HPC systems. This workshop focuses on AI methods and systems explicitly co-designed for extreme scale, including HPC-aware model architectures, scalable training and inference pipelines, physics-integrated learning algorithms, and efficient computing techniques for high-dimensional data. Through peer-reviewed papers, invited talks, and panel discussions, the workshop aims to set a research agenda, foster interdisciplinary collaboration, and build a community around AI that operates natively at HPC scale to transform scientific imaging and spatiotemporal analysis.

presentations.title: Scale Up Platform Enabled by RISC – SUPER
presentations.abstract:
Scale Up Platform Enabled by RISC-V (SUPER)
is an open source firmware extension that provides a remote
memory model implementation for RISC-V, mapping physical
memory operations, e.g., loads, stores, and atomics, to operations
over unmodified networks such as Slingshot, UAL or UEC. Unlike other remote memory, memory expansion, or scaleup
implementations, SUPER requires no hardware
beyond a packet-based network. Instead, SUPER uses unique
capabilities of the RISC-V architecture to intercept physical
memory accesses and convert them to remote memory accesses.
The overhead for this interception is less than 10 nanoseconds
on the new NextSilicon Arbel CPUs. Unlike previous systems,
SUPER requires no globally coherent address space map.
This paper describes

• what SUPER provides

• how it uses the unique properties of RISC-V

• its performance

presentations.title: ScaleTether: Graph Rewriting and Selective Timing Prediction for Megatron Parallelism
presentations.abstract: Automated planners for distributed training must evaluate configurations that have not yet run. ScaleTether transforms version-pinned Megatron executions into workload graphs for tensor, data, and pipeline parallelism. It exports graphs as Chakra traces for ASTRA-sim, while graph support and measured H100 timings determine whether it returns an estimate, requests measurements, or rejects an unsupported configuration. Six graphs created before their target runs matched later captures on every checked field, and all 72 injected corruptions were rejected. Across cases, median timing error ranged from 0.73% to 3.59%. In 80 four-GPU searches, all 35 estimates chose the measured optimum, while measurement intercepted all 19 ungated choices above 1% regret. Selective measurement cut acquisition by 30.3% to 7.58 H100 GPU-hours including calibration and by 44.0% to 6.09 with calibration reuse. Agents followed guidance in 120/120 offline sessions versus 52/120 with configuration numbers alone.

presentations.title: Scaling a Heterogeneous Metagenomics Workflow to 100,000 Samples with Nextflow on HPC
presentations.abstract: Running large-scale and heterogeneous metagenomics workflows is challenging not only because of CPU resources needed but also because of high requirements for storage and memory. We present GutMap, a thirteen-step Nextflow workflow that processes over 100{,}000 human gut metagenomes with a total size of 189~TB. We report the results of running GutMap on the Helios supercomputer using almost 1.5~million CPU-hours, describe memory-related optimisations and solutions to storage limitations and provide a detailed account of the resource profile of the workflow.

presentations.title: Scaling Computation, Expanding Discovery: From Medical Imaging to Continental-Scale Archaeology
presentations.abstract: Scientific discovery is increasingly limited not by the availability of data, but by our ability to analyze and interpret complex information across spatial and temporal scales. Advances in AI, scalable computational methods, and high-performance computing (HPC) are transforming these limits, enabling scientists to see, infer, and understand phenomena previously beyond reach. Drawing on examples from medical imaging to continental-scale archaeology, this talk explores how radical collaboration among domain scientists, AI researchers, and HPC experts unlocks new scientific insights from massive, heterogeneous imaging and spatiotemporal datasets. Beyond accelerating existing workflows, these collaborations demonstrate how scaling computation can fundamentally expand the boundaries of scientific discovery.

presentations.title: Scaling Laws for Physics-Aware ACOPF Surrogate Learning
presentations.abstract: Learning-based surrogates for AC optimal power flow (ACOPF) promise large speedups over classical solvers, but their operational value depends on physical feasibility as much as predictive accuracy. Physics-aware objectives such as the augmented Lagrangian (AL) improve constraint satisfaction at additional per-step cost, yet how this trade-off behaves with scale is uncharacterized. We sweep model and dataset sizes under MSE and AL training, and measure how violation changes with network size. Both objectives improve as power laws: MSE prediction loss depends more on model size than on data, while the AL composite of prediction loss and violation improves comparably along both axes. Violation grows markedly more slowly with network size under AL. On matched hardware and equal training samples, AL reduces violation about 19x with 2.4x training time and negligible added memory. The training objective shapes not only where a surrogate lands but how its quality evolves with scale.

presentations.title: Science-Aware Network Operations for Research Networks (SciNet)
presentations.abstract:
The emergence of AI-driven autonomous laboratories is changing how scientific experiments are designed, executed, and analyzed.
Research networks, however, remain passive communication infrastructures that optimize packet delivery while being agnostic to the scientific workflows they support, a disconnect that creates bottlenecks in distributed experimentation, multi-facility workflows, and real-time scientific decision making.
This paper presents Science-Aware Autonomous Networks (SciNet), a networking paradigm in which artificial intelligence (AI) embedded in the network control plane continuously observes scientific workflows, predicts future network demands, reasons about workflow dependencies, and autonomously adapts network behavior.
Unlike conventional AIOps systems that optimize utilization or reliability, SciNet optimizes for scientific productivity through workflow-aware routing, predictive resource allocation, and autonomous failure mitigation.
We describe the SciNet layered architecture and its optimization objective, characterize the network requirements of Department of Energy (DOE) science workflows through stakeholder interviews, distill these requirements into six recurring use cases with associated quality-of-service classes, and outline ongoing research directions under the Genesis Mission toward AI-driven autonomous laboratories.

The emergence of AI-driven autonomous laboratories is changing how scientific experiments are designed, executed, and analyzed.
Research networks, however, remain passive communication infrastructures that optimize packet delivery while being agnostic to the scientific workflows they support, a disconnect that creates bottlenecks in distributed experimentation, multi-facility workflows, and real-time scientific decision making.
This paper presents Science-Aware Autonomous Networks (SciNet), a networking paradigm in which artificial intelligence (AI) embedded in the network control plane continuously observes scientific workflows, predicts future network demands, reasons about workflow dependencies, and autonomously adapts network behavior.

presentations.title: Scientific Software and the People Who Make It Happen: Building Our Communities and Practices
presentations.abstract:
Software has become central to all aspects of modern science and technology. Especially in high performance computing (HPC) and computational science and engineering (CSE), it is becoming ever larger and more complex while computer platforms evolve and become more diverse. Simultaneously, the teams behind the software are becoming larger, more technically diverse, and more geographically distributed. AI tools add both great potential and significant caution.

This BoF will address these issues and more, sharing experiences and best practices, and building community around software topics. Presentations and discussion notes will be made available at the BoF series website (http://bit.ly/swe-cse-bof).

presentations.title: SCinet — Technical Overview
SCinet Network Overview
presentations.abstract: This session provides a technical overview of SCinet’s architecture for both the Conference/Exhibitor network and the Science Connector Network.

presentations.title: SCinet Research and NRE Talk
SciNet: Science-Aware Network Operations for Research Networks
presentations.abstract:
Emergence of AI-driven autonomous laboratories is fundamentally changing how scientific experiments are designed, executed, and analyzed. However, research networks
remain passive communication infrastructures that seek to optimize packet delivery while being agnostic of the scientific workflows they support. This disconnect creates bottlenecks
in distributed experimentation, multi-facility workflows, and real-time scientific decision making. In this paper, we propose Science-Aware Autonomous Networks (SciNet), a new networking paradigm where artificial intelligence (AI) is integrated into the
network control plane to continuously observe scientific workflows, predict network demands, reason about workflow dependencies, and optimize network behavior, done autonomously. Unlike conventional AIOps systems that optimize utilization or reliability, SciNet is focused on optimizing for scientific productivity through workflow-aware routing, predictive resource allocation, and autonomous mitigation of failures. We present the architecture, mathematical formulation, learning framework, and evaluation methodology, and discuss how the proposed system aligns with the Department of Energy’s vision for AI-driven autonomous laboratories.

presentations.title: Secure integration and scaling for thousands of Jupyter sessions across hybrid cloud and HPC resources on Anvil
presentations.abstract: The Anvil Notebook Service is a highly scalable Kubernetes-based JupyterHub platform on Purdue University's NSF-funded Anvil supercomputer. We present technical solutions bridging Anvil's 1000-node Slurm HPC partition and its Kubernetes cloud resource to scale JupyterLab, VSCode and Linux Desktops for thousands of users. To scale beyond the capacity of the Kubernetes infrastructure, a locally developed, open-source software called Dynamic Node Manager converts idle HPC nodes to Kubernetes nodes on demand. To enable access to shared HPC filesystems from Jupyter pods, custom user identity integration allows containers to run as the logged-in user's UID. Users can access HPC Slurm queues for batch job submission. For efficient GPU utilization, users can dynamically slice GPUs based on vRAM requirements. Users can also run Apptainer containers and access AI agents and MCP tools. This talk shares the engineering insights for the hybrid HPC/cloud container orchestration of the service.

presentations.title: Security and Day-2 Resilience as First Class Control Plane Primitives for Heterogeneous Supercomputers
presentations.abstract: This experience report describes how reproducibility, security, and safe day-2 operations are handled in OpenCHAMI, an open, API-first, composable HPC control plane developed collaboratively under a Linux Foundation foundation and deployed in production across multiple sites. Modern centres run Slurm-scheduled HPC alongside Kubernetes-based AI, and maintenance windows test the management plane hardest. Rather than a controlled benchmarking study, we contribute a deployed open system, transferable operational practices, and an honest account of what is validated today versus roadmapped. We describe a composable microservices architecture with snapshot-based, predictably degrading state; a layered image-build pipeline with one-shot cloud-init convergence that removes configuration drift; and a WireGuard-based ephemeral bootstrapping model that keeps no long-lived credentials in images. We report author-reported outcomes, including a boot-to-scheduler-ready reduction from roughly eight minutes to ninety seconds, and evidence that the same control plane transfers across sites, architectures, and workload classes.

presentations.title: Security Mediation and Adversarial Evaluation for Agentic AI at HPC Facilities
presentations.abstract: For LLM agents at DOE facilities, prompt injection and unsupported citations share one shape: a value reaches a consequential action, a sink, from a forbidden origin. PALISADE, a sidecar gating six boundaries of the VISTA platform, labels values by origin outside the model, propagates labels by text matching, and admits a sink value only if its label permits. SIEGE, our 205-attack benchmark, enforces HPC job submission as a security boundary and scores detector evasion separately from sink access. The deterministic tier stops 19 of 32 sink-capable attacks and, with egress blocking, all 5 forged citations, at 0.28 ms/turn and 3.3% benign blocking. Adaptive attacks (PAIR, TAP) raise credited sink admissions to means of 28–31 of 32, but about 14 still carry the attack, none bearing an untrusted label at the check. Closing this propagation gap requires tracking dataflow or keeping untrusted values out of the planner.

presentations.title: Security Panel
Segments: A Reusable Sparse-Data Abstraction for Multicore CPUs and GPUs
presentations.abstract: Sparse matrices, graphs, numerical meshes, and particle methods differ in semantics, yet repeatedly process collections of variable-length groups such as matrix rows, adjacency lists, incidence relations, and particle neighborhoods. Implementations commonly bind these groups to a particular storage format and hardware-specific execution strategy, forcing traversal, reduction, and scheduling logic to be duplicated across data structures and backends. We present TNL Segments, a reusable C++ abstraction that separates irregular-data semantics from physical representation and parallel execution. Segments provide the mapping (segmentIdx, localIdx) → globalIdx, while application-specific values, column indices, edge weights, and mesh data remain in independent arrays. The same interface supports multicore CPUs, CUDA GPUs, and HIP GPUs.

presentations.title: SemQBench: Benchmarking Decomposition-Aware Runtime Policies for Quantum-HPC Search
presentations.abstract: Quantum processors increasingly act as accelerators in HPC workflows, where the runtime schedules the work. Many search problems split into independent parts, but the runtime can exploit this only if the workflow exposes those parts and a per-part validity check. SemQBench compares seven execution policies on the 20-qubit IQM Garnet processor, varying one choice at a time: whether to amplify, whether partial results combine across runs, and what a retry keeps. Amplifying the whole problem gives no clear gain over random sampling at 6.7-104x more device time. Collecting valid partial results across a batch cuts executions for 95% confidence by 2.20-4.00x and wins in 99/108 overhead settings. Fewer executions need not mean less device time: one workload drops from thirteen executions to four as device time rises from 7.44-9.81 μs. Exposed structure gives the runtime a strong default and the evidence to drop it when it does not pay.

presentations.title: Serving Masked Diffusion LLMs: Characterization and Design Principles from Real Hardware
presentations.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) promise faster generation than autoregressive (AR) models by denoising many tokens at once, but their behavior under concurrent serving load is unmeasured. We characterize dLLM serving using LLaDA-8B-Instruct with a D2F LoRA adapter on one NVIDIA H200 GPU, evaluated on GSM8K and HumanEval. First, request difficulty is discrete: denoising-step counts fall into 11 fixed levels, and no admission-time signal predicts the level (best R² = 0.150). Second, generation budgets below ~320 tokens understate serving variance through truncation. Third, 24% of single-request wall-clock time is GPU computation; the rest is CPU-side dispatch overhead. Sharing one forward pass per denoising step amortizes this overhead, reaching 16.0× single-request throughput at batch size 16. We also derive a batch-timeout stability rule for synchronized batching under Poisson arrivals. These results show that dLLM serving needs parallelism at the level of each denoising step. Code and data are available at https://github.com/flarebrienne/Serving-Masked-Diffusion-LLMS.

presentations.title: SHARD-DB: Scalable Hash-Based Retrieval for High-Throughput Reference Database Construction
presentations.abstract: Reference databases tailored to metabarcoding loci are essential for environmental-DNA analysis, but constructing them can require thousands of searches against multi-terabyte nucleotide collections. CRUX-style workflows commonly expand primer-derived sequences using BLAST. SHARD-DB instead performs broad approximate retrieval with densified one-permutation MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), followed by targeted locus localization. On a full NCBI NT MiFish workload of 10,292 queries, SHARD-DB completed retrieval and localization in 73:38 using 28.6 GiB peak RSS, while CRUX-style Merged BLAST completed in 52:16 using approximately 407 GB peak RSS. SHARD-DB retrieved 1,606,861 unique candidate accessions versus 133,387 for BLAST, providing a substantially broader reference pool for database construction. Historical matched-subset experiments also showed large SHARD-DB runtime advantages for MarVer3 16S and PR2 18S, demonstrating strong workload-dependent performance.

presentations.title: ShardTensor: Democratizing Domain Parallelism for Scientific Machine Learning
presentations.abstract:
Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) faces unique challenges for extreme-resolution
data, with mitigations that often fail to scale or degrade the accuracy of
trained models. Some specialized methods have achieved remarkable
results in training models or performing inference on massive spatial datasets
with bespoke techniques, but each is a model-specific effort; there is no general
framework that makes domain parallelism accessible to SciML practitioners at large.
We introduce
\texttt{ShardTensor}, a PyTorch-native abstraction that brings domain
parallelism into the standard training and inference workloads the way DDP brought
data parallelism: non-invasively, without model changes, and composable with
existing data- and model-parallel techniques.
We describe the dispatch design that makes this possible, and show on
benchmarks and production applications that unmodified models train beyond
single-GPU memory, scale near-linearly at large input sizes, and run faster
inference on high-resolution data.

presentations.title: Sharing a Fabric with Collective Communication: Two Storage Penalties in DL Training
presentations.abstract: Distributed DL training on HPC systems often shares one network fabric for collective communication and parallel-filesystem I/O. Using a real GNN workload on a Slingshot-11 system, we identify two costs. First, shared-fabric I/O causes heavy-tailed DataLoader stalls: typical waits are 15 ms but spike to seconds in 28% of Lustre iterations and 12% of VAST iterations. Second, traffic-class contention slows collective communication: Lustre stalls all-reduce by up to 145 times in isolation. The first effect affects any shared-fabric storage path, whereas the second occurs only when storage and collective traffic share a traffic class. A dedicated all-flash tier on a separate traffic class substantially reduces the secondary effect but leaves its DataLoader tail heavy. Nimbus, which stages data to node-local NVMe, eliminates both by removing storage I/O from the shared fabric. Nimbus achieves 7.4 times higher throughput than Lustre and 1.31 times higher throughput than VAST with a warm cache.

SIGHPC Annual Member Meeting
presentations.abstract: The SIGHPC Annual Member Meeting brings together ACM SIGHPC members and the broader HPC community to review the organization's activities, celebrate recent accomplishments, and discuss priorities for the coming year. The meeting provides an open forum where members can interact directly with SIGHPC leadership, learn about ongoing initiatives in education, awards, student programs, chapters, diversity and inclusion, publications, and conference activities, and help shape future directions. Whether you are a long-time member or new to the community, this session offers an opportunity to engage with SIGHPC leadership, provide feedback, ask questions, and become involved in the society's activities.

presentations.title: Simulation of Tungsten Transport in the ASDEX-U Tokamak Plasma
presentations.abstract: Simulation of tungsten transport in the ASDEX-U tokamak plasma reveals critical insights for fusion reactor design. Tungsten, used for its heat resistance, ionizes during operation and can penetrate the core, radiating energy and reducing efficiency. These simulations explore the interaction of tungsten ions with rotation and light impurities like boron and helium in the complex edge region near the wall. The study highlights the role of binary collisions and asymmetries in tungsten penetration. Confidence in the model is bolstered by recent validation on a separate physics problem.

presentations.title: Sixth International Symposium on Quantitative Co-Design of Supercomputers (SQCS)
presentations.abstract: The Sixth International Symposium on Quantitative Co-Design of Supercomputers, or SQCS'26, considers combining two methodologies — collaborative co-design and data-driven analysis — to realize the potential of supercomputing more fully. By narrowing in on these two proven methodologies with the broad-community attention of an SC26 audience, we will address a host of identified challenges impacting high performance computing (HPC). The 2026 workshop focus will focus on upcoming machines and emerging technologies. The state of HPC is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving beyond a sole focus on raw peak FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) to prioritizing time-to-solution, energy efficiency, and AI-simulation convergence. The landscape is defined by the rise of "post-exascale" machines, the integration of generative AI into scientific workflows, and the emergence of hybrid quantum-classical architectures. This symposium will bring together leaders in the field to review current efforts across centers and discuss areas that show potential.

presentations.title: Skip the SuperPOD - The User-Driven Case for Throughput-Optimized GPU Clusters
presentations.abstract: AI compute architectures are optimized for theneeds of the market, which today is hyperscaler AI training. It is critical for academic cyberinfrastructure leaders to understand the workload profiles in higher education and compare these to peer institutions to account for any local factors. This study seeks to compare and contrast the workload profiles across a set of university HPC centers to identify whether usage patterns are consistent across institutions and build out a data-driven model to capacity plan for GPU compute demand.

presentations.title: Skyway My Way! InfiniBand to Ethernet Optimization and Benchmarking
presentations.abstract: Modern high performance computing and AI/ML workloads increasingly require efficient bridges between InfiniBand compute fabrics and Ethernet storage systems to enable large data transfer capabilities. The NVIDIA Skyway is a gateway device designed to translate IPoIB (Internet Protocol over InfiniBand) for external Ethernet services. This work seeks to evaluate and optimize the Skyway by benchmarking bandwidth performance, validating multi-tenant partition security boundaries, and identifying optimal deployment strategies for HPC workloads. Testing is performed on a nine-node cluster with an InfiniBand, Ethernet, and Skyway switch. A modified version of GPCNeT is used to measure cluster bandwidth under congestion. NFS performance is benchmarked within both the Ethernet network and across the Skyway. Finally, the network is partitioned to separate traffic of two controller nodes, emulating a secure user compute system. Our experimentation paves the way for Skyway implementation on production clusters, providing insight on hashing and storage I/O improvements for future work.

presentations.title: SlingShot as a First-Class Kubernetes Resource: Bare-Metal RDMA for Multi-Tenant AI
presentations.abstract:
AI and HPC increasingly demand interconnects that are simultaneously high-performance, open, and cloud-native. HPE’s Ethernet-based Slingshot fabric substantially shaped the
Ultra Ethernet Consortium’s 1.0 transport, establishing it as a proven foundation for open, standards-based RDMA. Exposing its kernel-bypass RDMA plane to multi-tenant, bare-metal
Kubernetes is non-trivial: the fabric lives outside conventional Linux networking, and NIC particularities such as resource pools must be accommodated. Prior approaches depend on brittle, loosely-coupled external device plugins, chained CNI plugins, controllers, and databases. Building on a deployment on Isambard-AI, the UK’s sovereign AI Research Resource, we present a Cray eXascale Interconnect (CXI) Dynamic Resource Allocation
(DRA) driver making Slingshot devices first-class, scheduler-visible Kubernetes resources. It enables declarative, topology-aware allocation and native multi-tenant isolation without privileged pods, and coordinates cluster-wide Virtual Network Identifier lifecycle
through namespace attachment. We evaluate distributed LLM-serving workloads, demonstrating bare-metal RDMA performance with secure isolation within a Trusted Research Environment.

presentations.title: Software for Large Scale Application
presentations.abstract: This session surveys the software layers that make large-scale quantum-classical applications possible. Speakers will present the open Quantum Software Ecosystem (openQSE), the interfaces that connect quantum resources to HPC systems, and the workflow tools and libraries built on top of them. The talks highlight how these components fit together and what it takes to run real applications on integrated quantum-HPC systems today.

presentations.title: Software for Large Scale Application (2)
presentations.abstract: This session surveys the software layers that make large-scale quantum-classical applications possible. Speakers will present the open Quantum Software Ecosystem (openQSE), the interfaces that connect quantum resources to HPC systems, and the workflow tools and libraries built on top of them. The talks highlight how these components fit together and what it takes to run real applications on integrated quantum-HPC systems today.

presentations.title: SOO, MOO, and FOO: Transformer-Layer Execution on Ryzen AI NPUs
presentations.abstract: Consumer neural processing units (NPUs) make local large language model inference attractive, but limited resources make mapping transformer layers to them challenging. This paper categorizes and evaluates three ways to offload transformer layers on Ryzen AI NPUs. Single-operator offload (SOO) configures the NPU to execute one operation within a transformer layer. Multi-operator offload (MOO) submits an ordered list of operators to be executed sequentially on the NPU. We introduce fused-operator offload (FOO), which groups graph operators into subgraphs, maps their dataflows through the NPU, and adjusts the loop order to preserve intermediate data on-chip. Across encoder and decoder layers, FOO improves effective GFLOP/s over MOO and SOO by up to 2.22× and 6.30×, respectively. We further introduce a FOO method to speed up attention and feed-forward computations by 7.80× and 6.83×, respectively. Compared to the integrated GPU (iGPU), FOO improves energy efficiency by up to 9.15× higher effective GFLOP/s/W.

presentations.title: SORT: Slurm-Orchestrated ROCm Telemetry for Facility-wide GPU Observability on HPC Systems
presentations.abstract:
Nearly 300 projects use Frontier at the Oak Ridge
Leadership Computing Facility each year, with approximately
30% turnover in the project population. These projects execute
heterogeneous applications across CPUs and GPUs, and their
computational requirements evolve as new workloads enter the
facility. Planning next-generation systems requires OLCF lead-
ership to better understand accelerator usage across the facility
workload population.
We present SORT, a Slurm-Orchestrated ROCm Telemetry
framework that uses traditional prologue and epilogue hooks
to control a ROCprofiler-SDK-based telemetry collector over the
lifetime of a Slurm allocation. SORT integrates ROCprofiler-SDK
counter collection with the Slurm allocation lifecycle and joins
compact counter artifacts with scheduler metadata for offline
analysis. Deployed on Borg, SORT collected 88,269 valid counter files associated
with 67,373 jobs. The resulting telemetry supports population-
level characterization of instruction, memory-request, and FP64
activity and can help identify candidate jobs for deeper profiling.

presentations.title: Sovereignty above the scheduler: pluggable site policies and a federated view for AI/HPC with Waldur
presentations.abstract:
Sovereign AI and HPC infrastructure requires that sites can enforce their own policies and replace underlying components without breaking their participation in federations.

We present the architecture of Waldur, an MIT-licensed allocation and accounting platform that serves as the allocation component of the EuroHPC Federation Platform and runs in production at sites including CSCS, Isambard-AI, Cambridge Dawn and the Estonian Government Cloud. Waldur separates two concerns that are often entangled. At the site level, a pluggable agent model lets each site map federated allocations onto its own backends (Slurm, Kubernetes, OpenStack or others) and apply local policies for account provisioning, quota enforcement, usage reporting and access rules. Scheduler choice and local governance thus remain site decisions. At the federation level, a common data model for projects, allocations, users and usage gives funders, allocation committees and users a single view across heterogeneous sites, without requiring those sites to adopt the same stack.

We discuss the design of the plugin boundary: what must be standardised for federation to work, what should stay site-specific, and how this boundary limits the impact when any one component changes its license or stewardship. We close with open questions on shared allocation and accounting standards across sovereign federations.

presentations.title: Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication on Cerebras WSE-3
presentations.abstract: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is bounded by data movement rather than arithmetic, since every nonzero fetches from an unpredictable address. We present a general tile-wise SpMV kernel for the Cerebras WSE-3, whose ~893,000 processing elements (PE) hold the working set in on-chip SRAM. The kernel partitions the matrix with a deterministic host-side balancing algorithm and sums per-PE partials eastward along each grid row. Sweeping to the full wafer, the local compute scales linearly and a two-parameter model predicts it exactly across 17 configurations; the eastward reduction, parallel along one axis only, is the sole limit on total scaling, and a standalone chain-latency model underpredicts it by up to 26% once it overlaps compute. On a biobank-scale genotype matrix of 5.28 billion nonzeros the kernel sustains 64,700 GFLOP/s; on a matched smaller instance it completes in 59.6 μs against 5.46 ms for four A100 GPUs.

presentations.title: SPEAR: Semantic Partitioning and Edge-Adapted Routing for Distributed LLM Serving
presentations.abstract: Edge deployment of LLMs requires multiple devices working together, since no single device matches a cloud server's range. Existing edge routers treat each query as one unit and use fixed, offline-trained policies that break down as workloads change. We present SPEAR (Semantic Partitioning and Edge-Adapted Routing), which routes work at the subtask level and keeps adapting after deployment. We split each query into subtasks, send each to an edge device by capability score and risk threshold, and fall back to a cloud model only when confidence is too low. We also update each device's LoRA parameters from cloud feedback, so edge models and the router keep improving without cloud-side retraining. On a testbed of Raspberry Pi 4s, Jetson Orins, and an RTX 4090 server, SPEAR reaches 94.7% routing accuracy, beating baselines like RouteLLM, with only 32.4 ms overhead; local adaptation raises Banking77 accuracy from 31.0% to 56.5% over five rounds.
