presentations.title: SPHERE Research Infrastructure for Cybersecurity Experimentation
Spiral Wave: The Heart's Chaotic Dance
presentations.abstract:
A spiral of crimson, gold, mocha, and magenta moves through the heart, tracing the electrical activity that coordinates every heartbeat. Here, that rhythm has broken down. The spiral is a rotor, a self-sustaining electrical wave that drives atrial fibrillation, one of the most common and dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.

Every frame is generated directly from a high-performance cardiac electrophysiology simulation. The left atrium is modeled as a large network of electrically coupled tissue, simulated in near real time using custom CUDA code running on NVIDIA GPUs. This computational framework allows researchers to investigate how atrial fibrillation begins, evolves, and responds to targeted intervention.

The colors are not arbitrary; they are the language of physiology. Crimson marks tissue at rest, ready to activate. Gold follows the wave of depolarization as it propagates through the muscle. Mocha and magenta represent the refractory period, when the tissue is recovering before it can fire again. In this simulation, the refractory period is shortened, and a precisely timed electrical stimulus initiates the spiral wave.

Spiral Wave lives at the intersection of computation, medicine, and art. Every color, every curve, and every swirl emerges from the underlying physics of cardiac tissue. Nothing in this animation was designed to be beautiful. It simply is.

presentations.title: SplitFT: An Edge-Cloud Collaborative Federated Split Learning System for LLM Fine-Tuning
presentations.abstract:
Federated Split Learning (FSL) has emerged as an effective paradigm for mitigating the computational burden of edge clients in classical federated learning while preserving data privacy. However, applying FSL to large language model (LLM) fine-tuning introduces several critical challenges. In particular, cut-layer selection must be adaptively configured across clients to accommodate heterogeneous data distributions and device capabilities, which can significantly affect system performance. Moreover, reducing communication overhead during fine-tuning remains an important yet underexplored problem.

We propose SplitFT, an edge-cloud collaborative federated split learning system for LLM fine-tuning. SplitFT allows clients to select different cut layers according to their computational resources and model performance. It further reduces communication costs by decreasing the LoRA rank at the cut layer. To better emulate real-world data heterogeneity, we introduce a length-based Dirichlet partitioning strategy. Extensive experiments on popular benchmarks demonstrate that SplitFT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both fine-tuning efficiency and model performance.

presentations.title: SpSYRK: Half the Work in Distributed Sparse Matrix Multiplication
presentations.abstract:
The symmetric rank-k update (SYRK), C = AA^⊤,
computes the dot product between each pair of rows of A. Its sparse variant is central to
similarity-based approaches in machine learning, graph analytics,
and genomics. Existing distributed sparse
matrix multiplication algorithms, such as Sparse SUMMA, treat
sparse SYRK as a generic multiplication, leaving performance
untapped.

In this paper, we present a distributed sparse SYRK algorithm that leverages symmetry. The approach reduces per-process computation compared with state-of-the-art distributed SpGEMM. A second variant reorders
communication to avoid materializing A^⊤ and reduce communication volume.

The algorithm achieves a 2× speedup over an optimized Sparse
SUMMA on matrices. Our variant achieves
superior scaling at high process counts. The approach is a drop-
in replacement for any application computing C = AA^⊤ via
a distributed SpGEMM routine, and its triangular output can
be consumed directly by subsequent operations with reduced
compute and memory footprint.

presentations.title: Squid: Distributed-Memory k-mer Counting for Rack-Scale GPU Clusters
presentations.abstract: The problem of k-mer counting (KC) is to quantify the frequency of length-k substrings in a biological sequence. It is an essential and often limiting step in bioinformatics workloads. Despite the recent popularity of GPUs, the fastest distributed-memory KC solutions remain CPU-based. Existing GPU implementations have poor memory-bandwidth utilization and weak communication-computation overlap. To address these issues, we present Squid, a GPU-native distributed-memory, bulk-synchronous parallel k-mer counter. Squid introduces a transpose-based k-mer generation kernel that reaches up to 71% of peak high-bandwidth memory bandwidth and is 6× faster than prior approaches. On identical hardware, Squid runs 22× faster end-to-end than the previous state-of-the-art GPU counter, and scales to 256 GPUs on a modern GB200-NVL72 cluster at ≥85% intra-rack parallel efficiency. Squid is also the first GPU k-mer counter to outperform the CPU-based DAKC and HySortK, running on 1024 CPUs of Perlmutter, by up to 2× and 6.6×, respectively.

presentations.title: Stabilizing Autoregressive PDE Foundation Model Rollouts with Event-Triggered Context Healing
presentations.abstract: Autoregressive PDE foundation models enable fast full-field forecasting but accumulate errors as predicted states are recursively reused. We introduce Event-Triggered Context Healing (ETCH), which compares forecasts with measurements from 12 cylinder-surface pressure taps. When their discrepancy exceeds a threshold, pressure-conditioned hourglass diffusion transformers reconstruct the velocity--pressure context for subsequent predictions. On 43 RealPDEBench Cylinder trajectories, ETCH reduces velocity and pressure errors from 48.05 and 63.71% to 6.29 and 7.25% for DPOT, and from 74.97 and 76.91% to 5.16 and 6.84% for Poseidon-T, using the same reconstructors and threshold. For DPOT, correcting 14.56% of windows maintains errors close to reconstructing every window and supports average real-time forecasting and correction on an A100 GPU. These results show that sparse physical feedback stabilizes long autoregressive rollouts across PDE foundation models while reducing reconstruction cost.

presentations.title: StageOnce: Speculative Cross-Job Data Staging for LLM Agent Fleets
presentations.abstract: Scientific workflows increasingly run as fleets of LLM agents analyzing the same large immutable datasets. On a shared compute node, independent staging repeats source reads and creates storage contention, while each job discovers its inputs during reasoning. StageOnce coordinates these speculative path predictions through a node-local daemon, coalescing concurrent misses into one immutable copy while preserving dataset versions and private outputs. Tools read staged inputs directly from the filesystem, without per-read coordination. Recorded-session replays in genomics and astronomy on SSD and HDD backends reduce fleet makespan by 31%–51% at 12 concurrent jobs against independent staging. Logical staging remains one copy across every tested fleet size. An ablation isolates speculation, which reduces makespan by 8%–49% against reactive shared caching.

presentations.title: STARCH: RPC-Lifecycle Tracing of Margo-Based Distributed Systems for Performance Analysis
presentations.abstract: STARCH is a low-perturbation LTTng-based tracing system targeting RPC-Lifecycles, designed to instrument Margo-based applications without any code modification on the target. Per-node collectors aggregate events from clients and servers, while causal association of a client request to a server response is handled outside of the HPC job. The resulting trace database can be used to generate statistics and test many hypotheses without needing to run multiple manually instrumented experiments. In this paper we use STARCH to analyze a known CHFS performance degradation using IOR, and present the potential general applicability of STARCH on GekkoFS. STARCH typically incurs under 1.7\% overhead on our IOR+CHFS benchmark, and reliably collects and reconstructs tracing data in a manageable per-node data volume. STARCH was able to surface a nontrivial performance finding about CHFS, reducing the problem scope to a specific area of RPC handling.

presentations.title: StarLight Software Defined Staright Exchange for Data-Intensive Science
STORM: Scalable One-Sided Communication for Distributed Monte Carlo Particle Transport
presentations.abstract:
Domain-decomposed Monte Carlo transport moves particles between MPI ranks as they cross spatial subdomains. Transfers are irregular, bursty, and unpredictable. Existing asynchronous algorithms commonly use matched MPI messages, requiring receiver participation and progress polling.

STORM converts OFI/libfabric one-sided operations into a receiver-passive migration protocol with ordered publication, dynamic buffer growth, and termination accounting. On 2,240–13,440 ranks of Leonardo, STORM retains 88.3% constant global workload scaling efficiency under constant global transport work and more than 97% weak-scaling efficiency, with up to 1.27× speedup over optimized point-to-point MPI. In one three-dimensional Implicit Monte Carlo Hohlraum run, it is 1.41× faster at 4,480 ranks.

presentations.title: StrataVR: A Unity-Based Out-of-Core Pipeline for Interactive Exploration of Multi-Terabyte Volumes in Virtual Reality
presentations.abstract:
Large volumetric datasets often exceed GPU memory, making responsive exploration in virtual reality (VR) difficult. StrataVR is a Unity-based out-of-core volume renderer that stores datasets externally and loads a small multi-resolution working set as the view changes. To our knowledge, it is the first Unity-based out-of-core VR volume renderer demonstrated on a multi-terabyte dataset. A C++ tool prepares bricks and metadata, while view-aware planning and asynchronous streaming keep relevant data in a fixed GPU pool. Coarser resident bricks remain visible until finer data arrives, providing continuous feedback and progressive refinement. The working system supports multichannel visualization, empty-region skipping, channel controls, cross sections and cutouts.

The interactive e-poster will show how StrataVR turns a multi-teratbye dataset into a responsive VR experience. Animations will explain how StrataVR works, while Unity and headset footage will show it in use.

presentations.title: Strategies for Sustaining HPC Systems under Resource Constraints
Streaming Nuclear Physics at Scale
presentations.abstract: Nuclear physics experiments have long challenged the limits of high-rate and low-latency logic. Presently, streaming readout can move decision making from fixed detector electronics to software, allowing raw detector data to be processed continuously as they are produced. We highlight the state of Jefferson Lab and ESnet collaborative work with example workflows. First, existing data from the CLAS12 detector were replayed across ESnet through the EJFAT network load balancer to the Perlmutter supercomputer at NERSC, reaching 100 Gb/s as jobs dynamically scaled the workflow. Second, live data direct from the CLAS12 electromagnetic calorimeter were streamed, showing end-to-end capabilities and real-time cosmic ray identification. These demonstrations go beyond earlier transport benchmarks to physics-based streaming workflows, thus combining high-rate data transport with online scientific processing. We also discuss applying this approach to Jefferson Lab’s development of streaming-readout modules for positron emission tomography (PET) processing, enabling future whole-area, whole-body scanning otherwise considered impractical.

presentations.title: Stress-Testing Exascale Scientific Data Output - ADIOS2 Configuration Strategies for WarpX under Extreme Load Imbalance
presentations.abstract: Spatially imbalanced, temporally irregular simulation output challenges I/O configurations tuned for balanced workloads. This work evaluates ADIOS2 BP5 configurations through openPMD-api using WarpX on Frontier at ORNL and Perlmutter at NERSC, contrasting balanced 3D Cartesian output with boosted-frame back-transformed diagnostics (BTD). BTD combines rank-level output skew with snapshot contributions spanning multiple simulation steps. Balanced output reaches 3.64~TB/s without compression on 2,048 Frontier nodes and over 1~TB/s on 512 Perlmutter nodes; lossless Blosc2 compression achieves approximately 7~TB/s application-level effective throughput on Frontier. In the tested BTD configurations, SPAN combined with asynchronous writing provides the highest throughput on Frontier, FlattenSteps supports assembly of complete lab-frame snapshots for checkpointing without reader modification and with negligible write-time overhead and no penalty on read performance, and DataSizeBased aggregation improves throughput when subfile counts are constrained. These results identify complementary mechanisms for handling irregular output and provide configuration guidance for these workloads and systems.

presentations.title: Stretch Break
Structure-Aware Linear Solvers for Matrix-Free High-Order Finite-Element Simulations on GPUs
presentations.abstract: Higher-order finite-element simulations solve the same Poisson and shifted-Helmholtz systems repeatedly, and preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) needs iterations that climb with polynomial order and mesh grading, each ending in a latency-bound global reduction. We present two GPU solvers selected from the structure the mesh and the operator retain. On tensor-product meshes, an exact fast-diagonalization inverse needs one apply and no iterations. It is 138 to 4,570 times faster than converged Chebyshev-Jacobi PCG and 14 to 140 times faster than our own p-multigrid solve on uniform meshes. Where that structure is gone, a device-resident Chebyshev-Jacobi p-multigrid preconditioner converges in five to seven iterations against 106 to 668 for Jacobi PCG. Both are measured in DFT-FE on up to 128 A100 GPUs and 1,024 MI250X GCDs. This is unpublished work in preparation. The poster walks from the problem through the choice of solver to the measured gains and limits of each.

presentations.title: Student@SC: A Hands-On Introduction to HPC & AI
presentations.abstract:
Start your SC26 experience with a full-day, hands-on introduction to high performance computing and artificial intelligence.
This workshop will help students build practical familiarity with the tools, concepts, and workflows used in modern HPC and AI development. Through guided exercises, students will explore how to work in advanced computing environments, run computational workloads, and understand how AI applications connect with large-scale computing systems.
The workshop is designed for students with a range of backgrounds. Whether you are encountering HPC for the first time or looking to strengthen your foundation, this session will help you build confidence using technical computing resources.
Lunch will be provided to full-day participants.
Please see the SC26 Student Programming page for a detailed schedule.

presentations.title: Studying Silent Data Corruption Sensitivity of Precision Reduction Techniques during Deep Neural Network Training
presentations.abstract: High Performance Computing platforms have nurtured the development of deep learning (DL) models, particularly providing the massive computing power needed for training those models. However, the alarming growth rate of DL models has made their optimization, to reduce memory size and energy consumption, a priority. In particular, precision reduction techniques have been developed to tackle those challenges. The available literature provides a good description of how precision reduction affects the performance deep learning models. However, there is a knowledge gap of how sensitive precision reduction techniques are to silent data (SDCs), that can lead to unsuspected errors. SDCs are becoming more prevalent, for that reason, we set out to investigate how deep learning models, optimized with precision reduction techniques, react to bit flips caused by silent data corruption. Our results show that those optimized models are, in most cases, surprisingly resilient to bit flips compared to original model.

presentations.title: Sub-Cycle Measurement of AI Workload Energy, Flexibility, and Synchronization on Production GPU Racks
presentations.abstract: Different instruments report different power for the same AI workload. We show this on production H100 racks by recording the same events at three concurrent tiers: one-minute breakers, 100 ms per-GPU telemetry, and 10 kHz voltage and current on every rack feed. Disagreement between tiers shows what each instrument resolves. Coarse tiers return wrong numbers with no sign they are wrong: a training job pulses 5.75 times per second, and device telemetry, sampling ten times per second, reports 4.18. Only the feed record shows that a resumed job’s first pulse lands at full amplitude, and that an inference-serving instance under burst admission swings its whole rack from idle to peak twelve times per second. A resolution ladder states which tier resolves each phenomenon and how the others fail. For this load, ramp rates, transient magnitudes, and the coherence of aggregated units are sub-cycle quantities.

presentations.title: Subsurface to Stellar: HPC Enablement with Open OnDemand and ColdFront at bp and NASA
presentations.abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure continues to grow in capability and scale, yet user access models and support mechanisms often lag behind evolving user expectations. Through a collaboration under the NASA-bp Space Act Agreement, bp and NASA identified a common challenge: reducing friction between users and HPC resources through modern, web-based interfaces. This paper presents two independent but complementary approaches. At bp, Open OnDemand (OOD) was deployed and extended to provide a browser-first interface for HPC resources, integrating existing infrastructure while supporting application deployment, operational visibility, and governance of user-developed web applications. At NASA's Flight Sciences Laboratory, ColdFront was extended through a plugin-based architecture to provide self-service management of projects, storage, licenses, and access controls with integrated approval workflows and auditability. Together, these case studies demonstrate how web-based platforms can improve accessibility, accelerate onboarding, increase user autonomy, and reduce administrative burden without requiring fundamental changes to underlying HPC systems.

presentations.title: sundials4py: state-of-the-art time integrators for high-performance Python
presentations.abstract: We discuss sundials4py, a Python interface to the SUNDIALS suite of high-performance numerical time integrators, on AMD and NVIDIA GPU-based supercomputers. We show how sundials4py provides portable access to SUNDIALS’ accelerator-enabled solvers and zero-copy interoperability with numpy, PyTorch, and JAX. We also demonstrate how nanobind and litgen are used to generate much of the Python interface binding code, reducing the effort required to expose a large, evolving HPC library while integrating it naturally with the Python GPU ecosystem. Prepared by LLNL under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. LLNL-ABS-2023376.

presentations.title: Super(comptuing) Heroes
presentations.abstract: Members of underrepresented groups often lack access to role models within their minority. The HPC community is still predominantly male, making it difficult for young women to find female “superheroes” to identify with. Such role models are crucial for career planning and guidance. This session aims to provide especially women with the opportunity to meet influential, well-recognized female HPC “superheroes” from academia, research labs, HPC centers and industry. Join us to be inspired and find relatable role models as we work together to build a more inclusive and connected HPC community.

presentations.title: SuperSAM: Crafting a SAM Supernetwork via Structured Pruning and Unstructured Parameter Prioritization
presentations.abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates the design of efficient networks, with one-shot NAS enabling greater efficiency by training a single weight-sharing supernetwork that contains many subnetworks. Designing such search spaces is challenging due to considerations involving architectural space, scoring methods, and computational cost. We present SuperSAM, a one-shot NAS search space derived from the Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our proposed NAS approach involves automated search space design via layer-wise structured pruning and activations-based MLP parameter prioritization. The SAM supernetwork is trained with the sandwich rule, while deployment uses a program autotuner to discover efficient subnetworks. Discovered models are 30–70% smaller than the original SAM ViT-B, with some outperforming the pre-trained model.

presentations.title: Supporting a Fast-Paced National AI Resource: Portal, Identity, and Federated Access at Scale
presentations.abstract: The UK AI Research Resource (AIRR) has grown in two years to over 5,000 users and over 800 awarded projects, reached through a single front door onto autonomous sites. Supporting a resource this large and heterogeneous rests on three foundations: a shared gateway (AIRRPortal), in production; a shared identity layer (AIRR ConnectID), live for the gateway with site brokering in development; and federated user support, discussed as future work. Support is easy to mismeasure: a user whose sign-in is broken cannot raise a ticket through an authenticated helpdesk, so the failures that matter most go unseen. From 25 months of production data, identity proves a large, hidden source of support load whose cost tracks account-lifecycle ownership more closely than a user's sector: self-managed identities are 13% of accounts but generate 70% of identity-related support, a 15.3x per-user difference. We draw lessons for scaling federated user support.

presentations.title: Sustainable Supercomputing
presentations.abstract:
Providing a sustainable path for supercomputing is a pressing topic for our community, industry, and governments. Supercomputing has an insatiable appetite for computational cycles, while we face increasing challenges of delivering performance per Watt advances with silicon technology trends. All within the context of the converging needs of HPC and AI, climate change, the drive towards net-zero, and economic pressures driven by geo-political challenges.

Improving the sustainability of supercomputing provides many opportunities when the end-to-end cycle is considered. From the design of computational circuits and systems; to the power and cooling that is used to operate them, along with the suite of software tools used to administrate, maintain, and raise operational efficiency of HPC systems, with the increasing pressures from the AI aspects being added to traditional HPC workload and workflows. All elements of the system considered, from compute nodes and interconnects to IO and storage components of the system.

presentations.title: Sustaining Early-Career Talent Through an HPC Bootcamp Pipeline
presentations.abstract: The Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF), a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) user facility, hosts an annual Intro to HPC Bootcamp that introduces students to foundational high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) skills through a one-week, hands-on, project-based program. To retain early-career talent in HPC and DOE laboratories, the bootcamp has developed a workforce pipeline with progressively deeper opportunities for participant re-engagement. Approximately 25% of each cohort return as peer mentors, and two former peer mentors return as summer interns to further develop their skills while innovating the program. Evaluation data demonstrates increased participant-reported confidence in technical skills and interest in HPC and DOE careers following the bootcamp. Participants and peer mentors also pursue internships at DOE laboratories through connections made during the program. Together, these pathways provide continued access to HPC resources, mentorship, professional development, and community to support early-career professionals in pursuing HPC careers.

presentations.title: System Level Energy and Cost Characterization of Hybrid Quantum–Classical Cloud Workloads
presentations.abstract: Near-term quantum workloads depend on hybrid quantum-classical cloud architectures, yet their power and performance dynamics remain difficult to characterize. To address this, we present a high-level simulation framework to evaluate power, energy, and cost across heterogeneous QPU and CPU clouds. By modeling macro level interactions such as job arrivals, workflow iterations, and device power states, the framework orchestrates administrative-level evaluation without requiring detailed quantum properties. To demonstrate the framework with selected configurations and workload, we sweep the variational iteration count over a fixed fleet, holding circuit width, depth, shots, and arrival patterns constant, so that loop length serves as the sole independent variable. While computation and per-job energy scale linearly, QPU occupancy and turnaround depart abruptly from linearity beyond a critical iteration count: past it, nearly all quantum phase time is spent blocked on qubit connectivity rather than computing, and turnaround per job becomes heavily tailed.

presentations.title: T-CCL: Resource Efficient and Performant Collective Communication using Tensor Memory Accelerator
Talking to Your Users: Ask Better Questions Before You Build
presentations.abstract: User experience (UX) is often misunderstood as a nice-to-have, rather than a necessary element of scientific computing. In reality, UX encompasses all the ways a user interacts with a product and is highly relevant to HPC systems. This interactive BoF will introduce UX work as a practical approach for improving usability and adoption. Participants will discuss how to ask users better questions to uncover needs and identify opportunities to improve systems, services, and support. Participants will leave with practical methods, starter resources, and connections to a growing cross-institutional UX community. This session benefits developers, documentation specialists, and facility support staff.

presentations.title: Taming AI Storage Systems
presentations.abstract: Training and inferencing AI models require massively distributed GPU-based compute clusters. These clusters consume large amounts of data, via distributed storage solutions and high-speed networks. The storage solutions are facing huge amounts of clients accessing storage simultaneously while demanding low latency and high throughput. This tutorial directly supports SC’s focus on scalable high‑performance systems and AI/HPC convergence by providing practical methods to diagnose and alleviate storage-related bottlenecks in large GPU-based clusters. It will give an overview of existing and emerging distributed storage solutions. The audience will get tips from industry experts for configuring these storage systems and optimizing workloads to fully utilize the potential of these highly distributed storage systems.

Teaching HPC to Advanced High School Students at a Summer Program
presentations.abstract:
Since 2023, staff and students from Tennessee Tech's Information Technology Services department have participated as a research and exploration group for the Governor's School for Emerging Technologies (GSET), a 3-week summer program for Tennessee high school students. We introduce a subset of those students to a variety of topics and careers related to research computing, including having the students build small (but fully-functional) HPC clusters, both in virtual machines on their laptops, and also on recently-decommissioned desktop computers.
The students begin developing a broad set of skills including Linux systems administration, networking, benchmarking, parallel programming, and other concepts core to HPC. They also present their choice of computationally intensive applications, usually run on their own cluster, as a project presentation to other GSET students and staff.
This presentation will give an overview of our GSET experience and how it might be adapted to other institutions and audiences.

presentations.title: TEIR: A Tiled Execution IR for Tensor Contractions
presentations.abstract: Tensor contractions are core kernels in scientific computing and machine learning. Efficient execution requires hardware-aware tiling and a schedule across cores and over time that depends on the contraction and the microarchitecture. Existing systems search this space with auto-tuning (TVM), optimize it with library heuristics (BLIS, TBLIS), or transpose whole tensors around a GEMM (TTGT). Recent systems expose tiles explicitly, from programming environments (cuTile, Triton-CPU) to tile-based primitives (KleidiAI, CUTLASS, LIBXSMM). We introduce the Tiled Execution Intermediate Representation (TEIR), which explicitly represents what runs (kernels on tiles), when it runs (an execution schedule), and how data is laid out (per-tensor strides and offsets). We implement TEIR as an MLIR dialect whose optimization passes schedule a contraction and lower it to LIBXSMM kernels. Across 24 TCCG contractions on AVX-512, NEON, and SME, TEIR achieves 1.5×–1.9× the geometric-mean throughput of the next-best backends and leads in 54 of 72 cases.

presentations.title: Tensor Compilers for AI and HPC
presentations.abstract: The recent developments in AI have prompted an interest in tensor compilers, but their use is not universal and often they are coupled with hand optimized kernels in real deployments. In this work, we dive deep into tensor compilers and adjacent systems to build a holistic systems understanding of tensor program optimization. We define our own tensor operator taxonomy. Using a modern GPU as an example, we condense GPU kernel optimization into two principles, from which many optimization techniques emerge. Using the PyTorch 2.0 compiler backend, TorchInductor, and the Triton compiler as examples, we explain in detail what intermediate representations and optimization techniques are used during the compilation process. We find that kernel fusion is the most consequential optimization. In the end, we are able to understand the value proposition of tensor compilers, the type of optimizations they apply, their limitations and how they can be used effectively and augmented.

presentations.title: Tensor Contractions on AWS Trainium
presentations.abstract:
Tensor contractions are fundamental across computational science and machine learning, yet reaching high performance on domain-specific accelerators with large systolic arrays, such as AWS Trainium, remains challenging.

We present a compiler that optimizes a binary tensor contraction, given as an einsum equation with axis sizes, and lowers it into a Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) kernel. The core contribution of the poster is the automatic search: the contraction is lowered to an intermediate representation, and candidate kernel and SBUF tilings are ranked by a measurement-based model of Trainium2's engines. The compiler is evaluated on Trainium2, where the generated kernels reach 155 of 157 TFLOPS on square matrix multiplication and run 2.3 to 2.9 times faster than torch.einsum on four contractions from the TCCG benchmark.

In the poster session we walk visitors through the pipeline, from einsum equation to emitted NKI code, and discuss the tiling decisions behind the results.

presentations.title: Tessera: User-Defined Compiler Optimizations for High-Performance Scientific Computing
presentations.abstract: Despite the extensive capabilities of today's compilers, general-purpose compilers cannot exploit domain-specific properties for optimization in scientific software because the semantic meaning of the code is lost as it is transformed from the application and library layers down to the compiler and hardware. To solve this problem, we present Tessera, an MLIR-based framework that allows domain experts to annotate scientific code with high-level mathematical and structural properties — including symmetries, matrix properties, and algebraic identities — which are automatically compiled into performance optimizations. This enables scientists to benefit from domain-specific optimizations without needing to restructure their code or have deep compiler expertise. To demonstrate Tessera's generality, we show that our framework achieves performance improvements on benchmarks built on both linear algebra and arbitrary-precision floating-point libraries.

presentations.title: The 12th Computational Approaches for Cancer Workshop (CAFCW26)
presentations.abstract: Cancer touches everyone. Since being established in 2015, CAFCW continues to bring together the community interested in impacting cancer with HPC and the community with an interest in learning more about HPC impacting cancer challenges. The workshop continues to grow, inviting the cancer and HPC communities to converge at SC, interact, and share insights and advances. The workshop highlights the diversity of opportunities where HPC serves as an essential element for advances in cancer treatments, driving new approaches to understand cancer and enabling translation of insights and new treatments to reach clinical impact. This year, the workshop will emphasize the role of HPC in translating research to clinical application and reaching patients, uniting research, clinic and patient. For over a decade, this workshop has catalyzed new biomedical research by connecting industry, government research laboratories, and academia at the intersection of computation, biomedical science, cancer, and healthcare.

presentations.title: The 1st International Workshop on Edge-Cloud-HPC Operational Continuum (ECHO)
presentations.abstract: High performance computing (HPC) is decentralizing into a sensor-edge-cloud continuum. Modern edge AI pipelines for perception and control now face the same systemic bottlenecks that define supercomputing: data-management overhead, interconnect topology, and accelerator utilization. This workshop on Edge-Cloud-HPC Operational Continuum (ECHO) applies an HPC lens to resource-constrained environments, investigating how foundational principles must evolve for non-deterministic edge and cloud infrastructures. We focus on three pillars: (1) exporting HPC rigor to the edge through hierarchy-aware parallelism, co-designed memory management, and high-performance streaming I/O; (2) reclaiming predictability for cloud-native HPC by mitigating virtualization overheads, multi-tenant resource contention, and stochastic provisioning; and (3) expanding HPC influence into adjacent domains, including Edge/IoT, MLOps, and cyber-physical systems via shared metrics, reference workloads, and reproducible benchmarking that reports variance and tail behavior. We invite papers, experience reports, and demos, and we encourage artifact packaging for comparison.

presentations.title: The 2nd International Workshop for Software Frameworks and Workload Management on Quantum-HPC Ecosystems
presentations.abstract: The integration of quantum computing (QC) with high performance computing (HPC) is emerging as a transformative paradigm for addressing complex scientific and engineering challenges. Given current quantum hardware limitations, such as noise, limited qubit counts, and constrained circuit depth, hybrid quantum–HPC (Q-HPC) ecosystems provide a practical path forward by combining complementary strengths. This workshop focuses on software frameworks, AI-enabled orchestration, and workload management strategies essential for scalable Q-HPC integration. Topics include architecture co-design, heterogeneous resource management, networking, fault tolerance, error mitigation, programming models, middleware, benchmarking, and large-scale distributed Q-HPC systems. Emphasis will be placed on open, interoperable ecosystems such as openQSE and on ML/AI techniques for adaptive workflow orchestration, topology-aware scheduling, performance prediction, and autonomous runtime control. Through invited talks, technical presentations, panels, and special sessions, the workshop will foster collaboration across academia, industry, national laboratories, and funding agencies to define research priorities and accelerate AI-driven Q-HPC ecosystems.

presentations.title: The 50-State AI Plan: A Grassroots Approach to Building a US AI Continent
presentations.abstract: This session examines how state and regional initiatives can strengthen U.S. leadership in AI and quantum computing. Using Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Utah, Oklahoma, and others as examples, the panel will explore how states are aligning regional assets with America’s AI Action Plan, the Genesis Mission, and the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR). The discussion frames this work as a grassroots U.S. counterpart to the EU “AI Continent,” built through state-led, place-based innovation rather than a top-down model. Building on the NSF-CASC Workshop on Envisioning NAIRR State and Regional Hubs for Educational Transformation, the session will highlight pathways for expanding workforce development, research access, and regional cooperation. Panelists will discuss partnerships among academia, government, industry, philanthropy, and federal agencies, along with strategies for broadening access to computing and data resources, streamlining deployment, and engaging states in AI capacity building. Inclusive state-led hubs can drive innovation, attract investment, and grow the AI workforce.

presentations.title: The 9th Annual Parallel Applications Workshop, Alternatives to MPI+X (PAW-ATM)
presentations.abstract:
Supercomputers get faster and more complex every year. MPI, long the dominant model for distributed computation, has adapted by combining with models for intra-node parallelism (e.g., OpenMP, CUDA). These MPI+X hybrids offer performance but demand significant programmer effort to write, debug, and tune applications.

Alternatives to MPI+X are worth exploring as programmer productivity becomes a major component of the time to science. Alternatives include parallel programming languages (e.g., Chapel, Regent, Fortran), general purpose libraries (e.g., Charm++, COMPSs, HPX, Legion, UPC++), and domain-specific libraries (e.g., Arkouda, Dask, Spark). With many options to choose from, it is hard for programmers to know which alternative models are appropriate for their application and for programming model developers to understand the opportunities for improvement.

PAW-ATM brings together both application experts and programming model developers to disseminate knowledge about available applications and models, as well as advance their design.

presentations.title: The Agentic Memory Hierarchy: Cross-State I/O Characterization for a Unified Substrate
presentations.abstract:
LLM agents now run long, multi-agent, multi-user workloads whose state does not fit
a single store. An agent produces four kinds of state on one memory-storage hierarchy: the model context (KV cache), execution state of tool calls and checkpoints, cognitive memory of facts and skills, and bulk artifacts and embeddings. Each sits behind a separate, uncoordinated substrate, so lifetimes are uncorrelated, repeated content is unrecognized, evictions collide over one memory budget, and provenance is lost. We present the first cross-state I/O characterization, via an extract-normalize-replay method over real agent, serving, memory, and HPC I/O traces and the static footprint of four scientific agents. The states occupy distinct size regimes, span two stress axes, and contend in most windows; over half of KV prefix blocks are reusable, yet recency eviction captures only a third. Each finding maps to a unified-substrate requirement; we release the schema, extractors, and replay benchmark.

presentations.title: The American Science Cloud and the Genesis Mission
presentations.abstract: The Genesis Mission is a U.S. Department of Energy initiative to accelerate AI-driven scientific discovery across the national research complex. At its core is the American Science Cloud (AmSC),a secure, federated, and science-optimized platform connecting DOE leadership computing facilities, national laboratories, and experimental user facilities into a unified environment for large-scale scientific workflows. This talk will provide an overview of AmSC and Genesis from a project-wide perspective, representing contributions from across the DOE laboratory community. It describes the platform architecture and the central role that cloud-native technologies such as containers, Kubernetes, and cloud infrastructure play in enabling AmSC's vision. The talk will also discuss some of the major challenges the AmSC platform is designed to address and its future goals.

presentations.title: The Art of the Hack: Deconstruct--Reconstruct--Apply as a Constructionist Framework for AI-Enabled Gateway Development
presentations.abstract: Hackathons are widely used for technical workforce development, yet their effectiveness is attributed to informal learning rather than grounded in learning theory. We present Deconstruct–Reconstruct–Apply (DRA), a constructionist framework for training in the era of LLM coding assistants, and report its first formalized instantiation: the SGX3 Virtual Coding Institute (June 1–19, 2026) and HackHPC@ADMI26 (June 22–26, 2026). Instruction taught students to dismantle AI systems before rebuilding them; the hackathon required teams to redeploy that toolchain in untaught domains and ship user-facing science gateways.

presentations.title: The Bipartible Architecture Pattern: Transparently Directing HTTP Requests over InfiniBand
presentations.abstract:
Large-scale compute (HPC) systems often deploy InfiniBand (IB) networks for high-bandwidth and low latency communication. In an HPC system, a TCP network is typically used for control-plane and general-purpose communication. The last decade has seen the rise of cloud-native software patterns which are characterized by container based software distribution and communication over TCP/IP.

This paper introduces the Bipartible Architecture Pattern that transparently redirects HTTP traffic onto IB without changing workload implementation or network configuration. This is achieved by introducing a service on the host(s) that intercepts HTTP requests and transforms them into global filesystem requests. This maintains the HTTP interface while leveraging the IB network for data transfer.

The feasibility of this pattern is demonstrated by implementing a prototype for Garage (S3) and Pulp (repository). We offer this pattern as one of many alternative approaches to address the performance challenges of deploying scientific software containers at scale on HPC environments.

presentations.title: The case for unprivileged containerization in HPC, or: Does software simplicity still matter in 2026?
presentations.abstract:
Containerization is an increasingly popular way to encapsulate an application or workflow along with all of its dependencies (other than the Linux kernel). This has been effective for HPC applications, both old and new. However, the principles and practices of HPC collide with those of cloud computing, including in particular container standards such as OCI. Also, containerization is often presented as a complex technology, with many concepts entangled, but in fact it is pretty straightforward.
This talk revisits the motivation for Charliecloud, an HPC-focused container implementation that has prioritized simplicity and lack of privilege since the beginning, based on my decade of experience leading the project. I argue for a simplicity-first view of how containers work, explore how the assumptions of HPC and cloud computing clash (particularly in the era of ML/AI) and outline some possible solutions. These ideas are incomplete, and my hope is that discussion with the CANOPIE community will help build a more robust path forward.

presentations.title: The Computational and Economic Breakeven of Hybrid HPC/ML
presentations.abstract: High performance computing is rapidly integrating machine learning with traditional numerical solvers, creating hybrid workflows and digital twins. This panel audits the "total energy to solution" for hybrid HPC workloads, quantifying their operational power demands from silicon hardware to total cost of ownership. Panelists will address the following core questions: What is the energy required to generate large-scale, ground-truth training datasets versus the direct computational cost of ML training? What, if any, is the energy overhead of running traditional physics engines alongside ML for active validation? At what computational breakeven point does deploying an ML surrogate yield a net reduction in total energy use? Finally, how do these physical energy ledgers translate into real-world budgets and sustainability goals for scientific deployment? Bringing together perspectives from materials science, weather forecasting, hyperscale computing, and computing economics, this panel evaluates the physical and financial energy realities of ML integration in HPC.

presentations.title: The Cornell Virtual Workshop: Looking Back, Looking Forward
presentations.abstract: The Cornell Virtual Workshop (CVW), developed to deliver asynchronous training for high-performance computing (HPC), has served for more than three decades as an innovative platform for collecting and delivering training for HPC users and computational scientists. Created by the Cornell Center for Advanced Computing, the CVW service has followed the development of both HPC systems and generations of programming languages. We describe the evolution of the CVW over time across a series of experiments and innovations, through use by more than 300,000 visitors per year, and describe challenges in maintaining a long-standing training environment. Finally we offer some ideas for future innovations and tracking the direction of computational science research.

presentations.title: The Cost of Parallelism: A Measured Comparison of Sequential and Systolic INT8 GEMM on an FPGA
presentations.abstract: Matrix multiplication dominates neural-network inference, and hardware designers choose between reusing one multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit over time and instantiating many that run concurrently. That exchange rate is usually assumed rather than measured, and is least favorable at small problem sizes. This work measures it. Two INT8 architectures, a single-MAC baseline and a 4x4 output-stationary systolic array, were implemented in SystemVerilog behind one shared interface and compared on an Intel Cyclone 10 GX FPGA under identical operands, device, tools, and constraint. The array is 7.4x faster in cycles for 16x the DSP blocks and 1.62x the ALMs, with no loss of clock frequency. Per-cycle occupancy explains the sublinear return: the array peaks at 12 of 16 active elements and never fills. The work is complete and validated on silicon. The poster walks through both architectures, the measured tradeoff, and the occupancy analysis, with QR-linked RTL.

presentations.title: The Economic Value of Heat Reuse
presentations.abstract: Due to the AI frenzy, the energy demand of data centers continues to grow dramatically, and AI factories that consume hundreds of Megawatts have become the new normal. The heat that those data centers generate from their electricity consumption is typically rejected as waste heat to ambient air, although it has potential value for other industries to be reused. This paper proposes an economic model to assess the value of such heat. We describe a demand function tailored to data center waste heat, use it in combination with demand curves to determine the heat’s value, and validate it with cooling data from the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Garching, Germany. We also present industrial use cases for heat at varying temperatures and discuss the potential economic advantages of heat reuse. Finally, we consider infrastructure costs and provide supply equations that outline the return on investment and payback periods.

presentations.title: The Empty Shelf: Vertical Market Failure in Data Storage for HPC and AI
presentations.abstract: For decades, computing drew on a shelf of demonstrated, but undeployed, technology, stocked largely by government-funded research. HAMR, the technology now carrying the HDD roadmap, came off that shelf: a 2001 federal cooperative agreement co-funded its early development; volume shipment arrived two decades later. The government funding instrument retired in 2007 on the premise that industry would restock the shelf. In magnetic data storage, where few suppliers face few hyperscale buyers, that premise collapsed into a vertical market failure, with suppliers rationally declining to fund breakthrough R&D. Buyers feel the consequences in shortages, rising prices, year-long lead times, and missed technology roadmaps. Demonstrated technologies sit unfunded, and the market still lacks a tier combining tape's low cost with quick access. The panel debates whether this stall threatens other computing technologies and closes on two ways to restock the shelf: pooled and matched pre-competitive investment, and AI demand for near-storage processing.

presentations.title: The Evolution of the Coaraci HPC Infrastructure: Operational Lessons from a Brazilian Research Computing Center
presentations.abstract:
High-performance computing (HPC) is a necessary tool for many research fields. However, the cluster is not the only component necessary to operate an HPC environment. This paper presents the evolution of the Coaraci High-Performance Computing infrastructureat the Gleb Wataghin Institute of Physics (IFGW), University of Campinas (UNICAMP), Brazil; The project modernized an existing academic data center through upgrades to electrical power, backup generation, UPS systems, precision cooling, airflow management, high-speed networking, workload management, monitoring, user onboarding, and technical support. Thermal improvements included cold-aisle containment, high-flow floor panels, and high-airflow rack doors.
Average Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) decreased from 2.14 in April 2024 to 1.56 in June 2025, an observed reduction of about 27%. The optimized cooling strategy also enabled operation with two active cooling units and one standby unit. Since February 2024, Coaraci has operated 24/7 with 366 registered users, 284 of whom have executed workloads.

presentations.title: The Future of Dynamic Resource Utilization in HPC: Chances and Challenges
presentations.abstract:
The increasing computational demands are driving the deployment of ever-larger HPC and AI infrastructures. While these systems deliver unprecedented performance, they also pose critical challenges to their efficient use, particularly in terms of energy consumption.

This BoF will explore dynamic resource management as a key enabler of higher utilization and reduced energy consumption. Instead of traditional batch scheduling, dynamic resource control at the start or during a job’s runtime enables better allocation of compute capacity, memory, network availability, and storage. This BoF will address the two major key challenges of novel scheduling and its integration across the software stack.

presentations.title: The Future of NSF-Supported Advanced Cyberinfrastructure
presentations.abstract: The U.S. National Science Foundation's vision and investment plans for cyberinfrastructure (CI) are designed to address the evolving needs of the science and engineering research community. Senior leadership and program staff from NSF’s Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure (OAC) will discuss OAC's vision, strategic and national priorities, as well as highlights from the latest funding opportunities across all aspects of the research cyberinfrastructure ecosystem. Substantial time will be devoted to audience Q&A between attendees and NSF staff and unstructured time to meet informally with NSF staff.

presentations.title: The Future of P3HPC in the age of Agentic Development
The Future of Python on HPC Systems
presentations.abstract: Python is the most widely used programming language today — but on HPC systems, it’s often more pain than power. From slow module loading on shared filesystems to packaging headaches and incompatible distributions, these hurdles block new users and frustrate seasoned developers alike. Meanwhile, major changes to Python’s core — new array APIs, packaging reforms, JIT compilation, and threading primitives — are happening without HPC at the table. This BoF brings together language leaders and HPC practitioners to shape Python’s future, learn what’s coming, and connect with peers.

presentations.title: The Future of the HPC Workforce: Skills, Scale, and Sustainability
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing (HPC) is undergoing rapid transformation with the convergence of simulation, AI, data-intensive science, and emerging quantum computing. This evolution is reshaping the skills required to effectively use and advance these systems, creating urgent challenges in workforce development. This panel brings together perspectives from national laboratories, academia, and industry to discuss how to build a sustainable, inclusive, and future-ready HPC workforce.

Key questions include: What will the HPC workforce need to look like in the next 5–10 years? Where are the most critical gaps in skills, training pathways, and access? What skills are currently missing or undervalued in existing curricula? Which collaboration models across institutions have proven effective? How can we broaden participation and lower barriers to entry?

The session will include interactive audience engagement, with opportunities to submit and prioritize questions in real time, ensuring a dynamic and relevant discussion.

presentations.title: The Green500: Trends in Energy-Efficient Supercomputing
presentations.abstract: With power being a first-order design constraint on par with performance, it is important to measure and analyze energy-efficiency trends in supercomputing. To raise the awareness of greenness as a first-order design constraint, the Green500 seeks to characterize the energy efficiency of supercomputers for different metrics, workloads, and methodologies. This BoF discusses trends across the Green500 and highlights from the current Green500 list. In addition, the Green500, Top500, and Energy Efficient HPC Working Group have been working together on improving power-measurement methodology, and this BoF presents updates that will improve ease of submission without compromising accuracy.

presentations.title: The Ground Truth — AI’s Real Impact on Science and HPC
presentations.abstract: AI is impacting all aspects of science. As the global scientific community embraces these tools and methods, we anticipate a potential acceleration of discovery in many areas. This prestigious international panel will discuss the implications for how we successfully harness the immense potential of AI.

presentations.title: The Impact of GenAI on HPC Programming and Programming Models
presentations.abstract:
According to many mainstream media outlets and tech gurus, the age of computer programmers is fading away as GenAI proves itself capable of helping with programming tasks, or completing them independently. And many of us probably have positive (and negative) stories about using AI in our day-to-day lives. But what do we expect the impact of GenAI to be on programming for HPC systems and applications?

This session kicks off with opening statements from thought leaders representing various HPC programming models (MPI, OpenMP, NVIDIA, Kokkos, COMPSs, and Chapel), followed by an open session for audience opinions, Q&A, and healthy debate.

presentations.title: The International Post-Exascale (InPEx) Project
presentations.abstract:
Several (trans-)national initiatives have recognized the crucial importance of co-design between hardware, software, and application stakeholders in the path to exascale and beyond. However, these regional efforts are somehow disconnected while the community would benefit by sharing return of experience, common know-how, and advancing on the new problems arising as exascale machines become more and more available.

The International Post-Exascale (InPEx) Project will bring together researchers and engineers, companies, funding bodies, and policy organizations to contribute to the implementation of an international, shared, high-quality computing environment based on the principles and practices of co-design.

presentations.title: The Mission Continues: Veteran Voices in SC26
presentations.abstract: Active-duty servicemen and veterans are part of the workforce in high performance computing (HPC). This panel features speakers with a broad range of experience in HPC who will discuss strategies and leveraging training and skills, and how it translates into working in industry, academia and national laboratories.

presentations.title: The MQSS Benchmarking Framework: Extensible Orchestration Layer for Quantum Benchmarking in HPC-Integrated Ecosystems
presentations.abstract: HPCQC systems are emerging as the practical path toward quantum computation, given current constraints on quantum noise, qubit count, and circuit depth. Benchmarking orchestrators can help pave the way by providing a unified framework for executing and evaluating workloads across het- erogeneous quantum hardware, simulators, and circuit libraries, while remaining extensible as the quantum computing ecosystem evolves. In light of this, we present the MBF, an open-source orchestration layer that unifies several components, such as benchmark definition, device abstraction, and execution strategies. MBF achieves these via its abstract benchmark, adapter and provider interfaces while supporting profiling at various stages to capture performance metrics across both the HPC and QC components of quantum computation. Together, these capabilities enable consistent and extensible benchmarking throughout diverse HPCQC environments, enabling the evaluation and performance analysis of quantum workloads across the full computational stack.

presentations.title: The Next Scaling Law After LLMs: AI That Understands the Physical World
presentations.abstract: Scientific progress is limited not by a lack of new ideas but by the time and cost involved in physical experimentation. AI’s most transformative impact in enabling scientific discoveries lies in reducing the need for such experiments. To get there, we need to build AI models that are able to simulate and understand the physical world at all scales, which language models are unable to do. Neural operators lay the foundation for such multi-scale learning since they learn mappings between function spaces, and can accept inputs and outputs at any resolution. They have been successfully applied in weather and climate modeling, nuclear fusion, quantum chemistry, and designing novel medical devices. We are now bringing universality and scale, the key ingredients to the success of LLMs, to AI for physical understanding. I will share what we have already achieved and a glimpse of what lies ahead.

presentations.title: The NSF Leadership Computing Facility and the Rising Importance of Interconnects in the (AI+)HPC World
presentations.abstract: This talk will begin with updates on the deployment and early operations of the NSF's newest Leadership Computing and AI Inference systems. It will then discuss how the rise of the AI industry has Impacted the diversity and investment in interconnects in new AI and HPC platforms. Finally the talk will attempt to cover the ramifications of interconnect changes on old and new workloads.

presentations.title: The Oracle at DKRZ
presentations.abstract:
This video is a visualization of the algorithm used to generate "prophecies" from machine code — that will form part of a sculptural installation to be exhibited at the German Climate Computing Centre (DKRZ).

The work situates climate modeling in the broader, non-scientific history of humanity's attempts to grapple with the future. By reinterpreting the binary of the ICON climate model into words, and searching for where those words combine into statements about the future, ICON is reimagined as a modern-day oracle. The algorithm's lexicon comes from English translations of classical Greek texts. In these fictions, prophecies are true, and are intertwined with the distinct tragedy of not being believed or acted upon — a startling parallel to humanity's lackluster response to the climate crisis.

Inspiration for the project came through conversations with scientists at DKRZ; about the computation and storage of data, as well as the Centre's role in scientific research and weather prediction. On the computational side, the ability to abstract almost anything into a string of zeros and ones highlights a wonderful symmetry: if anything can be binary, then binary can be anything. From this perspective, binary becomes an interface between seemingly disparate media and raises questions about how the systems we use to interpret data give rise to meaning.

The connection to a history of fortune telling was developed through understanding the role DKRZ plays within the scientific landscape. The vast array of resources spent in the construction and maintenance of its supercomputers is a testament to how far humanity will go to fulfill a specific need — to know what the future will be like. From this perspective, it represents an incredibly sophisticated approach to something humans have been doing throughout history and across civilizations. The rulers of city-states in Ancient Greece would climb the steps to the Oracle at Delphi seeking counsel. Now, various clients come to DKRZ, looking to use its computing power for projections on the weather and climate.

presentations.title: The Other Half of Workflow Portability: Evidence-Backed HPC Site Profiles with Agentic Discovery
presentations.abstract: Moving a workflow developed at one HPC site to another rarely succeeds without trial and error. Package managers, containers, and workflow specifications such as backpacks all describe what a workflow needs, but none describes how a given site must be used, so even a portable workflow requires manual adjustment at each site. That missing half includes the site's resource shape, storage, network permissions, and operating policies, scattered across the batch system, prose documentation, and undocumented behavior. We propose the HPC site profile, a structured, evidence-backed description whose every field traces to the measurement, documentation, or pilot job that established it. A bounded language-model agent extracts documented fields with citations, each verified deterministically or discarded, while login measurements and pilot jobs supply the rest. The profile then preflights a workflow into an execution plan or an early, explainable failure. We build and evaluate profiles at three production sites.

presentations.title: The Price of a Single Source: Performance Portability of Chapel and Julia across CPUs and GPUs
presentations.abstract: Developing high-performance computing codes is challenging: exploiting modern hardware requires reasoning about architectural detail, and heterogeneity makes this harder still. Even portability frameworks leave much of a code specialised: across five C++ implementations of the same mini-application, only 16% of the source is shared by all backends. Languages such as Chapel/Julia promise a single-source approach, targeting CPUs and GPUs from multiple vendors while trading some control for productivity and portability. We implement BabelStream, CloverLeaf and TeaLeaf in Chapel and Julia, and compare them against CUDA, HIP and OpenMP C++ baselines across diverse hardware using the Pennycook performance-portability metric. Across three GPU platforms, CloverLeaf achieves P=89% (Julia) and 86% (Chapel); on TeaLeaf the ordering inverts, falling to 77% (Chapel) and 62% (Julia). Both languages need 45-64\% fewer lines of code, and where the C++ backends diverge by 0.63 on average, Chapel and Julia share almost all source between CPU and GPU.

presentations.title: The Relationship Between AI and Research Data Management
presentations.abstract:
With the scientific world focused on becoming ‘AI Ready’, a new opportunity has emerged: revisiting long-standing challenges and unmet needs in research data management and computation-heavy science. This talk examines that opportunity from two angles and the relative value propositions of both:
1. As newer AI technologies become more ubiquitous in science, what new approaches to research data management do they require?
2. How can research data management practices be applied to mine computational artifacts (e.g., benchmarks) for insight?

presentations.title: The Self-Driving Fusion Workflow: A Vision for Automated Scientific Discovery
presentations.abstract: Simulation-driven fusion research requires scientists to coordinate a complex sequence of activities, including application configuration, workflow composition, execution, data movement, and analysis. Although tools exist for individual stages, integrating them into a portable and automated end-to-end workflow remains difficult, particularly across heterogeneous leadership computing facilities. We present a vision for an AI agent-driven workflow framework that enables scientists to describe research objectives and constraints through a natural-language interface rather than manually orchestrating individual tasks. A composition layer translates this intent into an executable workflow assembled from a registry of containerized fusion applications and machine-readable application descriptions. Agent decisions are grounded in a curated knowledge vault of verified configurations and gated by declarative correctness hooks evaluated before, during, and after execution. The framework combines adaptive execution, application coupling, scientific data management, compression and reduction, in situ analysis and visualization, and campaign management into a cohesive ecosystem for executing end-to-end science workflows.

presentations.title: The Shape of Speed: Impacts of Partition Geometry and Rank Density in Distributed Quantum Circuit Simulations
presentations.abstract: In distributed quantum circuit simulation, a poorly shaped partition can halve performance before computation begins. Evaluation on Fugaku across 764 validated configurations (twelve algorithms, thirteen torus partition geometries, and six rank densities for 39-qubit simulations on 1,024 nodes) shows that partition geometry dominates runtime. All twelve algorithms run 1.73–2.31x slower on flat partitions than on near-cubic ones despite identical data transfer, proving the slowdown stems from network delivery rather than communication volume. This penalty scales with the 3D torus partition aspect ratio (runtime ∝ α^0.39, r = 0.72). Rank density is secondary, cutting runtime by 11% at 16 ranks per node only on compact geometries. Ultimately, requesting a near-cubic partition with 16 ranks per node roughly halves time-to-solution relative to flat partitions, which also consume 1.82x more energy. A simulator-free all-to-all microbenchmark confirms a similar geometry penalty for collective-dominated workloads.

presentations.title: The State of Open-Source Computer Architecture Simulators: Shared Problems and Community Action
presentations.abstract: Computer architecture simulators are central to exploring the design space of modern high-performance hardware and analyzing its performance. Many open-source simulators exist, targeting different hardware scopes, granularities, and metrics, yet none is perfect: issues with speed, accuracy, and usability limit their effectiveness for architecture researchers, accelerator designers, hardware-software co-designers, and performance engineers, among others. This BoF convenes an expert panel of users and developers from academia and industry to discuss these tools' shortcomings and possible responses. We invite all who build, use, or depend on these simulators to join the discussion and identify impactful community efforts, with outcomes shared publicly.

presentations.title: The Status and Future of Unified Shared Memory in the CPU+GPU Ecosystem
presentations.abstract: Originally GPU and CPU memory spaces were completely separate, with explicit data movements needed for interaction between CPU and GPU compute cores. Over time, all major GPU vendors have added hardware and software capabilities for transparent access to each other’s memory, with various levels of granularity and integration, with unified shared memory (USM) representing the most tight integration. This BoF will start by outlining the history, current state, and planned future of cross-memory technologies. We will then open the floor for discussion with conference attendees to gather their perspectives on where this technology should evolve going forward.

presentations.title: The Unassessed Attack Surface: Channel-Based Provenance in HPC and Quantum-Computing Open-Source Software
presentations.abstract: Software trust is negotiated in communication channels such as the README, the registry listing, or the maintainer's account. AI agents now consume these channels directly, and attackers enter through them: the XZ Utils backdoor arrived through a mailing list, the Shai-Hulud worms phished maintainers to compromise 1,000+ npm packages, and in 2026, AI agents repeatedly installed a hallucinated package that never existed. Existing tools assess repositories, builds, and artifacts, but not this layer. We present channel-based provenance, to our knowledge, the first assessment framework for this layer: 18 signals spanning identity and access, communication channels, knowledge infrastructure, and distribution metadata, measured on 87 HPC and quantum-computing projects with a hand-verified 30-project panel. We find near-total provenance blindness; no missing signal requires new infrastructure, so the gap is adoption. The poster walks viewers from attack timeline to framework to per-project results, closing with concrete calls for maintainers, software stacks, and facilities.

presentations.title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution
presentations.abstract: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth challenge efficient inference. Pruning often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity remains challenging due to irregular memory accesses and workload imbalance. In this work, we investigate standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance using roofline analysis, showing that a 3 × 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of ~10 FLOP/byte compared to ∼96 FLOP/byte for dense convolution. We propose techniques for efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results show that our approach achieves up to 1.65× speedup over dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and up to 1.52× on NVIDIA Tegra X1, demonstrating the potential of direct sparse convolution for efficient inference on modern GPUs and edge devices.

presentations.title: Thirteenth SC Workshop on Best Practices for HPC Training and Education
presentations.abstract:
The inherent wide distribution, heterogeneity, and dynamism of the current and emerging high performance computing and software environments increasingly challenge cyberinfrastructure facilitators, trainers, and educators. The challenge is how to support and train the current multidisciplinary users and prepare the future educators, researchers, developers, and policymakers to keep pace with the rapidly evolving HPC environments to advance discovery and economic competitiveness for many generations.

The 13th annual workshop on HPC training and education is an ACM SIGHPC Education Chapter coordinated effort, aimed at fostering more collaborations among the practitioners from traditional and emerging fields to explore educational needs in HPC, to develop and deploy HPC training, and to identify new challenges and opportunities for the latest HPC platforms. The workshop will also be a platform for disseminating results and lessons learned in these areas and will be captured in a special edition of the Journal of Computational Science Education.

presentations.title: Thirteenth Workshop on Accelerator Programming and Directives (WACCPD 2026)
presentations.abstract: Accelerators are now a central component of modern HPC systems, delivering an increasing share of computational capability and enabling tightly coupled, highly heterogeneous node architectures. This evolving landscape — spanning GPUs, AI/ML accelerators, FPGAs, dataflow devices, and emerging quantum processors — creates both new opportunities and significant challenges in algorithm design, performance portability, and programming model standardization. WACCPD 2026 brings together researchers and practitioners working on programming models, compilers, runtimes, and applications for accelerator-based systems. The workshop focuses on approaches that enable performance, scalability, and portability across diverse architectures, including directive-based models, standard language parallelism, portable frameworks, and task-based and data-centric systems. It also highlights mixed-precision techniques, AI-assisted programming, and hybrid classical–quantum workflows. Through peer-reviewed papers, invited talks, and a panel, WACCPD fosters exchange of ideas and showcases methods and case studies that advance programmable, sustainable, and high-performance heterogeneous computing.

presentations.title: This Data Will Self-Destruct in One Microsecond: Live Data Reduction and Steering at LCLS-II
presentations.abstract: The LCLS-II X-ray free electron laser at SLAC fires at repetition rates up to 1 MHz, generating raw data rates that start at 280 GB/s and will approach 1,120 GB/s by the end of the decade. At this scale, the traditional “write everything, analyze later” approach to science breaks down. Most raw data must be reduced, characterized, or discarded within moments of acquisition. At LCLS-II in situ processing is built into the architecture. This talk presents the overall design of the LCLS-II Data System, from detector readout through a distributed data reduction pipeline to fast feedback describing how LCLS measures, analyzes, and decides to steer experiments on the timescales of seconds, minutes, or hours. It also covers how the ILLUMINE project extends that pipeline with ML models that analyze high-rate data streams and steer experiments in near real time. I will discuss where AI/ML delivers today including event vetoing, rapid feature extraction and digital-twin aided reconstruction, and where it’s a work in progress. There are engineering realities that need to be reckoned with: latency budgets measured in microseconds, model deployment on heterogeneous edge hardware, coupling to remote HPC facilities, and earning scientists’ trust in decisions that are made before a human ever sees the data.

presentations.title: Three Axes for Scientific AI on HPC: Energy Efficiency, Uncertainty, and Verifiable Trust
presentations.abstract: Scientific AI on leadership-class HPC sits at the intersection of three concerns the community usually addresses separately: energy efficiency, uncertainty quantification (UQ), and verifiable trust. Compression and quantization change model behavior in ways that matter for scientific validity. Energy optimizations can quietly erode privacy and safety properties. And the HPC, UQ, and AI-safety communities rarely meet in one room. This BoF session brings them together to identify shared challenges, gaps in current practice, and concrete next steps toward AI systems for science that are simultaneously efficient, uncertainty-aware, and verifiably trustworthy on the world’s largest computing systems.

presentations.title: Tighter error bounds using structural floating-point properties and tail bounds
presentations.abstract: Traditional deterministic error analysis provide worst case error bounds and prior work on probabilistic error analysis do not model structural floating-point properties, leading to looser bounds for cancellation heavy cases. In this work, we use hybrid error analysis to provide tighter error bounds for long summation and dot product numerical kernels. We extend the FPChecker tool to track global and local rounding error to compute key statistics related to structural floating-point properties, such as the Sterbenz lemma, which is used to compute modified Bernstein's tail bound. We then compare our derived error bound with Higham and Mary's probabilistic error bound and show that our bound faithfully models the structural floating-point behavior. Finally, we show the applicability of the derived bounds on a physical example of computing the magnitude of Fourier modes for density wave function used in compressible-flow simulations.

presentations.title: Time Management
presentations.abstract: This session will cover systems and tools for time and task management in a fast-paced workplace. Participants will learn from others and share what works for them.

presentations.title: TMD - A Label-Free, Misalignment-Robust Distance for HPC Attack Detection
presentations.abstract: In this paper, we present the Temporal Mahalanobis Distance (TMD), a distortion-robust, label-free distance for attack detection in HPC networks. The telemetry from the distributed facility components in HPC ecosystem is temporally misaligned, since the components differ in sampling rate, in when an attack reaches them, and in sample ordering. Additionally, the operational monitoring is label-scarce. TMD makes the Mahalanobis distance separation-aware by scaling spatial deviations against the timestamp separation. TMD is a general distortion-robust distance, and we found it most valuable in the HPC regime, where the discriminative signal is the cross-node structure. TMD sustains the attack-normal separability under the offset and the ordering distortion, where Euclidean and DTW perform near chance. We lift TMD into a Sinkhorn distance, namely, TMSD, which helps under severe misalignment. As another contribution, we build a just-in-time streaming detector on a calibrated, semi-supervised TMD head that scores each window in sub-millisecond time.

presentations.title: To SIMD Or Not To SIMD: Comparing RVV vs. CGRA SoCs For Non-Linear Functions In AI
presentations.abstract:
Non-linear functions are an important class of operations in modern large language models, yet chip vendors have so far relied on traditional vector or
scalar units for them, whose performance has not kept pace with the matrix
multiplication units (MMUs) now found in high-performance and edge devices from
almost every vendor. Reconfigurable units such as FPGAs and CGRAs have been
