proposed, but never systematically compared against traditional units backed by
MMUs. We build two SoCs, one with an RVV vector processor and one with a
elastic CGRA, each coupled with an MMU and driven by a
single-core CPU. For FFNs, we find
the CGRA shows maximum speedup in clock cycles of 7.12x over RVV for the activation of
simple point-wise functions like SiLU, whereas RVV shows up to
9.8x over the CGRA on complex functions such as softmax; over the
enclosing feed-forward block the corresponding maxima are 3.16x and 4.24x.

presentations.title: ToolFuse: Provenance-Aware In-Flight Coalescing of Redundant Agent Tool Calls
presentations.abstract: Scientific workflows increasingly run as fleets of LLM agents analyzing immutable datasets. Independent agents can issue equivalent expensive read-only tool calls simultaneously, before a completed-result cache has anything to reuse. ToolFuse addresses this cold-wave gap by coalescing active calls at a gateway between agents and tool handlers. Its contribution is a provenance-aware execution identity that establishes equivalence from versioned dependencies and execution context, rather than arguments alone. Under contention on an exclusive HPC node, 16 equivalent requests become one execution, reducing CPU time by 11.79× and makespan by 2.36×. Peak memory growth falls from 6.44 GiB to 0.53 GiB. Trace replay shows that sharing depends on call duration and arrival timing. For cheap calls, coalescing remains inactive with negligible overhead.

presentations.title: TOP500 Supercomputers
presentations.abstract:
The TOP500 list of supercomputers serves as a “Who’s Who” in the field of high performance computing (HPC). It started as a list of the most powerful supercomputers in the world and has evolved to a major source of information about trends in HPC. The 68th TOP500 list will be published in November 2026, just in time for SC26.

This BoF will present detailed analyses of the TOP500 and discuss the changes in the HPC marketplace during the past years. The BoF is meant as an open forum for discussion and feedback between the TOP500 authors and the user community.

presentations.title: Topology-Aware Sparse Factorization for Multi-Socket NUMA Architectures
presentations.abstract: The numerical factorization of sparse symmetric matrices is an irregular, memory-bound kernel. State-of-the-art solvers leave the placement of the factor implicit on multi-socket NUMA architectures, binding it to a domain by first touch. This work instead binds the factor during the analysis phase, partitioning it along the elimination tree so that each supernode is placed close to those updating it. Each thread then factors the supernodes bound to its own memory and steals from the nearest domain. Furthermore, no thread binding or memory policy has to be chosen since every decision is derived from the discovered compute node topology. The method is implemented in a production-level LDL solver and evaluated on Intel Ice Lake, AMD Genoa, and NVIDIA Grace over 34 SuiteSparse matrices. It outperforms MKL PARDISO, Panua PARDISO, CHOLMOD, and PaStiX, achieving geometric-mean speedups from 1.3 to 9.5 and, at flop parity, 2.7 less cross-socket traffic than Panua PARDISO.

presentations.title: Toward a Foundation Plug-and-Play Prior for Computed Tomography Reconstruction via a Multimodal Diffusion Model
presentations.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) throughput is limited by scan time, which grows with both the number of projections acquired and the detector integration time for each. Reconstructing high-quality volumes from sparse-view or low-dose measurements therefore depends on an informative prior, typically a neural network trained for one specific scan setting and retrained whenever the modality, geometry, or material changes. We investigate whether a single diffusion model trained across several imaging domains can instead serve as a prior for many CT problems simultaneously. We evaluate the proposed method using the same frozen model on three datasets that differ in modality, beam geometry, material, and degradation type, spanning flaw analysis in additively manufactured metal parts imaged with cone-beam X-ray CT and concrete microstructure imaged with parallel-beam neutron CT. Our proposed method out-performs analytic reconstructions in all three cases, providing a step toward a reusable foundation prior for heterogeneous CT reconstruction problems.

presentations.title: Toward GPU-Resident Climate Models: A Feasibility Study on Lossy Compression for the Spherical Harmonic Transform’s Communication Bottleneck
presentations.abstract:
Operational pseudospectral atmospheric models such
as the ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) run today
almost exclusively on CPUs; GPU ports are under active
development but not yet used in production. These models rely
on the Spherical Harmonic Transform (SHT) to compute spatial
derivatives and to alternate between spectral and grid-space
representations. Each time-step requires forward and inverse
SHTs, and both passes depend on global pencil transposition:
row-wise/column-wise all-to-all collectives that redistribute multi-
dimensional arrays across compute nodes. While GPU floating-
point throughput has grown rapidly, inter-node network band-
width has not kept pace, and at large node counts these global
collectives dominate wall-clock time.
As an alternative to float16 truncation during communication,
we investigate GPU-resident lossy compression, a capability not
yet available to any operational CPU-bound pseudospectral model.
Using representative fields from the DYAMOND high-resolution
operational dataset as input, and combining measured GPU
compression throughput with SimGrid network simulation, we
show that ZFP at 16 bits per value (rate-16), about the same
storage budget as float16, matches the communication-time
reduction of float16 truncation while delivering approximately
1600× lower mean relative error. ZFP at 8 bits per value
(rate-8) achieves approximately 1.93× the speedup of float16
while retaining 4× lower mean relative error. We additionally
corroborate the simulated communication-time trend with real
measurements on the CPU partition of the CRESCO8 cluster.

presentations.title: Toward HEPScore4GPU: Scaling and Power of Real HEP GPU Applications on the A100 and H100
presentations.abstract: The HEPiX Benchmarking Working Group is developing HEPScore4GPU, a GPU benchmark for high-energy physics (HEP) built from real HEP applications for the High Lumi-LHC program. A key question is how efficiently GPUs can be used for HEP today. We take three candidate applications under development, a Monte Carlo Generator, a detector full simulation and an AI-based end-to-end simulation application, and run them on NVIDIA A100 and H100 GPUs, measuring how throughput scales from one to four GPUs and how much power they use. In this contribution we will describe the measurement process and the understanding of the different behaviors, with the objective of providing input to the application developers to further improve the software and exploit the maximum power of the GPUs.

presentations.title: Toward OpenSHMEM 2.0: Separating Memory from Execution in PGAS
presentations.abstract: OpenSHMEM and the wider Partitioned Global Address Space (PGAS) family were built for homogeneous, CPU-centric machines, and they rest on one design choice that modern hardware has outgrown. The agent that issues, orders, and completes communication, which we call the \term{executor}, is bound to the process (the PE) that owns symmetric memory, so that by default one PE is one executor. On a CPU node this costs nothing. On a heterogeneous node, where one process drives many CPU threads, GPU streams, and thousands of GPU blocks, it becomes the central obstacle. We argue that OpenSHMEM 2.0 turns on one decision: \term{split the executor from the process}. Within each executor the model attempts to stay OpenSHMEM 1.x, so a single-executor process is exactly a classic PE and existing programs keep working. This position paper makes the case; it offers no API and no measurements.

presentations.title: Toward Software-Defined Performance Optimization for Emerging Quantum Systems
presentations.abstract:
Abstract—Quantum computing provides a promising computing
paradigm, yet physical hardware remains constrained by short
qubit coherence times, gate operational errors, and scarce
quantum resources [1]. In near-term quantum execution, software
efficiency directly impacts program viability: every redundant
gate consumes precious coherence time, accumulates operational
noise, and lowers execution success probability. Our broader
research investigates how compiler, systems, and learning-guided
optimization can maximize the usable computational throughput
extracted from constrained quantum hardware.

presentations.title: Towards a Distributed QHPC Workflow for Gadget-Aware Circuit Cutting and Pulse Synthesis
presentations.abstract: Pulse-level synthesis of compound gadgets (repetitive macroscopic gate blocks) compresses quantum control footprints. However, classically optimizing these schedules via optimal control algorithms creates severe compute bottlenecks, while scaling deep algorithms exhausts classical memory. These constraints demand distributed quantum high-performance computing (QHPC) workflows, but current tools use gate- or wire-level cutting that destroy data boundaries required for compound pulse gadget synthesis. We introduce Kodoki, a pulse gadget optimization framework that enables gadget-aware circuit cutting. Coupled with Qdislib and PyCOMPSs, Kodoki provides a decoupled distributed workflow. PyCOMPSs orchestrates pulse synthesis offline. Online, workers are given subcircuits and query a lookup table (LUT) of pre-computed pulses to execute subcircuits. Evaluations show Kodoki's compound synthesis achieves a 4.38x reduction in pulse execution time (from > 1000𝜇s to 240𝜇s). Shifting synthesis offline replaces an 865.5s compute bottleneck with a 2.326ms online query (𝑃₉₉ = 3.35ms). Ongoing evaluations will quantify scaling behavior across variational ansatzes.

presentations.title: Towards Direct-to-Chip Liquid-Cooled Megawatt Racks: Characterization of a Multi-Kilowatt Chip-Scale Cooler & The Implications on Facility Energy Use
presentations.abstract: The power density of artificial-intelligence (AI) and high-performance-computing (HPC) accelerators continues to increase. Although the HPC community adopted liquid cooling years ago, the broader computing industry is now undergoing a similar transition. With 1, 3, and 5 kW accelerators appearing on technology roadmaps, removing multi-kilowatt chip-level heat loads without excessive facility-cooling energy or hydraulic demand remains a challenge. This study characterizes a liquid-cooled thermal stack and identifies the design parameters needed to support next-generation AI devices. Repeatable steady-state measurements yielded an inlet-referenced thermal resistance of 0.0383 K/W. A reduced-order model separated coolant warming, cold-plate convection, and flow-independent stack resistance. At a 100 °C average heater limit and 5 L/min, the baseline stack dissipated 3.04 kW, while a controlled thin liquid-metal interface increased the projected capacity to 6.41 kW. At 3 kW, this interface reduced the required flow from 4.61 to 0.92 L/min and increased allowable inlet-temperature margin by 40.5 °C.

presentations.title: Towards Distributed-Memory All-Pairs Reachability over Homomorphically Encrypted Graphs
presentations.abstract:
Transitive closure determines reachability between all pairs of vertices
in a directed graph. For encrypted graphs, this computation requires
many expensive ciphertext operations. This makes single-node execution
slow even for small matrices.

We implement transitive closure (all-pairs reachability) for BGV-encrypted graphs on distributed memory systems. The implementation stores matrix rows and columns in
separate ciphertexts. Each output entry is computed from one row
ciphertext and one column ciphertext. We distribute these computations
over a two-dimensional MPI process grid. The output remains distributed
and is reused in the next transitive-closure step.

We evaluate the implementation with up to 1,024 MPI ranks and compare
against a single-node baseline with 32 OpenMP threads. At N=16, the
distributed implementation achieves a 5.66 times speedup over the
single-node baseline.

presentations.title: Towards Efficient HPC Systems for Agents: Challenges and Opportunities
presentations.abstract:
Coding agents have become real users of high-performance computing (HPC) systems, yet today's HPC abstractions, interfaces, and policies remain designed for humans. We observed 19.5% of users running coding agent, which account for 55.8% of job submissions, 29.1% of CPU core-hours, and 42.7% of GPU-hours. Agents are not simply faster humans. They issue commands at 20.8x the human rate, decompose work into fine-grained explore-modify-execute loops.
These behaviors strain abstractions built for human timescales, surfacing as control-plane pressure on the scheduler, metadata-intensive I/O on bandwidth-provisioned filesystems, repeated rediscovery of what earlier sessions already learned, and new prompt-injection and policy-enforcement surfaces. Neither banning agents nor treating them as ordinary users is sustainable. We instead argue for co-design, that facilities should treat agents as first-class principals where agents become facility-aware tenants. We outline the resulting challenges and opportunities in compute, storage, agent memory, and safety.

presentations.title: Towards Efficient Vertical Federated Learning on Distributed Scientific Infrastructure
presentations.abstract:
Modern scientific collaborations rely on combining data from multiple organizations while preserving data privacy according to regulations and policies. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) enables collaborative model training without requiring participants to share raw data. However, deploying VFL across geographically distributed infrastructure introduces significant execution overhead, and requires balancing computational cost and privacy requirements.

To address the communication overhead introduced by distributed VFL execution, we investigate the deployment of multiple VFL execution strategies within DYNAMOS, a policy-aware middleware for privacy-preserving data exchange. We evaluate the baseline VFL protocol alongside two communication-efficient variants, including a novel adaptation of an asynchronous optimization technique from Horizontal Federated Learning. The strategies are deployed in both a local environment and on a distributed research testbed, enabling a comparative evaluation under realistic scientific networking conditions. These experiments support execution time, model utility, and privacy analysis, demonstrating that the optimized strategies substantially reduce runtime while preserving predictive performance.

presentations.title: Towards MPI Communication Modeling From Passive Network Telemetry
presentations.abstract: The distribution of MPI message sizes issued by an application is a first-order determinant of its communication behavior, yet recovering this distribution typically requires application-level instrumentation and/or a priori knowledge of the communication pattern. We present an application-agnostic model of MPI communication that reconstructs the MPI message-size distribution from passive network telemetry: packet-level counters that modern NICs expose and that facility operators already collect continuously, system-wide, at negligible cost. The model requires no knowledge of the network topology, the communication peers, or the MPI operations in use, and can be applied retroactively to archived telemetry. Instantiated on the Cassini counters of NERSC's Perlmutter, the model estimates OSU Micro-Benchmark message counts within 0.5% and the dominant LAMMPS size classes within 10%, which is a first step toward instrumentation-free prediction of communication time.

presentations.title: Towards PIM-Aware Expert Decomposition and Mapping for MoE Inference
presentations.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference presents system challenges because experts receive uneven workloads and exhibit different execution characteristics. This work explores how processing-in-memory (PIM) can complement GPUs to improve MoE inference efficiency. We propose a PIM-aware approach that selectively assigns suitable expert computation to PIM while retaining other computation on the GPU. The approach also considers how experts can be decomposed and mapped to available PIM resources. This WIP talk will briefly introduce the motivation and proposed solution, highlight the main design considerations, and outline the next steps toward evaluating the feasibility and potential benefits of PIM-assisted MoE inference.

presentations.title: Towards Server-Grade Device Pooling over Routable PCIe with Improved and Scalable Systems Software
presentations.abstract: Routable PCIe enables composable infrastructures and device pooling with native drivers, yet little is known about its end-to-end performance in production systems, leaving a gap between microbenchmark research and marketing whitepapers. We show routable PCIe challenges assumptions made by traditional operating systems, particularly in how DMA buffers are managed when accessed by remote devices. We resolve a cache incoherence issue in the IOMMU's interrupt remapping subsystem and adapt IOMMU scalability optimizations from the OS kernel to routable PCIe software, reducing median DMA deallocation latency by 90% versus prior work and enabling full parallelism for pooled devices. We further optimize the deallocation critical path via a novel IOMMU sidecore-offloading scheme, reducing median unmapping latency by 26% and tail latency by up to 89% compared to the kernel. Finally, we evaluate on server-grade storage and GPUs, showing routable PCIe achieves native IOPS at lower latency and CPU utilization than scale-out alternatives.

presentations.title: Towards Verifying OpenMP Target Offloading
presentations.abstract:
With the rise of LLM-generated and translated codes alongside the rise of heterogeneous computing, verification of concurrent programming dialects is becoming a necessity. OpenMP is one of those many concurrency dialects with support for heterogeneous computing using their target offloading feature. There is little work formalizing and verifying this feature. Existing work in OpenMP verification does not handle the added complexities that target offloading brings, such as host-device execution semantics and data mapping semantics.

We help address this by developing a formal model for target offloading using an existing verification tool that supports base OpenMP, CIVL. With this formal model, we simulate multiple simple bugs in OpenMP and show that our model can be used to catch these bugs.

The poster presents how the formal model represents OpenMP target offloading semantics and how some simple bugs were simulated and tested.

presentations.title: Tracking HPC Software Stack Drift and Performance with Benchpark
presentations.abstract: As HPC systems grow in architectural complexity, system software stacks undergo continuous, autonomous development separate from HPC applications. Existing benchmarking frameworks do not fully automate evaluation of the changing software stacks, and a binary pass/fail result provides insufficient information to root cause test failures or performance changes. We present a continuous integration (CI) methodology that tracks changes in the software stack, tests functionality and performance, and identifies software and configuration changes that may explain failures or performance regressions. We demonstrate our methodology on HPC systems in two different compute centers, and attribute performance regressions to updates in the ROCm runtime library. By associating experiment results with software changes, our methodology provides a basis for diagnosing and reviewing evolving HPC environments.

presentations.title: Training Without Sharing: Federated Learning on the World's HPC Systems for Science
presentations.abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets institutions train shared AI models without exchanging raw data — a capability increasingly essential for science where data is sensitive, proprietary, or too large to move. Yet FL on HPC remains uncharted: job schedulers, site firewalls, identity federation, and heterogeneous accelerators reshape the problem beyond what cloud-based FL assumes. This BoF brings together framework developers, HPC centers, and scientific users to discuss running trustworthy FL across the world's supercomputers. We will surface open algorithmic, systems, and governance challenges and work toward a community roadmap for cross-facility FL benchmarks, interoperability, and shared practice.

presentations.title: Training-Free Mixture-of-Agents for CUDA Kernel Translation and Optimization
presentations.abstract: This poster presents a kernel-aware multi-agent framework for CUDA optimization that analyzes both performance gains and optimization cost. We compare Fixed, Adaptive, and Collaborative optimization modes across two kernels: Lattice-Boltzmann Method (LBM) and SYMM. Fixed applies a predefined sequence of coalescing, tiling, and atomic-focused transformations, while Adaptive uses routing to stop when additional layers are unnecessary. Collaborative uses multi-model proposals with GPT-OSS aggregation. Our layer-influence analysis measures how strongly each intermediate optimization layer shapes the final kernel using similarity-based scores. Results show that LBM benefits from deeper staged refinement, with later layers contributing most to the final output, whereas SYMM converges earlier after coalescing and tiling. Cost analysis further shows that Adaptive optimization can reduce tokens, energy, and optimization time by avoiding unnecessary transformations. Overall, the results highlight the importance of kernel-aware routing and layer-aware stopping for practical LLM-driven GPU optimization.

presentations.title: Transit-Layer Tensor Representation for Serverless Inference
presentations.abstract: The scale of frontier machine learning systems has led to an increasing need to efficiently store and transfer model weights. Existing methods for serverless inference employ scheduling policies to reduce cold start and model swapping latency, but have largely reached the limitations of hardware. In this paper, we introduce Condense, an ultra-fast method of compressing tensor weights across applications. We implement Condense in a serverless runtime as a transit-layer representation and evaluate the latency reduction. Across Llama models from 1B to 13B parameters, Condense reduces stored weight sizes by 2.27x-2.38x and improves cold-start loading time by 1.92x-2.17x over ServerlessLLM while retaining competitive downstream accuracy. We demonstrate that compact tensor representations can be generated quickly to provide significant runtime reductions across machine learning applications.

presentations.title: Trigger-Gated Multimodal LLM Agents for In-situ Scientific Simulation Monitoring
presentations.abstract: Simulations routinely run to completion while computing the wrong answer. No production tool monitors whether a running simulation computes valid science; we call this blind spot dark waste. Multimodal LLM agents could supply the physics-aware judgment such monitoring needs, but no scientific field fits in a context window. A rendering does. Vigil is a trigger-render-reason pipeline built as an ADIOS2 plugin engine on the application's I/O path. Deterministic triggers run every timestep inline with the write. Only flagged states stream in-transit to a visualization node, where an agent drives ParaView through tool calls and returns a structured verdict. Across four codes, with zero per-application training, Vigil confirms every parameter-induced failure and dismisses a trigger deliberately fired on a healthy run. Halting at the alert saves 39--68\% of an under-resolved Taylor--Green run, and gating costs 0.05\% of run time at 256 processes.

presentations.title: Triple Overlap in Pipelined Krylov Methods on Multi-GPU Systems
presentations.abstract:
We introduce a novel triple-overlap implementation for the pipelined preconditioned conjugate gradient (Pipe-PCG) and pipelined stabilized biconjugate gradient (Pipe-BiCGStab) solvers. Our approach extends conventional computation-communication overlap to concurrently execute collective operations, point-to-point communication, and compute kernels. This enables true computation-communication-communication overlap across multiple GPUs.

We evaluate on the MareNostrum 5 (H100) and Leonardo (A100) supercomputers, comparing against PETSc and the state-of-the-art two-stream NCCL implementation using SuiteSparse matrices and three massive instances scaled up to 512 GPUs. The three-stream design consistently outperforms the two-stream baseline, with the margin widening from 2–6% at 4 GPUs to 18–47% at 64 GPUs.

At 64 GPUs, the geometric-mean speedup over the two-stream baseline is 1.33× on MareNostrum 5 and 1.23× on Leonardo for Pipe-PCG, reaching 1.30× for Pipe-BiCGStab. In large-scale experiments, we observed speedups of up to 35% (Pipe-PCG) and 33% (Pipe-BiCGStab) over the two-stream design, and up to 3.27× over PETSc for both solvers.

presentations.title: Triton Attention Backend: Portable High-Performance Paged Attention for Production-Grade LLM Inference
presentations.abstract:
Attention kernels represent the backbone of modern LLMs and are usually the most performance-critical GPU kernels. Today, state-of-the-art LLM inference relies primarily on attention kernels painstakingly hand-optimized for each GPU architecture. This approach delivers strong performance, but it also fragments the software ecosystem and requires substantial, ongoing engineering effort for every new model and hardware platform.

In this work, we present a case study on the performance portability of the paged attention kernel. We describe our platform-agnostic Triton Attention implementation and demonstrate that open-source domain-specific languages can deliver efficient, portable LLM inference across GPU vendors.

Our experimental evaluation shows that our Triton kernel matches the performance of platform-specific kernels on the latest NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and is up to 7x faster than existing portable attention implementations. We further discuss how our kernel improves the flexibility, portability, and developer productivity of vLLM, and share the design principles behind our approach.

presentations.title: Trusted Research Environments for AI and Integrated Science: Launching the Genesis Mission
presentations.abstract: This BoF aims to build on the successful launch at SC25 of a multi-national community of practice. This year we focus on the Genesis Mission and DOE’s American Science Cloud and AI Models Consortium projects, to include establishing best practices for multi-facility or multi-institutional workflows, lessons learned from international contexts, sharing and accessing resources, developing mixed public/private partnerships, and protecting sensitive data privacy and security. Our goal is to advance progress in developing secure and trustworthy infrastructures for AI and integrated science. We seek to understand trustworthiness in supercomputing environments from both technical and socio-technical perspectives.

presentations.title: Trustworthy Agentic AI for HPC Operational and Predictive Data Analytics and Forecasting
presentations.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer promising pathways for automating high performance computing (HPC) operations, yet their real-world deployment is severely constrained by silent operational failures, uncalibrated confidence, and brittle central control. In this work, we chart a new vision for reliable, agentic AI across supercomputing facilities. We explore the architectural paradigm shift from centralized orchestration to decentralized, peer-to-peer agent topologies, illustrating how typed dialogue and bounded knowledge limits ensure defensible, transparent operational guidance. Furthermore, we examine the critical challenge of stance fidelity, demonstrating how verbalized confidence must be audited as dynamic system telemetry rather than taken at face value. Based on these insights, we advocate for a fundamental re-architecting of facility AI: prioritizing honest refusal over raw recall, establishing auditable ground-truth benchmarks, and transitioning AI tools from passive historical log lookups to active, pre-submission job steering.

presentations.title: Trustworthy Data at Scale: HDF5 in the Age of AI-Driven Science
presentations.abstract: HDF5 has anchored HPC I/O for 25 years, and AI-driven science is redefining what "trustworthy data at scale" demands: verifiable provenance, concurrent I/O, and cloud-native interoperability. Short talks from domain scientists launch interactive segments where an opt-in agentic survey captures attendee priorities, pain points, and open questions in real time, with aggregate results used to steer the discussion. This session is for seasoned HDF5 developers and domain scientists, and anyone just starting out or wondering what HDF5 is about: bring the problems you'd like to solve, and help steer the discussion and provide input to future HDF5 roadmap planning.

presentations.title: TSVC-RVV: A Diagnostic Extension of TSVC for Evaluating RISC-V Auto-Vectorization
presentations.abstract:
RISC-V is attracting growing interest in high-performance computing (HPC), with the RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV) providing a vector-length-agnostic architecture for accelerating data-parallel workloads. Realizing this potential requires compiler toolchains that reliably generate efficient RVV code. Assessing and improving RVV auto-vectorization is therefore important to the RISC-V HPC software ecosystem.

The Test Suite for Vectorizing Compilers (TSVC) is widely used to evaluate auto-vectorization. It contains 151 loops, each designed to exercise a specific vectorization pattern. However, effective TSVC evaluation requires substantial manual effort, as the suite provides no reference vector implementations and each loop may admit multiple valid vectorization strategies.

We extend TSVC with two complementary RVV-focused references: (1) RVV intrinsic implementations for all 151 loops, providing vectorization strategies; and (2) source-code variants that expose limitations in RISC-V compiler toolchains. Together, these references enable more informative TSVC evaluation and provide actionable guidance for improving RVV support for HPC workloads.

presentations.title: TULCA-based Visual Analytics of HPC Operational Data: A Case Study of Fugaku Rack's Power Data
presentations.abstract: In this paper, we apply Tensor Unified Linear Comparative Analysis (TULCA) to rack-level power consumption data from the supercomputer Fugaku. The data are represented as a third-order tensor with temporal, spatial, and variable axes, with each time point labeled by its operational period. TULCA generates low-dimensional representations that emphasize differences among labeled groups while preserving the tensor structure. Based on this representation, we construct an analysis workflow that provides an overview of temporal behavior and traces differences between analyst-selected temporal clusters back to the contributing compute racks. We applied the workflow to power consumption data from Fugaku's 432 compute racks across two operational periods. In case studies, the racks contributing most strongly to the observed separation exhibited sharp, short-term power fluctuations. These results demonstrate the potential of the workflow for interactive comparative analysis of HPC operational data.

presentations.title: Twelfth International Workshop on Heterogeneous High-Performance Reconfigurable Computing (H2RC 2026)
presentations.abstract: As in the previous 11 years, this workshop will bring together application experts, software developers, and hardware engineers, both from industry and academia, to share experiences and best practices to leverage the practical application of reconfigurable logic to scientific computing, AI/ML, and “big data” applications. In particular, the workshop will focus on sharing experiences and techniques for accelerating applications and/or improving energy efficiency with FPGAs using high-level design flows, which enable and improve cross-platform functional and performance portability while also improving productivity. Particular emphasis is given to cross-platform comparisons and combinations that foster a better understanding within the industry and research community on what are the best mappings of applications to a diverse range of hardware architectures that are available today (e.g., FPGA, GPU, many-cores and hybrid devices, ASICs), and on how to most effectively achieve cross-platform compatibility.

presentations.title: Twenty Years of Sparsity on GPUs
presentations.abstract: The first CUDA-capable GPU was launched 20 years ago, and a sparse matrix-vector product (SpMV) kernel was one of the first CUDA kernels I attempted to write. The SIMT execution model of the GPU made it relatively easy to build a working implementation, but the simplest kernels suffered from several performance pitfalls. A couple of years later, Nathan Bell and I set out to design kernels that would deliver truly high throughput and utilize significant fractions of the high bandwidth that GPUs provide. The paper we published in SC09 demonstrated that this was indeed possible. It also highlighted two key ideas: selecting the right data structure that exploits known matrix structure makes high performance straightforward, and irregularity is easily managed if it is rare. Since that time, a great deal of work has been done for both sparse computations and linear algebra on the GPU. In this talk, I will look back at the lessons of our early work, some notable steps on the path since that time, and consider some of the challenges ahead of us.

presentations.title: Type-Safe, Dynamically Defined Metadata Support for Scientific Applications
presentations.abstract:
Earlier work on offering rich metadata, such as Empress, TagIt, SoMeta, and PDC all suffer from limitations on the type and structure of the metadata they process.
The most flexible of these, Empress, hard coded the work structure of application to include run and time step, forcing this view on users.
Further, it also assumes a mesh layout, which is not conducive to simulations or experimental data layouts which do not lay on a mesh. We have a multi-language, Rust-based approach for fully flexible, type safe metadata management.

presentations.title: U.S. National Science Foundation Cyberinfrastructure in an Age of Change and Challenge
presentations.abstract: The U.S. National Science Foundation asked the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to assess the evolving role of cyberinfrastructure in enabling 21st-century scientific discovery and innovation. This Birds of a Feather session will discuss the committee’s assessment of NSF’s advanced cyberinfrastructure portfolio in a rapidly changing environment shaped by artificial intelligence, cloud computing, rapidly expanding private-sector investment in AI, and the potential role of strategic partnership between government and industry. Committee members will summarize major themes from the report and invite community discussion on how NSF can sustain broad, effective, and forward-looking cyberinfrastructure for the research enterprise.

presentations.title: UDTS-Integrated SRCNet Data Control System

presentations.title: Ultra Ethernet: Next-Generation Networking for HPC Supercomputers and AI Factories
presentations.abstract: Ultra Ethernet has emerged as a major effort to create a scalable, open networking architecture for both AI factories and high-performance computing systems. As AI clusters continue to grow while HPC workloads demand ever-higher communication performance and efficiency, many networking requirements are beginning to converge. This BoF provides a forum for researchers, system architects, operators, application developers, and network vendors to discuss experiences, emerging requirements, unresolved challenges, and future directions for large-scale networking. The discussion aims to identify common needs across HPC and AI and foster collaboration toward open, interoperable networking solutions for next-generation computing systems.

presentations.title: Understanding AllReduce Performance Through Hardware Telemetry
presentations.abstract: Inter-GPU AllReduce operations traverse several tightly coupled hardware components, including the GPU, PCIe interface, NIC, and network. Each component exposes hardware telemetry for its local behavior, and no single telemetry source observes the complete communication path. A combined view is therefore needed to narrow where performance is limited and to guide optimization. We combine selected NVIDIA A100 GPU counters with Cassini NIC counters on HPE Slingshot-11 to analyze a 1 GiB inter-node AllReduce across NCCL protocols, NCCL channel counts, and GPU-aware MPI versus NCCL. Across the three studies, the joint telemetry associates performance differences with distinct behaviors: work amplification for NCCL LL, increased synchronization and reduced transfer progress at high channel counts, and slow transfer progress with additional rank imbalance for MPI. Joint GPU–NIC telemetry therefore helps distinguish different sources of AllReduce slowdown and narrows where optimization effort should be focused.

presentations.title: Understanding and Improving Multi-Rack Symmetric-Memory AllGather in NCCL
presentations.abstract: Rack-scale GPU systems such as the GB200 NVL72 extend the NVLink scale-up domain from four or eight GPUs per server to 72 GPUs per rack. Large language model (LLM) training still scales across many racks, with all-gathers spanning heterogeneous NVLink and InfiniBand fabrics. These all-gathers operate in a message-size regime where both latency and bandwidth matter. In this work, we characterize NCCL's symmetric-memory and legacy all-gather performance for this regime. We derive a closed-form topology-aware bandwidth bound and extend it with a latency term for comparison with empirical measurements. Based on observed trends and model insights, we design two new GPU-initiated symmetric-memory all-gather implementations that outperform NCCL's symmetric-memory all-gathers by up to 2.6x for 32-512MB messages.

presentations.title: Understanding Communication Performance in Large-Scale Codes: A Practical Guide
presentations.abstract: Communication has become a primary performance limiter for large-scale applications, from sparse solvers to AI workloads. This full-day tutorial introduces attendees to the practical use and performance analysis of modern communication libraries, including MPI, RCCL, and rocSHMEM, with a focus on profiling communication behavior using TAU. The tutorial will provide students, early-career researchers, and application developers, who are not necessarily specialists in communication libraries, a bottom-up understanding of communication performance. Participants will learn how to compile and run representative communication benchmarks, interpret latency and bandwidth results, and connect benchmark behavior to application-level communication patterns. Using hands-on examples, attendees will explore how communication choices affect performance on GPU-based systems and how profiling tools can reveal bottlenecks that are otherwise hidden at the source-code level. The tutorial emphasizes practical workflows for cross-referencing benchmark data with profiling output to guide optimization decisions. Built around a collaboratively developed, thoroughly tested code base, the session will provide a reproducible and accessible environment for live exercises. By the end of the day, attendees will be equipped to diagnose communication performance inefficiencies and make informed library and design choices for their own codes.

presentations.title: Understanding the NERSC User Community Through Network Analysis
presentations.abstract: NERSC users collaborate, forming a network. Which users occupy the most structurally influential positions in the NERSC user community? Using 2020–2026 NERSC allocation records, a proxy collaboration graph was analyzed to reveal the user community’s dynamics. Two definitions of user connectivity were compared using available data on project allocation size: unweighted degree and repository-size-adjusted (RSA) strength. Degree distributions, program-office affiliation, and user roles were analyzed. Results show that RSA strength is a more accurate measurement of user connectivity than unweighted degree. The strongest connectors in the network are career scientists and users associated with high-energy physics. These findings suggest that in HPC network data, unweighted connectivity is not a reliable measurement of network influence or cross-disciplinary reach. Findings also suggest that allocation networks reflect certain field-specific collaboration patterns, implying that allocation networks may provide a useful proxy for co-authorship networks in the same field.

presentations.title: Unified Communication X (UCX) Community
presentations.abstract:
In order to exploit the capabilities of new HPC systems and to meet their demands in scalability, communication software needs to scale to millions of cores and support applications with adequate functionality. UCX is a collaboration between industry, national labs, and academia that consolidates and provides a unified open-source framework.

The UCX project is managed by the UCF Consortium (http://www.ucfconsortium.org/). The session will serve as the UCX community meeting and will introduce the latest developments to HPC developers and the broader user community.

presentations.title: Union of Containers: Layered Software Stacks with Cross-Container Dependency Reuse for HPC
presentations.abstract: HPC software stacks are typically distributed as one container image per accelerator target, and every image duplicates the CPU-generic majority of the stack. This work splits the stack across containers. A shared provider holds the architecture-generic dependencies; thin specialized layers hold only GPU-compiled packages and reuse the provider's builds instead of recompiling them. The layers compose at run time through absolute RPATH entries under fixed paths, with no search-path configuration. With Spack and E4S recipes, each specialized layer compiled 1 of 20 buildable packages at two facilities, Midway3 and NSF ACCESS Anvil. On Anvil, each further GPU target adds 1,412 files where a monolithic build adds 10,772, rebuilding a layer is 1.8 to 2.8 times faster, and application performance is unchanged on A100 and H100 GPUs. The same install trees run unmodified under Apptainer and Charliecloud. The poster also reports four constraints on where reuse holds.

presentations.title: Unleashing Performance: How CXL and Disaggregated Memory Are Revolutionizing HPC and AI
presentations.abstract:
As memory-bound workloads begin to dominate HPC and AI, traditional architectures face severe limitations in memory bandwidth and capacity. Compute Express Link® (CXL®) is providing the means to create disaggregated and composable memory tiers to accelerate HPC and AI performance.

This panel, moderated by Dan Olds, features experts from Penguin Solutions, SemiconDx, and Intel, who will explore the evolving role of CXL in next-generation HPC/AI systems. Panelists will discuss emerging memory architectures, performance benchmarks, cost and scale trade-offs, alongside lessons learned from early implementations and incorporation of emerging technologies, such as silicon photonics, that should be on everyone’s roadmap.

Through interactive discussion and audience engagement, the session will highlight real-world benchmarks discussing CXL-enabled systems, as well as practical insights into memory-constrained workloads. Attendees will understand current limitations, gain actionable guidance, and leave better equipped to evaluate and resolve memory constraints in HPC and AI environments.

presentations.title: Useful Data, Not Just More Data: Cost-Aware Floating Car Data Generation in Large-Scale Traffic Simulation
presentations.abstract: Large-scale traffic simulations can generate millions of floating car data (FCD) records, but more output does not necessarily provide more useful information. Using Ruth on LUMI, we study a Chicago scenario with 6.9 million input vehicle trips and 748,509 road-network nodes. We compare output size, road-edge coverage, temporal coverage, and speed similarity against a high-detail simulation reference. With vehicle updates fixed at 20 seconds, increasing the FCD sampling period from 5 to 20 seconds halves output while retaining 97.1% road-edge coverage and 88.9% temporal coverage. Tests on 1–16 nodes show sublinear gains in the traffic-time interval recorded within a fixed wall-time budget. Reducing rerouting participation from 80% to 50% extends this interval by 18%–22% and lowers wall time per second of recorded traffic time by 15%–18%. We recommend selecting the smallest output meeting task-specific coverage and speed-error requirements; rerouting changes still require validation of traffic outcomes.

presentations.title: Using Containers To Accelerate HPC
presentations.abstract: The use of containers has revolutionized the way in which industries and enterprises have developed and deployed computational software and distributed systems. This containerization model has gained traction within the HPC community as well with the promise of improved reliability, reproducibility, portability, and levels of customization that were not previously possible on supercomputers. This adoption has been enabled by a number of HPC container runtimes that have emerged including Apptainer, Shifter, Sarus, Podman, and others. This hands-on tutorial looks to train users on the use of containers for HPC use cases. We will provide a detailed background on Linux containers, along with an introductory hands-on experience building a container image, sharing the container and running it on an HPC cluster. Furthermore, the tutorial will provide more advanced information on how to run MPI-based and GPU-enabled HPC applications, how to optimize I/O intensive workflows, how to set up GUI-enabled interactive sessions, and how to use containers for agentic AI and MCP servers. Users will leave the tutorial with a solid foundational understanding of how to utilize containers on HPC resources using Podman, Docker, and Apptainer, and in-depth knowledge to deploy custom containers for HPC and AI on their own resources.

presentations.title: Using ethtrace to debug AI networks
presentations.abstract:
We introduce ethtrace, a simple and lightweight on-demand network monitoring tool that generates probes from a source host at a specified frequency and relies on switch telemetry
extensions such as the in-band flow analyzer to collect per hop and interactively displays or logs it at the destination host. ethtrace usage is as simple as that of established
tools like ping and traceroute, but provides richer visibility and
finer grained insights than existing approaches. ethtrace can
be used to track the path of an existing queue-pair or TCP
connection, or to monitor one or all paths between two hosts.
We present several use-cases where ethtrace was used to
quickly debug RoCEv2 performance anomalies such as PFC is-
sues, DCQCN parameters settings, offering visibility into complex
network behaviour that today is very difficult to understand
and debug. ethtrace is deployable today, as a large fraction
of deployed datacenter switches have telemetry support.

presentations.title: Using Persistent Digital Twins as Spatial Environments for Robotics Simulation and Deployment
presentations.abstract:
Deploying autonomous robots into new industrial sites requires their simulation and control software to understand the environment in which they will operate. This can create duplicated engineering effort between environments prepared for robotics simulation and 3D representations of physical sites already maintained for operational applications.

In an ongoing industrial robotics project, we are exploring whether a persistent 3D digital twin can serve as a reusable spatial environment for an external robotics simulator, with the objective of reducing the time and engineering effort required to deploy autonomous robots on new customer sites.

The robotics company maintains its own simulation, perception, navigation, and control stack. Through a bidirectional interface, robot poses are sent to the 3D environment, virtual sensor viewpoints are updated, and depth information is returned to the robotics simulator. Users can simultaneously visualize the simulation within the customer site and issue commands back to the simulated robot.

Using an API-driven, web-based architecture, the two independent systems were integrated in only a few weeks. This Community Talk will share this early industrial implementation and discuss practical questions around real-time coupling, sensor feedback, latency, and the potential for persistent digital twins to become shared spatial infrastructure across simulation and operational applications.

presentations.title: Utilizing Deep Learning-Based Video Frame Interpolation for Scientific Visualization
presentations.abstract: Scientific visualization workflows must balance visual fidelity against the storage and I/O costs of large image databases. We investigate deep learning-based Video Frame Interpolation (VFI) to reduce these costs by reconstructing omitted visualization images from stored keyframes. We evaluate the FILM and RIFE models on scientific visualization images using perceptual quality metrics and integrate them into the PyCinema analysis framework. Based on these results, we develop a greedy keyframe selection algorithm that stores an image only when it cannot be reconstructed from neighboring keyframes within a user-defined error tolerance. Its reliance on local information enables integration into an in situ ParaView Catalyst workflow. Experiments show that VFI can accurately reconstruct omitted images while substantially reducing the number of frames written to disk, improving the storage efficiency of scientific visualization pipelines.

presentations.title: uv-manager: A Transparent Wrapper for Safe, Architecture-Aware Python Environments on Heterogeneous HPC Clusters
presentations.abstract: uv suits high-performance computing unusually well, but a cluster violates three of its assumptions: that $HOME has room for a package cache, that a shell profile is available, and that every node shares one CPU architecture. uv-manager, a transparent wrapper deployed as a site module, resolves all three. Users invoke uv and uvx unchanged while it relocates per-user state onto capacity storage and partitions that state by an architecture key resolved on the executing node, with architecture-neutral trampolines so one PATH entry works everywhere. Relocation is half a solution: capacity storage is purged file by file, and uv performs no integrity check on an environment it believes installed, so it executes what a purge leaves behind. uv-manager protects against this failure mode by detecting and repairing on the executing node, which is what makes the placement safe.

presentations.title: Validation of a Parallel and Distributed Computing Instrument for Early Computing Research
presentations.abstract:
Parallel and distributed computing (PDC) has become the dominant
computing model. Substantial research and advocacy efforts have been
made to introduce PDC early in computing curricula. However, much
of this research has relied on informal, ad-hoc measures of
intervention efficacy. We address this gap by developing and
validating an instrument designed to assess PDC knowledge of
introductory computing students. This instrument is intended for
use by researchers as a pre/post intervention assessment. We
validate our instrument using Item Response Theory under the Rasch
(1PL) model using data from multiple institutions. The
instrument demonstrated a broad range of item difficulties,
acceptable fit statistics, and evidence of unidimensionality.
After recalibration, the improved instrument demonstrates strong
reliability as a measure of foundational PDC knowledge. This
instrument will help improve the rigor and quality of future PDC
education research.

presentations.title: Variation-Aware Non-Uniform Node Power Capping for Exascale HPC Systems
presentations.abstract:
Exascale systems such as Aurora operate under stringent power and thermal constraints, yet their nominally identical nodes exhibit substantial performance-per-watt variation due to manufacturing, aging, and thermal differences. Under uniform node power caps, this variation slows the critical-path node in tightly coupled applications and reduces the effectiveness
of a fixed job-level power budget. We present a variation-aware, non-uniform node power allocation method for Aurora that (i) characterizes the power–performance response of individual nodes using a large-scale RAPL (Running Average Power Limit) power sweep, (ii) represents the characterization using either a quadratic or a piecewise-linear model, and (iii) uses the selected model to compute non-uniform per-node power caps under a fixed job-level power budget. Using measured Nekbone experiments at approximately 512 nodes and 8,210 nodes, non-uniform allocation improves normalized application performance by up to 7.5% at moderate scale and 6.8% at 8,210 nodes compared with matched uniform node power capping.

presentations.title: Verification of PETSc with CIVL]{Verification of PETSc with CIVL using LLM-generated ACSL contracts and deterministic driver generation
presentations.abstract:
PETSc is widely used in science and engineering applications where wrong results can have costly consequences. Despite this, numerical libraries are rarely formally verified. One challenge
is the need for an expert to hand-write a specification and verification driver, which can introduce additional bugs. With modern large language models (LLMs), it is tempting to generate
drivers and reference models automatically, but one-shot generation is brittle and produces unverified code that must be audited. We present an approach that uses LLMs in a limited setting
to generate a small, human-certifiable ACSL contract from a function’s documentation. A deterministic toolchain supporting a restricted ACSL profile then generates a driver that uses CIVL to check the implementation against the contract. We demonstrate the pipeline end-to-end on three PETSc functions and discover a bug in MatAYPX.

presentations.title: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) in a Real, Geographically Distributed Environment Using the FABRIC Testbed
presentations.abstract: We study Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) in a real, geographically distributed environment using the FABRIC testbed. VFL enables organizations to collaboratively train machine-learning models without sharing their underlying datasets, making it a promising approach where data-sharing requirements, regulations, or organizational policies would otherwise hinder collaboration.

presentations.title: VisionHPC: AI Generation of Expert-Level HPC Codes From High-Level Mathematical Abstractions
presentations.abstract: We present VisionHPC, an agentic AI framework that generates expert-level high performance computing (HPC) code directly from high-level mathematical abstractions. Following extensive expert-guided training, it produces HPC implementations for multicore CPUs and GPUs using widely adopted parallel programming models, including OpenMP, OpenACC, and CUDA/HIP. The framework accepts images of mathematical formulations from three representative scientific domains — linear algebra, partial differential equations, and computational fluid dynamics — and translates them into efficient parallel code. Compared with state-of-the-art multimodal models, including ChatGPT, MathGPT, and Claude, VisionHPC achieves up to 12× higher correctness than the strongest baseline, reaching an average correctness exceeding 95%. These results demonstrate that AI can reliably bridge high-level mathematical descriptions and expert-quality HPC software, substantially improving productivity for scientific software development.

presentations.title: VisKnacks: Agentic ParaView Visualization on HPC
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence can assist in prototyping scientific visualizations. To assist visualization experts, we introduce VisKnacks, an autonomous ParaView visualization agent enabled by large language models (LLMs). VisKnacks integrates multi-agent orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and containerized rendering services for high performance computing (HPC) systems while remaining compatible with existing agent harnesses. The system supports hybrid workflows in which ParaView rendering is distributed to HPC resources while pipeline creation and iterative refinement remain local. We present the system overview, initial benchmarks, visualization quality benchmarks, and lessons learned from deploying this system.

presentations.title: VLIW Scheduling: Timing Is All You Need
presentations.abstract:
AMD's XDNA2 NPU packs 32 six-issue VLIW cores where the schedule must resolve nearly all pipeline hazards. Each core achieves 1,843 GFLOPS by always issuing a VMAC.F operation, an 8×8×8 block-floating-point (BFP16) matrix multiply-accumulate. This corresponds to an array-wide performance of 59 TFLOPS. One obstacle is register pressure: a standard double-buffered 2×2 output block needs eight accumulator registers, whereas a core has only five.

We present a hand-scheduled VLIW BFP16 tensor-contraction kernel that time-multiplexes the output block's four accumulation chains onto two registers and issues a VMAC.F in every steady-state cycle.

On one core with L1-resident data, our kernel achieves 96.4% of theoretical peak (5.0× faster than the compiled mm_bfp.cc kernel). With the operands streamed from DRAM, a pre-tiled M3840×N3840×K8192 matrix multiplication reaches 21.4 TFLOPS on the whole NPU.

At the poster, we will walk visitors through the VLIW scheduling diagrams and the scannable artifact reproducing every measurement.

presentations.title: Vortex Bubbles in Anabatic Upslope Flow During Morning Transition
presentations.abstract: Sea of bubbling vortices arising in upslope (anabatic) flow at a slope angle of eight degrees after sudden imposition of surface heat flux against a constant ambient stratification. This serves as a simplified model for the morning transition from nighttime downslope (katabatic) drainage to daytime upslope flow occurring during sunrise in valleys or mountains when solar radiation starts to heat up the sloped terrain, reversing the buoyancy and pressure gradients established during the cooler nocturnal conditions. Flow shown here is in an intermediate regime between laminar and fully turbulent.

presentations.title: Wafer Scale Acceleration of Unstructured Finite Element Methods
presentations.abstract: Finite element simulations on unstructured meshes require high performance and bandwidth to solve realistic problems. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE) represents a paradigm shift in large-scale compute acceleration, integrating 900,000 processing elements (PEs) on a single device. While prior work has demonstrated strong performance for structured stencils on the WSE, FEM on unstructured meshes remains largely unexplored, owing to the dissonance between its irregular connectivity patterns and the WSE's structured dataflow model. We present an architectural mapping that reconciles the disparate mesh structures of the target architecture and application. For the heat equation, we demonstrate near-ideal weak scaling up to the wafer scale and sub-linear cost with increasing per-PE workload, showing the architecture's advantages for structured stencils extend to irregular connectivity. We establish unstructured FEM as a workload that wafer-scale architectures can serve, and identify per-PE capacity, rather than irregularity, as the constraint that governs how far the approach extends.

presentations.title: Wafer-Scale Unstructured Scientific Computing
Watts Behind the Weights: Characterizing Energy Consumption of the AI Training Lifecycle in HPC
presentations.abstract: Modern AI training workloads have become a leading contributor to energy consumption in HPC infrastructures. Yet this consumption is treated as a monolithic block, attributed to execution alone. The training lifecycle includes preparation and post-execution stages, and execution itself comprises multiple phases whose energy consumption varies with the task, model, dataset, and infrastructure-related factors. This work closes this gap by characterizing energy consumption across the entire AI training lifecycle in HPC infrastructures, following a fine-grained approach that attributes energy to individual phases and events, rather than to training as a whole. We apply this methodology on a production supercomputer, assessing preparation and post-execution using distinct datasets and models, and characterizing execution over workloads with distinct resource requirements, namely the I/O-intensive ResNet-50 and the GPU-bound Qwen3-8B. We draw several lessons to help HPC users accurately attribute energy consumption across their workloads and make their training pipelines more energy-efficient.

presentations.title: Watts, FLOPs, and Impact: Rethinking Energy in the Exascale Era
presentations.abstract: Energy consumption has become a key constraint in high performance computing (HPC), shaping system design, procurement, software, and scientific workflows in the exascale era. As large-scale simulations and AI-driven workloads increase power demand, the community must reconsider how performance is measured, optimized, and reported beyond FLOPs alone. This BoF session will convene researchers, facility operators, vendors, and application scientists to discuss energy measurement, performance-per-watt metrics, efficient algorithms and runtimes, workload scheduling, and carbon-aware computing. The session will identify practical gaps, share lessons from production systems, and define community priorities for sustainable, energy-efficient HPC at scale.

presentations.title: Welcome to S-HPC 2026
presentations.abstract: Welcome to the fifth international workshop on Security in High Performence Computing. We will introduce the agenda for the day. We have six technical papers that range from security algorithms, security infrastructure in the age of AI, and how it applies to security applies to HPC/AI workflows.

presentations.title: What is Your Cluster Actually Doing? Understanding Users, Utilization, and Performance Through Extensive Slurm Job Data Analysis
presentations.abstract:
Most HPC clusters collect and save job accounting data that can offer insights into how the cluster is used. Many others have looked at this and other data, with particular results and insights. This study adds a novel approach, looking at job data through a four-way job classification, and then analyzing cluster utilization through this lens. Additionally, we infer some amount of application usage data, and infer parallel configurations being utilized by users.

Some important results, among others, of our analysis are: a large fraction of HPC usage is from single-node jobs; user provided job walltime limits are largely unrelated to actual job walltime; and parallelism configurations (inferred) seem to be a place for significant user training and improvement.

presentations.title: What Your Job Queue Isn’t Telling You: Workflow Monitoring with Drona
presentations.abstract: Scientific workloads on high performance computing (HPC) systems often involve multi-stage workflows beyond simple job submission. Existing tools provide limited monitoring, exposing primarily scheduler-level metadata and forcing users to piece together workflow progress, performance behavior, and domain-specific results through fragmented interfaces. A new and improved version of the Drona Workflow Engine addresses this gap by providing a schema-driven framework combined with a support library for constructing integrated job monitoring artifacts throughout the workflow lifecycle. This paper presents Drona’s monitoring architecture, based on dynamic elements, retriever functions, workflow abstractions, and a support library, enabling real-time observability and interactive job management during execution within a unified interface. We demonstrate Drona monitoring dashboards for various domain-specific workflows.

presentations.title: When Agents Break the Memory Hierarchy: Understanding Data Stalls in Agentic HPC Workflows
presentations.abstract: Scientific workflows use storage-memory hierarchies to manipulate exascale data without data loading stalls at feasible resource costs. These systems exploit the fact that traditional HPC workflows have deterministic access patterns. Agentic HPC workflows break this assumption, allowing AI agents to decide what will run next. We find that on a representative workflow, a state-of-the-art DMSH system increases wall time by 3.18x because data needs are learned too late for staging. We also find that 93% of artifact-loading time is representation transformation rather than byte transfer. The cost of transformation makes some representations nearly 65x more valuable to keep than others in terms of end-to-end workflow stall avoided. Models and transformed data also compete for host memory, making capacity value dependent on correctly predicting reuse timing through agent framework signals, and tuning memory management based on representation needs and hardware availability. These findings motivate memory management designed for agentic HPC workflows.

presentations.title: When More Cores Hurts: The Vector Database Scaling Paradox in HPC
presentations.abstract: Vector databases have been designed and optimized for cloud environments; however, emerging scientific AI workloads (e.g., molecular search, meteorological trajectory detection, and literature-driven hypothesis generation) demand efficient, scalable execution on HPC systems. We present a large-scale evaluation of three state-of-the-art vector databases — Qdrant, Milvus, and Weaviate — on two production supercomputers, scaling to 256 distributed workers across 64 compute nodes. We evaluate VDBs using Yandex-T2I, a multimodal embedding dataset, and Pes2o-VE, a novel real-world scientific dataset. Our results reveal that insertion is bottlenecked by per-batch consistency requirements, additional cores can reduce query throughput by up to 30.67%, and scaling from 16 to 256 workers yields a 2.67x improvement with 16 nodes before QPS begins to decline. This scaling paradox exposes the fundamental mismatch between cloud-oriented designs and HPC systems, highlighting the need for new, HPC-aware vector database designs.

presentations.title: Where Data Becomes Light: The Beauty of Scientific Visualization
presentations.abstract:
Where Data Becomes Light is a digital light projection and immersive visual experience that celebrates the beauty of science through contemporary visualization. On view nightly, Thursday through Sunday, at THE MART (artonthemart.com) September through mid-November, the large-scale imagery transforms the 2.5-acre building façade into a luminous canvas, where sweeping animations and vivid imagery inspire curiosity and wonder, and invite audiences to witness the elegance and complexity of the natural world through modern scientific computing.

Scientific discovery often begins with numbers, signals, and equations, but its deepest insights emerge when those patterns become visible. Scientific visualization transforms complex data into images that reveal structure, motion, and meaning, allowing us to see phenomena that would otherwise remain hidden. In these images, turbulence becomes choreography, molecular interactions resemble intricate architecture, and the evolution of galaxies unfolds like a vast celestial landscape.

Like Art of HPC, Where Data Becomes Light celebrates creativity and beauty in computational science. The projection includes several works from past SC Art of HPC exhibits and Scientific Visualization and Data Analytics Showcases, bringing the SC community's work to the city's skyline.

The Collaboration

For decades, researchers have used visualization to transform massive datasets into images that reveal patterns hidden in raw numbers. As high-performance computing has grown in prominence to address the biggest challenges in science and engineering, Argonne National Laboratory has played a key role in this evolution, operating world-class supercomputers and producing visualizations that illuminate everything from the structure of materials and the behavior of turbulent flows to the formation of galaxies and the dynamics of climate systems.

At the same time, the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois Chicago helped define the modern field of visualization. EVL researchers’ work contributed to the landmark National Science Foundation report on scientific visualization, which helped establish visualization as a critical component of scientific discovery. EVL’s innovations in immersive visualization environments and collaborative visual computing have expanded the ways scientists and the public experience complex data.

presentations.title: Who and What Is on Your Machine? Meeting the Coming Rules for Shared AI Compute Without Slowing the Science
presentations.abstract: HPC systems were built for trusted users. Today they run a variety of HPC and AI workloads, serve GPU-as-a-service customers they've never met, and face rising regulatory attention. NIST is finalizing SP 800-234, the first HPC-specific security overlay, and advanced compute is one of the few genuinely bipartisan topics in Washington. The rules are coming. The question is whether operators shape them or inherit them. This BoF brings standards authors, security architects, supercomputing operators, and implementers into a candid, practitioner-level exchange with the audience on what works, what fails, and how the community secures shared compute without slowing the science.

presentations.title: Who Benefits from Federation? Heterogeneous Gains in Cross-Operator Network Traffic Representation Learning
presentations.abstract: Research and education networks, regional ISPs, and campus networks hold telemetry worth modeling jointly, but non-disclosure agreements and privacy policy prevent pooling it. We evaluate federated representation learning on real telemetry from ten Internet2 backbone routers and ten CESNET3 academic institutions, with a commercial ISP held out as an unseen-network probe, comparing centralized, federated, and local-only training at equal budget across five seeds. Federation is statistically equivalent to centralized pooling (5% equivalence bound, p = 0.020), so the data-custody constraint costs nothing in representation quality. Its benefit is not uniform: backbone clients gain a median 9.2% reduction in reconstruction error, campus clients 1.9% (p = 0.0003), an effect robust to outlier removal and training-set size that tracks a difference in traffic regularity we characterize but do not isolate. Two manipulations of local optimization selectively suppress the backbone benefit, identifying local adaptation as the mechanism.

presentations.title: Who Shapes the Future of Public HPC? Planning, Priorities, and Investment in the Age of AI and Quantum Computing
presentations.abstract:
HPC infrastructures are being reshaped by rapid hardware innovation, pressure for greater energy efficiency, and the rise of AI and data-intensive workloads. Simultaneously, future directions are influenced not only by scientific communities and public research agendas, but also by industry roadmaps and emerging QC ambitions.

This BoF will examine how different countries plan future public HPC investments, how priorities are set, and who has influence in that process. The aim is to better understand whether public HPC remains community-driven or is increasingly shaped by industrial and market forces, and what this means for the future of research infrastructures.

presentations.title: Who You Gonna CALL? Static Whole-Program Call Graphs for Fortran
presentations.abstract: Fortran retains continued relevance in high-performance and scientific computing, yet its tooling ecosystem lags behind that of C and C++. Call graphs are a common foundation for analysis tools, and constructing them for modern Fortran requires resolving language features that elude simple source analysis. We present a static call-graph generator for Fortran implemented as a Flang plugin. Building on LLVM Flang's parse tree and semantic information, it produces whole-program call graphs from source code and resolves type-bound procedures, polymorphic dispatch, finalizers, operator overloading, generic interfaces, and C interoperability. We evaluate it on the production codes ICON, NEKO, and CP2K, and on the Fortran benchmarks of SPEChpc 2021, comparing against static LLVM-IR and dynamic Score-P call graphs. Across all applications, our analysis produces a reliable and detailed representation of procedures and call relationships. A case study demonstrates that the resulting graphs are well suited to guide instrumentation for performance analysis.

presentations.title: WHPC Career Pathways
presentations.abstract: Three women working in industry, national laboratories, and academia will share their career journeys and perspectives on navigating professional transitions, mentorship, challenges, and opportunities. This session offers practical insights for students and early-career professionals exploring diverse pathways in careers within HPC.

presentations.title: WHPC Closing Remarks
WHPC Distinguished Speaker: From Silent 700s to El Capitan: Mentors and Community Made All the Difference
