presentations.abstract:
The WHPC@SC26 workshop has a goal of fostering a diverse and inclusive HPC community. We welcome all attendees who align with our goals and want to support broader participation in the HPC workforce.

The WHPC workshop series has become the leading SC event focused on DEI topics. We aim to cultivate skills for valuing a diverse workforce and creating a welcoming environment for all. Following the workshop held at SC24, we have an increased emphasis on diversity and inclusion of all people from underrepresented groups.

WHPC@SC26 will focus on the following topics:
- Building community through real-time networking
- Improving diversity and inclusion for all in the HPC workforce
- Highlighting and supporting early-career researchers from underrepresented groups
- Building a deeper understanding of what diversity, equity, and inclusion means for different groups
- Learning from, and valuing, different experiences and career paths

presentations.title: Women-Led Technical Project Spotlights
presentations.abstract:
Three women technical leaders give 5-minute lightning talks on innovative projects, from open-source CFD and AI infrastructure scalability to AI for cancer surveillance:
→ One Code, Two Worlds: Building an Open-Source CFD Code in Collaboration with Industry — Michele Weiland (EPCC, UK)
→ Scalability Issues on AI Infrastructures — Isabel Schwerdtfeger (IBM, Germany)
→ Cancer Surveillance in the Age of AI — Sally R. Ellingson (University of Kentucky, USA)

presentations.title: Workflow-Level Scheduling of Hybrid Quantum-Classical Applications on Heterogeneous Resources
presentations.abstract: Hybrid quantum--classical applications involve coordinated execution of quantum and classical tasks across heterogeneous resources. We model such applications as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and formulate workflow scheduling as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that captures task dependencies, heterogeneous resource assignment, communication costs, makespan, and tardiness. To account for the the stochastic nature of QPU execution times, we additionally develop a robust counterpart based on budgeted uncertainty. The proposed framework enables workflow-level optimization beyond the performance of individual quantum or classical components. We evaluate the approach using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), illustrating how optimized scheduling can improve resource utilization and reduce end-to-end execution time in hybrid quantum--classical environments.

presentations.title: Workflows Community: Next-Generation Workflows for HPC — AI, Agentic Systems, and Scientific Discovery
presentations.abstract:
This BoF will convene the workflows community to discuss the challenges of next-generation scientific workflows. A central focus will be on how the role of the human changes as workflows become increasingly autonomous: where people remain in the loop, how they steer and validate agentic systems, and how our community can support workflow developers.

The session will bring together workflow users, developers, theorists, and industrial collaborators, highlighting emerging research directions and practical needs from scientific campaigns. Through interactive discussions, participants will explore collaborative strategies to enable resilient, scalable, and adaptive workflows that meet the evolving demands of scientific discovery.

presentations.title: Workload-Derived Requirements for Reconfigurable AI/HPC Fabrics
presentations.abstract: Rack scale AI and HPC systems combine accelerators with high bandwidth fabrics but often impose fixed resource ratios and communication domains. We evaluate eleven applications and two bounds across training, inference, molecular dynamics, linear algebra, and graph analytics while varying host resources, accelerator count, and connectivity. Fabric sensitivity differs sharply. Disabling peer to peer communication reduces all to all bandwidth by 36.1× and all reduce by 16.3×; HPL fails to initialize and training slows 2.23×, while GPU HPCG and DeepDriveMD are unaffected. These results motivate software composition for resource changes and live optical reconfiguration for connectivity changes without destroying state. Our prototype matches native bandwidth, but state reconstruction adds substantial delay. Dynamic composition surpasses static goodput near 72 second idle windows and reaches 1.34× at 160 seconds. Reconfigurable fabrics therefore require topology, opportunity duration, predictability, and state preservation.

presentations.title: Workload-Manager-Agnostic QPU Integration with QRMI
presentations.abstract: Integrating quantum resources into HPC workflows is complicated by two layers of fragmentation: quantum hardware vendors expose incompatible APIs, and HPC centers run diverse job schedulers. The Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI), an open-source project developed by a growing community of 15 national laboratories, institutions, and quantum vendors, resolves both problems by exposing quantum resources as first-class schedulable resources alongside CPUs and GPUs, independent of vendor or scheduler. This hands-on, three-hour tutorial targets HPC engineers and administrators, and gives quantum vendors concrete motivation: implement QRMI once, and your backend becomes accessible from any scheduler. The tutorial spans three modules covering today's HPC scheduling landscape: traditional batch schedulers, where attendees choose one of Slurm, PBS, IBM LSF, or Open Cluster Scheduler for hands-on exercises; Kubernetes, increasingly adopted for AI workloads; and the Flux Framework, a graph-based scheduler for next-generation HPC systems. In each module, participants submit real QRMI-managed jobs targeting cloud quantum resources from providers such as IBM, Pasqal, and Alice & Bob. Attendees will leave having experienced firsthand how QRMI integrates with their own workload manager to deliver quantum workloads to HPC users, giving them a concrete starting point for building quantum-ready HPC infrastructure today.

presentations.title: Workshop on High Performance Fabrics for AI and HPC
presentations.abstract: As computing demands surge for AI and HPC applications, networking becomes essential for performance and scaling. AI and HPC fabrics are used in scale-up and scale-out communications. This workshop will cover innovations in AI/HPC fabric architecture, network transport, load balancing, congestion control, network resilience, and network visibility. The workshop will further focus on Ethernet technologies for AI and HPC including Scale-Up Ethernet Transport (SUE-T), Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN), Ultra Ethernet, advanced congestion control, lossless transport mechanisms, telemetry, and fabric management.

presentations.title: Workshop on Operational Data Analytics in HPC (HPC-ODA)
presentations.abstract:
Operational data analytics (ODA) provides unique opportunities to analyze, understand, and optimize HPC operations. Readily available open-source frameworks make the collection of telemetry from different operational domains of HPC increasingly easy. However, analyzing the data, extracting actionable knowledge from it, and leveraging it to optimize HPC operations is challenging. While most HPC sites have sophisticated monitoring capabilities in place, their analysis capabilities often do not go beyond visual inspection by humans via dashboards or static thresholds for alarms. Few early adopter sites have pioneered advanced usage of data, but its wider adoption will depend on success stories and the availability of analysis tools and models.

This workshop will bring together HPC users, practitioners in HPC operations, monitoring experts, and data analytics researchers to share experiences, discuss state-of-the-art research, and foster collaboration. It will solicit papers with concrete, reproducible, and empirical data gathered through case studies, research for practice, and surveys.

presentations.title: Wrap-up and Closing Remarks
Wrap-Up and Conclusion
XLOOP 2026: The 8th Annual Workshop on Extreme-Scale Experiment-in-the-Loop Computing
presentations.abstract: Advancement in computational power and high-speed networking is enabling a new model of scientific experiment, experiment-in-the-loop computing (EILC). In this model, simulation and/or learning modules are run as data is collected from observational and experimental sources. Presently, the amount and complexity of data generated by simulations and by observational and experimental sources, such as sensor networks and large-scale scientific facilities, continues to increase. Several research challenges exist, many of which are independent of the scientific application domain. New algorithms, including artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms, to merge simulation ensembles and experimental data sets must be developed. Data transfer techniques and workflows must be constructed to control the ensembles and integrate simulated and observed data sets. The Workshop on Extreme-Scale Experiment-in-the-Loop Computing (XLOOP 2026) will be a unique opportunity to promote this interdisciplinary topic area. We invite papers, presentations, and participants from the physical and computer sciences.

presentations.title: You Only Have Seven Seconds
presentations.abstract:
You Only Have Seven Seconds is a poetic, human–AI collaborative documentary that unfolds as both a visual archive of an internationally exhibited installation and a cinematic experiment in memory preservation. Against the backdrop of rising Alzheimer’s cases and the emergence of machine-generated false memories, the film reimagines remembrance through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Inspired by her grandmother’s cognitive decline, the artist developed a custom AI system that transforms fragmented spoken recollections into synthetic visual sequences. Presented as an interactive AI art installation, the project ReCollection has traveled worldwide, welcoming thousands of visitors to whisper their fading memories — each within seven seconds — into the artwork and generate visual memories in real time. These memories form the foundation of an evolving archive, constructed through speech recognition, text auto-completion, and text-to-image generation.

Drawing from this archive, the film incorporates emerging speech-to-video technology to weave a collective, culturally diverse montage of love and loss. The participatory datasets are curated to build dialogical relationships, forming patterns, counterpoints, and resonances that evoke a poetics of relation. Initially conceived as a personal reflection, the work has evolved into a living, breathing, shared world-building experience that reassembles the ephemeral past into a dynamic portrait of collective human selfhood.

presentations.title: Zero-Overhead Polymorphism on GPGPUs with LLVM Just-in-Time Compilation
presentations.abstract: An ahead-of-time compiler's ability to optimize strongly affects the runtime performance of an application, yet limited knowledge of runtime parameters restricts which optimizations it can apply. Just-in-time compilers can make more informed optimization decisions, but have seen limited adoption in high-performance computing due to build toolchain requirements and programming language restrictions. In this work, we use LLVM as a just-in-time compiler that can be tightly integrated into any application. We automatically specialize compute kernels by inspecting LLVM's intermediate representation to find simple loop-invariant conditionals, which we remove, and virtual function calls, which we inline. This suits C++ lambda functions better than previous work, which requires explicit annotation. We apply this method to a multiphysics simulation package that runs on general-purpose graphics processing units. This reduces iteration time by up to 35% by significantly simplifying control flow complexity of the compiled kernels and improves developer productivity through lower build times.

presentations.title: Towards Scalable and Efficient Deep Learning: Structured Optimization Across Training and Fine-Tuning
presentations.abstract:
Modern deep learning systems must balance optimization quality against computation, memory, communication, and reliability constraints, whose relative importance varies across supercomputing architectures. This dissertation develops controlled relaxation as a structured optimization strategy: preserve information essential to learning while relaxing costly requirements in synchronization, curvature representation, and parameterization.

The thesis develops this principle through three contributions. AD-KFAC relaxes global synchronization in distributed second-order optimization while retaining curvature information in asynchronous, versioned, and recoverable state. BD-KFAC replaces dense curvature representations with block-diagonal structure, exposing a controllable trade-off between statistical fidelity and resource cost. RRLoRA relaxes the requirement for an uninterrupted low-rank optimization trajectory by periodically refactorizing the learned update and restarting the learning-rate schedule, allowing the parameterization to evolve without discarding accumulated information.

Together, these methods address complementary bottlenecks in distributed second-order training, resource-efficient curvature estimation, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning while preserving the optimization structure that makes each approach effective. The results support controlled relaxation as a systems-aware design principle: preserve signal-carrying structure, relax constraints that impose disproportionate system cost, and keep the resulting approximation or asynchronous state observable and recoverable. This principle offers a practical framework for designing efficient and reliable machine-learning systems on large-scale supercomputing platforms.

presentations.title: Finite-Element Methods and Exascale Algorithms for Fully Relativistic Noncollinear Pseudopotential Density Functional Theory: From Mathematical Formulations to Efficient Computational Realization and Magnetic Materials Applications
presentations.abstract:
Fully relativistic noncollinear density functional theory (DFT) is essential for simulating spintronic and topological materials but costs 12–30 times more than unpolarized DFT, largely because each electron state becomes a two-component spinor. This cost is dominated by a sparse Hermitian eigenproblem with ~10^8 unknowns and ~10^5 eigenvectors, re-solved every self-consistent-field iteration in complex arithmetic. This thesis co-designs finite-element discretizations, eigensolvers, and GPU implementations within the open-source DFT-FE code.

The central contribution is residual-based Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration (R-ChFSI), which reformulates the Chebyshev recurrence around the residual so that errors from inexact operations shrink with it. Whereas standard Chebyshev filtering stalls, R-ChFSI converges to residuals of 10^-8 with approximate overlap-matrix inverses and FP32/TF32 arithmetic, making reduced precision and compressed communication safe. On Aurora, combining TF32 filtering with 10–12-bit block-floating-point compression of point-to-point messages accelerates filtering by up to 3.5x and the full ground-state solve by 2.27x over FP64, changing the energy by 1.3x10^-10 Ha/atom.

Band parallelization sustains 94% filtering efficiency when strong-scaling an 11,468-electron system to 384 nodes, and calculations reach 78,988 electrons on 800 Aurora nodes. On CPUs, DFT-FE achieves 8x–10x lower minimum wall time than Quantum ESPRESSO at equal accuracy, and GPU runs need 40x–70x fewer node-hours than CPU runs. The thesis also derives consistent forces and stresses and introduces adaptive-coordinate meshes that reduce energy errors up to 28x at fixed degrees of freedom. These capabilities enable a novel study of how vacancies reshape magnetism in the two-dimensional magnet Fe3GeTe2.

presentations.title: Embrace the Chaos: Harnessing Variability in Accelerator-Rich Systems
presentations.abstract:
HPC and ML workload scaling have led supercomputers to deploy large, heterogeneous systems with extreme power limits. Current GPU thermal design power limits (TDPs) range from 1,400–2,000W, scaling to extreme power budgets at scale. Thus, power has displaced performance as the dominant constraint. My research addresses this challenge by co-optimizing power and performance at scale through cross-stack approaches spanning hardware, firmware, systems, and applications.

Power management (PM) causes performance variation across accelerators, making it hard for users to get repeatable performance and for administrators to balance resource utilization. I was the first to characterize GPU variability across production clusters, uncovering consistent variability. This work guided MLCommons' benchmarking effort on handling variability. To harness this variability, I developed PAL, a cluster scheduler that leverages application-specific variability during job placement to optimize latencies and resource utilization.

Further investigating PM, we found GPU power often spikes above TDP (temporarily), triggering frequency throttling that hurts performance. I investigated these power excursions, especially frequent in compute-intensive workloads, and developed solutions that reduce excursions and improve latency.

As workloads rapidly evolve, new workloads often show different excursion characteristics as well as power/performance variability. To adapt our solutions to new, unseen workloads, I developed Minos, which groups similar workloads using power and utilization characteristics while reducing profiling overheads.

Overall, my research demonstrates the critical impact of excursions and GPU variability on large-scale systems. As power constraints intensify and hardware limits are pushed, this cross-stack co-design offers essential techniques to improve power-constrained supercomputing in the future.

presentations.title: Near-Real-Time Performance Visualization of MPI Applications: Integrating Performance Analysis Into HPC Education
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing (HPC) has become an essential capability in both industrial practice and scientific research, making the acquisition of practical HPC skills an increasingly important objective in higher education. Parallel programming with models such as MPI and OpenMP is central to this training, and students should gain experience on real HPC clusters rather than on local machines. However, universities often have access only to limited, partitioned, or decommissioned cluster resources, while learners must also master operational concepts such as SSH, SCP, and batch-based job management with systems such as SLURM. In addition, efficient MPI programs require performance analysis, yet established tools are designed for experts and assume prior knowledge of instrumentation, measurement, and interpretation.

EduMPI Suite addresses this gap by providing an educational environment for executing and analyzing MPI programs on HPC clusters in near-real-time. It automatically delivers visual feedback on MPI communication events during execution, enabling students to observe program behavior and understand the performance characteristics. A distinctive feature is the visualization of internal algorithmic communication patterns of collective operations, which are often hidden in professional tools but are crucial for understanding the performance implications of collective communication.

Usability evaluations over multiple semesters show that EduMPI Suite lowers the barriers to practical HPC performance analysis, is recommended by students, and improves the success rate of identifying and explaining performance problems to 96%, compared with 60% for professional analysis tools. Its near-real-time performance analysis is enabled by low measurement overhead <3.8% and low query latency <0.09 s.

presentations.title: Towards Resource-Efficient Parallel Concept Drift Detection in Data Streams
presentations.abstract:
Modern data science increasingly outpaces the efficient use of parallel hardware, creating a need for computational performance engineering. Because HPC tools are not embedded in exploratory data science environments, data scientists lack support for such investigations. This PhD project therefore bridges HPC and data science, using concept drift detection as a case study.

Concept drift—the change in data distributions after ML model deployment—must be detected to ensure robust streaming ML systems. However, the computational overhead of drift detectors (DDs) remains underexplored, even though directly affecting latency, energy consumption, and deployability. This gap motivates the thesis contributions.

First, a framework is introduced for systematically investigating the computational performance of DDs, including complexity analysis, benchmarking and performance analysis. Second, building on this framework, a survey and benchmark evaluate DDs bi-objectively, measuring both runtime and accuracy. The results reveal that computational performance is treated as secondary in the literature, no single detector dominates across scenarios, and higher accuracy consistently requires longer runtimes. Simultaneously, timely drift detection can reduce pipeline runtime by avoiding unnecessary model updates. Third, performance analysis identifies bottlenecks in state-of-the-art DD implementations, particularly inefficient BLAS and OpenMP usage in streaming scenarios. Consequently, the thesis presents MoPEDDs, a modular parallel ensemble of DDs that exploits unused parallel resources improving detection with negligible runtime overhead.

Finally, because performance engineering remains complex for most data scientists, the thesis introduces JUmPER (Jupyter meets Performance). It embeds performance engineering into Jupyter through coarse- and fine-grained monitoring, making HPC expertise accessible where data science happens.

presentations.title: Machine Learning-Based Multi-Objective Optimization for HPC Workload Scheduling
presentations.abstract: As high-performance computing (HPC) systems reach exascale, schedulers that optimize a single objective, typically throughput, prove inadequate for facilities that must simultaneously manage performance, energy consumption, and resilience under substantial workload uncertainty. This dissertation develops and empirically validates a three-component multi-objective scheduling framework built on graph neural networks (GNNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), testing the hypothesis that graph-structured representations of jobs and system state, combined with adaptive multi-objective learning, outperform traditional and single-objective learned schedulers in production HPC environments. The framework comprises (1) GNN-RL, a graph attention network and PPO-based scheduler encoding job dependencies and resource contention; (2) HARMONIC, a Bayesian uncertainty-aware optimizer that separates aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty and balances performance, energy, and resilience via a multi-objective DDPG agent with Pareto-front guarantees; and (3) EA-GATSched, a GATv2-based scheduler driven by a GEOPM-calibrated physics power model and a state-conditioned Pareto-weighting network. GNN-RL and HARMONIC evaluations are complete: GNN-RL improves utilization by 13.8%–20.2% and throughput by 15.0%–50.0% over EASY-backfilling across 377,234 production jobs on three ALCF systems; HARMONIC reduces energy by 10%–19%, improves throughput by 16%–25%, and cuts performance variability by 18%–32% across simulation and a 64-node testbed. EA-GATSched, the framework's in-progress third component, has achieved 27.3%–56.6% energy reduction and up to 95.8% utilization across 389,604 jobs on the same three systems, with cross-architecture GEOPM validation remaining as future work. These two studies draw on overlapping, not additive, job sets from the same ALCF systems and together establish relational, uncertainty-aware, and physics-grounded learning as jointly necessary for sustainable exascale HPC scheduling.

presentations.title: Real-Time High-Fidelity Bayesian Inference and Forecasting of Tsunamis: A Digital Twin for Tsunami Early Warning Applied to the Cascadia Subduction Zone
presentations.abstract:
Tsunamis resulting from megathrust earthquakes are rare events that can cause devastating socioeconomic damage and loss of life. State-of-the-art early-warning systems rely on simplified physics models that can be inaccurate for near-field predictions, leading to delayed, missed, or false warnings. Tsunami propagation codes typically use shallow-water equations, which omit coupled ocean-acoustic and surface-gravity wave dynamics, while high-fidelity hydrodynamics codes are too computationally expensive for real-time use. My doctoral research develops a digital twin framework for tsunami early warning that incorporates high-fidelity physics, uses Bayesian data assimilation, and leverages GPU-oriented algorithms to enable accurate, real-time forecasts with rigorously quantified uncertainties for the Cascadia Subduction Zone.

The computational advance is an offline–online decomposition exploiting time-shift invariance in the parameter-to-observable and parameter-to-prediction maps. Their block-triangular Toeplitz structure enables fast Fourier transform-based matrix-vector products, delivering approximately one-hundred-thousand-fold speedups over repeated partial differential equation solves. The Bayesian inverse problem is reformulated in the smaller observation space using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, enabling offline factorization and real-time inference.

For a margin-wide Cascadia rupture with 600 hypothetical pressure sensors, the method infers more than one billion parameters and predicts wave heights at 21 locations in under 0.2 seconds on 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, a ten-billion-fold speedup over state-of-the-art methods—a breakthrough recognized with the 2025 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The framework also enables scalable Bayesian optimal experimental design by recasting sensor placement as dense matrix subset selection to minimize uncertainty in inferred seafloor motion or wave-height forecasts. This digital twin paves the way toward accurate, uncertainty-aware tsunami forecasts worldwide.

presentations.title: Subgraph Counting: Methods, Frameworks, and Applications
presentations.abstract:
Subgraph counting and matching are core primitives in network analysis, underpinning applications from computational biology to fraud detection to performance analysis in HPC. Existing methods assume static, small networks, rely on hardware-specific kernels that do not scale across the accelerator ecosystem, and emphasize counting over the harder problem of locating pattern instances. This dissertation addresses all three.

We develop ParaDyMS, a parallel method for counting all motifs of size k ≤ 5 on fully dynamic networks under batched edge insertions and deletions. Rather than recomputing from scratch, ParaDyMS updates motif counts incrementally using only the delta induced by a batch of changes. Implemented in the Kokkos C++ Performance Portability ecosystem, ParaDyMS targets both OpenMP and CUDA from one source, achieving up to 124× speedup over the state-of-the-art static method and outperforming 112 CPU cores with a single GPU.

To address hardware portability, we present PyGB-LAPIS, a compilation pipeline lowering graph algorithms written in Python-GraphBLAS through MLIR and the LAPIS backend into Kokkos-flavored C++. PyGB-LAPIS generates kernels across five sparse storage formats and multiple hardware backends from one source, matching hand-written Kokkos performance while eliminating per-backend engineering effort.

Finally, we develop an exact subgraph matching method that decomposes query and host graphs into size-4 graphlets and searches a compressed graphlet-overlap representation. This supports arbitrary-size queries and, uniquely, resolves multiple simultaneous queries in one pass through a shared search tree rather than restarting per query, with the union graph traversed on the fly and pruned by graphlet frequency to control its size.

presentations.title: Efficient Representation Learning for Heterogeneous Systems and Continual Task Adaptation
presentations.abstract:
This dissertation addresses two fundamental challenges in distributed machine learning: client heterogeneity and continual adaptation to new tasks. It develops efficient fine-tuning and representation-learning frameworks that let distributed models acquire new knowledge and align it across clients without communication bottlenecks or catastrophic forgetting.

First, we introduce a dual-distilled federated learning framework for clients with heterogeneous systems and data. Trainable global prototypes with adaptive margins align local representations and logits without requiring a shared model architecture, enabling robust knowledge transfer and stable convergence.

Next, we propose a communication-efficient federated framework for large language models (LLMs) based on representation fine-tuning. By intervening on hidden states rather than weights, and combining All-But-Me aggregation with dynamic test-time computing, it reduces communication cost while balancing local personalization and global generalization.

We then present SETA, a mixture of sparse experts for task-agnostic continual learning in LLMs. SETA resolves the plasticity–stability dilemma by structurally decomposing the parameter space into shared and task-specific experts, protecting shared knowledge from semantic drift while preserving task-specific features.

Finally, we introduce FedSEAM, which extends sparse experts to federated continual learning. Clients learn experts on private task streams, and the server merges them through subspace agreement: it combines only the update directions clients share, keeps disagreeing directions as client-private experts, and protects prior-task subspaces from being overwritten.

Together, these contributions chart a path toward scalable, resource-aware machine learning systems that bridge decentralized efficiency and continual real-world deployment, learning new tasks across privacy-constrained environments without forgetting.

presentations.title: Genome Variant Representation in Genome LMs and Multi-Omic AI: Efficiency, Scalability, and Medical Actionability
presentations.abstract:
The recent rapid growth and curation of large multi-omic datasets, driven largely by high-throughput sequencing, have provided unprecedented opportunities in medical and clinical research, especially for precision medicine. This presents an opportunity for improved multi-omic deep learning implementations for oncology tasks. However, it comes with a set of challenges, namely:

1. Granularity in genomic variant representation: representing complex, arbitrary-length genomic variant data without destroying spatial context or non-coding regulatory signals in both standalone and multi-omic models

2. Scalability and efficiency: establishing efficient and domain-informed data loading strategies, hyperparameter optimization guidelines and computationally scalable architectural choices, especially for resource-intensive medical applications

3. Systematized multi-omic integration: How can we rigorously evaluate multi-omics integration strategies and assess which combinations of omics modalities yield the most informative biological representations for oncology tasks?

To address these issues, we have made the following contributions. First, we developed a feasibility study into the representation of genomic variant data, leveraging genome language models (gLMs) to capture nucleotide-level dependencies across variable-length somatic variant-associated sequences for pan-cancer classification and survival analysis. Next, we scaled our framework to combine both coding exomes and non-coding regions by implementing input load balancing and architectural changes, improving performance on chosen oncology tasks. Finally, we introduced a generalized, versatile, and modular framework that incorporates key autoencoder architectures for representation learning, enabling exploration and robust evaluation of multi-modal omics integration.

The cumulative findings bridge hardware-efficient scaling, biological representation learning, and cancer-specific multi-omics to drive medical actionability.

presentations.title: Foundation Models for Discovery and Exploration in Chemical Space
presentations.abstract:
Accurate, rapid prediction of molecular properties remains a bottleneck in materials innovation because experiments and conventional simulations are too costly to explore vast, high-dimensional chemical spaces. Scalable and interpretable molecular foundation models can accelerate discovery across chemical space while using computational resources efficiently. We demonstrate this with MIST, a family of molecular foundation models trained with up to an order of magnitude more data and parameters than prior work. To train MIST we developed Smirk, a tokenizer which preserves nuclear, electronic, and geometric information, enabling representation learning across chemical systems.

The largest MIST model has 1.8B parameters and was trained on 2B molecules. Training such a large model is an expensive endeavor. To make model development tractable on an academic compute budget we developed hyperparameter-penalized neural scaling laws which guided identification of compute-optimal model configurations without exhaustive sweeps at every scale, reducing model-development cost by an order of magnitude.

MIST models have been fine-tuned to predict over 400 structure–property relationships spanning domains from psychophysics to electrochemistry. They demonstrate state-of-the-art benchmark performance and enable real-world applications including stereochemical reasoning for organometallics, olfactory perception mapping, and electrolyte formulation design.

Beyond raw predictive accuracy, using mechanistic-interpretability methods we determine MIST learns chemically meaningful concepts during training. Analysis of token vectors, low-dimensional embedding projections and model logits reveals concept-aligned structures not explicitly labeled during training.

Together, these contributions connect molecular representation learning, compute-optimal scaling, and broad scientific validation, establishing scientific foundation models as robust tools for materials discovery and optimization.

presentations.title: Hardware-Aware Matrix-Free Algorithms for Accelerating Large-Scale Finite-Element Simulations on Distributed CPU and GPU Architectures
presentations.abstract:
Large-scale simulations governed by partial differential equations reduce, after finite-element (FE) discretization, to two kernels: operator action on large blocks of vectors inside eigensolvers, and the solution of Poisson or Helmholtz systems inside linear solvers. Both are limited by data movement rather than floating-point throughput, and the traditional assembled sparse-matrix and cell-matrix strategies scale poorly at high polynomial order, the first bound by memory traffic, the second by an operation count that grows as the sixth power of the order.

This dissertation develops hardware-aware matrix-free algorithms that evaluate operator actions on the fly through sum factorization, batched over the multivector dimension. The contributions are batched FE Helmholtz matrix-multivector products, using even-odd decomposition and SIMD vectorization on CPUs and fused register-blocked kernels on GPUs, a matrix-free Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonian action covering nonlocal projectors, real and complex arithmetic and inline constraint handling on AVX2/AVX-512/SVE CPUs and on GPUs with tensor cores and reduced-precision ghost exchange, a distributed-memory GPU fast-diagonalization solver that inverts the FE Laplacian exactly at O(N^(4/3)) FLOPs, and a device-native fused conjugate-gradient solver with a Chebyshev-Jacobi p-multigrid preconditioner.

Measured inside DFT-FE against existing baselines on Summit, Frontier, Fugaku, Polaris, Pravega and Aurora, the operator actions run 2.6x–5.8x faster than cell-matrix. The fused solve runs 5.86x faster than deal.II on 384 Aurora GPUs, and p-multigrid holds it at 5–7 iterations across polynomial orders. On tensor-product meshes one exact solve is 34x–3,186x faster than p-multigrid. The algorithms assume nothing specific to DFT and carry over to higher-order FE applications.

presentations.title: One-Sided: A Portrait of the New OpenSHMEM Standard
presentations.abstract:
In MPI, every memory transfer requires negotiation. The sender announces. The receiver posts a matching receive. Both wait. This is the contract at the heart of parallel communication — and this visualization begins there, in the weight of it: 256 processing elements, bilateral arcs crossing in every direction, a single REQUEST suspended at its target with no response coming.

Then the model changes.

OpenSHMEM eliminates the contract. Any process can write directly into any other's memory. No handshake. No prior agreement. The target is simply — a destination.

This 90-second visualization is a portrait of that principle, built entirely from real benchmark data captured on an HPE internal research cluster: four nodes, 256 processing elements, HPE Slingshot fabric.

The visual language is built around directionality. 256 PEs are arranged in four organic galaxy clusters — Realms α, β, γ, δ, 64 PEs each — with arcs cycling through one source cluster at a time so the viewer can track individual operations to their specific destinations, not interpret a global blur. Periodic spotlights isolate single PE-to-PE operations. The contrast with the MPI opening is deliberate and exact.

The data behind the animation is 500,000 real GUPS operations — Giga Updates Per Second, a standard benchmark for irregular remote atomic writes — captured live on the HPE Slingshot fabric. Each arc is a real operation. The pattern it makes is not designed; it is measured.

The closing act shows the full system in motion, with the GUPS source code, an operation counter climbing to 500,000, and the key argument: this workload cannot be handled without a global synchronization barrier in MPI — a cost that scales with every PE added. In OpenSHMEM, it just runs.

presentations.title: Fatal Attraction
presentations.abstract:
Supermassive black holes are among the largest objects in the Universe. Their masses range from at least one hundred thousand to many billions of times that of our Sun. In a tidal disruption event, a star is captured by the black hole’s gravitational field.

This artwork illustrates the different phases of destruction of a star by the tidal field of a supermassive black hole.

The right panel combines multiple instants of times highlighting the enormous stretch incurred by the star as it is pulled back toward the black hole.

The left panel shows the star after its first orbit around the black hole. The star is then subsequently destroyed when colliding with its own accretion stream.

presentations.title: Portrait of Data Center
presentations.abstract:
A supercomputer has vital signs: a temperature, a metabolism, and a heartbeat. This piece paints them. Streaming GPU telemetry (utilization, power draw, temperature, and interconnect traffic) drives a generative flow field: thousands of particles drift and glow, each colored by heat, brightened by power, their speed set by how hard the machine is thinking. Nothing is invented; every gesture is a reading of the machine's own body.

The work is deliberately multi-dimensional. One dimension is data, which is the honest mapping of live signals to light. Another is choreography, drawn from Martha Graham's foundational language of modern dance: contraction and release. Graham built movement from the body's core, a gathering inward that coils tension, then an expansive release outward. Here the machine's heartbeat performs exactly that: on each slow breath the particles are drawn toward the core, gathering; then, on the release, they are expelled outward in a bloom of light and sparks, timed to the pulse. As load climbs from idle to peak, the breath deepens and the release becomes a throw. A supercomputer that is moving through its own register, from rest to full, dramatic exertion.

The third dimension is metaphor: the data center as a living, feeling body, its telemetry the score to which it dances. By borrowing Graham's grammar of gather-and-expel, the piece asks the audience to read a machine not as cold infrastructure but as a performer; one whose choreography is authored not by a human hand but by the physics of computation itself. High performance computing, rendered as contemporary dance.

presentations.title: 2011 Tōhoku–Oki Earthquake and Tsunami: Dynamic Rupture and Acoustic–Gravity Simulations
presentations.abstract: This video visualizes data obtained from large-scale earthquake and tsunami simulations based on a dynamic rupture model of the 2011 Tōhoku–Oki earthquake, a magnitude 9.1 megathrust earthquake in the Japan Trench that caused over 20,000 deaths and $300B in damages. The 3D dynamic rupture simulation (Wong et al., Nature Communications, 2026) computes the seismic wave propagation in the Earth, generating the earthquake-induced seafloor motion that is visualized by the seafloor velocity and seafloor displacement fields in the video. These seafloor motion data are used as an input to a 3D acoustic–gravity simulation that computes the coupled ocean acoustic and tsunami wave propagation, which is visualized by the sea bottom pressure and surface wave height perturbations. The implementation of these earthquake and tsunami models is an integral part of an ongoing effort to develop a digital twin for tsunami early warning in the Japan Trench. This work is an extension of the Cascadia Subduction Zone digital twin that was recognized with the ACM Gordon Bell Prize at SC25 (Henneking et al., SC25 Proceedings, 2025).

presentations.title: An Exascale Universe in Warm and Cool
presentations.abstract:
This image opens onto a world that feels at once immense and intimate: a turbulent landscape constructed from data generated by one of the largest cosmology simulations run on exascale supercomputers. Vast orange forms move across the frame like heated clouds, molten currents, or a weather system caught mid-motion. Cooler blue structures gather around and beneath them, forming translucent streams and pockets that suggest an opposing climate. Their overlap turns temperature into a visual conversation — warm and cool masses pressing together, passing through one another, and creating a layered terrain with no familiar ground or horizon.

The orange and blue bodies are isosurfaces extracted from temperature data: boundaries that give form to conditions that cannot ordinarily be seen. Their fine wireframe skins deliberately retain the visual language of early computer graphics. Rather than conceal the construction of the image behind smooth, seamless surfaces, the mesh makes the digital scaffold visible. It recalls the moment when computer-generated worlds announced themselves through grids, polygons, and luminous lines — an artificial landscape honest about the machinery that makes it possible.

Across this shifting terrain, small magenta, violet, and pale spheres drift like beads, sparks, or distant lights. Each represents an element from the simulation and can stand for an extraordinary amount of matter — many solar masses compressed into a point of visual scale. Individually, they appear delicate; collectively, they trace a crowded and intricate environment.

By combining translucent temperature forms, deliberately exposed polygonal meshes, and floating matter, the work lets computational data become a place to linger. It invites the viewer to move between recognition and uncertainty: to see clouds, currents, constellations, and cellular structures, while remembering that the landscape is entirely constructed from a numerical model. The result is an artificial world with its own texture, atmosphere, and visual history — an image where calculation becomes environment.

presentations.title: JASMIN in July (Per Day): Brownian Bouquet
presentations.abstract:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Brownian Bouquet, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one day in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Stochastic Sea (which instead plots one spindle for one hour), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case a bouquet of flowers. The flower-like nature is encouraged by coercing the spindle centers into a sunflower-inspired pattern.

Brownian Bouquet invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

presentations.title: Entropy on the Edge of Collapse
presentations.abstract: This is a dynamical rendering of a detailed three-dimensional simulation of the explosion of the very-rapidly rotating core of a massive star that is exploding as a supernova. Rapid rotation leads to a powerful jet-like explosion along the two poles, accompanied by the generation and tangling of strong magnetic fields. This movie depicts the earliest phases of the supernova explosion that is simultaneously giving birth to a rapidly rotating radio pulsar.

presentations.title: Oil on Canvas: Galactic Center on Palette
presentations.abstract:
My painting (Oil on Canvas) translates a radio-astronomy observation of our galaxy's heart into a dusky, nebular atmosphere, its aubergine and violet field that surrounds the Milky Way's core.

The source of my interpretation of the galactic center stemmed from discussions with Prof. Florina Ciorba from the University of Basel (UniBas), Switzerland, who is the co-founder member and PI of the UniBas node of the SKACH project — The SKA (Square Kilometre Array) of Switzerland Consortium (SKACH, https://skach.org/about-skach/). The underlying data comes from the 1.28 GHz MeerKAT galactic center mosaic created by Heywood et al. (2022), released by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO). The image that inspired me and my painting is a re-rendered version by J.C. Muñoz-Mateos and branded by SKACH (the Swiss SKA Consortium) and SKAO (the Square Kilometre Array Observatory).

https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/milky-way-center-meerkat-and-webb/

presentations.title: Simulation of Tungsten Transport in the ASDEX-U Tokamak Plasma
presentations.abstract: Simulation of tungsten transport in the ASDEX-U tokamak plasma reveals critical insights for fusion reactor design. Tungsten, used for its heat resistance, ionizes during operation and can penetrate the core, radiating energy and reducing efficiency. These simulations explore the interaction of tungsten ions with rotation and light impurities like boron and helium in the complex edge region near the wall. The study highlights the role of binary collisions and asymmetries in tungsten penetration. Confidence in the model is bolstered by recent validation on a separate physics problem.

presentations.title: Open Polarity
presentations.abstract: This image depicts the 3D structure of the Sun's open coronal magnetic field from a snapshot of the “Live Prediction” HPC simulation developed by Predictive Science Inc. as part of their research for the August 12, 2026, total solar eclipse. See eclipse.predsci.com for more details on the simulation, which was created using the Magnetohydrodynamic Algorithm outside a Sphere Fortran code (github.com/predsci/mas) at a resolution of over 50 million cells. It ran faster than real time using 24 128-core EPYC Turin 9745 CPUs (3,072 total cores) on NASA's Athena supercomputer.

presentations.title: Flow Through a Pebble-Bed Reactor in NekRS
presentations.abstract: The pb146 case in NekRS is a benchmark computational fluid dynamics problem that simulates flow through a packed bed of 146 spherical particles, representing a simplified pebble-bed reactor geometry. It features a densely packed arrangement of spheres inside a cylindrical domain, producing complex flow behavior with tight gaps, recirculation zones, and turbulent interactions that are challenging to resolve numerically. Using NekRS’s high-order spectral element method, the case captures detailed boundary-layer physics and serves as a realistic yet standardized workload, making it widely used for testing solver accuracy, scalability, and performance on GPU-based high performance computing systems.

presentations.title: Fulfillment: Artistic Encounters with the Hidden Labor and Environmental Footprint of High Performance Computing
presentations.abstract:
High performance computing (HPC) has become one of the defining infrastructures of contemporary society. Beyond enabling scientific discovery, HPC increasingly powers artificial intelligence, climate modeling, logistics, digital commerce, autonomous systems, and large-scale simulation. Despite its transformative role, HPC largely remains invisible to the public, obscuring the vast networks of human labor, material extraction, energy consumption, and environmental impact required to sustain computational infrastructures.

This project argues that artistic practice can make HPC visible, not only by visualizing scientific data, but by revealing the social, ecological, and political systems in which computational infrastructures are embedded. Rather than treating HPC solely as a technological achievement, the work positions it as part of a cultural-material landscape whose hidden operations shape everyday life.

Fulfillment is an interdisciplinary virtual reality artwork developed at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory (EVL), University of Illinois Chicago, in collaboration with anthropologists, designers, and computer scientists from several research institutions spanning the U.S., Europe, and Asia with support from the National Science Foundation. This proposal is for a public exhibition of the Fulfillment project as part of the Art Gallery Program at the SC26 conference. While the original work investigates global logistics and supply chain capitalism, this exhibition reframes those systems through the computational infrastructures that increasingly govern them. Warehouses, AI-driven optimization, cloud computing, data centers, predictive algorithms, and real-time simulation are presented as interconnected expressions of contemporary HPC ecosystems.

presentations.title: Biological Interfaces
presentations.abstract:
Water at biological interfaces contributes substantially to the mechanical behavior of membranes, yet how it responds to mechanical stress is not well characterized. This artwork was developed from molecular simulations, which examined how lateral tension influences interfacial water in lipid model membranes representative of mammalian and bacterial composition under physiological conditions.

In the resting state, interfacial water organizes into hydrogen-bonded networks, with small ring-like arrangements linking adjacent lipid. In the video, these ring-like arrangements are highlighted by the glowing planes between golden spheres. When lateral stress is applied, these arrangements persist in one mammalian membrane type, while in the other, stress-induced flattening of the membrane surface causes interfacial water to become partially decoupled from the lipid interface. This differential behavior points to a close relationship between a membrane's mechanical properties and the structural organization of its associated water network, offering insight into the mechanisms by which interfacial water contributes to membrane resilience under mechanical load. Whilst the video is mostly for aesthetical purposes, the findings of the molecular simulations suggest that interfacial water is not merely a passive boundary layer but an active participant in membrane stability that responds dynamically to stress, with implications extending across biophysics, drug design, and the study of biological adaptation.

presentations.title: Spiral Wave: The Heart's Chaotic Dance
presentations.abstract:
A spiral of crimson, gold, mocha, and magenta moves through the heart, tracing the electrical activity that coordinates every heartbeat. Here, that rhythm has broken down. The spiral is a rotor, a self-sustaining electrical wave that drives atrial fibrillation, one of the most common and dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.

Every frame is generated directly from a high-performance cardiac electrophysiology simulation. The left atrium is modeled as a large network of electrically coupled tissue, simulated in near real time using custom CUDA code running on NVIDIA GPUs. This computational framework allows researchers to investigate how atrial fibrillation begins, evolves, and responds to targeted intervention.

The colors are not arbitrary; they are the language of physiology. Crimson marks tissue at rest, ready to activate. Gold follows the wave of depolarization as it propagates through the muscle. Mocha and magenta represent the refractory period, when the tissue is recovering before it can fire again. In this simulation, the refractory period is shortened, and a precisely timed electrical stimulus initiates the spiral wave.

Spiral Wave lives at the intersection of computation, medicine, and art. Every color, every curve, and every swirl emerges from the underlying physics of cardiac tissue. Nothing in this animation was designed to be beautiful. It simply is.

presentations.title: Antarctica: Looking Through the Ice Into the Past
presentations.abstract:
This work is an interdisciplinary collaboration between artists, designers, scientific researchers, and visualization experts. The team aimed to address two primary objectives. To start, we incorporated the human language of art to set the foundation for science communication to open the conversation between communities and the scientific endeavors of the scientist, a part of the NSF Center for Oldest Ice Exploration (COLDEX). The second aim was to assist the team, Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues, in understanding the ice sheet layers they are currently studying.

Dr. Duncan Young and colleagues use airborne ice-penetrating radar, gravity, and magnetic surveys to image the internal structure of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet and the geology hidden beneath more than three kilometers of ice. Their work spans three key regions of East Antarctica — the South Pole region, Dome A, the Allan Hills, and Dome C. These measurements reveal how ice has flowed, deformed, melted, and interacted with the underlying landscapes over millions of years. One of their primary goals is to locate regions where the oldest continuous ice has remained preserved and to understand how the ice sheet layers have changed over time to predict future movements.

Incorporated in the video are artistic representations of the data reflecting the ice sheet layers of Antarctica. These scientifically directed visualizations of the data were transformed into 3D prints that proved to be valuable in communicating with colleagues to determine the next drilling site in Antarctica to test hypotheses. Additionally, the 3D printing allowed the scientists to see and hold a physical representation of their findings.

presentations.title: Morphogenesis
presentations.abstract:
Long before computers, Alan Turing asked how a smooth egg becomes a spotted, striped, branching creature. His answer, reaction-diffusion, is the chemistry of pattern itself. Here that chemistry runs as living paint: two competing substances diffuse and react across a field, blooming into coral, fingerprints, dividing cells, and restless worms, cycling endlessly through nature's vocabulary of form.

But look closely, and the field is split into three vertical territories, each a separate GPU. The luminous seams between them are the secret of large-scale simulation: the halo exchange, where neighboring processors trade their edge values every timestep so the pattern can flow seamlessly across boundaries. Gold packets pulse along the seams and communication is made visible.

This is how we simulate weather, galaxies, and combustion: cut reality into pieces, solve each in parallel, and stitch the edges back together. The pattern is the phenomenon; the seams are the high performance computing. Turing's morphogenesis is computed the way modern science actually computes it.

presentations.title: Vortex Bubbles in Anabatic Upslope Flow During Morning Transition
presentations.abstract: Sea of bubbling vortices arising in upslope (anabatic) flow at a slope angle of eight degrees after sudden imposition of surface heat flux against a constant ambient stratification. This serves as a simplified model for the morning transition from nighttime downslope (katabatic) drainage to daytime upslope flow occurring during sunrise in valleys or mountains when solar radiation starts to heat up the sloped terrain, reversing the buoyancy and pressure gradients established during the cooler nocturnal conditions. Flow shown here is in an intermediate regime between laminar and fully turbulent.

presentations.title: Boiling the Ocean ... Literally
presentations.abstract:
The video shows monthly averaged sea surface temperature anomalies in the North Atlantic since 1980. The colors represent warming and cooling up to 2026 compared to the monthly averages from 1980 to 1995. The visualization highlights the rapid speed at which our oceans have been warming in a period of just over 45 years.

The video was made as realistic as possible with satellite imagery, realistic atmosphere thickness and density, a topography map and the use of ray-traced renders to present the data as realistically and prominently as possible.

presentations.title: Radiation: When Steels Fall Apart
presentations.abstract:
This visualization uses a high performance computing-based workflow to reveal the atomic-scale structure of neutron-irradiated steel. Highlighted in the image are nanoscale defects and chemical features that formed or evolved as a result of irradiation.

The specimen examined in this study was prepared from an HT-9 alloy irradiated to 0.68 displacements per atom (dpa) at 478 degrees Celsius in Idaho National Laboratory’s Advanced Test Reactor. The visualization combines two correlative datasets collected from the same specimen: a two-dimensional image acquired using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and a three-dimensional dataset acquired using atom probe tomography (APT).

The combined datasets reveal several complex microstructural features associated with radiation damage. These include spherical clusters enriched in nickel and silicon, dislocation lines decorated with solute clusters, and a grain boundary exhibiting radiation-induced solute segregation. The dataset also captures a pre-existing vanadium nitride precipitate. Characterizing these features is important because they can influence the physical and mechanical properties of the alloy.

Using high performance computing and advanced deep-learning methods, this image-based workflow improves feature identification and enables more accurate spatial correlation of the complementary TEM and APT datasets. The multimodal computational model under development uses structural information obtained from TEM to support further analysis of the APT dataset and improve the identification and characterization of solute clusters.

This visualization is composed entirely of experimental data obtained from TEM and APT measurements. Rendering the datasets in this form allows researchers to more effectively interpret correlative measurements, identify and analyze complex radiation-induced features, validate computational methods, and communicate scientific findings.

presentations.title: Ligand Dynamics Control Structure, Elasticity, and High-Pressure Behavior of Nanoparticle Superlattices
presentations.abstract: The spherical clusters in this image are a molecular dynamics simulation of lead sulfide nanocrystals, each seven nanometers wide, coated with radiating oleic acid ligands that allow such particles to self-assemble into an ordered crystal called a nanoparticle superlattice. The underlying research found that below a critical ligand coverage density, nanoparticles collapse and fuse together, while above it, the ligand layer cushions the structure enough to withstand applied pressures up to nearly 56 gigapascals while largely retaining its ordered arrangement. The image renders this simulated nanoscale structure alongside additional micrographs of nanoparticle superlattice material from the same body of research.

presentations.title: Colourful Wind Assistance
presentations.abstract:
The video shows the flow past two wing sails arranged in tandem, representative of wind-assisted propulsion devices. The simulation was performed with x3d2, a high-order finite-difference incompressible-flow solver developed within the Xcompact3d framework (https://www.incompact3d.com). The simulation uses the immersed-boundary method to represent the foil geometry, together with non-periodic streamwise inflow/outflow boundary conditions and periodic transverse boundaries.

The calculation uses a uniform Cartesian mesh of approximately 381 million grid points. Based on the wing-sail chord and imposed inflow velocity, the Reynolds number is approximately 28,000. The case is an illustrative demonstration of the numerical methodology rather than a full-scale wing-sail prediction. Simulations were run in double precision on an NVIDIA Grace Hopper GH200 GPU using x3d2’s CUDA backend.

presentations.title: JASMIN in July (Per Hour): Stochastic Sea
presentations.abstract:
This artwork explores the computational life of JASMIN, a UK research computing facility supporting environmental and Earth-system science. Rather than presenting activity as a conventional graph or dashboard, it translates the rhythms of a month of work on the facility to an abstract visual form.

In Stochastic Sea, each "spindle" form is a polar representation of Brownian motion representing one hour in the month of July where normalized power and job statistics were used to set the parameters controlling the Brownian motion and its relative appearance.

As with its sister piece Brownian Bouquet (which instead plots one spindle for one day), characteristics of JASMIN's computational workload from July 2026 are mapped to different properties of each spindle. Power consumption controls its overall scale; the number of completed jobs controls the variance and resulting diffuseness of its Brownian trajectories; running jobs control the number of points used to construct those trajectories; pending jobs determine their rotation; and failed jobs select the color palette. Each metric is independently normalized over the range observed in the dataset before being mapped to the corresponding visual parameter, to create an abstract piece which can be interpreted as a physical form, in this case suggestive of a filamentary superstructure such as galactic super-clusters or a network of synapses. The spindle centers are randomly distributed across the composition, reinforcing this impression of a complex, interconnected structure.

Stochastic Sea invites the viewer to see computational infrastructure not simply as an invisible technical resource, but as a dynamic system where countless individual processes combine to produce rhythms, fluctuations and patterns at a larger scale. The work deliberately occupies the space between data visualization and abstract art.

presentations.title: Where Data Becomes Light: The Beauty of Scientific Visualization
presentations.abstract:
Where Data Becomes Light is a digital light projection and immersive visual experience that celebrates the beauty of science through contemporary visualization. On view nightly, Thursday through Sunday, at THE MART (artonthemart.com) September through mid-November, the large-scale imagery transforms the 2.5-acre building façade into a luminous canvas, where sweeping animations and vivid imagery inspire curiosity and wonder, and invite audiences to witness the elegance and complexity of the natural world through modern scientific computing.

Scientific discovery often begins with numbers, signals, and equations, but its deepest insights emerge when those patterns become visible. Scientific visualization transforms complex data into images that reveal structure, motion, and meaning, allowing us to see phenomena that would otherwise remain hidden. In these images, turbulence becomes choreography, molecular interactions resemble intricate architecture, and the evolution of galaxies unfolds like a vast celestial landscape.

Like Art of HPC, Where Data Becomes Light celebrates creativity and beauty in computational science. The projection includes several works from past SC Art of HPC exhibits and Scientific Visualization and Data Analytics Showcases, bringing the SC community's work to the city's skyline.

The Collaboration

For decades, researchers have used visualization to transform massive datasets into images that reveal patterns hidden in raw numbers. As high-performance computing has grown in prominence to address the biggest challenges in science and engineering, Argonne National Laboratory has played a key role in this evolution, operating world-class supercomputers and producing visualizations that illuminate everything from the structure of materials and the behavior of turbulent flows to the formation of galaxies and the dynamics of climate systems.

At the same time, the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois Chicago helped define the modern field of visualization. EVL researchers’ work contributed to the landmark National Science Foundation report on scientific visualization, which helped establish visualization as a critical component of scientific discovery. EVL’s innovations in immersive visualization environments and collaborative visual computing have expanded the ways scientists and the public experience complex data.

Wednesday, November 18, 2026
7:30-8:00 pm
THE MART, Chicago Riverwalk between Wells and Franklin Streets

presentations.title: The Oracle at DKRZ
presentations.abstract:
This video is a visualization of the algorithm used to generate "prophecies" from machine code — that will form part of a sculptural installation to be exhibited at the German Climate Computing Centre (DKRZ).

The work situates climate modeling in the broader, non-scientific history of humanity's attempts to grapple with the future. By reinterpreting the binary of the ICON climate model into words, and searching for where those words combine into statements about the future, ICON is reimagined as a modern-day oracle. The algorithm's lexicon comes from English translations of classical Greek texts. In these fictions, prophecies are true, and are intertwined with the distinct tragedy of not being believed or acted upon — a startling parallel to humanity's lackluster response to the climate crisis.

Inspiration for the project came through conversations with scientists at DKRZ; about the computation and storage of data, as well as the Centre's role in scientific research and weather prediction. On the computational side, the ability to abstract almost anything into a string of zeros and ones highlights a wonderful symmetry: if anything can be binary, then binary can be anything. From this perspective, binary becomes an interface between seemingly disparate media and raises questions about how the systems we use to interpret data give rise to meaning.

The connection to a history of fortune telling was developed through understanding the role DKRZ plays within the scientific landscape. The vast array of resources spent in the construction and maintenance of its supercomputers is a testament to how far humanity will go to fulfill a specific need — to know what the future will be like. From this perspective, it represents an incredibly sophisticated approach to something humans have been doing throughout history and across civilizations. The rulers of city-states in Ancient Greece would climb the steps to the Oracle at Delphi seeking counsel. Now, various clients come to DKRZ, looking to use its computing power for projections on the weather and climate.

presentations.title: You Only Have Seven Seconds
presentations.abstract:
You Only Have Seven Seconds is a poetic, human–AI collaborative documentary that unfolds as both a visual archive of an internationally exhibited installation and a cinematic experiment in memory preservation. Against the backdrop of rising Alzheimer’s cases and the emergence of machine-generated false memories, the film reimagines remembrance through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Inspired by her grandmother’s cognitive decline, the artist developed a custom AI system that transforms fragmented spoken recollections into synthetic visual sequences. Presented as an interactive AI art installation, the project ReCollection has traveled worldwide, welcoming thousands of visitors to whisper their fading memories — each within seven seconds — into the artwork and generate visual memories in real time. These memories form the foundation of an evolving archive, constructed through speech recognition, text auto-completion, and text-to-image generation.

Drawing from this archive, the film incorporates emerging speech-to-video technology to weave a collective, culturally diverse montage of love and loss. The participatory datasets are curated to build dialogical relationships, forming patterns, counterpoints, and resonances that evoke a poetics of relation. Initially conceived as a personal reflection, the work has evolved into a living, breathing, shared world-building experience that reassembles the ephemeral past into a dynamic portrait of collective human selfhood.

presentations.title: A Study of 4D Julia Sets: Iterations of Z = Z2 + K in the Quaternions
presentations.abstract:
Created in 2005, this work is an exploration of quaternion Julia sets. Quaternions are a four-dimensional number system.

Real numbers: 1 dimension — ( a )
Complex numbers: 2 dimensions — a + bia + bia + bi
Quaternions: 4 dimensions — a + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dka + bi + cj + dk

A quaternion Julia set is the set of starting points ( (a, b, c, d) ) whose iterates remain bounded (they do not escape to infinity). Complex Julia sets typically appear as curves or fractal lines in the plane. Quaternion Julia sets live in four dimensions; the slices we can see often appear as evolving 3D solids. This animation explores those solids as the parameters that generate the set are changed. Motion through the 4D parameter space is created with Hermite splines connecting successive 4D target values. For much of the work, new targets are set every four seconds, producing a slow largo pace of about 60 beats per minute.

Credits

Animation: Dan Sandin
Algorithms: John Hart, Yumei Dang
Programming: Dan Sandin, Shalini Venkataraman
Visionary Leadership: Tom DeFanti
Mathematical Leadership: Louis Kauffman

presentations.title: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night
presentations.abstract: INSTRUMENT | One Antarctic Night (IOAN) is a multi-player VR experience that brings the rhythms of the cosmos to life in an endless remix instrument. Created from 758,457,209 magnitude readings for 817‚373 astronomical objects captured by the AST3 robotic telescopes in Antarctica, the experience transports players inside of a field of objects at the heart of the Large Magellanic Cloud. Within a multiplayer VR arena, and floating inside a luminous field between the Earth and the Large Magellanic Cloud, multiple players explore and collaboratively create new visual and sound remixes to perform the AST3 dataset as a soundscape for external visitors to the VR arena. The collaborative experience is inspired by communal percussion and multiplayer instruments. Real-time database queries, selections, and filtering operations enable multiple players in VR to collaboratively interact with the objects in the field to create data remixes from astronomical data. Visitors to the arena see and hear the virtual world in correct spatial relation to their real-world positions through spatialized 4K portals and spatialized ambisonic audio that align the physical space of the arena installation with the inner space of the multiplayer virtual environment.
